## **ADR-033 — Argo CD GitOps & Continuous Delivery Architecture**

This is the correct next ADR because the responsibility chain now looks like:

```text
ADR-030
Docker / OCI
      │
      ▼
What do we deploy?

ADR-031
Kubernetes
      │
      ▼
Where/how does it run?

ADR-032
Helm
      │
      ▼
How do we package Kubernetes configuration?

ADR-033
Argo CD / GitOps
      │
      ▼
How does declared configuration safely reach
DEV → UAT → PROD?
```

ADR-033 should go deep into **GitOps principles → push vs pull deployment → Argo CD selection → application repository vs GitOps repository → repository architecture → Application vs ApplicationSet → App-of-Apps → environment organization → DEV/UAT/PROD → cluster registration → projects → RBAC → SSO → repository credentials → Helm integration → values management → immutable image promotion → CI/CD separation → automatic vs manual sync → sync policies → prune → self-heal → sync waves → hooks → health checks → drift detection → reconciliation → deployment approvals → PR-based promotion → Git commit as audit trail → rollback/revert → secrets and External Secrets → Sealed Secrets evaluation → Argo CD Image Updater boundary → multi-cluster GitOps → cluster bootstrapping → disaster recovery → HA Argo CD → notifications → metrics → Prometheus/Grafana → audit → security hardening → least privilege → production access → Git repository compromise → supply-chain controls → signed commits → OCI artifacts → deployment windows → progressive delivery → Argo Rollouts boundary → blue/green → canary → failure handling → sync errors → OutOfSync → Degraded → Missing → Unknown → troubleshooting → emergency changes → break-glass procedures → GitOps anti-patterns → governance → production reference architecture.**


# ADR-033 — Argo CD GitOps & Continuous Delivery Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-033
**Status:** Accepted
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-032 established **Helm** as the Kubernetes application packaging standard. ADR-033 establishes how those packages move safely and consistently through **DEV → UAT → PROD**.

> **CI builds artifacts. Git declares desired state. Argo CD reconciles desired state. Kubernetes executes it.**

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Application Git
    │
    ▼
CI Pipeline
    │
    ├── Test
    ├── Scan
    ├── Build OCI Image
    ├── Sign
    └── Publish
    │
    ▼
Container Registry
    │
    ▼
GitOps Repository
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Helm
    │
    ▼
Kubernetes
```

---

# 1. Problem

Traditional CI/CD commonly follows a **push deployment model**:

```text
Jenkins / GitHub Actions
          │
          │ Kubernetes credentials
          ▼
      kubectl / Helm
          │
          ▼
     Production
```

This creates several problems:

```text
CI requires production credentials
Deployment state may exist only in pipeline history
Manual cluster changes create drift
Rollback becomes inconsistent
Auditability becomes fragmented
Environment promotion becomes harder to govern
```

Mediverse needs a declarative deployment architecture.

---

# 2. Decision

Mediverse shall adopt:

**GitOps + Argo CD**

as the standard Kubernetes continuous-delivery architecture.

```text
Git
 │
 │ Desired State
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 │ Reconciliation
 ▼
Kubernetes
```

---

# 3. GitOps Principle

GitOps means the desired state of the deployment platform is represented declaratively in Git.

Example:

```yaml
image:
  repository: registry.example.com/mediverse/content-service
  tag: "2.4.7"
```

Git answers:

> What should production currently be running?

---

# 4. Git Becomes Desired-State Authority

For GitOps-managed Kubernetes resources:

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Desired State
```

becomes authoritative.

The cluster represents:

```text
Actual State
```

Argo CD continuously compares them.

---

# 5. Reconciliation

```text
Desired State
     │
     │ compare
     ▼
Actual State
     │
     ├── Same → Synced
     │
     └── Different → OutOfSync
```

This reconciliation model is fundamentally different from simply running deployment scripts.

---

# 6. Why Argo CD?

Argo CD provides:

```text
GitOps reconciliation
Kubernetes-native operation
Helm support
Kustomize support
Multi-cluster management
Drift detection
Application health
RBAC
SSO integration
Auditability
Sync automation
Rollback visibility
```

---

# 7. Alternatives Considered

| Technology                       | Decision                 |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Argo CD                          | ✅ Selected               |
| Flux CD                          | 🟡 Strong alternative    |
| Jenkins direct deployment        | ❌ Rejected as primary CD |
| GitHub Actions direct deployment | ❌ Rejected as primary CD |
| Manual Helm                      | ❌ Rejected               |
| Manual kubectl                   | ❌ Rejected               |

Flux is technically capable.

The decision is standardization, not an assertion that Flux is inferior.

---

# 8. CI and CD Separation

Mediverse shall explicitly separate CI and CD.

```text
CI
│
├── Compile
├── Unit Test
├── Integration Test
├── Security Scan
├── Build Image
├── Generate SBOM
├── Sign Artifact
└── Publish Artifact


CD
│
├── Observe Git
├── Render Desired State
├── Compare Cluster
├── Synchronize
├── Detect Drift
└── Report Health
```

---

# 9. CI Must Not Become CD

Avoid:

```text
CI Pipeline
     │
     ├── docker build
     ├── docker push
     ├── kubectl apply
     └── helm upgrade PROD
```

This couples artifact creation with production control.

---

# 10. Pull-Based Deployment

Preferred:

```text
                 Production Cluster
                         │
                         ▼
                      Argo CD
                         │
                         │ Pull
                         ▼
                        Git
```

The deployment controller operates from the target environment rather than allowing CI to push arbitrary commands into production.

---

# 11. Security Benefit

CI no longer needs broad production Kubernetes credentials.

```text
CI
 │
 X
 │
Production Kubernetes API
```

Instead:

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
Registry / Git

Argo CD
 │
 ▼
Kubernetes
```

This reduces credential exposure.

---

# 12. Application Repository

Application repositories contain source code.

Example:

```text
content-service/
├── src/
├── pom.xml
├── Dockerfile
├── helm/
└── tests/
```

The repository answers:

> How do we build the application?

---

# 13. GitOps Repository

The GitOps repository answers:

> What should each environment run?

Example:

```text
mediverse-gitops/

├── dev/
├── uat/
└── prod/
```

---

# 14. Why Separate Repositories?

A source-code merge should not automatically equal a production deployment.

Separation provides:

```text
Deployment approval boundary
Independent deployment history
Environment governance
Clear artifact promotion
Reduced production coupling
```

---

# 15. Repository Architecture

Recommended conceptual structure:

```text
mediverse-gitops/
│
├── applications/
│
├── environments/
│   ├── dev/
│   ├── uat/
│   └── prod/
│
├── platform/
│
└── bootstrap/
```

---

# 16. Environment Separation

Each environment should have explicitly declared desired state.

```text
DEV
 │
 ├── content-service 2.5.0
 └── assessment-service 3.1.0

UAT
 │
 ├── content-service 2.4.9
 └── assessment-service 3.0.8

PROD
 │
 ├── content-service 2.4.7
 └── assessment-service 3.0.7
```

Different environments do not need to run identical versions simultaneously.

---

# 17. Artifact Promotion

The same artifact should move forward.

```text
Build Once
    │
    ▼
sha256:ABC
    │
    ├── DEV
    │
    ▼
   UAT
    │
    ▼
  PROD
```

Do not rebuild production artifacts after UAT approval.

---

# 18. Why Build Once?

If:

```text
DEV artifact ≠ UAT artifact ≠ PROD artifact
```

then the thing tested is not necessarily the thing released.

Artifact promotion should preserve identity.

---

# 19. Immutable Artifact References

Production should increasingly use immutable image references.

```text
registry/mediverse/content-service@sha256:...
```

rather than mutable tags.

---

# 20. Promotion Through Pull Requests

Preferred production flow:

```text
Artifact Ready
     │
     ▼
GitOps PR
     │
     ▼
Review
     │
     ▼
Approval
     │
     ▼
Merge
     │
     ▼
Argo CD
     │
     ▼
PROD
```

The Git history becomes part of the deployment audit trail.

---

# 21. Argo CD Application

An Argo CD `Application` defines:

```text
Source
Destination
Project
Sync Policy
```

Conceptually:

```text
Git Repository
      │
      ▼
Application
      │
      ▼
Namespace / Cluster
```

---

# 22. Application Boundary

A deployable Mediverse service may map to an Argo CD Application.

Example:

```text
content-service-prod
assessment-service-prod
learning-service-prod
gateway-prod
```

This provides independent lifecycle and health visibility.

---

# 23. Avoid One Giant Application

Bad:

```text
mediverse-production
      │
      └── everything
```

One failure can complicate synchronization and ownership across the entire platform.

---

# 24. ApplicationSet

As environments and clusters grow, manually maintaining hundreds of Applications becomes repetitive.

Argo CD ApplicationSet can generate Applications from structured configuration.

```text
ApplicationSet
      │
      ├── content-dev
      ├── content-uat
      ├── content-prod
      ├── assessment-dev
      ├── assessment-uat
      └── assessment-prod
```

---

# 25. ApplicationSet Use Case

Suppose:

```text
40 services × 3 environments
```

results in:

```text
120 Applications
```

ApplicationSet can reduce repetitive definitions.

---

# 26. ApplicationSet Warning

ApplicationSet should eliminate mechanical duplication.

It should not hide deployment architecture behind incomprehensible generators.

Automation that nobody can reason about is not good platform engineering.

---

# 27. App-of-Apps Pattern

Argo CD can bootstrap collections of Applications through a parent application.

```text
Root Application
       │
       ├── Gateway
       ├── Content
       ├── Assessment
       └── Learning
```

This pattern can be useful for platform bootstrap.

---

# 28. App-of-Apps Limitation

Do not create deep trees such as:

```text
Root
 └── Platform
      └── Domain
           └── Team
                └── Application
                     └── Component
```

unless there is a concrete operational reason.

Hierarchy should remain understandable.

---

# 29. Argo CD Projects

`AppProject` shall provide boundaries around:

```text
Repositories
Clusters
Namespaces
Resource types
Application teams
```

Projects are an important security boundary.

---

# 30. Default Project

Production workloads should not simply use an unrestricted Argo CD `default` project forever.

Dedicated projects should express actual permissions.

---

# 31. Example Project Model

```text
mediverse-platform

mediverse-backend

mediverse-frontend

mediverse-ai
```

Exact boundaries should follow ownership and security requirements rather than arbitrary service categories.

---

# 32. Source Repository Restrictions

Projects should restrict which Git repositories applications may consume.

A production application should not be allowed to deploy from arbitrary repositories.

---

# 33. Destination Restrictions

Projects should restrict deployment destinations.

Example:

```text
Backend DEV project
        │
        X
        │
Production namespace
```

A configuration mistake should not casually cross environment boundaries.

---

# 34. Resource Restrictions

Application teams generally do not need permission to GitOps-manage:

```text
ClusterRole
ClusterRoleBinding
CRD
Node
Namespace infrastructure
```

Platform-level resources require stronger control.

---

# 35. Argo CD RBAC

Argo CD itself requires role-based access control.

Potential roles:

```text
Viewer
Developer
Operator
Release Manager
Platform Administrator
```

---

# 36. Least Privilege

A developer who needs to view DEV applications does not automatically require:

```text
Delete production application
Force production sync
Modify Argo CD projects
Manage repositories
```

Permissions must follow actual responsibilities.

---

# 37. SSO

Enterprise Argo CD should integrate with centralized identity.

Conceptually:

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Enterprise Identity Provider
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 ▼
RBAC
```

Avoid unmanaged local administrator accounts as the normal access model.

---

# 38. Administrative Accounts

Built-in/local administrative credentials should be tightly controlled.

Normal engineering access should use organizational identity.

---

# 39. Repository Credentials

Argo CD needs controlled access to Git repositories.

Credentials must not be embedded directly in application manifests.

---

# 40. Repository Authentication

Preferred mechanisms depend on Git infrastructure and may include:

```text
SSH credentials
Short-lived tokens
Workload identity/integration
Repository-specific credentials
```

Long-lived broad credentials should be minimized.

---

# 41. Helm Integration

ADR-032 established Helm.

Argo CD shall consume Helm charts and values to generate desired Kubernetes manifests.

```text
GitOps Configuration
        │
        ▼
      Argo CD
        │
        ▼
       Helm
        │
        ▼
Rendered Kubernetes Resources
```

---

# 42. Helm Responsibility Remains Separate

Argo CD does not change Helm's architectural responsibility.

```text
Helm
→ Packaging / templating

Argo CD
→ Reconciliation / deployment
```

---

# 43. Environment Values

DEV/UAT/PROD may use different values:

```text
values-dev.yaml
values-uat.yaml
values-prod.yaml
```

while consuming the same chart.

---

# 44. Secrets

Plaintext production secrets shall not be committed into the GitOps repository.

GitOps does not mean:

> Put every piece of configuration, including passwords, directly into Git.

---

# 45. External Secrets

Preferred architecture:

```text
Secret Manager / Vault
          │
          ▼
External Secrets Operator
          │
          ▼
Kubernetes Secret
          │
          ▼
Application Pod
```

Git stores the secret reference/declaration rather than the secret value.

---

# 46. Sealed Secrets

Sealed Secrets may be evaluated where encrypted secrets-in-Git are operationally justified.

However, Mediverse's preferred production direction remains external secret management.

---

# 47. Secret Rotation

GitOps deployments must support secret rotation without rebuilding application images.

Secret lifecycle and application artifact lifecycle are separate.

---

# 48. Automatic Synchronization

Argo CD can automatically synchronize changes.

This is useful for environments such as DEV.

```text
Git Change
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Automatic Sync
```

---

# 49. Production Synchronization

Production synchronization requires stronger governance.

A production Git merge should already represent an approved deployment decision.

Whether synchronization is automatic after merge or requires an additional control depends on release policy.

Avoid duplicating approvals merely for ceremony.

---

# 50. Self-Heal

Self-healing allows Argo CD to correct drift.

```text
Git says replicas=3

Cluster manually changed to 8
          │
          ▼
       OutOfSync
          │
          ▼
       Argo CD
          │
          ▼
      replicas=3
```

---

# 51. Pruning

Pruning removes resources no longer present in desired state.

```text
Resource removed from Git
          │
          ▼
        Argo CD
          │
          ▼
Resource removed from cluster
```

This is powerful and potentially destructive.

---

# 52. Pruning Governance

Production pruning should be enabled only with proper repository protection, reviews and resource lifecycle controls.

Deleting YAML can become deleting infrastructure state.

---

# 53. Drift Detection

One of Argo CD's core advantages is continuous drift detection.

```text
Git
 │
 ├─────────────┐
 │             │
 ▼             ▼
Desired       Actual
 │             │
 └────Compare──┘
       │
       ▼
 Synced / OutOfSync
```

---

# 54. Manual `kubectl edit`

Routine production configuration changes through:

```bash
kubectl edit deployment ...
```

are prohibited as the normal operational workflow.

They create drift.

---

# 55. Emergency Manual Changes

Emergency manual changes may occasionally be necessary.

They must be:

```text
Authorized
Audited
Temporary
Documented
Back-ported into Git
```

Otherwise Argo CD may overwrite them.

---

# 56. Break-Glass Procedure

Production shall define a break-glass process for exceptional cases.

```text
Incident
   │
   ▼
Authorized Engineer
   │
   ▼
Temporary Elevated Access
   │
   ▼
Emergency Change
   │
   ▼
Incident Stabilized
   │
   ▼
Git Reconciliation
   │
   ▼
Access Revoked
```

---

# 57. Sync Status

Important Argo CD synchronization states include:

```text
Synced

OutOfSync
```

Sync state tells us whether desired and actual configuration align.

---

# 58. Health Status

Health is different from synchronization.

An application can be:

```text
Synced
```

but:

```text
Degraded
```

because the declared configuration itself produced an unhealthy application.

---

# 59. Critical Distinction

```text
Synced ≠ Healthy
```

GitOps guarantees reconciliation toward desired state.

It does not guarantee that the desired state is good.

---

# 60. Application Health

Health evaluation should consider Kubernetes resources such as:

```text
Deployment
StatefulSet
DaemonSet
Job
Ingress
PersistentVolumeClaim
```

and supported custom resources.

---

## ADR-033 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The next section should continue directly with **61. Sync Waves**, then cover ordering/dependencies, hooks, custom health checks, failure states, retry strategy, rollback/revert, deployment windows, notifications, Prometheus/Grafana observability, audit/security hardening, repository compromise, multi-cluster GitOps, HA/DR, progressive delivery, Argo Rollouts, blue-green/canary, anti-patterns, governance, risks and the final Mediverse GitOps reference architecture.

# ADR-033 — Argo CD GitOps & Continuous Delivery Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Application Health**.

---

# 61. Sync Waves

Some Kubernetes resources require controlled deployment ordering.

Argo CD sync waves provide explicit ordering.

```text
Wave -2 → Prerequisites
Wave -1 → Migration/Initialization
Wave  0 → Application
Wave  1 → Supporting resources
Wave  2 → Post-deployment resources
```

Lower-numbered waves execute before higher-numbered waves.

---

# 62. Why Ordering Matters

Consider:

```text
External Secret
      │
      ▼
Kubernetes Secret
      │
      ▼
Deployment
```

If the Deployment starts before required configuration exists, Pods may fail immediately.

Ordering should be used only where a real dependency exists.

---

# 63. Sync Wave Anti-Pattern

Do not encode the entire distributed-system dependency graph through sync waves.

Bad:

```text
Database
  ↓
Kafka
  ↓
Identity
  ↓
Gateway
  ↓
Service A
  ↓
Service B
  ↓
Service C
```

Microservices should tolerate temporary dependency unavailability through correct application resilience.

---

# 64. Sync Phases

Argo CD synchronization may involve lifecycle phases conceptually such as:

```text
PreSync
   │
   ▼
Sync
   │
   ▼
PostSync
```

Failure handling can also involve `SyncFail`.

---

# 65. PreSync

`PreSync` can support operations that genuinely must complete before application synchronization.

Potential example:

```text
Database Migration Job
        │
        ▼
      PreSync
        │
        ▼
Application Deployment
```

This should not become a dumping ground for arbitrary scripts.

---

# 66. PostSync

`PostSync` may support post-deployment operations such as:

```text
Smoke testing
Deployment verification
Controlled notifications
```

where appropriate.

---

# 67. SyncFail

Failure hooks may perform narrowly defined failure-handling operations.

They should not attempt to build a second orchestration engine inside Argo CD.

---

# 68. Hooks vs Declarative Resources

Preferred:

```text
Declarative Kubernetes Resource
```

over:

```text
Complex imperative hook
```

whenever normal Kubernetes reconciliation can solve the problem.

---

# 69. Database Migration Strategy

Database migration deserves explicit orchestration.

Preferred conceptual flow:

```text
New Artifact
     │
     ▼
Migration Job
     │
     ├── Failure → STOP
     │
     └── Success
             │
             ▼
       Application Rollout
```

---

# 70. Migration Compatibility

Migrations should favor backward compatibility.

```text
Old Application
       │
       ├────► Schema N+1
       │
New Application
       │
       └────► Schema N+1
```

during rolling transitions where possible.

GitOps cannot make destructive schema changes automatically reversible.

---

# 71. Custom Health Checks

Standard Kubernetes resources have known health semantics.

Custom resources may require custom health evaluation.

Examples could include:

```text
ExternalSecret
Certificate
Rollout
Custom Operator Resource
```

Health customization should remain centralized and governed.

---

# 72. Healthy

`Healthy` means Argo CD considers the managed application resources operational according to its health assessment.

It does not mean every business transaction is working correctly.

---

# 73. Degraded

A `Degraded` application requires investigation.

Potential causes include:

```text
Deployment unavailable
Pod failures
Failed rollout
Failed Job
Broken custom resource
```

---

# 74. Progressing

`Progressing` commonly indicates that resources are moving toward the desired healthy state.

For example:

```text
Deployment
    │
    ▼
New ReplicaSet
    │
    ▼
Pods starting
```

---

# 75. Missing

A resource expected from desired state but absent from the cluster may appear missing.

Potential causes:

```text
Deletion
Failed creation
Permission problem
Pruning interaction
Controller problem
```

---

# 76. Unknown

`Unknown` means Argo CD cannot reliably determine resource health.

Do not automatically treat `Unknown` as healthy.

---

# 77. OutOfSync

`OutOfSync` means:

```text
Desired State
      ≠
Actual State
```

It does **not** automatically mean the application is unavailable.

---

# 78. Persistent OutOfSync

Repeated OutOfSync conditions may indicate:

```text
Manual mutation
Mutating admission webhook
Controller-generated fields
Incorrect ignore rules
Helm nondeterminism
External operator behavior
```

Fix the cause rather than repeatedly pressing Sync.

---

# 79. Deterministic Rendering

Helm rendering used by GitOps should be deterministic.

Avoid templates generating values such as:

```text
Random passwords
Random IDs
Current timestamps
Random annotations
```

on every render.

Otherwise Argo CD may continuously detect artificial drift.

---

# 80. Ignore Differences

Argo CD can ignore selected differences when another legitimate controller owns specific fields.

But ignore rules are dangerous when overused.

Bad strategy:

> Ignore everything that keeps becoming OutOfSync.

That hides real configuration drift.

---

# 81. Retry Strategy

Transient synchronization failures may justify controlled retries.

Examples:

```text
Temporary API failure
Short registry/network interruption
Eventually available CRD/controller
```

Retries should be bounded.

---

# 82. Retry Is Not Repair

If a deployment fails because:

```text
Wrong image
Invalid configuration
Missing Secret
Invalid resource
```

retrying twenty times accomplishes nothing.

The desired state itself must be corrected.

---

# 83. Deployment Failure Flow

```text
Argo CD Sync
     │
     ▼
Resource Apply
     │
     ▼
Health Evaluation
     │
     ├── Healthy
     │      │
     │      ▼
     │   Success
     │
     └── Failure
            │
            ▼
        Diagnose Layer
            │
     ┌──────┼──────┐
     ▼      ▼      ▼
   Git    K8s     App
```

---

# 84. Rollback Philosophy

In GitOps, rollback should generally mean:

```text
Revert Desired State
```

not:

```text
Manipulate Production
without changing Git
```

---

# 85. Git Revert

Preferred:

```text
Bad Commit
    │
    ▼
Git Revert
    │
    ▼
Merge
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Previous Desired State
```

Git remains authoritative.

---

# 86. Rollback Limitation

Reverting Git cannot automatically reverse:

```text
Destructive database migration
Published Kafka event
External API side effect
Deleted business data
Object transformation
```

Release architecture must account for irreversible state transitions.

---

# 87. Deployment Windows

Production may require controlled synchronization windows.

Example:

```text
Business Hours
      │
      X
High-risk deployment

Approved Release Window
      │
      ▼
Deployment
```

This depends on Mediverse operational policy.

---

# 88. Sync Windows

Argo CD sync windows can restrict or permit synchronization during configured periods.

Use them for genuine operational governance, not bureaucratic friction.

---

# 89. Emergency Override

Critical incident remediation may require authorized override of normal deployment windows.

Such overrides must be auditable.

---

# 90. Notifications

Argo CD notifications should surface meaningful deployment events.

Examples:

```text
Synchronization failed
Application degraded
Deployment succeeded
Health changed
```

---

# 91. Notification Fatigue

Do not notify every engineer for every successful DEV synchronization.

Notifications should be:

```text
Relevant
Actionable
Environment-aware
Ownership-aware
```

Otherwise engineers will ignore them.

---

# 92. Observability

Argo CD itself is production infrastructure and must be monitored.

Important areas include:

```text
Application health
Sync failures
Reconciliation latency
API health
Repository access
Controller performance
Queue behavior
```

---

# 93. Prometheus

Argo CD metrics should integrate with the Mediverse Prometheus observability platform.

---

# 94. Grafana

Grafana dashboards should expose useful GitOps operational indicators.

```text
Applications Synced
Applications OutOfSync
Applications Degraded
Sync Failures
Reconciliation Performance
Controller Health
```

---

# 95. Alerting

Alerts should focus on operational impact.

Examples:

```text
Production application degraded
Production sync repeatedly failing
Argo CD controller unavailable
Repository inaccessible
Persistent reconciliation failures
```

---

# 96. Logs

Argo CD component logs should flow into centralized logging.

Relevant components may include:

```text
API Server
Application Controller
Repository Server
ApplicationSet Controller
Authentication components
```

---

# 97. Audit Trail

Production deployment investigation should answer:

```text
Who changed desired state?

What changed?

Who reviewed it?

When was it merged?

Which artifact was promoted?

When did Argo CD synchronize?

What happened afterward?
```

---

# 98. Git Auditability

Git provides strong change history, but Git alone does not magically provide governance.

Repository protections are still required.

---

# 99. Protected Production Branch

Production GitOps branches should use controls such as:

```text
Pull request required
Review required
Restricted direct push
Status checks
Controlled administrators
```

according to organizational policy.

---

# 100. CODEOWNERS Direction

Sensitive deployment paths should require appropriate owners.

Conceptually:

```text
/prod/platform/       → Platform Team
/prod/security/       → Security/Platform
/prod/content/        → Content Service Owners
```

Ownership should correspond to responsibility.

---

# 101. Git Repository Compromise

GitOps creates a critical security implication:

```text
Compromise Git Write Access
          │
          ▼
Modify Desired State
          │
          ▼
Potential Production Change
```

Therefore Git security becomes part of production security.

---

# 102. Repository Security

Production GitOps repositories require strong controls around:

```text
Authentication
MFA
Branch protection
Review policy
Token scope
Audit logs
Repository ownership
Automation identities
```

---

# 103. CI Compromise

Even though CI does not directly deploy to production, compromised CI may attempt to publish malicious artifacts or alter GitOps configuration.

GitOps reduces one attack path.

It does not eliminate software supply-chain risk.

---

# 104. Artifact Trust

The deployment architecture should eventually enforce:

```text
Trusted Source
     │
     ▼
CI Build
     │
     ▼
SBOM
     │
     ▼
Security Scan
     │
     ▼
Signed Artifact
     │
     ▼
Approved Registry
     │
     ▼
GitOps Reference
     │
     ▼
Admission Verification
```

---

# 105. Signed Container Images

ADR-030 established signed-image direction.

Argo CD should deploy only artifact references permitted by cluster supply-chain policy.

---

# 106. Signed Git Commits

Signed commits may provide additional provenance for sensitive repositories.

However, signed commits do not replace:

```text
Identity security
Review
Branch protection
Artifact verification
```

---

# 107. Repository Server Security

Argo CD's repository-processing components interact with potentially complex deployment content.

Repository access and plugin execution should therefore be tightly controlled.

---

# 108. Custom Plugins

Custom configuration-management plugins increase attack surface.

They require explicit platform review.

Avoid arbitrary shell execution inside the GitOps rendering path.

---

# 109. Argo CD Credentials

Argo CD credentials must follow least privilege.

Avoid one credential capable of unrestricted access to every repository and every infrastructure system.

---

# 110. Kubernetes Permissions

Argo CD itself requires Kubernetes permissions to reconcile resources.

Those permissions should match the resources it actually owns.

Do not automatically grant unrestricted cluster-admin access everywhere.

---

# 111. Namespace-Scoped Applications

Where possible, application-level Argo CD permissions should be constrained to appropriate namespaces/resources.

Cluster-wide resources require stronger governance.

---

# 112. Multi-Cluster GitOps

Mediverse may operate multiple Kubernetes clusters.

Example:

```text
Argo CD
   │
   ├── DEV Cluster
   ├── UAT Cluster
   └── PROD Cluster
```

Argo CD can manage multiple target clusters.

---

# 113. Central vs Per-Cluster Argo CD

Two broad patterns exist:

```text
Central Argo CD
      │
      ├── Cluster A
      ├── Cluster B
      └── Cluster C
```

versus:

```text
Cluster A → Argo CD A
Cluster B → Argo CD B
Cluster C → Argo CD C
```

Neither is universally correct.

---

# 114. Central Argo CD Benefits

Centralization can simplify:

```text
Management
Visibility
Policy
Configuration
Application discovery
```

but increases blast radius.

---

# 115. Per-Environment Argo CD Benefits

Separate instances can provide:

```text
Environment isolation
Reduced credential concentration
Independent failure domains
Stronger PROD separation
```

at the cost of additional operations.

---

# 116. Mediverse Direction

Production should have stronger isolation than DEV/UAT.

A reasonable enterprise direction is:

```text
Non-Production GitOps Plane
      │
      ├── DEV
      └── UAT


Production GitOps Plane
      │
      └── PROD
```

rather than one unrestricted Argo CD instance controlling everything.

---

# 117. Cluster Registration

Remote cluster credentials must be securely managed.

Registering a cluster effectively grants Argo CD deployment authority over some or all of that cluster.

This is a high-value credential boundary.

---

# 118. Cluster Bootstrap

A new cluster needs a reproducible bootstrap process.

```text
Terraform
    │
    ▼
Kubernetes Cluster
    │
    ▼
Bootstrap Components
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Root GitOps Configuration
    │
    ▼
Platform + Applications
```

---

# 119. Bootstrap Paradox

Argo CD cannot GitOps-manage itself before it exists.

Therefore a small initial bootstrap mechanism is unavoidable.

After bootstrap, ongoing Argo CD configuration should become declarative where practical.

---

# 120. Terraform Boundary

Terraform should provision:

```text
Cloud
Network
Kubernetes
IAM
Foundational infrastructure
```

It may bootstrap Argo CD.

It should not then compete with Argo CD for ownership of ordinary application Kubernetes resources.

---

# 121. Resource Ownership

Every managed resource should have one clear primary owner.

Bad:

```text
Terraform ─┐
Helm CLI ──┼──► Same Deployment
Argo CD ───┘
```

This guarantees eventual conflict.

---

# 122. Disaster Recovery

Argo CD disaster recovery is simpler when desired state already exists externally in Git.

```text
Argo CD Lost
     │
     ▼
Cluster/Application State Continues
     │
     ▼
Recreate Argo CD
     │
     ▼
Reconnect Git
     │
     ▼
Reconcile
```

But credentials and configuration still require recovery planning.

---

# 123. Argo CD Is Not Application Runtime

If Argo CD goes down:

```text
Existing Pods
Existing Services
Existing Deployments
```

do not automatically stop.

Kubernetes continues running existing desired state.

What is lost temporarily is GitOps reconciliation and deployment control.

---

# 124. Argo CD High Availability

Production Argo CD should use an HA-capable architecture appropriate to workload scale and availability requirements.

Critical components should avoid unnecessary single points of failure.

---

# 125. Git Availability

Argo CD depends on Git availability for reconciliation and new deployment state.

A temporary Git outage should not terminate already running applications.

---

# 126. Registry Availability

New deployments may fail if required artifacts cannot be pulled.

Running workloads may remain unaffected until restart/rescheduling requires the image.

---

# 127. Recovery Testing

DR documentation that has never been tested is speculation.

Mediverse should periodically validate:

```text
Can Argo CD be recreated?
Can repositories reconnect?
Can cluster credentials be restored?
Can applications reconcile?
How long does recovery take?
```

---

# 128. Progressive Delivery

Standard Kubernetes Deployments provide rolling updates.

Some Mediverse workloads may eventually require more controlled release strategies.

Examples:

```text
Canary
Blue/Green
Progressive traffic shifting
Automated analysis
```

---

# 129. Argo Rollouts

Argo Rollouts may be introduced for workloads requiring advanced progressive delivery.

It is **not mandated for every service**.

---

# 130. Why Not Every Service?

Progressive delivery introduces:

```text
Additional CRDs
Controllers
Traffic-management integration
Metrics analysis
More release states
Operational complexity
```

Use it where failure risk justifies that complexity.

---

# 131. Canary Deployment

Conceptually:

```text
100% Version A

        │
        ▼

95% Version A
 5% Version B

        │
        ▼

75% Version A
25% Version B

        │
        ▼

50 / 50

        │
        ▼

100% Version B
```

Progression should depend on measurable health.

---

# 132. Canary Analysis

Useful signals may include:

```text
5xx rate
Latency
Business transaction failures
CPU/memory anomalies
Application-specific SLIs
```

A deployment should not be promoted merely because Pods are `Running`.

---

# 133. Blue/Green Deployment

Conceptually:

```text
              Traffic
                 │
                 ▼
             BLUE v1
                 │
             validated

GREEN v2 deployed separately
                 │
                 ▼
             validation
                 │
                 ▼
          Traffic Switch
                 │
                 ▼
             GREEN v2
```

This can simplify rapid traffic rollback but requires additional capacity.

---

# 134. Progressive Delivery Boundary

Preferred responsibility:

```text
Argo CD
   │
   ▼
Desired Rollout Resource
   │
   ▼
Argo Rollouts
   │
   ▼
Progressive Deployment
```

Argo CD remains GitOps controller.

Argo Rollouts manages rollout mechanics.

---

# 135. ApplicationSet at Scale

As Mediverse expands across:

```text
Services
Environments
Regions
Clusters
```

ApplicationSet may generate consistent application definitions.

Example:

```text
40 Services
×
3 Environments
×
2 Regions

=
240 deployment targets
```

Manual Application YAML becomes inefficient at that scale.

---

# 136. ApplicationSet Governance

Generation logic must remain reviewable.

One incorrect generator can affect many applications simultaneously.

Automation increases both productivity and blast radius.

---

# 137. GitOps Troubleshooting Workflow

When deployment fails:

```text
1. Check Argo CD Application status
              │
              ▼
2. Synced or OutOfSync?
              │
              ▼
3. Healthy or Degraded?
              │
              ▼
4. Inspect sync operation
              │
              ▼
5. Inspect rendered resources
              │
              ▼
6. Inspect Kubernetes events
              │
              ▼
7. Inspect Pods
              │
              ▼
8. Inspect application logs
              │
              ▼
9. Inspect metrics/traces
              │
              ▼
10. Correct desired state in Git
```

---

# 138. GitOps Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

❌ CI pipelines with broad production cluster credentials

❌ Routine `kubectl apply` to production

❌ Routine `helm upgrade` from laptops

❌ Production configuration existing only in pipeline variables

❌ Plaintext secrets in Git

❌ Mutable production image references

❌ Rebuilding artifacts per environment

❌ Direct production branch pushes

❌ One unrestricted Argo CD project

❌ Every engineer having Argo CD admin

❌ One Git credential with unlimited repository access

❌ Automatic pruning without governance

❌ Ignoring every drift difference

❌ Random Helm-generated values

❌ Excessive sync hooks

❌ Encoding runtime service dependencies through sync waves

❌ Manual cluster changes never reconciled to Git

❌ Terraform and Argo CD managing the same resources

❌ Treating `Synced` as proof the application works

❌ Treating Git revert as database rollback

❌ Progressive delivery for every trivial service

---

# 139. Governance Model

```text
Application Team
      │
      ├── Source code
      ├── Application Helm configuration
      ├── Resource requirements
      └── Application health

Platform Team
      │
      ├── Argo CD platform
      ├── GitOps standards
      ├── Cluster integration
      ├── ApplicationSet standards
      └── Platform policies

Security Team
      │
      ├── Access policies
      ├── Supply-chain controls
      ├── Secret governance
      └── Audit requirements

Release Owners
      │
      ├── Environment promotion
      └── Production approval
```

---

# 140. Production Deployment Contract

Every production deployment should identify:

```text
Application
Artifact digest
Application version
Helm chart version
Git commit
Environment
Configuration version
Approval
Deployment timestamp
Health outcome
```

This provides traceability from code to runtime.

---

# 141. Production Readiness Checklist

Before an application becomes GitOps-managed in production:

```text
GitOps repository defined              ✅
Argo CD Application defined            ✅
AppProject restrictions                ✅
Repository permissions                 ✅
Cluster/namespace destination          ✅
Helm values validated                  ✅
Immutable artifact reference           ✅
External secrets                       ✅
RBAC                                   ✅
Resource limits                        ✅
Health probes                          ✅
NetworkPolicy                          ✅
Observability                          ✅
Rollback/revert strategy               ✅
Database migration strategy            ✅
Branch protection                      ✅
Deployment ownership                   ✅
Alerting                               ✅
Break-glass process                    ✅
```

---

# 142. Security Architecture

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Enterprise Identity
    │
    ▼
Git Repository
    │
    ├── Branch Protection
    ├── PR Review
    ├── CODEOWNERS
    └── Audit
    │
    ▼
GitOps Desired State
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ├── SSO
    ├── RBAC
    ├── AppProject
    └── Restricted Credentials
    │
    ▼
Kubernetes API
    │
    ├── RBAC
    ├── Admission Policy
    ├── Image Verification
    └── NetworkPolicy
    │
    ▼
Workload
```

Security is layered.

GitOps is not itself a security boundary sufficient for the entire platform.

---

# 143. Complete Delivery Architecture

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Application Repository
    │
    ▼
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
CI Pipeline
    │
    ├── Compile
    ├── Unit Tests
    ├── Integration Tests
    ├── SAST
    ├── Dependency Scan
    ├── Build OCI Image
    ├── Generate SBOM
    ├── Container Scan
    ├── Sign Image
    └── Publish
    │
    ▼
OCI Registry
    │
    ▼
Immutable Artifact
    │
    ▼
GitOps Promotion PR
    │
    ▼
GitOps Repository
    │
    ├───────────────┬───────────────┐
    ▼               ▼               ▼
   DEV             UAT             PROD
    │               │               │
    └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
                 Argo CD
                    │
                    ▼
                  Helm
                    │
                    ▼
             Kubernetes API
                    │
                    ▼
                 Workload
```

---

# 144. Environment Promotion Architecture

```text
                        BUILD ONCE
                            │
                            ▼
                      IMAGE DIGEST
                        sha256:ABC
                            │
                            ▼
                           DEV
                            │
                     Automated Tests
                            │
                            ▼
                      Promotion PR
                            │
                            ▼
                           UAT
                            │
                     Validation / QA
                            │
                            ▼
                      Promotion PR
                            │
                     Review + Approval
                            │
                            ▼
                          PROD
                            │
                            ▼
                       sha256:ABC
```

The artifact does not change.

Only its promotion state changes.

---

# 145. GitOps Control Plane Architecture

```text
                    ┌───────────────────────┐
                    │      GitOps Git       │
                    │                       │
                    │ Desired State         │
                    │ Environment Config    │
                    │ Artifact References   │
                    └───────────┬───────────┘
                                │
                                ▼
                    ┌───────────────────────┐
                    │       ARGO CD         │
                    │                       │
                    │ ApplicationSet        │
                    │ Application           │
                    │ AppProject            │
                    │ Reconciliation        │
                    │ Drift Detection       │
                    │ Health                │
                    └───────────┬───────────┘
                                │
                                ▼
                    ┌───────────────────────┐
                    │      Kubernetes       │
                    │                       │
                    │ Deployments           │
                    │ Services              │
                    │ ConfigMaps            │
                    │ HPA                   │
                    │ PDB                   │
                    │ NetworkPolicy         │
                    └───────────────────────┘
```

---

# 146. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                              | Mitigation                          |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Git compromise                    | MFA + branch protection + audit     |
| Malicious artifact                | Signing + scanning + admission      |
| Argo CD compromise                | RBAC + isolation + least privilege  |
| Secret leakage                    | External secret management          |
| Accidental production change      | PR approval + CODEOWNERS            |
| Configuration drift               | Continuous reconciliation           |
| Bad automatic pruning             | Governance + review                 |
| Invalid desired state             | CI validation                       |
| Database incompatibility          | Expand/contract migrations          |
| Git unavailable                   | Existing workloads continue         |
| Argo CD unavailable               | HA + recovery process               |
| Shared control-plane blast radius | PROD isolation                      |
| Manual emergency drift            | Break-glass + Git reconciliation    |
| ApplicationSet mistake            | Review + staged validation          |
| Rollback failure                  | Backward compatibility              |
| Supply-chain compromise           | Provenance + signatures             |
| Excessive permissions             | AppProjects + RBAC                  |
| Alert fatigue                     | Actionable environment-aware alerts |

---

# 147. Consequences

### Positive

```text
Declarative deployments
Strong auditability
Automatic drift detection
Reproducible environments
Reduced CI production privileges
Controlled artifact promotion
Consistent rollback mechanism
Multi-cluster scalability
Helm integration
Improved operational visibility
Disaster recovery simplification
```

### Negative

```text
Additional platform complexity
Git becomes critical infrastructure
Argo CD requires operational expertise
Bad Git changes can propagate quickly
Secret architecture must be solved separately
Database rollback remains difficult
ApplicationSet increases blast radius
Multi-cluster management increases complexity
```

GitOps does not eliminate deployment risk.

It makes deployment state **explicit, reproducible and governable**.

---

| **Risk Level**                      | Critical                     |

# 150. Relationship With Previous ADRs

```text
ADR-030 — Docker / OCI
       │
       └──► Defines immutable deployable artifact
                    │
                    ▼
ADR-031 — Kubernetes
       │
       └──► Defines runtime/orchestration platform
                    │
                    ▼
ADR-032 — Helm
       │
       └──► Defines Kubernetes application package
                    │
                    ▼
ADR-033 — Argo CD
       │
       └──► Defines GitOps delivery/reconciliation
                    │
                    ▼
             PRODUCTION DELIVERY
```

The complete responsibility chain is now:

```text
Terraform
    │
    └──► Provision Infrastructure

Docker / OCI
    │
    └──► Package Application

Helm
    │
    └──► Package Kubernetes Configuration

Git
    │
    └──► Declare Desired State

Argo CD
    │
    └──► Reconcile Desired State

Kubernetes
    │
    └──► Execute Workloads

Prometheus / Grafana / OTel
    │
    └──► Observe Runtime
```
