```text
ADR-030  Docker & OCI Container Architecture          ✅
ADR-031  Kubernetes Cluster Architecture              ✅
ADR-032  Helm Application Packaging                   ✅
ADR-033  Argo CD GitOps & Continuous Delivery         ✅
ADR-034  Terraform Infrastructure as Code             ✅
ADR-035  AWS Cloud & Multi-Account Architecture       ✅
```

# Next — ADR-036

## **ADR-036 — CI Platform & Enterprise Software Supply Chain Architecture**

This is the correct next boundary. We have defined **where Mediverse runs and how CD works**, but we have not yet made the enterprise decision for **how source code becomes a trusted OCI artifact**.

ADR-036 should cover **GitHub Actions vs Jenkins vs GitLab CI evaluation → CI platform selection → hosted vs self-hosted runners → repository workflows → reusable workflows → pipeline-as-code → trigger strategy → PR validation → branch protection → Java/Maven pipeline → React/Vite pipeline → Docker BuildKit → build caching → parallelization → test stages → JUnit → frontend tests → integration tests → ephemeral services → quality gates → SonarQube → SAST → SCA → secret scanning → container scanning → IaC scanning → SBOM → CycloneDX/SPDX → artifact provenance → SLSA direction → Cosign signing → OIDC → AWS role federation → eliminating static AWS credentials → ECR publishing → immutable digests → Maven dependency/repository architecture → Nexus boundary → npm dependency governance → dependency pinning → lockfiles → third-party action pinning → CI secrets → runner isolation → untrusted PR security → fork security → self-hosted runner risks → cache poisoning → artifact retention → build reproducibility → promotion rather than rebuilding → GitOps update → CI-to-Argo boundary → production credential separation → release tagging → semantic versioning → monorepo vs polyrepo pipeline strategy → path filtering → concurrency → cancellation → flaky-test governance → CI observability → metrics → audit → cost controls → disaster recovery → compromise response → supply-chain threat model → governance → anti-patterns → production reference architecture.**

# ADR-036 — CI Platform & Enterprise Software Supply Chain Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-036
**Status:** Accepted
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-035 established the AWS runtime foundation. ADR-036 now defines the missing half of delivery: **how Mediverse source code becomes a tested, scanned, traceable, signed, immutable artifact that is safe to promote through GitOps.**

> **CI builds and verifies artifacts. CI does not deploy production workloads. Argo CD remains the CD authority.**

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Git Repository
    │
    ▼
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│            CI               │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│ Compile                     │
│ Test                        │
│ Quality Gate                │
│ SAST / SCA                  │
│ Secret Scan                 │
│ Build OCI Image             │
│ Generate SBOM               │
│ Container Scan              │
│ Generate Provenance         │
│ Sign Artifact               │
└──────────────┬──────────────┘
               │
               ▼
              ECR
               │
        Immutable Digest
               │
               ▼
         GitOps Update
               │
               ▼
             Argo CD
```

---

# 1. Problem

Mediverse already has decisions for:

```text
Source Code
    │
    ▼
Docker / OCI
    │
    ▼
ECR
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
EKS
```

But the process transforming source into a trusted artifact has not yet been formally defined.

Without a standardized CI architecture, teams eventually create incompatible pipelines with inconsistent security.

---

# 2. Decision

Mediverse shall adopt **GitHub Actions** as the primary CI automation platform.

The CI architecture shall support:

```text
Java / Maven
React / TypeScript / Vite
Docker / OCI
Terraform
Helm
Security scanning
Testing
SBOM generation
Artifact signing
AWS federation
ECR publishing
GitOps integration
```

---

# 3. CI Platforms Evaluated

| Platform                   | Decision                          |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| GitHub Actions             | ✅ Selected                        |
| Jenkins                    | 🟡 Supported only where justified |
| GitLab CI/CD               | 🟡 Strong alternative             |
| AWS CodeBuild/CodePipeline | 🟡 Specialized use                |
| CircleCI                   | ❌ Not selected                    |
| Manual build/release       | ❌ Prohibited                      |

---

# 4. Why GitHub Actions?

GitHub Actions integrates naturally with:

```text
Git repositories
Pull requests
Branch protection
CODEOWNERS
Release tags
OIDC
Security workflows
Reusable workflows
Environment approvals
```

It also avoids operating a Jenkins control plane unless there is a genuine requirement.

---

# 5. Why Not Jenkins as Primary?

Jenkins is powerful.

Its weakness is operational overhead.

An enterprise Jenkins environment requires management of:

```text
Controller
Agents
Plugins
Plugin vulnerabilities
Upgrades
Backups
Credentials
Scaling
Availability
Security hardening
```

Mediverse should not operate that infrastructure without a concrete advantage.

---

# 6. Jenkins Boundary

Jenkins remains acceptable for:

```text
Legacy pipelines
Specialized internal environments
Unsupported integration requirements
Migration workloads
```

It should not become a second default CI standard.

---

# 7. GitHub Actions Is Not CD

This distinction is mandatory:

```text
GitHub Actions
      │
      └──► Continuous Integration

Argo CD
      │
      └──► Continuous Delivery / Deployment
```

CI must not gradually regain direct production deployment responsibility.

---

# 8. CI Responsibility

CI owns:

```text
Compilation
Testing
Static analysis
Dependency analysis
Artifact construction
SBOM generation
Security scanning
Artifact signing
Registry publication
Release metadata
```

---

# 9. CD Responsibility

Argo CD owns:

```text
Desired-state reconciliation
Deployment
Drift detection
Kubernetes synchronization
Health assessment
Self-healing where enabled
```

---

# 10. CI/CD Trust Boundary

```text
                CI
                 │
                 ▼
          Trusted Artifact
                 │
                 ▼
              Registry
                 │
                 ▼
           GitOps Change
                 │
                 ▼
               Git
                 │
                 ▼
             Argo CD
                 │
                 ▼
            Kubernetes
```

No direct:

```text
CI ─────────────► kubectl PROD
```

---

# 11. Pipeline as Code

CI workflows shall live in version control.

Example:

```text
.github/
└── workflows/
    ├── backend-ci.yml
    ├── frontend-ci.yml
    ├── container.yml
    ├── terraform-ci.yml
    └── release.yml
```

Pipeline behavior therefore receives normal Git review.

---

# 12. Workflow Review

CI workflow changes are security-sensitive.

A malicious workflow could:

```text
Steal secrets
Publish malicious images
Assume cloud roles
Modify artifacts
Tamper with releases
```

Workflow files require protected review.

---

# 13. CODEOWNERS for CI

Sensitive paths should require platform/security ownership.

Conceptually:

```text
.github/workflows/   → Platform Team
security/            → Security Team
terraform/           → Platform Team
```

This prevents arbitrary pipeline privilege changes.

---

# 14. Workflow Triggers

Typical triggers include:

```text
Pull Request
Push
Release Tag
Manual approved execution
Scheduled security jobs
```

Triggers should match actual workflow purpose.

---

# 15. Pull Request Pipeline

Every significant pull request should execute relevant validation.

```text
PR
 │
 ▼
Compile
 │
 ▼
Unit Tests
 │
 ▼
Lint
 │
 ▼
Security Checks
 │
 ▼
Quality Gate
 │
 ▼
Merge Eligibility
```

---

# 16. PR Pipeline Objective

The PR pipeline answers:

> **Should this change be allowed into the protected branch?**

It should be fast enough that engineers do not learn to ignore CI.

---

# 17. Main Branch Pipeline

After merge:

```text
main
 │
 ▼
Trusted CI Context
 │
 ▼
Build
 │
 ▼
Test
 │
 ▼
Package
 │
 ▼
Scan
 │
 ▼
Sign
 │
 ▼
Publish
```

Artifact publication should happen from trusted repository context.

---

# 18. Untrusted Pull Requests

Pull requests from forks or untrusted contributors must not automatically receive sensitive credentials.

```text
Untrusted Code
     │
     X
     │
AWS Credentials
Signing Keys
Production Secrets
```

This is a major CI security boundary.

---

# 19. PR Secret Exposure

Never design a pipeline where arbitrary pull-request code can execute while production credentials are available.

That is effectively remote credential extraction.

---

# 20. Branch Protection

Protected branches should require:

```text
Pull request
Required reviews
Required CI checks
CODEOWNERS where appropriate
Restricted force push
Restricted deletion
```

Production integrity starts before artifact construction.

---

# 21. Java CI Pipeline

Spring Boot services should follow:

```text
Checkout
   │
   ▼
JDK Setup
   │
   ▼
Dependency Resolution
   │
   ▼
Compile
   │
   ▼
Unit Tests
   │
   ▼
Integration Tests
   │
   ▼
Static Analysis
   │
   ▼
Package JAR
```

---

# 22. Java Version

ADR-011 selected Java 21.

CI shall therefore build using Java 21 rather than whatever Java version happens to exist on a runner.

```text
Developer → Java 21
CI        → Java 21
Container → Java 21-compatible runtime
```

---

# 23. Maven

ADR-019 selected Maven.

CI shall use Maven's reproducible project configuration rather than manually constructing classpaths or downloading dependencies with scripts.

---

# 24. Maven Wrapper

Repositories should strongly prefer:

```text
./mvnw
```

over depending on arbitrary globally installed Maven versions.

This improves build reproducibility.

---

# 25. Maven Dependency Cache

CI may cache Maven dependencies.

```text
~/.m2
```

Caching should improve performance without becoming a source of untrusted artifact substitution.

---

# 26. Cache Is Not Artifact Trust

A cache is an optimization.

It must never become the authoritative release artifact store.

```text
CI Cache
   ≠
Artifact Repository
```

---

# 27. Unit Tests

Unit tests should run on every relevant pull request.

They should be:

```text
Fast
Deterministic
Isolated
Repeatable
```

Tests that randomly fail destroy confidence in CI.

---

# 28. Integration Tests

Integration tests should validate interactions such as:

```text
Spring Boot ↔ PostgreSQL
Spring Boot ↔ Redis
Spring Boot ↔ Kafka
Repository layer
API layer
Security behavior
```

where appropriate.

---

# 29. Testcontainers

Testcontainers should be considered/preferred for realistic integration dependencies where practical.

Conceptually:

```text
CI Test
  │
  ├── PostgreSQL Container
  ├── Redis Container
  └── Kafka Container
```

This can reduce dependence on permanently shared test infrastructure.

---

# 30. Shared Test Database Anti-Pattern

Avoid:

```text
Every CI Build
      │
      ▼
One Shared PostgreSQL
```

Parallel builds will contaminate each other's test state and create flaky tests.

---

# 31. Frontend CI

React/TypeScript/Vite pipeline:

```text
Checkout
   │
   ▼
Node Setup
   │
   ▼
npm ci
   │
   ▼
Lint
   │
   ▼
Type Check
   │
   ▼
Unit Tests
   │
   ▼
Build
```

---

# 32. `npm ci`

CI should prefer deterministic installation based on the committed lockfile.

```text
package.json
     +
package-lock.json
     │
     ▼
npm ci
```

---

# 33. Lockfiles

Dependency lockfiles shall be committed.

They provide deterministic dependency resolution and improve supply-chain traceability.

---

# 34. Dependency Pinning

Dependencies should not rely unnecessarily on uncontrolled floating versions.

Bad:

```text
"some-package": "*"
```

Production builds require predictable dependency graphs.

---

# 35. TypeScript Validation

Type errors should fail CI.

Do not allow:

```text
CI build succeeds
       │
       ▼
Browser discovers type-related defect
```

when static validation could catch it earlier.

---

# 36. Frontend Build

Vite production builds should generate immutable hashed assets.

Example:

```text
assets/index-a92f81.js
assets/vendor-f10c22.js
```

This aligns with ADR-035 CloudFront caching architecture.

---

# 37. Parallelization

Independent CI jobs should execute concurrently.

```text
             PR
              │
     ┌────────┼─────────┐
     ▼        ▼         ▼
   Tests    SAST      Lint
     │        │         │
     └────────┼─────────┘
              ▼
          Quality Gate
```

Do not serialize unrelated work.

---

# 38. Pipeline Critical Path

Optimization should focus on the longest dependency chain rather than blindly caching everything.

CI speed is an engineering productivity concern.

---

# 39. Fail Fast

Cheap validation should execute early.

Example:

```text
Formatting
    │
Lint
    │
Compile
    │
Unit Tests
    │
Integration Tests
    │
Container Build
```

There is little value spending ten minutes building an image for code that fails formatting or compilation.

---

# 40. Quality Gates

A pipeline should prevent artifact promotion when required quality criteria fail.

Potential gates:

```text
Compilation
Tests
Coverage policy
Static analysis
Security severity thresholds
Container scan
Required reviews
```

---

# 41. SonarQube

SonarQube should provide centralized code-quality/static-analysis governance where adopted by Mediverse.

It can evaluate:

```text
Bugs
Vulnerabilities
Code smells
Duplications
Coverage
Maintainability
```

---

# 42. SonarQube Quality Gate

The quality gate should be actionable.

A pipeline that reports:

```text
Quality Gate FAILED
```

and then publishes the production artifact anyway has no meaningful gate.

---

# 43. Coverage

Code coverage is a useful signal.

It is not a measure of correctness.

```text
100% coverage
     ≠
100% correct software
```

Teams should not write meaningless tests merely to satisfy a percentage.

---

# 44. SAST

Static Application Security Testing should inspect source/code patterns for security weaknesses.

SAST belongs before artifact promotion.

---

# 45. SCA

Software Composition Analysis should inspect third-party dependencies.

This is particularly important because Mediverse depends on large ecosystems:

```text
Maven Central
npm
Container base images
GitHub Actions
```

---

# 46. Dependency Vulnerabilities

A secure application can still become vulnerable through a compromised or vulnerable dependency.

Supply-chain security therefore includes dependencies, not just Mediverse source code.

---

# 47. Secret Scanning

CI should detect accidentally committed secrets.

Examples:

```text
AWS access keys
API tokens
Private keys
Database passwords
JWT signing secrets
```

---

# 48. Secret Scanning Is Not Enough

Once a real secret has entered Git history, deleting the line is insufficient.

The secret should normally be considered compromised and rotated.

---

# 49. Docker Build Architecture

Container builds should use modern OCI-compatible tooling such as Docker BuildKit/buildx where appropriate.

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
BuildKit
  │
  ▼
OCI Image
```

---

# 50. Multi-Stage Builds

Spring Boot container builds should use multi-stage techniques where they improve image hygiene.

```text
BUILD STAGE
     │
     ▼
Compile / Package
     │
     ▼
RUNTIME STAGE
     │
     ▼
Minimal Runtime Image
```

Build tools do not need to exist inside the final production image.

---

# 51. Runtime Images

Production runtime images should contain only what the workload requires.

Avoid shipping:

```text
Maven
Compilers
Source repositories
Debug utilities
Package managers
```

without operational justification.

---

# 52. Non-Root Containers

Production containers should run as non-root where application requirements permit.

This supports the Kubernetes security architecture established earlier.

---

# 53. Base Image Governance

Container base images should come from approved sources.

Avoid random public images selected because they appeared first in a search result.

---

# 54. Base Image Pinning

Base images should use controlled versions/digests where reproducibility and supply-chain policy require it.

Otherwise:

```text
FROM image:latest
```

may produce different binaries from identical source code.

---

# 55. Container Scanning

The final OCI image should be scanned before release publication/promotion.

Scanning should evaluate:

```text
OS packages
Application dependencies
Known vulnerabilities
Configuration issues where supported
```

---

# 56. Scan Severity Policy

Not every vulnerability should automatically block every environment.

Policies should consider:

```text
Severity
Exploitability
Runtime exposure
Fix availability
Environment
Accepted risk
```

Security gates must be strict enough to matter and rational enough to remain usable.

---

# 57. Vulnerability Exceptions

Temporary exceptions require:

```text
Owner
Reason
Expiry
Risk assessment
Tracking
```

Permanent "ignore" lists become vulnerability graveyards.

---

# 58. SBOM

Every production release should generate a Software Bill of Materials.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
SBOM
    │
    ├── Components
    ├── Versions
    ├── Dependencies
    └── Relationships
```

---

# 59. SBOM Formats

Preferred interoperable formats include:

```text
CycloneDX
SPDX
```

The exact standard should align with the selected security tooling.

---

# 60. Why SBOM Matters

During a major vulnerability incident, Mediverse should be able to answer:

```text
Which services contain library X?

Which version?

Which container?

Which environments?

Which releases?
```

without manually inspecting every repository.

---

## ADR-036 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

Part 2 should continue from **Section 61 — Artifact Provenance**, then cover SLSA direction, Cosign signing, signature verification, OIDC and AWS federation, ECR publication, immutable digests, Nexus/Maven repository boundaries, npm dependency governance, third-party GitHub Action security, runner architecture and isolation, self-hosted runner risks, cache poisoning, CI secrets, artifact retention, reproducible builds, release/version strategy, GitOps update mechanics, promotion without rebuilding, CI-to-Argo trust boundaries, concurrency, flaky-test governance, CI observability, compromise response, supply-chain threat model, governance, anti-patterns, risks and the final Mediverse enterprise CI/supply-chain reference architecture.

# ADR-036 — CI Platform & Enterprise Software Supply Chain Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Why SBOM Matters**.

---

# 61. Artifact Provenance

Every production artifact should carry evidence describing how it was produced.

Provenance should establish:

```text
Source Repository
       │
       ▼
Source Commit
       │
       ▼
CI Workflow
       │
       ▼
Build Environment
       │
       ▼
Artifact Digest
```

The objective is traceability from running workload back to source.

---

# 62. Why Provenance Matters

Without provenance, possessing an image in ECR does not prove:

```text
Who built it
Which source produced it
Which commit was used
Which workflow produced it
Whether CI controls were executed
Whether the artifact was modified afterward
```

Artifact existence and artifact trust are different things.

---

# 63. SLSA Direction

Mediverse should align its software supply-chain architecture with **SLSA principles**.

The objective is progressive maturity around:

```text
Build integrity
Provenance
Build isolation
Source integrity
Artifact traceability
Tamper resistance
```

This ADR does not mandate chasing a specific SLSA level merely for certification optics.

---

# 64. Build Provenance

Conceptually:

```text
Git Commit
    │
    ▼
GitHub Actions
    │
    ├── Workflow Identity
    ├── Repository Identity
    ├── Commit SHA
    └── Build Metadata
    │
    ▼
OCI Artifact
    │
    ▼
Provenance Attestation
```

---

# 65. Artifact Signing

Production OCI artifacts should be cryptographically signed.

Selected direction:

```text
OCI Image
    │
    ▼
Cosign
    │
    ▼
Signature
```

Signing allows downstream systems to verify artifact identity and provenance.

---

# 66. Cosign

Cosign should be used as the preferred OCI signing technology.

Conceptually:

```text
CI
 │
 ├── Build
 ├── Scan
 ├── SBOM
 └── Sign
      │
      ▼
     ECR
```

---

# 67. Keyless Signing Direction

Where supported by the security model, Mediverse should prefer identity-based/keyless signing over distributing long-lived private signing keys through CI.

```text
GitHub Actions Identity
        │
        ▼
      OIDC
        │
        ▼
Signing Identity
        │
        ▼
OCI Signature
```

This reduces private-key management burden.

---

# 68. Signing Is Not Enough

A signed malicious artifact is still malicious.

Signing proves identity/integrity relationships.

It does not prove software correctness.

Therefore:

```text
Testing
+
Scanning
+
Provenance
+
Signing
+
Admission Policy
```

work together.

---

# 69. Signature Verification

Signing without verification has little security value.

The Kubernetes supply-chain architecture should eventually enforce:

```text
Incoming Image
      │
      ▼
Admission Policy
      │
      ▼
Verify Signature
      │
      ├── Trusted → Admit
      │
      └── Untrusted → Reject
```

---

# 70. Artifact Digest

Every OCI image has a content-addressed digest.

Example:

```text
sha256:7e35...
```

This identifies exact image content.

---

# 71. Tags vs Digests

Tags are human-friendly references.

```text
content-service:1.8.0
```

Digests are immutable content identities.

```text
content-service@sha256:...
```

Production deployment should ultimately resolve to immutable artifact identity.

---

# 72. Mutable Tag Risk

This is dangerous:

```text
content-service:prod
```

if somebody can replace what `prod` points to.

Then Git may remain unchanged while production artifact content changes.

That breaks GitOps traceability.

---

# 73. ECR Publication

Only trusted CI contexts should publish release artifacts to production ECR repositories.

```text
Untrusted PR
    │
    X
    │
Production ECR


Protected Branch
    │
    ▼
Trusted CI
    │
    ▼
Production ECR
```

---

# 74. AWS Authentication

GitHub Actions should authenticate to AWS using short-lived federation.

Preferred:

```text
GitHub Actions
      │
      ▼
     OIDC
      │
      ▼
AWS IAM Trust Policy
      │
      ▼
Temporary Role Session
```

---

# 75. No Permanent AWS Keys

Avoid storing:

```text
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```

as long-lived GitHub secrets when OIDC federation can replace them.

Long-lived credentials increase rotation and theft risk.

---

# 76. OIDC Trust Policy

AWS trust policies must restrict which GitHub identities can assume sensitive roles.

Do not configure:

```text
Any GitHub repository
      │
      ▼
Production AWS Role
```

Trust should account for repository, organization, branch/environment, and workflow context as appropriate.

---

# 77. AWS Role Separation

CI roles should be separated by responsibility.

Example:

```text
CI Build Role
     │
     └── Limited AWS access

ECR Publisher Role
     │
     └── Push approved artifacts

Terraform Role
     │
     └── Infrastructure operations

PROD Runtime Roles
     │
     └── Workload-specific access
```

---

# 78. CI Does Not Need EKS Admin

Because Argo CD owns deployment:

```text
GitHub Actions
      │
      X
      │
EKS cluster-admin
```

should be the normal architecture.

Removing production Kubernetes credentials from CI materially reduces blast radius.

---

# 79. Maven Repository Architecture

Maven dependencies and internally produced Java artifacts require explicit repository governance.

Potential sources:

```text
Maven Central
Internal Nexus
Approved vendor repositories
```

---

# 80. Nexus Boundary

Nexus may provide:

```text
Maven proxy
Internal Maven releases
Internal snapshots
Dependency caching
Repository governance
```

where Mediverse requires centralized artifact repository management.

It should not duplicate ECR's role for OCI images without a reason.

---

# 81. Artifact Responsibility

Recommended boundary:

```text
Amazon ECR
    │
    └── OCI/container artifacts

Nexus
    │
    └── Maven/internal package artifacts

GitHub
    │
    └── Source + workflow definitions
```

Clear ownership avoids repository sprawl.

---

# 82. Maven Snapshot vs Release

Internal libraries should distinguish:

```text
SNAPSHOT
→ Development artifact

Release
→ Immutable published version
```

Released library versions must not be silently overwritten.

---

# 83. Internal Shared Libraries

Shared Java libraries should be created cautiously.

Excessive shared libraries create tight coupling between microservices.

Good candidates:

```text
Observability conventions
Security integration utilities
Stable platform clients
```

Bad candidate:

```text
One giant mediverse-common.jar
containing every domain model
```

That recreates a distributed monolith.

---

# 84. npm Dependency Governance

Frontend dependencies should follow similar supply-chain controls.

Requirements include:

```text
Committed lockfile
npm ci
Dependency scanning
Controlled registries
Version governance
Minimal package set
```

---

# 85. npm Package Risk

Adding a package is adding executable third-party code to the software supply chain.

Do not install a dependency for functionality that could reasonably be implemented in a few stable lines merely because an npm package exists.

---

# 86. Dependency Update Automation

Automated dependency update tooling may create pull requests for:

```text
Maven dependencies
npm packages
GitHub Actions
Container base images
```

Updates must still pass normal CI and review.

---

# 87. Third-Party GitHub Actions

GitHub Actions themselves are software dependencies.

Example:

```yaml
uses: vendor/action@...
```

A compromised action can compromise CI.

---

# 88. Action Pinning

Security-sensitive workflows should pin third-party actions to immutable commit SHAs where appropriate.

Conceptually:

```text
uses: vendor/action@<commit-sha>
```

rather than blindly trusting a mutable branch reference.

---

# 89. Action Allowlist

Enterprise governance may restrict Actions to:

```text
GitHub-maintained actions
Verified/approved vendors
Internally reviewed actions
```

Unknown Actions should not automatically receive privileged workflow access.

---

# 90. Runner Architecture

GitHub Actions can use:

```text
GitHub-hosted runners
```

or:

```text
Self-hosted runners
```

The choice affects security, networking, cost, and operational complexity.

---

# 91. GitHub-Hosted Runners

Hosted runners are preferred for ordinary CI where they satisfy requirements.

Benefits:

```text
Ephemeral execution
Low operational burden
Managed updates
Elastic capacity
Reduced persistent-runner compromise
```

---

# 92. Self-Hosted Runners

Self-hosted runners may be justified for:

```text
Private network access
Special hardware
Large builds
GPU builds
Custom tooling
Compliance constraints
```

But they create significant security responsibilities.

---

# 93. Persistent Runner Risk

Dangerous architecture:

```text
Untrusted PR
     │
     ▼
Persistent Runner
     │
     ▼
Malicious Persistence
     │
     ▼
Future Trusted Build
     │
     ▼
Credential Theft
```

Persistent self-hosted runners should not casually execute untrusted code.

---

# 94. Ephemeral Self-Hosted Runners

Where self-hosting is required, ephemeral runners are strongly preferred.

```text
Job Requested
     │
     ▼
Create Runner
     │
     ▼
Execute One Job
     │
     ▼
Destroy Runner
```

This reduces persistence opportunities.

---

# 95. Runner Network Access

A CI runner should have only the network access required for its job.

Do not place general-purpose CI runners inside a network from which every production database and internal system is reachable.

---

# 96. CI Secrets

Secrets should be scoped according to:

```text
Repository
Environment
Workflow
Job
```

and exposed only where required.

---

# 97. Environment Secrets

Production-specific credentials should use protected environments and approval controls where applicable.

DEV workflows should not automatically receive PROD secrets.

---

# 98. Secret Masking

Log masking is useful but not a security architecture.

Once arbitrary code receives a secret, that code may exfiltrate it through mechanisms other than plain log output.

The real control is avoiding unnecessary secret exposure.

---

# 99. Cache Poisoning

CI caches create a supply-chain risk when untrusted workflows can populate cache entries later consumed by privileged builds.

Cache keys and trust boundaries must therefore be designed carefully.

---

# 100. Cache Separation

Where necessary:

```text
Untrusted PR Cache
       │
       X
       │
Trusted Release Cache
```

Trusted builds should not blindly consume artifacts produced by untrusted execution contexts.

---

# 101. Build Artifacts

Intermediate build outputs may be stored temporarily for:

```text
Testing
Debugging
Pipeline handoff
Coverage reports
Security reports
```

Artifact retention should match actual operational requirements.

---

# 102. Artifact Retention

Do not retain every intermediate CI artifact forever.

Define retention based on:

```text
Audit requirements
Debugging needs
Release lifecycle
Storage cost
Security sensitivity
```

Production OCI artifacts follow separate registry-retention governance.

---

# 103. Reproducible Builds

The architecture should move toward reproducible builds.

Conceptually:

```text
Same Source
+
Same Dependencies
+
Same Build Configuration
       │
       ▼
Equivalent Artifact
```

Perfect byte-for-byte reproducibility may not always be immediate, but unnecessary nondeterminism should be removed.

---

# 104. Build Metadata

Avoid uncontrolled build inputs such as:

```text
Current timestamp embedded everywhere
Unpinned dependency versions
latest base images
Environment-specific compilation
Random generated content
```

when they undermine reproducibility.

---

# 105. Build Once

Mediverse shall follow:

> **Build once, promote many.**

```text
Commit ABC
    │
    ▼
Build Image
    │
    ▼
sha256:XYZ
    │
    ├── DEV
    ├── UAT
    └── PROD
```

---

# 106. Do Not Rebuild Per Environment

Rejected:

```text
Source
 ├── DEV Build
 ├── UAT Build
 └── PROD Build
```

Those are three different artifacts even when they originate from the same commit.

Testing one does not prove another is identical.

---

# 107. Runtime Configuration

Environment differences belong in runtime configuration.

```text
Same OCI Artifact
       │
       ├── DEV configuration
       ├── UAT configuration
       └── PROD configuration
```

This aligns with Helm + GitOps architecture.

---

# 108. Release Versioning

Mediverse should use clear release identifiers.

For appropriate artifacts:

```text
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
```

can provide semantic versioning.

Example:

```text
2.4.1
```

---

# 109. Commit SHA

Every artifact should also retain source commit identity.

Example metadata:

```text
Version:       2.4.1
Commit:        a82f71...
Image Digest:  sha256:...
Build:         GitHub Actions run ...
```

---

# 110. OCI Labels

Container metadata should expose useful provenance such as:

```text
Source repository
Revision
Version
Creation metadata where appropriate
Vendor/project
```

using standardized OCI annotations where practical.

---

# 111. GitOps Update

After publishing an approved artifact, automation may propose a GitOps repository update.

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
New Digest
 │
 ▼
GitOps Pull Request
 │
 ▼
Review / Policy
 │
 ▼
Merge
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
```

---

# 112. CI Should Propose, Not Secretly Deploy

Preferred production flow:

```text
CI
 │
 └──► Creates/updates GitOps PR

Human/Policy
 │
 └──► Approves promotion

Argo CD
 │
 └──► Deploys
```

The exact approval model may vary by environment.

---

# 113. DEV Promotion

DEV may permit highly automated promotion.

Example:

```text
main merged
    │
    ▼
Build + Verify
    │
    ▼
Publish
    │
    ▼
Update DEV GitOps
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
```

Fast feedback is desirable.

---

# 114. UAT Promotion

UAT should promote an artifact already validated in DEV.

```text
sha256:XYZ
    │
    ▼
DEV
    │
    ▼
Promotion
    │
    ▼
UAT
```

No rebuild occurs.

---

# 115. Production Promotion

Production promotion should use the same immutable artifact.

```text
DEV ─────┐
         │
UAT ─────┼──► sha256:XYZ
         │
PROD ────┘
```

Production approval changes deployment authorization, not binary contents.

---

# 116. GitOps Repository Credentials

Automation updating GitOps repositories should receive narrowly scoped credentials.

It does not need unrestricted access to every repository in the organization.

---

# 117. CI-to-Argo Boundary

There should normally be no need for:

```text
GitHub Actions
      │
      ▼
Argo CD Admin API Token
```

CI updates desired state.

Argo CD observes Git.

This decoupling is one of GitOps's strongest properties.

---

# 118. Release Tagging

Release tags should correspond to known source commits.

Protected release workflows should prevent arbitrary users from manufacturing trusted releases from unreviewed code.

---

# 119. Monorepo vs Polyrepo

CI architecture must support both repository models.

Mediverse should not choose repository topology merely because one CI configuration is easier.

---

# 120. Polyrepo

Potential advantages:

```text
Independent ownership
Independent releases
Smaller repository scope
Service-specific permissions
```

Potential disadvantages:

```text
Workflow duplication
Cross-service changes
Dependency coordination
Repository sprawl
```

---

# 121. Monorepo

Potential advantages:

```text
Atomic cross-project changes
Shared tooling
Central visibility
Consistent CI
```

Potential disadvantages:

```text
Larger CI graph
Permission complexity
Repository scale
Unnecessary builds
```

---

# 122. Path Filtering

For monorepos, CI should execute only affected pipelines where reliable.

```text
services/content/**
        │
        ▼
Content Service CI
```

rather than rebuilding 40 unrelated services for every README change.

---

# 123. Path Filtering Risk

Incorrect filtering can skip required builds.

Dependency relationships must be understood before optimizing.

Speed is not worth silently bypassing validation.

---

# 124. Concurrency

CI should control concurrent executions.

Example:

```text
PR Commit A → CI running
PR Commit B → arrives
                │
                ▼
Cancel obsolete A where safe
                │
                ▼
Run B
```

This saves capacity and reduces irrelevant feedback.

---

# 125. Release Concurrency

Release workflows require stricter serialization.

Two concurrent release processes should not race to update the same version or GitOps target.

---

# 126. Flaky Tests

A test that fails randomly is a production engineering defect in the test system.

Repeated:

```text
Re-run
Re-run
Re-run
Finally green
```

is not a valid quality strategy.

---

# 127. Flaky-Test Governance

Flaky tests should be:

```text
Detected
Tracked
Assigned
Fixed
```

Temporary quarantine may be necessary, but permanent quarantine defeats the purpose of the test.

---

# 128. CI Performance Metrics

Mediverse should observe:

```text
Pipeline duration
Queue time
Failure rate
Flaky-test rate
Cache effectiveness
Runner utilization
Build frequency
Security-gate failures
```

CI is production infrastructure for engineering.

---

# 129. Developer Feedback Time

Long pipelines directly reduce development velocity.

Target:

```text
Fast PR checks
        +
Deeper asynchronous/merge validation
        +
Strict release validation
```

rather than putting every possible test into one 90-minute PR pipeline.

---

# 130. CI Logs

CI logs should contain enough information to diagnose failures without exposing:

```text
Secrets
Tokens
Private keys
Sensitive environment values
```

Debug logging must not bypass security.

---

# 131. Auditability

For each release, Mediverse should be able to identify:

```text
Source commit
Pull request
Reviewers
Workflow
Workflow version
Test results
Security results
SBOM
Provenance
Artifact digest
Signature
Registry location
GitOps promotion
```

---

# 132. CI Cost

CI has real cost.

Major drivers include:

```text
Runner minutes
Large runners
Storage
Artifact retention
Container builds
Integration tests
Repeated unnecessary builds
Self-hosted infrastructure
```

Optimization should target waste without weakening validation.

---

# 133. Self-Hosted Runner Cost

Self-hosted does not mean free.

Costs include:

```text
Compute
Scaling
Patching
Security
Monitoring
Networking
Operations
Incident response
```

Hosted runners may be cheaper overall even when per-minute pricing appears higher.

---

# 134. CI Availability

A CI outage should prevent new releases but should not stop existing Mediverse production workloads.

This is another reason CI must not sit inside the runtime request path.

---

# 135. Disaster Recovery

Critical CI configuration already exists in Git:

```text
Workflow definitions
Build scripts
Dockerfiles
Maven configuration
Security configuration
```

External dependencies still require recovery planning.

---

# 136. Supply-Chain Threat Model

Important threats include:

```text
Compromised developer account
Malicious pull request
Compromised dependency
Dependency confusion
Compromised GitHub Action
Compromised runner
Cache poisoning
Credential theft
Malicious base image
Artifact replacement
Registry compromise
Signing identity compromise
GitOps repository compromise
```

---

# 137. Compromise Response

If CI compromise is suspected:

```text
Detect
  │
  ▼
Disable affected workflow/runner
  │
  ▼
Revoke credentials/sessions
  │
  ▼
Identify affected artifacts
  │
  ▼
Invalidate/revoke trust
  │
  ▼
Rebuild from trusted source
  │
  ▼
Re-sign
  │
  ▼
Re-promote
```

Incident response must consider artifacts already produced.

---

# 138. Artifact Trust Revocation

Mediverse must be able to identify which deployed artifacts were built during a compromised window.

This is why provenance, digest tracking, and deployment auditability matter.

---

# 139. Security Governance

```text
Development Teams
      │
      ├── Tests
      ├── Build configuration
      └── Dependency maintenance

Platform Team
      │
      ├── Reusable workflows
      ├── Runner architecture
      ├── Registry integration
      └── GitOps integration

Security Team
      │
      ├── SAST/SCA policy
      ├── Secret scanning
      ├── Signing policy
      ├── Provenance requirements
      └── Vulnerability exceptions

Release Owners
      │
      └── Production promotion governance
```

---

# 140. Reusable Workflows

Common CI behavior should be centralized through reusable workflows where appropriate.

Example:

```text
Reusable Java Workflow
       │
       ├── Service A
       ├── Service B
       ├── Service C
       └── Service D
```

This reduces copy-paste drift.

---

# 141. Reusable Workflow Versioning

Centralized workflows create dependency risk.

A breaking change to one shared workflow could break every repository.

Therefore reusable workflow changes require:

```text
Versioning
Testing
Compatibility management
Controlled rollout
```

---

# 142. CI Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ CI directly deploying production with kubectl
❌ CI with unrestricted EKS cluster-admin
❌ Long-lived AWS keys in GitHub
❌ Secrets available to untrusted PRs
❌ Persistent runners executing arbitrary fork code
❌ Unpinned third-party Actions
❌ Mutable production container tags
❌ Rebuilding separately for DEV/UAT/PROD
❌ Skipping failed security gates
❌ Permanent vulnerability exceptions
❌ Plaintext secrets in workflow YAML
❌ latest container base images for controlled releases
❌ Shared test databases across concurrent builds
❌ npm install instead of deterministic CI installation
❌ Missing dependency lockfiles
❌ Blind cache sharing across trust boundaries
❌ Publishing artifacts from untrusted branches
❌ Giant mediverse-common shared library
❌ Retaining every CI artifact forever
❌ Treating coverage as correctness
❌ Ignoring flaky tests
❌ Running every monorepo pipeline for every trivial change
❌ Giving CI direct Argo CD admin tokens
❌ Signing artifacts without verifying signatures
❌ Generating SBOMs nobody stores or uses
```

---

# 143. Production Quality Gate

A production-candidate artifact should conceptually satisfy:

```text
Source Protected
      │
      ▼
Compilation          ✅
Unit Tests           ✅
Integration Tests    ✅
Frontend Validation  ✅
Quality Gate         ✅
SAST                 ✅
SCA                  ✅
Secret Scan          ✅
OCI Build            ✅
Container Scan       ✅
SBOM                  ✅
Provenance            ✅
Signature             ✅
      │
      ▼
Trusted Artifact
```

Failure of mandatory gates prevents release eligibility.

---

# 144. Release Metadata Contract

Every production artifact should have traceability to:

| Metadata            | Required |
| ------------------- | -------: |
| Application/service |        ✅ |
| Version             |        ✅ |
| Git repository      |        ✅ |
| Git commit SHA      |        ✅ |
| Pull request/change |        ✅ |
| CI workflow         |        ✅ |
| CI run              |        ✅ |
| OCI digest          |        ✅ |
| SBOM                |        ✅ |
| Security scan       |        ✅ |
| Provenance          |        ✅ |
| Signature           |        ✅ |
| Build timestamp     |        ✅ |
| Promotion history   |        ✅ |

---

# 145. CI Security Architecture

```text
                     DEVELOPER
                         │
                         ▼
                    GitHub / Git
                         │
                         ▼
                   Pull Request
                         │
              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
              ▼                     ▼
       Untrusted Context       Trusted Context
              │                     │
              ▼                     ▼
       No Production         Protected Branch
         Credentials                │
                                    ▼
                              GitHub Actions
                                    │
                     ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
                     ▼              ▼              ▼
                   Tests         Security        Build
                                    │              │
                                    ▼              ▼
                                SBOM/Scan      OCI Image
                                                   │
                                                   ▼
                                              Provenance
                                                   │
                                                   ▼
                                                 Sign
                                                   │
                                                   ▼
                                                  ECR
```

---

# 146. Complete CI/CD Architecture

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Application Git
    │
    ▼
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│        GITHUB ACTIONS        │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│ Compile                      │
│ Unit Tests                   │
│ Integration Tests            │
│ Lint / Type Check            │
│ SonarQube                    │
│ SAST                         │
│ SCA                          │
│ Secret Scan                  │
│ Docker BuildKit              │
│ Container Scan               │
│ SBOM                         │
│ Provenance                   │
│ Cosign                       │
└───────────────┬──────────────┘
                │
                ▼
            Amazon ECR
                │
                ▼
       Immutable OCI Digest
                │
                ▼
         GitOps Update PR
                │
                ▼
        GitOps Repository
                │
                ▼
             Argo CD
                │
                ▼
               Helm
                │
                ▼
              EKS
```

---

# 147. Trust Chain

The final software supply-chain trust path becomes:

```text
Developer Identity
        │
        ▼
Protected Git
        │
        ▼
Reviewed Source
        │
        ▼
Trusted CI Workflow
        │
        ▼
Tests + Security Gates
        │
        ▼
OCI Artifact
        │
        ├── SBOM
        ├── Provenance
        └── Signature
        │
        ▼
Trusted Registry
        │
        ▼
GitOps Promotion
        │
        ▼
Admission Verification
        │
        ▼
Kubernetes Runtime
```

Every major transition introduces an explicit trust decision.

---

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                         | Mitigation                        |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Developer account compromise | MFA + branch protection           |
| Malicious PR                 | Untrusted execution isolation     |
| AWS credential theft         | OIDC + temporary credentials      |
| Dependency compromise        | SCA + lockfiles + SBOM            |
| GitHub Action compromise     | SHA pinning + allowlist           |
| Runner compromise            | Ephemeral runners                 |
| Cache poisoning              | Trust-aware cache isolation       |
| Malicious base image         | Approved/pinned images            |
| Vulnerable artifact          | Container scanning                |
| Artifact replacement         | Immutable digest                  |
| Registry tampering           | Signing + verification            |
| Build tampering              | Provenance                        |
| Secret leakage               | Scoped secrets + secret scanning  |
| CI→PROD compromise           | No direct cluster credentials     |
| Rebuild inconsistency        | Build once/promote                |
| Flaky tests                  | Tracking + remediation            |
| CI workflow compromise       | CODEOWNERS + protection           |
| Excessive CI cost            | Parallelization + path filtering  |
| Compromised release          | Traceability + revocation/rebuild |

---
