# Next — ADR-038

## **ADR-038 — Kubernetes Autoscaling, Capacity Management & Performance Architecture**

This is the logical next decision because ADR-037 gives us the telemetry needed to make scaling decisions. Now we need to define **how Mediverse reacts when traffic changes instead of merely observing it**.

ADR-038 should cover **capacity philosophy → requests/limits → CPU/memory sizing → JVM container awareness → HPA → custom/external metrics → KEDA → Kafka lag-based scaling → event-driven consumers → VPA → recommendation vs automatic mode → HPA/VPA conflicts → Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter → node provisioning → instance-family selection → Spot/On-Demand strategy → topology spread → pod anti-affinity → PodDisruptionBudget → priority classes → system workload isolation → GPU pools → GPU scheduling → AI workload scaling → queue-based load leveling → concurrency limits → backpressure → connection pools → database bottlenecks → Redis/Kafka capacity → load testing → stress testing → spike testing → soak testing → performance budgets → SLO-driven capacity → headroom → graceful degradation → load shedding → circuit breakers → scaling stabilization → scale-up/scale-down behavior → cold starts → Java startup optimization → cost-performance trade-offs → capacity forecasting → rightsizing → failure scenarios → governance → anti-patterns → production reference architecture.**

# ADR-038 — Kubernetes Autoscaling, Capacity Management & Performance Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-038
**Status:** Accepted
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-037 established the telemetry required to understand system behavior. ADR-038 defines how Mediverse uses that information to **allocate capacity, absorb traffic spikes, scale workloads, control resource consumption, and prevent overload from cascading through the platform.**

> **Autoscaling is not a substitute for capacity engineering. Scaling a bottleneck simply moves the bottleneck somewhere else.**

```text
                         USER LOAD
                             │
                             ▼
                       CloudFront / ALB
                             │
                             ▼
                         API Gateway
                             │
                             ▼
                     ┌─────────────────┐
                     │       EKS       │
                     │                 │
                     │      Pods       │
                     └────────┬────────┘
                              │
                     HPA / KEDA Decisions
                              │
                    ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                    ▼                   ▼
               More Pods          Fewer Pods
                    │
                    ▼
             Need More Nodes?
                    │
                    ▼
                Karpenter
                    │
                    ▼
               EC2 Capacity
```

# 1. Problem

Mediverse workloads will not experience constant demand.

Traffic may change because of:

```text
Student login peaks
Exam periods
Faculty activity
Large content releases
AI requests
Video/media workloads
Kafka event bursts
Background processing
Scheduled workloads
Unexpected traffic spikes
```

Static infrastructure sizing creates two bad outcomes:

```text
Too little capacity
       │
       ▼
Latency / Errors / Outage

Too much capacity
       │
       ▼
Idle Infrastructure / Waste
```

---

# 2. Decision

Mediverse shall implement a layered capacity-management architecture based on:

| Layer                          | Primary Mechanism              |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| Pod resource allocation        | Kubernetes requests/limits     |
| Stateless workload scaling     | HPA                            |
| Event-driven scaling           | KEDA                           |
| Resource recommendations       | VPA                            |
| Node provisioning              | Karpenter                      |
| Infrastructure diversity       | EC2 instance families          |
| Failure distribution           | Topology spread constraints    |
| Availability during disruption | PodDisruptionBudget            |
| Critical workload protection   | PriorityClass                  |
| Load protection                | Backpressure + load shedding   |
| Dependency protection          | Concurrency/connection limits  |
| Validation                     | Load/stress/spike/soak testing |
| Decision telemetry             | Prometheus/OpenTelemetry       |

---

# 3. Scaling Layers

Scaling must be considered at multiple layers.

```text
Traffic
   │
   ▼
Application Scaling
   │
   ▼
Pod Scaling
   │
   ▼
Node Scaling
   │
   ▼
Database / Cache / Kafka Capacity
   │
   ▼
AWS Infrastructure
```

Increasing pod count alone does not guarantee higher system capacity.

---

# 4. Capacity Philosophy

The platform shall use:

```text
Measure
   │
   ▼
Understand
   │
   ▼
Size
   │
   ▼
Load Test
   │
   ▼
Scale
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
   ▼
Right-size
```

not:

```text
Guess
 │
 ▼
Deploy
 │
 ▼
Hope
```

---

# 5. Kubernetes Resource Requests

Every production workload should define resource requests.

Example:

```yaml
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 768Mi
```

Requests influence Kubernetes scheduling.

---

# 6. CPU Requests

CPU requests represent expected baseline compute requirements.

If:

```text
Pod A requests 500m
Pod B requests 1000m
```

the scheduler uses those requests when deciding where the Pods can fit.

---

# 7. Memory Requests

Memory requests are particularly important because insufficient memory capacity can prevent scheduling.

They should be based on measured workload behavior rather than copied blindly between services.

---

# 8. Resource Limits

Limits define upper resource boundaries where appropriate.

Example:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    memory: 1Gi
```

CPU and memory limits behave differently and should not be treated as equivalent controls.

---

# 9. Memory Limits

A container exceeding its effective memory boundary can be terminated.

Typical symptom:

```text
Memory Growth
     │
     ▼
Container Limit
     │
     ▼
OOMKilled
     │
     ▼
Restart
```

This can create repeated production instability.

---

# 10. CPU Limits

CPU limits may cause throttling rather than process termination.

```text
Application needs CPU
        │
        ▼
CPU limit reached
        │
        ▼
Throttling
        │
        ▼
Latency increases
```

Overly aggressive CPU limits can therefore damage latency while dashboards still show the Pod as healthy.

---

# 11. CPU Limit Policy

CPU limits should not be mechanically imposed using arbitrary ratios such as:

```text
request = 500m
limit   = 500m
```

for every Java workload.

Their use must be validated against actual performance and cluster governance requirements.

---

# 12. Resource Right-Sizing

Resource configuration should use data from ADR-037:

```text
Prometheus
   │
   ├── CPU usage
   ├── Memory usage
   ├── CPU throttling
   ├── GC behavior
   └── Latency
        │
        ▼
Right-Sizing Decision
```

---

# 13. Java Container Awareness

Spring Boot workloads run inside containers.

The JVM must therefore operate according to container resource boundaries rather than assuming it owns the underlying EC2 host.

Modern supported Java versions provide container awareness, but JVM behavior still requires validation.

---

# 14. JVM Heap

Container memory is not equivalent to Java heap.

A container also requires memory for:

```text
Heap
Metaspace
Thread stacks
Direct buffers
JIT/code cache
Native libraries
Agents
Other native allocations
```

Therefore:

```text
-Xmx = container memory limit
```

is generally unsafe.

---

# 15. JVM Memory Budget

Conceptually:

```text
Container Memory
      │
      ├── Java Heap
      ├── Metaspace
      ├── Threads
      ├── Direct Memory
      ├── Native Memory
      └── Safety Headroom
```

Heap sizing must leave space for non-heap/native memory.

---

# 16. JVM Percentage-Based Sizing

Percentage-based heap sizing may be preferable in containerized environments where validated.

Example conceptually:

```text
Container Memory
       │
       ▼
JVM MaxRAMPercentage
       │
       ▼
Heap Budget
```

Exact values must come from workload testing.

---

# 17. Garbage Collection

Monitor:

```text
GC pause duration
GC frequency
Heap utilization
Allocation rate
Old-generation pressure
```

Autoscaling CPU while ignoring pathological GC behavior will not solve memory-related application problems.

---

# 18. Thread Pools

Spring Boot services also have concurrency limits.

Potential constrained resources include:

```text
HTTP worker threads
Database connections
Kafka consumer threads
Async executors
External API client pools
```

Scaling decisions must consider these internal limits.

---

# 19. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

HPA shall be the primary autoscaling mechanism for ordinary stateless request-driven workloads.

```text
Metrics
   │
   ▼
HPA
   │
   ▼
Desired Replicas
   │
   ▼
Deployment
```

---

# 20. HPA Example

Conceptually:

```text
Current Pods = 4
CPU target   = 60%
Observed CPU = 90%

        │
        ▼

HPA calculates additional replicas

        │
        ▼

Current Pods → 6
```

Actual scaling behavior depends on HPA calculations and policy.

---

# 21. Minimum Replicas

Critical production services should usually maintain more than one replica.

```text
minReplicas: 1
```

for a critical synchronous API creates unnecessary availability risk.

---

# 22. Maximum Replicas

Every HPA must define a realistic upper bound.

Unlimited application scaling can overload downstream dependencies.

```text
API Pods
  10
   │
   ▼
  100
   │
   ▼
 1000
   │
   ▼
PostgreSQL destroyed by connections
```

Autoscaling needs dependency-aware boundaries.

---

# 23. CPU-Based Scaling

CPU is useful when workload demand correlates strongly with CPU consumption.

Examples may include:

```text
Request processing
Computation-heavy transformations
Some Spring Boot APIs
```

But CPU is not universally the best scaling metric.

---

# 24. Memory-Based Scaling

Memory-based HPA should be used cautiously.

Many JVM applications retain memory after load decreases.

This can make memory a poor direct signal for elastic scale-down.

---

# 25. Request-Based Scaling

For HTTP workloads, more meaningful metrics may include:

```text
Requests per second
Concurrent requests
In-flight requests
Request queue depth
Latency
```

depending on service behavior.

---

# 26. Custom Metrics

Prometheus-backed custom metrics can provide workload-specific scaling signals.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Prometheus
    │
    ▼
Metrics Adapter
    │
    ▼
HPA
```

This should be introduced where CPU/memory metrics fail to represent actual demand.

---

# 27. Scaling on Latency

Latency alone can be a dangerous autoscaling signal.

Example:

```text
Database becomes slow
       │
       ▼
API latency rises
       │
       ▼
HPA creates more API Pods
       │
       ▼
More DB connections
       │
       ▼
Database becomes slower
```

This is a positive feedback loop.

---

# 28. Dependency-Aware Scaling

Scaling policies must understand downstream capacity.

Important dependencies include:

```text
PostgreSQL
Redis
Kafka
External APIs
AI services
Search infrastructure
```

Horizontal scaling is not infinite capacity.

---

# 29. KEDA

KEDA shall be the preferred event-driven autoscaling mechanism where workloads scale according to event sources rather than ordinary CPU utilization.

```text
Event Source
     │
     ▼
KEDA
     │
     ▼
Scaling Decision
     │
     ▼
Kubernetes Workload
```

---

# 30. KEDA Use Cases

Potential Mediverse candidates include:

```text
Kafka consumers
Background workers
Media processors
Notification workers
AI task workers
Queue-driven jobs
```

---

# 31. Kafka Lag-Based Scaling

Kafka consumer workloads may scale based on consumer lag.

```text
Producer Rate ↑
      │
      ▼
Kafka Backlog ↑
      │
      ▼
KEDA
      │
      ▼
Consumer Replicas ↑
```

This is often more meaningful than consumer CPU.

---

# 32. Kafka Partition Constraint

Kafka consumer scaling has an important limit.

For one consumer group:

```text
Useful consumer concurrency
        ≤
Relevant partition count
```

If a topic has 10 partitions, scaling the group to 100 consumers does not produce 100 actively consuming workers for those 10 partitions.

---

# 33. Scale-to-Zero

Some asynchronous workloads may support:

```text
0 replicas
```

when no work exists.

This can reduce cost.

It is inappropriate for synchronous APIs requiring immediate availability unless the cold-start behavior is explicitly acceptable.

---

# 34. Cold Starts

Scaling from zero introduces startup delay.

For Java:

```text
Event arrives
    │
    ▼
KEDA detects demand
    │
    ▼
Pod scheduled
    │
    ▼
Image starts
    │
    ▼
JVM starts
    │
    ▼
Spring context initializes
    │
    ▼
Ready
```

That delay may be seconds or longer.

---

# 35. Startup Optimization

Spring Boot startup should be measured where rapid scaling matters.

Potential areas include:

```text
Application initialization
Dependency initialization
Class loading
Image size
Readiness behavior
JVM configuration
Framework configuration
```

Optimization should follow profiling, not guesswork.

---

# 36. Readiness and Scaling

A newly created Pod must not receive traffic before it is actually ready.

```text
Pod Started
    │
    ▼
Startup
    │
    ▼
Readiness Probe
    │
    ├── Fail → No traffic
    │
    └── Pass → Endpoint available
```

Autoscaling without correct readiness probes can worsen incidents.

---

# 37. Startup Probes

Slow-starting workloads may use startup probes to distinguish legitimate initialization from a failed application.

This prevents liveness checks from repeatedly killing an application before startup completes.

---

# 38. Liveness Probe

Liveness answers:

> Should Kubernetes restart this container?

It must not simply test whether every downstream dependency is healthy.

Otherwise a database outage could cause every application Pod to restart continuously.

---

# 39. Readiness Probe

Readiness answers:

> Should this Pod currently receive traffic?

This is the correct mechanism for temporarily removing an unhealthy instance from service routing.

---

# 40. Vertical Pod Autoscaler

VPA analyzes resource usage and can recommend or adjust resource requests.

```text
Observed Usage
      │
      ▼
VPA
      │
      ▼
CPU / Memory Recommendation
```

---

# 41. VPA Initial Direction

Mediverse should initially use VPA primarily for **recommendations/right-sizing analysis** on workloads already controlled by HPA.

Automatic VPA mutation requires careful testing.

---

# 42. HPA/VPA Conflict

If:

```text
HPA scales on CPU utilization
```

while:

```text
VPA automatically changes CPU requests
```

the systems can influence each other's calculations.

This interaction must be deliberately designed.

---

# 43. Rightsizing Loop

Preferred:

```text
Prometheus
   │
   ▼
Historical Usage
   │
   ▼
VPA Recommendations
   │
   ▼
Engineering Review
   │
   ▼
Git Change
   │
   ▼
Argo CD
```

This keeps important resource decisions auditable.

---

# 44. Node Capacity

Pod autoscaling works only if nodes have sufficient capacity.

```text
HPA
 │
 ▼
More Pods
 │
 ▼
No Node Capacity
 │
 ▼
Pending Pods
```

Therefore pod and node autoscaling must work together.

---

# 45. Karpenter

ADR-035 identified Karpenter as the preferred future dynamic node-provisioning direction.

ADR-038 adopts **Karpenter for elastic application capacity** once production operational maturity is sufficient.

Managed node groups remain appropriate for stable baseline/system capacity.

---

# 46. Hybrid Node Architecture

Recommended:

```text
                       EKS
                        │
          ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
          ▼             ▼             ▼
      System MNG    Karpenter      GPU Capacity
                      Nodes
```

System-critical workloads retain predictable baseline infrastructure.

Application capacity can scale dynamically.

---

# 47. Karpenter Flow

```text
HPA / KEDA
     │
     ▼
New Pods
     │
     ▼
Unschedulable
     │
     ▼
Karpenter
     │
     ▼
Select EC2 Capacity
     │
     ▼
Launch Node
     │
     ▼
Schedule Pods
```

---

# 48. Instance Flexibility

Karpenter should generally be allowed to select from multiple compatible EC2 instance types.

Rigid dependence on one exact instance type reduces:

```text
Availability
Spot flexibility
Cost optimization
Provisioning success
```

---

# 49. Instance Families

Different workloads may favor:

```text
General purpose
Compute optimized
Memory optimized
GPU accelerated
```

Workload profiling should determine placement.

---

# 50. On-Demand Capacity

Critical baseline workloads should have reliable On-Demand capacity.

This includes components where interruption would create unacceptable operational risk.

---

# 51. Spot Capacity

Spot should be used for interruption-tolerant elastic capacity.

Potential candidates:

```text
Stateless application replicas
Kafka workers with graceful handling
Batch workloads
Background processing
Some AI workloads
CI capacity
```

---

# 52. Spot Diversification

Spot architecture should avoid dependency on one instance type.

```text
Several instance families
        +
Several sizes
        +
Several AZs
```

improves capacity availability.

---

# 53. Spot Interruption

Applications running on Spot must tolerate interruption.

```text
Interruption Signal
       │
       ▼
Drain / Terminate
       │
       ▼
Work Rescheduled
```

State must not depend on the continued existence of one EC2 node.

---

# 54. Stateful Workloads

Stateful managed services such as PostgreSQL should not be treated like stateless Kubernetes Pods.

The scaling model for:

```text
RDS
ElastiCache
MSK
Search
```

requires separate service-specific capacity planning.

---

# 55. Topology Spread

Production replicas should be distributed across failure domains.

```text
Service Replicas
      │
 ┌────┼────┐
 ▼    ▼    ▼
AZ-A AZ-B AZ-C
```

Kubernetes topology spread constraints should be used where appropriate.

---

# 56. Replica Distribution

Bad:

```text
5 replicas
   │
   ▼
All on Node A
```

A node failure then removes all capacity despite having multiple replicas.

---

# 57. Zone Distribution

Similarly:

```text
6 replicas
   │
   ▼
All in AZ-A
```

provides little protection from AZ failure.

Replica count without failure-domain distribution is misleading.

---

# 58. Pod Anti-Affinity

Pod anti-affinity may be used for workloads requiring stronger separation.

However, overly strict anti-affinity can make Pods unschedulable during constrained capacity.

Topology spread is often more flexible.

---

# 59. PodDisruptionBudget

Critical services should use appropriate PodDisruptionBudgets.

Example conceptually:

```yaml
minAvailable: 2
```

This protects availability during voluntary disruptions such as node maintenance.

---

# 60. PDB Limitation

A PodDisruptionBudget does not prevent:

```text
Application crashes
Node hardware failure
AZ failure
OOMKilled
```

It governs voluntary Kubernetes disruptions.

It is not a universal availability guarantee.

---

## ADR-038 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

Part 2 should continue with **Section 61 — Priority Classes**, then cover system workload isolation, graceful termination, connection draining, HPA stabilization, scaling oscillation, database connection budgets, concurrency controls, backpressure, load shedding, circuit breakers, bulkheads, queue-based load leveling, PostgreSQL/Redis/Kafka capacity limits, GPU scheduling and AI scaling, performance testing, load/stress/spike/soak tests, performance budgets, SLO-driven capacity, headroom, capacity forecasting, rightsizing, FinOps, failure scenarios, governance, anti-patterns and the final Mediverse production autoscaling/capacity architecture.

# ADR-038 — Kubernetes Autoscaling, Capacity Management & Performance Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — PDB Limitation**.

---

# 61. Priority Classes

Kubernetes `PriorityClass` should distinguish critical platform workloads from ordinary application workloads.

Conceptually:

```text
Priority
   │
   ├── Critical Platform
   ├── Critical Application
   ├── Standard Application
   └── Batch / Background
```

This helps Kubernetes make scheduling decisions when cluster capacity becomes constrained.

---

# 62. Priority Is Not Free Capacity

Priority does not create resources.

If the cluster has:

```text
CPU available = 0
Memory available = 0
```

assigning everything a higher priority merely creates competing high-priority workloads.

Priority must therefore be selective.

---

# 63. Pod Preemption

When necessary, Kubernetes may evict lower-priority workloads to make room for higher-priority Pods.

```text
Cluster Full
    │
    ▼
Critical Pod Pending
    │
    ▼
Lower-Priority Pod Preempted
    │
    ▼
Critical Pod Scheduled
```

This behavior must be understood before introducing PriorityClasses.

---

# 64. System Workload Isolation

Critical cluster/platform components should not compete indiscriminately with application workloads.

Potential system workloads include:

```text
CoreDNS
Observability
Argo CD
Ingress components
Security agents
OTel Collectors
Controllers
```

A runaway application should not starve the infrastructure required to operate the cluster.

---

# 65. Dedicated System Capacity

Baseline managed node groups may provide stable capacity for critical platform workloads.

```text
EKS
 │
 ├── System Node Group
 │      └── Platform workloads
 │
 └── Karpenter Capacity
        └── Application workloads
```

Taints, tolerations and affinity rules may enforce this boundary.

---

# 66. Taints and Tolerations

Dedicated nodes can use taints.

```text
System Node
    │
    └── Taint: workload=system
```

Only approved workloads receive the matching toleration.

This prevents arbitrary application Pods from consuming reserved system capacity.

---

# 67. Graceful Termination

Applications must tolerate Pod termination correctly.

```text
Termination Requested
        │
        ▼
Pod stops receiving new traffic
        │
        ▼
In-flight requests finish
        │
        ▼
Resources close
        │
        ▼
Process exits
```

Autoscaling depends on safe termination just as much as safe startup.

---

# 68. SIGTERM Handling

Spring Boot services should respond correctly to termination signals.

The application should have enough time to:

```text
Stop accepting work
Finish eligible requests
Commit/rollback transactions
Stop consumers
Close connections
Flush required telemetry
```

before forced termination.

---

# 69. Termination Grace Period

`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` should match actual shutdown behavior.

Setting it arbitrarily low can kill valid in-flight work.

Setting it excessively high can make deployments and scale-down unnecessarily slow.

---

# 70. Connection Draining

Load-balancing behavior must allow terminating Pods to drain connections.

```text
ALB / Service
      │
      X──► Terminating Pod
      │
      └──► Healthy Pods
```

Otherwise users may receive errors during routine scaling or deployments.

---

# 71. Kafka Consumer Shutdown

Kafka consumers should stop gracefully.

```text
Consumer
   │
   ▼
Termination
   │
   ▼
Stop polling
   │
   ▼
Finish/commit eligible work
   │
   ▼
Leave consumer group
```

Abrupt termination can increase duplicate processing and rebalance disruption.

---

# 72. Scale-Up Behavior

Scale-up should normally react faster than scale-down.

```text
Demand ↑
   │
   ▼
Scale quickly

Demand ↓
   │
   ▼
Observe stability
   │
   ▼
Scale cautiously
```

Capacity shortage hurts users faster than temporary excess capacity hurts cost.

---

# 73. Scale-Down Stabilization

A stabilization window can prevent immediate scale-down after a short demand reduction.

Without it:

```text
Load ↑ → Scale Up
Load ↓ → Scale Down
Load ↑ → Scale Up
Load ↓ → Scale Down
```

produces oscillation.

---

# 74. Scaling Thrashing

Repeated scale-up/scale-down cycles waste resources and destabilize applications.

Causes may include:

```text
Noisy metrics
Bad thresholds
Insufficient stabilization
Long startup times
Incorrect requests
Highly bursty traffic
```

Scaling behavior itself must be monitored.

---

# 75. Minimum Capacity as Headroom

Critical services should maintain enough baseline capacity to absorb normal short-term spikes without waiting for:

```text
HPA
+
Scheduler
+
Karpenter
+
EC2 startup
+
Pod startup
```

Autoscaling has latency.

---

# 76. Capacity Headroom

Production should deliberately maintain headroom.

Conceptually:

```text
Available Capacity
████████████████████

Normal Load
████████████

Headroom
            ████████
```

Running permanently at 95–100% utilization leaves little room for failures or spikes.

---

# 77. Headroom Is Workload-Specific

There is no universal rule such as:

```text
Always keep exactly 30% free
```

Appropriate headroom depends on:

```text
Traffic volatility
Scaling latency
SLO
Failure model
Cost
Dependency limits
```

---

# 78. Concurrency Limits

Applications should limit how much concurrent work they accept.

```text
Incoming Requests
       │
       ▼
Concurrency Gate
   ┌───┴────┐
   ▼        ▼
Accept    Reject/Queue
```

Unlimited concurrency usually becomes resource exhaustion.

---

# 79. Little's Law Reality

If request latency increases while arrival rate remains high, the number of concurrent in-flight requests grows.

This means downstream slowness can consume:

```text
Threads
Memory
Connections
Queues
```

even when application CPU remains moderate.

---

# 80. Database Connection Budget

PostgreSQL connections are finite.

Suppose:

```text
20 Pods
×
20 connections per Pod
=
400 potential connections
```

Scaling to 100 Pods would create:

```text
100 × 20 = 2000
```

potential connections.

HPA limits must therefore account for database capacity.

---

# 81. Connection Pool Formula

Capacity planning should explicitly model:

```text
Maximum Application Pods
        ×
Maximum Connections Per Pod
        +
Administrative/System Connections
        <
Database Safe Connection Capacity
```

Do not discover this constraint during a production traffic spike.

---

# 82. HikariCP

Spring Boot's HikariCP pool should be tuned from actual concurrency requirements.

Bigger pools are not automatically faster.

Oversized pools can increase database contention.

---

# 83. Connection Acquisition

Monitor:

```text
Active
Idle
Pending
Timeout
Acquisition duration
```

A growing pending count is often an early saturation signal.

---

# 84. PgBouncer Direction

If connection scalability becomes a genuine constraint, a PostgreSQL connection proxy/pooler such as PgBouncer or an appropriate managed alternative may be evaluated.

It should not be introduced merely to hide fundamentally bad connection management.

---

# 85. Backpressure

When downstream systems cannot keep up, upstream systems must reduce or regulate demand.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Consumer Capacity Reached
   │
   ▼
Backpressure
   │
   ▼
Producer Slows / Queue Builds
```

Without backpressure, overload propagates.

---

# 86. Queue-Based Load Leveling

Kafka can absorb temporary differences between producer and consumer rates.

```text
Traffic Spike
     │
     ▼
Producer
     │
     ▼
Kafka
██████████████
     │
     ▼
Consumers
```

This prevents every workload from needing instantaneous scaling.

---

# 87. Queue Is Not Infinite

Kafka backlog cannot be used as an excuse for permanently insufficient consumer capacity.

Monitor:

```text
Lag size
Lag growth rate
Oldest message age
Recovery time
```

A queue merely moves the overload boundary.

---

# 88. Load Shedding

When capacity is exhausted, intentionally rejecting lower-priority work can protect critical functionality.

```text
Overload
   │
   ▼
Load Shedding
   │
   ├── Critical request → Accept
   └── Non-critical request → Reject/defer
```

Controlled degradation is better than total collapse.

---

# 89. HTTP Overload Response

Where appropriate, overloaded services may return meaningful responses such as:

```text
429 Too Many Requests
503 Service Unavailable
```

rather than accepting work that will inevitably time out.

---

# 90. Retry-After

When the service can reasonably estimate recovery behavior, `Retry-After` may help clients avoid immediate aggressive retries.

Retries without coordination can amplify overload.

---

# 91. Retry Storm

Dangerous sequence:

```text
Service slows
    │
    ▼
Requests timeout
    │
    ▼
Clients retry
    │
    ▼
Traffic doubles
    │
    ▼
Service slows further
```

This can turn degradation into an outage.

---

# 92. Retry Policy

Retries should generally have:

```text
Maximum attempts
Timeout
Exponential backoff
Jitter
Idempotency awareness
```

Infinite or immediate retries are prohibited.

---

# 93. Circuit Breaker

Circuit breakers can prevent repeated calls to a dependency already known to be failing.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Circuit Breaker
 ┌──┴─────┐
 ▼        ▼
Closed    Open
 │          X
 ▼          │
Dependency  Fast Failure/Fallback
```

---

# 94. Circuit Breaker States

Conceptually:

```text
CLOSED
  │ failures
  ▼
OPEN
  │ wait
  ▼
HALF-OPEN
  │ test
  ├── success → CLOSED
  └── failure → OPEN
```

Thresholds must be tuned from observed behavior.

---

# 95. Bulkhead Pattern

Failures should be isolated so one dependency cannot consume all application capacity.

Example:

```text
Application
   │
   ├── AI Worker Pool
   ├── Content API Pool
   └── Notification Pool
```

A blocked AI integration should not consume every thread required for core learning functionality.

---

# 96. Timeout Architecture

Every remote call should have a finite timeout.

```text
Service A
    │
    ▼
Service B

Timeout = bounded
```

Waiting forever is not resilience.

---

# 97. Timeout Hierarchy

Timeouts should make architectural sense.

Example:

```text
User request timeout        10s
   │
Service A downstream call    5s
   │
Service B DB operation        2s
```

A downstream timeout longer than the entire upstream request budget is often useless.

Exact values require testing.

---

# 98. Graceful Degradation

When non-critical dependencies fail, Mediverse should preserve useful functionality where possible.

Examples:

```text
Recommendation engine unavailable
        │
        ▼
Core learning content still works

Analytics pipeline delayed
        │
        ▼
Assessment submission still works
```

Not every dependency deserves the power to take down the entire platform.

---

# 99. Criticality Classification

Services/workflows should be classified.

Example:

```text
Tier 0 → Platform-critical
Tier 1 → Critical user journey
Tier 2 → Important
Tier 3 → Background / deferrable
```

Capacity, scaling and availability policies can then differ appropriately.

---

# 100. PostgreSQL Capacity

Database scaling requires monitoring and planning around:

```text
CPU
Memory
Connections
Storage
IOPS
Locks
Query latency
Replication
Vacuum behavior
```

Adding application Pods cannot compensate for an overloaded database indefinitely.

---

# 101. Query Optimization Before Scaling

If one query consumes 80% of database resources, increasing RDS size may postpone rather than solve the problem.

The preferred order is:

```text
Identify query
    │
    ▼
Analyze execution plan
    │
    ▼
Fix query/index/schema where appropriate
    │
    ▼
Measure
    │
    ▼
Scale infrastructure if still required
```

---

# 102. Read Scaling

Read-heavy workloads may eventually use:

```text
Primary
   │
   ├── Writes
   │
   └── Replicas → Reads
```

where consistency requirements permit.

Application architecture must explicitly understand replication lag.

---

# 103. Redis Capacity

Redis/ElastiCache capacity planning should consider:

```text
Memory
Evictions
Connections
CPU
Network
Hit ratio
Key distribution
TTL behavior
```

A cache at its memory boundary can create cascading database load.

---

# 104. Cache Stampede

When a popular cached object expires:

```text
Cache Entry Expires
       │
       ▼
1000 Requests
       │
       ▼
1000 DB Queries
```

This is a cache stampede.

Mitigation may involve:

```text
Request coalescing
TTL jitter
Background refresh
Stale-while-revalidate patterns
```

where appropriate.

---

# 105. Kafka Capacity

Kafka/MSK capacity planning should account for:

```text
Partitions
Replication
Broker CPU
Disk
Network
Producer throughput
Consumer throughput
Retention
Consumer lag
```

Partition count is both a scalability and operational design decision.

---

# 106. Partition Planning

Too few partitions restrict parallelism.

Too many partitions create additional metadata and operational overhead.

Partition count should reflect:

```text
Expected throughput
Consumer parallelism
Ordering requirements
Future growth
```

---

# 107. AI Workload Capacity

AI workloads may have fundamentally different resource characteristics:

```text
High CPU
High memory
GPU
Long-running requests
Large model memory
Batch processing
External model APIs
```

They should not be mixed blindly with ordinary Spring Boot capacity policies.

---

# 108. Dedicated AI Node Pools

GPU or specialized AI workloads should use dedicated node capacity.

```text
EKS
 │
 ├── General Application Nodes
 │
 └── AI/GPU Nodes
          │
          └── AI workloads
```

Taints/tolerations and node affinity should enforce placement.

---

# 109. GPU Scheduling

GPU workloads should request explicit GPU resources.

Conceptually:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1
```

A GPU is a scarce and expensive schedulable resource.

---

# 110. GPU Scale-to-Zero

Where startup latency permits, non-interactive GPU workloads may scale aggressively down or to zero.

Keeping expensive GPU nodes idle continuously without a latency requirement is wasteful.

---

# 111. AI Concurrency

AI endpoints require explicit concurrency control.

One model instance may only support a limited number of concurrent operations before:

```text
Memory exhaustion
Latency explosion
GPU saturation
External API throttling
```

HPA alone cannot infer all of these constraints.

---

# 112. External AI APIs

If Mediverse uses external AI providers, local autoscaling cannot increase provider quota.

Capacity planning must include:

```text
Rate limits
Token limits
Concurrent request limits
Provider latency
Provider availability
Cost
```

---

# 113. Performance Testing

No production scaling policy should be considered mature without performance testing.

The primary test classes are:

```text
Load
Stress
Spike
Soak
```

Each answers a different question.

---

# 114. Load Testing

Load testing validates expected workload.

Question:

> Can Mediverse satisfy its performance objectives at anticipated traffic levels?

Example:

```text
Expected peak = X requests/sec
```

The actual target must come from product usage assumptions and measurement.

---

# 115. Stress Testing

Stress testing intentionally exceeds expected capacity.

Question:

> Where does Mediverse break, and how does it fail?

The goal is to identify the bottleneck and failure behavior.

---

# 116. Spike Testing

Spike testing applies sudden demand.

```text
100 RPS
   │
   │ sudden
   ▼
5000 RPS
```

This evaluates whether:

```text
HPA reacts
Karpenter reacts
Queues absorb load
Dependencies survive
```

---

# 117. Soak Testing

Soak testing maintains sustained load over an extended period.

It can expose:

```text
Memory leaks
Connection leaks
GC degradation
Disk growth
Queue accumulation
Resource fragmentation
```

that short tests miss.

---

# 118. Performance Test Environment

A tiny DEV environment does not accurately predict production behavior.

Meaningful tests require sufficiently production-like:

```text
Topology
Resource ratios
Dependencies
Data volumes
Configuration
```

without requiring every test environment to equal full production scale.

---

# 119. Test Data

Performance tests require realistic data characteristics.

Testing a database with 100 rows does not prove performance against millions of records.

Data volume and distribution matter.

---

# 120. Performance Budgets

Critical operations should have explicit performance objectives.

Examples:

```text
API latency
Frontend load performance
Database query latency
Kafka processing delay
AI response latency
```

Exact numbers belong to service SLOs and product requirements.

---

# 121. SLO-Driven Capacity

Capacity should ultimately be tied to user-visible objectives.

```text
Traffic
   │
   ▼
Capacity
   │
   ▼
Latency / Availability
   │
   ▼
SLI
   │
   ▼
SLO
```

A system with low CPU but failing latency SLOs is not sufficiently provisioned or designed.

---

# 122. Capacity Forecasting

Autoscaling handles short-term elasticity.

Forecasting handles longer-term growth.

Forecast:

```text
Users
Traffic
Storage
Kafka volume
Database growth
AI consumption
Network
```

over appropriate planning horizons.

---

# 123. Autoscaling Cannot Solve Everything

If traffic doubles every quarter, autoscaling does not eliminate the need for:

```text
Database planning
Partition planning
Quota increases
Architecture changes
Cost forecasting
Capacity reservations
```

Elasticity and capacity planning are complementary.

---

# 124. Rightsizing

Resources should periodically be compared against actual usage.

```text
Requested CPU: 4 cores
Observed p95:   0.3 cores
```

may indicate severe over-provisioning.

Conversely:

```text
Requested CPU: 0.2 cores
Observed:      constantly throttled
```

indicates under-provisioning.

---

# 125. Rightsizing Is Not Minimization

The objective is not:

```text
Use the smallest possible resources
```

The objective is:

```text
Meet reliability/performance targets
at economically reasonable capacity
```

Aggressive cost cutting that creates outages is not optimization.

---

# 126. FinOps Integration

Capacity telemetry should inform:

```text
Cost per environment
Cost per workload
Idle capacity
Spot usage
Node utilization
GPU utilization
Rightsizing opportunities
```

Engineering and cost decisions should use the same underlying capacity data.

---

# 127. Resource Ownership

Every workload should have identifiable ownership.

Without ownership, nobody is accountable for:

```text
Bad requests/limits
Waste
Scaling failures
Unbounded replicas
Performance regressions
```

---

# 128. Namespace Quotas

ResourceQuota may prevent one namespace/team from consuming unbounded cluster capacity.

Conceptually:

```text
Namespace
   │
   ├── CPU budget
   ├── Memory budget
   └── Object limits
```

Quotas should protect shared infrastructure without preventing legitimate scaling.

---

# 129. LimitRange

LimitRange may provide namespace-level defaults/bounds for resource configuration.

It should act as a guardrail, not replace explicit workload sizing.

---

# 130. Capacity Failure Scenario

Consider:

```text
Traffic × 10
    │
    ▼
HPA scales Pods
    │
    ▼
Nodes full
    │
    ▼
Karpenter adds nodes
    │
    ▼
Pods start
    │
    ▼
DB connections explode
    │
    ▼
PostgreSQL saturates
    │
    ▼
Latency rises
    │
    ▼
Retries increase
    │
    ▼
System collapses
```

This demonstrates why "enable autoscaling" is not a complete architecture.

---

# 131. Corrected Failure Architecture

A resilient version introduces:

```text
Traffic Spike
    │
    ▼
Rate / Concurrency Controls
    │
    ▼
HPA / KEDA
    │
    ▼
Bounded Replica Count
    │
    ▼
Connection Budget
    │
    ▼
Queue / Backpressure
    │
    ▼
Dependency Protection
    │
    ▼
Graceful Degradation
```

---

# 132. Availability During Node Loss

Capacity planning must assume node failure.

If normal operation consumes virtually all cluster capacity, losing one node can immediately cause service degradation.

This is why failure headroom matters.

---

# 133. Availability During AZ Loss

For high-criticality services, capacity design should consider whether remaining Availability Zones can carry required traffic after an AZ failure.

```text
AZ-A  X

AZ-B + AZ-C
     │
     ▼
Can they sustain required service?
```

Multi-AZ placement alone does not answer that question.

---

# 134. Scaling During Incident

Autoscaling systems should remain observable during incidents.

ADR-037 should expose:

```text
HPA desired/current replicas
KEDA activity
Pending Pods
Karpenter provisioning
Node capacity
CPU throttling
OOM events
DB saturation
Kafka lag
```

Otherwise operators cannot tell whether scaling is helping.

---

# 135. Scaling Alerts

Useful alerts may include:

```text
HPA at maximum replicas
Pods unschedulable
Karpenter provisioning failures
Persistent CPU throttling
Repeated OOMKilled
DB connection exhaustion
Kafka lag continuously growing
Node capacity shortage
GPU capacity unavailable
```

These should be actionable, not noisy.

---

# 136. Scaling Auditability

Important scaling configuration belongs in Git.

```text
Deployment resources
HPA
KEDA ScaledObject
PDB
PriorityClass
Topology constraints
NodePool
NodeClass
```

Changes therefore flow through review and GitOps.

---

# 137. Capacity Governance

```text
Application Teams
      │
      ├── Application performance
      ├── Requests/limits
      ├── HPA policy
      └── Concurrency behavior

Platform Team
      │
      ├── Karpenter
      ├── Node pools
      ├── Quotas
      ├── Scheduling policy
      └── Cluster capacity

Database Team / Platform
      │
      ├── PostgreSQL capacity
      ├── Connection budgets
      └── Storage/IOPS

SRE
      │
      ├── SLOs
      ├── Headroom
      ├── Performance testing
      └── Capacity forecasting

FinOps
      │
      └── Cost efficiency
```

---

# 138. Capacity Review

Critical services should periodically review:

```text
Peak demand
Resource utilization
HPA behavior
Startup latency
DB connection usage
Dependency saturation
Error budget
Cost
Forecast growth
```

Autoscaling configurations should not be written once and forgotten.

---

# 139. Performance Regression

CI/release processes should eventually detect major performance regressions for critical workloads.

A release that passes unit tests but doubles API latency is still defective.

Performance validation should be proportionate to service criticality.

---

# 140. Capacity Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ No CPU/memory requests
❌ Copying identical resources to every service
❌ Setting JVM heap equal to container memory
❌ Treating CPU limits as harmless
❌ HPA without maxReplicas
❌ Scaling APIs without DB connection budgets
❌ Scaling solely on latency without dependency analysis
❌ KEDA consumers beyond useful Kafka partition concurrency
❌ Scale-to-zero for latency-critical APIs without justification
❌ One replica for critical production services
❌ All replicas on one node/AZ
❌ Missing PDBs for critical workloads
❌ Making every workload highest priority
❌ No graceful shutdown
❌ Immediate scale-down after traffic drops
❌ Unlimited application concurrency
❌ Infinite retries
❌ No timeout on remote calls
❌ Treating Kafka as infinite storage for overload
❌ Increasing DB size before investigating pathological queries
❌ Unbounded database connection pools
❌ Mixing expensive GPU workloads with general nodes
❌ Idle GPU fleets without latency justification
❌ Performance testing only after production incidents
❌ Testing with unrealistic data
❌ Running cluster capacity permanently near exhaustion
❌ Assuming autoscaling replaces forecasting
❌ Optimizing cost at the expense of SLOs
```

---

# 141. Scaling Decision Hierarchy

When load increases:

```text
                 Demand
                    │
                    ▼
          Is service healthy?
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ▼                   ▼
         YES                  NO
          │                   │
          ▼                   ▼
Is demand signal valid?   Find bottleneck
          │                   │
          ▼                   ▼
      Scale Pods       DB / Cache / Kafka /
          │            external dependency?
          ▼                   │
Enough nodes?                 ▼
    │                    Protect dependency
 ┌──┴──┐                 │
 ▼     ▼                  ▼
YES    NO             Backpressure /
 │      │             load shedding
 ▼      ▼
Serve Karpenter
        │
        ▼
      Nodes
```

---

# 142. Application Scaling Architecture

```text
                   HTTP TRAFFIC
                        │
                        ▼
                       ALB
                        │
                        ▼
                  API / Gateway
                        │
                        ▼
                 Spring Services
                        │
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              ▼                   ▼
          Prometheus          Dependencies
              │                   │
              ▼                   ├── PostgreSQL
             HPA                  ├── Redis
              │                   └── External APIs
              ▼
        Desired Replicas
              │
              ▼
       Kubernetes Scheduler
              │
              ▼
          Karpenter
              │
              ▼
           EC2 Nodes
```

---

# 143. Event-Driven Scaling Architecture

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
 Kafka
   │
   ├──────────────► Prometheus
   │
   │                   │
   │                   ▼
   │                  KEDA
   │                   │
   ▼                   ▼
Backlog           Consumer Replicas
                       │
                       ▼
                    Workers
```

Scaling is based on work waiting to be processed.

---

# 144. Resource Management Architecture

```text
                    WORKLOAD
                       │
            ┌──────────┼──────────┐
            ▼          ▼          ▼
          CPU        Memory    Concurrency
            │          │          │
            ▼          ▼          ▼
        Requests     Limits      Pools
            │          │          │
            └──────────┼──────────┘
                       ▼
                   Kubernetes
                       │
             ┌─────────┴─────────┐
             ▼                   ▼
            HPA                 VPA
             │             Recommendations
             ▼
          Replicas
```

---

# 145. Dependency Protection Architecture

```text
Incoming Traffic
       │
       ▼
Rate / Concurrency Limit
       │
       ▼
Application
       │
       ├── Timeout
       ├── Retry + Backoff
       ├── Circuit Breaker
       ├── Bulkhead
       └── Backpressure
             │
             ▼
        Dependencies
       ┌─────┼─────┐
       ▼     ▼     ▼
      DB    Redis Kafka
```

This boundary is critical. Horizontal scaling without it can turn application elasticity into dependency overload.

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                       | Mitigation                                 |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Pod resource starvation    | Requests + rightsizing                     |
| OOMKilled                  | JVM/container memory budgeting             |
| CPU throttling             | Measure before enforcing aggressive limits |
| Insufficient replicas      | HPA                                        |
| Event backlog              | KEDA                                       |
| No node capacity           | Karpenter                                  |
| Spot interruption          | Diversification + graceful rescheduling    |
| AZ/node concentration      | Topology spread                            |
| Maintenance outage         | PDB                                        |
| System workload starvation | Dedicated system capacity                  |
| Scaling oscillation        | Stabilization                              |
| Cold-start latency         | Minimum replicas + startup optimization    |
| DB overload from HPA       | Connection budget + max replicas           |
| Retry storm                | Backoff + jitter + bounded attempts        |
| Dependency cascade         | Circuit breakers + bulkheads               |
| Overload collapse          | Backpressure + load shedding               |
| Kafka backlog              | Lag monitoring + consumer scaling          |
| Cache stampede             | TTL/request-coalescing strategies          |
| GPU waste                  | Dedicated elastic GPU capacity             |
| Unknown breaking point     | Stress testing                             |
| Long-term degradation      | Soak testing                               |
| Traffic spike failure      | Spike testing                              |
| Cost waste                 | Rightsizing + FinOps                       |
| Capacity exhaustion        | Forecasting + headroom                     |
