# Next — ADR-040

## **ADR-040 — Enterprise API Gateway, Traffic Management, Rate Limiting & Resilience Architecture**

This should be the next decision because we have already designed **how services run and recover**, but we still need a formal architecture governing **how external and internal traffic actually enters and moves through Mediverse**.

ADR-040 should cover **CloudFront → WAF → ALB → Kubernetes ingress/Gateway → Spring Cloud Gateway → API routing → public vs private APIs → north-south vs east-west traffic → TLS termination → authentication boundary → JWT validation → CORS → request-size limits → timeout hierarchy → connection management → rate limiting → Redis-backed distributed rate limits → quotas → per-user/per-client policies → burst control → concurrency limiting → 429 semantics → retries → idempotency → circuit breakers → bulkheads → load shedding → health checks → API version routing → canary traffic → blue/green routing → header-based routing → WebSocket/SSE handling → upload/download paths → large media bypass → service discovery → internal traffic → correlation/trace propagation → gateway metrics → security logging → DDoS/WAF interaction → failure scenarios → HA → scaling → performance → governance → anti-patterns → production traffic reference architecture.**

# ADR-040 — Enterprise API Gateway, Traffic Management, Rate Limiting & Resilience Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-040
**Status:** Accepted
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-039 established how Mediverse survives catastrophic infrastructure and data failures. ADR-040 now defines the **traffic control plane**: how requests enter Mediverse, how they are authenticated and routed, how overload is controlled, and how downstream failures are prevented from propagating across the platform.

> **A gateway is not just a router. It is an enforcement boundary for traffic, security, resilience, observability, and API governance.**

```text
                         INTERNET
                            │
                            ▼
                       CloudFront
                            │
                            ▼
                          AWS WAF
                            │
                            ▼
                           ALB
                            │
                            ▼
                    Kubernetes Ingress
                            │
                            ▼
                  Spring Cloud Gateway
                            │
          ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
          ▼                 ▼                 ▼
       Auth API        Learning API       Content API
          │                 │                 │
          └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                            ▼
                    Internal Services
```

# 1. Problem

Mediverse contains multiple backend services, but exposing every service directly to clients would create an uncontrolled API surface.

Without a defined traffic architecture:

```text
Client
 ├──► auth-service
 ├──► user-service
 ├──► content-service
 ├──► assessment-service
 ├──► media-service
 ├──► AI-service
 └──► notification-service
```

clients become coupled directly to internal topology.

This creates problems with:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
TLS
CORS
Rate limiting
API versioning
Routing
Service discovery
Observability
Traffic shaping
Resilience
Security policies
Deployment changes
```

---

# 2. Decision

Mediverse shall implement a layered ingress architecture:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
AWS WAF
   │
   ▼
Application Load Balancer
   │
   ▼
Kubernetes Traffic Entry
   │
   ▼
Spring Cloud Gateway
   │
   ▼
Application Services
```

Responsibilities shall be deliberately separated rather than duplicated at every layer.

---

# 3. Traffic Categories

Traffic shall be classified into:

```text
North-South
     │
     ▼
External client ↔ Mediverse

East-West
     │
     ▼
Service ↔ Service
```

These traffic classes have different security and routing requirements.

---

# 4. North-South Traffic

Examples:

```text
Browser → Mediverse API
Mobile App → Mediverse API
Faculty Portal → Mediverse API
Admin Portal → Mediverse API
External Integration → Mediverse API
```

North-south traffic passes through controlled public entry points.

---

# 5. East-West Traffic

Examples:

```text
Learning Service
      │
      ▼
Content Service

Assessment Service
      │
      ▼
User Service
```

Internal service communication should not unnecessarily leave the private platform network.

---

# 6. Public API Boundary

Only explicitly approved endpoints should be reachable externally.

Bad:

```text
Internet
   │
   ├──► PostgreSQL
   ├──► Redis
   ├──► Kafka
   ├──► Internal Services
   └──► Actuator
```

Preferred:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
Controlled Gateway
   │
   ▼
Approved APIs
```

---

# 7. CloudFront

CloudFront shall provide the global edge layer where appropriate.

Responsibilities may include:

```text
Static-content delivery
Caching
TLS
Origin protection
WAF integration
Global edge distribution
```

CloudFront should not become the application authorization engine.

---

# 8. AWS WAF

AWS WAF shall provide edge-level HTTP filtering.

Potential protections include:

```text
Known malicious patterns
IP reputation controls
Request anomalies
Bot-related controls
Rate-based rules
Application-specific blocking rules
```

WAF and application rate limiting solve overlapping but different problems.

---

# 9. DDoS Boundary

AWS edge/network protections should absorb infrastructure-level attacks while WAF and application controls manage HTTP/application-level abuse.

Conceptually:

```text
Attack
  │
  ▼
AWS Edge Protection
  │
  ▼
WAF
  │
  ▼
Gateway Limits
  │
  ▼
Application
```

Defense should be layered.

---

# 10. Application Load Balancer

ALB provides AWS-to-Kubernetes HTTP/HTTPS traffic distribution.

```text
CloudFront / Internet
        │
        ▼
       ALB
        │
        ▼
    Kubernetes
```

ALB should not contain Mediverse business logic.

---

# 11. Kubernetes Traffic Entry

The Kubernetes entry layer maps external traffic into cluster services.

The exact implementation may evolve between Ingress and Kubernetes Gateway API as platform maturity changes.

Application contracts should avoid unnecessary dependence on the implementation.

---

# 12. Spring Cloud Gateway

Spring Cloud Gateway shall provide Mediverse's application-aware API gateway.

Responsibilities include:

```text
API routing
Authentication integration
Rate limiting
Request policy
Header processing
Resilience controls
Observability
API version routing
```

---

# 13. Gateway Responsibility Boundary

The gateway should handle cross-cutting traffic concerns.

It should not become:

```text
❌ Business logic service
❌ Database access layer
❌ Data aggregation monolith
❌ Replacement for service authorization
```

Business logic belongs in domain services.

---

# 14. Gateway Routing

Example:

```text
/api/v1/auth/**
        │
        ▼
auth-service

/api/v1/content/**
        │
        ▼
content-service

/api/v1/assessments/**
        │
        ▼
assessment-service
```

Routing rules should be explicit and version controlled.

---

# 15. Client Decoupling

Clients should know:

```text
api.mediverse.example
```

rather than internal addresses such as:

```text
content-service.mediverse.svc.cluster.local
```

Internal service topology may therefore change without changing external clients.

---

# 16. Service Discovery

Inside Kubernetes:

```text
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Kubernetes Service
   │
   ▼
Pods
```

Kubernetes DNS/service discovery should normally provide internal endpoint discovery.

---

# 17. API Contract Stability

The gateway may hide infrastructure topology.

It cannot hide arbitrary breaking API contract changes.

API compatibility must still be governed explicitly.

---

# 18. TLS

External production traffic shall use HTTPS.

```text
Client
   │
   │ HTTPS
   ▼
Mediverse
```

Plain HTTP should not carry authenticated production application traffic.

---

# 19. TLS Termination

TLS may terminate at an AWS-controlled entry layer such as ALB/CloudFront according to the final network design.

Internal encryption requirements must be determined separately.

---

# 20. Internal TLS

TLS termination at the edge does not automatically mean all internal traffic should be plaintext.

The requirement depends on:

```text
Threat model
Compliance
Network trust boundaries
Service sensitivity
Operational complexity
```

A future service-mesh decision may address stronger east-west mTLS.

---

# 21. Authentication Boundary

The gateway should validate authentication for protected external routes.

Conceptually:

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
JWT Validation
 ┌─┴─────────┐
 ▼           ▼
Valid      Invalid
 │           │
 ▼           ▼
Route       401
```

---

# 22. JWT Validation

JWT validation should verify relevant properties including:

```text
Signature
Issuer
Audience
Expiration
Required claims
```

Merely decoding a JWT is not authentication.

---

# 23. Authorization

Gateway-level authorization may enforce coarse route-level rules.

Example:

```text
/admin/**
     │
     ▼
Requires ADMIN authority
```

But domain authorization still belongs inside services.

---

# 24. Defense in Depth

Bad:

```text
Gateway says user is ADMIN
       │
       ▼
Service trusts everything
```

Preferred:

```text
Gateway
  │
  ├── Authentication
  └── Coarse authorization
           │
           ▼
Domain Service
  │
  └── Resource/business authorization
```

A gateway bypass or internal call must not automatically bypass domain security.

---

# 25. 401 vs 403

Mediverse APIs should distinguish:

```text
401 Unauthorized
→ Authentication missing/invalid

403 Forbidden
→ Authenticated but insufficient permission
```

Using them interchangeably makes security troubleshooting harder.

---

# 26. Authentication Failure Behavior

Invalid authentication should fail early.

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   X
Backend services
```

There is no reason to consume backend capacity for obviously invalid requests.

---

# 27. Token Forwarding

Services requiring user identity may receive validated token/context according to the security architecture.

The gateway must not create untrusted identity headers that downstream services blindly accept from arbitrary callers.

---

# 28. Trusted Identity Headers

If identity context is propagated through headers:

```text
X-User-Id
X-Roles
```

the architecture must guarantee that external clients cannot spoof them.

Gateway-controlled headers should overwrite/remove untrusted client values.

---

# 29. CORS

CORS should be centrally governed for browser-facing APIs.

Production should explicitly allow approved origins.

Bad:

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

combined indiscriminately with authenticated browser APIs.

---

# 30. Environment-Specific Origins

Example:

```text
DEV
→ localhost development origins

UAT
→ uat.mediverse.example

PROD
→ mediverse.example
```

Development convenience must not silently become production policy.

---

# 31. Preflight Requests

The gateway should correctly handle browser `OPTIONS` preflight requests.

Incorrect authentication/CORS ordering can cause legitimate browser requests to fail before reaching application APIs.

---

# 32. Request Size Limits

The platform shall impose bounded request sizes.

```text
Client
   │
   ▼
Request Size Check
   │
 ┌─┴──────┐
 ▼        ▼
Valid   Too Large
 │        │
 ▼        ▼
Route    413
```

Unlimited request bodies create resource-exhaustion risk.

---

# 33. Upload Architecture

Large file/media uploads should not automatically traverse:

```text
CloudFront
→ ALB
→ Gateway
→ Spring Boot
→ Memory
→ S3
```

That is expensive and inefficient.

---

# 34. Direct Object Upload

For suitable media workflows:

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Backend requests upload authorization
   │
   ▼
Presigned S3 URL
   │
   ▼
Browser ─────────► S3
```

This removes large binary transfer from application Pods.

---

# 35. Upload Security

Direct upload does not mean unrestricted upload.

Controls may include:

```text
Short-lived authorization
Object-key restrictions
Size limits
Content-type constraints
Malware scanning workflow
Ownership validation
Post-upload processing
```

---

# 36. Download Architecture

Large downloadable content should similarly use object storage/CDN delivery where appropriate.

```text
User
  │
  ▼
CloudFront
  │
  ▼
S3
```

Spring Boot should not become an expensive file proxy without a reason.

---

# 37. Timeout Architecture

Every network layer should use bounded timeouts.

```text
Client
   │
   ▼
Edge
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service
   │
   ▼
Dependency
```

Unbounded waiting is prohibited.

---

# 38. Timeout Hierarchy

Timeouts should shrink toward downstream dependencies.

Conceptually:

```text
Client budget           15s
Gateway budget          12s
Service call             8s
Database operation       3s
```

Exact values must come from workload requirements.

---

# 39. Timeout Contradiction

Bad:

```text
Gateway timeout = 5s
Backend timeout = 30s
```

The backend may continue consuming resources long after the client has already received failure.

Timeout budgets must be coordinated.

---

# 40. Connection Timeouts

Connection establishment should have a separate bounded timeout.

A dead dependency should fail quickly rather than tying up threads/connections indefinitely.

---

# 41. Read Timeouts

Read/response timeouts protect against dependencies that accept connections but fail to produce responses within acceptable time.

---

# 42. Gateway Connection Pools

The gateway itself has finite:

```text
Connections
Memory
CPU
Event-loop capacity
```

It must be monitored and scaled like any other production service.

---

# 43. Rate Limiting

Mediverse shall implement rate limiting at appropriate layers.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Rate Limiter
 ┌─┴────────┐
 ▼          ▼
Allowed    Exceeded
 │          │
 ▼          ▼
Backend     429
```

---

# 44. Why Rate Limiting?

Rate limiting protects against:

```text
Abuse
Accidental client loops
Credential attacks
Runaway integrations
Expensive AI requests
Resource exhaustion
Traffic bursts
```

---

# 45. Rate Limiting Is Not Autoscaling

Autoscaling asks:

> How much capacity should we create?

Rate limiting asks:

> How much demand should we permit?

Both are necessary.

---

# 46. Rate-Limit Dimensions

Limits may apply by:

```text
IP
Authenticated user
API client
Tenant/organization
Endpoint
Operation type
Subscription tier
```

depending on product requirements.

---

# 47. IP-Based Limits

IP limits are useful for unauthenticated traffic.

They are weak as the only user-level policy because:

```text
Many users may share one NAT
One user may change IP
Attackers may distribute traffic
```

---

# 48. User-Based Limits

Authenticated APIs should generally support limits tied to stable authenticated identity where appropriate.

Example:

```text
user:123
→ 100 requests/minute
```

The exact quota is product-specific.

---

# 49. Endpoint-Specific Limits

Not all endpoints have equal cost.

Example:

```text
GET /content
→ relatively cheap

POST /ai/generate
→ expensive
```

Applying one global limit to both is poor capacity governance.

---

# 50. Distributed Rate Limiting

With multiple gateway replicas:

```text
Gateway 1
Gateway 2
Gateway 3
```

purely local counters can allow each replica to independently permit the full quota.

A distributed limiter may therefore be required.

---

# 51. Redis-Backed Rate Limiting

Redis may provide distributed rate-limit state.

```text
Gateway Replicas
      │
      ▼
    Redis
      │
      ▼
Shared Counter State
```

This provides more consistent policy across gateway replicas.

---

# 52. Rate-Limiter Dependency

Making Redis mandatory for every request introduces another dependency.

The architecture must decide behavior if rate-limit storage becomes unavailable.

Possible strategies:

```text
Fail open
Fail closed
Local fallback
Endpoint-specific policy
```

There is no universally correct answer.

---

# 53. Fail-Open Rate Limiting

For lower-risk endpoints:

```text
Rate limiter unavailable
        │
        ▼
Allow traffic temporarily
```

may preserve availability.

But abuse protection becomes weaker.

---

# 54. Fail-Closed Rate Limiting

For highly sensitive or expensive operations:

```text
Rate limiter unavailable
        │
        ▼
Reject operation
```

may be safer.

This trades availability for protection.

---

# 55. Token Bucket

Token-bucket algorithms are useful where controlled bursts should be allowed.

```text
Bucket
██████████

Request
   │
   ▼
Consume token

Tokens replenish over time
```

---

# 56. Burst Capacity

A client may be allowed:

```text
Steady rate = X
Burst        = Y
```

This accommodates normal short bursts without permitting sustained overload.

---

# 57. Quotas

Rate limits and quotas are related but different.

```text
Rate Limit
→ Requests per short interval

Quota
→ Consumption over longer period
```

Example:

```text
100 requests/minute
```

versus:

```text
10,000 AI generations/month
```

---

# 58. AI Traffic Governance

AI endpoints deserve separate limits because their cost and resource characteristics differ significantly.

Potential controls:

```text
Requests/user
Concurrent generations
Token budget
Daily quota
Organization quota
Model-specific quota
```

---

# 59. Concurrency Limiting

Rate limiting alone does not bound concurrent work.

Example:

```text
100 requests/sec
×
30-second operation
=
potentially ~3000 concurrent operations
```

Concurrency limits are therefore critical for long-running workloads.

---

# 60. Concurrency Gate

```text
Requests
   │
   ▼
Concurrency Limiter
   │
 ┌─┴──────────────┐
 ▼                ▼
Capacity         Full
available         │
 │                ▼
 ▼             Reject/
Execute          Queue
```

This protects finite resources such as:

```text
Threads
DB connections
GPU slots
External API capacity
Memory
```

---

## ADR-040 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The critical architecture established so far is:

```text
                  INTERNET
                     │
                     ▼
                 CloudFront
                     │
                     ▼
                   WAF
                     │
                     ▼
                    ALB
                     │
                     ▼
             Kubernetes Entry
                     │
                     ▼
            Spring Cloud Gateway
                     │
          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
          │          │          │
       Security   Traffic    Resilience
          │       Control       │
          │          │          │
          ▼          ▼          ▼
         JWT      Rate Limit   Timeout
         CORS     Quotas       Concurrency
      AuthZ       Burst        Protection
          │          │          │
          └──────────┼──────────┘
                     ▼
               Microservices
```

The most important boundary is that **CloudFront, WAF, ALB, Kubernetes traffic entry, and Spring Cloud Gateway are not five interchangeable gateway products**. Each layer needs a deliberately limited responsibility; otherwise Mediverse ends up with duplicated routing, timeout, security, and rate-limit configuration scattered across the stack.

**Part 2** should continue with **Section 61 — 429 and Rate-Limit Response Semantics**, followed by retry/backoff architecture, idempotency, retry storms, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding, graceful degradation, gateway failure handling, WebSocket/SSE traffic, API versioning, backward compatibility, canary and blue/green traffic routing, header-based routing, service-to-service traffic, internal APIs, trace propagation, access logging, gateway RED metrics, WAF/gateway security events, health/readiness, HA, HPA, connection exhaustion, failure scenarios, API governance, anti-patterns and the final Mediverse production traffic architecture.

# ADR-040 — Enterprise API Gateway, Traffic Management, Rate Limiting & Resilience Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Concurrency Gate**.

---

# 61. HTTP 429 Semantics

When a client exceeds an enforced rate limit, the gateway should normally return:

```http
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
```

This communicates that the request is valid, but the caller has exceeded the permitted request rate.

---

# 62. Rate-Limit Response

Where useful, the response should provide enough information for well-behaved clients to react correctly.

Conceptually:

```text
HTTP 429
   │
   ├── Retry-After
   ├── Correlation ID
   └── Standard error body
```

Avoid exposing sensitive internal capacity information.

---

# 63. Retry-After

Where recovery timing is meaningful:

```http
Retry-After: 30
```

can instruct the client not to immediately retry.

This helps reduce retry storms.

---

# 64. Standard Error Contract

Gateway-generated failures should follow Mediverse's standardized API error model.

Example conceptually:

```json
{
  "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED",
  "message": "Request limit exceeded.",
  "correlationId": "..."
}
```

Clients should not need completely different parsing logic for gateway and service errors.

---

# 65. Retry Architecture

Retries are appropriate only for failures likely to be transient.

Potential candidates:

```text
Connection reset
Temporary service unavailability
Selected 5xx responses
Transient network failure
```

Retries should never be blindly applied to every failure.

---

# 66. Retry Boundaries

A request may cross several components:

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Gateway
  │
  ▼
Service A
  │
  ▼
Service B
  │
  ▼
Database
```

If every layer independently retries three times, one user request can multiply into a large number of downstream operations.

Retry ownership must therefore be explicit.

---

# 67. Retry Storm

```text
Dependency slows
      │
      ▼
Requests fail
      │
      ▼
Clients retry
      │
      ▼
Gateway retries
      │
      ▼
Services retry
      │
      ▼
Dependency receives MORE traffic
      │
      ▼
Dependency collapses
```

This is one of the most dangerous resilience anti-patterns.

---

# 68. Bounded Retries

Retries must have a maximum attempt count.

Conceptually:

```text
Attempt 1
   │ failure
   ▼
Attempt 2
   │ failure
   ▼
Attempt 3
   │ failure
   ▼
STOP
```

Infinite retries are prohibited.

---

# 69. Exponential Backoff

Retry delays should generally increase between attempts.

```text
Retry 1 → 100 ms
Retry 2 → 200 ms
Retry 3 → 400 ms
```

Exact values depend on workload requirements.

---

# 70. Jitter

Randomized jitter should be introduced where large numbers of clients could retry simultaneously.

Without jitter:

```text
10,000 clients fail
      │
      ▼
All wait 1 second
      │
      ▼
All retry together
      │
      ▼
Another traffic spike
```

With jitter, retries become distributed over time.

---

# 71. Retry Safety

A retry must consider whether the operation is safe to repeat.

Generally:

```text
GET
→ commonly retryable

POST
→ may create duplicate state
```

HTTP method alone is not enough; actual operation semantics matter.

---

# 72. Idempotency

An idempotent operation produces the same intended business outcome when repeated.

This is critical for operations such as:

```text
Assessment submission
Payment-like operations
Content creation
AI job creation
File-processing requests
```

where duplicate execution could be harmful.

---

# 73. Idempotency Keys

For appropriate APIs:

```text
Client
   │
   │ Idempotency-Key: abc123
   ▼
Gateway / Service
   │
   ▼
Has abc123 already completed?
   │
 ┌─┴────────────┐
 ▼              ▼
NO             YES
 │              │
 ▼              ▼
Process       Return previous
request       result
```

The business service should normally own durable idempotency semantics.

---

# 74. Gateway Idempotency Boundary

The gateway may propagate and validate an idempotency key.

It should not automatically become the authoritative database for every business operation.

Business-level duplicate prevention belongs near the business transaction.

---

# 75. Circuit Breakers

Circuit breakers should protect services from repeatedly calling dependencies known to be unhealthy.

```text
Service
   │
   ▼
Circuit Breaker
   │
 ┌─┴──────────┐
 ▼            ▼
CLOSED       OPEN
 │            │
 ▼            X
Dependency   Fast failure
```

---

# 76. Circuit Breaker States

```text
CLOSED
   │
   │ failure threshold reached
   ▼
OPEN
   │
   │ recovery interval
   ▼
HALF-OPEN
   │
   ├── success → CLOSED
   └── failure → OPEN
```

Thresholds must be tuned rather than copied blindly between services.

---

# 77. Gateway Circuit Breaker

Gateway-level circuit breakers may protect external routing paths.

However, downstream services still need resilience for their own dependencies.

```text
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

The gateway cannot protect `Service A → Service B` if it never sees that call.

---

# 78. Fallbacks

Fallbacks should only be used when a meaningful degraded response exists.

Good candidate:

```text
Recommendation service unavailable
        │
        ▼
Return learning page without recommendations
```

Bad candidate:

```text
Assessment submission failed
        │
        ▼
Pretend submission succeeded
```

Fallbacks must preserve correctness.

---

# 79. Bulkheads

Independent traffic/resource pools should prevent one workload from consuming everything.

```text
Gateway / Service
       │
 ┌─────┼─────────┐
 ▼     ▼         ▼
Core   AI      Background
Pool   Pool       Pool
```

An overloaded AI feature should not consume all capacity needed for authentication.

---

# 80. Load Shedding

When capacity is exhausted, the platform should reject lower-value work deliberately.

```text
Incoming Load
      │
      ▼
Capacity Boundary
      │
 ┌────┴────┐
 ▼         ▼
Critical   Non-critical
 │         │
 ▼         X
Serve     Shed
```

Controlled rejection is preferable to uncontrolled system collapse.

---

# 81. Load-Shedding Priority

Potential priority order:

```text
Authentication
Core learning
Assessment operations
Content retrieval
Recommendations
Analytics
Background work
```

Actual business criticality must determine final policy.

---

# 82. HTTP 503

When the platform cannot temporarily serve an otherwise valid request:

```http
503 Service Unavailable
```

may be appropriate.

This differs from:

```text
429 → Caller exceeded allowed rate
503 → Service currently unable to serve
```

---

# 83. Graceful Degradation

Mediverse should preserve critical workflows when optional dependencies fail.

```text
AI Service ✕
     │
     ▼
Core Learning Platform
     │
     └── Still Available
```

Architecture should explicitly identify optional dependencies.

---

# 84. Gateway Failure

The gateway itself is critical infrastructure.

If there is only one gateway Pod:

```text
Gateway Pod
    X
    │
    ▼
Entire API unavailable
```

Therefore production requires redundant gateway replicas.

---

# 85. Gateway High Availability

```text
ALB
 │
 ├──► Gateway Pod A
 ├──► Gateway Pod B
 └──► Gateway Pod C
```

Replicas should be distributed across nodes and Availability Zones where practical.

---

# 86. Gateway HPA

Spring Cloud Gateway should scale horizontally according to measured demand.

Potential signals include:

```text
CPU
Request rate
Concurrent connections
Event-loop pressure
Latency
```

CPU alone may not represent gateway saturation.

---

# 87. Gateway Resource Requests

Gateway Pods require explicit:

```text
CPU requests
Memory requests
Validated limits
```

Because every API request may pass through them, resource starvation here has platform-wide impact.

---

# 88. Gateway Readiness

A gateway Pod should receive traffic only after:

```text
Application initialized
Routes loaded
Required configuration available
Critical dependencies ready
```

Readiness must not simply mean that the JVM process exists.

---

# 89. Gateway Liveness

Liveness should answer:

> Can this gateway process recover only by restarting it?

It should not restart every gateway Pod simply because one downstream service is unavailable.

---

# 90. WebSocket Traffic

WebSockets have different characteristics from ordinary request/response APIs.

```text
Client
  │
  │ persistent connection
  ▼
Gateway
  │
  ▼
Realtime Service
```

Connections may remain open for long periods.

---

# 91. WebSocket Capacity

Capacity planning should consider:

```text
Concurrent connections
Connection lifetime
Memory per connection
Heartbeat traffic
Reconnect storms
Node draining
Gateway scaling
```

RPS alone is a poor capacity metric for WebSockets.

---

# 92. WebSocket Reconnect Storm

If a gateway node fails:

```text
10,000 connections lost
        │
        ▼
10,000 clients reconnect
        │
        ▼
Sudden traffic spike
```

Clients should use reconnect backoff and jitter.

---

# 93. Server-Sent Events

SSE may be used for server-to-client streaming where full bidirectional WebSocket communication is unnecessary.

SSE also creates long-lived HTTP connections and therefore requires separate capacity consideration.

---

# 94. Long-Running HTTP Requests

Long-running operations such as AI generation should not automatically keep gateway requests open indefinitely.

Where appropriate:

```text
POST /ai/jobs
      │
      ▼
202 Accepted
      │
      ▼
Background Processing
      │
      ▼
Job Status / SSE / WebSocket
```

may be more resilient.

---

# 95. API Versioning

Externally consumed APIs require explicit version management.

Preferred initial pattern:

```text
/api/v1/...
```

Future incompatible contracts may use:

```text
/api/v2/...
```

---

# 96. Versioning Is Not for Every Change

Adding a backward-compatible optional field does not necessarily require `/v2`.

Version changes should correspond to meaningful incompatible contract changes.

---

# 97. Backward Compatibility

During migration:

```text
Clients v1
   │
   ▼
API v1

Clients v2
   │
   ▼
API v2
```

Both may need to coexist for a defined transition period.

---

# 98. API Deprecation

Deprecated APIs should have:

```text
Owner
Replacement
Deprecation date
Usage telemetry
Migration plan
Removal date
```

"Deprecated forever" creates permanent maintenance cost.

---

# 99. API Consumer Visibility

Before removing an API version, Mediverse should know who still uses it.

Gateway telemetry should help identify:

```text
Endpoint
Version
Client
Traffic volume
Error rate
```

where identity/privacy policies permit.

---

# 100. Canary Traffic

The traffic layer may support gradual rollout.

```text
Users
  │
  ▼
Gateway / Routing
  │
  ├── 95% → Version A
  └──  5% → Version B
```

This limits blast radius during releases.

---

# 101. Canary Progression

Example conceptually:

```text
1%
 │
 ▼
5%
 │
 ▼
25%
 │
 ▼
50%
 │
 ▼
100%
```

Promotion should depend on health signals rather than elapsed time alone.

---

# 102. Canary Metrics

Important comparison signals include:

```text
Error rate
Latency
Resource consumption
Business failures
Dependency errors
SLO impact
```

A technically healthy canary can still contain business defects.

---

# 103. Canary Rollback

If the new version violates defined thresholds:

```text
Canary
  │
  ▼
Regression detected
  │
  ▼
Traffic → Stable Version
```

Rollback should be fast and controlled.

---

# 104. Blue/Green Routing

Another deployment model:

```text
BLUE
Current production

GREEN
New release
```

Traffic switches only after GREEN is validated.

---

# 105. Blue/Green Trade-Off

Advantages:

```text
Fast rollback
Clear environment separation
```

Costs:

```text
Temporary duplicate capacity
Database compatibility challenges
Operational complexity
```

It should not be forced onto every service.

---

# 106. Database Compatibility

Traffic switching cannot fix incompatible database migrations.

During progressive delivery:

```text
Old App
   │
   ├──► Database
   │
New App
   └──► Same Database
```

schema changes must often remain compatible with both versions during transition.

---

# 107. Expand-Contract Migration

Preferred approach for many schema changes:

```text
EXPAND
Add backward-compatible schema
        │
        ▼
DEPLOY
Old + new applications coexist
        │
        ▼
MIGRATE
Move data/usage
        │
        ▼
CONTRACT
Remove obsolete schema
```

This reduces deployment coupling.

---

# 108. Header-Based Routing

Selected test traffic may route according to trusted headers.

```text
X-Mediverse-Canary: true
        │
        ▼
Canary Service
```

External clients must not be allowed to abuse privileged routing headers.

---

# 109. Cookie-Based Routing

Controlled cookies may support preview or session-affinity scenarios where justified.

Sticky routing should not be introduced without understanding its effect on scaling and failure recovery.

---

# 110. Internal APIs

Not every API should be exposed through the public gateway.

```text
Public APIs
   │
   ▼
External Gateway

Internal APIs
   │
   ▼
Private Kubernetes Network
```

Internal-only interfaces should remain private.

---

# 111. Service-to-Service Calls

Internal communication should use stable service identities.

```text
assessment-service
       │
       ▼
user-service
```

rather than calling public internet endpoints for routine internal communication.

---

# 112. Public Hairpinning

Bad:

```text
Service A
   │
   ▼
Public CloudFront/WAF/ALB
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

for ordinary internal service communication.

This adds unnecessary:

```text
Latency
Cost
Failure points
External exposure
```

---

# 113. Internal Authentication

Private network location alone is not sufficient authorization.

Internal services should authenticate/authorize calls according to the security architecture.

A future ADR may introduce workload identity and mTLS.

---

# 114. East-West Resilience

Service-to-service calls still require:

```text
Timeouts
Retries where safe
Circuit breakers
Concurrency limits
Observability
```

The public gateway does not solve east-west resilience.

---

# 115. Correlation IDs

Every incoming request should receive or carry a correlation identifier.

```text
Client
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │ correlation-id
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

This helps trace failures across distributed systems.

---

# 116. Trace Context

ADR-037 established OpenTelemetry.

The gateway should propagate standard distributed tracing context across downstream requests.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
   │
   ▼
Database
```

The trace should reveal the end-to-end request path.

---

# 117. Request Logging

Gateway access logs should capture useful metadata such as:

```text
Timestamp
Route
Method
Status
Latency
Correlation ID
Client/application identity where appropriate
Response size
```

Sensitive request bodies or credentials should not be logged indiscriminately.

---

# 118. Sensitive Headers

Logs must avoid exposing:

```text
Authorization tokens
Cookies
API keys
Secrets
Sensitive personal data
```

Observability cannot be allowed to become a credential-leak mechanism.

---

# 119. RED Metrics

Gateway monitoring should include RED metrics:

```text
Rate
Errors
Duration
```

broken down by useful dimensions such as:

```text
Route
Status class
API version
Upstream service
```

while controlling metric-cardinality growth.

---

# 120. Gateway Saturation

Additional signals include:

```text
CPU
Memory
Active connections
Connection-pool utilization
Pending requests
Event-loop saturation
Rate-limit rejections
Circuit-breaker state
```

These help distinguish gateway saturation from backend saturation.

---

# 121. Rate-Limit Metrics

Monitor:

```text
Allowed requests
Rejected requests
Limit policy
Endpoint
Client class
```

A sudden increase in 429 responses may indicate:

```text
Attack
Bad client
Incorrect policy
Unexpected product usage
Capacity problem
```

---

# 122. Security Telemetry

Traffic architecture should expose relevant events from:

```text
CloudFront
WAF
ALB
Gateway
Authentication
```

into the broader security/observability architecture.

---

# 123. WAF vs Gateway Metrics

WAF blocking and gateway rejection are different signals.

```text
WAF Block
→ Request never reaches application boundary

Gateway 429
→ Valid traffic boundary reached but policy rejected request
```

Dashboards should preserve this distinction.

---

# 124. Health Endpoints

Health endpoints should be separated appropriately.

Potential concepts:

```text
/actuator/health/liveness
/actuator/health/readiness
```

They should not expose unnecessary internal details publicly.

---

# 125. Actuator Exposure

Bad:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
/actuator/**
```

with unrestricted access.

Only explicitly required operational endpoints should be exposed, and sensitive management endpoints should remain private/protected.

---

# 126. Gateway Configuration

Routes and policies should be version controlled.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Gateway Configuration
 │
 ▼
CI validation
 │
 ▼
GitOps
 │
 ▼
Gateway
```

Manual production route editing should not be the normal operating model.

---

# 127. Configuration Validation

Gateway configuration should be tested before deployment.

Examples:

```text
Duplicate routes
Invalid predicates
Broken filters
Missing upstream services
Unsafe CORS
Invalid timeout values
```

A malformed gateway configuration can affect the entire platform.

---

# 128. Route Ownership

Every externally exposed API route should have:

```text
Owning team
Backend service
API version
Security classification
Rate-limit policy
SLO
Lifecycle status
```

Unowned public APIs become permanent liabilities.

---

# 129. API Catalog

Mediverse should maintain an API inventory/catalog containing at least:

```text
API
Owner
Purpose
Consumers
Authentication
Version
Lifecycle
Documentation
```

This complements OpenAPI specifications.

---

# 130. OpenAPI

Externally consumed REST APIs should maintain OpenAPI contracts.

```text
Service Code
   │
   ▼
OpenAPI Contract
   │
   ├── Documentation
   ├── Testing
   ├── Client integration
   └── Governance
```

The API contract should not drift silently from implementation.

---

# 131. Contract Testing

Service/gateway changes should eventually include automated contract validation.

This can detect:

```text
Removed fields
Changed types
Removed endpoints
Breaking status-code changes
```

before production deployment.

---

# 132. Gateway SLO

Because the gateway sits on critical request paths, it requires its own availability and latency objectives.

A gateway that adds significant latency to every API call becomes a systemic performance problem.

---

# 133. Failure Scenario — Gateway Saturation

```text
Traffic Spike
    │
    ▼
Gateway CPU/Connections saturated
    │
    ▼
Latency rises
    │
    ▼
Client retries
    │
    ▼
More traffic
```

Mitigation:

```text
Rate limiting
Concurrency controls
HPA
Capacity headroom
Retry governance
```

---

# 134. Failure Scenario — Redis Rate Limiter

```text
Redis unavailable
      │
      ▼
Distributed limiter unavailable
      │
      ▼
Endpoint policy
   ┌────┴────┐
   ▼         ▼
Fail Open   Fail Closed
```

The behavior must be deliberate per traffic class.

---

# 135. Failure Scenario — Backend Down

```text
Gateway
   │
   ▼
content-service ✕
   │
   ▼
Timeout / Circuit Breaker
   │
   ▼
Controlled 5xx / Fallback
```

The gateway should not queue unbounded requests waiting for recovery.

---

# 136. Failure Scenario — Authentication Service

If authentication requires synchronous introspection on every request:

```text
Auth Service ✕
      │
      ▼
Entire Platform ✕
```

This is a major availability dependency.

Self-contained JWT validation can reduce that dependency where consistent with the security design.

---

# 137. Failure Scenario — Bad Client

```text
Buggy Client
    │
    ▼
Infinite request loop
    │
    ▼
Rate Limit
    │
    X
Backend overload
```

Traffic governance protects the platform from accidental abuse as well as attackers.

---

# 138. Failure Scenario — AI Endpoint

```text
10,000 AI Requests
       │
       ▼
Rate Limit
       │
       ▼
Concurrency Limit
       │
       ▼
Job Queue
       │
       ▼
AI Workers
```

Allowing all 10,000 requests to synchronously occupy gateway and backend resources would be poor architecture.

---

# 139. Traffic Governance Ownership

```text
Platform Team
   │
   ├── CloudFront
   ├── WAF
   ├── ALB
   ├── Kubernetes entry
   └── Gateway platform

Application Teams
   │
   ├── API contracts
   ├── Domain authorization
   ├── Idempotency
   └── Service resilience

Security
   │
   ├── WAF policy
   ├── Authentication requirements
   └── Exposure governance

SRE
   │
   ├── Gateway SLO
   ├── Capacity
   ├── Alerts
   └── Failure testing
```

---

# 140. Traffic Architecture Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Exposing every microservice publicly
❌ Public databases, Redis or Kafka
❌ Business logic inside gateway filters
❌ Treating gateway authentication as complete domain authorization
❌ Blind trust of client-supplied identity headers
❌ Wildcard production CORS without justification
❌ Unlimited request bodies
❌ Proxying every large S3 upload through Spring Boot
❌ Missing network timeouts
❌ Retrying every failure
❌ Retries at every architectural layer
❌ Retries without backoff/jitter
❌ Retrying non-idempotent operations blindly
❌ Infinite concurrency
❌ One rate limit for every endpoint
❌ IP address as the only authenticated-user identity
❌ Unlimited expensive AI requests
❌ One gateway replica
❌ Liveness dependent on every backend
❌ Long synchronous AI operations without justification
❌ Mutable API contracts without version governance
❌ Public hairpinning for internal calls
❌ Public Actuator exposure
❌ Logging JWTs/API keys
❌ Manual production route configuration
❌ Removing API versions without usage telemetry
❌ Canary rollout without rollback criteria
❌ Assuming private network = trusted caller
```

---

```text
                     REQUEST
                        │
                        ▼

                        │
                        ▼
                       WAF
                        │
```


```text

              │                │

USER ───────────────────────► S3
```

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                        | Mitigation                           |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Malicious edge traffic      | WAF + AWS edge protection            |
| Direct service exposure     | Controlled gateway boundary          |
| Invalid authentication load | Early JWT validation                 |
| Header spoofing             | Gateway-controlled trusted headers   |
| Browser CORS failure        | Centralized explicit CORS            |
| Oversized payloads          | Request-size limits                  |
| Large media overhead        | S3 presigned uploads + CloudFront    |
| Runaway clients             | Rate limiting                        |
| Expensive AI abuse          | Dedicated quota/concurrency policies |
| Gateway overload            | HPA + headroom                       |
| Retry storm                 | Bounded retries + backoff + jitter   |
| Duplicate writes            | Idempotency                          |
| Dependency collapse         | Circuit breakers                     |
| Resource starvation         | Bulkheads                            |
| Platform overload           | Load shedding                        |
| Optional dependency failure | Graceful degradation                 |
| Gateway failure             | Multi-replica HA                     |
| WebSocket reconnect storm   | Backoff + jitter                     |
| API breaking change         | Versioning + contract testing        |
| Bad release                 | Canary/blue-green rollback           |
| Internal service exposure   | Private east-west traffic            |
| Debugging difficulty        | Correlation + tracing                |
| Sensitive log leakage       | Logging controls                     |
| Configuration drift         | GitOps                               |
