```text
       ▼
ACL Filtering
       │
       ▼
Reranking
       │
       ▼
Context Builder
       │
       ▼
Prompt Registry
       │
       ▼
Model Router
       │
       ▼
LLM
       │
       ▼
Grounding Validation
       │
       ▼
Answer + Verified Sources
```

---

# 144. Agent Architecture

```text
                       USER
                        │
                        ▼
                  Agent Gateway
                        │
                        ▼
                  Agent Runtime
                        │
             ┌──────────┼──────────┐
             ▼          ▼          ▼
          Planner    Policy     Budget
             │          │          │
             └──────────┼──────────┘
                        ▼
                  Tool Registry
                        │
           ┌────────────┼────────────┐
           ▼            ▼            ▼
        Search       Read APIs    Write APIs
           │            │            │
           │            │            ▼
           │            │      Human Approval
           │            │            │
           └────────────┼────────────┘
                        ▼

```

---

# 145. AI Reliability Architecture

```text
AI Request
    │
    ▼
Primary Model
    │
 ┌──┴────┐
 ▼       ▼
OK     Failure
 │       │
 │       ▼
 │   Circuit Breaker
 │       │
 │       ▼
 │   Approved Fallback
 │       │
 └───────┼───────
         ▼
   Output Validation
         │
         ▼
      Response
```

If all AI providers fail:

```text
AI unavailable
      │
      ▼
Graceful degradation
      │
      ▼
Core Mediverse remains available
```

---

# 146. Complete Mediverse AI Architecture

```text
                         CLIENT
                           │
                           ▼
                      API GATEWAY
                           │
                           ▼
                    DOMAIN SERVICES
                           │
                           ▼
                       AI PLATFORM
                           │
      ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
      ▼                    ▼                    ▼
Prompt Registry       RAG Engine          Agent Runtime
      │                    │                    │
      │                    ▼                    ▼
      │                OpenSearch          Tool Registry
      │                    │                    │
      └────────────┬───────┴────────────┬───────┘
                   ▼                    ▼
              Safety Layer        Policy Engine
                   │                    │

                             ▼

                             │
```

---

# 147. AI Governance Lifecycle

```text
Use Case Proposed
       │
       ▼
Risk Classification
       │
       ▼
Model / Prompt Selection
       │
       ▼
Offline Evaluation
       │
       ▼
Security / Privacy Review
       │
       ▼
Faculty Review
       │
       ▼
Canary Release
       │
       ▼
Production Monitoring
       │
       ▼
Continuous Evaluation
       │
       ▼

```

AI deployment is therefore a lifecycle, not an API call.

---

# 148. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk                              | Primary Mitigation                   |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Hallucination                     | RAG + grounding evaluation           |
| Medical misinformation            | Faculty-reviewed evaluation          |
| Prompt injection                  | Trust boundaries + tool controls     |
| Sensitive-data leakage            | Minimization + redaction             |
| Cross-tenant leakage              | Tenant-aware retrieval/state         |
| Fake citations                    | Programmatic source mapping          |
| Provider outage                   | Circuit breaker + approved fallback  |
| Provider lock-in                  | AI platform abstraction              |
| Unexpected spend                  | Quotas + budgets + attribution       |
| Prompt regression                 | Versioning + evaluation              |
| Model regression                  | Model upgrade testing                |
| Incorrect structured output       | Schema + business validation         |
| Unauthorized tool execution       | Authorization + least privilege      |
| Agent runaway                     | Step/token/time/cost limits          |
| Duplicate write actions           | Idempotency                          |
| Excessive agency                  | Human confirmation                   |
| Poisoned RAG corpus               | Ingestion authorization + provenance |
| Bad automated evaluation          | Human/faculty review                 |
| AI incident                       | Kill switches + feature flags        |
| Privacy exposure through logs     | Metadata-first logging               |
| AI dependency breaks core product | Graceful degradation                 |

## Next — ADR-046

### **ADR-046 — Enterprise File, Media, Object Storage, CDN & Digital Asset Management Architecture**

This should come next because Mediverse is fundamentally a **content-heavy medical education platform**. We have referenced S3, CloudFront, images, PDFs, videos, audio and 3D assets repeatedly, but we have not yet formally decided how those assets are stored, uploaded, secured, transformed, versioned and delivered.

ADR-046 should cover **file taxonomy → S3 architecture → bucket strategy → object-key conventions → metadata → database vs object-store ownership → presigned upload/download → multipart upload → large video uploads → upload lifecycle → validation → MIME/type verification → malware scanning → quarantine → image processing → thumbnails → audio processing → video transcoding → HLS/DASH → 3D GLB/glTF assets → compression → range requests → CloudFront → origin access → signed URLs/cookies → private educational content → public assets → tenant isolation → faculty upload permissions → object versioning → immutable assets → content hashes → deduplication → lifecycle tiers → archive → deletion → orphan cleanup → event-driven processing → S3 events/Kafka boundary → processing workflows → idempotency → media-service design → CDN cache keys → invalidation → cache-control → bandwidth → hot assets → DRM evaluation → download protection limitations → encryption → KMS → metadata privacy → backup/replication → cross-region DR → observability → cost governance → testing → anti-patterns → final Mediverse digital asset architecture.**


# ADR-046 — Enterprise File, Media, Object Storage, CDN & Digital Asset Management Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-046
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-046 defines how Mediverse stores, processes, secures, versions and delivers its digital educational assets.

Mediverse is not just a REST application. It will handle substantial binary and media content:

```text
Images
PDFs
Lecture notes
Audio
Videos
Animations
3D models
GLB / glTF assets
Thumbnails
Generated diagrams
AI-generated assets
Faculty uploads
Certificates
```

The architectural question is:

> **How should Mediverse manage potentially millions of large digital assets without storing binaries inside PostgreSQL, routing every download through Spring Boot, exposing S3 directly, or creating an insecure and expensive media architecture?**

---

# 1. Digital Assets Are a Separate Data Class

Mediverse contains two fundamentally different categories of information.

```text
Structured Domain Data
──────────────────────
Student
Course
Chapter
Assessment
Enrollment
Progress
Permissions

Binary / Digital Assets
───────────────────────
Images
Videos
Audio
PDF
3D models
Documents
```

They should not automatically use the same persistence technology.

---

# 2. Core Decision

Mediverse shall use object storage as the authoritative binary asset store.

Within AWS:

```text
Amazon S3
```

shall be the primary object-storage architecture.

Conceptually:

```text
Domain Metadata
      │
      ▼
 PostgreSQL

Binary Content
      │
      ▼
     S3
```

---

# 3. Why Not PostgreSQL BLOB Storage?

Technically PostgreSQL can store binary data.

That does not make it the correct default.

Storing large videos, images and 3D models in PostgreSQL would increase:

```text
Database size
Backup size
Replication traffic
Restore time
I/O pressure
Operational complexity
```

while providing little benefit.

---

# 4. Metadata vs Binary Separation

Preferred:

```text
PostgreSQL
────────────────
asset_id
owner_id
course_id
object_key
media_type
status
size
checksum
version
created_at

S3
────────────────
actual binary object
```

The database understands the business asset.

S3 stores its bytes.

---

# 5. Asset Identity

A Mediverse asset should have a stable application-level identifier.

Example:

```text
assetId = 7f8d...
```

The application should not use the S3 object key itself as the primary business identity.

---

# 6. Why Separate Asset ID?

Storage layout can change.

For example:

```text
S3 Key v1
courses/123/video.mp4

↓

S3 Key v2
tenant/abc/course/123/assets/video/uuid
```

The application's stable asset ID should survive such migrations.

---

# 7. Asset Metadata Model

Conceptually:

```text
Asset
────────────────────────
asset_id
tenant_id
owner_id
asset_type
original_filename
object_key
content_type
size_bytes
checksum
status
version
visibility
created_at
updated_at
```

Additional metadata should be domain-specific rather than turning one table into an uncontrolled metadata dump.

---

# 8. Asset Lifecycle

Assets should have explicit states.

```text
INITIATED
    │
    ▼
UPLOADING
    │
    ▼
UPLOADED
    │
    ▼
SCANNING
    │
    ▼
PROCESSING
    │
    ▼
READY
```

Failure states may include:

```text
REJECTED
INFECTED
PROCESSING_FAILED
DELETED
```

---

# 9. Never Trust Upload Completion Alone

An object appearing in S3 does not mean:

```text
Safe
Valid
Authorized
Processable
Ready for students
```

Upload completion is only one lifecycle transition.

---

# 10. Object-Key Design

Poor:

```text
lecture1.mp4
```

Better:

```text
tenant/<tenant-id>/course/<course-id>/asset/<asset-id>/source
```

Keys should support operational organization without embedding unnecessary sensitive data.

---

# 11. Avoid PII in Object Keys

Bad:

```text
students/john-smith@example.com/report.pdf
```

Object keys can appear in:

```text
Logs
Metrics
Audit records
URLs
Operational tools
```

Use opaque identifiers where possible.

---

# 12. Environment Isolation

Production, UAT and development assets should not accidentally share storage boundaries.

Conceptually:

```text
DEV Storage
UAT Storage
PROD Storage
```

Infrastructure-level separation is preferable for important environments.

---

# 13. Bucket Strategy

Do not create:

```text
one bucket per user
```

or:

```text
one bucket per course
```

without a concrete reason.

Bucket boundaries should primarily reflect:

```text
Environment
Security boundary
Lifecycle
Replication requirements
Asset class
```

---

# 14. Logical Asset Classes

Mediverse may distinguish:

```text
Original Uploads
Processed Media
Public Assets
Private Assets
Temporary Uploads
Quarantine
Logs/Processing Artifacts
```

Whether these become separate buckets or prefixes is an infrastructure decision based on security and lifecycle requirements.

---

# 15. Public S3 Access

Production educational asset buckets should not simply be publicly readable.

Bad:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
Public S3 Bucket
```

Private origin access should be the default.

---

# 16. CDN Architecture

Delivery should use:

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
CloudFront
  │
  ▼
S3
```

rather than having every student retrieve large files directly through Spring Boot.

---

# 17. Why CDN?

A student in one region and another student elsewhere may request the same content.

Without CDN:

```text
Student A ──► Origin
Student B ──► Origin
Student C ──► Origin
```

With CDN:

```text
              Origin
                │
                ▼
            CloudFront
           /     |      \
          ▼      ▼       ▼
      Student Student Student
```

Frequently requested content can be served closer to users.

---

# 18. Spring Boot Is Not a Video Proxy

Bad:

```text
Student
   │
   ▼
Spring Boot
   │
   ▼
S3
   │
   ▼
Spring Boot
   │
   ▼
Student
```

This wastes:

```text
Pod bandwidth
Connections
CPU
Memory
Network capacity
```

Spring Boot should generally authorize access and issue delivery credentials/URLs rather than stream every byte itself.

---

# 19. Upload Architecture

Likewise, large uploads should not necessarily travel through application Pods.

Bad:

```text
Faculty
   │
   ▼
Spring Boot
   │
  5 GB
   ▼
S3
```

Preferred:

```text
Faculty
   │
   ▼
Mediverse API
   │
   ▼
Authorize
   │
   ▼
Presigned Upload
   │
   ▼
Faculty ─────────► S3
```

---

# 20. Presigned Upload

Workflow:

```text
1. Client requests upload

2. Backend authenticates user

3. Backend validates upload intent

4. Backend creates asset record

5. Backend generates presigned operation

6. Client uploads directly to S3

7. Backend verifies completion

8. Processing pipeline begins
```

This preserves application control while removing large binary transfer from the API tier.

---

# 21. Presigned URL Is a Capability

A presigned URL effectively grants temporary permission.

Therefore it must be:

```text
Short-lived
Scoped
Operation-specific
Object-specific
```

Do not generate broad, long-lived upload credentials.

---

# 22. Client Cannot Choose Arbitrary Key

Bad:

```text
POST /upload-url

{
  "key": "anything/i/want"
}
```

The backend should derive the permitted storage location from trusted application context.

---

# 23. Upload Authorization

Before generating an upload URL:

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Authentication
 │
 ▼
Authorization
 │
 ▼
Domain Validation
 │
 ▼
Asset Creation
 │
 ▼
Upload Permission
```

The storage layer must not bypass Mediverse business permissions.

---

# 24. Upload Intent

The API should know what the user intends to upload.

Example:

```text
assetType = LECTURE_VIDEO
courseId = 123
```

This allows different:

```text
Maximum sizes
Allowed types
Processing pipelines
Security rules
```

---

# 25. Multipart Upload

Large files should use multipart upload where appropriate.

```text
Large Video
     │
     ├── Part 1
     ├── Part 2
     ├── Part 3
     └── Part N
           │
           ▼
       Complete
```

This improves reliability for large media uploads.

---

# 26. Multipart Advantages

Multipart upload allows:

```text
Parallel transfer
Retry of individual parts
Large object support
Better recovery from unstable connections
```

A failed 5 GB upload should not necessarily restart from byte zero.

---

# 27. Abandoned Multipart Uploads

Users may start uploads and never finish them.

```text
Initiate
   │
   ▼
Upload 20%
   │
   X
```

Incomplete multipart uploads consume storage.

Lifecycle policies should clean them up after an appropriate period.

---

# 28. Upload Size Limits

Every asset type should have explicit size limits.

Example categories:

```text
Profile image
Diagram
PDF
Audio
Video
3D model
```

Do not allow arbitrary multi-gigabyte uploads simply because S3 technically supports them.

---

# 29. Filename Is Untrusted Input

Uploaded filenames may contain:

```text
Path-like strings
Special characters
Misleading extensions
Extremely long names
Unexpected Unicode
```

The original filename should be treated as metadata, not trusted storage structure.

---

# 30. File Extension Is Not Validation

This:

```text
heart-diagram.jpg
```

does not prove the object is a JPEG.

Likewise:

```text
lecture.pdf
```

does not prove it is a valid PDF.

---

# 31. Content-Type Validation

The platform should evaluate:

```text
Declared MIME type
File signature / magic bytes
Expected asset type
Processing result
```

where appropriate.

Never trust only the client's `Content-Type`.

---

# 32. Malware Scanning

Untrusted faculty/user uploads should enter a scanning pipeline before becoming generally accessible.

```text
Upload
  │
  ▼
Quarantine
  │
  ▼
Malware Scan
 ┌┴─────────────┐
 ▼              ▼
CLEAN         INFECTED
 │              │
 ▼              ▼
Process        Reject
```

---

# 33. Quarantine Boundary

Newly uploaded objects should not automatically be delivered to students.

```text
Untrusted Upload
      │
      X
Student Delivery
```

until required validation/scanning succeeds.

---

# 34. Scan Failure

If scanning infrastructure is unavailable:

```text
Upload
  │
  ▼
SCAN_PENDING
```

is safer than:

```text
"Scanner failed, therefore assume clean."
```

for untrusted content.

---

# 35. Malware Result

The asset lifecycle may become:

```text
UPLOADED
   │
   ▼
SCANNING
   │
   ├── CLEAN ─────► PROCESSING
   │
   └── INFECTED ──► REJECTED
```

Audit metadata should record the result.

---

# 36. Processing Architecture

Different asset types require different processing.

```text
                 Asset
                   │
      ┌────────────┼────────────┐
      ▼            ▼            ▼
    Image         Video        Audio
      │            │            │
      ▼            ▼            ▼
 Resize        Transcode      Encode
      │            │            │
      ▼            ▼            ▼
 Thumbnail       HLS         Waveform
```

---

# 37. Asynchronous Processing

Video transcoding should not occur inside an HTTP request.

Bad:

```text
POST /video
    │
    ▼
Wait 20 minutes
    │
    ▼
HTTP Response
```

Processing must be asynchronous.

---

# 38. Processing Workflow

```text
Upload Complete
      │
      ▼
Validation
      │
      ▼
Scan
      │
      ▼
Processing Job
      │
      ▼
Derived Assets
      │
      ▼
READY
```

The client can query or receive status updates separately.

---

# 39. Event-Driven Processing

Object lifecycle changes can generate processing events.

Conceptually:

```text
S3
 │
 ▼
Event
 │
 ▼
Processing Coordinator
 │
 ▼
Worker
```

But raw infrastructure events should not automatically become Mediverse enterprise domain events.

---

# 40. S3 Event vs Domain Event

These are different:

```text
S3:
ObjectCreated

Mediverse:
LectureVideoReady
```

The first describes infrastructure.

The second describes a business-relevant state.

Do not confuse them.

---

# 41. Domain Event Publication

After processing succeeds:

```text
Asset Processing
      │
      ▼
Asset DB state = READY
      │
      ▼
Transactional Outbox
      │
      ▼
Kafka
      │
      ▼
AssetReady
```

ADR-042's reliability model still applies.

---

# 42. Processing Idempotency

Infrastructure events can be duplicated.

Therefore:

```text
ObjectCreated
ObjectCreated
```

must not create uncontrolled duplicate processing jobs or duplicate asset records.

---

# 43. Image Processing

Images may require:

```text
Resize
Thumbnail
Format normalization
Optimization
Metadata stripping
```

depending on use case.

---

# 44. Image Variants

Rather than resizing dynamically on every request:

```text
Original
   │
   ├── Thumbnail
   ├── Small
   ├── Medium
   └── Large
```

can be generated ahead of time where predictable sizes exist.

---

# 45. Original Preservation

For important content, preserve the original upload separately from processed variants.

```text
Original
   │
   ├── Derived v1
   ├── Derived v2
   └── Future reprocessing
```

This enables new processing pipelines without asking faculty to re-upload.

---

# 46. Video Processing

Uploading:

```text
lecture.mp4
```

and serving that exact file to every device is not a complete video architecture.

Students may have:

```text
Different bandwidth
Different screen sizes
Different network quality
Different devices
```

---

# 47. Adaptive Bitrate Streaming

Preferred video architecture:

```text
Original Video
      │
      ▼
Transcoding
      │
      ├── 360p
      ├── 480p
      ├── 720p
      └── 1080p
            │
            ▼
         HLS/DASH
            │
            ▼
        CloudFront
```

The player can adapt quality to network conditions.

---

# 48. HLS

HTTP Live Streaming divides video into segments plus manifests.

Conceptually:

```text
master.m3u8

├── 360p playlist
├── 720p playlist
└── 1080p playlist
```

Each playlist references media segments.

---

# 49. Video Range Requests

For downloadable/progressive media where appropriate, HTTP range requests allow clients to request parts of an object rather than always transferring the entire file.

CDN/origin configuration must support the selected delivery model.

---

# 50. Video Thumbnail

Processing may generate:

```text
Poster image
Preview thumbnail
Duration
Resolution
Codec metadata
```

for the application UI.

---

# 51. Audio Processing

Audio assets may require:

```text
Normalization
Format conversion
Bitrate variants
Duration extraction
Waveform generation
```

depending on product requirements.

---

# 52. PDF Processing

PDF uploads may require:

```text
Malware scan
Page-count extraction
Thumbnail generation
Metadata extraction
Text extraction
```

where product features require them.

Text extraction belongs to a derived processing pipeline, not the authoritative binary object.

---

# 53. 3D Assets

Mediverse's 3D learning capabilities require special handling.

Primary web-friendly formats may include:

```text
glTF
GLB
```

depending on the 3D architecture.

---

# 54. 3D Asset Pipeline

Conceptually:

```text
Original 3D Asset
       │
       ▼
Validation
       │
       ▼
Optimization
       │
       ├── Geometry optimization
       ├── Texture optimization
       ├── Compression
       └── Metadata
              │
              ▼
             CDN
```

---

# 55. 3D Performance

A technically valid 500 MB anatomy model may still be unusable in a browser.

3D governance must consider:

```text
Polygon count
Texture size
Material count
Compression
Initial download
GPU memory
Mobile hardware
```

---

# 56. 3D Level of Detail

Complex models may require:

```text
High Detail
Medium Detail
Low Detail
```

variants.

Device and camera distance can influence which representation is loaded.

---

# 57. 3D Compression

Technologies such as geometry and texture compression may materially reduce asset size.

But compression compatibility and decoding cost must be evaluated against supported browsers/devices.

---

# 58. Asset Derivatives

One source asset can generate multiple derived objects.

```text
Source Asset
     │
     ├── Thumbnail
     ├── Optimized image
     ├── HLS stream
     ├── Transcript
     └── Preview
```

These relationships should be represented explicitly.

---

# 59. Content Hash

Assets may store a cryptographic checksum.

```text
Object Bytes
    │
    ▼
SHA-256
    │
    ▼
Content Hash
```

This can support:

```text
Integrity verification
Deduplication analysis
Processing identity
```

---

# 60. Deduplication

Suppose faculty upload the same 1 GB video five times.

A content hash can identify identical binary content.

But automatic physical deduplication introduces lifecycle and authorization complexity.

```text
Asset A ─┐
Asset B ─┼──► Same Object
Asset C ─┘
```

Deleting one logical asset must not accidentally delete content still referenced by another.

Therefore deduplication should be deliberate rather than an automatic initial optimization.

---

## ADR-046 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The architecture established so far is:

```text
                     FACULTY / USER
                           │
                           ▼
                     Mediverse API
                           │
                    Authorization
                           │
                           ▼
                    Asset Metadata
                      PostgreSQL
                           │
                           ▼
                  Presigned Upload
                           │
                           ▼
                           S3
                           │
                           ▼
                      QUARANTINE
                           │
                           ▼
                    Malware Scan
                           │
                           ▼
                     Validation
                           │
                           ▼
                 Processing Pipeline
                 ┌─────────┼─────────┐
                 ▼         ▼         ▼
               Image      Video      3D
                 │         │         │
                 ▼         ▼         ▼
             Variants     HLS    Optimized GLB
                 │         │         │
                 └─────────┼─────────┘
                           ▼
                         READY
                           │
                           ▼
                      CloudFront
                           │
                           ▼
                        Student
```

And the core storage boundary is:

```text
PostgreSQL
=
Asset business metadata

S3
=
Authoritative binary objects

CloudFront
=
Delivery

Processing Pipeline
=
Derived representations

Kafka
=
Business/event integration
```

The critical rule is:

> **Mediverse application services manage asset identity, authorization and lifecycle; S3 manages binary storage; CloudFront manages scalable delivery. Spring Boot should not become a multi-gigabyte file-transfer proxy.**

# ADR-046 — Enterprise File, Media, Object Storage, CDN & Digital Asset Management Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Deduplication**.

---

# 61. Asset Versioning & Immutability

Published educational assets should preferably behave as immutable objects.

Instead of:

```text
course/video.mp4
        │
        ▼
overwrite same object
```

prefer:

```text
asset-123/version-1/source.mp4
asset-123/version-2/source.mp4
```

This makes caching, rollback and auditability substantially safer.

---

# 62. Logical Version vs S3 Version

Mediverse should distinguish:

```text
Application Asset Version
        ≠
S3 Object Version
```

Application versioning represents business meaning.

S3 Versioning is an infrastructure protection mechanism.

Do not make application workflows dependent directly on opaque S3 version IDs.

---

# 63. S3 Versioning

Versioning should be enabled where recovery requirements justify it.

```text
Object v1
   │
   ▼
Object v2
   │
   ▼
Object v3
```

This can protect against accidental overwrite or deletion.

---

# 64. Replacement Semantics

When faculty replaces a lecture PDF:

```text
Asset
 ├── Version 1
 └── Version 2
```

the system should explicitly decide whether existing course references:

```text
Automatically follow latest
```

or remain pinned:

```text
Course Publication → Asset Version 1
```

For auditable educational releases, explicit version references are safer.

---

# 65. Immutable Object Keys

Preferred:

```text
/assets/<asset-id>/<version>/<variant>
```

Once published, that object should not normally change.

A new binary produces a new version/key.

---

# 66. Why Immutability Helps CDN

If:

```text
URL A
=
Always same bytes
```

CloudFront can cache aggressively.

If the same URL constantly changes, invalidation and stale-content problems increase.

---

# 67. Content-Addressable Storage

An alternative architecture derives storage identity from content:

```text
SHA-256
   │
   ▼
objects/ab/cd/<hash>
```

This can simplify deduplication and integrity verification.

However, it complicates logical asset lifecycle and access semantics.

Mediverse should not make this its initial business-facing storage model.

---

# 68. Asset References

Domain entities should reference:

```text
assetId
```

or a controlled asset/version identifier.

Avoid storing raw S3 URLs throughout domain tables.

---

# 69. Why Raw URLs Are Dangerous

Infrastructure changes:

```text
Bucket A
   ↓
Bucket B

CloudFront A
   ↓
CloudFront B
```

should not require updating millions of domain records.

Asset resolution belongs behind an asset abstraction.

---

# 70. Asset Resolver

Conceptually:

```text
assetId
   │
   ▼
Asset Service
   │
   ▼
Authorization
   │
   ▼
Delivery Policy
   │
   ▼
CloudFront URL / Cookie
```

Storage implementation remains hidden.

---

# 71. Deletion Is a Workflow

Bad:

```text
DELETE FROM asset
DELETE S3 object
```

inside one HTTP operation.

Asset deletion may involve:

```text
References
Versions
Derivatives
CDN
Retention
Audit
Legal requirements
Processing jobs
```

It should therefore be lifecycle-driven.

---

# 72. Soft Delete

First transition:

```text
READY
  │
  ▼
DELETE_REQUESTED
  │
  ▼
DELETED
```

can prevent immediate destructive removal.

---

# 73. Reference Validation

Before deleting:

```text
Asset
 │
 ├── Course A
 ├── Chapter B
 └── Assessment C
```

Mediverse must determine whether those references block deletion.

---

# 74. Physical Deletion

Physical object removal should happen only after:

```text
Authorization
Reference validation
Retention checks
Lifecycle transition
```

succeed.

---

# 75. Derived Asset Cleanup

Deleting the source may require deleting:

```text
Thumbnail
HLS segments
Manifest
Transcript
Waveform
Optimized 3D models
Preview images
```

Derived assets must not become permanent garbage.

---

# 76. Orphan Detection

Possible inconsistency:

```text
S3 Object
   │
   ▼
No PostgreSQL asset record
```

or:

```text
PostgreSQL Asset
   │
   ▼
Missing S3 object
```

Periodic reconciliation should detect these conditions.

---

# 77. Orphan Cleanup Safety

Never implement:

```text
Not referenced?
    │
    ▼
DELETE immediately
```

Use:

```text
Detect
  │
  ▼
Mark Candidate
  │
  ▼
Grace Period
  │
  ▼
Revalidate
  │
  ▼
Delete
```

This prevents destructive cleanup from temporary inconsistencies.

---

# 78. Temporary Assets

Temporary objects may include:

```text
Upload fragments
Processing intermediates
Generated previews
Failed transformations
Temporary exports
```

They require shorter lifecycle policies than published educational content.

---

# 79. S3 Lifecycle Policies

Storage lifecycle can automatically transition objects based on age and category.

Conceptually:

```text
Hot
 │
 ▼
Warm
 │
 ▼
Archive
 │
 ▼
Delete
```

Policies must align with actual access requirements.

---

# 80. Archive Tier

Rarely accessed historical material may move to archival storage.

But archive retrieval may not be immediate.

Do not archive content students expect to open interactively.

---

# 81. Retention Policy

Retention should be defined by asset class.

Example:

```text
Published course content
Assessment evidence
Temporary uploads
Processing artifacts
Audit-related exports
```

should not all share one arbitrary retention period.

---

# 82. CDN Security Boundary

Primary delivery architecture:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
Private S3 Origin
```

Users should not bypass CloudFront and access private origin objects directly.

---

# 83. Origin Access Control

CloudFront should use controlled origin access so S3 permits the distribution while denying general public access.

```text
CloudFront
     │
     │ authorized origin access
     ▼
    S3
```

---

# 84. Public vs Private Assets

Not every asset requires identical access controls.

Potential classes:

```text
PUBLIC
──────
Marketing image
Public logo

AUTHENTICATED
─────────────
General learning resource

ENROLLMENT_RESTRICTED
─────────────────────
Course content

FACULTY_ONLY
────────────
Answer keys
Draft materials
```

Delivery policy must follow business authorization.

---

# 85. Private Content Delivery

For protected material:

```text
Student
   │
   ▼
Mediverse API
   │
   ▼
Authorization
   │
   ▼
Temporary CDN Access
   │
   ▼
CloudFront
```

The application authorizes; the CDN transfers.

---

# 86. Signed URLs

A signed URL grants temporary access to a specific resource.

Useful for:

```text
Single PDF
Single download
Specific private asset
```

Access should expire.

---

# 87. Signed Cookies

Signed cookies can be useful when access covers many related objects.

This matters particularly for streaming:

```text
master.m3u8
segment001
segment002
segment003
...
```

Generating separate signed URLs for hundreds of segments may be unnecessarily cumbersome.

---

# 88. Signed URL vs Signed Cookie

```text
Single object
    │
    ▼
Signed URL

Multiple related protected objects
    │
    ▼
Signed Cookie
```

The exact mechanism should follow the delivery pattern.

---

# 89. URL Expiration

Shorter expiry reduces exposure but increases renewal frequency.

Longer expiry improves convenience but increases sharing risk.

Expiry should therefore depend on:

```text
Asset sensitivity
Session duration
Streaming requirements
User experience
```

---

# 90. Signed URLs Are Not DRM

A signed URL controls initial access.

It does **not** guarantee that an authorized user cannot:

```text
Download
Copy
Screen record
Redistribute
```

This distinction matters.

---

# 91. Content Protection Reality

There is no architecture that can perfectly prevent an authorized user from capturing content displayed on their device.

Claims of:

```text
100% download prevention
```

are unrealistic.

Mediverse should distinguish access control from perfect copying prevention.

---

# 92. DRM Evaluation

If premium video content requires stronger controls, DRM may be evaluated.

Possible architecture:

```text
Encrypted Stream
      │
      ▼
DRM License
      │
      ▼
Authorized Player
```

But DRM introduces:

```text
Cost
Player complexity
Browser/device compatibility
License infrastructure
Operational burden
```

It should be requirement-driven.

---

# 93. Cache-Control

Immutable public/static assets can use aggressive caching.

Conceptually:

```text
Cache-Control:
public, max-age=..., immutable
```

Protected assets require policies consistent with authorization and privacy.

---

# 94. Immutable Asset URLs

Best CDN behavior:

```text
/content/v1/hash-or-version/file
```

Then when content changes:

```text
/content/v2/...
```

instead of overwriting v1.

---

# 95. CDN Invalidation

Sometimes content must be removed or corrected immediately.

Then:

```text
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
Invalidate Path
```

may be necessary.

But routine deployment should not depend on massive invalidations.

---

# 96. Why Excessive Invalidation Is Bad

Frequent invalidation suggests poor cache identity.

Prefer:

```text
New content
=
New URL
```

where possible.

---

# 97. CDN Cache Key

Cache identity may consider:

```text
Path
Query parameters
Headers
Cookies
```

Adding unnecessary dimensions reduces cache hit ratio.

---

# 98. Cache-Key Explosion

Bad:

```text
Asset URL
+
Unique user ID
=
Unique CDN cache entry per student
```

This destroys CDN efficiency.

Authorization and cache identity should be designed separately where possible.

---

# 99. Query Parameters

Only query parameters that genuinely alter representation should normally influence cache identity.

Tracking parameters should not automatically create distinct cached objects.

---

# 100. Hot Assets

A newly released lecture may suddenly receive:

```text
10 requests
100 requests
10,000 requests
```

CDN caching protects the origin from repeated identical delivery.

---

# 101. Origin Shielding

For sufficiently large global traffic, an additional centralized caching layer/origin-shield strategy may reduce repeated origin fetches.

This should be introduced based on measured traffic, not speculation.

---

# 102. Geographic Delivery

CloudFront edge locations can improve latency for geographically distributed students.

But application APIs, databases and dynamic content still require separate regional architecture.

CDN does not make the entire application globally distributed.

---

# 103. Encryption at Rest

S3 assets must use approved server-side encryption.

Potential choices include:

```text
SSE-S3
SSE-KMS
```

Selection depends on security and key-management requirements.

---

# 104. SSE-S3

SSE-S3 provides managed encryption at rest with comparatively low operational complexity.

It may be sufficient for asset classes without dedicated KMS governance requirements.

---

# 105. SSE-KMS

SSE-KMS provides additional key-control and audit capabilities.

It may be preferred where requirements demand:

```text
Explicit key policies
Key-level audit
Controlled key ownership
Separation of duties
```

---

# 106. KMS Is Not Free Complexity

Using a customer-managed key for every conceivable object class can create:

```text
Policy complexity
API cost
Operational dependencies
Quota pressure
Key-management burden
```

Use KMS deliberately.

---

# 107. Tenant Encryption

A separate KMS key per tenant should not be assumed automatically.

It may be appropriate for specific enterprise contractual requirements, but it materially increases lifecycle and operational complexity.

Logical tenant isolation remains mandatory regardless of key strategy.

---

# 108. Encryption in Transit

All upload and delivery traffic should use TLS.

```text
Client
  │ HTTPS
  ▼
CloudFront / S3 / API
```

Plain HTTP should not be accepted for protected production content.

---

# 109. Metadata Privacy

Even when object bytes are encrypted, metadata may expose information.

Avoid keys such as:

```text
/HIV-patient/john-smith/...
```

Sensitive meaning should not be unnecessarily encoded in object names.

---

# 110. Event Notification Architecture

Infrastructure events may feed a queue:

```text
S3
 │
 ▼
Event Notification
 │
 ▼
Queue
 │
 ▼
Processing Worker
```

A queue decouples upload rate from processing capacity.

---

# 111. Why Queue Processing?

Suppose:

```text
1,000 videos uploaded
```

while workers can process:

```text
20 concurrently
```

A queue absorbs the difference.

Without backpressure, workers or downstream services may collapse.

---

# 112. Processing Concurrency

Concurrency should be controlled by:

```text
Asset type
CPU
Memory
GPU
Transcoder capacity
External quotas
Cost
```

More parallelism is not automatically better.

---

# 113. Processing Retry

Transient processing failures may retry.

Example:

```text
Job
 │
 ▼
Worker
 │
 ✕
 ▼
Retry with backoff
```

Retries must be bounded.

---

# 114. Processing Dead-Letter Path

After repeated failure:

```text
Processing Queue
      │
      ▼
Retries exhausted
      │
      ▼
DLT / Failure Queue
      │
      ▼
Investigation / Replay
```

The asset should transition to a clear failure state.

---

# 115. Transcoding Infrastructure

Video transcoding is computationally expensive.

Mediverse should evaluate managed media-processing services rather than building an entire transcoding platform inside Kubernetes by default.

---

# 116. MediaConvert Evaluation

For AWS-centric deployment, a managed transcoding service such as AWS Elemental MediaConvert is a reasonable architectural candidate for:

```text
HLS packaging
Resolution variants
Codec conversion
Audio tracks
Thumbnails
```

The exact adoption remains workload/cost driven.

---

# 117. Lambda vs Containers

Small transformations:

```text
Metadata extraction
Thumbnail generation
Lightweight validation
```

may suit short-lived serverless execution.

Heavy workloads:

```text
Complex 3D processing
Large media manipulation
Long CPU jobs
GPU workloads
```

may require containers or specialized managed services.

---

# 118. Do Not Force Everything Into Lambda

A 30-minute 3D optimization pipeline should not be forced into a serverless function merely because S3 can trigger one.

Compute choice must follow workload characteristics.

---

# 119. Asset Service

Mediverse should expose an explicit Asset/Media Service boundary.

Responsibilities:

```text
Asset metadata
Upload authorization
Upload sessions
Lifecycle
Access authorization
Delivery resolution
Processing status
Deletion orchestration
```

It should not necessarily perform all binary processing itself.

---

# 120. Asset API

Representative APIs may include:

```text
POST   /assets/uploads
POST   /assets/{id}/complete
GET    /assets/{id}
GET    /assets/{id}/status
GET    /assets/{id}/access
DELETE /assets/{id}
```

Exact contracts belong in the ADS.

---

# 121. Upload Session

Large uploads benefit from an explicit session:

```text
Create Upload Session
       │
       ▼
Receive assetId
       │
       ▼
Upload parts
       │
       ▼
Complete
       │
       ▼
Verify
```

This creates a clean application-level lifecycle.

---

# 122. Upload Completion Verification

Never accept:

```text
Client says upload completed
```

as sufficient evidence.

The backend/processing workflow should verify the expected object exists and matches required properties.

---

# 123. Checksum Verification

Where appropriate:

```text
Expected Checksum
       │
       ▼
Uploaded Object
       │
       ▼
Verify
```

This protects against corruption and supports integrity guarantees.

---

# 124. Resumable Upload

For unreliable/mobile networks:

```text
Upload
  │
  ✕ network failure
  │
  ▼
Resume remaining parts
```

is far better UX than restarting a multi-gigabyte lecture.

Multipart architecture enables this.

---

# 125. Status API

Processing may take minutes.

Therefore:

```text
GET /assets/{id}/status
```

might return:

```json
{
  "status": "PROCESSING"
}
```

rather than holding the original request open.

---

# 126. Event Notification to UI

Where justified:

```text
Processing Complete
      │
      ▼
Backend Event
      │
      ▼
WebSocket / SSE / Notification
      │
      ▼
Faculty UI
```

can reduce polling.

Do not add real-time infrastructure if simple polling adequately meets the requirement.

---

# 127. Cleanup Jobs

Scheduled reconciliation may handle:

```text
Expired upload sessions
Abandoned multipart uploads
Orphan objects
Failed processing artifacts
Expired temporary exports
Deletion candidates
```

Cleanup is part of the architecture, not an afterthought.

---

# 128. Backup Philosophy

Remember:

```text
S3 durability
≠
Complete backup strategy
```

Accidental application deletion, malicious actions or logical corruption still require recovery controls.

---

# 129. Versioning + Replication

Depending on recovery requirements:

```text
S3 Versioning
+
Replication
+
Retention controls
```

may provide layered protection.

---

# 130. Cross-Region Replication

For sufficiently strict disaster-recovery requirements:

```text
Primary Region S3
       │
       ▼
Replication
       │
       ▼
Secondary Region S3
```

can reduce asset recovery risk.

It should be justified by RPO/RTO and cost.

---

# 131. Replication Is Not Backup

A bad deletion or corruption may also propagate.

Therefore:

```text
Replication
≠
Immutable historical recovery
```

Recovery architecture must consider the actual failure scenarios.

---

# 132. Asset RPO

RPO asks:

> How much recently uploaded asset data can Mediverse tolerate losing?

For critical published content, the answer may approach zero.

Temporary uploads may tolerate more.

---

# 133. Asset RTO

RTO asks:

> How long can asset delivery remain unavailable?

Different services may have different objectives:

```text
Public images
Course PDFs
Lecture video
3D models
Faculty uploads
```

---

# 134. DR Architecture

Conceptually:

```text
Primary Region
 ├── PostgreSQL metadata
 ├── S3
 └── CloudFront Origin
        │
        ▼
Disaster
        │
        ▼
Secondary Recovery
 ├── Metadata recovery
 ├── Asset recovery
 └── Delivery restoration
```

Metadata and binaries must remain consistent enough to recover together.

---

# 135. Observability

Asset infrastructure should expose telemetry for:

```text
Uploads
Failures
Processing duration
Queue depth
Malware results
Storage growth
Delivery latency
CDN hit ratio
Origin requests
Bandwidth
4xx/5xx
```

---

# 136. Processing Metrics

Important metrics include:

```text
Jobs queued
Jobs running
Jobs completed
Jobs failed
Retry count
Processing latency
Queue age
```

Queue age is particularly important because a healthy worker count can still hide growing delays.

---

# 137. CDN Metrics

Monitor:

```text
Request volume
Cache hit ratio
Origin fetches
4xx
5xx
Bytes transferred
Latency
Geographic traffic
```

A low cache hit ratio on highly reusable content should trigger investigation.

---

# 138. Storage Metrics

Track:

```text
Total bytes
Object count
Asset class
Environment
Storage tier
Growth rate
Incomplete uploads
Derived/original ratio
```

Without classification, cost optimization becomes guesswork.

---

# 139. Cost Model

Digital asset cost roughly includes:

```text
Storage
+
Requests
+
Processing
+
Transcoding
+
CDN delivery
+
Internet egress
+
Replication
+
Encryption/key operations
```

The largest bill may not be S3 storage itself.

---

# 140. Video Cost

Video is particularly expensive because it combines:

```text
Large storage
Transcoding
Multiple renditions
High bandwidth
Long consumption sessions
```

Architecture should track cost per delivered hour where useful.

---

# 141. 3D Cost

3D assets can similarly become expensive through:

```text
Large textures
Large models
Repeated downloads
Multiple LODs
Processing
```

Optimization directly affects both performance and cost.

---

# 142. Egress Optimization

The main strategy is not:

```text
Compress the API response harder
```

but:

```text
Efficient formats
      +
Asset optimization
      +
CDN caching
      +
Adaptive streaming
      +
Correct cache lifetime
```

---

# 143. Asset Testing

Testing should cover:

```text
Authorization
Upload limits
MIME spoofing
Malformed files
Malware workflow
Multipart upload
Interrupted upload
Checksum mismatch
Processing retry
Duplicate events
Private delivery
Signed URL expiry
Deletion
Orphan cleanup
CDN behavior
```

---

# 144. Security Testing

Explicitly test attempts to:

```text
Upload executable disguised as image
Access another tenant's asset
Modify object key
Reuse expired URL
Bypass CloudFront
Upload oversized file
Inject path-like filename
Access quarantined content
Retrieve faculty-only material
```

---

# 145. Chaos Testing

Failure scenarios should include:

```text
S3 temporarily unavailable
Processing worker crash
Queue backlog
Transcoder failure
Malware scanner failure
Database unavailable
CDN origin failure
Duplicate infrastructure event
Partial multipart upload
```

The system should fail predictably.

---

# 146. Asset Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Large binaries stored in PostgreSQL by default
❌ Videos streamed through Spring Boot Pods
❌ Multi-GB uploads proxied through application Pods without need
❌ Public production S3 buckets
❌ Client-controlled arbitrary object keys
❌ Trusting file extensions
❌ Trusting client Content-Type
❌ Making uploaded content immediately public
❌ Skipping malware scanning for untrusted uploads
❌ Synchronous video transcoding inside HTTP requests
❌ Using one source MP4 as complete streaming architecture
❌ Treating S3 ObjectCreated as a business event
❌ Non-idempotent processing consumers
❌ Raw S3 URLs stored throughout domain tables
❌ PII embedded in object keys
❌ Overwriting published assets under the same CDN URL
❌ Massive routine CloudFront invalidations
❌ Unique CDN cache entry per user without necessity
❌ Assuming signed URLs prevent copying
❌ Claiming screen recording can be completely prevented
❌ Using DRM without a real business requirement
❌ Permanent abandoned multipart uploads
❌ Immediate destructive orphan cleanup
❌ Unlimited processing concurrency
❌ Infinite retries
❌ Heavy transcoding forced into Kubernetes without justification
❌ Heavy workloads forced into Lambda without workload analysis
❌ Treating replication as backup
❌ No asset lifecycle/status model
❌ No cleanup architecture
❌ No asset cost attribution
```

---

# 147. Upload Decision Flow

```text
                    UPLOAD REQUEST
                          │
                          ▼
                     Authenticate
                          │
                          ▼
                      Authorize
                          │
                          ▼
                  Validate Intent
                          │
                          ▼
                  Create Asset Record
                          │
                          ▼
                     Asset Size?
                    ┌─────┴─────┐
                    ▼           ▼
                  SMALL        LARGE
                    │           │
                    ▼           ▼
               Presigned     Multipart
                 Upload       Upload
                    │           │
                    └─────┬─────┘
                          ▼
                    Verify Object
                          │
                          ▼
                      Quarantine
                          │
                          ▼
                    Malware Scan
                    ┌─────┴─────┐
                    ▼           ▼
                  CLEAN      INFECTED
                    │           │
                    ▼           ▼
                Validate      Reject
                    │
                    ▼
                 Process
                    │
                    ▼
                  READY
```

---

# 148. Delivery Decision Flow

```text
                     ASSET REQUEST
                          │
                          ▼
                     Asset Lookup
                          │
                          ▼
                     Visibility?
             ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
             ▼            ▼             ▼
           PUBLIC    AUTHENTICATED   RESTRICTED
             │            │             │
             │            ▼             ▼
             │       Authenticate    Authorize
             │            │             │
             └────────────┼─────────────┘
                          ▼
                   Delivery Policy
                          │
               ┌──────────┴──────────┐
               ▼                     ▼
          Single Object        Protected Stream
               │                     │
               ▼                     ▼
          Signed URL          Signed Cookie /
                              Stream Policy
               │                     │
               └──────────┬──────────┘
                          ▼
                      CloudFront
                          │
                          ▼
                      Private S3
```

---

# 149. Final Reference Architecture

```text
                       MEDIVERSE CLIENT
                              │
              ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
              │                                │
              ▼                                ▼
        CONTROL PLANE                     DATA PLANE
              │                                │
              ▼                                │
        API Gateway                            │
              │                                │
              ▼                                │
         Asset Service                         │
              │                                │
       ┌──────┼─────────┐                      │
       ▼      ▼         ▼                      │
     Auth   Metadata   Upload Session           │
              │         │                      │
              ▼         ▼                      │
         PostgreSQL  Presigned Upload           │
                        │                      │
                        └──────────┐           │
                                   ▼           │
                                  S3 ◄─────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼
                              Quarantine
                                   │
                                   ▼
                             Malware Scan
                                   │
                                   ▼
                          Processing Coordinator
                                   │
                ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
                ▼                  ▼                  ▼
              Image              Video                3D
            Processor          Transcoder          Processor
                │                  │                  │
                ▼                  ▼                  ▼
             Variants          HLS/DASH          GLB / LOD
                │                  │                  │
                └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                   ▼
                           Processed Asset Store
                                   │
                                   ▼
                              CloudFront
                                   │
                    ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
                    ▼                             ▼
                Public Assets              Private Assets
                                                  │
                                           Signed Access
                                                  │
                                                  ▼
                                               Student
```

Supporting event architecture:

```text
S3 Event
   │
   ▼
Processing Queue
   │
   ▼
Worker
   │
   ▼
Asset Metadata Update
   │
   ▼
Transactional Outbox
   │
   ▼
Kafka
   │
   ├──► Search Indexing
   ├──► Notification
   ├──► AI/RAG Ingestion
   └──► Analytics
```

This connects ADR-046 directly to the architecture already established in ADR-042 through ADR-045.

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                   | Decision                                  |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Binary source of truth | **Amazon S3**                             |
| Business metadata      | **PostgreSQL**                            |
| Asset identity         | Application-level UUID/ID                 |
| Large upload path      | Direct-to-S3                              |
| Upload authorization   | Backend-controlled                        |
| Large files            | Multipart upload                          |
| Public S3 access       | Disabled by default                       |
| Delivery               | **CloudFront**                            |
| Origin                 | Private S3                                |
| Private content        | Signed CDN access                         |
| Video delivery         | Adaptive streaming where required         |
| Video processing       | Asynchronous                              |
| 3D format              | glTF/GLB-oriented web pipeline            |
| Uploaded content       | Untrusted until validated                 |
| Malware scanning       | Required for applicable untrusted uploads |
| Published assets       | Prefer immutable/versioned objects        |
| Raw S3 URLs in domains | Avoid                                     |
| Asset references       | Stable asset/version IDs                  |
| Encryption             | Required                                  |
| CDN caching            | Version-aware                             |
| Processing             | Queue/event driven                        |
| Processing consumers   | Idempotent                                |
| Domain events          | Outbox + Kafka                            |
| Orphan cleanup         | Reconciliation + grace period             |
| Lifecycle policies     | Required                                  |
| DR                     | RPO/RTO driven                            |
| Observability          | Required                                  |
| Cost governance        | Required                                  |
| Asset Service          | Dedicated application boundary            |
| Status                 | **Accepted**                              |
| Priority               | **Critical**                              |

The architectural separation is now:

```text
PostgreSQL
=
Asset metadata / business truth

S3
=
Binary truth

CloudFront
=
Scalable asset delivery

Processing Pipeline
=
Derived representations

Kafka
=
Business integration

OpenSearch
=
Searchable projection

AI Platform
=
AI/RAG consumption
```

# ADR-046 — COMPLETE ✅

The recent architecture sequence is now:

```text
ADR-040  API Gateway                                      ✅
ADR-041  Service Communication                            ✅
ADR-042  Distributed Consistency & Event Reliability      ✅
ADR-043  Enterprise Caching & Redis                       ✅
ADR-044  Enterprise Search & Semantic Retrieval           ✅
ADR-045  Enterprise AI Platform, RAG & Agents             ✅
ADR-046  File, Media, Object Storage & CDN                ✅
```

## Next — ADR-047

### **ADR-047 — Enterprise Observability, OpenTelemetry, Logging, Metrics, Tracing, Alerting & SRE Architecture**

This should come next. At this stage Mediverse has PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, OpenSearch, AI workflows, S3/CDN, asynchronous processing and many microservices. Without a unified observability architecture, troubleshooting this system would become guesswork.

ADR-047 should establish **observability principles → logs vs metrics vs traces → OpenTelemetry → instrumentation standards → correlation IDs → trace/span propagation → W3C Trace Context → Spring Boot/Micrometer → Kubernetes telemetry → structured JSON logging → centralized log pipeline → CloudWatch/ELK/OpenSearch evaluation → log levels → PII/secrets redaction → log retention → Prometheus → metric naming → labels/cardinality → RED/USE methods → histograms → business metrics → Kafka metrics → PostgreSQL → Redis → OpenSearch → S3/media processing → AI observability → RAG traces → token/cost/quality metrics → distributed tracing → sampling → tail sampling → baggage → Grafana dashboards → service dashboards → golden signals → SLIs → SLOs → error budgets → alert design → symptom vs cause alerts → Alertmanager/on-call integration → severity → escalation → runbook links → synthetic monitoring → health/readiness/liveness boundaries → black-box monitoring → frontend RUM → Core Web Vitals → Kubernetes/node/container observability → audit logs vs operational logs → security telemetry → observability access control → retention → high-cardinality cost controls → telemetry pipeline resilience → collector architecture → multi-environment isolation → incident investigation workflow → observability testing → anti-patterns → final Mediverse observability reference architecture.**

# ADR-047 — Enterprise Observability, OpenTelemetry, Logging, Metrics, Distributed Tracing, Alerting & SRE Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-047
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-047 defines how Mediverse observes, diagnoses and operates the distributed platform established by the preceding architecture decisions.

Mediverse now contains:

```text
React / Web Clients
API Gateway
Spring Boot Microservices
PostgreSQL
Redis
Kafka
OpenSearch
AI / RAG Platform
S3
CloudFront
Media Processing
Kubernetes
External Dependencies
```

At this complexity level, logs alone are insufficient.

The architectural question is:

> **How should Mediverse build a unified observability platform that allows engineers to understand what is happening across thousands of distributed requests, detect failures before users report them, correlate logs/metrics/traces across services, define measurable reliability objectives, and operate the platform without drowning in telemetry noise and cost?**

---

# 1. Monitoring vs Observability

These terms are related but not identical.

Monitoring asks:

```text
Is the system healthy?
Is CPU high?
Is the API returning errors?
```

Observability asks:

```text
Why is checkout/search/tutoring slow?

Which dependency caused it?

Which tenant/users are affected?

Where did the request spend its time?

What changed?
```

Monitoring detects known conditions.

Observability helps investigate both known and unexpected conditions.

---

# 2. The Three Primary Telemetry Signals

Mediverse shall standardize around:

```text
                 OBSERVABILITY
                      │
         ┌────────────┼────────────┐
         ▼            ▼            ▼
       LOGS         METRICS       TRACES
```

Each solves a different problem.

---

# 3. Logs

Logs describe discrete events.

Example:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "...",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "course-service",
  "traceId": "...",
  "message": "Course retrieval failed"
}
```

Logs provide detailed diagnostic context.

---

# 4. Metrics

Metrics represent numeric measurements over time.

Examples:

```text
http_requests_total

http_request_duration_seconds

jvm_memory_used_bytes

kafka_consumer_lag

database_connections_active
```

Metrics are efficient for:

```text
Dashboards
Alerting
Trend analysis
SLO calculations
Capacity planning
```

---

# 5. Traces

Distributed traces show the path of a request through multiple components.

```text
Student
   │
   ▼
API Gateway
   │
   ▼
Course Service
   │
   ├──► Redis
   │
   └──► PostgreSQL
```

Each operation becomes a span.

Together they form a trace.

---

# 6. Why All Three?

Suppose students report:

```text
Course page takes 8 seconds.
```

Metrics reveal:

```text
p95 latency increased.
```

Trace reveals:

```text
Course Service
   │
   └── PostgreSQL query = 7.2 seconds
```

Logs reveal:

```text
Query timeout / execution details.
```

The signals complement one another.

---

# 7. Core Decision

Mediverse shall adopt **OpenTelemetry** as the primary vendor-neutral telemetry instrumentation standard.

Conceptually:

```text
Applications
     │
     ▼
OpenTelemetry
     │
     ▼
OTel Collector
     │
 ┌───┼───────────────┐
 ▼   ▼               ▼
Logs Metrics        Traces
```

---

# 8. Why OpenTelemetry?

Without standardization:

```text
Service A → Vendor SDK A

Service B → Vendor SDK B

Service C → Custom tracing

Service D → Different metrics
```

This creates observability coupling and inconsistency.

OpenTelemetry provides a common instrumentation and telemetry model.

---

# 9. Vendor Neutrality

Application instrumentation should not be unnecessarily tied to:

```text
Grafana
Datadog
New Relic
AWS
Elastic
```

The backend may change.

Instrumentation should survive that change wherever practical.

---

# 10. OpenTelemetry Architecture

```text
Spring Boot Services
        │
        ▼
OpenTelemetry SDK / Instrumentation
        │
        ▼
OTLP
        │
        ▼
OpenTelemetry Collector
        │
        ├──► Metrics Backend
        ├──► Trace Backend
        └──► Log Backend
```

The collector becomes a telemetry processing layer.

---

# 11. Collector Responsibilities

The OpenTelemetry Collector may perform:

```text
Receive
Batch
Filter
Transform
Enrich
Sample
Redact
Export
```

telemetry.

Application Pods should not need direct integrations with every observability backend.

---

# 12. Collector Deployment

A Kubernetes environment may use multiple collector roles.

Conceptually:

```text
Application Pods
      │
      ▼
Node / Agent Collectors
      │
      ▼
Gateway Collectors
      │
      ▼
Observability Backends
```

The exact topology should depend on telemetry volume and reliability requirements.

---

# 13. Collector Is Infrastructure

Do not embed the collector into every application container.

Preferred:

```text
Application
     │
     ▼
OTLP
     │
     ▼
Collector Infrastructure
```

This preserves separation of concerns.

---

# 14. Telemetry Resource Attributes

Every telemetry item should identify its origin.

Core attributes should include concepts such as:

```text
service.name
service.version
deployment.environment
cloud.region
k8s.namespace.name
```

where appropriate.

---

# 15. Service Naming Standard

Avoid:

```text
service
backend
app1
spring-app
```

Use stable canonical names:

```text
auth-service
course-service
assessment-service
search-service
asset-service
ai-platform
```

Dashboards and alerts depend heavily on consistent naming.

---

# 16. Environment Attribute

Telemetry must distinguish:

```text
DEV
UAT1
UAT2
STAGING
PRODUCTION
```

A production alert should never be confused with a UAT failure.

---

# 17. Correlation ID

Every inbound request should receive or propagate a correlation identifier.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Gateway
  │ correlation-id
  ▼
Service A
  │
  ▼
Service B
```

This supports operational investigation.

---

# 18. Trace ID vs Correlation ID

With distributed tracing, the trace ID already provides powerful request correlation.

Do not create unnecessary duplicate identifiers without a concrete requirement.

Conceptually:

```text
traceId
=
Distributed technical request identity
```

A separate business correlation ID may still be useful for workflows spanning multiple traces/events.

---

# 19. W3C Trace Context

HTTP trace propagation should use standardized W3C Trace Context.

Conceptually:

```text
traceparent
tracestate
```

rather than inventing proprietary tracing headers across Mediverse.

---

# 20. Trace Propagation

Suppose:

```text
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Course Service
   │
   ▼
Content Service
```

all spans should share the same trace.

```text
Trace ABC
 ├── Gateway
 ├── Course Service
 └── Content Service
```

---

# 21. Broken Trace Propagation

If one service fails to propagate trace context:

```text
Trace ABC
 ├── Gateway
 └── Course Service

Trace XYZ
 └── Content Service
```

the end-to-end request becomes fragmented.

Propagation testing is therefore important.

---

# 22. Kafka Trace Propagation

Tracing does not stop at HTTP.

```text
Course Service
      │
      ▼
Kafka
      │
      ▼
Indexer
```

trace context can be propagated through message metadata/headers where appropriate.

---

# 23. Asynchronous Trace Semantics

Do not pretend asynchronous workflows behave exactly like synchronous HTTP calls.

A Kafka consumer may process an event:

```text
seconds
minutes
hours
```

later.

Trace relationships should represent asynchronous causality correctly rather than manufacturing misleading parent-child timing.

---

# 24. Span

A span represents one operation.

Example:

```text
HTTP GET /courses/{id}
```

or:

```text
SELECT course
```

or:

```text
Redis GET
```

---

# 25. Span Attributes

Useful span attributes may include:

```text
HTTP method
Route
Status code
Database system
Messaging destination
Service name
Error status
```

Avoid sensitive or uncontrolled values.

---

# 26. Span Naming

Bad:

```text
GET /courses/123
GET /courses/456
GET /courses/789
```

Better:

```text
GET /courses/{courseId}
```

Dynamic IDs in span names create unnecessary cardinality.

---

# 27. Cardinality

Cardinality is one of the most important observability cost concepts.

Low cardinality:

```text
status = SUCCESS | FAILURE
```

High cardinality:

```text
userId = millions of possible values
```

High-cardinality dimensions can dramatically increase telemetry cost and backend load.

---

# 28. Never Use User IDs as Metric Labels

Bad:

```text
requests_total{
  user_id="123456"
}
```

This can create millions of metric series.

Use logs/traces/audit systems when individual request investigation is required.

---

# 29. Metric Labels

Good labels typically include bounded values such as:

```text
service
environment
method
route
status_class
region
```

provided their cardinality remains controlled.

---

# 30. Metric Naming

Metric names must be:

```text
Consistent
Meaningful
Unit-aware
Stable
```

Avoid multiple teams creating:

```text
request_time
api_latency
http_speed
response_duration
```

for the same concept.

---

# 31. Counters

Counters monotonically increase.

Example:

```text
http_requests_total
```

Useful for counting:

```text
Requests
Errors
Events
Retries
Jobs
```

---

# 32. Gauges

Gauges represent values that rise and fall.

Examples:

```text
active_connections

queue_depth

memory_usage

running_jobs
```

---

# 33. Histograms

Histograms are critical for latency.

Instead of:

```text
average latency = 200 ms
```

measure distributions.

Then derive:

```text
p50
p90
p95
p99
```

---

# 34. Average Latency Can Mislead

Suppose:

```text
99 requests = 100 ms

1 request = 20 sec
```

Average latency can hide severe tail behavior.

Students experiencing those slow requests do not care that the average looks healthy.

---

# 35. RED Method

For request-driven services, monitor:

```text
R = Rate
E = Errors
D = Duration
```

Example:

```text
course-service

Rate      → requests/sec
Errors    → error rate
Duration  → p95 latency
```

---

# 36. USE Method

For infrastructure resources:

```text
U = Utilization
S = Saturation
E = Errors
```

Useful for:

```text
CPU
Memory
Disk
Network
Connection pools
```

---

# 37. Golden Signals

Mediverse shall use the classic operational signals:

```text
Latency
Traffic
Errors
Saturation
```

as a baseline.

---

# 38. Technical vs Business Metrics

Technical:

```text
HTTP requests
CPU
Kafka lag
DB latency
```

Business:

```text
Course enrollments
Assessment submissions
Video processing completions
AI tutor sessions
```

Both matter.

---

# 39. Business Metrics Warning

Do not turn Prometheus into an analytics warehouse.

Metrics should support operational decisions.

Detailed product analytics belongs in the analytics platform.

---

# 40. Spring Boot Observability

Spring Boot services should standardize instrumentation using:

```text
Spring Boot Actuator
Micrometer
OpenTelemetry integration
```

rather than each service implementing custom telemetry frameworks.

---

# 41. Actuator

Actuator provides operational endpoints and instrumentation hooks for:

```text
Health
Metrics
Application state
```

But actuator endpoints require security controls.

---

# 42. Actuator Security

Never expose every management endpoint publicly.

```text
Internet
   │
   X
/actuator/*
```

Management access should follow network and authentication policies.

---

# 43. JVM Metrics

Monitor:

```text
Heap
Non-heap
GC
Threads
Class loading
CPU
```

for Spring Boot workloads.

---

# 44. GC Monitoring

A service may show:

```text
CPU normal
HTTP latency high
```

while suffering excessive garbage collection.

GC metrics can expose this.

---

# 45. Connection Pool Metrics

For PostgreSQL-backed services:

```text
Active
Idle
Pending
Maximum
Timeouts
```

should be monitored.

Connection pool exhaustion can appear as application latency.

---

# 46. PostgreSQL Observability

Monitor:

```text
Connections
Query latency
Slow queries
Locks
Deadlocks
Cache hit behavior
Replication lag
Storage
CPU
I/O
```

according to deployment architecture.

---

# 47. Database Query Tracing

Traces may identify:

```text
Course Service
    │
    ▼
PostgreSQL
    │
    ▼
2.7 sec
```

But SQL telemetry must not expose sensitive parameter values unnecessarily.

---

# 48. Redis Observability

From ADR-043, monitor:

```text
Hit ratio
Misses
Latency
Memory
Evictions
Connections
Keyspace behavior
Replication
```

---

# 49. Cache Hit Ratio

A cache with:

```text
5% hit rate
```

may be adding infrastructure complexity without meaningful benefit.

Metrics should validate caching assumptions.

---

# 50. Kafka Observability

Critical Kafka telemetry includes:

```text
Producer errors
Consumer lag
Consumer throughput
Broker health
Partition state
Under-replicated partitions
Request latency
DLT growth
```

---

# 51. Consumer Lag

Consumer lag answers:

```text
How far behind is processing?
```

Example:

```text
Produced offset: 1,000,000
Consumed offset:   950,000

Lag = 50,000
```

Lag growth can indicate overloaded or failed consumers.

---

# 52. Lag Alone Is Insufficient

A lag of:

```text
10,000
```

could mean:

```text
1 second behind
```

or:

```text
2 hours behind
```

depending on throughput.

Monitor both lag count and age/time delay where possible.

---

# 53. OpenSearch Observability

ADR-044 requires monitoring:

```text
Query latency
Indexing latency
Rejected requests
Shard health
Disk
Heap
GC
Search failures
Indexing failures
Kafka indexing lag
```

---

# 54. Search Quality Observability

Infrastructure can report:

```text
HTTP 200
```

while search relevance is terrible.

Therefore search also needs quality signals such as:

```text
Zero-result rate
Click-through behavior
Retrieval metrics
```

from ADR-044.

---

# 55. S3 / Media Observability

ADR-046 introduced:

```text
Uploads
Processing
Scanning
Transcoding
CDN delivery
```

Monitor the full asset lifecycle.

---

# 56. Media Processing Metrics

Examples:

```text
processing_queue_depth

processing_duration

processing_failure_rate

transcoding_jobs_active

asset_ready_latency
```

---

# 57. Asset Ready Latency

A useful product-facing metric:

```text
Upload completed
      │
      ▼
Asset READY
```

Measure the elapsed time.

This is more meaningful than monitoring worker CPU alone.

---

# 58. CloudFront Observability

Monitor:

```text
Requests
Cache hit ratio
Origin requests
4xx
5xx
Bytes transferred
Latency
```

from ADR-046.

---

# 59. AI Observability

ADR-045 requires a dedicated AI telemetry layer.

Monitor:

```text
Model calls
Latency
Tokens
Cost
Failures
Timeouts
Safety blocks
Fallbacks
RAG retrieval
Tool calls
```

---

# 60. AI Trace

An AI request may produce:

```text
AI Tutor Request
      │
      ├── Authorization
      ├── Query Processing
      ├── OpenSearch Retrieval
      ├── Reranking
      ├── Prompt Construction
      ├── LLM Invocation
      ├── Validation
      └── Response
```

This should appear as one correlated operational trace where practical.

---

## ADR-047 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The architecture established so far is:

```text
                         MEDIVERSE
                             │
           ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
           ▼                 ▼                 ▼
     Spring Boot           Kafka          Infrastructure
           │                 │                 │
           └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                             ▼
                       OpenTelemetry
                             │
                             ▼
                    OTel Collectors
                             │
              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
              ▼              ▼              ▼
             LOGS          METRICS         TRACES
              │              │              │
              └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                             ▼
                       Visualization
                             │
                             ▼
                       Alerting / SRE
```

The primary correlation model is:

```text
                       Trace ID
                          │
          ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼               ▼                ▼
       Gateway        Service A        Service B
                          │
                 ┌────────┼─────────┐
                 ▼        ▼         ▼
              PostgreSQL Redis     Kafka
                                    │
                                    ▼
                                Consumer
```

And the initial operational model is:

```text
Application Services
      │
      ├── RED
      │   ├── Rate
      │   ├── Errors
      │   └── Duration
      │
Infrastructure
      │
      └── USE
          ├── Utilization
          ├── Saturation
          └── Errors
```

The most important rule established so far is:

> **Telemetry must help answer operational questions. Collecting more logs, metrics and traces is not automatically better observability; uncontrolled telemetry creates noise, high cardinality, storage cost and slower incident investigation.**

**Part 2** should continue from **Section 61 — AI Quality & Cost Telemetry**, then cover RAG quality traces, prompt/model version attributes, tool-call telemetry, structured logging, JSON logs, log levels, exception logging, stack traces, sensitive-data redaction, secrets, PII, audit logs vs application logs, centralized logging architecture, CloudWatch vs OpenSearch/Loki evaluation, retention, log sampling, trace sampling, head vs tail sampling, exemplar correlation, Prometheus architecture, scraping, ServiceMonitor, recording rules, federation/long-term metrics, Grafana dashboards, dashboard hierarchy, service golden dashboards, Kubernetes observability, kube-state-metrics, node/container telemetry, HPA signals, liveness/readiness/startup probes, synthetic monitoring, black-box probes, frontend RUM, Core Web Vitals, SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, burn-rate alerts, alert design, severity, symptom-vs-cause alerts, Alertmanager/on-call routing, escalation, runbooks, incident correlation, deployment/change markers, security telemetry, observability RBAC, telemetry retention, collector resilience, backpressure, observability during observability failure, cost governance, testing, anti-patterns and the final Mediverse enterprise observability + SRE reference architecture.


# ADR-047 — Enterprise Observability, OpenTelemetry, Logging, Metrics, Distributed Tracing, Alerting & SRE Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — AI Trace**.

---

# 61. AI Quality & Cost Telemetry

Traditional observability tells us whether the AI request succeeded technically.

That is insufficient.

```text
HTTP 200
Model responded
Latency = 1.8s
```

does **not** mean:

```text
Answer correct
Answer grounded
Citation correct
Answer safe
Cost acceptable
```

AI requires additional quality and economic telemetry.

---

# 62. AI Operational Metrics

Track:

```text
ai_requests_total

ai_request_duration

ai_errors_total

ai_timeouts_total

ai_fallback_total

ai_input_tokens

ai_output_tokens

ai_cost

ai_safety_blocks_total
```

Dimensions must remain cardinality-controlled.

---

# 63. Model Identity

AI telemetry should identify:

```text
provider
model
modelVersion
feature
environment
```

where operationally useful.

This allows comparison such as:

```text
Model A
p95 = 1.2 sec

Model B
p95 = 4.8 sec
```

---

# 64. Prompt Version Telemetry

From ADR-045, prompts are versioned artifacts.

Telemetry should therefore correlate:

```text
Feature
   │
   ▼
Prompt Version
   │
   ▼
Model Version
   │
   ▼
Outcome
```

This is essential when a prompt deployment causes quality regression.

---

# 65. Do Not Log Full Prompts by Default

A prompt may contain:

```text
Student information
Conversation history
Retrieved course content
Assessment answers
System instructions
```

Therefore:

```text
promptVersion = v17
```

is usually safer operational metadata than indiscriminately storing the complete prompt.

---

# 66. RAG Telemetry

A RAG trace should expose stages such as:

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Query Processing
   │
   ▼
Retrieval
   │
   ▼
Reranking
   │
   ▼
Context Building
   │
   ▼
Generation
```

This allows engineers to determine whether a poor answer originated from retrieval or generation.

---

# 67. Retrieval Telemetry

Useful operational attributes include:

```text
retrieved_document_count
retrieval_duration
reranking_duration
selected_chunk_count
zero_result
```

Quality evaluation remains governed by ADR-044 and ADR-045.

---

# 68. AI Tool Telemetry

Agent traces should show:

```text
Agent
 │
 ├── Search Tool
 ├── Course Tool
 ├── Progress Tool
 └── Draft Tool
```

including:

```text
Tool name
Duration
Result status
Retry
Authorization outcome
```

without leaking sensitive arguments.

---

# 69. Agent Loop Metrics

Monitor:

```text
agent_steps
tool_calls
agent_duration
agent_token_usage
agent_cost
agent_failures
human_approval_requests
```

Unexpectedly increasing step counts may indicate agent loops or degraded reasoning.

---

# 70. Structured Logging

Mediverse application logs shall be machine-readable structured events.

Preferred:

```json
{
```
