```json
  "timestamp": "2026-08-03T10:15:30Z",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "service": "course-service",
  "environment": "production",
  "traceId": "abc123",
  "event": "COURSE_FETCH_FAILED",
  "message": "Course retrieval failed"
}
```

instead of uncontrolled text.

---

# 71. Why JSON Logging?

Structured logs allow queries such as:

```text
service = course-service
AND
level = ERROR
AND
environment = production
```

without unreliable text parsing.

---

# 72. Common Log Schema

Core fields should be standardized.

For example:

```text
timestamp
severity
service
serviceVersion
environment
traceId
spanId
event
message
```

Optional domain-safe attributes may be added where justified.

---

# 73. Log Event Names

Stable event identifiers are valuable.

Example:

```text
ASSET_PROCESSING_FAILED
COURSE_PUBLICATION_FAILED
KAFKA_EVENT_RETRY
AI_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT
```

Humans can change message wording without breaking dashboards and searches.

---

# 74. Log Levels

Standard semantics:

```text
TRACE
DEBUG
INFO
WARN
ERROR
```

Teams must use them consistently.

---

# 75. INFO Abuse

Bad:

```text
INFO Entering method
INFO variable x = ...
INFO leaving method
```

across every request.

This creates enormous noise.

INFO should represent meaningful operational events.

---

# 76. DEBUG Logging

DEBUG may provide detailed diagnostics but should normally be disabled or tightly controlled in production.

Dynamic temporary enablement may be useful during incidents.

---

# 77. ERROR Logging

ERROR should indicate genuine failures requiring investigation or meaningful operational awareness.

If every expected 404 produces an ERROR, the signal becomes useless.

---

# 78. Exception Logging

Avoid logging the same exception at every layer.

Bad:

```text
Repository logs exception
    │
Service logs same exception
    │
Controller logs same exception
    │
Global handler logs same exception
```

One failure becomes four noisy events.

---

# 79. Stack Traces

Stack traces are valuable for unexpected failures.

But they are:

```text
Large
Expensive
Potentially sensitive
```

Use them where they improve diagnosis rather than for every expected business error.

---

# 80. Sensitive Data Redaction

Logs must not contain uncontrolled:

```text
Passwords
JWTs
API keys
Authorization headers
Session tokens
Secrets
Sensitive personal data
```

Logging policy must be enforced through code review, libraries and telemetry processing.

---

# 81. Never Log Credentials

This:

```text
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
```

must never become normal application telemetry.

Credential leakage into logging systems expands the security blast radius.

---

# 82. Request/Response Body Logging

Logging complete HTTP bodies is dangerous.

A body may contain:

```text
Student profile
Assessment answer
Password
AI prompt
Uploaded metadata
```

Body logging should be disabled by default and explicitly controlled.

---

# 83. Audit Logs vs Operational Logs

These are separate concerns.

```text
Operational Log
=
Why did software fail?

Audit Log
=
Who performed a consequential action?
```

Do not treat application logs as the authoritative audit trail.

---

# 84. Audit Event

Example:

```text
Faculty X
published
Assessment Y
at Time Z
```

Audit requirements may demand:

```text
Immutability
Longer retention
Restricted access
Integrity protection
```

beyond ordinary logs.

---

# 85. Centralized Logging

Architecture:

```text
Applications
     │
     ▼
Log Collection
     │
     ▼
Central Log Backend
     │
     ▼
Search / Dashboards
```

Engineers should not SSH into individual Pods to investigate production.

---

# 86. Pods Are Ephemeral

A Kubernetes Pod can disappear.

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
Crash
 │
 ▼
Replacement Pod
```

If logs exist only on the container filesystem, evidence may disappear with it.

---

# 87. Log Backend Selection

Possible architectures include:

```text
CloudWatch Logs
OpenSearch
Grafana Loki
Managed observability platforms
```

The decision should consider:

```text
Search requirements
Retention
Scale
Cost
Operational complexity
Existing AWS architecture
Security
```

---

# 88. Do Not Automatically Use OpenSearch for Everything

Mediverse already uses OpenSearch for application search.

That does not mean the same cluster should automatically store enormous observability logs.

Search workloads and log workloads have different:

```text
Retention
Scaling
Index patterns
Failure characteristics
```

Separate architecture may be necessary.

---

# 89. Log Retention

Retention should vary by class.

Example:

```text
Debug/diagnostic logs
Operational logs
Security logs
Audit logs
```

A universal "keep everything forever" policy is expensive and often unnecessary.

---

# 90. Log Sampling

High-volume repetitive events may be sampled.

But never blindly sample:

```text
Security incidents
Rare errors
Audit events
```

Sampling policy must preserve important signals.

---

# 91. Distributed Trace Sampling

Tracing every request at massive scale can become expensive.

Therefore Mediverse shall support trace sampling.

```text
Requests
   │
   ▼
Sampling
 ┌─┴─┐
 ▼   ▼
Keep Drop
```

---

# 92. Head Sampling

Decision occurs near trace start.

Example:

```text
Keep 10%
```

Advantages:

```text
Simple
Low overhead
Predictable volume
```

Disadvantage:

An important failed trace may be discarded before the failure occurs.

---

# 93. Tail Sampling

Decision occurs after enough of the trace is observed.

This allows rules such as:

```text
Keep errors
Keep slow traces
Keep rare operations
Sample normal traffic
```

This provides richer control but requires more collector infrastructure.

---

# 94. Recommended Sampling Strategy

Production should prioritize retaining:

```text
Errors
High latency
Critical workflows
Rare conditions
```

while sampling routine successful traffic according to volume.

---

# 95. Exemplars

Metrics can reference representative traces.

Conceptually:

```text
p99 latency spike
       │
       ▼
Example Trace ID
       │
       ▼
Distributed Trace
```

This creates a powerful metrics → traces investigation path.

---

# 96. Prometheus Architecture

Prometheus should be the primary Kubernetes/service operational metrics model where appropriate.

```text
Applications
     │
     ▼
Metrics Endpoints
     │
     ▼
Prometheus
     │
     ▼
Grafana
```

OpenTelemetry can participate in the telemetry pipeline without eliminating Prometheus-native infrastructure requirements.

---

# 97. Metrics Scraping

Spring Boot applications expose approved metrics endpoints.

Prometheus discovers and scrapes them.

```text
course-service
      │
      ▼
/actuator/prometheus
      │
      ▼
Prometheus
```

Management endpoints remain network-controlled.

---

# 98. ServiceMonitor

Where the Prometheus Operator is used, resources such as:

```text
ServiceMonitor
PodMonitor
```

can declaratively define scraping targets.

This fits Kubernetes-native operations.

---

# 99. Recording Rules

Expensive or frequently used PromQL expressions can be precomputed.

Conceptually:

```text
Raw Metrics
    │
    ▼
Recording Rule
    │
    ▼
Precomputed Series
```

This improves dashboard/query efficiency.

---

# 100. Long-Term Metrics

Local Prometheus storage alone may not satisfy long retention or multi-cluster requirements.

At larger scale, evaluate systems such as:

```text
Thanos
Grafana Mimir
Managed Prometheus
```

based on requirements.

Do not add them before those requirements exist.

---

# 101. Grafana

Grafana should provide unified operational visualization across:

```text
Services
Infrastructure
Databases
Kafka
Search
Media
AI
SLOs
```

where corresponding data sources are available.

---

# 102. Dashboard Hierarchy

Avoid one giant dashboard containing 200 panels.

Prefer hierarchy:

```text
Platform Overview
       │
       ├── Service Overview
       ├── Kubernetes
       ├── PostgreSQL
       ├── Kafka
       ├── Redis
       ├── OpenSearch
       ├── Media
       └── AI
```

---

# 103. Service Golden Dashboard

Every production service should have a baseline dashboard showing:

```text
Request rate
Error rate
Latency
Resource saturation
Dependency health
Deployment version
```

This creates consistent first-line investigation.

---

# 104. Dashboard Variables

Useful bounded variables:

```text
Environment
Cluster
Namespace
Service
Region
```

allow the same dashboard design to serve multiple deployments.

---

# 105. Deployment Markers

Dashboards should display deployment/change events.

```text
Latency
   │
   │       ↑ deployment
   │       │
   └───────┼────────────
           │
           └── errors rise
```

This makes change correlation much faster.

---

# 106. Kubernetes Observability

Monitor:

```text
Cluster
Node
Namespace
Pod
Container
Deployment
StatefulSet
Job
HPA
Persistent Volume
```

not merely application endpoints.

---

# 107. kube-state-metrics

Kubernetes object-state telemetry can expose:

```text
Desired replicas
Available replicas
Pod states
Deployment status
Job status
Resource requests
Resource limits
```

for monitoring.

---

# 108. Node Metrics

Node-level monitoring should cover:

```text
CPU
Memory
Disk
Filesystem
Network
Load
```

to detect infrastructure saturation.

---

# 109. Container Metrics

Track:

```text
CPU usage
Memory usage
Throttling
Restarts
OOM kills
Network
```

Container restart count alone is not sufficient.

---

# 110. CPU Throttling

A Pod may have:

```text
CPU usage apparently below node capacity
```

while aggressive CPU limits cause throttling.

This can create unexplained application latency.

Monitor throttling when diagnosing performance.

---

# 111. OOMKill

If:

```text
Container memory
     │
     ▼
Limit exceeded
     │
     ▼
OOMKilled
```

Kubernetes restarts the container.

Telemetry should make the reason obvious.

---

# 112. HPA Observability

If Horizontal Pod Autoscaling is used, monitor:

```text
Current replicas
Desired replicas
Scaling metric
Scaling events
Maximum replicas
```

A service pinned at maximum replicas while latency rises indicates capacity problems.

---

# 113. Health Endpoints

Different health concepts must remain separate:

```text
Liveness
Readiness
Startup
```

They solve different Kubernetes problems.

---

# 114. Liveness Probe

Liveness asks:

> Is this process stuck or irrecoverably unhealthy such that Kubernetes should restart it?

Do not include every downstream dependency.

---

# 115. Bad Liveness Check

If liveness depends on PostgreSQL:

```text
PostgreSQL outage
      │
      ▼
Every application fails liveness
      │
      ▼
Kubernetes restarts everything
```

This makes an outage worse.

---

# 116. Readiness Probe

Readiness asks:

> Can this instance currently serve traffic correctly?

If not:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
Removed from Service endpoints
```

without necessarily restarting it.

---

# 117. Startup Probe

Slow-starting services can use startup probes to prevent premature liveness failures during initialization.

This is particularly useful when startup time legitimately varies.

---

# 118. Synthetic Monitoring

Internal metrics alone are insufficient.

Synthetic tests can periodically execute workflows such as:

```text
Open application
Login
Load course
Search chapter
```

to test user-visible availability.

---

# 119. Black-Box Monitoring

Black-box monitoring asks:

```text
Can the service be reached from outside?
Does DNS resolve?
Does TLS work?
Does HTTP respond?
```

rather than relying on internal application metrics.

---

# 120. Frontend Observability

Backend telemetry cannot explain every student experience.

React should support appropriate frontend observability for:

```text
JavaScript errors
Page load
API failures
Navigation performance
User-perceived latency
```

while respecting privacy requirements.

---

# 121. Real User Monitoring

RUM captures actual user experience.

This can reveal differences caused by:

```text
Device
Browser
Network
Geography
```

that backend monitoring cannot see.

---

# 122. Core Web Vitals

For web experience, monitor relevant user-facing performance signals such as:

```text
LCP
INP
CLS
```

rather than relying only on server response time.

---

# 123. SLI

A **Service Level Indicator** is a measured reliability signal.

Example:

```text
Successful requests
───────────────────
Total valid requests
```

or:

```text
Percentage of requests
completed below 500 ms
```

---

# 124. SLO

A **Service Level Objective** defines the target.

Example:

```text
99.9% of valid API requests
succeed over 30 days.
```

SLOs should represent user-relevant reliability.

---

# 125. SLA vs SLO

```text
SLO
=
Internal reliability target

SLA
=
Contractual/business commitment
```

They should not be casually treated as identical.

---

# 126. Availability SLI

Conceptually:

```text
Good Requests
──────────────
Valid Requests
```

But defining "good" requires care.

For example, a correct:

```text
404
```

may be a successful application response rather than system failure.

---

# 127. Latency SLI

Instead of:

```text
average latency < 500 ms
```

prefer user-oriented distributions:

```text
99% of requests
under threshold
```

for important workflows.

---

# 128. Workflow SLOs

Some Mediverse SLOs should measure complete experiences.

Examples:

```text
Course page availability

Assessment submission success

Search response success

Asset playback startup

AI tutor response availability
```

not merely individual microservice uptime.

---

# 129. Error Budget

If SLO is:

```text
99.9%
```

then:

```text
0.1%
```

of the measurement window is the reliability error budget.

This makes reliability trade-offs explicit.

---

# 130. Error Budget Use

If a team rapidly consumes its error budget:

```text
Feature velocity
      ↓

Reliability work
      ↑
```

may be required.

An SLO without operational consequences is just a dashboard number.

---

# 131. Burn Rate

Burn rate measures how quickly the error budget is being consumed.

```text
Burn rate = 1
```

roughly means consumption at the expected sustainable rate.

A very high burn rate signals a serious reliability problem.

---

# 132. Burn-Rate Alerting

Instead of alerting on every small error spike, alerts can detect:

```text
Fast severe burn
```

and:

```text
Slow sustained burn
```

across different windows.

This reduces noise while protecting SLOs.

---

# 133. Alert Philosophy

An alert should generally mean:

> **A human may need to act.**

If no one needs to do anything, it probably belongs on a dashboard rather than paging an engineer.

---

# 134. Symptom vs Cause Alerts

Prefer:

```text
Students cannot submit assessments
```

over paging first on:

```text
Pod CPU = 81%
```

CPU may be a cause.

User-visible failure is the symptom.

Cause metrics remain useful for diagnosis.

---

# 135. Alert Severity

Example classification:

```text
SEV1 / CRITICAL
Major production outage

SEV2 / HIGH
Significant degradation

SEV3 / MEDIUM
Non-critical operational issue

INFO
Non-paging notification
```

Exact definitions must be documented.

---

# 136. Alert Routing

Architecture:

```text
Metrics / Events
       │
       ▼
Alert Rules
       │
       ▼
Alertmanager / Alert Platform
       │
       ▼
Routing
   ┌───┼─────────┐
   ▼   ▼         ▼
On-call Team   Chat   Ticket
```

Routing depends on severity and ownership.

---

# 137. Alert Ownership

Every production alert must have:

```text
Owner
Severity
Meaning
Action
Runbook
Escalation path
```

An orphan alert is operational debt.

---

# 138. Runbooks

A useful alert links to a runbook containing:

```text
What the alert means
Likely causes
Dashboards
Queries
Immediate checks
Mitigation
Escalation
Recovery verification
```

This directly connects ADR-047 with the future Operations Runbook.

---

# 139. Alert Noise

If engineers receive hundreds of meaningless alerts:

```text
Alert
Alert
Alert
Alert
Alert
```

they will stop trusting alerts.

Alert fatigue is an architecture failure, not merely a human problem.

---

# 140. Security Telemetry

Security-relevant events should include appropriate monitoring for:

```text
Authentication failures
Authorization failures
Suspicious access
Credential abuse
Privilege changes
Administrative operations
WAF/security events
```

Security telemetry and operational telemetry may have different retention/access policies.

---

# 141. Observability RBAC

Telemetry itself can contain sensitive operational information.

Access should be role-controlled.

Not every developer automatically needs unrestricted access to:

```text
Production logs
Audit events
Security telemetry
Potentially sensitive traces
```

---

# 142. Telemetry Pipeline Reliability

The observability system must not take down the application.

Bad:

```text
Telemetry backend unavailable
        │
        ▼
Application request blocks
        │
        ▼
Production outage
```

Telemetry export should generally be asynchronous and failure-tolerant.

---

# 143. Backpressure

If collectors cannot export fast enough:

```text
Applications
    │
    ▼
Collectors
    │
    X
Backend
```

the system requires:

```text
Queues
Batching
Memory limits
Dropping policy
Retry limits
```

Telemetry must not grow without bounds.

---

# 144. Observing the Observability System

Monitor:

```text
Collector health
Dropped telemetry
Export failures
Queue utilization
Backend ingestion latency
Prometheus scrape failures
Storage capacity
```

Otherwise telemetry can silently disappear.

---

# 145. Cost Governance

Observability cost grows through:

```text
Log volume
Metric cardinality
Trace volume
Retention
Indexing
Dashboard queries
Data transfer
```

Cost controls must be designed from the beginning.

---

# 146. Observability Testing

CI/CD and environment validation should test:

```text
Trace propagation
Required metrics
Structured log schema
Sensitive-data redaction
Health endpoints
Alert rules
Dashboard queries
SLO calculations
Collector configuration
```

Observability configuration is production code.

---

# 147. Observability Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject or strongly discourage:

```text
❌ Logs as the only observability mechanism
❌ SSHing into Pods as the standard debugging workflow
❌ Unstructured production logging
❌ Logging passwords/JWTs/API keys
❌ Full request/response logging by default
❌ User IDs as Prometheus labels
❌ Dynamic IDs in metric names
❌ Dynamic IDs in span names
❌ Unlimited metric cardinality
❌ INFO log for every method entry/exit
❌ Same exception logged at every layer
❌ Every HTTP 4xx treated as ERROR
❌ Keeping all telemetry forever
❌ Tracing 100% forever without cost analysis
❌ Sampling away every error
❌ Publicly exposed Actuator endpoints
❌ Database dependency inside liveness probe
❌ Treating readiness and liveness as identical
❌ Monitoring CPU while ignoring user symptoms
❌ Alerting on everything measurable
❌ Alerts without owners
❌ Alerts without runbooks
❌ SLOs without error-budget consequences
❌ Monitoring AI only through HTTP status
❌ Logging complete AI prompts indiscriminately
❌ Treating audit logs as ordinary application logs
❌ One gigantic Grafana dashboard
❌ Using the production search cluster as a log dump by default
❌ Telemetry export blocking application requests
❌ No monitoring of telemetry collectors themselves
```

---

# 148. Incident Investigation Flow

```text
                  USER IMPACT DETECTED
                          │
                          ▼
                      SLO Alert
                          │
                          ▼
                 Platform Dashboard
                          │
                          ▼
                  Identify Service
                          │
              ┌───────────┼───────────┐
              ▼           ▼           ▼
            Metrics      Traces       Logs
              │           │           │
              └───────────┼───────────┘
                          ▼
                    Dependency?
              ┌───────────┼────────────┐
              ▼           ▼            ▼
          PostgreSQL     Kafka      OpenSearch
              │           │            │
              ├───────────┼────────────┤
              ▼           ▼            ▼
            Redis        AI         Asset/CDN
              │           │            │
              └───────────┼────────────┘
                          ▼
                     Root Cause
                          │
                          ▼
                      Mitigation
                          │
                          ▼
                  Verify SLI Recovery
                          │
                          ▼
                   Incident Review
```

---

# 149. Final Mediverse Observability Architecture

```text
                         MEDIVERSE USERS
                               │
                 ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
                 ▼                           ▼
              React                       Synthetic
               RUM                         Probes
                 │                           │
                 └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                               ▼
                          API GATEWAY
                               │
                               ▼
                       MICROSERVICES
                               │
       ┌───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
       ▼                       ▼                        ▼
 PostgreSQL / Redis           Kafka               OpenSearch
                                                       │
       ┌───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
       ▼                       ▼                        ▼
   AI Platform              S3/CDN               Kubernetes
       │                       │                        │
       └───────────────────────┼────────────────────────┘
                               ▼
                        OpenTelemetry
                               │
                               ▼
                      OTel Collectors
                               │
              ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐
              ▼                ▼                 ▼
            LOGS            METRICS            TRACES
              │                │                 │
              ▼                ▼                 ▼
        Log Backend       Prometheus        Trace Backend
              │                │                 │
              └────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                               ▼
                            Grafana
                               │
                  ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                  ▼            ▼            ▼
              Dashboards      SLOs        Alerts
                                            │
                                            ▼
                                       Alertmanager
                                            │
                                            ▼
                                          On-call
                                            │
                                            ▼
                                         Runbook
```

The operational correlation model becomes:

```text
Deployment Version
        +
Trace ID
        +
Service
        +
Environment
        +
Metrics
        +
Logs
        +
Distributed Trace
        +
SLO State
        =
Investigable Production System
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                   |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Observability standard     | **OpenTelemetry**                          |
| Primary signals            | Logs + Metrics + Traces                    |
| Spring instrumentation     | Actuator + Micrometer + OTel               |
| Trace propagation          | W3C Trace Context                          |
| Telemetry transport        | OTLP where appropriate                     |
| Telemetry processing       | OpenTelemetry Collector                    |
| Metrics model              | Prometheus-compatible                      |
| Visualization              | Grafana                                    |
| Logging                    | Structured JSON                            |
| Central logging            | Required                                   |
| Audit vs operational logs  | Separate concerns                          |
| Sensitive data             | Redact / prohibit                          |
| Metric cardinality         | Strictly controlled                        |
| User IDs as metric labels  | Prohibited                                 |
| Trace sampling             | Required at scale                          |
| Error/slow traces          | Preferential retention                     |
| Kubernetes metrics         | Required                                   |
| Liveness/readiness/startup | Separate semantics                         |
| Synthetic monitoring       | Required for critical workflows            |
| Frontend RUM               | Recommended                                |
| Reliability model          | SLI + SLO + Error Budget                   |
| Alert model                | User-impact/action oriented                |
| Burn-rate alerts           | Preferred for SLOs                         |
| Alert ownership            | Mandatory                                  |
| Runbook association        | Mandatory for actionable production alerts |
| AI observability           | Operational + cost + quality               |
| Telemetry RBAC             | Required                                   |
| Collector resilience       | Required                                   |
| Cost governance            | Required                                   |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                               |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                               |

The architecture now establishes an important distinction:

```text
LOGS
=
Detailed events

METRICS
=
System behavior over time

TRACES
=
Request causality

AUDIT
=
Accountability

RUM
=
Actual user experience

SYNTHETICS
=
Externally tested experience

SLIs
=
Measured reliability

SLOs
=
Reliability targets

ERROR BUDGET
=
Allowed unreliability

ALERTS
=
Human action required
```

## Next — ADR-048

### **ADR-048 — Enterprise Identity, Authentication, Authorization, RBAC/ABAC, OAuth 2.0, OIDC & Zero-Trust Security Architecture**

This is the correct next ADR because security concepts have already appeared throughout the previous decisions, but Mediverse still needs one authoritative decision defining **who a caller is, what they can do, how identity propagates through the distributed system, and where authorization decisions belong**.

ADR-048 should cover **identity architecture → students/faculty/admin/institution identities → authentication vs authorization → IdP boundary → Keycloak/Cognito/Auth0 evaluation → OAuth 2.0 → OpenID Connect → authorization code + PKCE → SPA authentication → BFF evaluation → access vs ID vs refresh tokens → JWT architecture → opaque token evaluation → signing algorithms → JWKS → key rotation → token lifetime → refresh rotation → logout/revocation → session management → MFA/passkeys → account recovery → password policy → brute-force protection → federation/SSO → Google/Microsoft/institutional SSO → SAML evaluation → tenant-aware identity → RBAC → ABAC → resource-level authorization → course/enrollment/faculty ownership rules → policy enforcement points → gateway vs service authorization → Spring Security → method authorization → service identity → workload identity → Kubernetes service accounts → OAuth client credentials → mTLS/service mesh relationship → token propagation vs token exchange → confused-deputy prevention → least privilege → admin privilege → break-glass access → impersonation/support access → audit → authorization caching → policy engine/OPA evaluation → secrets → credential rotation → frontend token security → XSS/CSRF/CORS boundaries → rate limiting/account lockout → zero-trust principles → threat modeling → testing → anti-patterns → final Mediverse identity and authorization reference architecture.**

# ADR-048 — Enterprise Identity, Authentication, Authorization, RBAC/ABAC, OAuth 2.0, OIDC & Zero-Trust Security Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-048
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-048 defines the authoritative identity and access-control architecture for Mediverse.

Mediverse has several fundamentally different actors:

```text
Students
Faculty
Institution Administrators
Platform Administrators
Support Personnel
Microservices
Background Workers
CI/CD Systems
AI Agents
External Integrations
```

The architectural question is:

> **How does Mediverse establish identity, authenticate humans and workloads, authorize every sensitive operation, propagate identity safely across distributed services, support institutional SSO, and prevent a compromised user, service or token from gaining excessive access?**

---

# 1. Authentication ≠ Authorization

These must remain separate concepts.

```text
Authentication
=
Who are you?

Authorization
=
What are you allowed to do?
```

A successfully authenticated student is not automatically authorized to access every course.

---

# 2. Identity Architecture

Conceptually:

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Identity Provider
 │
 ▼
Authentication
 │
 ▼
Identity / Tokens
 │
 ▼
Mediverse
 │
 ▼
Authorization
 │
 ▼
Protected Resource
```

Authentication should not be independently reinvented by every microservice.

---

# 3. Core Decision

Mediverse shall use a centralized **Identity Provider (IdP)** implementing standards-based identity protocols.

Primary standards:

```text
OAuth 2.x
OpenID Connect
```

Application services shall integrate with the identity architecture rather than maintaining independent authentication systems.

---

# 4. Identity Provider Boundary

The IdP owns capabilities such as:

```text
User authentication
Credential handling
MFA
Federated identity
Token issuance
Identity sessions
Account recovery
Authentication policies
```

Domain services own business authorization.

This distinction matters.

---

# 5. Identity Provider Candidates

Depending on deployment and operational requirements, candidates include:

```text
Keycloak
Amazon Cognito
Auth0
Microsoft Entra External ID
Other standards-compliant IdPs
```

Mediverse should not build a custom OAuth/OIDC server unless a compelling requirement exists.

---

# 6. Keycloak Evaluation

Keycloak provides strong control over:

```text
OIDC
OAuth
SAML
Federation
Roles
Identity brokering
MFA
Administrative policies
```

Advantages:

```text
Open source
Self-hostable
Highly configurable
Avoids strong SaaS dependency
```

Trade-off:

```text
Mediverse operates it.
```

That means:

```text
Availability
Scaling
Upgrades
Database
Security patches
Backup
Monitoring
```

become Mediverse responsibilities.

---

# 7. Managed Identity Evaluation

A managed IdP reduces operational burden.

Conceptually:

```text
Mediverse
    │
    ▼
Managed Identity Platform
```

Advantages:

```text
Less infrastructure
Managed availability
Managed security updates
Simpler operations
```

Trade-offs include:

```text
Vendor coupling
Pricing
Feature constraints
Migration complexity
```

---

# 8. Initial Architectural Position

Mediverse should keep application integration standards-based regardless of provider.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
OIDC / OAuth
    │
    ▼
Identity Provider
```

not:

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Vendor-specific identity logic everywhere
```

This keeps future provider migration feasible.

---

# 9. Identity Types

Mediverse must distinguish:

```text
Human Identity
      │
      ├── Student
      ├── Faculty
      ├── Admin
      └── Support

Workload Identity
      │
      ├── Microservice
      ├── Worker
      ├── CI/CD
      └── Automation

Agent Identity
      │
      └── AI agent acting within delegated authority
```

These should not share one universal credential model.

---

# 10. User Identity

A stable internal identifier should represent the Mediverse user.

Example:

```text
userId = UUID
```

Avoid using:

```text
email
username
phone
```

as immutable primary identity.

These can change.

---

# 11. External Identity Mapping

A user may authenticate through:

```text
Google
Microsoft
Institution SSO
Local IdP account
```

but map to one Mediverse identity.

```text
External Identity
       │
       ▼
Identity Mapping
       │
       ▼
Mediverse User ID
```

---

# 12. OAuth 2.x

OAuth primarily addresses delegated authorization.

Conceptually:

```text
Resource Owner
      │
      ▼
Authorization Server
      │
      ▼
Access Token
      │
      ▼
Resource Server
```

Do not treat OAuth itself as the complete user-authentication protocol.

---

# 13. OpenID Connect

OIDC adds identity semantics on top of OAuth.

```text
OAuth
+
Identity Layer
=
OpenID Connect
```

OIDC is the preferred standard for Mediverse interactive user authentication.

---

# 14. Authorization Code Flow

For interactive applications:

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Authorization Endpoint
   │
   ▼
User Authentication
   │
   ▼
Authorization Code
   │
   ▼
Token Exchange
```

This avoids delivering credentials directly to Mediverse application code.

---

# 15. PKCE

Authorization Code with PKCE protects the authorization-code exchange.

Conceptually:

```text
Client creates verifier
       │
       ▼
Challenge sent
       │
       ▼
Authorization Code
       │
       ▼
Code + Verifier
       │
       ▼
Token
```

PKCE should be required for applicable public clients.

---

# 16. SPA Security Problem

A React SPA executes in the browser.

Therefore:

```text
Browser
=
Untrusted execution environment
```

Any credential accessible to JavaScript is potentially exposed through XSS.

This must influence token architecture.

---

# 17. BFF Pattern Evaluation

Mediverse should strongly evaluate a **Backend-for-Frontend (BFF)** architecture for security-sensitive browser authentication.

```text
React
  │
  ▼
BFF
  │
  ▼
Identity Provider
```

The BFF can keep OAuth tokens out of browser JavaScript.

---

# 18. BFF Session Architecture

```text
Browser
   │
   │ Secure HttpOnly Cookie
   ▼
BFF
   │
   │ Access Token
   ▼
Backend APIs
```

JavaScript does not directly handle the access token.

This materially reduces token theft through XSS.

---

# 19. BFF Trade-Off

BFF adds:

```text
Backend state/session concerns
CSRF considerations
Infrastructure
Routing complexity
```

Therefore it is not "free security."

But for Mediverse's enterprise architecture, the security benefits can justify the additional layer.

---

# 20. Token Types

Do not confuse:

```text
ID Token
Access Token
Refresh Token
```

They have different purposes.

---

# 21. ID Token

An ID token communicates authentication information to the client.

Conceptually:

```text
"This user authenticated."
```

It is not automatically the correct credential for calling every Mediverse API.

---

# 22. Access Token

The access token authorizes API access.

```text
Client / BFF
     │
     │ Access Token
     ▼
Resource Server
```

Backend APIs validate it before protected operations.

---

# 23. Refresh Token

Refresh tokens allow obtaining new access tokens without repeating interactive login.

Because they are longer-lived and powerful:

```text
Refresh Token
>
Access Token
```

in security sensitivity.

Their storage and rotation require stronger controls.

---

# 24. JWT Access Tokens

Mediverse may use signed JWT access tokens.

Structure:

```text
Header
Payload
Signature
```

Advantages:

```text
Local verification
Reduced authorization-server dependency
Standard ecosystem support
Useful distributed architecture
```

---

# 25. JWT Is Not Encrypted by Default

A common mistake:

```text
JWT
=
Secret data
```

No.

A signed JWT's claims can generally be decoded by whoever possesses it.

Do not place sensitive information in JWT claims merely because the token is signed.

---

# 26. JWT Signature

Resource servers must verify:

```text
Signature
Issuer
Audience
Expiration
Relevant claims
```

before trusting the token.

Parsing a JWT is not authentication.

---

# 27. JWKS

Public verification keys can be distributed through a JWKS endpoint.

```text
Identity Provider
       │
       ▼
      JWKS
       │
       ▼
Resource Services
```

Services can verify tokens without possessing the IdP's private signing key.

---

# 28. Signing Algorithm

Use approved asymmetric signing algorithms.

Conceptually:

```text
Private Key
    │
    ▼
Identity Provider signs

Public Key
    │
    ▼
Services verify
```

Private signing keys should not be distributed to application services.

---

# 29. Key Rotation

Signing keys must be rotatable.

```text
Key A
  │
  ▼
Key A + Key B
  │
  ▼
Key B
```

JWKS and token validation should tolerate controlled overlap during rotation.

---

# 30. Token Lifetime

Access tokens should be short-lived.

Why?

A stolen bearer token generally remains usable until:

```text
Expiration
Revocation mechanism
Other enforcement
```

Short lifetimes reduce exposure.

---

# 31. Do Not Create 30-Day Access Tokens

Long-lived bearer access tokens dramatically increase compromise impact.

Use:

```text
Short access token
      +
Controlled session/refresh mechanism
```

instead.

---

# 32. Refresh Token Rotation

Where refresh tokens are exposed to clients that require them, rotation can work as:

```text
Refresh Token A
      │
      ▼
Use
      │
      ├── Access Token
      └── Refresh Token B

Token A becomes invalid
```

Reuse detection can indicate token theft.

---

# 33. Opaque Tokens

JWT is not mandatory for every situation.

Opaque tokens can use:

```text
Resource Server
      │
      ▼
Token Introspection
      │
      ▼
Authorization Server
```

Advantages include stronger centralized revocation semantics.

Trade-off:

```text
Runtime dependency
Additional network calls
Latency
Availability coupling
```

---

# 34. JWT vs Opaque Decision

For Mediverse distributed APIs, signed JWTs are a reasonable default where local validation matters.

Opaque tokens should remain available for use cases requiring stronger centralized control.

Do not make token format an ideological decision.

---

# 35. Logout

Logout is more complicated than:

```text
delete frontend variable
```

A complete logout may involve:

```text
Application session
IdP session
Refresh token
Browser cookie
Federated session
```

depending on architecture.

---

# 36. Token Revocation

JWT local verification creates a trade-off:

```text
Fast decentralized validation
        ↕
Immediate revocation complexity
```

Mitigations include:

```text
Short access-token lifetime
Refresh-token revocation
Session termination
Selective denylist where justified
```

---

# 37. Do Not Build Giant JWT Denylists

If every JWT requires a database lookup against a global denylist:

```text
JWT's local-validation advantage
=
largely lost
```

Use revocation mechanisms based on actual requirements.

---

# 38. Session Management

Mediverse should explicitly track security-relevant sessions where the architecture requires:

```text
Login time
Last activity
Device/session metadata
Refresh state
Revocation state
```

rather than treating authentication as one permanent token.

---

# 39. Concurrent Sessions

Policy may define:

```text
Unlimited devices
Limited active sessions
User-visible session management
Administrative session revocation
```

depending on product/security requirements.

---

# 40. MFA

Higher-risk accounts should support stronger authentication.

Priority candidates:

```text
Platform administrators
Institution administrators
Faculty with sensitive privileges
Support personnel
```

MFA policy can be risk/role based.

---

# 41. Phishing-Resistant Authentication

Where practical, Mediverse should support stronger authentication mechanisms such as:

```text
Passkeys / WebAuthn
Security keys
```

particularly for privileged administration.

SMS should not be treated as the strongest available MFA method.

---

# 42. Password Storage

If Mediverse/its IdP manages passwords:

```text
Plaintext password storage
=
Prohibited
```

Passwords must use an approved password-hashing algorithm and parameters.

Application microservices should not independently store user passwords.

---

# 43. Password Policy

Avoid arbitrary complexity rules such as:

```text
Exactly:
1 uppercase
1 lowercase
1 symbol
1 number
```

as the sole security strategy.

More meaningful controls include:

```text
Adequate length
Compromised-password screening
Rate limiting
MFA
Secure recovery
```

---

# 44. Login Brute-Force Protection

Authentication should resist:

```text
Password spraying
Credential stuffing
Brute force
Automated attacks
```

through appropriate:

```text
Rate limiting
Risk detection
Progressive controls
MFA
Monitoring
```

---

# 45. Account Lockout Warning

Permanent lockout after a tiny number of failures enables denial-of-service attacks against known accounts.

Controls should balance:

```text
Attack resistance
Availability
User recovery
```

---

# 46. Account Recovery

Account recovery is effectively another authentication mechanism.

If recovery is weak:

```text
Strong MFA
   │
   X
Weak recovery process
```

the entire authentication architecture becomes weak.

---

# 47. Recovery Security

Recovery should consider:

```text
Verified channels
Short-lived tokens
Single-use tokens
Rate limits
Audit
Notification
```

and stronger procedures for privileged accounts.

---

# 48. Email Verification

Email verification proves control over an email address at a point in time.

It does not prove:

```text
Medical qualification
Faculty employment
Institution membership
Administrative authority
```

Those require separate business verification.

---

# 49. Federation

Institutions may already maintain identities.

Preferred:

```text
University Identity Provider
          │
          ▼
      Federation
          │
          ▼
       Mediverse
```

rather than forcing every institutional user to maintain another independent password.

---

# 50. Institutional SSO

Potential protocols:

```text
OIDC
SAML 2.0
```

OIDC should generally be preferred for modern integrations where available.

SAML remains relevant for enterprise institutions with existing SAML infrastructure.

---

# 51. Identity Brokering

Mediverse's IdP may broker external identities:

```text
Google ───────┐
Microsoft ────┤
University ───┼──► Mediverse IdP ─► Mediverse
SAML IdP ─────┘
```

This prevents every microservice from integrating directly with external identity providers.

---

# 52. Federation Does Not Equal Authorization

University SSO may prove:

```text
"This is Alice from University X."
```

It does not automatically prove:

```text
"Alice can publish Pharmacology assessments."
```

Business authorization remains Mediverse's responsibility.

---

# 53. Tenant-Aware Identity

A user may participate in:

```text
Institution A
Institution B
```

with different privileges.

Therefore:

```text
User Identity
≠
Tenant Membership
```

Membership must be modeled explicitly.

---

# 54. Membership Model

Conceptually:

```text
User
 │
 ├── Membership → Institution A → FACULTY
 │
 └── Membership → Institution B → STUDENT
```

A global `role=FACULTY` claim cannot correctly represent this situation.

---

# 55. RBAC

Role-Based Access Control grants permissions through roles.

Example:

```text
STUDENT
FACULTY
INSTITUTION_ADMIN
PLATFORM_ADMIN
```

Roles simplify broad permission management.

---

# 56. Permission Model

Prefer:

```text
Role
 │
 ▼
Permissions
```

Example:

```text
FACULTY
   │
   ├── course:create
   ├── content:create
   ├── assessment:create
   └── assessment:grade
```

rather than scattering:

```text
if role == FACULTY
```

through every code path.

---

# 57. RBAC Is Not Enough

Suppose two faculty members exist.

```text
Faculty A
Faculty B
```

Faculty A should not automatically edit Faculty B's private draft merely because both have:

```text
ROLE_FACULTY
```

Resource context matters.

---

# 58. ABAC

Attribute-Based Access Control evaluates attributes.

Examples:

```text
user.tenantId
resource.tenantId

user.department
resource.department

resource.ownerId

enrollment.status
course.visibility
```

Authorization becomes contextual.

---

# 59. RBAC + ABAC

Mediverse should use a hybrid approach:

```text
RBAC
=
Broad capability

ABAC / Resource Policy
=
Contextual permission
```

Example:

```text
FACULTY
+
owns course
+
same tenant
=
may edit course
```

---

# 60. Resource-Level Authorization

Critical operations should evaluate the actual resource.

```text
Request:
PUT /courses/123

Identity:
Faculty A

Authorization:
Can Faculty A edit Course 123?
```

Checking only:

```text
Is Faculty?
```

is insufficient.

---

## ADR-048 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The identity boundary established so far is:

```text
                     HUMAN USER
                         │
                         ▼
                  Identity Provider
                         │
               ┌─────────┴─────────┐
               ▼                   ▼
         Authentication        Federation
               │                   │
               └─────────┬─────────┘
                         ▼
                   OIDC / OAuth
                         │
                         ▼
                  Browser / BFF
                         │
                         ▼
                    API Gateway
                         │
                         ▼
                  Resource Service
                         │
                         ▼
                    Authorization
                         │
              ┌──────────┼──────────┐
              ▼          ▼          ▼
             RBAC       ABAC      Resource
                                  Ownership
                         │
                         ▼
                    Domain Action
```

For browser authentication, the preferred security direction is:

```text
React Browser
      │
      │ Secure + HttpOnly
      │ Session Cookie
      ▼
     BFF
      │
      │ OAuth Access Token
      ▼
API Gateway / APIs
      │
      ▼
Resource Authorization
```

And the most important distinction is:

```text
IdP
=
Authentication Authority

Token
=
Identity / Delegated Access Evidence

RBAC
=
Broad Capability

ABAC
=
Contextual Policy

Domain Service
=
Resource Authorization Authority
```

The core rule is:

> **Authentication proves an identity; it never grants unrestricted access. Every sensitive Mediverse operation must still be authorized against the tenant, resource, action and relevant business context.**

**Part 2** continues from **Section 61 — Authorization Policy Enforcement Points**, covering gateway vs service authorization, Spring Security, method-level authorization, IDOR/BOLA prevention, tenant isolation, policy engines/OPA, authorization caching, service identities, workload identity, Kubernetes ServiceAccounts, client credentials, mTLS, service mesh identity, token propagation vs exchange, confused-deputy attacks, AI-agent delegated identity, least privilege, privileged administration, break-glass access, support impersonation, secrets and credential management, browser security, cookies, CSRF, XSS, CORS, CSP, logout/session invalidation, zero trust, auditability, threat modeling, security testing, anti-patterns and the final Mediverse identity/security reference architecture.


# ADR-048 — Enterprise Identity, Authentication, Authorization, RBAC/ABAC, OAuth 2.0, OIDC & Zero-Trust Security Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Resource-Level Authorization**.

---

# 61. Authorization Policy Enforcement Points

Authorization must happen at explicit enforcement points.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
API Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service
   │
   ▼
Domain Operation
```

Possible enforcement exists at multiple layers, but those layers have different responsibilities.

---

# 62. Gateway Authorization

The gateway can enforce coarse-grained controls such as:

```text
Valid access token?
Correct issuer?
Correct audience?
Required broad scope?
Known client?
```

Example:

```text
GET /admin/*
      │
      ▼
Require authenticated request
```

This reduces obviously unauthorized traffic reaching backend services.

---

# 63. Gateway Authorization Is Not Enough

The gateway usually cannot safely determine:

```text
Does Faculty A own Course 123?

Is Student B enrolled in Course 123?

Can Admin C modify Institution X?

Is Assessment 42 currently editable?
```

These require domain knowledge.

Therefore:

> Gateway authentication/authorization must never replace service-level resource authorization.

---

# 64. Defense in Depth

Preferred:

```text
                   Request
                      │
                      ▼
                 API Gateway
                      │
              Token Validation
                      │
                      ▼
               Resource Service
                      │
               Authorization
                      │
                      ▼
                Domain Policy
                      │
                      ▼
                  Resource
```

Security does not depend on one perimeter.

---

# 65. Spring Security

Spring Boot services shall use Spring Security as the standard application security framework.

Responsibilities may include:

```text
JWT validation
Security context
Authority mapping
Endpoint rules
Method authorization
Authentication integration
```

Teams should not implement custom token parsers and authorization frameworks independently.

---

# 66. Resource Server

Spring Boot APIs act as OAuth resource servers.

Conceptually:

```text
Access Token
     │
     ▼
Spring Security
     │
     ├── Verify signature
     ├── Verify issuer
     ├── Verify audience
     ├── Verify expiry
     └── Map authorities
            │
            ▼
        Controller
```

---

# 67. Method-Level Authorization

Sensitive service operations may use method authorization.

Conceptually:

```java
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('course:create')")
public Course createCourse(...) {
    ...
}
```

But annotations alone do not solve resource ownership.

---

# 68. Domain Authorization

Example:

```text
Faculty has:
course:update

             +
Course belongs to faculty's tenant

             +
Faculty owns/manages course

             +
Course state permits editing

             =
ALLOW
```

This logic belongs near the domain boundary.

---

# 69. IDOR / BOLA

One of the most important API authorization risks is:

```text
GET /students/1001
```

changing to:

```text
GET /students/1002
```

and receiving another user's protected resource.

This is an authorization failure, not an authentication failure.

---

# 70. Never Trust Resource IDs

An authenticated caller supplying:

```text
courseId
studentId
tenantId
assessmentId
```

does not prove they are authorized to access that resource.

Every protected object reference requires authorization.

---

# 71. Tenant Isolation

Tenant isolation must be enforced systematically.

Conceptually:

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Membership
 │
 ▼
Tenant
 │
 ▼
Resource
```

The resource must belong to an authorized tenant context.

---

# 72. Never Trust Client Tenant ID

Bad:

```json
{
  "tenantId": "institution-B",
  "courseId": "123"
}
```

followed by:

```text
Use tenantId directly
```

The server must derive or validate tenant context against authenticated membership.

---

# 73. Tenant Context

A request may resolve:

```text
Authenticated User
       │
       ▼
Selected Tenant
       │
       ▼
Membership Validation
       │
       ▼
Authorized Tenant Context
```

Only then should tenant-scoped operations proceed.

---

# 74. Database Isolation

Application authorization should be reinforced by data-access patterns.

Bad:

```text
SELECT *
FROM course
WHERE id = ?
```

when tenant isolation is required.

Safer conceptual query:

```text
SELECT *
FROM course
WHERE id = ?
AND tenant_id = ?
```

Authorization should be difficult to accidentally bypass.

---

# 75. Global Administrators

Platform administrators may legitimately operate across tenants.

This must be an explicit privileged capability.

Do not implement:

```text
if admin
   skip all security
```

Administrative actions still require:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Audit
Scope
```

---

# 76. Policy Decision Architecture

Complex authorization can be conceptualized as:

```text
PEP
Policy Enforcement Point

PDP
Policy Decision Point

PIP
Policy Information Point
```

Flow:

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
PEP
   │
   ▼
PDP
   │
   ├── Identity
   ├── Resource
   ├── Environment
   └── Attributes
         │
         ▼
      ALLOW / DENY
```

---

# 77. Policy Engine Evaluation

External policy engines such as OPA may be evaluated when authorization rules become sufficiently complex.

Potential advantages:

```text
Central policy language
Policy-as-code
Consistent evaluation
Independent testing
```

But introducing one too early can create unnecessary architecture.

---

# 78. Do Not Centralize All Authorization Blindly

A global policy engine cannot magically understand every business invariant.

For example:

```text
Assessment can be modified
only before publication
unless revision workflow active
```

may belong directly in the assessment domain.

External policy systems should complement domain authorization, not replace domain modeling.

---

# 79. Default Deny

Authorization should follow:

```text
No explicit permission
        │
        ▼
       DENY
```

not:

```text
No rule found
     │
     ▼
Probably allow
```

Default-deny is fundamental.

---

# 80. Authorization Decision Logging

Important authorization outcomes should produce appropriate telemetry.

Examples:

```text
Denied administrative action
Cross-tenant access attempt
Privilege escalation attempt
Policy evaluation failure
```

But logging every successful authorization check at high volume may create useless noise.

---

# 81. Authorization Caching

Some authorization information may be cached.

Examples:

```text
Role mappings
Tenant membership
Static permission mappings
```

But caching introduces stale-authorization risk.

---

# 82. Permission Revocation vs Cache

Suppose:

```text
Faculty permission removed
        │
        ▼
Authorization cache still says ALLOW
```

The cache TTL determines how long the stale privilege remains.

Security-sensitive permissions therefore require carefully bounded caching.

---

# 83. Workload Identity

Humans are not the only callers.

```text
Course Service
Search Indexer
Media Worker
Notification Worker
AI Platform
```

also require identities.

Using shared passwords between services is unacceptable.

---

# 84. Service Identity

Each workload should have its own identity.

```text
course-service
      │
      ▼
Identity A

asset-service
      │
      ▼
Identity B
```

not:

```text
all-backend-services
      │
      ▼
Shared Credential
```

This enables least privilege and attribution.

---

# 85. Kubernetes ServiceAccount

Within Kubernetes:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
ServiceAccount
 │
 ▼
Workload Identity
```

should form part of the workload identity architecture.

Avoid distributing static cloud credentials into Pods.

---

# 86. Cloud Workload Identity

In AWS-oriented Kubernetes deployments:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
Kubernetes ServiceAccount
 │
 ▼
AWS Workload Identity Mechanism
 │
 ▼
IAM Role
```

can grant narrowly scoped cloud access without embedding long-lived AWS access keys.

---

# 87. Least-Privilege IAM

Example:

```text
asset-service
```

may need access to:

```text
specific S3 asset resources
specific KMS operations
```

It does not therefore need:

```text
s3:*
kms:*
*
```

across the AWS account.

---

# 88. Client Credentials

For appropriate machine-to-machine OAuth scenarios:

```text
Service A
    │
    ▼
Authorization Server
    │
    ▼
Access Token
    │
    ▼
Service B
```

OAuth client-credentials flow may be used.

This represents the service itself, not an end user.

---

# 89. User Context vs Service Context

Suppose:

```text
Student
   │
   ▼
Course Service
   │
   ▼
Progress Service
```

Progress Service may need to know:

```text
Student identity
```

while also knowing:

```text
Course Service is the caller
```

These are different security contexts.

---

# 90. Token Propagation

Simple architecture:

```text
User Token
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

Service A forwards the original token.

This preserves user identity but can create excessive token reach.

---

# 91. Token Reach

Suppose the user's token permits:

```text
Course API
Assessment API
Profile API
```

but Service A only needs to call:

```text
Profile API
```

forwarding the broad original token gives Service A more delegated capability than necessary.

---

# 92. Token Exchange

For higher-security workflows:

```text
User Token
    │
    ▼
Service A
    │
    ▼
Token Exchange
    │
    ▼
Narrow Token
    │
    ▼
Service B
```

can reduce downstream privilege.

This should be introduced where threat/risk justifies the complexity.

---

# 93. Confused Deputy Problem

Suppose:

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Service A
 │
 ▼
Privileged Service B
```

Service A must not accidentally use its own broad privilege to perform an operation the user was never allowed to request.

Authorization must consider:

```text
Caller identity
+
Delegated user authority
+
Requested operation
```

where applicable.

---

# 94. mTLS

Mutual TLS can authenticate both sides of a service connection.

```text
Service A
   │
   │ mTLS
   ▼
Service B
```

Both endpoints establish cryptographic workload identity.

---

# 95. mTLS Does Not Replace Authorization

mTLS proves something like:

```text
This connection came from course-service.
```

It does not prove:

```text
course-service may delete assessment 123.
```

Authentication and authorization remain separate.

---

# 96. Service Mesh Identity

If ADR-041 adopts a service mesh, workload certificates and mTLS can provide:

```text
Workload identity
Encrypted east-west traffic
Service authentication
Policy enforcement
```

But the mesh does not understand all Mediverse business authorization.

---

# 97. Zero Trust

Mediverse shall follow zero-trust principles.

The simplified principle is:

> **Network location is not sufficient evidence of trust.**

Being:

```text
inside Kubernetes
inside VPC
inside corporate network
```

does not automatically authorize access.

---

# 98. Zero Trust Request

Conceptually:

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Authenticate identity
   │
   ▼
Evaluate authorization
   │
   ▼
Evaluate context
   │
   ▼
Apply least privilege
   │
   ▼
Allow / Deny
```

for sensitive boundaries.

---

# 99. AI Agent Identity

ADR-045 introduced agents capable of calling tools.

An AI agent must not receive magical unrestricted system access.

```text
AI Agent
   │
   ▼
Delegated Identity
   │
   ▼
Authorized Tools
```

Agent capabilities must remain bounded.

---

# 100. Agent Delegation

If a student asks:

```text
"Show my progress."
```

the AI system may call the Progress API using authority derived from that student's permitted context.

It must not call:

```text
GET /students/*
```

with unrestricted backend privilege simply because the AI service itself is trusted.

---

# 101. Agent Tool Authorization

Every tool call remains subject to authorization.

```text
LLM Decision
    │
    ▼
Tool Invocation
    │
    ▼
Authorization
    │
    ├── ALLOW
    └── DENY
```

The LLM is never the authorization authority.

---

# 102. Privileged AI Actions

High-impact actions such as:

```text
Publishing content
Changing grades
Deleting course material
Changing permissions
Sending institutional communication
```

should not automatically execute merely because an agent generated the request.

ADR-045's human-approval architecture remains applicable.

---

# 103. Administrative Privileges

Privileged accounts require stronger controls.

Examples:

```text
Platform Admin
Security Admin
Institution Admin
Support Admin
```

Avoid one universal:

```text
SUPER_ADMIN
```

role with unrestricted permanent access whenever finer separation is practical.

---

# 104. Separation of Duties

Sensitive operations may require distinct privileges.

For example:

```text
Identity Administration
Infrastructure Administration
Security Administration
Content Administration
```

should not automatically collapse into one role.

---

# 105. Just-in-Time Privilege

Where operational maturity supports it:

```text
Normal Account
     │
     ▼
Request Elevation
     │
     ▼
Approval / Verification
     │
     ▼
Temporary Privilege
     │
     ▼
Expiry
```

is safer than permanent privileged access.

---

# 106. Break-Glass Access

Emergency access may be required during severe incidents.

A break-glass mechanism should be:

```text
Rare
Strongly authenticated
Time-limited
Audited
Alert-generating
Reviewed afterward
```

It should not become the normal administrative workflow.

---

# 107. Support Access

Support personnel may need to investigate user issues.

Bad:

```text
Support employee
=
Can access every student's account whenever desired
```

Support access requires explicit scope and auditing.

---

# 108. Impersonation

If user impersonation is required:

```text
Support Identity
      │
      ▼
Impersonation Session
      │
      ▼
User Context
```

the system must preserve both:

```text
Actual actor
Impersonated subject
```

in audit records.

---

# 109. Impersonation UI

The UI should make impersonation obvious.

```text
YOU ARE IMPERSONATING:
Student 123
```

Silent impersonation creates severe security and audit risks.

---

# 110. Secrets Management

Secrets include:

```text
Database credentials
API keys
OAuth client secrets
Signing material
Third-party credentials
```

They should be managed through an approved secrets-management architecture.

---

# 111. Secrets Are Not Configuration

This:

```text
application-prod.yml

database.password=...
```

committed to Git is unacceptable.

Git history makes secret removal difficult even after deleting the visible line.

---

# 112. Kubernetes Secrets

Kubernetes Secrets alone should not automatically be treated as a complete enterprise secrets-management solution.

The architecture must consider:

```text
Encryption at rest
RBAC
Secret distribution
Rotation
Audit
External secret stores
```

---

# 113. External Secrets

An architecture may use:

```text
AWS Secrets Manager
        │
        ▼
External Secrets mechanism
        │
        ▼
Kubernetes workload
```

where appropriate.

The source of truth should remain controlled.

---

# 114. Secret Rotation

Credentials should be rotatable without:

```text
manual editing across 40 services
```

Rotation architecture should support:

```text
New credential
      │
      ▼
Controlled overlap
      │
      ▼
Workloads refresh
      │
      ▼
Old credential revoked
```

where the credential type permits it.

---

# 115. Browser Cookies

For BFF sessions, cookies should use appropriate controls such as:

```text
Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
```

according to the deployment architecture.

---

# 116. HttpOnly

`HttpOnly` prevents normal JavaScript access to the cookie.

This reduces session theft through XSS.

It does not eliminate XSS itself.

---

# 117. Secure Cookie

`Secure` ensures the browser sends the cookie only over HTTPS.

Production authentication must not rely on plaintext HTTP.

---

# 118. SameSite

`SameSite` can reduce cross-site request risks.

But the correct mode depends on:

```text
Frontend domain
BFF domain
Federated login flow
Cross-site requirements
```

Do not set it blindly.

---

# 119. CSRF

Cookie-based authentication creates CSRF considerations because browsers may automatically attach cookies.

Therefore state-changing requests require an appropriate CSRF defense.

---

# 120. CSRF Protection

Possible architecture:

```text
Browser
   │
   ├── Session Cookie
   │
   └── CSRF Token
          │
          ▼
         BFF
```

Combined with:

```text
SameSite
Origin validation
CSRF tokens
```

as appropriate.

---

# 121. XSS

XSS can allow attacker-controlled JavaScript to execute in the Mediverse frontend.

Potential consequences include:

```text
Act as user
Read page data
Call APIs
Steal non-HttpOnly credentials
Manipulate content
```

Frontend security is therefore part of identity security.

---

# 122. localStorage Token Risk

Storing long-lived authentication tokens in:

```text
localStorage
```

makes them directly accessible to JavaScript.

An XSS vulnerability can therefore extract them.

This is one major reason the BFF architecture is preferred for sensitive browser sessions.

---

# 123. CSP

Content Security Policy can reduce some XSS attack paths.

A production CSP should be deliberately designed rather than:

```text
script-src *
unsafe-inline
unsafe-eval
```

which destroys much of its protection.

---

# 124. CORS

CORS controls which browser origins can access APIs.

It is **not authentication**.

Bad assumption:

```text
CORS allows only mediverse.com
therefore API is secure
```

Non-browser attackers are not constrained by browser CORS enforcement.

---

# 125. CORS Policy

Production should explicitly allow required origins.

Avoid:

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

for credentialed sensitive APIs.

---

# 126. Rate Limiting

Identity endpoints require dedicated abuse protection.

Examples:

```text
/login
/password-reset
/token
/MFA verification
/account recovery
```

These should not necessarily use the same limits as ordinary course APIs.

---

# 127. Authentication Telemetry

ADR-047 observability should monitor:

```text
Login success/failure
MFA challenges
Token failures
Suspicious refresh activity
Account recovery
Authorization denials
Administrative elevation
Break-glass use
```

with privacy-aware telemetry.

---

# 128. Audit Trail

Security-sensitive actions require durable audit events.

Conceptually:

```text
Actor
Action
Resource
Tenant
Timestamp
Outcome
Relevant Context
```

Examples:

```text
Role changed
Course published
Grade modified
User impersonated
Admin privilege elevated
Break-glass activated
```

---

# 129. Audit Integrity

Audit data should be protected against unauthorized modification or deletion.

An administrator capable of performing an action should not automatically have unrestricted ability to erase evidence of that action.

---

# 130. Security Event Correlation

From ADR-047:

```text
Authentication Event
        │
        ▼
Trace / Request
        │
        ▼
Authorization Event
        │
        ▼
Domain Action
        │
        ▼
Audit Event
```

should be correlatable where appropriate.

---

# 131. Threat Modeling

Security architecture must be threat-driven.

For important workflows, evaluate:

```text
Who is the attacker?

What asset are they targeting?

What trust boundary is crossed?

What privilege is required?

What happens if compromised?
```

rather than simply adding security products.

---

# 132. STRIDE

A threat-modeling framework such as STRIDE can help evaluate:

```text
Spoofing
Tampering
Repudiation
Information Disclosure
Denial of Service
Elevation of Privilege
```

across major Mediverse trust boundaries.

---

# 133. Identity Threat Example

```text
Attacker
   │
   ▼
Steals refresh token
   │
   ▼
Obtains access tokens
   │
   ▼
Acts as student
```

Controls:

```text
Secure token storage
Rotation
Reuse detection
Session revocation
Short access-token lifetime
Telemetry
```

---

# 134. Authorization Threat Example

```text
Student A
   │
   ▼
GET /assessment/123
   │
   ▼
Changes ID to 124
   │
   ▼
Receives restricted assessment
```

Control:

```text
Resource-level authorization
```

not simply JWT validation.

---

# 135. Tenant Threat Example

```text
Institution A Admin
        │
        ▼
Changes tenantId
        │
        ▼
Institution B data
```

Controls:

```text
Server-derived tenant context
Membership validation
Tenant-scoped queries
Audit
Security testing
```

---

# 136. Service Compromise

Assume eventually a workload may be compromised.

If:

```text
notification-service
```

is compromised, it should not automatically have credentials allowing:

```text
Database administration
S3 deletion
User-role changes
Assessment modification
```

Least privilege limits blast radius.

---

# 137. Key Compromise

Security design must answer:

> What happens if a signing key, API key, client secret or workload credential is compromised?

Required capabilities include:

```text
Detection
Revocation
Rotation
Replacement
Audit
Blast-radius analysis
```

---

# 138. Security Testing

Testing should include:

```text
Authentication bypass
Expired tokens
Wrong issuer
Wrong audience
Invalid signature
Role escalation
IDOR/BOLA
Cross-tenant access
CSRF
CORS misconfiguration
Session fixation
Refresh-token reuse
Privilege revocation
Admin workflows
```

---

# 139. Automated Authorization Tests

Every sensitive endpoint should have negative tests.

Example:

```text
Student → Student resource     ALLOW
Student → Other private user   DENY
Faculty → Own course           ALLOW
Faculty → Other tenant course  DENY
Admin A → Tenant B             DENY
```

Testing only happy paths is inadequate.

---

# 140. Dependency Security

Identity/security libraries require active patching.

Critical dependencies include:

```text
Spring Security
OAuth/OIDC libraries
JWT libraries
IdP
Ingress/Gateway
Service Mesh
Secrets tooling
```

Security architecture degrades if dependencies remain unpatched.

---

# 141. Zero-Trust Decision Flow

```text
                     REQUEST
                        │
                        ▼
                  Establish Identity
                        │
                        ▼
                  Validate Credential
                        │
                        ▼
                  Resolve Tenant
                        │
                        ▼
                  Resolve Resource
                        │
                        ▼
                  Evaluate RBAC
                        │
                        ▼
                  Evaluate ABAC
                        │
                        ▼
                 Domain Constraints
                        │
               ┌────────┴────────┐
               ▼                 ▼
             ALLOW              DENY
               │                 │
               ▼                 ▼
          Execute Action     Security/Audit
               │
               ▼
             Audit
```

---

# 142. Human Identity Flow

```text
                       USER
                        │
                        ▼
                 Identity Provider
                        │
              ┌─────────┴─────────┐
              ▼                   ▼
          Password /            External
          Passkey/MFA             IdP
              │                   │
              └─────────┬─────────┘
                        ▼
                 OIDC Authorization
                        │
                        ▼
                       BFF
                        │
                Secure Session
                        │
                        ▼
                     Browser
```

Backend interaction:

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
BFF
   │ Access Token
   ▼
API Gateway
   │
   ▼
Spring Boot Resource Server
   │
   ▼
RBAC + ABAC + Domain Policy
```

---

# 143. Workload Identity Flow

```text
                   Kubernetes Pod
                         │
                         ▼
                  ServiceAccount
                         │
             ┌───────────┴───────────┐
             ▼                       ▼
      Cloud Workload Identity   Service Identity
             │                       │
             ▼                       ▼
           AWS APIs              Service APIs
             │                       │
             ▼                       ▼
         IAM Policy          OAuth / mTLS Policy
```

No static universal backend credential is required.

---

# 144. AI Agent Security Flow

```text
                      STUDENT
                         │
                         ▼
                     AI Tutor
                         │
                  User Context
                         │
                         ▼
                     AI Agent
                         │
                         ▼
                   Tool Request
                         │
                         ▼
                    Tool Gateway
                         │
                         ▼
                    Authorization
                  ┌──────┴──────┐
                  ▼             ▼
                ALLOW          DENY
                  │
                  ▼
             Domain Service
                  │
                  ▼
              Audit / Trace
```

The rule is:

```text
AI reasoning
≠
authorization decision
```

---

# 145. Identity & Security Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject:

```text
❌ Authentication implemented independently by every microservice
❌ Custom OAuth server without compelling reason
❌ Passwords stored by domain services
❌ Plaintext passwords
❌ Email used as immutable user ID
❌ JWT decoded without signature validation
❌ ID token used blindly as API access token
❌ Sensitive data stored inside JWT claims
❌ 30-day bearer access tokens
❌ Long-lived browser tokens in localStorage by default
❌ Shared service credentials
❌ Static AWS keys inside Pods
❌ One universal SUPER_ADMIN for everything
❌ Global role=FACULTY without tenant context
❌ Gateway-only authorization
❌ Checking role without resource ownership
❌ Trusting tenantId supplied by client
❌ Cross-tenant queries without tenant constraints
❌ mTLS treated as business authorization
❌ Internal network treated as trusted
❌ AI agents given unrestricted backend credentials
❌ LLM allowed to decide authorization
❌ Secrets committed to Git
❌ Secrets stored in application.yml
❌ Logging JWTs/passwords/API keys
❌ CORS treated as authentication
❌ Wildcard credentialed CORS
❌ Cookie sessions without CSRF consideration
❌ Support impersonation without audit
❌ Permanent unrestricted break-glass accounts
❌ Authorization tests covering only successful cases
```

---

# 146. Security Boundaries

The Mediverse security architecture now contains explicit trust boundaries:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
────────────────────────
Edge Boundary
────────────────────────
   │
API Gateway / BFF
   │
   ▼
────────────────────────
Application Boundary
────────────────────────
   │
Microservices
   │
   ▼
────────────────────────
Data Boundary
────────────────────────
   │
PostgreSQL / Redis /
Kafka / OpenSearch / S3

Separate:

────────────────────────
Identity Boundary
────────────────────────
Identity Provider

────────────────────────
Administration Boundary
────────────────────────
Privileged Operations

────────────────────────
Cloud Boundary
────────────────────────
IAM / KMS / Secrets
```

Crossing a boundary requires explicit trust evaluation.

---

# 147. Authorization Responsibility Matrix

| Layer                 | Responsibility                                    |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Identity Provider     | Authenticate identity                             |
| BFF                   | Browser session and token handling                |
| API Gateway           | Coarse authentication/access controls             |
| Spring Security       | Token validation and application security context |
| Domain Service        | Resource/business authorization                   |
| RBAC                  | Broad capability                                  |
| ABAC                  | Contextual authorization                          |
| Database access layer | Tenant-aware data constraints                     |
| Service Mesh          | Workload transport identity/mTLS                  |
| IAM                   | AWS resource authorization                        |
| Kubernetes RBAC       | Kubernetes API authorization                      |
| Secrets Manager       | Credential protection                             |
| Audit Platform        | Accountability                                    |
| AI Tool Gateway       | Agent capability enforcement                      |

No single layer replaces the others.
