But automatic changes can restart Pods and interact with HPA.

Use deliberately.

---

# 57. HPA + VPA

Using HPA and VPA on the same resource signal without understanding their interaction can produce unstable behavior.

Example:

```text
VPA changes CPU request
       │
       ▼
HPA utilization calculation changes
       │
       ▼
Replica behavior changes
```

Platform policy should define allowed combinations.

---

# 58. Node Autoscaling

Pod autoscaling alone is insufficient.

```text
HPA creates Pods
      │
      ▼
No node capacity
      │
      ▼
Pods Pending
```

The cluster also needs capacity autoscaling.

---

# 59. Cluster Autoscaler

Traditional architecture:

```text
Pending Pods
     │
     ▼
Cluster Autoscaler
     │
     ▼
Node Group scales
```

This works well with predefined node groups.

---

# 60. Karpenter

Karpenter can provision capacity more dynamically based on unscheduled workload requirements.

Conceptually:

```text
Pending Pod
    │
    ▼
Requirements
    │
    ▼
Karpenter
    │
    ▼
Appropriate EC2 Capacity
```

For Mediverse's diverse workload profile, this is strategically attractive.

---

## ADR-050 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The Kubernetes architecture established so far is:

```text
                       AWS ORGANIZATION
                              │
             ┌────────────────┴────────────────┐
             ▼                                 ▼
       NON-PRODUCTION                      PRODUCTION
        AWS ACCOUNT                        AWS ACCOUNT
             │                                 │
             ▼                                 ▼
         EKS Cluster                       EKS Cluster
             │                                 │
       ┌─────┼─────┐                     ┌─────┼─────┐
       ▼     ▼     ▼                     ▼     ▼     ▼
      AZ-A  AZ-B  AZ-C                   AZ-A  AZ-B  AZ-C
             │                                 │
             ▼                                 ▼
        Node Pools                         Node Pools
       ┌─────┼─────┐                 ┌────────┼────────┐
       ▼     ▼     ▼                 ▼        ▼        ▼
    System General AI             System   General     AI
             │                                 │
             ▼                                 ▼
         Namespaces                        Namespaces
             │                                 │
             ▼                                 ▼
          Workloads                         Workloads
```

The scaling chain is:

```text
Application Demand
       │
       ▼
Workload Metric
       │
       ▼
HPA / Event Autoscaler
       │
       ▼
More Pods
       │
       ▼
Scheduler
       │
       ├── Capacity available ──► Schedule
       │
       └── Capacity missing
                 │
                 ▼
          Node Autoscaler
                 │
                 ▼
             EC2 Capacity
```

And the resilience model is:

```text
Multiple Replicas
       +
Multi-AZ Placement
       +
Topology Spread
       +
Readiness
       +
Graceful Shutdown
       +
PodDisruptionBudget
       +
Autoscaling
       =
Application-Level Kubernetes Resilience
```

The critical rule is:

> **Kubernetes does not create high availability from a badly configured application. A one-replica service, incorrect probes, missing resource requests, single-AZ placement and broken shutdown behavior remain unreliable even when deployed to EKS.**

**Part 2** should continue from **Section 61 — Karpenter vs Cluster Autoscaler Decision**, then cover Spot capacity, interruption handling, consolidation, scheduling governance, EBS/EFS/CSI, StatefulSets, Jobs/CronJobs, ConfigMaps, ServiceAccounts/workload identity, Kubernetes RBAC, NetworkPolicy, Pod Security Standards, admission control, Kyverno/Gatekeeper evaluation, image policies, ECR, supply-chain controls, ingress/Gateway API, AWS Load Balancer Controller, ALB/NLB, Route 53, ExternalDNS, cert-manager, service mesh integration, observability, Kubernetes audit, GitOps/Argo CD, Helm, environment promotion, cluster upgrades, add-on lifecycle, node rotation, backup/Velero, disaster recovery, AZ/region/cluster failure, capacity planning, cost governance, platform SLOs, operational ownership, anti-patterns and the final Mediverse EKS reference architecture.


# ADR-050 — Enterprise Kubernetes Platform, EKS, Multi-Environment, Namespace, Autoscaling, Scheduling & Cluster Governance Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Karpenter**.

---

# 61. Karpenter vs Cluster Autoscaler Decision

Both solve node-capacity scaling, but differently.

```text
Cluster Autoscaler
      │
      ▼
Existing Node Groups
      │
      ▼
Scale Group Capacity
```

Karpenter is more workload-driven:

```text
Pending Pods
     │
     ▼
Scheduling Requirements
     │
     ▼
Karpenter
     │
     ▼
Select EC2 Capacity
     │
     ▼
Launch Node
```

For Mediverse, **Karpenter is the preferred strategic node autoscaler**, subject to production validation.

---

# 62. Why Karpenter?

Mediverse has heterogeneous workloads:

```text
Spring Boot APIs
Kafka consumers
Media workers
AI workloads
Batch jobs
Platform services
```

Karpenter can provision capacity matching actual Pod requirements rather than forcing every workload through a small fixed set of node groups.

---

# 63. Do Not Remove All Stable Capacity

Dynamic provisioning does not mean:

```text
Cluster starts with zero reliable nodes
```

Critical platform components need dependable baseline capacity.

Preferred:

```text
Stable System Capacity
        +
Dynamic Application Capacity
```

---

# 64. Spot Instances

Spot capacity can substantially reduce compute cost.

Suitable candidates include:

```text
Stateless workers
Fault-tolerant consumers
Batch jobs
Media processing
Horizontally scalable services
```

provided interruption is handled correctly.

---

# 65. Spot Is Interruptible

Spot instances can disappear.

Therefore:

```text
Cheap
≠
Reliable
```

A workload using Spot must tolerate node termination.

---

# 66. Critical Workload Strategy

Do not place all replicas of a critical API exclusively on one Spot capacity type.

Preferred:

```text
Critical Service
     │
     ├── On-Demand baseline
     └── Spot burst capacity
```

where economics justify it.

---

# 67. Capacity Diversification

Spot reliability improves when capacity requirements are flexible across:

```text
Instance families
Instance sizes
Availability Zones
```

Over-constraining:

```text
exact-instance-type = X
exact-AZ = Y
```

reduces Karpenter's options.

---

# 68. Interruption Handling

Node interruption should trigger:

```text
Interruption Notice
      │
      ▼
Cordon / Drain
      │
      ▼
Pods rescheduled
      │
      ▼
Replacement capacity
```

Applications must already support graceful termination.

---

# 69. Consolidation

Karpenter can potentially consolidate inefficient nodes.

```text
Node A → 20% utilized
Node B → 25% utilized
Node C → 15% utilized
```

may become:

```text
Fewer better-utilized nodes
```

when scheduling constraints permit.

---

# 70. Consolidation Safety

Aggressive consolidation can create unnecessary Pod churn.

Critical workloads require:

```text
PDB
Graceful shutdown
Topology controls
Correct readiness
```

before aggressive optimization.

Cost optimization must not destroy reliability.

---

# 71. Persistent Storage

Kubernetes Pods are ephemeral.

Persistent data therefore requires separate storage.

Primary AWS options:

```text
EBS
EFS
S3
Managed databases
```

These solve different problems.

---

# 72. EBS

EBS provides block storage.

Typical:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
PersistentVolumeClaim
 │
 ▼
EBS CSI
 │
 ▼
EBS Volume
```

Suitable for workloads requiring persistent block devices.

---

# 73. EBS Availability-Zone Constraint

An EBS volume exists in an Availability Zone.

Therefore:

```text
EBS Volume in AZ-A
       │
       ▼
Pod must attach appropriately in AZ-A
```

This matters during scheduling and failure recovery.

---

# 74. EFS

EFS provides shared network filesystem capabilities.

```text
Pod A ─┐
Pod B ─┼──► EFS
Pod C ─┘
```

Useful where multiple Pods genuinely need shared POSIX filesystem access.

Do not use EFS simply because persistent storage is required.

---

# 75. S3 Is Not a Filesystem Replacement

ADR-046 established S3 for object storage.

Use:

```text
S3
```

for object semantics.

Use:

```text
EBS / EFS
```

when filesystem/block semantics are actually required.

Do not hide architectural mismatches behind filesystem adapters.

---

# 76. CSI

Kubernetes storage integrations should use CSI drivers.

Examples:

```text
EBS CSI
EFS CSI
```

CSI decouples storage implementations from Kubernetes core.

---

# 77. StatefulSets

StatefulSets provide stable identities and storage relationships for workloads that require them.

```text
service-0
service-1
service-2
```

But StatefulSet does not magically make a distributed database reliable.

---

# 78. Managed Stateful Infrastructure

Where practical, Mediverse should prefer managed AWS services for critical data infrastructure rather than operating everything inside EKS.

Examples:

```text
PostgreSQL → RDS/Aurora where selected
Object storage → S3
Managed Redis where selected
Managed search where selected
```

Kubernetes is not a requirement to self-host every database.

---

# 79. Jobs

Finite workloads should use Kubernetes Jobs where appropriate.

Examples:

```text
Data migration
One-time processing
Maintenance
Batch operations
```

A Job represents work expected to complete.

---

# 80. CronJobs

Recurring tasks may use CronJobs.

Examples:

```text
Cleanup
Periodic reconciliation
Scheduled exports
```

But critical enterprise scheduling may require stronger workflow systems if jobs have complex dependencies and recovery semantics.

---

# 81. CronJob Concurrency

A scheduled job taking longer than its schedule can overlap.

```text
Job A ────────────────
       Job B ────────────────
```

Concurrency policy must be explicitly considered.

---

# 82. Job Idempotency

Retries can occur.

Therefore jobs should be designed so that:

```text
Execute once
Execute again
```

does not corrupt state.

This aligns with ADR-042's distributed reliability principles.

---

# 83. ConfigMaps

Non-sensitive runtime configuration can use ConfigMaps.

Examples:

```text
Feature configuration
Service endpoints
Operational settings
```

Secrets belong to ADR-049's secret-management architecture.

---

# 84. Configuration Changes

Changing a ConfigMap does not guarantee every application automatically reloads it correctly.

Teams must define whether configuration changes require:

```text
Dynamic reload
Pod restart
New deployment
```

---

# 85. ServiceAccounts

Every application workload should use an appropriate ServiceAccount.

Avoid relying universally on:

```text
default
```

ServiceAccount.

Identity should map to workload responsibility.

---

# 86. Workload Identity

From ADR-048/049:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
ServiceAccount
 │
 ▼
AWS Workload Identity
 │
 ▼
IAM Role
 │
 ▼
AWS Resource
```

This eliminates the need for long-lived AWS credentials in Pods.

---

# 87. Kubernetes RBAC

Kubernetes API authorization should follow least privilege.

Roles may govern:

```text
Pods
Deployments
ConfigMaps
Secrets
Jobs
Namespaces
```

Application workloads generally do not need broad Kubernetes API access.

---

# 88. `cluster-admin`

Routine application deployment should not require:

```text
cluster-admin
```

Giving every engineer or CI pipeline cluster-admin privileges destroys the security boundary.

---

# 89. Human Kubernetes Access

Human production access should be:

```text
Identity-based
Role-controlled
Audited
Time-bound where appropriate
```

rather than shared kubeconfig credentials.

---

# 90. NetworkPolicy

Kubernetes networking should follow:

```text
Default Deny
     │
     ▼
Explicitly Allow Required Traffic
```

where the CNI/network architecture supports enforcement.

---

# 91. East-West Isolation

Without network policies:

```text
Compromised Pod
      │
      ├──► Service A
      ├──► Service B
      ├──► Redis
      ├──► Internal APIs
      └──► Anything reachable
```

Network segmentation reduces blast radius.

---

# 92. NetworkPolicy Is Not Authorization

Allowing:

```text
course-service → assessment-service
```

does not prove that a specific operation is authorized.

ADR-048 application authorization remains mandatory.

---

# 93. Pod Security Standards

Mediverse should enforce Kubernetes Pod Security Standards or equivalent admission policies.

Target production posture should strongly prefer:

```text
restricted
```

semantics unless a workload has documented exceptions.

---

# 94. Containers Should Not Run as Root by Default

Preferred:

```text
runAsNonRoot
```

with an appropriate application user.

Running every application as root unnecessarily increases compromise impact.

---

# 95. Privileged Containers

Production application workloads should not use:

```text
privileged: true
```

without exceptional infrastructure-level justification.

Privileged containers can severely weaken node isolation.

---

# 96. Linux Capabilities

Containers should drop unnecessary Linux capabilities.

Conceptually:

```text
Drop ALL
   │
   ▼
Add only explicitly required capabilities
```

where compatible.

---

# 97. Read-Only Root Filesystem

Where application design permits:

```text
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
```

reduces runtime modification opportunities.

Writable paths should be explicit.

---

# 98. Admission Control

Security and governance should be enforced before workloads enter the cluster.

```text
Deployment
    │
    ▼
Admission
    │
    ├── Policy satisfied ─► Admit
    └── Policy violated ──► Reject
```

This is stronger than discovering bad configuration after deployment.

---

# 99. Admission Policy Examples

Policies may enforce:

```text
No privileged Pods
Required resource requests
Approved registries
Required labels
No hostPath
No hostNetwork
Non-root execution
Required probes
Restricted capabilities
```

according to workload category.

---

# 100. Kyverno vs Gatekeeper

Both are valid policy-engine candidates.

```text
Kyverno
=
Kubernetes-native policy model

Gatekeeper
=
OPA/Rego-based policy enforcement
```

Mediverse should choose **one primary admission-policy framework**, not deploy both without a concrete reason.

---

# 101. Policy-as-Code

Admission policies should be:

```text
Versioned
Reviewed
Tested
Promoted
Audited
```

through Git.

Cluster governance is software.

---

# 102. Policy Rollout

Do not immediately enforce hundreds of policies in production.

Preferred:

```text
Audit
  │
  ▼
Measure violations
  │
  ▼
Fix workloads
  │
  ▼
Enforce
```

This avoids breaking legitimate workloads blindly.

---

# 103. Container Registry

Mediverse should use a controlled registry such as Amazon ECR for production images.

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
Build
 │
 ▼
Scan
 │
 ▼
ECR
 │
 ▼
EKS
```

---

# 104. Never Deploy `latest`

Bad:

```text
image: mediverse/course-service:latest
```

because deployment state becomes ambiguous.

Use immutable identifiers such as:

```text
Version tag
+
Image digest
```

with digest pinning preferred for strong reproducibility.

---

# 105. Image Immutability

A release should identify exactly one image.

```text
course-service:1.7.3
       │
       ▼
sha256:...
```

The same release identifier must not silently point to different binaries later.

---

# 106. Image Scanning

Container pipelines should scan for:

```text
Known vulnerabilities
Secrets
Malware where appropriate
Unsupported packages
```

before promotion.

A scanner does not automatically make a vulnerable image safe; policy must define what findings block deployment.

---

# 107. Software Supply Chain

The deployment pipeline should establish:

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
Build
  │
  ▼
Artifact
  │
  ▼
Provenance
  │
  ▼
Registry
  │
  ▼
Deployment
```

so production artifacts can be traced back to controlled source and build processes.

---

# 108. Image Signing

Mediverse should progressively support signed/verifiable container artifacts.

Admission can eventually enforce:

```text
Trusted signer?
Known provenance?
Approved repository?
```

before allowing production deployment.

---

# 109. Ingress Architecture

External traffic should not directly target arbitrary Pods.

Preferred:

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
AWS Edge / DNS
   │
   ▼
Load Balancer
   │
   ▼
Ingress / Gateway
   │
   ▼
Kubernetes Service
   │
   ▼
Pods
```

---

# 110. AWS Load Balancer Controller

The AWS Load Balancer Controller should manage AWS load-balancing integration where selected.

It can provision/manage resources such as:

```text
ALB
NLB
```

from Kubernetes resources.

---

# 111. ALB

Application Load Balancer is appropriate for HTTP/HTTPS layer-7 routing.

Capabilities include:

```text
Host routing
Path routing
TLS termination
HTTP semantics
```

---

# 112. NLB

Network Load Balancer is appropriate for layer-4 requirements such as:

```text
TCP
TLS pass-through/termination scenarios
High-throughput network traffic
```

depending on service requirements.

Do not use ALB and NLB interchangeably.

---

# 113. Gateway API

Mediverse should evaluate Kubernetes Gateway API as the strategic successor for richer traffic-management configuration.

Conceptually:

```text
GatewayClass
     │
     ▼
Gateway
     │
     ▼
HTTPRoute / GRPCRoute
```

It provides cleaner separation between infrastructure ownership and application routing.

---

# 114. Ingress vs Gateway API

Existing Ingress remains valid.

Do not migrate solely because Gateway API is newer.

Adopt Gateway API when:

```text
Controller support
Operational maturity
Traffic requirements
Ownership model
```

justify the change.

---

# 115. Route 53

Public/private DNS should integrate with Route 53 where consistent with the AWS architecture.

```text
api.mediverse...
       │
       ▼
Route 53
       │
       ▼
Load Balancer
```

DNS becomes part of the production dependency chain and must be monitored.

---

# 116. ExternalDNS

ExternalDNS can automate Kubernetes-driven DNS record management.

```text
Service / Gateway
       │
       ▼
ExternalDNS
       │
       ▼
Route 53
```

Its IAM permissions must be tightly scoped.

A compromised DNS controller with unrestricted zone access has significant blast radius.

---

# 117. TLS Certificates

Public certificate lifecycle should follow ADR-049.

Typically:

```text
ACM
 │
 ▼
ALB / CloudFront
```

or cert-manager where Kubernetes-managed certificate issuance is appropriate.

Do not create competing certificate systems without clear ownership boundaries.

---

# 118. Service Mesh Relationship

ADR-041's service mesh, if adopted, operates inside the Kubernetes architecture.

```text
External Traffic
      │
      ▼
Gateway
      │
      ▼
Service Mesh
      │
      ▼
Microservices
```

The mesh may provide:

```text
mTLS
Traffic policy
Workload identity
Telemetry
```

but Kubernetes remains responsible for scheduling and workload lifecycle.

---

# 119. Observability

ADR-047 becomes mandatory platform infrastructure.

Every production cluster must expose visibility into:

```text
Nodes
Pods
Deployments
Autoscaling
Scheduling
Network
Storage
Control-plane interactions
Applications
```

---

# 120. Cluster Metrics

Core dashboards should include:

```text
Node utilization
Pending Pods
Pod restarts
OOMKills
CPU throttling
Unschedulable Pods
HPA status
Karpenter activity
Volume failures
Ingress errors
```

---

# 121. Kubernetes Events

Events can provide useful short-lived diagnostic context:

```text
FailedScheduling
BackOff
Unhealthy
FailedMount
Evicted
```

But Kubernetes Events are not a durable observability database by themselves.

---

# 122. Kubernetes Audit Logs

Production Kubernetes API activity should be audited according to security requirements.

This helps answer:

```text
Who changed this Deployment?

Who read this Secret?

Who deleted this namespace?

Who created this privileged Pod?
```

---

# 123. GitOps

Production Kubernetes state should primarily be managed through GitOps.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Desired State
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 ▼
EKS
```

rather than manual `kubectl` mutation.

---

# 124. Argo CD

Argo CD should continuously reconcile approved desired state.

```text
Git
 │
 │ desired
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 ▼
Cluster
 │
 │ drift?
 └────────► Reconcile
```

This creates a controlled deployment model.

---

# 125. `kubectl edit` in Production

Routine:

```text
kubectl edit deployment
```

creates configuration drift.

Emergency changes may occasionally be necessary, but must be:

```text
Audited
Temporary
Back-ported to Git
Reviewed
```

Git remains authoritative.

---

# 126. Helm

Helm should package reusable Kubernetes application configuration.

Example:

```text
Chart
 ├── Deployment
 ├── Service
 ├── HPA
 ├── PDB
 ├── ServiceAccount
 └── Config
```

Helm is packaging/templating.

It is not the deployment authority when GitOps owns reconciliation.

---

# 127. Helm Values

Avoid enormous environment-specific values files containing arbitrary differences.

Prefer:

```text
Common defaults
      +
Small explicit environment overrides
```

Production should not become an entirely different application architecture hidden inside `values-prod.yaml`.

---

# 128. Environment Promotion

Preferred:

```text
Build Once
    │
    ▼
Immutable Artifact
    │
    ▼
DEV
    │
    ▼
UAT
    │
    ▼
STAGING
    │
    ▼
PRODUCTION
```

Do not rebuild application binaries independently for every environment.

---

# 129. Promotion Changes Configuration, Not Binary

The same image digest should move through environments.

```text
sha256:ABC
   │
   ├── DEV
   ├── UAT
   ├── STAGING
   └── PROD
```

Environment-specific configuration may differ.

The application binary should not.

---

# 130. Cluster Upgrades

Kubernetes versions have finite support windows.

Mediverse needs a routine upgrade process:

```text
Review compatibility
       │
       ▼
Upgrade non-production
       │
       ▼
Validate
       │
       ▼
Upgrade control plane
       │
       ▼
Rotate nodes
       │
       ▼
Validate production
```

Waiting until forced upgrade deadlines is poor platform management.

---

# 131. Add-On Compatibility

Before Kubernetes upgrades, validate:

```text
CNI
CoreDNS
kube-proxy
CSI drivers
Karpenter
Argo CD
Ingress controller
Service mesh
Observability stack
Admission controllers
```

The Kubernetes API version is only one part of compatibility.

---

# 132. Deprecated APIs

Application manifests must be checked for Kubernetes APIs removed in future versions.

A cluster upgrade can fail workloads that still depend on obsolete resource versions.

CI should detect this before production.

---

# 133. Node Rotation

Worker nodes should be treated as replaceable.

```text
Old Node
   │
   ▼
Cordon
   │
   ▼
Drain
   │
   ▼
Replacement Node
   │
   ▼
Terminate Old Node
```

Do not maintain pet worker nodes indefinitely.

---

# 134. Backup Scope

Kubernetes backup must distinguish:

```text
Cluster configuration
Persistent volumes
Application databases
Object storage
External managed services
```

Backing up Kubernetes YAML does not back up PostgreSQL.

---

# 135. Velero Evaluation

Velero may be used for:

```text
Kubernetes resource backup
Selected volume backup/snapshots
Restore workflows
```

where appropriate.

But it does not replace native database backup and DR strategies.

---

# 136. Git as Recovery Source

Much Kubernetes configuration already exists in Git.

Therefore:

```text
GitOps repository
+
Terraform
+
Helm
```

should allow reconstruction of substantial cluster state.

Backups should focus particularly on state that cannot simply be regenerated.

---

# 137. Cluster Failure

Architecture must assume an entire cluster can become unavailable.

Recovery should answer:

```text
Can infrastructure be recreated?
Can applications be redeployed?
Can secrets be restored/referenced?
Can DNS be redirected?
Can persistent data be recovered?
```

---

# 138. AZ Failure

With multi-AZ placement:

```text
AZ-B fails
   │
   ▼
Pods lost
   │
   ▼
Remaining replicas continue
   │
   ▼
Replacement capacity elsewhere
```

provided application dependencies also tolerate the AZ failure.

Multi-AZ Pods do not help if the database remains a single-AZ dependency.

---

# 139. Regional Failure

Kubernetes alone does not solve regional DR.

Regional resilience requires coordinated decisions across:

```text
EKS
PostgreSQL
S3
Kafka
Redis
OpenSearch
KMS
Secrets
DNS
Identity
```

The DR architecture must be end-to-end.

---

# 140. Capacity Planning

Autoscaling does not eliminate capacity planning.

Mediverse still needs to understand:

```text
Baseline load
Peak load
Growth
Instance availability
Service quotas
IP capacity
Pod density
Database limits
Kafka partitioning
```

Autoscaling cannot create resources beyond cloud/account constraints.

---

# 141. IP Exhaustion

Large EKS environments can exhaust VPC/subnet IP capacity.

Symptoms:

```text
Nodes available
     │
     ▼
Pods cannot obtain IPs
     │
     ▼
Scheduling/network failures
```

VPC and CNI capacity planning are part of Kubernetes architecture.

---

# 142. Cost Governance

Kubernetes cost should be attributable by:

```text
Environment
Namespace
Workload
Team
Capacity type
```

where practical.

Without allocation data, cost optimization becomes guesswork.

---

# 143. Requests Drive Cost

If a service requests:

```text
4 CPU
8 GiB RAM
```

but normally consumes:

```text
0.2 CPU
1 GiB RAM
```

the scheduler reserves capacity based largely on requests.

Bad requests create real infrastructure cost.

---

# 144. Platform SLOs

The Kubernetes platform itself should have reliability objectives.

Examples:

```text
Deployment success
Scheduling availability
Ingress availability
DNS availability
GitOps reconciliation
Critical controller availability
```

Application SLOs depend on platform reliability.

---

# 145. Ownership Model

Platform team owns:

```text
EKS
Node lifecycle
Core add-ons
Ingress
GitOps platform
Admission policy
Cluster observability
Platform security baseline
```

Application teams own:

```text
Application manifests
Resource sizing
Probes
HPA behavior
PDB
Application availability
Domain telemetry
```

Shared ownership must be explicit.

---

# 146. Kubernetes Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject:

```text
❌ Production and DEV sharing one unrestricted cluster
❌ Namespace treated as equivalent to AWS-account isolation
❌ Single-AZ production worker capacity
❌ One replica for every critical API
❌ No resource requests
❌ Arbitrary copied resource limits
❌ JVM Xmx equal to container memory limit
❌ Every workload marked high priority
❌ All replicas scheduled on one node/AZ
❌ Liveness checking every downstream dependency
❌ CPU-only autoscaling for every workload
❌ HPA without node-capacity scaling
❌ Spot-only critical services without resilience design
❌ GPU nodes accepting ordinary workloads
❌ StatefulSet assumed to make databases highly available
❌ Self-hosting every managed data service inside Kubernetes
❌ Application Pods using default ServiceAccount everywhere
❌ Static AWS keys inside Pods
❌ Broad cluster-admin for CI/CD
❌ Every engineer having permanent cluster-admin
❌ No NetworkPolicy strategy
❌ Privileged application containers
❌ Containers running as root without need
❌ Mutable `latest` image tags
❌ Production images without vulnerability controls
❌ Manual production deployment as standard practice
❌ `kubectl edit` as configuration management
❌ Secrets committed to Helm values
❌ Rebuilding binaries separately for PROD
❌ Ignoring deprecated Kubernetes APIs
❌ Worker nodes treated as permanent servers
❌ Assuming Git backup equals database backup
❌ Autoscaling without capacity/quota planning
```

---

# 147. Cluster Governance Model

```text
                       PLATFORM POLICY
                             │
             ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
             ▼               ▼                ▼
         Security         Reliability        Cost
             │               │                │
             ▼               ▼                ▼
        Admission         Resources        Quotas
         Policies           PDB/HPA        Right-size
             │               │                │
             └───────────────┼────────────────┘
                             ▼
                          GitOps
                             │
                             ▼
                           EKS
```

Governance should be automated rather than dependent on engineers remembering dozens of rules.

---

# 149. Core Kubernetes Invariants

These must remain true regardless of future implementation changes:

```text
1. Production has a stronger isolation boundary than a namespace alone.

2. Production workloads span multiple failure domains.

3. Worker nodes are disposable infrastructure.

4. Critical APIs use multiple replicas.

5. Production workloads define meaningful resource requests.

6. Resource sizing is driven by measurement.

7. Liveness, readiness and startup have distinct semantics.

8. Workloads terminate gracefully.

9. Pod scaling and node scaling operate together.

10. Specialized capacity is isolated through scheduling policy.

11. Workloads use dedicated identities.

12. Static cloud credentials are not embedded in Pods.

13. Kubernetes API permissions follow least privilege.

14. Network reachability does not imply authorization.

15. Security policy is enforced through admission controls.

16. Production artifacts are immutable and identifiable.

17. Git is the authoritative desired-state source.

18. The same binary artifact is promoted between environments.

19. Kubernetes upgrades are routine engineering work.

20. Persistent data has an explicit backup/recovery owner.

21. Autoscaling does not replace capacity planning.

22. Platform and application ownership boundaries are explicit.
```

---

| Area                      | Decision                                       |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Container platform        | **Amazon EKS**                                 |
| Control plane             | AWS managed                                    |
| Production isolation      | Dedicated production cluster/account preferred |
| Worker architecture       | Multi-AZ                                       |
| General compute           | EC2                                            |
| Node lifecycle            | Replaceable/immutable                          |
| Node autoscaling          | **Karpenter preferred**                        |
| Stable system capacity    | Required                                       |
| Spot                      | Selective, interruption-tolerant workloads     |
| Specialized capacity      | Dedicated node pools                           |
| ARM/Graviton              | Evaluate/use where compatible                  |
| GPU                       | Dedicated capacity                             |
| Resource requests         | Mandatory production baseline                  |
| Resource limits           | Workload-specific                              |
| JVM sizing                | Container-aware                                |
| Namespace quotas          | Required where appropriate                     |
| Replica topology          | Multi-node/AZ                                  |
| PDB                       | Required for relevant critical workloads       |
| Graceful shutdown         | Required                                       |
| Probes                    | Liveness + readiness + startup as appropriate  |
| HPA                       | Workload-specific metrics                      |
| Worker autoscaling        | Queue/lag metrics preferred where appropriate  |
| VPA                       | Right-sizing/selective automation              |
| Storage                   | CSI-based                                      |
| Object storage            | S3                                             |
| Shared filesystem         | EFS where justified                            |
| Block storage             | EBS where justified                            |
| Critical databases        | Managed services preferred                     |
| Workload identity         | ServiceAccount + AWS identity                  |

| Privileged containers     | Exception only                                 |
| Admission control         | Mandatory governance layer                     |
| Policy-as-code            | Required                                       |
| Registry                  | ECR                                            |
| `latest`                  | Prohibited in production                       |
| Image immutability        | Required                                       |
| Supply-chain verification | Progressive enforcement                        |
| External traffic          | Controlled gateway/load-balancer path          |
| DNS                       | Route 53                                       |
| GitOps                    | **Argo CD**                                    |
| Packaging                 | Helm                                           |

CODE

IMMUTABLE IMAGE
 │

ECR
 │
 ▼
GITOPS
 │
 ▼
ARGO CD
 │

EKS
 │
 ├── Admission Policy
 ├── Workload Identity
 ├── Scheduling
 ├── HPA
