## Next — ADR-051

### **ADR-051 — Enterprise CI/CD, GitOps, Argo CD, Helm, Release Engineering & Software Supply-Chain Architecture**

ADR-050 established **where Mediverse runs**. ADR-051 should establish exactly **how trusted software gets there**.

It should cover **Git repository strategy → trunk-based development vs GitFlow → branch protection → pull requests → CODEOWNERS → semantic versioning → conventional commits evaluation → CI triggers → Maven/Gradle → npm builds → unit/integration/contract/E2E tests → quality gates → SonarQube → dependency scanning → SAST → secret scanning → SBOM → SCA → container builds → BuildKit → multi-stage Dockerfiles → reproducible builds → ECR → immutable tags/digests → artifact signing → provenance → SLSA → Cosign/Sigstore → admission verification → Helm chart architecture → chart versioning → environment values → GitOps repository strategy → Argo CD → ApplicationSets → sync policies → drift detection → self-healing → pruning → secrets integration → image promotion → DEV/UAT/STAGING/PROD promotion → approvals → progressive delivery → rolling vs blue/green vs canary → Argo Rollouts evaluation → automated rollback → database migration strategy → backward-compatible schemas → feature flags → release toggles → deployment markers → release observability → DORA metrics → change failure rate → MTTR → rollback architecture → hotfixes → break-glass deployment → Jenkins vs GitHub Actions evaluation → CI worker security → OIDC workload federation → cache security → artifact retention → dependency pinning → build hermeticity → supply-chain threat model → compromised dependency/build runner/registry scenarios → disaster recovery → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise software delivery reference architecture.**

# ADR-051 — Enterprise CI/CD, GitOps, Argo CD, Helm, Release Engineering & Software Supply-Chain Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-051
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-050 established **where Mediverse workloads run**.

ADR-051 establishes:

> **How source code becomes a verified, immutable, traceable production workload—and how Mediverse prevents unreviewed source, compromised dependencies, mutable artifacts, leaked credentials, insecure CI workers or manual production changes from bypassing that chain.**

The fundamental delivery chain is:

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
Source Control
   │
   ▼
Review
   │
   ▼
CI
   │
   ▼
Test / Analyze / Scan
   │
   ▼
Build
   │
   ▼
Immutable Artifact
   │
   ▼
Registry
   │
   ▼
GitOps Desired State
   │
   ▼
Argo CD
   │
   ▼
EKS
   │
   ▼
Runtime Verification
```

---

# 1. CI and CD Are Different Responsibilities

CI answers:

```text
Can this source safely produce
a releasable artifact?
```

CD answers:

```text
Which approved artifact
should run in this environment?
```

Mediverse shall keep these responsibilities logically separated.

---

# 2. Core Decision

The strategic delivery model shall be:

```text
Source Repository
      │
      ▼
CI Pipeline
      │
      ▼
Immutable Artifact
      │
      ▼
ECR / Artifact Repository
      │
      ▼
GitOps Repository
      │
      ▼
Argo CD
      │
      ▼
Amazon EKS
```

CI builds artifacts.

Argo CD reconciles runtime state.

CI should not normally execute arbitrary imperative production deployment commands.

---

# 3. Push vs Pull Deployment

Traditional push deployment:

```text
CI Server
   │
   ▼
kubectl apply
   │
   ▼
Production
```

Preferred GitOps pull/reconciliation model:

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
GitOps Repository
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 ▼
Production
```

This reduces direct production credentials inside CI.

---

# 4. Why GitOps?

GitOps provides:

```text
Versioned desired state
Peer review
Audit history
Drift detection
Rollback history
Environment visibility
Reproducibility
```

Git becomes the declarative record of intended runtime state.

---

# 5. Git Is Desired State, Not Secret Storage

ADR-049 remains authoritative:

```text
Git
├── Kubernetes manifests       ✅
├── Helm configuration         ✅
├── Application versions       ✅
├── Policies                   ✅
├── Secret references          ✅
├── Encrypted secret material  ⚠️ where justified
└── Plaintext secrets          ❌
```

---

# 6. Repository Categories

Mediverse should distinguish at least:

```text
Application Repositories
Infrastructure Repositories
GitOps Repositories
Platform Configuration
```

These have different ownership and lifecycle characteristics.

---

# 7. Application Repository

Example:

```text
course-service/
├── src/
├── pom.xml
├── Dockerfile
├── tests/
├── helm/
└── docs/
```

Application teams own the application lifecycle.

---

# 8. Infrastructure Repository

Infrastructure-as-code may contain:

```text
Terraform
AWS infrastructure
EKS configuration
IAM
Networking
KMS
Databases
```

Infrastructure changes require different permissions from ordinary application releases.

---

# 9. GitOps Repository

Example:

```text
mediverse-gitops/
├── dev/
├── uat/
├── staging/
└── production/
```

or a structured application/environment model.

It defines what artifact versions environments should run.

---

# 10. Monorepo vs Polyrepo

Neither is universally superior.

Monorepo advantages:

```text
Atomic cross-service changes
Central standards
Simplified discovery
```

Polyrepo advantages:

```text
Independent ownership
Independent lifecycle
Smaller permission boundaries
```

Mediverse should choose based on bounded contexts and team ownership rather than fashion.

---

# 11. Microservice Repository Independence

Independent microservices should not require synchronized releases merely because they happen to live in the same repository.

Repository topology must not accidentally recreate a distributed monolith.

---

# 12. Branching Strategy

Mediverse should prefer a trunk-oriented model.

Conceptually:

```text
Feature Branch
     │
     ▼
Pull Request
     │
     ▼
main
```

Feature branches should generally be short-lived.

---

# 13. Long-Lived Branch Problem

A model such as:

```text
develop
release/*
uat
staging
production
```

can create:

```text
Merge divergence
Cherry-pick errors
Environment branches
Unclear source of truth
Slow integration
```

Branches should represent code-development concerns, not environments.

---

# 14. Environment ≠ Branch

Avoid:

```text
dev branch      → DEV
uat branch      → UAT
prod branch     → PROD
```

because code divergence can become environment divergence.

Environment state belongs in deployment configuration.

---

# 15. Pull Requests

Changes to protected branches should pass through pull requests.

PRs provide:

```text
Review
Automated checks
Discussion
Auditability
Ownership validation
```

---

# 16. Branch Protection

Critical branches should enforce controls such as:

```text
No direct push
Required reviews
Required status checks
No unresolved discussions
Restricted force push
Controlled deletion
```

according to repository criticality.

---

# 17. CODEOWNERS

Sensitive areas should require review by appropriate owners.

Examples:

```text
/security/
 /terraform/
 /kubernetes/
 /database/migrations/
 /auth/
```

A frontend developer should not be able to silently alter production IAM policy without relevant review.

---

# 18. Two-Person Control

High-impact changes may require stronger review.

Examples:

```text
Production IAM
KMS policy
Cluster admission policy
Authentication configuration
Production database migration
```

Not every typo needs two approvals.

Controls should follow risk.

---

# 19. Commit Identity

Repository history should provide reliable attribution.

Critical repositories should avoid anonymous/shared identities.

```text
Change
  │
  ▼
Known Author
  │
  ▼
Reviewed PR
```

---

# 20. Conventional Commits

Conventional Commits may standardize messages such as:

```text
feat:
fix:
docs:
refactor:
chore:
```

This can support automated changelogs and versioning.

But commit-message formatting is not itself a release architecture.

---

# 21. Semantic Versioning

Versioned Mediverse components should generally follow:

```text
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
```

Example:

```text
3.7.2
```

Version semantics should reflect compatibility contracts rather than arbitrary build numbers.

---

# 22. Version Is Not Deployment Identity

A human-readable version helps operations.

For exact artifact identity, use:

```text
Image Digest
```

Example conceptually:

```text
course-service:3.7.2
+
sha256:ABC...
```

The digest identifies exact image content.

---

# 23. CI Trigger

Typical CI flow:

```text
Pull Request
     │
     ▼
Fast Validation

Merge to main
     │
     ▼
Full Build
     │
     ▼
Release Artifact
```

Expensive work should be structured intelligently without weakening required validation.

---

# 24. Pipeline Stages

A mature pipeline may contain:

```text
Checkout
   │
   ▼
Dependency Resolution
   │
   ▼
Compile
   │
   ▼
Unit Tests
   │
   ▼
Static Analysis
   │
   ▼
Security Analysis
   │
   ▼
Integration Tests
   │
   ▼
Package
   │
   ▼
Container Build
   │
   ▼
Container Scan
   │
   ▼
SBOM / Provenance
   │
   ▼
Sign
   │
   ▼
Publish
```

Not every stage must execute serially.

Independent checks should run in parallel where practical.

---

# 25. Fail Fast

Cheap validation should generally happen before expensive work.

```text
Formatting
Compile
Unit tests
Basic static analysis
```

should not wait behind a 30-minute integration environment if they can reject the change in two minutes.

---

# 26. Maven / Gradle

Spring Boot services should use a deterministic build tool configuration.

If Maven:

```text
mvnw
```

If Gradle:

```text
gradlew
```

Repository-provided wrappers reduce CI dependence on globally installed versions.

---

# 27. Build Tool Pinning

Do not rely on:

```text
whatever Maven happens
to be installed on Jenkins
```

Build environments should explicitly control tool versions.

This improves reproducibility.

---

# 28. Node Builds

React applications similarly require controlled:

```text
Node version
Package manager
Lockfile
Build command
```

A CI worker should not silently upgrade dependencies because no lockfile exists.

---

# 29. Dependency Locking

Dependency manifests and lock mechanisms should constrain dependency resolution.

For frontend:

```text
package-lock.json
pnpm-lock.yaml
yarn.lock
```

depending on the selected package manager.

Equivalent dependency-control principles apply to backend builds.

---

# 30. Dependency Pinning

Unbounded dependency versions such as:

```text
latest
*
floating snapshots
```

reduce reproducibility and increase supply-chain risk.

Dependencies should be intentionally upgraded.

---

# 31. Unit Tests

Unit tests should run early and quickly.

They validate isolated application behavior.

They should not require:

```text
Production database
Production Kafka
Internet dependency
```

to execute.

---

# 32. Integration Tests

Integration tests validate real integration behavior.

Examples:

```text
Spring Boot ↔ PostgreSQL
Spring Boot ↔ Kafka
Spring Boot ↔ Redis
```

Testcontainers or equivalent ephemeral infrastructure can provide realistic CI environments.

---

# 33. Contract Tests

Microservices should validate API/event contracts.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Contract
   │
   ▼
Consumer
```

Contract testing helps detect incompatible independent releases before production.

---

# 34. End-to-End Tests

E2E tests validate critical user journeys.

Examples:

```text
Login
Course enrollment
Assessment submission
Content access
```

Do not attempt to test every possible condition through E2E tests.

They are slower and more fragile than lower-level tests.

---

# 35. Testing Pyramid

Preferred emphasis:

```text
             /\
            /E2E\
           /─────\
          /Integration\
         /───────────\
        /  Unit Tests  \
       /_______________\
```

Large numbers of stable low-level tests with fewer carefully selected E2E scenarios.

---

# 36. Flaky Tests

A test that fails randomly is not harmless.

Teams eventually learn to ignore it.

```text
Flaky Quality Gate
       │
       ▼
Repeated Retry
       │
       ▼
Trust Lost
```

Flaky tests must be fixed, quarantined with ownership, or removed.

---

# 37. SonarQube

SonarQube may enforce code-quality/security analysis.

Typical concerns:

```text
Bugs
Vulnerabilities
Code smells
Coverage
Duplication
Security hotspots
```

Quality gates should focus especially on changed code rather than demanding unrealistic historical perfection before any progress is possible.

---

# 38. Quality Gate

A pipeline should fail when mandatory quality requirements fail.

Bad:

```text
SonarQube failed
     │
     ▼
"Ignore it and deploy"
```

A gate that everyone bypasses is not a gate.

---

# 39. SAST

Static Application Security Testing should inspect source/build artifacts for known vulnerability patterns.

SAST complements:

```text
Review
Testing
Dependency scanning
Runtime controls
```

It does not replace them.

---

# 40. Software Composition Analysis

SCA identifies risk in third-party dependencies.

```text
Application
    │
    ├── Spring libraries
    ├── npm packages
    └── Other dependencies
```

Most modern applications contain far more third-party code than custom code.

---

# 41. Vulnerability Severity Alone Is Insufficient

A CVSS number should not be the only decision input.

Consider:

```text
Exploitability
Reachability
Exposure
Known exploitation
Fix availability
Runtime context
```

A theoretical vulnerability in unreachable code differs from an actively exploited internet-facing flaw.

---

# 42. Secret Scanning

ADR-049 requires repository and CI secret detection.

```text
Commit
  │
  ▼
Secret Scanner
  │
  ├── Clean ─────► Continue
  │
  └── Credential ► Block + Rotate if exposed
```

Once committed, a real credential should be treated as compromised.

---

# 43. Infrastructure Scanning

Terraform, Kubernetes and other infrastructure definitions should be scanned for dangerous configurations.

Examples:

```text
Public storage
Open security groups
Privileged containers
Missing encryption
Overbroad IAM
```

---

# 44. Container Build

Applications should use controlled container builds.

Typical Spring Boot model:

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
Build Stage
  │
  ▼
Application Artifact
  │
  ▼
Runtime Stage
  │
  ▼
Minimal Runtime Image
```

---

# 45. Multi-Stage Dockerfile

Multi-stage builds reduce final-image contents.

```text
Builder Image
├── compiler
├── Maven
├── source
└── build tools

        │
        ▼

Runtime Image
├── JRE
└── application
```

Build tooling generally does not belong in production images.

---

# 46. Minimal Runtime Image

Smaller runtime images reduce:

```text
Attack surface
Package count
Download size
Scanning noise
```

But minimalism should not destroy debuggability without an operational alternative.

---

# 47. Non-Root Runtime

Production application containers should normally run as non-root, consistent with ADR-050.

The Dockerfile and Kubernetes security context must agree.

---

# 48. BuildKit

Modern container builds should use secure BuildKit-style capabilities where appropriate.

Particularly important for:

```text
Caching
Multi-platform builds
Secret mounts
SSH forwarding
```

Secrets required during builds must not become image layers.

---

# 49. Build Secrets

Bad:

```dockerfile
ARG TOKEN
RUN curl ... "$TOKEN"
```

if the token can leak through history or build metadata.

Preferred:

```text
Ephemeral build-secret mount
       │
       ▼
Build operation
       │
       ▼
Secret discarded
```

---

# 50. Build Once

A release artifact should be built once.

```text
Commit ABC
    │
    ▼
Build
    │
    ▼
Image sha256:XYZ
```

That exact image is promoted through environments.

---

# 51. Do Not Rebuild for Production

Bad:

```text
DEV build
UAT build
STAGING build
PROD build
```

Even from the same commit, builds may differ because dependencies, timestamps or tooling changed.

Preferred:

```text
One Artifact
    │
    ├── DEV
    ├── UAT
    ├── STAGING
    └── PROD
```

---

# 52. Reproducible Builds

Where practical, Mediverse should improve build reproducibility so identical controlled inputs produce equivalent outputs.

Inputs include:

```text
Source
Dependencies
Build tool
Base image
Compiler/runtime
Build configuration
```

---

# 53. Base Images

Container base images should be:

```text
Approved
Version controlled
Scanned
Maintained
```

Avoid blindly inheriting:

```text
openjdk:latest
```

or another floating base image.

---

# 54. Base Image Refresh

Immutable artifacts do not mean never rebuilding.

If a critical base-image vulnerability appears:

```text
Source unchanged
      │
      ▼
Rebuild with patched base
      │
      ▼
New image digest
```

The new artifact must go through normal validation/promotion.

---

# 55. Container Registry

ADR-050 selected Amazon ECR.

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
ECR
 │
 ▼
EKS
```

ECR becomes part of the trusted software-delivery boundary.

---

# 56. Registry Permissions

CI may require:

```text
Push
```

EKS/runtime generally requires:

```text
Pull
```

Those permissions should not be interchangeable.

---

# 57. Immutable Tags

Where supported/configured, release repositories should prevent accidental tag overwrites.

Bad:

```text
3.4.0 → Digest A

later

3.4.0 → Digest B
```

The meaning of `3.4.0` has now changed.

---

# 58. Digest Pinning

GitOps production state should ultimately identify the exact image.

```text
repository:
  course-service

digest:
  sha256:...
```

rather than relying only on mutable tag resolution.

---

# 59. Artifact Retention

Registry lifecycle policies must balance:

```text
Storage cost
Rollback requirements
Audit
Incident investigation
Compliance
```

Deleting yesterday's production image immediately after deployment makes rollback impossible.

---

# 60. SBOM

Every significant release should progressively generate a Software Bill of Materials.

Conceptually:

```text
Application
   │
   ├── Component A
   ├── Component B
   ├── Library C
   └── Runtime D
```

An SBOM answers:

> **What software components are actually inside this release?**

---

## ADR-051 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The delivery architecture established so far is:

```text
                     DEVELOPER
                         │
                         ▼
                  Feature Branch
                         │
                         ▼
                    Pull Request
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼───────────────┐
          ▼              ▼               ▼
        Tests          SAST          Secret Scan
          │              │               │
          └──────────────┼───────────────┘
                         ▼
                        main
                         │
                         ▼
                     CI BUILD
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼───────────────┐
          ▼              ▼               ▼
     Unit/Integration   SCA          SonarQube
          │              │               │
          └──────────────┼───────────────┘
                         ▼
                 Container Build
                         │
                         ▼
                Container Scanning
                         │
                         ▼
                 SBOM / Provenance
                         │
                         ▼
                 IMMUTABLE IMAGE
                         │
                         ▼
                        ECR
```

The release identity becomes:

```text
Git Commit
    │
    ▼
Application Version
    │
    ▼
Container Image
    │
    ▼
Image Digest
    │
    ▼
SBOM / Provenance
```

And the critical separation is:

```text
             CI PLANE
                │
                ▼
          Build + Verify
                │
                ▼
             Artifact
                │
                X
       No routine direct
        PROD mutation
                │
                ▼
         GITOPS PLANE
                │
                ▼
            Argo CD
                │
                ▼
               EKS
```

The most important rule established in Part 1 is:

> **Production should run an immutable artifact that can be traced back to reviewed source, a controlled build, successful quality/security gates and an exact image digest. Environment promotion changes desired deployment state; it does not rebuild the application.**

**Part 2** should continue from **Section 61 — SBOM Formats & Lifecycle**, then cover **CycloneDX/SPDX → provenance → SLSA → artifact attestation → Cosign/Sigstore → signing-key vs keyless signing → verification → admission enforcement → dependency provenance → package repositories → Nexus relationship → Helm chart architecture → library charts → chart version vs app version → values hierarchy → schema validation → Helm security → GitOps repository design → Argo CD architecture → Projects → Applications → ApplicationSets → automated sync → self-healing → pruning → sync waves/hooks → health checks → drift → GitOps secret integration → multi-cluster delivery → promotion mechanics → DEV/UAT/STAGING/PROD approvals → release candidates → progressive delivery → rolling/blue-green/canary → Argo Rollouts → metrics-based promotion → rollback → feature flags → database migrations → expand-contract → Flyway/Liquibase → release observability → deployment markers → DORA metrics → Jenkins vs GitHub Actions → CI runner isolation → ephemeral runners → OIDC federation → cache poisoning → dependency confusion → malicious PRs → compromised runner → compromised registry → supply-chain threat model → break-glass releases → hotfixes → disaster recovery → anti-patterns → final Mediverse software-delivery reference architecture.**


# ADR-051 — Enterprise CI/CD, GitOps, Argo CD, Helm, Release Engineering & Software Supply-Chain Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — SBOM**.

---

# 61. SBOM Formats

Mediverse should standardize on an industry-supported SBOM format.

Primary candidates:

```text
CycloneDX
SPDX
```

The exact format matters less than maintaining a consistent, automated and machine-readable inventory.

---

# 62. SBOM Generation

The SBOM should be generated by CI from the actual release artifact.

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
Build
  │
  ▼
Container Image
  │
  ├──► SBOM
  │
  └──► Vulnerability Scan
```

Generating an SBOM manually from `pom.xml` alone may miss components introduced through the runtime image.

---

# 63. SBOM Lifecycle

The SBOM belongs to the release.

```text
course-service:3.7.2
        │
        ├── Image Digest
        ├── SBOM
        ├── Provenance
        └── Signature
```

These artifacts together establish release identity.

---

# 64. Provenance

SBOM answers:

```text
What is inside?
```

Provenance answers:

```text
Where did this artifact come from?
How was it built?
Which source produced it?
Which build system produced it?
```

Both are required for mature supply-chain security.

---

# 65. Build Provenance

A provenance record should connect:

```text
Git Repository
      │
      ▼
Commit SHA
      │
      ▼
Build Workflow
      │
      ▼
Build Environment
      │
      ▼
Artifact Digest
```

This creates traceability from source to binary.

---

# 66. SLSA

Mediverse should progressively align its build architecture with SLSA-style software supply-chain principles.

The goal is not:

```text
"Achieve a badge"
```

The goal is reducing opportunities for attackers to replace trusted source or artifacts during the build pipeline.

---

# 67. Artifact Attestation

An attestation makes a verifiable statement about an artifact.

Examples:

```text
Artifact X

was built by
→ Trusted CI

from
→ Repository Y

at
→ Commit Z
```

Other attestations may represent:

```text
SBOM
Test result
Vulnerability scan
Provenance
Policy compliance
```

---

# 68. Artifact Signing

Mediverse should progressively sign production artifacts.

```text
Artifact Digest
      │
      ▼
Signing Process
      │
      ▼
Signature
```

Consumers can verify that the artifact came through an approved release process.

---

# 69. Cosign

Cosign/Sigstore should be evaluated as the strategic container-signing mechanism.

Conceptually:

```text
Container Image
      │
      ▼
Cosign
      │
      ▼
Signature / Attestation
      │
      ▼
Registry
```

---

# 70. Signing Keys

Traditional signing:

```text
Private Signing Key
        │
        ▼
CI
        │
        ▼
Artifact Signature
```

creates another highly sensitive secret requiring ADR-049 lifecycle management.

---

# 71. Keyless Signing

Where supported, Mediverse should prefer identity-backed/keyless signing.

Conceptually:

```text
CI Workload Identity
        │
        ▼
OIDC Identity
        │
        ▼
Short-Lived Signing Identity
        │
        ▼
Artifact Signature
```

This reduces dependence on permanent signing private keys stored in CI.

---

# 72. Signing Is Useless Without Verification

This architecture is incomplete:

```text
CI → Sign Image → ECR
```

if Kubernetes accepts any unsigned image anyway.

The complete model is:

```text
Build
  │
  ▼
Sign
  │
  ▼
Registry
  │
  ▼
Verify
  │
  ▼
Admission
  │
  ▼
Deploy
```

---

# 73. Admission Verification

ADR-050's admission layer should progressively enforce:

```text
Approved registry
        +
Valid signature
        +
Trusted identity
        +
Required provenance
```

for production workloads.

---

# 74. Enforcement Rollout

Do not enable strict signature enforcement before the build pipeline consistently signs artifacts.

Preferred:

```text
Generate
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
   ▼
Audit
   │
   ▼
Warn
   │
   ▼
Enforce
```

---

# 75. Dependency Provenance

Supply-chain trust must include dependencies.

```text
Mediverse Source
      │
      ├── Maven dependencies
      ├── npm dependencies
      ├── Container base images
      └── Build tools
```

A secure application build can still be compromised through a malicious dependency.

---

# 76. Package Repository

External dependencies should be consumed through controlled repository infrastructure where appropriate.

Conceptually:

```text
Maven Central / npm
        │
        ▼
Repository Manager
        │
        ▼
CI
```

This allows additional governance and caching.

---

# 77. Nexus Relationship

If Mediverse uses Nexus Repository:

```text
External Repositories
        │
        ▼
      Nexus
        │
        ├── Maven Proxy
        ├── npm Proxy
        ├── Internal Packages
        └── Release Artifacts
```

ECR should remain the preferred production container registry in the AWS architecture.

Do not duplicate every artifact across Nexus and ECR without a purpose.

---

# 78. Dependency Confusion

An attacker may attempt to publish a public package matching an internal package name.

Mitigations include:

```text
Controlled namespaces
Private repository priority
Dependency pinning
Repository configuration
Package provenance
```

---

# 79. Helm Architecture

ADR-050 established Helm as the Kubernetes packaging layer.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Helm Chart
    │
    ├── Deployment
    ├── Service
    ├── HPA
    ├── PDB
    ├── ServiceAccount
    └── Configuration
```

Helm packages resources.

Argo CD controls deployment state.

---

# 80. Standard Application Chart

A standardized Mediverse chart pattern should reduce copy/paste configuration.

Common capabilities include:

```text
Deployment
Service
ServiceAccount
Probes
Resources
Autoscaling
PDB
ConfigMap
Ingress/Gateway integration
Observability metadata
```

---

# 81. Library Charts

Reusable Helm library charts may centralize common templates.

But excessive abstraction creates:

```text
Template
   │
   ▼
Template
   │
   ▼
Template
   │
   ▼
Nobody understands generated YAML
```

Reuse should reduce duplication without hiding Kubernetes.

---

# 82. Chart Version vs Application Version

These are separate concepts.

```text
Chart Version
=
Packaging/template version

App Version
=
Application release
```

Example:

```text
Chart: 2.4.1
App:   7.8.3
```

Do not assume they must always be identical.

---

# 83. Values Hierarchy

Preferred:

```text
Base Defaults
      │
      ├── DEV overrides
      ├── UAT overrides
      ├── STAGING overrides
      └── PROD overrides
```

Overrides should remain small and explicit.

---

# 84. Environment Differences

Reasonable differences include:

```text
Replica count
Resource sizing
Autoscaling thresholds
External endpoint references
Feature configuration
```

Unreasonable differences include entirely different service architectures hidden inside environment values.

---

# 85. Helm Schema Validation

Charts should use values schema validation where useful.

Bad configuration:

```text
replicaCount: "banana"
```

should fail before reaching Kubernetes.

---

# 86. Render Validation

CI should render Helm templates and validate resulting Kubernetes resources.

```text
Helm Chart
    │
    ▼
helm template
    │
    ▼
Rendered YAML
    │
    ▼
Schema / Policy Validation
```

Template compilation success alone is insufficient.

---

# 87. Helm Secrets

Plaintext production credentials must never exist in:

```text
values-prod.yaml
values.yaml
Chart templates
```

Use ADR-049 secret references/external-secret mechanisms.

---

# 88. GitOps Repository Design

A practical structure may resemble:

```text
mediverse-gitops/
│
├── applications/
│   ├── course-service/
│   ├── assessment-service/
│   └── search-service/
│
├── environments/
│   ├── dev/
│   ├── uat/
│   ├── staging/
│   └── production/
│
└── platform/
```

Exact directory structure is less important than clear ownership.

---

# 89. GitOps Repository Permissions

Changing application source and changing production desired state are separate privileges.

```text
Application Developer
        │
        ▼
Application Repository

Release Authority
        │
        ▼
Production GitOps State
```

This separation provides another control boundary.

---

# 90. Argo CD Architecture

```text
GitOps Repository
       │
       ▼
    Argo CD
       │
       ▼
Desired vs Actual
       │
       ├── Equal → Healthy
       │
       └── Drift → Reconcile
```

Argo CD continuously compares Git with Kubernetes.

---

# 91. Argo CD Projects

Projects should constrain:

```text
Allowed repositories
Allowed clusters
Allowed namespaces
Allowed resource types
```

Application teams should not automatically gain permission to deploy anywhere Argo CD itself can reach.

---

# 92. Argo CD Applications

An Argo CD Application maps:

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
Repository/path/chart
  │
  ▼
Destination cluster
  │
  ▼
Namespace
```

This mapping should be declarative and reviewed.

---

# 93. ApplicationSets

ApplicationSets can generate repeated application definitions.

Useful for:

```text
Multiple environments
Multiple clusters
Repeated service patterns
```

Example:

```text
Applications
     │
     ├── DEV
     ├── UAT
     ├── STAGING
     └── PROD
```

without manually maintaining identical Argo Application objects.

---

# 94. ApplicationSet Restraint

Do not build a highly dynamic generator system before deployment topology requires it.

Simple GitOps structures are easier to debug.

Complexity should solve an actual scaling problem.

---

# 95. Automated Sync

DEV may use aggressive automated synchronization:

```text
Git change
    │
    ▼
Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Automatic Sync
```

Production automation should align with release approval requirements.

Automation and governance are not opposites.

---

# 96. Self-Healing

If runtime state differs from Git:

```text
Git
 │
 │ replicas = 3
 ▼
Cluster
 │
 │ replicas = 7 manually
 ▼
Drift
```

Argo CD may restore the declared state.

This discourages permanent manual mutation.

---

# 97. Pruning

When a resource is removed from desired state, Argo CD can delete it.

```text
Git resource removed
        │
        ▼
Argo Prune
        │
        ▼
Cluster resource deleted
```

This is powerful and potentially destructive.

Production pruning requires careful controls.

---

# 98. Sync Waves

Some resources require ordering.

Example:

```text
Namespace
   │
   ▼
Configuration
   │
   ▼
Database Migration
   │
   ▼
Application
```

Argo CD sync waves/hooks can coordinate controlled ordering where required.

---

# 99. Hooks

Hooks may support lifecycle tasks such as:

```text
PreSync
Sync
PostSync
SyncFail
```

But business workflows should not be forced into Argo hooks merely because the mechanism exists.

---

# 100. Health Checks

Argo CD should determine whether deployed resources are:

```text
Healthy
Progressing
Degraded
Missing
```

Custom resources may require custom health logic.

A successful Git sync does not prove the application works.

---

# 101. Drift Detection

Drift may indicate:

```text
Manual change
Controller mutation
Configuration error
Attack
Emergency intervention
```

Not all drift is malicious, but unexplained production drift should be investigated.

---

# 102. GitOps Secrets

Preferred:

```text
GitOps
  │
  ▼
Secret Reference
  │
  ▼
External Secrets
  │
  ▼
AWS Secrets Manager
```

rather than storing secret values directly in Git.

---

# 103. Multi-Cluster GitOps

Argo CD can manage multiple clusters.

Conceptually:

```text
                 Argo CD
                    │
         ┌──────────┼──────────┐
         ▼          ▼          ▼
       DEV         UAT        PROD
```

However, production blast-radius requirements may justify separate Argo CD control planes.

---

# 104. Production GitOps Isolation

A single Argo CD instance with unrestricted access to every environment creates a high-value compromise target.

Preferred evaluation:

```text
Non-Prod Argo CD
       │
       ▼
Non-Prod Clusters

Prod Argo CD
       │
       ▼
Production
```

for stronger isolation.

---

# 105. Promotion

Promotion means changing which already-built artifact an environment references.

```text
Digest ABC
   │
   ▼
DEV
   │
   ▼
UAT
   │
   ▼
STAGING
   │
   ▼
PROD
```

No rebuild occurs.

---

# 106. Promotion Commit

A promotion may be represented by a Git change:

```yaml
image:
  digest: sha256:ABC...
```

The PR history then records:

```text
Who promoted?
What artifact?
When?
What approvals?
```

---

# 107. DEV Promotion

DEV should optimize for rapid feedback.

Typical:

```text
Merge main
    │
    ▼
Build + Verify
    │
    ▼
Publish Artifact
    │
    ▼
Automatically update DEV
```

assuming quality gates pass.

---

# 108. UAT Promotion

UAT should receive release candidates that have passed required automated validation.

Promotion may remain automated or controlled depending on testing workflow.

---

# 109. Staging

Staging should resemble production in architecture sufficiently to expose deployment problems.

It does not need identical scale.

It should validate:

```text
Deployment behavior
Configuration
Migrations
Observability
Networking
Security integration
```

---

# 110. Production Approval

Production promotion should require risk-appropriate approval.

Not:

```text
Every deployment requires
six managers and a CAB meeting.
```

Not:

```text
Anyone can deploy anything
at any time.
```

Use automation with proportionate controls.

---

# 111. Release Candidate

A release candidate should identify an immutable artifact.

```text
RC
 │
 ▼
Image Digest ABC
```

If testing discovers a defect, the fix creates:

```text
Digest DEF
```

Do not mutate ABC.

---

# 112. Deployment Strategies

Primary strategies:

```text
Rolling
Blue/Green
Canary
```

Each solves different risk and infrastructure problems.

---

# 113. Rolling Deployment

Default for ordinary stateless services:

```text
v1 v1 v1
   │
   ▼
v2 v1 v1
   │
   ▼
v2 v2 v1
   │
   ▼
v2 v2 v2
```

Simple and resource-efficient.

---

# 114. Blue/Green

```text
BLUE
v1 v1 v1

GREEN
v2 v2 v2
```

Traffic switches between environments.

Advantages:

```text
Fast rollback
Strong version separation
```

Cost:

```text
Temporary duplicate capacity
```

---

# 115. Canary

```text
95% → v1
 5% → v2
```

then progressively:

```text
75/25
50/50
0/100
```

based on observed health.

Canary releases reduce blast radius but require reliable metrics.

---

# 116. Argo Rollouts

Argo Rollouts should be evaluated for services requiring advanced progressive delivery.

It can manage:

```text
Canary
Blue/Green
Traffic progression
Analysis
Automated rollback
```

Do not replace every ordinary Deployment with Rollouts without a reason.

---

# 117. Metrics-Based Promotion

A canary should advance based on objective signals.

Examples:

```text
5xx rate
Latency
Saturation
Business failures
Crash rate
```

ADR-047 provides the observability foundation.

---

# 118. Bad Canary Metric

If a release causes:

```text
HTTP 200
```

while returning incorrect business data, infrastructure metrics may still look healthy.

Progressive delivery should include domain-level signals for critical flows.

---

# 119. Automatic Rollback

Example:

```text
Canary
  │
  ▼
Error Rate > Threshold
  │
  ▼
Stop Promotion
  │
  ▼
Route traffic back
```

Automatic rollback is useful when failure signals are trustworthy.

---

# 120. Rollback Is Not Always Safe

Application rollback may fail if the new version performed an incompatible database migration.

Therefore:

```text
Application Rollback
        +
Database Compatibility
```

must be designed together.

---

# 121. Database Migration Ownership

Database schema changes belong to the application release lifecycle.

Use controlled tools such as:

```text
Flyway
Liquibase
```

according to service standards.

Manual production SQL should not be the normal migration mechanism.

---

# 122. Migration Versioning

Migrations should be:

```text
Versioned
Reviewed
Tested
Auditable
Repeatable where appropriate
```

and associated with application evolution.

---

# 123. Expand-Contract Pattern

For zero/low-downtime evolution:

```text
Phase 1 — Expand

Old Schema
    │
    ▼
Add compatible new structure

Phase 2 — Migrate

Old + New
    │
    ▼
Applications transition

Phase 3 — Contract

Remove obsolete structure
```

This is safer than immediate destructive replacement.

---

# 124. Example

Bad:

```text
Release v2:
Rename column user_name → username
```

while v1 Pods still expect `user_name`.

Better:

```text
Add username
      │
      ▼
Support both
      │
      ▼
Migrate data
      │
      ▼
Deploy consumers
      │
      ▼
Remove user_name later
```

---

# 125. Destructive Migrations

Operations such as:

```text
DROP COLUMN
DROP TABLE
Change incompatible type
```

require stronger review and recovery planning.

They should usually be separated from the initial application rollout.

---

# 126. Migration Job

A migration may run through a controlled deployment job:

```text
Argo CD
   │
   ▼
Migration Job
   │
   ▼
Database
   │
   ▼
Application Rollout
```

Concurrency must ensure multiple Pods do not execute destructive migrations independently.

---

# 127. Feature Flags

Deployment and feature release should be separable.

```text
Deploy Code
    │
    ▼
Feature Disabled
    │
    ▼
Validate
    │
    ▼
Enable Feature
```

This can reduce release risk.

---

# 128. Feature Flag Debt

Flags are temporary control structures unless intentionally permanent.

Old flags create:

```text
Dead code
Combinatorial complexity
Confusing behavior
Testing burden
```

Each temporary flag needs an owner and cleanup plan.

---

# 129. Kill Switches

Critical integrations may benefit from operational kill switches.

Example:

```text
External AI Provider
       │
       X
Feature Flag
       │
       ▼
Fallback
```

This can mitigate incidents without rebuilding software.

---

# 130. Release Observability

Every deployment should emit/record:

```text
Application
Version
Digest
Commit
Environment
Timestamp
Deployment ID
```

ADR-047 dashboards should make release events visible against telemetry.

---

# 131. Deployment Markers

A graph should allow operators to see:

```text
Error Rate
   │
   │       ↑ deployment v3.7.2
   │       │
   │       │       /────
   │_______│______/
```

This dramatically improves incident correlation.

---

# 132. DORA Metrics

Mediverse should measure:

```text
Deployment Frequency
Lead Time for Changes
Change Failure Rate
Time to Restore Service
```

These measure delivery-system outcomes.

They should not become targets teams manipulate.

---

# 133. Deployment Frequency

More deployments are not automatically better.

The useful question is whether Mediverse can safely deliver small changes when needed.

---

# 134. Change Failure Rate

Track how often releases cause:

```text
Incident
Rollback
Hotfix
Significant degradation
```

A pipeline that deploys 100 times daily but breaks production constantly is not high-performing.

---

# 135. Jenkins vs GitHub Actions

Both can implement Mediverse CI.

Jenkins provides:

```text
Deep customization
Self-hosted control
Large plugin ecosystem
Existing enterprise integration
```

but brings substantial operational responsibility.

GitHub Actions provides tighter source-platform integration where GitHub is the authoritative SCM.

---

# 136. Strategic CI Direction

If Mediverse already operates Jenkins effectively, replacing it purely for modernization provides little value.

However, new architecture should reduce dependency on:

```text
Permanent Jenkins agents
Long-lived cloud keys
Huge shared controllers
Uncontrolled plugins
```

Regardless of CI product, the security model matters more than the logo.

---

# 137. Ephemeral CI Runners

Preferred:

```text
Job starts
   │
   ▼
Fresh runner
   │
   ▼
Build
   │
   ▼
Publish
   │
   ▼
Runner destroyed
```

This reduces cross-build contamination and persistence opportunities.

---

# 138. CI Runner Isolation

Untrusted PR code can execute inside CI.

Therefore runners should not automatically have:

```text
Production credentials
Production network access
Signing authority
Deployment authority
```

A malicious PR should not become a path to production compromise.

---

# 139. OIDC Federation

Preferred cloud authentication:

```text
CI Job
  │
  ▼
OIDC Token
  │
  ▼
AWS STS
  │
  ▼
Short-Lived Role
```

rather than:

```text
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
```

stored permanently in CI.

---

# 140. CI Cache Security

Build caches can improve performance but introduce poisoning risks.

Cache boundaries should consider:

```text
Repository
Branch
Trust level
Dependency source
Artifact identity
```

Untrusted PRs should not be able to poison trusted release caches.

---

# 141. Supply-Chain Threat Model

Primary threats include:

```text
Malicious dependency
Dependency confusion
Compromised developer account
Malicious pull request
Compromised CI runner
CI credential theft
Build-script manipulation
Compromised base image
Registry compromise
Mutable artifact replacement
GitOps repository compromise
Argo CD compromise
Unsigned artifact deployment
Secret leakage
Compromised package repository
```

The architecture must assume more than application-code vulnerabilities.

---

# 142. Compromised Runner

If a runner is compromised, controls should limit the attacker to the minimum current-job privileges.

Preferred:

```text
Ephemeral runner
+
Short-lived identity
+
Least privilege
+
Network isolation
+
No reusable secrets
```

Then destruction of the runner removes persistence.

---

# 143. Registry Compromise

Artifact signing and digest pinning provide additional defenses.

```text
Registry
   │
   ▼
Artifact
   │
   ▼
Digest Verification
   │
   ▼
Signature Verification
```

If content is replaced, verification should fail.

---

# 144. GitOps Compromise

The GitOps repository effectively controls production desired state.

Therefore it requires:

```text
Strong authentication
Branch protection
CODEOWNERS
Review
Audit
Restricted write access
```

Treat it as production infrastructure.

---

# 145. Break-Glass Deployment

A production emergency may occasionally require bypassing normal automation.

A break-glass mechanism should be:

```text
Rare
Explicit
Time-bound
Strongly authenticated
Audited
Reviewed afterward
```

It must not become:

```text
"The pipeline is slow,
so use kubectl."
```

---

# 146. Hotfixes

Hotfixes should still preserve traceability.

```text
Incident
   │
   ▼
Fix
   │
   ▼
PR / Review
   │
   ▼
CI
   │
   ▼
Immutable Artifact
   │
   ▼
Accelerated Promotion
```

Emergency does not justify creating an unknown binary manually on a laptop.

---

# 147. Delivery Disaster Recovery

Mediverse must be able to reconstruct the delivery platform.

Critical recovery assets include:

```text
Source repositories
GitOps repositories
Infrastructure code
CI configuration
Artifact registry
Artifact metadata
Signing/trust configuration
Argo CD configuration
Secret references
```

The delivery system itself is production infrastructure.

---

# 148. CI/CD Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject:

```text
❌ CI directly using permanent cluster-admin credentials

❌ Jenkins storing permanent AWS administrator keys

❌ CI rebuilding binaries separately for every environment

❌ Mutable production image tags

❌ Production using :latest

❌ Unreviewed direct pushes to protected branches

❌ Environment-per-branch deployment architecture

❌ Long-lived feature branches

❌ Production secrets in Git/Helm values

❌ Secrets passed insecurely through Docker ARG

❌ Build tools depending on random runner-installed versions

❌ Dependencies floating to latest

❌ Ignoring lockfiles

❌ Deploying when mandatory tests fail

❌ Permanently ignoring flaky quality gates

❌ Security scanners that never block anything

❌ Treating CVSS alone as complete risk analysis

❌ SBOM generation with no lifecycle association

❌ Signing artifacts but never verifying signatures

❌ One permanent signing key exposed to every CI job

❌ Untrusted PR jobs receiving production credentials

❌ Shared persistent CI workers without isolation

❌ Registry tags overwritten after release

❌ Manual kubectl as standard deployment mechanism

❌ Argo CD with unrestricted cross-environment privileges

❌ Blind automated pruning without safeguards

❌ Rebuilding release candidates after approval

❌ Canary rollout without meaningful telemetry

❌ Assuming HTTP 200 means business correctness

❌ Application rollback without DB compatibility

❌ Destructive migrations coupled directly to rollout

❌ Feature flags never removed

❌ Hotfix binaries built manually on engineer laptops

❌ Break-glass becoming the normal deployment path
```

---

# 149. Final Mediverse Software Delivery Architecture

```text
                           DEVELOPER
                               │
                               ▼
                        SOURCE REPOSITORY
                               │
                               ▼
                         PULL REQUEST
                               │
             ┌─────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             ▼                 ▼                  ▼
          Review             Tests             Security
             │                 │                  │
             │        ┌────────┼────────┐         │
             │        ▼        ▼        ▼         │
             │      Unit   Integration Contract   │
             │                                     │
             │          SAST / SCA / Secrets       │
             └─────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                               ▼
                              MAIN
                               │
                               ▼
                         TRUSTED CI JOB
                               │
              ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
              ▼                ▼                ▼
           Compile         Quality Gate      Security
              │                                 │
              ▼                                 ▼
          Package                           Scan
              │                                 │
              └────────────────┬────────────────┘
                               ▼
                        CONTAINER BUILD
                               │
                               ▼
                       IMMUTABLE IMAGE
                               │
             ┌─────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             ▼                 ▼                  ▼
           SBOM            Provenance          Scan
             │                 │                  │
             └─────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                               ▼
                         SIGN / ATTEST
                               │
                               ▼
                              ECR
                               │
                               │ Digest
                               ▼
                       GITOPS REPOSITORY
                               │
                   ┌───────────┼───────────┐
                   ▼           ▼           ▼
                  DEV         UAT       STAGING
                   │           │           │
                   └───────────┼───────────┘
                               ▼
                         PROD APPROVAL
                               │
                               ▼
                           PRODUCTION
                               │
                               ▼
                            ARGO CD
                               │
                               ▼
                     ADMISSION VERIFICATION
                               │
                 ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
                 ▼             ▼             ▼
             Registry      Signature      Policy
                 │             │             │
                 └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                               ▼
                              EKS
                               │
                               ▼
                      Progressive Delivery
                               │
                    ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                    ▼          ▼          ▼
                 Rolling     Canary    Blue/Green
                               │
                               ▼
                       ADR-047 TELEMETRY
                               │
                    ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                    ▼                     ▼
                  Healthy               Failure
                    │                     │
                    ▼                     ▼
                 Promote               Rollback
```

The trust chain becomes:

```text
Developer Identity
        │
        ▼
Reviewed Source
        │
        ▼
Trusted CI Identity
        │
        ▼
Controlled Build
        │
        ▼
Immutable Digest
        │
        ├── SBOM
        ├── Provenance
        └── Signature
        │
        ▼
Trusted Registry
        │
        ▼
Reviewed GitOps State
        │
        ▼
Argo CD
        │
        ▼
Admission Verification
        │
        ▼
Production
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                            | Decision                                               |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Delivery architecture           | **CI + GitOps**                                        |
| Deployment authority            | **Argo CD**                                            |
| CI direct production mutation   | Avoid/prohibit by default                              |
| Branching                       | Trunk-oriented                                         |
| Environment branches            | Rejected                                               |
| Protected branches              | Mandatory                                              |
| Pull requests                   | Required                                               |
| CODEOWNERS                      | Risk-based                                             |
| Build model                     | **Build once, promote**                                |
| Spring build                    | Maven/Gradle wrapper                                   |
| Frontend dependencies           | Lockfile required                                      |
| Unit/integration/contract tests | CI required                                            |
| E2E                             | Critical journeys                                      |
| Code quality                    | SonarQube/quality gate                                 |
| SAST                            | Required                                               |
| SCA                             | Required                                               |
| Secret scanning                 | Required                                               |
| Infrastructure scanning         | Required                                               |
| Container builds                | Multi-stage/minimal/non-root                           |
| Build secrets                   | Ephemeral secure mounts                                |
| Base images                     | Approved + pinned                                      |
| Registry                        | **Amazon ECR**                                         |
| Production artifact             | Immutable                                              |
| `latest`                        | Prohibited                                             |
| Deployment identity             | Digest                                                 |
| SBOM                            | Required strategic capability                          |
| SBOM format                     | CycloneDX/SPDX                                         |
| Provenance                      | Required strategic capability                          |
| Supply-chain framework          | SLSA-aligned direction                                 |

| Keyless signing                 | Preferred where supported                              |
| Runtime signature verification  | Progressive enforcement                                |
| Helm                            | Kubernetes packaging                                   |
| GitOps repository               | Authoritative desired state                            |
| GitOps secrets                  | External secret references                             |
| Argo CD Projects                | Required isolation mechanism                           |
| ApplicationSets                 | Use where scale justifies                              |
| Self-healing                    | Enabled where appropriate                              |
| Pruning                         | Controlled                                             |
| Promotion                       | Git-based artifact-reference change                    |
| DEV                             | Fast/automated                                         |
| UAT                             | Validated release candidates                           |
| Staging                         | Production-like validation                             |
| PROD                            | Controlled approval                                    |
| Rolling                         | Default                                                |
| Canary                          | High-risk services                                     |
| Blue/green                      | Where instant switch/rollback is valuable              |
| Argo Rollouts                   | Selective progressive delivery                         |
| Rollout analysis                | Metrics + business signals                             |
| DB migration                    | Flyway/Liquibase                                       |
| Schema evolution                | Expand-contract                                        |
| Destructive migration           | Separate/high control                                  |
| Feature flags                   | Controlled lifecycle                                   |
| Release telemetry               | Mandatory                                              |
| DORA metrics                    | Measure delivery outcomes                              |
| CI platform                     | Jenkins/GitHub Actions based on organizational context |
| CI workers                      | Ephemeral preferred                                    |
| AWS CI authentication           | **OIDC + short-lived STS**                             |
| Permanent AWS CI keys           | Rejected                                               |

| Status                          | **Accepted**                                           |

## Next — ADR-052

### **ADR-052 — Enterprise Infrastructure as Code, Terraform, AWS Landing Zone, Environment Provisioning & Infrastructure Lifecycle Architecture**

This is the logical next ADR because ADR-050 and ADR-051 assume that EKS, VPCs, IAM, KMS, databases, registries, DNS and supporting AWS infrastructure already exist. We still need one authoritative architecture defining **how that infrastructure itself is created and changed**.

ADR-052 should cover **AWS Organizations/account topology → landing zone → Control Tower evaluation → DEV/UAT/STAGING/PROD accounts → shared services/security/logging accounts → SCPs → IAM boundaries → Terraform as primary IaC → Terraform repository architecture → root modules vs reusable modules → module versioning → provider version pinning → `.terraform.lock.hcl` → state → remote S3 backend → state encryption → locking → state sensitivity → state isolation → workspace limitations → environment directories/stacks → backend bootstrap problem → Terraform execution identity → OIDC → plan/apply separation → PR plans → production approvals → drift → import → moved blocks → lifecycle rules → `prevent_destroy` → replacement risk → dependency graph → outputs → secrets in state → KMS → VPC architecture → subnets → routing → NAT → endpoints → security groups → EKS provisioning → RDS → Redis → OpenSearch → MSK → S3 → ECR → Route 53 → ACM → IAM → observability → policy-as-code → Checkov/tfsec/Terrascan evaluation → cost estimation → tagging → ownership → FinOps → Terraform testing → Terratest evaluation → ephemeral environments → Ansible relationship → configuration management → immutable infrastructure → AMI/node lifecycle → GitOps boundary → Terraform vs Helm responsibility → CI/CD integration → break-glass infrastructure changes → state recovery → disaster recovery → provider/module supply-chain security → multi-region infrastructure → deletion safeguards → anti-patterns → final Mediverse AWS IaC reference architecture.**


# ADR-052 — Enterprise Infrastructure as Code, Terraform, AWS Landing Zone, Environment Provisioning & Infrastructure Lifecycle Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-052
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-050 established the **EKS runtime platform**.

ADR-051 established the **trusted software delivery chain**.

ADR-052 establishes the infrastructure layer beneath both:

> **How does Mediverse create, modify, secure, reproduce, audit and recover AWS infrastructure without depending on manual console configuration or uncontrolled infrastructure changes?**

The target infrastructure lifecycle becomes:

```text
Architecture Decision
        │
        ▼
Terraform Code
        │
        ▼
Pull Request
        │
        ▼
Validate / Test / Security
        │
        ▼
Terraform Plan
        │
        ▼
Review / Approval
        │
        ▼
Terraform Apply
        │
        ▼
AWS Infrastructure
        │
        ▼
Drift Detection
```

---

# 1. Infrastructure Is Software

Infrastructure configuration must receive the same engineering discipline as application code.

That means:

```text
Version control
Peer review
Automated validation
Testing
Security scanning
Release control
Auditability
Reproducibility
```

Production infrastructure should not exist primarily as knowledge inside an engineer's head.

---

# 2. Core Decision

Mediverse shall adopt:

```text
Terraform
```

as the primary declarative Infrastructure-as-Code mechanism for AWS infrastructure.

Conceptually:

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Terraform
 │
 ▼
AWS APIs
 │
 ▼
Infrastructure
```

---

# 3. Terraform Responsibility

Terraform should manage infrastructure such as:

```text
AWS Accounts integration
VPC
Subnets
Routing
Security Groups
IAM
KMS
EKS
RDS
ElastiCache
MSK
OpenSearch
S3
ECR
Route 53
ACM
Load-balancing foundations
Observability infrastructure
```

Application Kubernetes resources remain primarily under Helm/GitOps ownership.

---

# 4. Terraform Is Not Configuration Management

Terraform answers:

```text
What infrastructure should exist?
```

Ansible answers more naturally:

```text
How should an existing machine
be configured?
```

Helm answers:

```text
What Kubernetes application
resources should exist?
```

These boundaries should not be blurred unnecessarily.

---

# 5. AWS Landing Zone

Mediverse should establish a governed AWS organizational foundation before scaling workloads.

Conceptually:

```text
AWS Organization
       │
       ├── Security
       ├── Log Archive
       ├── Shared Services
       ├── Development
       ├── Testing/UAT
       ├── Staging
       └── Production
```

Account topology becomes part of the security architecture.

---

# 6. Why Multiple AWS Accounts?

AWS accounts provide stronger isolation than:

```text
Tags
VPCs
Namespaces
IAM conventions
```

inside one giant account.

They provide boundaries for:

```text
IAM
Billing
Quotas
CloudTrail
Resources
Security controls
Blast radius
```

---

# 7. Production Account

Production should have a dedicated account boundary.

Avoid:

```text
One AWS account
 ├── dev
 ├── uat
 ├── staging
 └── prod
```

for a mature enterprise platform.

Production deserves stronger isolation.

---

# 8. Non-Production Accounts

Non-production may initially consolidate some environments if cost and operational scale justify it.

Example:

```text
Non-Production Account
 ├── DEV
 ├── UAT1
 └── UAT2
```

But this is a cost/complexity tradeoff, not equivalent isolation to separate accounts.

---

# 9. Security Account

Central security capabilities may live in a dedicated account.

Examples:

```text
Security tooling
Threat detection
Security aggregation
Delegated administration
Security automation
```

This reduces the ability of an application-account compromise to disable central security controls.

---

# 10. Log Archive Account

Security/audit logs should be centrally retained where appropriate.

```text
Workload Accounts
       │
       ▼
CloudTrail / Security Logs
       │
       ▼
Log Archive Account
```

Attackers compromising a workload account should not trivially erase the authoritative audit trail.

---

# 11. Shared Services Account

Shared infrastructure may include:

```text
CI/CD supporting services
Artifact infrastructure
DNS components
Network services
Observability components
Enterprise integrations
```

But "shared" should not become an excuse to create one enormous account containing everything.

---

# 12. AWS Control Tower

AWS Control Tower should be evaluated for landing-zone governance.

It can assist with:

```text
Account provisioning
Organizational units
Guardrails/controls
Logging foundations
Governance
```

The decision should depend on organizational scale and existing AWS governance.

---

# 13. Organizational Units

Accounts should be grouped according to governance needs.

Example:

```text
Root
 │
 ├── Security OU
 │
 ├── Infrastructure OU
 │
 ├── NonProduction OU
 │
 └── Production OU
```

OU design should support policy boundaries.

---

# 14. Service Control Policies

SCPs can establish organization-level maximum permissions.

Example:

```text
IAM allows action
       │
       ▼
SCP denies action
       │
       ▼
Action denied
```

SCPs are guardrails, not ordinary application authorization policies.

---

# 15. SCP Use Cases

Potential controls include restrictions around:

```text
Disabling security services
Leaving the organization
Unapproved regions
Dangerous root operations
Audit-log modification
```

Policies must be tested carefully.

A badly designed SCP can break entire environments.

---

# 16. Region Governance

Mediverse should explicitly define approved AWS regions.

Reasons include:

```text
Data residency
Cost
Service availability
Operational support
Security
DR architecture
```

Uncontrolled region usage creates shadow infrastructure.

---

# 17. Root User

AWS account root users should not participate in routine operations.

Root credentials require strong protection and should only be used for operations requiring root.

---

# 18. Human AWS Access

Human access should use centralized identity/federation.

Avoid:

```text
Individual long-lived IAM users
+
Permanent access keys
```

as the normal enterprise access model.

---

# 19. Workload AWS Access

ADR-048/049/050 established workload identity.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Short-Lived Identity
    │
    ▼
IAM Role
    │
    ▼
AWS Resource
```

Terraform must provision these identity relationships declaratively.

---

# 20. Terraform Repository

Infrastructure should live in version-controlled repositories.

Example:

```text
infrastructure/
├── modules/
├── environments/
├── policies/
├── tests/
└── docs/
```

Repository organization must make ownership obvious.

---

# 21. Root Modules

A root module represents deployable infrastructure composition.

Example:

```text
production/
├── main.tf
├── variables.tf
├── outputs.tf
├── providers.tf
└── backend.tf
```

Root modules orchestrate reusable components.

---

# 22. Reusable Modules

Common infrastructure patterns should be encapsulated into reusable modules.

Examples:

```text
VPC module
EKS module
RDS module
KMS module
S3 module
IAM module
```

But abstraction should solve repetition, not hide AWS completely.

---

# 23. Over-Abstraction

Bad module:

```text
enterprise_everything_module
```

with 250 variables controlling unrelated infrastructure.

This creates a monolithic infrastructure abstraction nobody can safely evolve.

Prefer cohesive modules with clear responsibility.

---

# 24. Module Interfaces

A module should expose a deliberate interface:

```text
Inputs
  │
  ▼
Module
  │
  ▼
Outputs
```

Consumers should not need knowledge of every internal implementation detail.

---

# 25. Module Versioning

Reusable modules should be versioned.

```text
v1.4.0
v1.5.0
v2.0.0
```

Production environments should not automatically consume whatever currently exists on `main`.

---

# 26. Module Pinning

Bad:

```text
source = "...//vpc?ref=main"
```

Preferred:

```text
source = "...//vpc?ref=v3.2.1"
```

or an equivalent immutable source reference.

Infrastructure dependencies should be reproducible.

---

# 27. Terraform Provider Pinning

Provider versions must be constrained.

```text
Terraform
    │
    ▼
AWS Provider Version
```

An unexpected provider upgrade can change resource behavior.

---

# 28. Terraform Lock File

`.terraform.lock.hcl` should normally be committed.

It records selected provider versions/checksums and improves reproducibility.

---

# 29. Terraform Version

The Terraform CLI version itself should be controlled.

Avoid:

```text
Developer A → Terraform X
Developer B → Terraform Y
CI          → Terraform Z
```

without compatibility governance.

---

# 30. Remote State

Production Terraform state must not primarily live on developer laptops.

Conceptually:

```text
Terraform
    │
    ▼
Remote Backend
    │
    ▼
Shared Controlled State
```

State is critical infrastructure metadata.

---

# 31. S3 Backend

For AWS-oriented Terraform, an S3-based remote state architecture is appropriate.

```text
Terraform
    │
    ▼
S3 Backend
```

with appropriate locking mechanism, encryption, versioning and access controls.

---

# 32. State Encryption

Terraform state may contain sensitive infrastructure information.

Therefore remote state must be encrypted:

```text
At rest
+
In transit
```

KMS-backed controls should be used where appropriate.

---

# 33. State Is Sensitive

Even when Terraform code contains no password, state may contain:

```text
Resource identifiers
Endpoints
Policy data
Configuration
Generated credentials
Potential secret values
```

Treat state as sensitive.

---

# 34. Never Publish State

Terraform state must not be:

```text
Committed to public Git
Attached casually to tickets
Shared over chat
Stored in unsecured file shares
```

State access requires least privilege.

---

# 35. State Locking

Concurrent infrastructure modifications can corrupt or conflict with state.

Required model:

```text
Apply A
  │
  ▼
Acquire Lock
  │
  ├── Success → Apply
  │
  └── Failure → Wait/Fail
```

Only one writer should modify a state unit at a time.

---

# 36. State Versioning

Backend storage should retain state history.

If state becomes damaged:

```text
Current State
     │
     X
Corruption
     │
     ▼
Previous Version
```

may provide recovery options.

This is not a substitute for careful state operations.

---

# 37. State Isolation

Do not store the entire enterprise in one Terraform state.

Bad:

```text
terraform.tfstate
 ├── VPC
 ├── EKS
 ├── RDS
 ├── Security
 ├── DNS
 ├── DEV
 ├── UAT
 ├── STAGING
 └── PROD
```

Blast radius becomes enormous.

---

# 38. State Boundaries

Separate state according to:

```text
Lifecycle
Ownership
Security boundary
Failure domain
Change frequency
```

not merely arbitrary file size.

---

# 39. Environment State

Production and development must not share one writable Terraform state.

Preferred:

```text
DEV State
UAT State
STAGING State
PROD State
```

with appropriate access separation.

---

# 40. Component State

Large environments may further separate:

```text
Network
EKS
Data
Security
Shared services
```

when their ownership/lifecycle warrants it.

Too many tiny states, however, create dependency-management overhead.

---

# 41. Terraform Workspaces

CLI workspaces can isolate state instances.

But using workspaces alone for major enterprise environment separation can hide important differences.

```text
terraform workspace select prod
```

is too easy to misuse as the only production boundary.

---

# 42. Preferred Environment Structure

Prefer explicit environment/stack configuration.

Example:

```text
live/
├── dev/
│   ├── network/
│   ├── eks/
│   └── data/
├── uat/
├── staging/
└── production/
```

The filesystem/repository itself makes the target environment obvious.

---

# 43. Environment Duplication

Do not copy thousands of lines between:

```text
dev/
uat/
staging/
prod/
```

Use reusable modules plus small environment-specific composition.

---

# 44. Backend Bootstrap Problem

Terraform's backend infrastructure must exist before Terraform can use it.

This creates:

```text
Terraform needs S3 backend
        │
        ▼
S3 backend must already exist
```

The bootstrap process must therefore be explicitly defined.

---

# 45. Bootstrap Stack

A minimal bootstrap process may provision:

```text
State bucket
Locking capability
KMS key
Terraform execution roles
Basic audit controls
```

After bootstrap, normal Terraform pipelines take ownership.

---

# 46. Bootstrap Security

Bootstrap credentials are unusually powerful.

They should not become permanent daily-use credentials.

After landing-zone initialization, normal operations should use constrained Terraform execution roles.

---

# 47. Terraform Execution Identity

CI should authenticate to AWS through short-lived identity.

From ADR-051:

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
OIDC
 │
 ▼
AWS STS
 │
 ▼
Terraform Role
```

Avoid permanent AWS access keys.

---

# 48. Environment-Specific Roles

Terraform roles should differ by environment.

```text
Terraform-DEV
Terraform-UAT
Terraform-STAGING
Terraform-PROD
```

Compromise of a DEV pipeline should not automatically provide production infrastructure permissions.

---

# 49. Least Privilege Challenge

Terraform frequently requires broad permissions because it creates infrastructure.

That does not justify:

```text
AdministratorAccess
```

forever.

Permissions should be scoped by infrastructure responsibility wherever operationally feasible.

---

# 50. Plan and Apply Separation

Terraform has two critical phases:

```text
PLAN
 │
 ▼
What will change?

APPLY
 │
 ▼
Perform the change
```

Production processes should preserve this distinction.

---

# 51. Pull Request Plan

Infrastructure PRs should automatically run:

```text
terraform fmt
terraform validate
Security checks
Policy checks
terraform plan
```

The reviewer should see expected infrastructure impact before approval.

---

# 52. Saved Plans

Where architecture permits, the reviewed plan and applied change should correspond closely.

Avoid:

```text
Review Plan A
     │
     ▼
Later generate unrelated Plan B
     │
     ▼
Apply B without review
```

especially for high-risk infrastructure.

---

# 53. Production Apply

Production apply should execute from controlled automation.

Preferred:

```text
Approved PR
    │
    ▼
Trusted CI
    │
    ▼
Short-lived PROD role
    │
    ▼
Terraform Apply
```

not from an engineer's laptop as the normal workflow.

---

# 54. Manual Terraform Apply

Local apply against production should be a break-glass operation.

If routine infrastructure work requires:

```text
terraform apply
```

from individual laptops, the operating model is incomplete.

---

# 55. Pull Request Review

Infrastructure review should examine actual consequences.

A PR containing:

```text
- instance_type = "..."
+ instance_type = "..."
```

may appear trivial while forcing replacement of a critical resource.

Review the plan, not only the HCL diff.

---

# 56. Destructive Plans

Changes containing:

```text
destroy
replace
recreate
```

must receive explicit attention.

Production pipelines should highlight destructive operations.

---

# 57. `prevent_destroy`

Terraform lifecycle protection may be appropriate for critical resources.

Examples:

```text
Production database
Critical KMS key
State bucket
```

But `prevent_destroy` is a safety mechanism, not disaster recovery.

---

# 58. `create_before_destroy`

Some resources can use replacement sequencing:

```text
Create New
    │
    ▼
Transition
    │
    ▼
Destroy Old
```

to reduce downtime.

This only works when the AWS resource supports parallel existence and transition.

---

# 59. `ignore_changes`

`ignore_changes` should be used sparingly.

Excessive use effectively tells Terraform:

```text
Stop managing this field
```

which can hide drift.

Every ignored field should have a documented external owner.

---

# 60. Drift

Drift occurs when:

```text
Terraform Desired State
          │
          ≠
          │
AWS Actual State
```

Common causes:

```text
Console changes
Other automation
Incident response
External controllers
Manual CLI operations
```

Drift must be visible rather than silently accepted.

---

## ADR-052 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The infrastructure control architecture is now:

```text
                       AWS ORGANIZATION
                              │
          ┌───────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          ▼                   ▼                    ▼
       SECURITY          NON-PRODUCTION        PRODUCTION
       ACCOUNT              ACCOUNTS             ACCOUNT
          │                   │                    │
          └───────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                       GOVERNANCE LAYER
                              │
                 ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                 ▼            ▼            ▼
                SCP         IAM/KMS       Audit
                              │
                              ▼
                         TERRAFORM
                              │
                ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
                ▼             ▼             ▼
              Network        EKS           Data
                │             │             │
                └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                              ▼
                             AWS
```

The Terraform change path is:

```text
Engineer
   │
   ▼
Terraform Code
   │
   ▼
Pull Request
   │
   ├── fmt
   ├── validate
   ├── security scan
   ├── policy check
   └── plan
   │
   ▼
Review
   │
   ▼
Approval
   │
   ▼
Trusted CI
   │
   ▼
OIDC / STS
   │
   ▼
Environment Terraform Role
   │
   ▼
Apply
   │
   ▼
AWS
```

The state architecture is:

```text
                    TERRAFORM STATE
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
           Encrypted     Locked      Versioned
              │            │            │
              └────────────┼────────────┘
                           ▼
                    Remote Backend
                           │
            ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
            ▼              ▼              ▼
           DEV            UAT            PROD
          State          State           State
```

The critical rule established in Part 1 is:

> **If production infrastructure can be materially changed through an undocumented console click that bypasses Git, review, Terraform plan and controlled execution, then Infrastructure as Code is not actually the source of truth—it is merely documentation that happens to resemble the infrastructure.**

**Part 2** should continue from **Section 61 — Drift Detection & Reconciliation**, then cover **Terraform import → adopting existing resources → `moved` blocks → refactoring without destruction → dependency graph → remote-state dependencies → outputs → sensitive outputs → secret generation/state leakage → Secrets Manager integration → VPC architecture → CIDR planning → public/private/isolated subnets → route tables → IGW → NAT Gateway → VPC endpoints/PrivateLink → DNS → security groups → NACLs → EKS provisioning → Karpenter infrastructure → RDS/Aurora → Redis → MSK/Kafka → OpenSearch → S3 → ECR → KMS → Route 53 → ACM → CloudTrail/Config → tagging → FinOps → policy-as-code → Checkov/tfsec/Terrascan → OPA/Sentinel evaluation → Terraform tests → Terratest → ephemeral infrastructure → Ansible boundary → immutable infrastructure → Terraform/Helm/GitOps ownership → CI/CD integration → provider/module supply-chain security → break-glass changes → state recovery → infrastructure DR → multi-region strategy → deletion protection → cost controls → anti-patterns → final Mediverse AWS Landing Zone + Terraform reference architecture.**


# ADR-052 — Enterprise Infrastructure as Code, Terraform, AWS Landing Zone, Environment Provisioning & Infrastructure Lifecycle Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Drift**.

---

# 61. Drift Detection

Terraform should regularly detect infrastructure drift.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Terraform Code
 │
 ▼
terraform plan
 │
 ▼
No Changes?
 │
 ├── Yes → Healthy
 └── No  → Drift Investigation
```

Detection is only useful when drift results in investigation and remediation.

---

# 62. Drift Does Not Always Mean Malice

Drift may originate from:

```text
Emergency repair
AWS automatic behavior
Another automation
Manual console change
Terraform bug
Provider behavior
```

The objective is understanding why the infrastructure changed.

---

# 63. Drift Reconciliation

When drift is discovered, the organization should choose one of three paths:

```text
Infrastructure
      │
      ├── Terraform correct
      │       │
      │       ▼
      │   Reconcile AWS
      │
      ├── AWS correct
      │       │
      │       ▼
      │ Update Terraform
      │
```
