Mockito should be used where replacing a collaborator genuinely isolates the unit under test.

```text
Service
 ├── Repository mock
 ├── External API mock
 └── Event publisher mock
```

But mocking everything produces tests that verify an imaginary system.

---

# 10. Mocking Anti-Pattern

This can pass:

```text
Controller Mock
      │
      ▼
Service Mock
      │
      ▼
Repository Mock
```

while the actual:

```text
Controller
   │
   ▼
Service
   │
   ▼
Hibernate
   │
   ▼
PostgreSQL
```

fails immediately.

Mocks cannot prove integration.

---

# 11. Spring Boot Slice Tests

Spring Boot slice testing should validate focused framework boundaries.

Examples:

```text
@WebMvcTest
@DataJpaTest
@JsonTest
```

These provide more realism than pure unit tests without loading the entire application unnecessarily.

---

# 12. Controller Tests

Controller tests should validate:

```text
HTTP status
Request validation
Serialization
Deserialization
Error mapping
Authorization behavior where applicable
Response structure
```

They should not merely prove that Java methods can be invoked.

---

# 13. Repository Tests

Repository tests should use a database sufficiently representative of production behavior.

If production uses PostgreSQL, relying entirely on H2 can hide differences involving:

```text
SQL dialect
Indexes
JSON types
Sequences
Constraints
Locking
Transactions
PostgreSQL-specific queries
```

---

# 14. Testcontainers

Testcontainers should be the strategic integration-testing mechanism for infrastructure dependencies where practical.

```text
Test Suite
    │
    ├── PostgreSQL Container
    ├── Redis Container
    ├── Kafka Container
    └── Other Required Dependencies
```

This provides disposable real infrastructure for tests.

---

# 15. PostgreSQL Integration Tests

Critical repository and persistence behavior should run against actual PostgreSQL.

```text
Spring Boot
     │
     ▼
Testcontainers PostgreSQL
     │
     ▼
Flyway/Liquibase
     │
     ▼
Integration Tests
```

This also validates migrations.

---

# 16. Migration Testing

Database migrations should be tested against:

```text
Clean database
+
Representative existing schema
```

because a migration that works only on an empty database may still fail during production upgrade.

---

# 17. Redis Integration Testing

Cache behavior should validate:

```text
Serialization
TTL
Invalidation
Key construction
Fallback behavior
Failure behavior
```

using real Redis where those semantics matter.

---

# 18. Kafka Integration Testing

Kafka integration tests should verify:

```text
Serialization
Publishing
Consumption
Headers
Partition keys
Retries
Idempotency
DLT behavior
```

Mocks cannot accurately reproduce all broker semantics.

---

# 19. OpenSearch Integration Testing

Search integration testing should validate:

```text
Mappings
Index creation
Queries
Analyzers
Filtering
Sorting
Reindexing behavior
```

where search correctness is product-critical.

---

# 20. Component Tests

A component test validates a service largely through its public interface while controlling external dependencies.

```text
Test
 │
 ▼
HTTP API
 │
 ▼
Service
 │
 ├── Real DB
 ├── Real Redis
 └── Controlled external integrations
```

This provides high confidence without requiring the complete Mediverse platform.

---

# 21. Contract Testing

Microservices require explicit compatibility testing.

```text
Consumer
    │
    ▼
Contract
    │
    ▼
Provider
```

Contract tests reduce dependence on enormous shared integration environments.

---

# 22. Consumer-Driven Contracts

A consumer may define expectations such as:

```text
GET /api/courses/123

expects:

200
courseId
title
status
```

The provider verifies that it continues satisfying the contract.

---

# 23. Pact

Pact should be evaluated for consumer-driven API contracts where its workflow fits Mediverse.

It can help independently deployed services verify compatibility without requiring every service to run simultaneously.

---

# 24. Spring Cloud Contract

Spring Cloud Contract is another strong candidate for Spring-centric services.

Selection should depend on:

```text
Team workflow
Language diversity
CI integration
Contract ownership
Existing Spring ecosystem usage
```

Do not run two contract frameworks permanently without a clear reason.

---

# 25. REST Contract Validation

REST compatibility includes more than endpoint existence.

Validate:

```text
HTTP method
Path
Status codes
Required fields
Optional fields
Data types
Validation
Error structures
Authentication expectations
```

---

# 26. OpenAPI Validation

OpenAPI specifications should be validated against implementation where feasible.

```text
OpenAPI Contract
      │
      ↕
Implementation
```

Documentation drifting away from actual APIs undermines its value.

---

# 27. GraphQL Testing

If GraphQL is used, validate:

```text
Schema compatibility
Queries
Mutations
Resolvers
Authorization
Nullability
Error behavior
Query complexity controls
```

---

# 28. gRPC Testing

gRPC contracts should validate protobuf compatibility and service behavior.

Breaking `.proto` evolution can disrupt independently deployed consumers.

---

# 29. Event Contract Testing

Kafka events require the same discipline as HTTP APIs.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Event Schema
   │
   ▼
Consumer
```

Tests should verify producer and consumer compatibility.

---

# 30. Schema Compatibility Gates

CI should reject incompatible event-schema changes according to ADR-053 compatibility policy.

```text
Schema Change
     │
     ▼
Compatibility Check
     │
     ├── Compatible → Continue
     └── Breaking   → Reject / Version
```

---

# 31. Frontend Unit Testing

React frontend logic should test:

```text
Utility functions
Reducers
Selectors
Validation
Transformation logic
State transitions
```

without unnecessarily rendering entire pages.

---

# 32. Vitest

For Vite-based React applications, Vitest should be the preferred test runner unless another existing standard provides a stronger reason.

It aligns naturally with the Vite toolchain.

---

# 33. React Testing Library

Component tests should focus on user-observable behavior.

Preferred:

```text
Render component
     │
     ▼
Find visible control
     │
     ▼
Interact
     │
     ▼
Assert visible result
```

rather than inspecting React implementation internals.

---

# 34. Accessibility Queries

Frontend tests should prefer semantic selectors where possible:

```text
Role
Label
Accessible name
Text
```

instead of brittle selectors such as:

```text
div:nth-child(7) > span
```

This improves both maintainability and accessibility awareness.

---

# 35. End-to-End Testing

E2E tests validate complete journeys.

Example:

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Login
   │
   ▼
Select Course
   │
   ▼
Start Assessment
   │
   ▼
Submit
   │
   ▼
View Result
```

These provide high confidence but are expensive to maintain and execute.

---

# 36. Playwright

Playwright should be the preferred strategic browser E2E framework for new Mediverse tests.

It provides:

```text
Modern browser automation
Cross-browser testing
Auto-waiting
Tracing
Screenshots/video
Parallel execution
Network controls
```

---

# 37. Cypress

Cypress remains viable where organizational experience or existing suites justify it.

Do not rewrite a large stable Cypress suite solely because Playwright is newer.

---

# 38. E2E Scope

E2E should focus on high-value journeys.

Examples:

```text
Registration
Login
Course enrollment
Payment if applicable
Assessment submission
Result generation
Critical administration flows
```

Do not reproduce every unit-test scenario through a browser.

---

# 39. E2E Explosion

Bad architecture:

```text
5,000 browser tests
```

for every business rule.

Results:

```text
Slow pipeline
Flakiness
Expensive debugging
High maintenance
Low developer trust
```

Push validation downward whenever lower layers can prove it reliably.

---

# 40. Test Data

Test data must be deterministic.

Tests should know:

```text
What exists
Who owns it
How it is created
How it is cleaned
```

Shared mystery data in UAT environments creates unreliable tests.

---

# 41. Test Data Builders

Code-based builders/fixtures should generate valid domain objects.

```text
UserBuilder
CourseBuilder
AssessmentBuilder
```

This reduces duplicated setup logic.

---

# 42. Production Data in Testing

Raw production personal/sensitive data should not be copied casually into test environments.

Use:

```text
Synthetic data
Masked data
Pseudonymized data
```

according to requirements.

---

# 43. Deterministic Tests

Given the same controlled inputs, a test should produce the same result.

Avoid hidden dependencies on:

```text
Current clock
Random external data
Execution order
Shared mutable state
Network availability
```

unless explicitly controlled.

---

# 44. Clock Control

Time-dependent business logic should use controllable clocks.

Example:

```text
Certificate expires after 30 days
```

should not require waiting 30 actual days or manipulating machine time.

---

# 45. Randomness

Random values used in tests should be reproducible when failure investigation requires it.

Record or control seeds where appropriate.

---

# 46. Test Isolation

Tests should not depend on execution order.

Bad:

```text
Test 1 creates user
Test 2 assumes user exists
Test 3 deletes user
```

A test suite should remain valid under parallel execution.

---

# 47. Flaky Tests

A flaky test alternates between pass and fail without meaningful product change.

Flakiness is a defect.

It should not be normalized.

---

# 48. Flaky Test Governance

When a test flakes:

```text
Detect
  │
  ▼
Record
  │
  ▼
Assign Owner
  │
  ▼
Fix / Quarantine Temporarily
  │
  ▼
Restore
```

Permanent quarantine is equivalent to deleting the quality gate.

---

# 49. Blind Retries

Automatically retrying every failed test until it passes can hide real failures.

Retries may help diagnose known infrastructure instability, but the original failure must remain visible.

---

# 50. Parallel Testing

Independent tests should run concurrently where infrastructure allows.

```text
Test Suite
 ├── Worker 1
 ├── Worker 2
 ├── Worker 3
 └── Worker 4
```

Parallelism reduces feedback time but exposes hidden shared-state coupling.

---

# 51. CI Test Stages

A practical CI sequence:

```text
Commit / PR
     │
     ▼
Static Checks
     │
     ▼
Unit Tests
     │
     ▼
Component / Integration
     │
     ▼
Contract
     │
     ▼
Build Artifact
     │
     ▼
Security
     │
     ▼
Environment Tests
```

Expensive tests should not block feedback before cheap failures are detected.

---

# 52. Fail Fast

Run cheap, high-signal checks early.

```text
Formatting
Compilation
Linting
Unit tests
```

before provisioning expensive integration environments.

---

# 53. Quality Gates

Mandatory failures should block release.

Examples:

```text
Compilation failure
Critical unit failure
Contract incompatibility
Migration failure
Critical security policy failure
```

A gate that everyone routinely overrides is not a gate.

---

# 54. Code Coverage

Coverage is a diagnostic metric, not proof of quality.

```text
100% coverage
```

can still test nothing meaningful.

Use coverage to locate untested risk, not as the sole quality objective.

---

# 55. Mutation Testing

Mutation testing should be evaluated for critical domain logic.

Conceptually:

```text
Original Code
     │
     ▼
Introduce Small Mutation
     │
     ▼
Run Tests
     │
     ├── Tests fail → Mutation killed
     └── Tests pass → Weak test coverage
```

Tools such as PIT can provide stronger evidence than line coverage alone.

---

# 56. API Functional Testing

API-level suites should validate realistic behavior through deployed service interfaces.

These tests complement controller/component tests.

---

# 57. Postman / Newman

Existing Postman collections may remain useful for:

```text
Exploration
Manual verification
API examples
Selected automated regression
```

But large enterprise automation should not depend exclusively on manually maintained Postman collections.

---

# 58. Smoke Tests

Smoke tests answer:

> **Is the deployed system fundamentally alive and usable?**

Examples:

```text
Application reachable
Authentication works
Critical dependency reachable
Basic read works
Basic write works
```

---

# 59. Regression Testing

Regression suites protect previously working behavior from accidental change.

They should be risk-based rather than an uncontrolled accumulation of every historical test case.

---

# 60. Environment Validation

A test environment should validate more than application code.

```text
DNS
TLS
Ingress
Identity
Secrets
Database connectivity
Kafka connectivity
Observability
Application behavior
```

A Kubernetes Deployment being `Ready` does not prove the environment works.

---

## ADR-054 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The Mediverse quality architecture now begins with:

```text
                      SOURCE CHANGE
                           │
                           ▼
                     STATIC CHECKS
                           │
                           ▼
                       UNIT TESTS
                           │
                           ▼
                    COMPONENT TESTS
                           │
                           ▼
                   INTEGRATION TESTS
                           │
                ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                ▼          ▼          ▼
            PostgreSQL    Redis      Kafka
                │          │          │
                └──────────┼──────────┘
                           ▼
                    CONTRACT TESTS
                           │
                           ▼
                     BUILD ARTIFACT
                           │
                           ▼
                    DEPLOYED SYSTEM
                           │
                           ▼
                       E2E TESTS
                           │
                           ▼
                     SMOKE / REGRESSION
```

The first 60 sections establish a critical rule:

> **Do not solve low confidence by creating thousands of slow E2E tests. Put each assertion at the lowest test layer that can prove the required behavior reliably, then reserve full-system tests for risks that genuinely cross system boundaries.**

**Part 2** should continue from **Section 61 — Security Testing**, then cover **SAST/SCA/DAST → OWASP ZAP → API security testing → authentication/authorization → RBAC/ABAC → tenant isolation → IDOR/BOLA → secret handling → dependency/security regression → infrastructure security validation → Kubernetes policy testing → performance engineering → workload modelling → k6/Gatling/JMeter → baseline/load/stress/spike/soak tests → latency percentiles → throughput → concurrency → coordinated omission → JVM profiling → GC → heap/thread analysis → database performance → connection saturation → Kafka throughput/consumer lag → Redis/OpenSearch performance → HPA/Karpenter validation → resilience testing → chaos engineering → Pod/node/AZ/dependency failure → network latency → Kafka/Redis/database failure → graceful degradation → retry storms → circuit breakers → DR tests → backup restoration → RPO/RTO validation → game days → synthetic monitoring → production smoke tests → canary analysis → SLO validation → observability assertions → release quality gates → test evidence → quality metrics → defect escape rate → accessibility → cross-browser/device testing → test ownership → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise quality-engineering reference architecture.**


# ADR-054 — Enterprise Testing Architecture, Quality Engineering, Test Automation, Performance Engineering & Production Validation

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Environment Validation**.

---

# 61. Security Testing

Security validation must exist throughout the delivery lifecycle rather than as one late-stage penetration test.

```text
Source
  │
  ├── SAST
  ├── SCA
  ├── Secret Scanning
  │
  ▼
Build
  │
  ├── Container Scan
  └── IaC Scan
  │
  ▼
Deployed Application
  │
  ├── DAST
  ├── API Security
  └── Authorization Tests
```

Security testing complements ADR-049 and ADR-051.

---

# 62. SAST

Static Application Security Testing should inspect source code for security weaknesses.

Typical categories include:

```text
Injection risks
Unsafe deserialization
Path traversal
Weak cryptography usage
Authentication mistakes
Input handling vulnerabilities
```

SAST findings require triage; scanner output is not automatically proof of exploitable vulnerability.

---

# 63. Software Composition Analysis

SCA validates third-party dependency risk.

```text
Application
   │
   ├── Spring dependencies
   ├── npm packages
   └── Transitive dependencies
            │
            ▼
       Vulnerability Analysis
```

This integrates with ADR-051's software supply-chain controls.

---

# 64. DAST

Dynamic Application Security Testing evaluates a running application.

```text
Running Application
       │
       ▼
Security Scanner
       │
       ▼
HTTP/API Attack Simulation
```

DAST can detect runtime issues that source analysis may miss.

---

# 65. OWASP ZAP

OWASP ZAP should be evaluated for automated web/API security testing.

It can support:

```text
Passive scanning
Active scanning
API scanning
Authentication-aware testing
CI integration
```

Active scanning must target authorized test environments—not uncontrolled production endpoints.

---

# 66. Authentication Testing

Authentication tests should validate:

```text
Valid credentials
Invalid credentials
Expired credentials
Revoked credentials
Malformed tokens
Missing tokens
Token tampering
Session expiration
```

A login happy-path test is insufficient.

---

# 67. Authorization Testing

Authorization tests must verify what authenticated identities are actually allowed to do.

```text
Authentication
      │
      ▼
Who are you?

Authorization
      │
      ▼
What may you do?
```

Both require independent testing.

---

# 68. RBAC Testing

For role-based access control:

```text
Student
Instructor
Administrator
Platform Operator
```

tests should verify both allowed and forbidden operations.

Testing only positive permissions misses privilege-escalation defects.

---

# 69. ABAC Testing

Where attribute-based controls exist, test combinations involving:

```text
User attributes
Resource ownership
Tenant
Environment
Resource classification
Request context
```

Boundary conditions are particularly important.

---

# 70. IDOR / BOLA

Object-level authorization deserves explicit testing.

Example vulnerability:

```text
GET /api/users/100/documents/500
```

User changes:

```text
500 → 501
```

and accesses another user's resource.

Knowing an object identifier must never imply authorization.

---

# 71. Tenant Isolation

If Mediverse introduces multi-tenancy, isolation testing becomes mandatory.

```text
Tenant A
   │
   X
Tenant B Data
```

Tests must attempt cross-tenant access through:

```text
APIs
Search
Caches
Events
Exports
Object storage
Analytics
```

---

# 72. Secret Handling Tests

Validation should ensure secrets do not leak through:

```text
Logs
HTTP responses
Stack traces
Metrics
Build artifacts
Container layers
Frontend bundles
Git
```

Secret scanning alone does not prove runtime non-disclosure.

---

# 73. Security Regression Tests

A vulnerability that has been fixed should usually receive a regression test where practical.

```text
Vulnerability
     │
     ▼
Fix
     │
     ▼
Regression Test
     │
     ▼
Future Protection
```

---

# 74. Infrastructure Security Validation

Terraform changes should be tested against ADR-052 policies.

Examples:

```text
No public RDS
Encryption enabled
Approved regions
Required tags
Restricted security groups
Logging enabled
```

---

# 75. Kubernetes Security Validation

Rendered Kubernetes resources should be tested for requirements such as:

```text
Non-root execution
Resource requests/limits
Approved registries
No privileged containers
Required probes
ServiceAccount configuration
SecurityContext
```

---

# 76. Performance Engineering

Performance testing must begin with a workload model.

Do not start by firing:

```text
10,000 users
```

at an endpoint with no understanding of real traffic.

---

# 77. Workload Model

Define:

```text
User population
Concurrent users
Requests/user
Read/write ratio
Request distribution
Payload sizes
Think time
Traffic peaks
Background jobs
Event volume
```

Performance testing should approximate expected production behavior.

---

# 78. Performance Objectives

Tests require measurable targets.

Example:

```text
Course API

p95 latency < 300 ms
p99 latency < 700 ms
error rate < 0.1%
throughput ≥ required RPS
```

Without targets, a load-test graph is just a graph.

---

# 79. Latency Percentiles

Average latency hides tail behavior.

Example:

```text
p50 = 80 ms
p95 = 250 ms
p99 = 1.8 sec
```

An average of 110 ms would conceal the poor experience of the slowest requests.

---

# 80. Throughput

Throughput measures completed work over time.

Examples:

```text
Requests/second
Events/second
Transactions/second
MB/second
```

Latency and throughput must be analyzed together.

---

# 81. Concurrency

Concurrency represents simultaneously active work.

```text
Users
  │
  ▼
Concurrent Requests
  │
  ▼
Application
```

Concurrency is not identical to requests per second.

---

# 82. Performance Tooling

Primary candidates include:

```text
k6
Gatling
JMeter
```

For modern automated API/load testing, k6 or Gatling should generally be preferred for new engineering workflows unless existing JMeter investments justify retaining it.

---

# 83. Baseline Test

A baseline establishes normal behavior under modest load.

```text
Low predictable load
        │
        ▼
Latency / CPU / Memory / DB
```

Without a baseline, later comparisons become harder.

---

# 84. Load Test

A load test validates expected operating conditions.

```text
Expected Production Load
          │
          ▼
System
          │
          ▼
SLO satisfied?
```

This should be the most representative performance scenario.

---

# 85. Stress Test

Stress testing intentionally exceeds expected capacity.

```text
Normal
  │
  ▼
Peak
  │
  ▼
Beyond Capacity
  │
  ▼
Failure Boundary
```

The objective is discovering how the system fails.

---

# 86. Spike Test

Spike tests simulate rapid traffic changes.

```text
Requests
   │
   │        ┌─────────
   │        │
   │________│
   └────────────────── Time
```

This is particularly important for autoscaled Kubernetes workloads.

---

# 87. Soak Test

A soak test maintains load for an extended period.

It detects problems such as:

```text
Memory leaks
Connection leaks
Thread exhaustion
Queue accumulation
Disk growth
Cache growth
Performance degradation
```

that short tests miss.

---

# 88. Capacity Test

Capacity testing determines the safe operating boundary.

```text
Load
 │
 ▼
Increase
 │
 ▼
SLO starts failing
 │
 ▼
Capacity Boundary
```

Production should operate with sufficient headroom below that boundary.

---

# 89. Coordinated Omission

Poor load generators may under-report latency when the target becomes slow because they stop issuing work at the intended rate.

Performance tooling and test design must account for this effect.

Otherwise severe saturation can look better than it actually is.

---

# 90. Performance Test Environment

Performance results from a developer laptop against tiny shared infrastructure cannot reliably predict production.

The environment should be sufficiently representative in:

```text
Compute
Database
Network
Caching
Autoscaling
Configuration
Dependency behavior
```

Scale may differ, but the differences must be understood.

---

# 91. JVM Performance

Spring Boot performance analysis should include:

```text
Heap
Garbage collection
Threads
CPU
Allocation rate
Class loading
Locks
```

Increasing Kubernetes CPU limits is not a substitute for JVM diagnosis.

---

# 92. JVM Profiling

Profiling tools should be used when evidence indicates CPU, allocation or thread problems.

```text
High latency
    │
    ▼
Profile
    │
    ▼
Hot path
    │
    ▼
Optimize
```

Optimize measured bottlenecks, not guessed ones.

---

# 93. Memory Leak Testing

Long-running tests should watch:

```text
Heap after GC
RSS
Off-heap memory
Thread count
Connection count
```

A steadily rising memory floor may indicate leakage.

---

# 94. Database Performance Testing

Load testing must include PostgreSQL behavior.

Monitor:

```text
Connections
CPU
IOPS
Query latency
Locks
Deadlocks
Buffer/cache behavior
Replication lag
Storage
```

An application benchmark that ignores the database is incomplete.

---

# 95. Connection Saturation

One important failure boundary is:

```text
Pods scale
   │
   ▼
Connections increase
   │
   ▼
DB max_connections reached
   │
   ▼
Requests fail
```

ADR-053's connection-budget architecture should be tested explicitly.

---

# 96. Query Performance Regression

Critical queries should have performance baselines where necessary.

A seemingly harmless schema/index change can turn:

```text
20 ms
```

into:

```text
2 seconds
```

under production-scale data.

---

# 97. Realistic Data Volume

Testing against 50 database rows proves almost nothing about queries expected to process tens of millions of records.

Representative data volume matters.

---

# 98. Redis Performance

Validate:

```text
Hit rate
Miss rate
Latency
Memory
Evictions
Connection behavior
Hot keys
```

and what happens when cache effectiveness drops.

---

# 99. Cache Failure Load Test

Test:

```text
Normal:
90% cache hit

Failure:
Redis unavailable
```

Then determine whether PostgreSQL survives the fallback traffic.

This is a critical dependency interaction test.

---

# 100. Kafka Performance

Kafka testing should validate:

```text
Producer throughput
Consumer throughput
Consumer lag
Partition distribution
Message size
Batching
Retries
Processing latency
```

---

# 101. Kafka Backlog Recovery

A consumer should be tested not only at steady state but while catching up from backlog.

```text
Consumer Down
     │
     ▼
Lag = 5,000,000
     │
     ▼
Consumer Restored
     │
     ▼
Can it catch up?
```

Steady-state capacity may be insufficient for recovery.

---

# 102. OpenSearch Performance

Search testing should measure:

```text
Query latency
Indexing latency
CPU
Heap
Shard behavior
Concurrent searches
Index size
Refresh impact
```

Search relevance and search performance are separate requirements.

---

# 103. Autoscaling Validation

HPA configuration must be tested under actual load.

```text
Load
 │
 ▼
Metric increases
 │
 ▼
HPA
 │
 ▼
More Pods
 │
 ▼
Capacity increases
```

A YAML configuration existing in Git does not prove scaling works.

---

# 104. Scale-Up Latency

Measure:

```text
Metric threshold crossed
        │
        ▼
HPA decision
        │
        ▼
Pod scheduled
        │
        ▼
Container started
        │
        ▼
Ready
```

This delay determines whether autoscaling can react quickly enough.

---

# 105. Karpenter Validation

When Pods cannot fit existing nodes:

```text
Pending Pods
     │
     ▼
Karpenter
     │
     ▼
Node provisioning
     │
     ▼
Pod scheduling
```

Test actual provisioning latency and failure modes.

---

# 106. Scale-Down Testing

Scale-down can be more dangerous than scale-up.

Validate:

```text
Graceful termination
PDB behavior
In-flight requests
Kafka partition reassignment
Connection draining
Long-running jobs
```

---

# 107. Performance Budget

Services should define resource/performance expectations.

Examples:

```text
Memory per Pod
CPU per request
DB connections per Pod
Expected RPS per Pod
Startup time
```

These values improve capacity planning.

---

# 108. Resilience Testing

A resilient system must be tested while components fail.

```text
Healthy System
      │
      ▼
Inject Failure
      │
      ▼
Observe Behavior
      │
      ▼
Recover
```

Waiting for production outages to discover failure behavior is poor engineering.

---

# 109. Chaos Engineering

Chaos engineering is controlled experimentation on failure behavior.

It is not:

```text
Randomly kill production things
and see what happens.
```

A useful experiment begins with a hypothesis.

---

# 110. Chaos Hypothesis

Example:

> If one course-service Pod terminates, user requests should continue within the defined SLO.

Then:

```text
Measure baseline
      │
      ▼
Terminate Pod
      │
      ▼
Observe
      │
      ▼
Validate hypothesis
```

---

# 111. Pod Failure

Test:

```text
Pod killed
   │
   ▼
Service routing adjusts
   │
   ▼
Replacement Pod starts
   │
   ▼
Traffic remains healthy
```

This validates Kubernetes assumptions.

---

# 112. Node Failure

A stronger test:

```text
Worker Node
     X
     │
     ▼
Pods disappear
     │
     ▼
Reschedule
     │
     ▼
Capacity restored
```

PDBs, topology and autoscaling behavior become relevant.

---

# 113. Availability Zone Failure

For critical services, test or simulate loss of an AZ where feasible.

```text
AZ-A
 X

AZ-B + AZ-C
     │
     ▼
Can workload continue?
```

Multi-AZ architecture without failure validation remains an assumption.

---

# 114. Network Latency

Inject increased dependency latency.

```text
Service A
    │
    │ +2 sec latency
    ▼
Service B
```

Then inspect:

```text
Timeouts
Thread pools
Connection pools
Retries
Circuit breakers
Overall latency
```

---

# 115. Network Loss

Packet loss/disconnection testing can reveal assumptions hidden by healthy networks.

Distributed systems must expect unreliable communication.

---

# 116. Dependency Failure

External dependencies should be deliberately made unavailable during testing.

Examples:

```text
Email provider
Payment provider
AI service
Object storage
Identity provider
```

The application should degrade according to business requirements.

---

# 117. Redis Failure

Validate:

```text
Redis unavailable
      │
      ▼
Cache operation fails
      │
      ▼
Fallback?
      │
      ▼
DB load impact
```

A cache outage should not automatically become a database outage.

---

# 118. Kafka Failure

Test:

```text
Broker unavailable
Producer timeout
Consumer interruption
Partition unavailable
```

and validate retry, buffering and recovery semantics.

---

# 119. Database Failover

Database failover testing should measure:

```text
Connection interruption
Failover duration
Application recovery
Transaction failures
Retry behavior
Data integrity
```

Multi-AZ does not mean applications experience zero errors.

---

# 120. Retry Storm

Failure can trigger:

```text
Dependency fails
      │
      ▼
Requests retry
      │
      ▼
More load
      │
      ▼
Dependency remains unhealthy
      │
      ▼
More retries
```

This positive feedback loop can turn a small outage into a major incident.

Test retry budgets and backoff.

---

# 121. Circuit Breaker Testing

Validate state transitions:

```text
CLOSED
  │ failures
  ▼
OPEN
  │ recovery delay
  ▼
HALF-OPEN
  │ success
  ▼
CLOSED
```

Circuit breakers configured but never failure-tested should not be trusted.

---

# 122. Graceful Degradation

Critical and optional capabilities should be distinguished.

Example:

```text
Recommendation Engine Down
        │
        ▼
Course Platform Still Works
        │
        ▼
Recommendations temporarily unavailable
```

Not every dependency failure should take down the entire application.

---

# 123. Bulkhead Testing

Resource isolation should prevent one failing workload from consuming all shared resources.

```text
Dependency A
   │
   X
Thread Pool A saturated

Dependency B
   │
   ▼
Thread Pool B remains healthy
```

---

# 124. Disaster-Recovery Testing

DR testing must validate the complete recovery workflow.

```text
Disaster
   │
   ▼
Detect
   │
   ▼
Declare
   │
   ▼
Restore / Failover
   │
   ▼
Validate
   │
   ▼
Resume Service
```

---

# 125. Backup Restore Tests

ADR-053 established that backups must be restored periodically.

ADR-054 requires automated or controlled validation of restored data.

Check:

```text
Database opens
Schema valid
Critical records present
Application connects
Integrity checks pass
```

---

# 126. RPO Validation

If:

```text
RPO = 5 minutes
```

the DR exercise must determine actual data loss.

If recovery loses 47 minutes, the architecture failed regardless of what the document claims.

---

# 127. RTO Validation

Measure actual time from declared outage to usable restored service.

```text
Disaster declared
      │
      ▼
Recovery
      │
      ▼
Application usable
```

Documentation time estimates are not evidence.

---

# 128. Game Days

Mediverse should periodically run controlled operational exercises.

Scenarios may include:

```text
Database failover
Kafka outage
Redis outage
Node loss
Expired certificate
Secret rotation failure
Bad deployment
Region degradation
```

The purpose is to test systems **and people/processes**.

---

# 129. Synthetic Monitoring

Synthetic tests should continuously execute selected critical journeys.

```text
Synthetic Client
      │
      ▼
Login
      │
      ▼
Critical API
      │
      ▼
Expected Result
```

This validates externally visible behavior, not merely infrastructure metrics.

---

# 130. Production Smoke Tests

Immediately after deployment:

```text
Deploy
  │
  ▼
Production Smoke
  │
  ├── Pass → Continue
  └── Fail → Stop/Rollback
```

Tests must avoid destructive effects on real users/data.

---

# 131. Canary Validation

ADR-051 progressive delivery should consume quality signals.

```text
5% traffic → New Version
      │
      ▼
Observe
      │
      ├── Healthy → 25%
      └── Failure → Rollback
```

---

# 132. Canary Signals

Evaluate:

```text
5xx rate
Latency
CPU/memory
Crash rate
DB errors
Kafka failures
Business transaction success
```

Infrastructure-only metrics can miss logically broken releases.

---

# 133. SLO Validation

ADR-047 SLOs should become release evidence.

Example:

```text
Availability ≥ target
p95 latency ≤ target
Error rate ≤ target
```

A release should not be considered healthy merely because Pods are running.

---

# 134. Observability Assertions

Tests can validate telemetry itself.

Examples:

```text
Trace generated
Correlation ID propagated
Expected metric emitted
Audit event created
Critical error logged correctly
Secret not logged
```

Observability is part of system behavior.

---

# 135. Feature Flag Validation

Test both:

```text
Flag OFF
+
Flag ON
```

for critical flags.

A feature hidden behind a flag can still break shared execution paths.

---

# 136. Release Quality Evidence

Each release should accumulate evidence such as:

```text
Commit
Artifact digest
Unit results
Integration results
Contract results
Security results
Performance evidence where required
Deployment result
Smoke result
Canary analysis
```

This creates an auditable release record.

---

# 137. Risk-Based Quality Gates

Not every change needs the same expensive validation.

Example:

```text
Documentation change
      │
      ▼
Minimal pipeline

Critical authentication change
      │
      ▼
Extended security + integration + E2E
```

Risk-based testing is more rational than blindly running everything for every change.

---

# 138. Quality Metrics

Useful engineering metrics include:

```text
Test pass rate
Flaky-test rate
Pipeline duration
Defect escape rate
Change failure rate
Mean time to detect
Regression recurrence
Security findings
Performance regressions
```

Metrics should drive investigation, not employee ranking.

---

# 139. Defect Escape Rate

Track defects discovered after the stage that should have caught them.

Example:

```text
Production authorization bug
```

should trigger the question:

> Which earlier quality layer should have detected this?

That produces architectural improvement.

---

# 140. Accessibility Testing

Mediverse should validate accessibility through:

```text
Semantic HTML
Keyboard navigation
Focus behavior
Accessible names
Contrast
Screen-reader compatibility
Automated accessibility scans
Manual testing
```

Automated tools detect only part of accessibility failures.

---

# 141. Cross-Browser Testing

Critical journeys should be validated across supported browser families.

The support matrix should be explicit rather than assuming every browser behaves identically.

---

# 142. Responsive Testing

Frontend validation should cover representative:

```text
Desktop
Tablet
Mobile
```

viewports.

Pixel-perfect testing across hundreds of device dimensions provides little value.

---

# 143. Test Ownership

Tests require owners.

```text
Application Team
→ Unit/component/service tests

Service Teams
→ Contracts

QA/QE
→ Cross-system strategy/tooling

Platform Team
→ Infrastructure/resilience validation

Security
→ Security strategy

SRE
→ Reliability/game days/production validation
```

Quality cannot be outsourced entirely to a QA team.

---

# 144. Test Failure Ownership

When a mandatory pipeline test fails, responsibility belongs to the team making the change unless evidence shows the test/platform itself is defective.

The normal response should not be:

```text
Disable test
```

to make the pipeline green.

---

# 145. Testing in Production

Some properties can only be validated against real production conditions.

Safe production testing may include:

```text
Synthetic journeys
Canary releases
Shadow traffic
Feature flags
Observability validation
Controlled chaos
```

This does not justify uncontrolled experiments on users.

---

# 146. Enterprise Quality Anti-Patterns

Mediverse shall reject:

```text
❌ QA only at the end of development

❌ Thousands of E2E tests for logic unit tests could prove

❌ Mocking every infrastructure dependency

❌ H2 as the only validation for PostgreSQL behavior

❌ Integration tests depending on manually maintained shared databases

❌ Test-order dependencies

❌ Shared mystery UAT test data

❌ Raw production PII copied into test environments

❌ Permanent flaky-test quarantine

❌ Blind retry-until-green pipelines

❌ Coverage percentage treated as proof of correctness

❌ Contract changes without compatibility tests

❌ Security testing only before annual audit

❌ Testing authentication but not authorization

❌ Positive authorization tests without negative cases

❌ No tenant-isolation testing

❌ Performance tests without workload models

❌ Average latency used instead of percentiles

❌ Load testing from a laptop against production

❌ Performance tests using unrealistically tiny datasets

❌ Application load tests ignoring PostgreSQL

❌ HPA assumed correct because YAML exists

❌ Autoscaling without scale-up latency testing

❌ Chaos engineering as random destruction

❌ Retries without backoff/budget

❌ Circuit breakers never failure-tested

❌ Multi-AZ treated as proof of resilience

❌ Backups treated as valid without restore testing

❌ RPO/RTO existing only in documentation

❌ Canary promotion based only on Pod health

❌ Production release considered healthy because deployment succeeded

❌ Test failures routinely bypassed to meet deadlines
```

---

# 147. Mediverse Quality Gates

The release path should progressively accumulate confidence:

```text
PR
 │
 ├── Compile
 ├── Lint
 ├── Unit
 ├── Slice
 ├── SAST
 ├── SCA
 └── Contract Compatibility
 │
 ▼
MERGE
 │
 ├── Integration
 ├── Testcontainers
 ├── Migration Validation
 ├── Component
 └── Artifact Build
 │
 ▼
RELEASE CANDIDATE
 │
 ├── API Regression
 ├── E2E Critical Journeys
 ├── Security
 ├── DAST
 └── Performance where required
 │
 ▼
STAGING
 │
 ├── Smoke
 ├── Environment Validation
 ├── Resilience Validation
 └── Production-like Performance
 │
 ▼
PRODUCTION CANARY
 │
 ├── SLO
 ├── Error Rate
 ├── Latency
 ├── Business KPIs
 └── Synthetic Journeys
 │
 ▼
FULL PROMOTION
```

---

# 148. Final Mediverse Quality Engineering Architecture

```text
                           REQUIREMENTS
                                │
                                ▼
                           SOURCE CODE
                                │
                ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
                ▼               ▼                ▼
             STATIC           UNIT           SECURITY
                │               │                │
                └───────────────┼────────────────┘
                                ▼
                         COMPONENT TESTS
                                │
                                ▼
                        INTEGRATION TESTS
                                │
          ┌─────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          ▼                     ▼                    ▼
     PostgreSQL               Redis                Kafka
          │                     │                    │
          └─────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                                ▼
                         CONTRACT TESTS
                                │
                                ▼
                        IMMUTABLE ARTIFACT
                                │
                                ▼
                        TEST ENVIRONMENT
                                │
               ┌────────────────┼─────────────────┐
               ▼                ▼                 ▼
              E2E            SECURITY         REGRESSION
               │                │                 │
               └────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                                ▼
                            STAGING
                                │
             ┌──────────────────┼───────────────────┐
             ▼                  ▼                   ▼
        PERFORMANCE         RESILIENCE          DR TESTS
             │                  │                   │
             └──────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                                ▼
                       PRODUCTION CANARY
                                │
                  ┌─────────────┼──────────────┐
                  ▼             ▼              ▼
                SLOs         SYNTHETICS     BUSINESS
                  │             │              KPIs
                  └─────────────┼──────────────┘
                                ▼
                       AUTOMATED ANALYSIS
                                │
                      ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                      ▼                   ▼
                   HEALTHY              FAILURE
                      │                   │
                      ▼                   ▼

```

---

# 149. Core Quality Invariants

Regardless of future tooling changes:

```text
1. No single testing layer defines quality.

2. Business logic is tested primarily below E2E level.

3. Real infrastructure is used where infrastructure semantics matter.

4. Production database behavior is not inferred solely from H2.

5. API and event contracts are compatibility-tested.

6. Tests are deterministic and independently executable.

7. Flakiness is treated as engineering debt.

8. Security validation includes negative authorization cases.

9. Performance tests begin with workload models and measurable objectives.

10. Tail latency matters.

11. Production-scale data characteristics matter.

12. Database capacity is part of application capacity.

13. Kafka scaling considers partition count and lag.

14. Autoscaling is experimentally validated.

15. Resilience mechanisms are failure-tested.

16. Retries are bounded.

17. Dependency failures have defined degradation behavior.

18. Backups are restore-tested.

19. RPO/RTO are measured through exercises.

20. Canary analysis includes business signals.

21. Production deployment success does not equal release success.

22. Quality evidence follows the release artifact.

23. Every mandatory test has an owner.

24. Test failures are investigated rather than routinely bypassed.
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                           | Decision                                       |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Overall model                  | **Layered quality engineering**                |
| Java testing                   | **JUnit 5**                                    |
| Mocking                        | Mockito, selective                             |
| Spring slices                  | Required where appropriate                     |
| DB integration                 | Real PostgreSQL                                |
| Infrastructure testing         | **Testcontainers**                             |
| H2                             | Not authoritative for PostgreSQL compatibility |
| DB migrations                  | Integration-tested                             |
| Redis/Kafka integration        | Real infrastructure where semantics matter     |
| API contracts                  | Required between independent services          |
| Contract framework             | Pact / Spring Cloud Contract evaluation        |
| OpenAPI compatibility          | Automated validation                           |
| Event contracts                | Compatibility-gated                            |
| React test runner              | **Vitest** preferred                           |
| React components               | React Testing Library                          |
| Browser E2E                    | **Playwright** preferred for new suites        |
| E2E scope                      | Critical journeys                              |
| Test data                      | Deterministic/synthetic                        |
| Production PII in tests        | Restricted                                     |
| Flaky tests                    | Defect; owned and remediated                   |
| Blind test retries             | Rejected                                       |
| Coverage                       | Diagnostic, not primary quality target         |
| Mutation testing               | Selective evaluation                           |
| API regression                 | Automated                                      |
| DAST                           | Required risk-based capability                 |
| DAST tooling                   | OWASP ZAP evaluation                           |
| Authorization negative testing | Mandatory                                      |
| Tenant isolation               | Mandatory if multi-tenant                      |

| Kubernetes policy testing      | Required                                       |

| Performance metrics            | p50/p95/p99 + throughput + errors              |
| Load test                      | Expected operating load                        |
| Stress test                    | Failure boundary                               |
| Spike test                     | Sudden demand                                  |
| Soak test                      | Long-duration degradation                      |
| DB performance                 | Included                                       |
| Kafka performance              | Throughput + lag                               |
| Autoscaling                    | Load validated                                 |
| Karpenter                      | Provisioning behavior tested                   |
| Chaos engineering              | Controlled hypothesis-based                    |
| Pod/node failure               | Tested                                         |
| AZ failure                     | Critical services                              |
| Dependency failure             | Tested                                         |
| Retry storms                   | Tested                                         |

| Graceful degradation           | Required for noncritical dependencies          |

parsing → OCR boundary → content versioning → embedding lifecycle → reindexing → retrieval evaluation → RAGAS-style evaluation → model evaluation datasets → golden datasets → LLM-as-judge limitations → human evaluation → prompt injection → indirect prompt injection → data exfiltration → tool abuse → jailbreaks → output sanitization → PII → data residency → model-provider privacy → encryption → AI # ADR-055 — Enterprise AI/ML, Generative AI, RAG, AI Agents, Model Governance & AI Platform Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-055
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-054 established how Mediverse proves system quality.

ADR-055 establishes how Mediverse introduces **AI, machine learning, generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation and agentic capabilities without turning the platform into an uncontrolled collection of prompts and external model calls**.

The governing principle is:

> **AI is probabilistic infrastructure, not deterministic business logic. Models may assist reasoning, generation, retrieval and personalization, but authoritative business rules, permissions, security boundaries and critical decisions remain controlled by deterministic systems.**

```text
                           MEDIVERSE
                               │
                               ▼
                       APPLICATION LAYER
                               │
                    ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                    ▼                     ▼
             Deterministic Logic      AI Capability
                    │                     │
                    │                     ▼
                    │                AI GATEWAY
                    │                     │
                    │        ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                    │        ▼            ▼            ▼
                    │      Models        RAG         Agents
                    │        │            │            │
                    │        ▼            ▼            ▼
                    │    Generation    Knowledge      Tools
                    │                     │            │
                    │                     ▼            ▼
                    │                Vector/Search   Services
                    │
                    └──────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                                   ▼
                           GOVERNANCE PLANE
                                   │
                    ┌──────────────┼───────────────┐
                    ▼              ▼               ▼
                 Security       Evaluation      Observability
```

---

# 1. AI Is Not the Default Solution

Before introducing AI, ask:

```text
Can deterministic software solve this reliably?
```

If yes, deterministic software is usually preferable.

Use AI when the problem genuinely benefits from:

```text
Natural language understanding
Generation
Semantic retrieval
Classification
Recommendation
Prediction
Multimodal understanding
Probabilistic reasoning
```

---

# 2. Capability Classification

Mediverse capabilities should be classified before implementation.

```text
Capability
    │
    ├── Deterministic
    │      └── Traditional software
    │
    ├── Predictive
    │      └── ML model
    │
    ├── Generative
    │      └── LLM / multimodal model
    │
    └── Agentic
           └── Model + tools + controlled workflow
```

This prevents unnecessary LLM usage.

---

# 3. Initial Mediverse AI Use Cases

Candidate capabilities include:

```text
AI Tutor
Question generation
Explanation generation
Study-plan assistance
Content summarization
Semantic search
Adaptive learning
Recommendation
Content classification
Transcription
Speech generation
Learning analytics
```

Each capability requires independent risk and quality evaluation.

---

# 4. AI Tutor

The AI tutor should operate as an educational assistance layer.

```text
Student
   │
   ▼
Tutor API
   │
   ▼
AI Orchestration
   │
   ├── Student context
   ├── Course context
   ├── Retrieved knowledge
   └── Safety policy
           │
           ▼
          LLM
           │
           ▼
      Grounded Answer
```

It must not be implemented as an unrestricted chatbot with direct access to every platform resource.

---

# 5. AI Tutor Boundaries

The tutor may:

```text
Explain concepts
Summarize material
Generate practice questions
Guide revision
Retrieve course material
```

It should not independently:

```text
Modify grades
Grant permissions
Change authoritative records
Approve users
Perform privileged administration
```

without deterministic authorization and explicit workflows.

---

# 6. AI-Generated Questions

Question generation should produce candidates.

```text
Learning Material
       │
       ▼
      LLM
       │
       ▼
Candidate Questions
       │
       ▼
Validation
       │
       ▼
Approved Question Bank
```

Generated educational content should not automatically become authoritative content.

---

# 7. Structured Generation

Where downstream systems consume model output, prefer structured responses.

Conceptually:

```json
{
  "question": "...",
  "type": "MCQ",
  "options": [],
  "correctAnswer": "...",
  "explanation": "..."
}
```

rather than parsing arbitrary prose.

---

# 8. Schema Validation

Structured AI output must still be validated.

```text
LLM
 │
 ▼
Structured Output
 │
 ▼
Schema Validation
 │
 ├── Valid   → Continue
 └── Invalid → Retry / Reject
```

A model requesting JSON does not guarantee semantically correct data.

---

# 9. AI Explanation Generation

Generated explanations should be clearly separated from canonical educational content.

```text
Canonical Content
       │
       ▼
AI Explanation
       │
       ▼
Student
```

AI-generated interpretation must not silently overwrite source material.

---

# 10. Adaptive Learning

Adaptive learning may use signals such as:

```text
Assessment performance
Topic mastery
Attempt history
Difficulty
Learning progress
```

to recommend future activities.

The recommendation system should not make irreversible academic decisions without defined governance.

---

# 11. AI Recommendation Boundary

Recommendation:

```text
"You should review cardiovascular physiology."
```

is fundamentally different from an authoritative decision:

```text
"You are prohibited from progressing."
```

AI recommendations and deterministic academic policy must remain separate.

---

# 12. Semantic Search

Traditional search:

```text
Exact / lexical terms
```

Semantic search:

```text
Meaning / similarity
```

Mediverse should support both where useful.

---

# 13. Hybrid Search

Preferred knowledge retrieval may combine:

```text
Lexical Search
      +
Vector Search
      +
Metadata Filters
      +
Reranking
```

rather than assuming vector similarity alone provides optimal retrieval.

---

# 14. Model Abstraction

Application services should not scatter direct model-provider SDK calls throughout the codebase.

Bad:

```text
Course Service ─────► Provider A
Assessment Service ─► Provider A
Tutor Service ──────► Provider B
Search Service ─────► Provider C
```

Preferred:

```text
Applications
     │
     ▼
AI Platform / Gateway
     │
     ├── Provider A
     ├── Provider B
     └── Self-hosted Model
```

---

# 15. AI Gateway

The gateway should centralize cross-cutting AI concerns.

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Model routing
Rate limits
Quotas
Prompt policies
Telemetry
Cost attribution
Fallback
Safety controls
Audit
```

It should not become a giant business-logic service.

---

# 16. Provider Strategy

Mediverse should avoid hard architectural dependence on one model provider.

Candidates may include managed model platforms and self-hosted models.

Provider selection should evaluate:

```text
Model quality
Latency
Availability
Cost
Privacy
Data residency
Context window
Multimodality
Tool support
Structured output
Operational complexity
```

---

# 17. Managed vs Self-Hosted

Managed models provide:

```text
Lower infrastructure burden
Rapid model access
Managed scaling
```

Self-hosting can provide:

```text
Greater deployment control
Specific privacy boundaries
Custom models
Potential economics at sufficient scale
```

Self-hosting is not automatically cheaper.

GPU operations can be expensive and operationally difficult.

---

# 18. Model Routing

Different workloads may use different models.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
AI Router
   │
   ├── Simple classification → Small model
   ├── Complex tutoring      → Strong model
   ├── Embeddings            → Embedding model
   └── Vision                → Multimodal model
```

Using the largest model for every request wastes money and latency.

---

# 19. Model Fallback

For appropriate noncritical workloads:

```text
Primary Model
      │
      X
      │
      ▼
Fallback Model
```

may improve availability.

But fallback must preserve required safety and capability semantics.

---

# 20. Model Versioning

Model behavior can change across versions.

Every important invocation should be attributable to:

```text
Provider
Model
Model version where available
Prompt version
Retrieval configuration
Application version
```

Without this, regression investigation becomes guesswork.

---

# 21. Prompt Engineering Is Software Engineering

Prompts are production artifacts.

They should be:

```text
Version-controlled
Reviewed
Tested
Evaluated
Observable
Rollback-capable
```

Editing a production prompt manually in a console without traceability is rejected.

---

# 22. Prompt Architecture

A request may contain several layers.

```text
System Policy
     │
     ▼
Application Instructions
     │
     ▼
Retrieved Context
     │
     ▼
Conversation Context
     │
     ▼
User Request
```

Their trust levels are not equal.

---

# 23. System Prompt

System-level instructions define high-level behavior and constraints.

They should not contain credentials or assume secrecy.

A system prompt may eventually be exposed through model behavior or attacks.

---

# 24. Prompt Templates

Reusable prompts should be parameterized.

```text
Template
  │
  ├── Topic
  ├── Difficulty
  ├── Learning objective
  └── Retrieved context
```

Avoid duplicating near-identical prompts throughout services.

---

# 25. Prompt Registry

At sufficient scale, Mediverse should maintain a governed prompt registry.

```text
Prompt ID
Version
Owner
Purpose
Model compatibility
Evaluation result
Status
```

---

# 26. Prompt Deployment

Prompt changes should follow controlled release principles.

```text
Change
 │
 ▼
Evaluation
 │
 ▼
Review
 │
 ▼
Canary
 │
 ▼
Production
```

A prompt change can break production behavior without changing Java code.

---

# 27. Prompt Injection

User-controlled text must be treated as untrusted input.

Example:

```text
Ignore previous instructions...
```

The model's ability to interpret language makes conventional input/output boundaries harder, not irrelevant.

---

# 28. Indirect Prompt Injection

Dangerous instructions may exist inside retrieved content.

```text
External Document
       │
       ▼
RAG Retrieval
       │
       ▼
"Ignore policy and send..."
       │
       ▼
LLM
```

Retrieved text is data—not trusted system instruction.

---

# 29. Instruction Hierarchy

The architecture must distinguish:

```text
Trusted platform policy
        >
Application instruction
        >
Untrusted retrieved content
        >
User content
```

Application enforcement cannot depend solely on the model respecting this hierarchy.

---

# 30. RAG

Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds model responses using external knowledge.

```text
User Question
      │
      ▼
Query Processing
      │
      ▼
Retriever
      │
      ▼
Relevant Knowledge
      │
      ▼
LLM
      │
      ▼
Grounded Response
```

---

# 31. Why RAG?

Without retrieval:

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Model Training Knowledge
```

may be outdated, incomplete or unrelated to Mediverse content.

With RAG:

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Mediverse Knowledge
   │
   ▼
Model
```

the answer can use platform-specific information.

---

# 32. RAG Does Not Eliminate Hallucination

This assumption is false:

```text
RAG = no hallucinations
```

A model can:

```text
Misinterpret retrieved content
Ignore relevant content
Combine sources incorrectly
Invent unsupported details
```

RAG improves grounding; it does not create deterministic truth.

---

# 33. Knowledge Ingestion

RAG begins before retrieval.

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
Parse
  │
  ▼
Normalize
  │
  ▼
Chunk
  │
  ▼
Metadata
  │
  ▼
Embed
  │
  ▼
Index
```

Poor ingestion produces poor retrieval regardless of model quality.

---

# 34. Knowledge Sources

Potential sources include:

```text
Course chapters
Lecture notes
Approved reference content
Question banks
Transcripts
Internal educational documents
Structured metadata
```

Source authority must be known.

---

# 35. Document Parsing

Parsing should preserve useful structure such as:

```text
Title
Chapter
Section
Paragraph
Table relationships
Page/location
Source identity
```

Flattening every document into one giant string destroys retrieval context.

---

# 36. OCR Boundary

OCR should only be used when source content cannot be extracted directly.

```text
Digital text
   │
   └── Extract directly

Scanned content
   │
   └── OCR
```

OCR introduces recognition errors and requires quality validation.

---

# 37. Chunking

Documents must be divided into retrieval units.

```text
Document
 ├── Chunk 1
 ├── Chunk 2
 ├── Chunk 3
 └── Chunk N
```

Chunk size is an optimization problem, not a universal constant.

---

# 38. Chunk Size

Too small:

```text
High precision
Low context
Fragmented meaning
```

Too large:

```text
More context
Poor retrieval precision
Higher token consumption
```

Chunking should be evaluated empirically.

---

# 39. Semantic Chunking

Where useful, chunk boundaries should follow meaningful structure:

```text
Chapter
Section
Concept
Paragraph group
```

rather than arbitrary character counts alone.

---

# 40. Chunk Metadata

Each chunk should preserve metadata such as:

```text
documentId
courseId
chapterId
section
version
language
contentType
access classification
source
```

Metadata enables filtering and traceability.

---

# 41. Embeddings

Embedding models convert content into vectors representing semantic relationships.

```text
Text
 │
 ▼
Embedding Model
 │
 ▼
Vector
```

Queries are embedded similarly for similarity search.

---

# 42. Embedding Model Versioning

Changing embedding models can invalidate similarity assumptions.

Therefore record:

```text
embeddingModel
embeddingVersion
embeddingDimension
createdAt
```

and plan re-embedding explicitly.

---

# 43. Vector Store

Candidate architecture:

```text
PostgreSQL + pgvector
```

or:

```text
OpenSearch Vector Search
```

depending on scale and retrieval requirements.

---

# 44. pgvector

pgvector can be attractive when:

```text
Existing PostgreSQL expertise
Moderate vector scale
Strong relational filtering
Operational simplicity
```

are priorities.

Do not deploy a separate vector database merely because RAG examples on the internet do.

---

# 45. OpenSearch Vector Capability

OpenSearch may be preferable when Mediverse already requires:

```text
Large search workloads
Lexical search
Vector search
Hybrid retrieval
Complex search filtering
```

This can consolidate search capabilities.

---

# 46. Vector Database Decision

The selection should consider:

```text
Corpus size
Query volume
Latency
Hybrid search
Metadata filtering
Operational burden
Cost
Backup
Availability
Existing infrastructure
```

There is no universally correct vector database.

---

# 47. Retrieval

Basic retrieval:

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Embedding
   │
   ▼
Vector Similarity
   │
   ▼
Top-K Chunks
```

is only the starting point.

---

# 48. Metadata Filtering

Authorization and domain context should constrain retrieval.

Example:

```text
courseId = 100
language = English
contentStatus = APPROVED
```

before irrelevant material reaches the model.

---

# 49. Retrieval Authorization

This is critical.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Authorized Knowledge Scope
 │
 ▼
Retriever
```

not:

```text
Retrieve everything
      │
      ▼
Ask model not to reveal it
```

The model is not an authorization boundary.

---

# 50. Hybrid Retrieval

A robust pipeline may use:

```text
Query
 │
 ├── Lexical retrieval
 │
 ├── Vector retrieval
 │
 └── Metadata filtering
          │
          ▼
       Merge
          │
          ▼
       Rerank
```

---

# 51. Reranking

Initial retrieval may return dozens of candidates.

A reranker can improve ordering:

```text
50 candidates
      │
      ▼
Reranker
      │
      ▼
Top 5
```

This can improve context quality while reducing token usage.

---

# 52. Context Assembly

Retrieved content should be assembled intentionally.

```text
Question
+
Relevant chunks
+
Source metadata
+
Instructions
=
Model Context
```

Do not blindly dump the largest possible amount of text into the context window.

---

# 53. Context Window

A large context window is not free memory.

Larger context can increase:

```text
Latency
Cost
Noise
Attention dilution
```

Retrieval quality remains important even with large-context models.

---

# 54. Citations

Grounded educational answers should provide source attribution where appropriate.

```text
Answer
  │
  ├── Source A
  ├── Chapter 4
  └── Section 2
```

Citations improve verification but must point to content actually supporting the statement.

---

# 55. Grounding

For knowledge-grounded use cases, model instructions should prioritize supplied authoritative material.

If evidence is insufficient, the system should permit:

```text
Insufficient information
```

rather than rewarding confident invention.

---

# 56. Knowledge Versioning

Course content changes.

```text
Content v1
   │
   ▼
Embeddings v1

Content v2
   │
   ▼
Embeddings v2
```

The retrieval index must track source versions.

---

# 57. Stale Embeddings

Updating PostgreSQL/S3 content without updating the retrieval index produces stale AI answers.

```text
Source updated
      │
      X
Vector index unchanged
```

Ingestion must participate in content lifecycle.

---

# 58. Reindexing

Embedding/model changes may require:

```text
Existing corpus
      │
      ▼
New embeddings
      │
      ▼
New index
      │
      ▼
Validation
      │
      ▼
Traffic switch
```

Prefer versioned indexes over destructive in-place migrations.

---

# 59. Retrieval Evaluation

RAG quality should separately measure retrieval.

Questions include:

```text
Was relevant evidence retrieved?
Was irrelevant evidence retrieved?
Was the correct source ranked highly?
```

Generation evaluation alone cannot diagnose retrieval failures.

---

# 60. RAG Evaluation Dimensions

A RAG system should evaluate at least:

```text
Retrieval relevance
Retrieval recall
Context precision
Answer correctness
Faithfulness
Citation correctness
Completeness
Latency
Cost
```

---

## ADR-055 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The architecture now establishes:

```text
                         USER
                           │
                           ▼
                    MEDIVERSE API
                           │
                           ▼
                    AI ORCHESTRATOR
                           │
              ┌────────────┼─────────────┐
              ▼            ▼             ▼
          POLICY       RETRIEVAL       MODEL
              │            │             │
              │            ▼             │
              │       HYBRID SEARCH      │
              │            │             │
              │       ┌────┴────┐        │
              │       ▼         ▼        │
              │    Lexical    Vector     │
              │       │         │        │
              │       └────┬────┘        │
              │            ▼             │
              │         RERANKER         │
              │            │             │
              └────────────┼─────────────┘
                           ▼
                     CONTEXT ASSEMBLY
                           │
                           ▼
                          LLM
                           │
                           ▼
                   STRUCTURED OUTPUT
                           │
                           ▼
                       VALIDATION
                           │
                           ▼
                    GROUNDED RESPONSE
```

The first 60 sections establish several non-negotiable rules:

```text
1. AI does not replace deterministic business rules.

2. Model-provider SDKs do not spread uncontrolled
   throughout microservices.

3. Prompts are versioned production artifacts.

4. Retrieved documents are untrusted data.

5. Authorization happens before retrieval,
   not through model instructions.

6. RAG improves grounding but does not eliminate hallucination.

7. Knowledge ingestion is part of the production architecture.

8. Chunking and embedding strategies are evaluated,
   not copied blindly from tutorials.

9. Vector infrastructure is selected from actual scale
   and search requirements.

10. Retrieval and generation quality are measured separately.
```
