# ADR-055 — Enterprise AI/ML, Generative AI, RAG, AI Agents, Model Governance & AI Platform Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — RAG Evaluation Dimensions**.

---

# 61. AI Evaluation Architecture

Traditional software testing asks:

```text
Expected Output == Actual Output?
```

Generative AI often requires a different model:

```text
Input
  │
  ▼
AI System
  │
  ▼
Probabilistic Output
  │
  ▼
Evaluation
  │
  ├── Correctness
  ├── Faithfulness
  ├── Relevance
  ├── Safety
  ├── Completeness
  ├── Style
  └── Cost / Latency
```

AI quality therefore requires **evaluation systems**, not just assertions.

---

# 62. Golden Evaluation Dataset

Every important AI capability should maintain representative evaluation cases.

```text
Evaluation Dataset
      │
      ├── Normal cases
      ├── Difficult cases
      ├── Edge cases
      ├── Adversarial cases
      └── Safety cases
```

For the AI tutor, examples should span subjects, difficulty levels and question types.

---

# 63. Golden Dataset Structure

A case may contain:

```text
Input
Expected facts
Approved sources
Expected behavior
Forbidden behavior
Evaluation criteria
```

The expected answer does not always need to be one exact string.

---

# 64. Evaluation Dataset Versioning

Evaluation data is a production engineering artifact.

Track:

```text
Dataset ID
Version
Owner
Purpose
Created date
Domain
Risk category
```

Changing the evaluation set can change perceived model quality even when the model has not changed.

---

# 65. Offline Evaluation

Before deployment:

```text
Candidate
   │
   ▼
Golden Dataset
   │
   ▼
Evaluation Runner
   │
   ▼
Metrics
   │
   ▼
Baseline Comparison
```

Candidate prompts/models/retrieval strategies should be compared against established baselines.

---

# 66. Regression Evaluation

A new model should not be accepted merely because it improves one metric.

Example:

```text
Candidate Model

Correctness     +8%
Latency         +40%
Cost            +120%
Safety          -5%
Citation quality -12%
```

This is a trade-off requiring explicit evaluation.

---

# 67. Human Evaluation

Some qualities require expert judgment.

For educational content:

```text
Subject Matter Expert
        │
        ▼
AI Response
        │
        ▼
Evaluate
        │
        ├── Correctness
        ├── Clarity
        ├── Pedagogical quality
        └── Safety
```

Automated scoring cannot completely replace expert review.

---

# 68. LLM-as-Judge

A model may evaluate another model's output.

```text
Response
   │
   ▼
Judge Model
   │
   ▼
Score
```

This can scale evaluation, but judge output is itself probabilistic.

---

# 69. Judge Limitations

LLM judges may exhibit:

```text
Position bias
Verbosity bias
Model-family bias
Prompt sensitivity
Inconsistent scoring
Preference for confident answers
```

Therefore LLM-as-judge should not become unquestioned ground truth.

---

# 70. Multi-Layer Evaluation

Preferred:

```text
Deterministic Checks
        +
Retrieval Metrics
        +
LLM Judge
        +
Human Evaluation
        +
Production Signals
```

No single metric should determine AI quality.

---

# 71. Hallucination Evaluation

For grounded answers:

```text
Generated Claim
      │
      ▼
Supporting Evidence?
      │
      ├── Yes → Grounded
      └── No  → Unsupported
```

Unsupported factual claims should be measurable.

---

# 72. Faithfulness

Faithfulness asks:

> Is the generated answer supported by the supplied context?

This differs from general factual correctness.

An answer can be factually true but unsupported by the retrieved Mediverse source.

---

# 73. Citation Evaluation

Citations should be evaluated for:

```text
Existence
Correct source
Correct location
Claim support
Source authority
```

Attaching arbitrary citations to an answer is worse than admitting insufficient evidence.

---

# 74. Retrieval Evaluation

Retrieval must be tested independently.

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Retriever
   │
   ▼
Expected Source Found?
```

If the correct document never reaches the model, prompt engineering cannot fix the underlying retrieval failure.

---

# 75. Safety Evaluation

Evaluation datasets should include unsafe/adversarial requests appropriate to Mediverse's risk profile.

The objective is verifying that AI behavior remains within defined product and security policy.

---

# 76. AI Red Teaming

High-risk AI capabilities should undergo adversarial testing.

Test categories include:

```text
Prompt injection
Indirect injection
Jailbreak attempts
Sensitive-data extraction
Tool abuse
Privilege escalation
Cross-user leakage
Memory poisoning
Retrieval manipulation
```

---

# 77. Prompt Injection Defense

There is no reliable universal prompt such as:

```text
"Never follow malicious instructions."
```

that solves prompt injection.

Defense requires architectural controls.

---

# 78. Prompt Injection Control Layers

```text
Untrusted Input
      │
      ▼
Input Handling
      │
      ▼
Restricted Context
      │
      ▼
Model
      │
      ▼
Tool Authorization
      │
      ▼
Output Validation
```

The model itself must not be the only security boundary.

---

# 79. Indirect Injection Defense

Retrieved documents may contain hostile instructions.

Therefore:

```text
Retrieved Content
      │
      ▼
Treat as DATA
      │
      X
Trusted Instructions
```

Tool permissions must never be derived directly from retrieved text.

---

# 80. Data Exfiltration

Attackers may attempt to make models reveal:

```text
Other users' data
System configuration
Private documents
Credentials
Internal prompts
Retrieved restricted data
```

The strongest control is preventing unauthorized information from entering model context in the first place.

---

# 81. Context Isolation

AI contexts must respect identity and authorization boundaries.

```text
User A
  │
  ▼
Authorized Context A

User B
  │
  ▼
Authorized Context B
```

Conversation or retrieval context must never accidentally cross those boundaries.

---

# 82. Tool Calling

Models may request execution of structured tools.

```text
LLM
 │
 ▼
Tool Request
 │
 ▼
Validation
 │
 ▼
Authorization
 │
 ▼
Tool Execution
 │
 ▼
Result
 │
 ▼
LLM
```

The model requests an action.

The platform decides whether it is permitted.

---

# 83. Tool Schemas

Tools should expose narrow typed contracts.

Example:

```text
getCourse(courseId)
```

is safer than:

```text
executeArbitrarySQL(query)
```

Agent tools should expose business capabilities, not unrestricted infrastructure primitives.

---

# 84. Tool Authorization

Every tool invocation must independently validate:

```text
Identity
Permission
Resource scope
Arguments
Policy
```

Never assume:

```text
The model already checked permission.
```

---

# 85. Agent Architecture

An agent combines:

```text
Model
+
Context
+
Tools
+
State
+
Control Loop
```

Conceptually:

```text
Goal
 │
 ▼
Reason
 │
 ▼
Select Tool
 │
 ▼
Execute
 │
 ▼
Observe
 │
 ▼
Continue / Finish
```

This creates significantly more risk than ordinary text generation.

---

# 86. Workflow vs Agent

Prefer deterministic workflows when steps are known.

```text
Known Process
    │
    ▼
Workflow Engine
```

Use agentic reasoning when the path genuinely requires dynamic decision-making.

Do not turn every workflow into an agent.

---

# 87. Bounded Agent

Preferred:

```text
Agent
 │
 ├── Approved Tools
 ├── Maximum Steps
 ├── Token Budget
 ├── Time Budget
 ├── Resource Scope
 └── Human Approval Gates
```

Unbounded autonomous loops are rejected.

---

# 88. Agent Identity

An agent must operate under an identifiable principal.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Agent Session
 │
 ▼
Delegated Identity
 │
 ▼
Tools
```

The agent should not automatically receive platform-admin privileges.

---

# 89. Least Privilege for Agents

Example:

```text
Study Assistant Agent

ALLOW:
Read enrolled course content
Read student's progress
Create draft study plan

DENY:
Modify grades
Change IAM
Delete users
Access other students
```

Capabilities should match the use case.

---

# 90. Human Approval

Sensitive actions require explicit confirmation.

```text
Agent proposes action
        │
        ▼
Human Approval
        │
        ├── Approve → Execute
        └── Reject  → Stop
```

Approval should happen before irreversible side effects.

---

# 91. Irreversible Actions

Actions involving:

```text
Deletion
Financial transactions
Account privileges
External communication
Authoritative academic records
Sensitive data disclosure
```

require stronger safeguards than read-only operations.

---

# 92. Agent Step Limits

Agents require bounded execution.

```text
maxSteps = N
timeout = T
tokenBudget = B
costBudget = C
```

Otherwise reasoning loops can consume uncontrolled resources.

---

# 93. Agent Failure

Agents must fail safely.

```text
Cannot determine next action
        │
        ▼
Stop / Escalate
```

not:

```text
Keep trying random tools forever
```

---

# 94. Agent Audit Trail

Record significant agent operations:

```text
Agent ID
User identity
Model
Prompt/version
Tool requested
Authorization result
Tool arguments classification
Execution result
Timestamp
```

Sensitive content should still follow logging/redaction rules.

---

# 95. AI Memory

AI memory should be deliberately separated into:

```text
Conversation Context
       +
Session State
       +
Long-Term Memory
```

They have different privacy and retention requirements.

---

# 96. Short-Term Memory

Conversation context supports continuity within an interaction.

```text
Message 1
Message 2
Message 3
   │
   ▼
Current Context
```

It should be bounded by relevance, tokens and privacy requirements.

---

# 97. Long-Term Memory

Long-term personalization may retain selected durable information.

But storing everything a user ever says is a poor architecture.

Memory requires:

```text
Purpose
Consent/expectation
Retention
Deletion
Access control
Relevance
```

---

# 98. Memory Minimization

Only retain information that materially improves future functionality.

Do not treat AI memory as an unlimited surveillance log.

---

# 99. Memory Poisoning

Attackers or erroneous model output may attempt to persist false instructions or facts.

```text
Malicious Input
      │
      ▼
Memory
      │
      ▼
Future Sessions Compromised
```

Memory writes therefore require validation and policy.

---

# 100. Memory Authorization

Memory is user-scoped data.

```text
User A Memory
      X
User B
```

Cross-user retrieval is a critical security failure.

---

# 101. External Tool Integration

External AI tools/connectors should follow the same security principles as internal services.

```text
AI
 │
 ▼
Tool Gateway
 │
 ▼
Authorization
 │
 ▼
External System
```

Model-generated tool arguments are untrusted input.

---

# 102. Tool Result Trust

Tool output is not automatically safe model instruction.

```text
External Tool
     │
     ▼
Untrusted Result
     │
     ▼
Model Context
```

This is another indirect prompt-injection boundary.

---

# 103. Output Validation

AI output consumed by software should pass:

```text
Schema validation
Type validation
Business validation
Authorization checks
Safety validation
```

before causing side effects.

---

# 104. Output Sanitization

Generated content rendered in web interfaces must be treated as untrusted content.

Protect against issues such as:

```text
Unsafe HTML
Script injection
Malicious links
Unexpected markup
```

Frontend security boundaries remain applicable to AI output.

---

# 105. PII and AI

Before sending information to a model, ask:

```text
Does the model actually require this data?
```

Apply ADR-053 data minimization principles.

---

# 106. Provider Privacy

Model providers must be evaluated for:

```text
Data retention
Training-data usage
Regional processing
Subprocessors
Security controls
Contractual commitments
Deletion
Logging
```

Provider privacy policy is part of architecture.

---

# 107. Data Residency

Sensitive workloads may require processing within approved regions or environments.

```text
Data Classification
       │
       ▼
Approved Model Deployment
```

Model quality alone does not determine provider eligibility.

---

# 108. AI Auditability

For high-value interactions, Mediverse should be able to reconstruct:

```text
Who requested?
Which model?
Which prompt?
Which knowledge?
Which tools?
Which output?
Which policy?
When?
```

subject to privacy and retention constraints.

---

# 109. Token Budget

Every AI capability should define token budgets.

```text
Input Tokens
+
Output Tokens
=
Cost + Latency
```

Unlimited context is not a sensible production default.

---

# 110. Context Budgeting

Context should prioritize:

```text
System policy
Required conversation state
Highest-value retrieved evidence
User request
```

Low-value history should be summarized or discarded.

---

# 111. AI Caching

Deterministic or sufficiently reusable AI results may be cached where semantics permit.

```text
Request
 │
 ▼
Cache
 │
 ├── Hit → Return
 └── Miss → Model
```

Caching user-specific or sensitive output requires careful isolation.

---

# 112. Semantic Caching

Semantically similar queries may reuse previous answers.

This can reduce:

```text
Cost
Latency
Provider traffic
```

but introduces risks of:

```text
Incorrect equivalence
Stale answers
Authorization leakage
Personalization mismatch
```

Use selectively.

---

# 113. Rate Limiting

AI endpoints require explicit rate controls.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Rate Limit
 │
 ▼
AI Gateway
```

This protects capacity and cost.

---

# 114. Quotas

Quota dimensions may include:

```text
User
Tenant
Feature
Model
Token count
Time period
```

A flat request count may be inadequate because AI requests can vary dramatically in cost.

---

# 115. Cost Attribution

Every model invocation should be attributable where practical.

```text
Request
 │
 ├── Application
 ├── Feature
 ├── Tenant/User category
 ├── Model
 ├── Tokens
 └── Estimated Cost
```

Without attribution, AI spending becomes difficult to govern.

---

# 116. AI Cost Optimization

Optimize in this order:

```text
Do we need AI?
       │
       ▼
Do we need this much context?
       │
       ▼
Do we need this model?
       │
       ▼
Can result be cached?
       │
       ▼
Can work be asynchronous/batched?
```

Do not start by degrading answer quality blindly.

---

# 117. Latency

AI latency includes more than inference.

```text
Request
 │
 ▼
Authorization
 │
 ▼
Retrieval
 │
 ▼
Reranking
 │
 ▼
Model Queue
 │
 ▼
Inference
 │
 ▼
Validation
```

End-to-end latency should be measured.

---

# 118. Streaming Responses

For long generation:

```text
Model
 │
 ▼
Token Stream
 │
 ▼
Client
```

can improve perceived responsiveness.

Streaming does not reduce total inference time.

---

# 119. Asynchronous AI Jobs

Long-running workloads such as:

```text
Large document summarization
Question-bank generation
Bulk embeddings
Transcription
Content processing
```

should often run asynchronously.

```text
API
 │
 ▼
Job Queue
 │
 ▼
Worker
 │
 ▼
AI
 │
 ▼
Result Store
```

---

# 120. AI Retries

Model calls may fail transiently.

Retry only appropriate failures using:

```text
Bounded attempts
Exponential backoff
Jitter
Timeouts
```

Do not retry every 4xx or policy rejection.

---

# 121. AI Fallback

Fallback may operate across:

```text
Model
Region
Provider
Capability mode
```

Example:

```text
Premium Model unavailable
        │
        ▼
Approved Secondary Model
```

Only if secondary behavior remains acceptable.

---

# 122. AI Circuit Breaker

Repeated provider failure should trigger protective behavior.

```text
Calls
 │
 ▼
Failures
 │
 ▼
Circuit Open
 │
 ▼
Fallback / Degraded Experience
```

This prevents retry storms.

---

# 123. AI Observability

Monitor:

```text
Request volume
Model latency
Time to first token
Total latency
Input tokens
Output tokens
Cost
Error rate
Rate-limit events
Fallback rate
Retrieval latency
Tool failures
Safety interventions
```

---

# 124. AI Tracing

A single AI interaction may span:

```text
API
 │
 ▼
Retriever
 │
 ▼
Vector Store
 │
 ▼
Reranker
 │
 ▼
LLM
 │
 ▼
Tool
 │
 ▼
LLM
```

Distributed tracing should expose these stages without logging sensitive raw content indiscriminately.

---

# 125. RAG Telemetry

Record metrics such as:

```text
Chunks retrieved
Retrieval scores
Reranking scores
Context size
Source IDs
Citation count
Retrieval latency
```

This helps diagnose whether failures originate from retrieval or generation.

---

# 126. AI SLOs

AI capabilities require explicit objectives.

Example:

```text
Tutor availability ≥ target
p95 first-token latency ≤ target
p95 completion latency ≤ target
Grounded-answer score ≥ target
Unsafe-response rate ≤ target
```

AI SLOs may include quality as well as infrastructure reliability.

---

# 127. Model Registry

Models used by Mediverse should be cataloged.

```text
Model
 │
 ├── Provider
 ├── Version
 ├── Purpose
 ├── Owner
 ├── Evaluation
 ├── Risk classification
 └── Approval status
```

Unknown models should not quietly appear in production.

---

# 128. Model Lifecycle

```text
Evaluate
   │
   ▼
Approve
   │
   ▼
Deploy
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
   ▼
Re-evaluate
   │
   ▼
Deprecate
```

Model lifecycle is continuous because model/provider behavior changes.

---

# 129. Fine-Tuning Decision

Fine-tuning should not be the first response to poor AI quality.

Evaluate first:

```text
Prompt improvement
Retrieval improvement
Better context
Better model
Tool use
```

Fine-tune only when evidence indicates it solves the actual problem.

---

# 130. Fine-Tuning Use Cases

Fine-tuning may be useful for:

```text
Stable output behavior
Specialized style
Classification
Domain-specific patterns
Repeated structured tasks
```

It is generally not the preferred mechanism for injecting frequently changing factual knowledge.

RAG is usually more appropriate for that.

---

# 131. Training Data Governance

Fine-tuning/training datasets require:

```text
Provenance
Usage rights
Quality
Classification
PII review
Retention
Versioning
Approval
```

"You found the dataset online" is not sufficient governance.

---

# 132. Traditional ML Boundary

Not every AI capability requires an LLM.

Examples:

```text
Risk prediction
Recommendation ranking
Dropout prediction
Difficulty estimation
Classification
```

may be better served by conventional ML.

---

# 133. MLOps

Traditional/self-hosted ML requires lifecycle management:

```text
Data
 │
 ▼
Training
 │
 ▼
Evaluation
 │
 ▼
Model Registry
 │
 ▼
Deployment
 │
 ▼
Monitoring
 │
 ▼
Retraining
```

---

# 134. Feature Store

A feature store should only be introduced when Mediverse operates enough reusable ML features to justify it.

```text
User mastery score
Course engagement
Assessment history
```

may eventually become shared features.

Premature feature-store infrastructure is rejected.

---

# 135. Online vs Batch Inference

Online:

```text
Request
 │
 ▼
Model
 │
 ▼
Immediate prediction
```

Batch:

```text
Dataset
 │
 ▼
Model
 │
 ▼
Bulk predictions
```

Use batch processing where immediate inference is unnecessary.

---

# 136. GPU Infrastructure

Self-hosted generative models may require GPU infrastructure.

Potential architecture:

```text
Kubernetes
    │
    ▼
GPU Node Pool
    │
    ▼
Inference Runtime
    │
    ▼
Model
```

GPU capacity must not be introduced merely for architectural prestige.

---

# 137. Inference Autoscaling

Self-hosted inference scaling should consider:

```text
Request concurrency
Queue depth
Tokens/sec
GPU utilization
Model memory
Startup/model-loading time
```

CPU-based HPA alone may be meaningless for GPU inference.

---

# 138. Model Loading

Large models may require significant startup time.

```text
Pod starts
   │
   ▼
Load model
   │
   ▼
Allocate GPU memory
   │
   ▼
Warm up
   │
   ▼
Ready
```

Autoscaling design must account for this delay.

---

# 139. Model Rollout

Model changes should use progressive validation.

```text
Current Model
      │
      ├──────────────┐
      ▼              ▼
Most Traffic     Candidate
                     │
                     ▼
                 Evaluation
```

---

# 140. Shadow Evaluation

A candidate model can receive copied production requests without serving its responses.

```text
Request
   │
   ├──► Production Model → User
   │
   └──► Candidate Model → Evaluation only
```

This enables realistic comparison with reduced user risk.

---

# 141. AI Canary

After offline/shadow validation:

```text
1%
 │
 ▼
5%
 │
 ▼
25%
 │
 ▼
100%
```

traffic may progressively move to the candidate when metrics remain acceptable.

---

# 142. Educational & Medical Content Governance

Mediverse's educational domain requires stricter treatment of medically relevant generated content.

AI-generated educational explanations should distinguish:

```text
Educational information
        vs
Authoritative clinical guidance
```

The platform must not imply that probabilistic generation is equivalent to verified medical instruction or patient-specific clinical advice.

---

# 143. Human-in-the-Loop

High-impact generated content may require expert approval.

```text
AI Generates
    │
    ▼
Draft
    │
    ▼
Expert Review
    │
    ├── Approve
    ├── Edit
    └── Reject
```

Human review should occur before publication when risk warrants it.

---

# 144. AI Incident Response

AI incidents may include:

```text
Unsafe output
Cross-user data leakage
Prompt injection
Tool misuse
Cost runaway
Model degradation
Incorrect educational content
Provider outage
Retrieval corruption
```

Incident procedures should capture AI-specific evidence.

---

# 145. AI Supply-Chain Security

AI dependencies include:

```text
Models
Model providers
Embedding models
Python packages
Inference containers
Datasets
Prompt libraries
Agent tools
Vector infrastructure
```

All require provenance and security governance appropriate to their risk.

---

# 146. AI Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ LLM for every problem
❌ Direct provider SDK calls scattered across services
❌ Largest model for every request
❌ Provider lock-in without deliberate decision
❌ Prompts edited manually in production
❌ Secrets inside prompts
❌ Treating retrieved documents as trusted instructions
❌ Using the model as an authorization engine
❌ Retrieving unauthorized data then asking the model not to reveal it
❌ Assuming RAG eliminates hallucination
❌ Vector database introduced without workload justification
❌ Arbitrary chunk size copied from tutorials
❌ Embeddings without source/version metadata
❌ Stale indexes after source changes
❌ AI evaluation based on a few demo prompts
❌ LLM-as-judge treated as objective truth
❌ Agent with unrestricted tools
❌ Agent running as platform administrator
❌ Arbitrary SQL/shell exposed as general-purpose agent tools
❌ Irreversible actions without approval
❌ Unlimited agent loops
❌ Unlimited token budgets
❌ Persisting every conversation as long-term memory
❌ Cross-user memory/context leakage
❌ Blind trust in tool output
❌ Raw AI output directly causing privileged side effects
❌ Sending unnecessary PII to model providers
❌ No provider privacy/residency review
❌ No AI cost attribution
❌ Retrying policy failures
❌ No fallback/degradation strategy
❌ Logging every raw prompt containing sensitive information
❌ Fine-tuning before diagnosing retrieval/prompt problems
❌ Training on datasets without provenance
❌ GPU clusters before workload justification
❌ Model rollout directly from 0% to 100%
❌ AI-generated medical educational content treated as automatically authoritative
```

---

# 147. AI Ownership Model

```text
Application Teams
      │
      ├── AI feature behavior
      ├── Business integration
      ├── Feature evaluation
      └── User experience

AI Platform Team
      │
      ├── AI Gateway
      ├── Model integrations
      ├── Prompt infrastructure
      ├── RAG platform
      ├── Evaluation platform
      ├── Model registry
      └── AI observability

Data Platform Team
      │
      ├── Knowledge pipelines
      ├── Data quality
      ├── Vector/index lifecycle
      └── Training datasets

Security Team
      │
      ├── Threat model
      ├── Prompt-injection testing
      ├── Tool security
      ├── Privacy
      └── AI red teaming

Domain Experts
      │
      ├── Educational correctness
      ├── Golden datasets
      ├── Content review
      └── High-risk approvals

SRE / Platform
      │
      ├── Reliability
      ├── Capacity
      ├── GPU infrastructure
      └── Incident response
```

---

                              USERS
                                │
                                ▼
                         MEDIVERSE APIs
                                │
                                ▼
                      AI ORCHESTRATION LAYER

---

# 149. Core AI Invariants

Regardless of future providers, models or frameworks:

```text
1. AI never becomes the authorization boundary.

2. Deterministic rules remain deterministic where correctness demands it.

3. AI capabilities are isolated behind governed platform interfaces.

4. Models, prompts, retrieval configuration and datasets are versioned.

5. Prompt changes are production changes.

6. Retrieved content is untrusted input.

7. Authorization occurs before knowledge reaches the model.

8. RAG does not guarantee factuality.

9. Retrieval quality and generation quality are evaluated independently.

10. AI quality is measured against representative evaluation datasets.

11. LLM judges are evidence, not ground truth.

12. High-risk outputs receive appropriate human oversight.

13. Agent tools are narrow, typed and independently authorized.

14. Agents operate with delegated least privilege.

15. Irreversible actions require stronger controls.

16. Agent execution is bounded by steps, time, tokens and cost.

17. AI memory is minimized, scoped and governed.

18. Model-generated tool arguments are untrusted input.

19. Sensitive data is minimized before model invocation.

20. Provider privacy and residency are architecture concerns.

21. AI usage has explicit rate, token and cost budgets.

22. AI telemetry measures retrieval, inference, tools, quality and cost.

23. Models undergo evaluation before production rollout.

24. Model changes use progressive delivery.

25. Fine-tuning is introduced only when evidence justifies it.

26. Training data has provenance and governance.

27. Self-hosted GPU infrastructure requires demonstrated need.

28. Educational/medical AI content is not automatically authoritative.

29. AI incidents are observable, auditable and recoverable.

30. Humans remain accountable for the system's behavior.
```

---

| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| AI architecture                       | **Central governed AI platform**                      |
| AI vs deterministic logic             | Requirement-driven                                    |
| Direct provider calls across services | Rejected                                              |
| Provider abstraction                  | AI Gateway                                            |
| Multi-model strategy                  | Supported                                             |
| Model routing                         | Capability/cost/quality aware                         |
| Model fallback                        | Controlled                                            |
| Prompt management                     | Version-controlled                                    |
| Prompt registry                       | Required at scale                                     |
| Structured output                     | Preferred for machine consumption                     |
| Output validation                     | Mandatory before side effects                         |
| RAG                                   | Strategic knowledge-grounding pattern                 |
| RAG authorization                     | Before retrieval                                      |
| Retrieval                             | Hybrid where justified                                |
| Vector platform                       | pgvector/OpenSearch evaluation                        |
| Vector DB proliferation               | Rejected without justification                        |
| Reranking                             | Selective                                             |
| Knowledge versioning                  | Required                                              |
| Citation support                      | Required for appropriate grounded educational answers |
| RAG evaluation                        | Retrieval + generation                                |
| Golden datasets                       | Required                                              |

| Rate limits / quotas                  | Required                                              |
| Cost attribution                      | Required                                              |
| Streaming                             | User-experience optimization                          |
| Long AI workloads                     | Async jobs                                            |
| Retries                               | Bounded + backoff                                     |

| AI observability                      | Required                                              |
| AI SLOs                               | Reliability + quality                                 |
| Model registry                        | Required                                              |
| Fine-tuning                           | Evidence-driven                                       |

| Traditional ML                        | Preferred when problem fits                           |

| Status                                | **Accepted**                                          |
| Priority                              | **Critical**                                          |

## Next — ADR-056

### **ADR-056 — Enterprise Identity, Authentication, Authorization, IAM, Zero Trust & Digital Identity Architecture**

This is the next major gap. Security has already been addressed broadly, but identity is important enough that leaving it buried inside general security architecture will eventually create inconsistent authentication and authorization across microservices, Kubernetes, AWS, CI/CD, AI agents and administrative systems.

ADR-056 should define **human identity → student/instructor/admin/operator personas → workforce vs customer identity → identity provider architecture → OIDC/OAuth 2.x → authorization code + PKCE → JWT vs opaque tokens → access/refresh tokens → token lifetime → token rotation → JWKS/key rotation → session management → logout/revocation → MFA/passkeys/WebAuthn → account recovery → federation → social/enterprise login → service identities → workload identity → Kubernetes ServiceAccounts → EKS Pod Identity/IRSA → AWS IAM roles → CI/CD OIDC federation → machine-to-machine authentication → client credentials boundaries → SPIFFE/SPIRE evaluation → mTLS → API gateway authentication → token propagation → token exchange → confused deputy → RBAC → ABAC → ReBAC evaluation → policy decision/enforcement points → OPA/Cedar-style policy evaluation → resource-level authorization → tenant isolation → admin privilege → just-in-time access → PAM → break-glass → AI-agent delegated identity → tool authorization → impersonation → audit → identity lifecycle → provisioning/deprovisioning → SCIM → dormant accounts → credential compromise → risk-based authentication → rate limiting → brute-force defense → session theft → CSRF → CORS boundaries → secretless workloads → zero trust → identity observability → authorization testing → identity incident response → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise identity reference architecture.**
