# ADR-057 — Enterprise API Architecture, API Gateway, REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets, Versioning & API Governance

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — RED Method**.

---

# 61. GraphQL Architecture

GraphQL should be introduced when consumer-driven data composition provides measurable value.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
GraphQL API
  │
  ▼
Schema
  │
  ▼
Resolvers
  │
  ├── Course Service
  ├── User Service
  └── Assessment Service
```

GraphQL is **not automatically superior to REST**.

---

# 62. GraphQL Schema

The schema is the GraphQL contract.

```graphql
type Course {
  id: ID!
  title: String!
  description: String
  instructor: Instructor!
}
```

Schema design should model consumer-facing domain concepts rather than database tables.

---

# 63. Queries

Queries represent read operations.

```graphql
query {
  course(id: "123") {
    title
    description
  }
}
```

Queries should not secretly perform destructive operations.

---

# 64. Mutations

State-changing operations belong in mutations.

```graphql
mutation {
  enroll(courseId: "123") {
    enrollmentId
    status
  }
}
```

Mutation names should express domain intent.

---

# 65. GraphQL Over-Fetching Advantage

REST may require:

```text
GET /courses/123
GET /courses/123/instructor
GET /courses/123/progress
```

GraphQL can potentially retrieve the required shape through one client operation.

This can benefit complex frontend experiences.

---

# 66. GraphQL Is Not One Database Query

This misconception is rejected:

```text
One GraphQL request
       =
One backend query
```

One request may trigger dozens or hundreds of resolver operations if poorly implemented.

---

# 67. N+1 Problem

Example:

```text
1 query → 100 courses

Then:

100 queries → instructor for each course
```

Total:

```text
101 backend operations
```

This is a classic GraphQL performance failure.

---

# 68. DataLoader / Batching

Resolvers should batch compatible lookups.

```text
100 instructor requests
        │
        ▼
      Batch
        │
        ▼
getInstructors(ids[])
```

Batching and caching can dramatically reduce N+1 behavior.

---

# 69. Query Depth

Clients can construct deeply nested queries.

```text
course
 └── instructor
      └── courses
           └── students
                └── courses
                     └── ...
```

Unbounded depth creates resource-exhaustion risk.

---

# 70. Query Complexity

Depth alone is insufficient.

A shallow query returning huge collections can still be expensive.

GraphQL gateways should evaluate:

```text
Depth
Field cost
Collection cardinality
Resolver cost
Overall complexity
```

---

# 71. GraphQL Pagination

Large collections must remain paginated.

GraphQL does not justify returning an entire dataset.

Connection/cursor patterns are appropriate where stable traversal is required.

---

# 72. GraphQL Authorization

Authorization must occur at the correct resource/domain boundary.

```text
Resolver
  │
  ▼
Load Resource
  │
  ▼
Authorization
  │
  ├── ALLOW
  └── DENY
```

A valid GraphQL query does not imply permission to access every requested field.

---

# 73. Field-Level Authorization

Some fields may require stronger privileges.

```text
User
 ├── displayName
 ├── avatar
 └── administrativeMetadata
```

The final field may require administrative authorization.

Do not assume object-level authorization automatically covers every field.

---

# 74. GraphQL Introspection

Introspection is valuable for tooling and development.

Whether it remains available publicly in production should follow the threat model.

Disabling introspection alone is not meaningful API security.

---

# 75. Persisted Queries

For controlled clients:

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Known Query ID
  │
  ▼
GraphQL Gateway
```

persisted queries can improve:

```text
Governance
Caching
Security controls
Traffic predictability
```

They are especially useful for first-party clients.

---

# 76. GraphQL Federation

Federation may allow multiple domains to contribute to a larger graph.

```text
                GraphQL Router
                      │
       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
       ▼              ▼              ▼
     Course        Student       Assessment
    Subgraph       Subgraph        Subgraph
```

This should only be introduced when organizational/domain scale justifies its operational complexity.

---

# 77. GraphQL Federation Boundary

Federation must not erase bounded contexts.

Each domain remains responsible for:

```text
Data ownership
Authorization
Schema ownership
Performance
Compatibility
```

A unified graph is not a unified database.

---

# 78. REST vs GraphQL

Use REST when:

```text
Resource operations are straightforward
HTTP caching matters
Simple integrations dominate
API consumers need conventional contracts
```

Consider GraphQL when:

```text
Frontend data requirements vary significantly
Many related resources must be composed
Consumer-controlled projections provide clear value
```

---

# 79. GraphQL Decision

Mediverse will **not replace REST globally with GraphQL**.

Preferred architecture:

```text
REST
→ Primary service/public API style

GraphQL
→ Selective consumer-facing composition layer
```

---

# 80. gRPC Architecture

gRPC should primarily target controlled service-to-service communication requiring:

```text
Strong contracts
Low overhead
High throughput
Streaming
Generated clients
```

---

# 81. Protocol Buffers

gRPC contracts should use Protobuf schemas.

```protobuf
message CourseRequest {
  string course_id = 1;
}
```

The `.proto` file is a production contract.

---

# 82. Protobuf Field Numbers

Field numbers are part of wire compatibility.

```protobuf
string course_id = 1;
```

Once published, numbers should not be casually reused for different meanings.

---

# 83. Protobuf Evolution

Prefer additive changes.

```text
Add new field
→ Usually compatible

Remove/reuse field number
→ Dangerous
```

Removed fields should be reserved when appropriate.

---

# 84. gRPC Unary Calls

Unary RPC:

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
One Request
  │
  ▼
Server
  │
  ▼
One Response
```

This resembles conventional synchronous request/response communication.

---

# 85. Server Streaming

```text
Client Request
      │
      ▼
Server
      │
      ├── Response 1
      ├── Response 2
      └── Response N
```

Useful where one request naturally produces a stream of results.

---

# 86. Client Streaming

```text
Client
  ├── Message 1
  ├── Message 2
  └── Message N
       │
       ▼
     Server
       │
       ▼
    Response
```

Use only where the domain naturally benefits from streamed input.

---

# 87. Bidirectional Streaming

```text
Client ◄════════════► Server
```

Both sides communicate through a persistent stream.

This adds lifecycle, backpressure and failure-handling complexity.

---

# 88. gRPC Deadlines

Every synchronous gRPC request should have a deadline.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Deadline
  │
  ▼
Service
```

Without deadlines, failed downstream calls can consume resources indefinitely.

---

# 89. Deadline Propagation

Downstream calls should respect the remaining upstream deadline.

```text
3s original budget
      │
      ▼
1.8s remaining
      │
      ▼
Downstream must not wait 10s
```

---

# 90. REST vs gRPC

Use REST when:

```text
Browser/external interoperability dominates
Human-readable debugging matters
HTTP ecosystem is valuable
```

Consider gRPC when:

```text
Internal high-throughput communication
Strong generated contracts
Low serialization overhead
Streaming
```

Mediverse should not convert every internal API to gRPC without evidence.

---

# 91. WebSocket Architecture

WebSockets support persistent bidirectional communication.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
HTTP Upgrade
  │
  ▼
Persistent Connection
  │
  ⇅
Server
```

Potential Mediverse uses include real-time notifications and collaborative experiences.

---

# 92. WebSocket Authentication

Authentication must occur when establishing the connection using a secure architecture appropriate to the client.

```text
Connection
    │
    ▼
Authenticate
    │
    ▼
Authorize
    │
    ▼
Accept
```

A connected client is not automatically authorized for every channel.

---

# 93. WebSocket Authorization

Subscription authorization must be resource-aware.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Subscribe course:123
 │
 ▼
Is user authorized for course 123?
```

Channel names are not authorization.

---

# 94. Connection Lifetime

Long-lived connections introduce:

```text
Authentication expiration
Network interruption
Server restart
Load balancer timeout
Client sleep
Deployment
```

Connection lifecycle must explicitly handle these events.

---

# 95. Heartbeats

Heartbeat/ping mechanisms can detect dead connections.

```text
Client ◄── ping/pong ──► Server
```

Timeout values must avoid excessive traffic.

---

# 96. Reconnection

Clients should use bounded reconnection with:

```text
Backoff
Jitter
Maximum delay
State recovery
```

Immediate reconnection loops during outages can overload the platform.

---

# 97. Backpressure

If:

```text
Producer rate
   >
Consumer rate
```

the architecture needs a policy.

Possible responses include:

```text
Buffer
Drop
Aggregate
Throttle
Disconnect
```

Unlimited memory buffering is not acceptable.

---

# 98. Horizontal WebSocket Scaling

Persistent connections complicate scaling.

```text
Client A ─► Pod 1
Client B ─► Pod 2
Client C ─► Pod 3
```

Events may require a shared messaging backbone so the correct connected client can receive them.

---

# 99. Real-Time Backbone

Conceptually:

```text
Domain Event
    │
    ▼
Kafka / Messaging
    │
    ▼
Realtime Service
    │
    ▼
Connected Clients
```

WebSocket servers should not become the authoritative source of domain state.

---

# 100. SSE

Server-Sent Events provide server-to-client streaming over HTTP.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
HTTP Connection
  │
  ◄──── Events ─── Server
```

SSE can be simpler than WebSockets when communication is primarily one-directional.

---

# 101. SSE vs WebSocket

Use SSE when:

```text
Server → client dominates
Browser support fits
Simple event streaming is sufficient
```

Use WebSockets when:

```text
Frequent bidirectional communication is required
```

Do not choose WebSockets merely because "real-time" appears in the requirement.

---

# 102. Webhooks

Webhooks notify external systems.

```text
Mediverse
    │
    ▼
HTTPS POST
    │
    ▼
External Consumer
```

Unlike normal APIs, Mediverse becomes the caller.

---

# 103. Webhook Signing

Webhook payloads should be cryptographically authenticated.

Conceptually:

```text
Payload
 +
Secret/Key
   │
   ▼
Signature
```

The receiver verifies authenticity before processing.

---

# 104. Webhook Replay Protection

Signed payloads alone may still be replayed.

Include appropriate:

```text
Timestamp
Event ID
Signature context
Acceptance window
```

and receiver-side duplicate detection.

---

# 105. Webhook Delivery

Webhook delivery should generally be asynchronous.

```text
Domain Event
    │
    ▼
Webhook Queue
    │
    ▼
Delivery Worker
    │
    ▼
Consumer
```

A slow external webhook endpoint must not block the core business transaction.

---

# 106. Webhook Retries

Transient failures should use:

```text
Bounded retries
Exponential backoff
Jitter
Dead-letter handling
```

Permanent failures must not retry forever.

---

# 107. Webhook Idempotency

Consumers may receive duplicate events.

```text
eventId = evt_123
```

should allow duplicate detection.

Webhook architecture should assume **at-least-once delivery** unless a stronger guarantee is explicitly implemented.

---

# 108. Synchronous Communication

Synchronous calls are appropriate when the caller needs an immediate result.

```text
Service A
    │
    ▼
Service B
    │
    ▼
Response required now
```

But synchronous chains increase temporal coupling.

---

# 109. Long Synchronous Chains

Avoid:

```text
Gateway
  ▼
A
  ▼
B
  ▼
C
  ▼
D
  ▼
E
```

for ordinary user requests when the architecture can avoid it.

Latency and failure probability compound across the chain.

---

# 110. Asynchronous Communication

Use events/messages when immediate completion is unnecessary.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Broker
   │
   ▼
Consumer
```

ADR-052 messaging architecture remains authoritative for delivery semantics.

---

# 111. API vs Event

Use API:

```text
"I need this answer now."
```

Use event:

```text
"This happened; interested consumers may react."
```

Do not model every integration as synchronous REST.

---

# 112. API Composition

A consumer may require data owned by several services.

```text
Client
  │
  ▼
Composition Layer
  │
  ├── User Service
  ├── Course Service
  └── Progress Service
```

Composition should avoid leaking backend topology directly to clients.

---

# 113. Backend-for-Frontend

A BFF may provide client-specific orchestration.

```text
Web
 │
 ▼
Web BFF
 │
 ├── Course
 ├── User
 └── Assessment
```

A mobile BFF may expose a different optimized contract.

---

# 114. BFF Boundary

BFFs may handle:

```text
Aggregation
Client-specific shaping
Session/token handling
Protocol adaptation
```

They should not become the new home of core domain business rules.

---

# 115. Mobile Contracts

Mobile clients may remain deployed for months.

Breaking API changes therefore have longer compatibility implications than web clients that can be updated immediately.

Version/deprecation policy must account for this.

---

# 116. API Versioning

Versioning exists to manage incompatible contract evolution.

The goal is not:

```text
Create v2 every month.
```

The goal is:

```text
Avoid unnecessary breaking changes.
```

---

# 117. URI Versioning

Example:

```text
/api/v1/courses
/api/v2/courses
```

Advantages:

```text
Visible
Simple
Easy to route
```

Disadvantages include URL proliferation.

---

# 118. Header Versioning

Version information can instead be negotiated through headers.

This can keep resource URIs stable but is less visible during debugging and consumer usage.

---

# 119. Media-Type Versioning

Custom media types can encode versions.

This provides sophisticated negotiation but often adds unnecessary complexity for ordinary application APIs.

---

# 120. Mediverse Versioning Strategy

Preferred:

```text
Additive evolution first
        │
        ▼
Avoid version bump
        │
        ▼
Breaking change unavoidable?
        │
        ▼
Introduce explicit major API version
```

URI major versioning is acceptable for externally consumed REST APIs where clarity is valuable.

---

# 121. Breaking Changes

Examples include:

```text
Removing field
Renaming field
Changing type
Changing requiredness
Changing status semantics
Changing enum semantics
Removing endpoint
Changing authorization assumptions
```

A syntactically compatible change can still be behaviorally breaking.

---

# 122. Additive Changes

Usually safer:

```text
New optional field
New endpoint
New optional query parameter
New operation
```

But consumers must tolerate unknown fields where contract conventions require it.

---

# 123. Enum Evolution

Adding a new enum value can break clients that assume exhaustive known values.

Therefore even apparently additive schema changes require consumer-awareness.

---

# 124. Breaking-Change Detection

CI should compare API contracts.

```text
Current OpenAPI
      │
      ▼
Candidate OpenAPI
      │
      ▼
Compatibility Check
      │
      ├── Compatible
      └── Breaking
```

The same principle applies to Protobuf and GraphQL schemas.

---

# 125. Consumer Inventory

Providers should know important consumers.

```text
API
 │
 ├── Web
 ├── Mobile
 ├── Internal Service
 ├── Partner
 └── External Integration
```

Deprecation without knowing consumers is operational gambling.

---

# 126. Deprecation

Deprecation should define:

```text
Deprecated capability
Replacement
Migration guidance
Timeline
Owner
```

"Deprecated" without removal planning is meaningless.

---

# 127. Sunset

A removal lifecycle should resemble:

```text
Announce
  │
  ▼
Deprecate
  │
  ▼
Measure Usage
  │
  ▼
Migrate Consumers
  │
  ▼
Sunset
  │
  ▼
Remove
```

Do not silently remove active APIs.

---

# 128. Contract Testing

Provider/consumer contracts should be validated automatically where useful.

```text
Consumer expectation
       │
       ▼
Contract Test
       │
       ▼
Provider Build
```

This catches compatibility failures before deployment.

---

# 129. API Mocking

Contract-based mocks can enable frontend/mobile development before backend completion.

Mocks must derive from the actual API contract, otherwise they create false confidence.

---

# 130. Generated SDKs

For stable externally consumed APIs, generated clients may reduce repetitive integration work.

```text
OpenAPI / Protobuf
       │
       ▼
Code Generation
       │
       ├── Java
       ├── TypeScript
       └── Other approved clients
```

Generated code still requires lifecycle/version governance.

---

# 131. API Documentation

Documentation should include:

```text
Purpose
Authentication
Endpoints/operations
Schemas
Errors
Examples
Rate limits
Pagination
Versioning
Deprecation
```

A Swagger page alone is not always sufficient developer documentation.

---

# 132. Developer Portal

If Mediverse exposes significant partner/public APIs, a developer portal should eventually provide:

```text
Documentation
Credentials/onboarding
API catalog
Examples
SDKs
Changelog
Deprecation notices
Status
```

Do not build a portal before there is a real external developer ecosystem.

---

# 133. API Security

Every API should be reviewed for:

```text
Authentication
Object authorization
Function authorization
Input validation
Mass assignment
Rate limits
Resource exhaustion
Sensitive-data exposure
Injection
Logging
```

ADR-056 remains authoritative for identity.

---

# 134. Excessive Data Exposure

Do not return entire internal objects and expect the frontend to hide sensitive fields.

Bad:

```text
Database Entity
      │
      ▼
Huge JSON
      │
      ▼
Frontend displays only 3 fields
```

The API should expose only necessary data.

---

# 135. Injection

User-controlled values must never become trusted query/code fragments.

Applies to:

```text
SQL
Search queries
GraphQL resolver backends
Shell commands
Template engines
NoSQL queries
```

Parameterized and constrained interfaces remain mandatory.

---

# 136. API Caching

Caching can reduce latency and backend load.

```text
Client
 │
 ▼
Cache
 │
 ├── HIT
 │
 └── MISS → Origin
```

Only cache responses whose authorization and freshness semantics permit it.

---

# 137. Cache-Control

HTTP caching directives should explicitly describe intended caching behavior.

Sensitive/private responses should not accidentally become shared-cache content.

---

# 138. ETag

ETags enable conditional retrieval.

```text
Client
 │
 ▼
If-None-Match
 │
 ▼
Server
 │
 ├── Changed → 200
 └── Same    → 304
```

This reduces unnecessary payload transfer.

---

# 139. Optimistic Concurrency

ETag/version concepts may also protect updates.

```text
Client reads version 5
       │
       ▼
Update requires version 5
       │
       ▼
Current version 6?
       │
       ▼
Reject conflict
```

This prevents silent lost updates.

---

# 140. CDN

Static/publicly cacheable API responses may benefit from edge caching.

Do not place personalized authenticated content into shared CDN caches without correct cache-key and privacy controls.

---

# 141. Compression

Compression can reduce network transfer for sufficiently large textual payloads.

Trade-offs include:

```text
CPU
Latency
Payload size
Security context
```

Tiny responses do not need aggressive compression.

---

# 142. API Performance Budget

Critical APIs should define targets such as:

```text
p50 latency
p95 latency
p99 latency
Maximum payload size
Dependency budget
Throughput target
Error-rate target
```

"Fast" is not a measurable requirement.

---

# 143. API Ownership

Every production API requires an accountable owner.

```text
API
 │
 ├── Owning team
 ├── Repository
 ├── Documentation
 ├── On-call path
 ├── Contract
 └── Lifecycle status
```

Orphaned APIs become security and operational liabilities.

---

# 144. API Catalog

At sufficient scale, Mediverse should maintain an API catalog containing:

```text
API name
Owner
Domain
Classification
Protocol
Version
Consumers
Authentication
Documentation
Lifecycle state
```

This supports discoverability and governance.

---

# 145. API Lifecycle

```text
Design
  │
  ▼
Review
  │
  ▼
Implement
  │
  ▼
Test
  │
  ▼
Publish
  │
  ▼
Observe
  │
  ▼
Evolve
  │
  ▼
Deprecate
  │
  ▼
Retire
```

APIs require lifecycle management beyond implementation.

---

# 146. API Governance

Governance should enforce minimum standards without creating an architecture committee bottleneck for every endpoint.

Automate:

```text
Schema linting
Compatibility checks
Security checks
Contract tests
Documentation validation
Ownership metadata
```

Use human review for high-impact design decisions.

---

# 147. API Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ POST for every operation
❌ 200 for every outcome
❌ Database entities exposed directly
❌ Business logic in API Gateway
❌ Gateway authentication treated as complete authorization
❌ UUIDs treated as authorization
❌ Unbounded collection endpoints
❌ Unlimited page sizes
❌ Arbitrary SQL-like filtering
❌ Uncontrolled bulk operations
❌ Retryable side effects without idempotency strategy
❌ Infinite/stacked retries
❌ Synchronous calls without timeouts
❌ Internal APIs treated as disposable contracts
❌ OpenAPI documentation drifting from implementation
❌ Breaking API changes without consumer analysis
❌ New major version for trivial additive changes
❌ APIs deprecated forever but never removed
❌ GraphQL introduced merely to replace REST
❌ GraphQL resolver N+1 ignored
❌ Unlimited GraphQL query depth/complexity
❌ GraphQL gateway becoming domain owner
❌ gRPC introduced everywhere because it benchmarks faster
❌ Protobuf field numbers reused
❌ gRPC calls without deadlines
❌ WebSockets used when SSE is sufficient
❌ WebSocket channel name treated as authorization
❌ Infinite reconnect loops
❌ Unlimited real-time buffering
❌ Core transactions blocked on external webhooks
❌ Unsigned webhooks
❌ Webhook duplicates assumed impossible
❌ BFF becoming a giant business-logic service
❌ Entire internal objects returned to clients
❌ Shared caching of sensitive personalized responses
❌ No API owner
❌ No consumer inventory
```

---

# 148. Final Mediverse Enterprise API Reference Architecture

```text
                             CONSUMERS
             ┌──────────────────┼───────────────────┐
             ▼                  ▼                   ▼
            WEB               MOBILE             PARTNER
             │                  │                   │
             └──────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                                ▼
                        CDN / EDGE SECURITY
                                │
                                ▼
                           API GATEWAY
                                │
          ┌─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
          ▼                     ▼                      ▼
        REST                 GraphQL             REAL-TIME
          │                     │                 ┌────┴────┐
          │                     │                 ▼         ▼
          │                     │             WebSocket    SSE
          │                     │
          └─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
                                ▼                      │
                         BFF / COMPOSITION             │
                                │                      │
                                ▼                      │
                         DOMAIN SERVICES ◄─────────────┘
                                │
              ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
              ▼                 ▼                 ▼
             REST              gRPC             EVENTS
              │                 │                 │
              │                 │                 ▼
              │                 │             Kafka/Broker
              │                 │                 │
              │                 │        ┌────────┴────────┐
              │                 │        ▼                 ▼
              │                 │     Workers          Webhooks
              │                 │
              └─────────────────┼────────────────────────────┐
                                ▼                            │
                         DOMAIN / DATA                       │
                                                             │
                                                             ▼
                                                     EXTERNAL SYSTEMS


                         CROSS-CUTTING CONTROL

        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ Authentication / Authorization                     │
        │ Rate Limits / Quotas                               │
        │ Validation                                         │
        │ Idempotency                                        │
        │ Timeouts / Deadlines                               │
        │ Retries / Circuit Breakers                         │
        │ Trace Context                                      │
        │ Logging / Metrics                                  │
        │ OpenAPI / Protobuf / GraphQL Contracts             │
        │ Compatibility                                      │
        │ Security                                           │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


                         GOVERNANCE PLANE

        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ API Catalog                                        │
        │ Ownership                                          │
        │ Contract Registry                                  │
        │ Schema Linting                                     │
        │ Breaking-Change Detection                          │
        │ Consumer Inventory                                 │
        │ Documentation                                      │
        │ Deprecation / Sunset                               │
        │ SLOs                                               │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

# 149. Core API Invariants

Regardless of future frameworks or gateway products:

```text
1. Every API is a contract.

2. Internal APIs are still contracts.

3. REST remains the default conventional API style.

4. Protocol choice follows workload requirements.

5. HTTP semantics are respected.

6. Persistence models do not become external contracts.

7. Inputs are validated at trust boundaries.

8. Domain invariants remain domain responsibilities.

9. Object-level authorization is mandatory.

10. Collections are bounded and paginated.

11. Retryable side effects have idempotency strategy.

12. Every synchronous dependency has a timeout/deadline.

13. Retries are bounded and coordinated.

14. API Gateway does not own domain business logic.

15. GraphQL is introduced only where consumer composition warrants it.

16. GraphQL query cost is controlled.

17. GraphQL authorization remains resource-aware.

18. gRPC contracts evolve compatibly.

19. gRPC calls have deadlines.

20. Real-time connections have authentication,
    authorization and lifecycle controls.

21. Backpressure is explicit.

22. Webhooks are signed, retryable and duplicate-safe.

23. Synchronous chains are kept shallow.

24. Events are preferred when immediate responses are unnecessary.

25. BFFs shape consumer experiences but do not own core domains.

26. API evolution prefers additive compatibility.

27. Breaking changes are automatically detected.

28. Deprecation includes migration and sunset.

29. Important consumers are inventoried.

30. API performance is measured through explicit SLOs.

31. Sensitive responses are not carelessly cached.

32. Every production API has an accountable owner.

33. Contracts, documentation and implementation remain synchronized.

34. API security is continuously tested.

35. API governance is automated wherever practical.
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                                  | Decision                                               |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Primary application API               | **REST/HTTPS**                                         |
| REST design                           | Resource-oriented                                      |
| HTTP semantics                        | Mandatory                                              |
| API entities                          | Explicit DTOs                                          |
| Problem responses                     | Standardized Problem Details                           |
| Validation                            | Boundary + domain                                      |
| Pagination                            | Mandatory for growing collections                      |
| Offset pagination                     | Standard/simple workloads                              |
| Cursor pagination                     | Large/high-change datasets                             |
| Idempotency                           | Required where retries can duplicate effects           |
| OpenAPI                               | Required for REST                                      |
| API Gateway                           | Edge/API-management concerns                           |
| Business logic in gateway             | Rejected                                               |
| GraphQL                               | Selective composition layer                            |
| GraphQL as universal REST replacement | Rejected                                               |
| GraphQL complexity controls           | Required                                               |
| GraphQL federation                    | Only when organizational scale justifies               |
| gRPC                                  | Selective internal communication                       |
| Protobuf compatibility                | Mandatory                                              |
| gRPC deadlines                        | Mandatory                                              |
| WebSockets                            | Bidirectional real-time workloads                      |
| SSE                                   | Preferred for simpler server→client streams            |
| WebSocket auth                        | Connection + resource authorization                    |
| Backpressure                          | Explicit                                               |
| Webhooks                              | Async + signed + retryable                             |
| Webhook delivery                      | At-least-once assumption                               |
| Sync communication                    | Immediate-result workflows                             |
| Async communication                   | Decoupled/background workflows                         |
| BFF                                   | Client-specific composition                            |
| API evolution                         | Additive first                                         |
| Major versions                        | Breaking changes only                                  |
| Contract compatibility checks         | CI-enforced                                            |
| Consumer inventory                    | Required for significant APIs                          |
| Deprecation                           | Defined migration + sunset                             |
| Contract testing                      | Required where consumer/provider independence warrants |
| Generated SDKs                        | Selective                                              |
| API catalog                           | Required at sufficient scale                           |
| Caching                               | Explicit + authorization-aware                         |
| ETag                                  | Supported                                              |
| API performance budgets               | Required for critical APIs                             |
| API ownership                         | Mandatory                                              |
| Status                                | **Accepted**                                           |
| Priority                              | **Critical**                                           |
