## Next — ADR-058

### **ADR-058 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, React Platform, Micro-Frontends, State Management, Design System, Web Performance & Frontend Security**

The backend and communication architecture is now extensive, but the React side needs the same architectural discipline.

ADR-058 should establish **React application topology → Vite/build architecture → TypeScript → feature/domain-based structure → routing → layouts → component boundaries → container/presentation patterns → server vs client state → TanStack Query evaluation → Redux Toolkit boundaries → Context → local state → normalized state → forms → React Hook Form → schema validation → API client → generated OpenAPI clients → Axios/fetch decision → authentication integration → BFF/token strategy → protected routes vs real authorization → error boundaries → Suspense → lazy loading → code splitting → bundle budgets → caching → optimistic updates → offline behavior → WebSocket/SSE integration → accessibility/WCAG → responsive/mobile-first design → design tokens → component library → Storybook → MUI/Tailwind boundary → theming → dark mode → internationalization → localization → date/time → frontend observability → Web Vitals → RUM → error monitoring → source maps → CSP → XSS → DOM sanitization → dependency security → supply-chain controls → frontend secrets → environment configuration → feature flags → experimentation → testing pyramid → Vitest → React Testing Library → MSW → Playwright → visual regression → contract testing → frontend CI/CD → static asset/CDN architecture → cache busting → deployment → rollback → micro-frontends decision framework → module federation → team ownership → frontend governance → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise frontend reference architecture.**



# ADR-058 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, React Platform, State Management, Design System, Web Performance & Frontend Security

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-058
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-057 established the communication contracts connecting Mediverse clients, APIs and services.

ADR-058 establishes how the **Mediverse web platform is structured, developed, secured, tested, optimized, deployed and evolved as a production React application**.

The governing principle is:

> **The frontend is an application architecture, not a collection of pages and components. Domain boundaries, state ownership, API contracts, security, accessibility, performance and operational visibility must be deliberately engineered.**

```text
                              USER
                               │
                               ▼
                         BROWSER / PWA
                               │
                               ▼
                      MEDIVERSE REACT APP
                               │
       ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
       ▼                       ▼                       ▼
    ROUTING                  FEATURES              PLATFORM
       │                       │                       │
       │              ┌────────┼────────┐              │
       │              ▼        ▼        ▼              │
       │           Course   Learning  Assessment       │
       │                                               │
       └───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┘
                               ▼
                         STATE LAYER
                               │
             ┌─────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             ▼                 ▼                  ▼
          LOCAL UI         SERVER STATE       GLOBAL STATE
             │                 │                  │
             ▼                 ▼                  ▼
           React          Query/Cache        Redux/Context
                               │
                               ▼
                         API CLIENT
                               │
                               ▼
                      BFF / API GATEWAY
                               │
                               ▼
                         MEDIVERSE APIs

                     CROSS-CUTTING PLANE

        Design System │ Security │ Accessibility
        Observability │ Testing  │ Performance
        i18n           │ Flags    │ Configuration
```

# 1. Frontend Is a Platform

Mediverse should not evolve into:

```text
src/
├── components/
│   ├── 700 unrelated components
├── pages/
├── utils/
└── api/
```

with every feature importing everything else.

The frontend requires explicit architectural boundaries.

# 2. Technology Baseline

The preferred web baseline is:

```text
React
TypeScript
Vite
React Router
TanStack Query where justified
Redux Toolkit where justified
React Hook Form
Schema validation
MUI / governed design system
Playwright
Vitest
React Testing Library
```

Individual libraries remain replaceable implementation decisions.

# 3. TypeScript

Production frontend code should use TypeScript.

```text
API Contract
     │
     ▼
Type Definitions
     │
     ▼
Application
     │
     ▼
Components
```

TypeScript reduces classes of integration and refactoring errors but does not replace runtime validation.

# 4. Strict TypeScript

Prefer strict compiler settings.

Conceptually:

```text
strict: true
noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true
```

where practical.

Avoid turning the application into:

```typescript
const response: any = ...
```

because that removes most of TypeScript's architectural value.

# 5. Vite

Vite should remain the default React build/development platform unless future requirements justify replacement.

It provides:

```text
Fast development startup
Modern module handling
Production bundling
Environment configuration
Plugin ecosystem
```

Build tooling should not become application architecture.

# 6. Domain-Oriented Structure

Prefer organization around business capabilities.

```text
src/
├── app/
├── features/
│   ├── auth/
│   ├── courses/
│   ├── assessments/
│   ├── learning/
│   ├── profile/
│   └── administration/
├── shared/
├── design-system/
└── infrastructure/
```

This scales better than organizing the entire application only by technical file type.

# 7. Feature Boundary

A feature may own:

```text
features/courses/
├── api/
├── components/
├── hooks/
├── pages/
├── schemas/
├── state/
├── types/
└── utils/
```

Feature-internal code should remain internal unless deliberately exported.

# 8. Public Feature API

Features should expose controlled entry points.

```text
courses/
   │
   ├── internal components
   ├── internal hooks
   └── index.ts
         │
         ▼
      Public API
```

This prevents arbitrary deep imports.

# 9. Dependency Direction

Preferred:

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Features
    │
    ▼
Shared Platform
    │
    ▼
Infrastructure
```

Avoid circular dependencies between unrelated domains.

# 10. Shared Folder Discipline

`shared/` must not become:

```text
shared/
└── everything-we-did-not-know-where-to-put/
```

Shared code should be genuinely domain-neutral and reused.

# 11. Component Architecture

Components should have focused responsibilities.

```text
Page
 │
 ├── Feature Components
 │      ├── Domain behavior
 │      └── Composition
 │
 └── UI Components
        └── Presentation
```

Do not force every component into an artificial "smart/dumb" classification, but preserve separation where it improves maintainability.

# 12. Page Components

Pages should primarily coordinate:

```text
Route parameters
Feature composition
Page-level loading/error state
Navigation
```

They should not contain thousands of lines of unrelated domain logic.

# 13. Component Size

There is no meaningful enterprise rule such as:

```text
Component must be < 100 lines
```

Complexity and responsibility matter more than raw line count.

Extract components when boundaries become clearer—not merely to satisfy arbitrary metrics.

# 14. Hooks

Custom hooks should encapsulate reusable React behavior.

```typescript
useCourse()
useAssessmentAttempt()
useCurrentUser()
```

Hooks should not become hidden global service locators.

# 15. Routing

Routing should be centrally understandable while allowing feature ownership.

Conceptually:

```text
/
├── /login
├── /dashboard
├── /courses
│    └── /:courseId
├── /assessments
└── /admin
```

URLs are part of the user-facing application contract.

# 16. Nested Routes

Nested routes should reflect meaningful UI hierarchy.

```text
/courses/:courseId
       │
       ├── overview
       ├── chapters
       └── assessments
```

Do not create route nesting simply because component nesting exists.

# 17. Route-Level Lazy Loading

Large features should be loaded on demand.

```text
User visits /admin
       │
       ▼
Load Admin Bundle
```

Users who never access administration should not necessarily download its entire codebase.

# 18. Protected Routes

Frontend route guards improve UX.

```text
Route
 │
 ▼
Authenticated?
 │
 ├── Yes → Render
 └── No  → Login
```

But:

> **Protected React routes are not authorization controls.**

ADR-056 server-side authorization remains mandatory.

# 19. Role-Based UI

The UI may hide operations the user cannot perform.

```text
Student
   X
"Delete Course" button
```

This prevents confusing UX.

It does **not** secure the backend endpoint.

# 20. Layout Architecture

Common layouts should be explicit.

```text
Root Layout
 │
 ├── Public Layout
 ├── Student Layout
 ├── Instructor Layout
 └── Admin Layout
```

Avoid duplicating navigation and shell logic across pages.

# 21. State Classification

Before choosing a state library, classify the state.

```text
State
 │
 ├── Local UI State
 ├── Form State
 ├── URL State
 ├── Server State
 └── Global Client State
```

Treating all five identically creates unnecessary complexity.

# 22. Local State

Use React local state for local UI concerns.

Examples:

```text
Modal open/closed
Selected tab
Temporary toggle
Expanded section
```

Do not put every boolean into Redux.

# 23. URL State

State affecting navigation/shareability often belongs in the URL.

Examples:

```text
Search query
Filters
Sort
Pagination
Selected section
```

```text
/courses?page=2&level=advanced
```

This improves refresh, bookmarking and navigation behavior.

# 24. Server State

Server state includes:

```text
Courses
User profile
Assessments
Notifications
Progress
```

It has characteristics such as:

```text
Remote ownership
Caching
Staleness
Refetching
Synchronization
```

Server state should not automatically be copied into global client stores.

# 25. TanStack Query

TanStack Query should be preferred for suitable REST/server-state management.

```text
Component
   │
   ▼
Query
   │
   ▼
Cache
   │
   ▼
API
```

It can manage:

```text
Caching
Deduplication
Refetching
Mutation lifecycle
Invalidation
Retries
Loading/error state
```

# 26. Query Keys

Query keys form part of cache architecture.

Example:

```typescript
['course', courseId]
['courses', filters]
['assessment', assessmentId]
```

Keys should be deterministic and centrally understandable.

# 27. Cache Staleness

Not all data has identical freshness requirements.

```text
Reference data
→ relatively stable

Notifications
→ rapidly changing
```

Configure freshness based on actual domain semantics.

# 28. Cache Invalidation

The hard question is not:

```text
Can we cache this?
```

but:

```text
When does it become invalid?
```

Mutation flows must deliberately invalidate/update affected queries.

# 29. Optimistic Updates

For appropriate low-risk interactions:

```text
User Action
    │
    ▼
Update UI Immediately
    │
    ▼
Send Mutation
    │
    ├── Success → Keep
    └── Failure → Roll Back
```

Optimistic UI should not imply an authoritative action succeeded before the backend confirms it.

# 30. Redux Toolkit

Redux Toolkit should be introduced for genuinely global complex client state.

Potential examples:

```text
Complex editor state
Cross-feature workflow state
Rich client-side coordination
```

Not:

```text
All API responses
Every input
Every modal
Every loading flag
```

# 31. Redux Boundary

Preferred:

```text
Server State
→ TanStack Query

Complex Global Client State
→ Redux Toolkit

Local State
→ React

Form State
→ Form library

Navigation State
→ URL
```

This prevents one state mechanism from swallowing the entire application.

# 32. Context

React Context is suitable for relatively stable cross-tree concerns such as:

```text
Theme
Localization
Feature context
Small scoped configuration
```

Context is not automatically a replacement for a state-management architecture.

# 33. Context Performance

A frequently changing large Context can cause broad rerenders.

Avoid:

```text
<AppContext value={everythingInTheApplication}>
```

Use focused contexts where appropriate.

# 34. Derived State

Do not store values that can be reliably derived.

Bad:

```text
firstName
lastName
fullName
```

if `fullName` is always:

```text
firstName + lastName
```

Duplicated state creates synchronization bugs.

# 35. State Normalization

Complex relational client state may benefit from normalized structures.

```text
entities:
  courses:
    123 → Course
    456 → Course
```

But server-state libraries may already solve enough caching concerns that manual normalization is unnecessary.

# 36. Forms

Forms require dedicated architecture because they combine:

```text
Input state
Validation
Accessibility
Submission
Errors
Dirty state
Server errors
```

# 37. React Hook Form

React Hook Form should be preferred for substantial forms where its model fits.

It reduces unnecessary rerenders and provides structured form lifecycle handling.

# 38. Schema Validation

Client validation schemas should define runtime expectations.

Potential approach:

```text
Form
 │
 ▼
Schema
 │
 ▼
Validated DTO
 │
 ▼
API Client
```

Server validation remains authoritative.

# 39. Client Validation Is UX

This is rejected:

```text
Frontend validated it
       │
       ▼
Backend can trust it
```

Attackers can call APIs directly.

Client validation improves UX; server validation provides trust-boundary enforcement.

# 40. Server Validation Errors

Backend validation responses should map cleanly to fields.

```text
API Error
   │
   ▼
email → already registered
```

Do not force forms to parse arbitrary strings.

# 41. API Client Layer

Components should not scatter low-level HTTP calls everywhere.

Bad:

```text
CourseCard.tsx → axios.get(...)
Navbar.tsx     → axios.get(...)
Dashboard.tsx  → axios.get(...)
```

Preferred:

```text
Components
    │
    ▼
Feature API Layer
    │
    ▼
Shared HTTP Client
    │
    ▼
Gateway/BFF
```

# 42. Generated API Clients

Where OpenAPI contracts are stable, generated TypeScript clients should be evaluated.

```text
OpenAPI
   │
   ▼
Generate
   │
   ▼
Typed API Client
```

This reduces contract duplication.

Generated clients should be wrapped where application-specific behavior requires it.

# 43. Fetch vs Axios

Either can support Mediverse.

Selection should be based on required capabilities rather than habit.

Modern `fetch` provides a strong native baseline.

Axios may still be useful where its abstraction provides measurable value.

The architecture should not depend heavily on library-specific behavior.

# 44. HTTP Client Responsibilities

A shared client may handle:

```text
Base URL
Credentials
Standard headers
Correlation context
Error normalization
Timeout/abort behavior
```

It should not hide arbitrary business behavior.

# 45. Authentication Integration

Authentication should follow ADR-056.

Conceptually:

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
IdP / BFF
   │
   ▼
Authenticated Session
   │
   ▼
Frontend
```

Do not build a second authentication system inside React.

# 46. BFF Strategy

For security-sensitive browser architecture:

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
HttpOnly Session Cookie
   │
   ▼
BFF
   │
   ▼
OAuth Tokens
   │
   ▼
APIs
```

should be evaluated.

This reduces direct exposure of OAuth tokens to JavaScript.

# 47. Token Storage

Avoid defaulting to:

```javascript
localStorage.setItem("accessToken", token)
```

for long-lived sensitive credentials merely because tutorials do it.

Browser token strategy must follow the actual threat model.

# 48. Frontend Secrets

There are no meaningful long-term secrets in browser JavaScript.

Anything shipped to the browser can be inspected.

Therefore:

```text
VITE_SECRET_API_KEY
```

is not secret merely because it came from an environment variable.

# 49. Environment Configuration

Frontend configuration should contain public runtime/build configuration only.

Examples:

```text
API base URL
Public feature configuration
Telemetry endpoint
Environment identifier
```

Credentials belong server-side.

# 50. Error Boundaries

React error boundaries should isolate rendering failures.

```text
Feature
  │
  X
Rendering Error
  │
  ▼
Fallback UI
```

A single broken widget should not necessarily destroy the entire application shell.

# 51. Error Boundary Placement

Potential levels:

```text
Application
Page
High-risk feature
```

Too few boundaries increase blast radius.

Too many make behavior fragmented.

# 52. User Error Experience

Do not show users:

```text
TypeError:
Cannot read properties of undefined
at CourseCard.jsx:157
```

Provide meaningful recovery UI while sending technical diagnostics to observability systems.

# 53. Loading Architecture

Loading states should distinguish:

```text
Initial loading
Background refetch
Mutation pending
Streaming
Lazy bundle loading
```

One global spinner for every network interaction produces poor UX.

# 54. Suspense

React Suspense may be used where supported by the selected data/router architecture.

It should simplify loading composition rather than be introduced purely because it is a newer React feature.

# 55. Code Splitting

Large features should be split into independently loadable bundles.

```text
Core Application
      │
      ├── Student Bundle
      ├── Admin Bundle
      ├── 3D Module
      └── Analytics Bundle
```

The Mediverse 3D learning capability is an obvious candidate because its dependencies may be large.

# 56. Bundle Analysis

Production builds should be analyzed periodically.

Look for:

```text
Duplicate libraries
Unexpected large dependencies
Unused modules
Large media
Multiple library versions
```

Bundle growth is otherwise gradual and invisible.

# 57. Bundle Budget

Define measurable limits.

Example architecture:

```text
Initial JS
Critical CSS
Largest feature chunk
Third-party JS
```

should each have budgets.

The exact numbers should be established from performance testing rather than invented globally.

# 58. Lazy Loading

Lazy-load expensive functionality that is not required for initial interaction.

Candidates:

```text
3D viewers
Charts
Rich editors
Admin tools
Large media experiences
```

Do not lazy-load tiny critical components merely to maximize chunk count.

# 59. Prefetching

Likely next-navigation resources may be prefetched selectively.

```text
Current Course
     │
     ▼
Likely Next Chapter
     │
     ▼
Prefetch
```

Aggressive prefetching wastes bandwidth, especially on mobile networks.

# 60. Performance Is an Architecture Requirement

Frontend performance should be treated like backend latency.

```text
User Action
    │
    ▼
Browser Work
    │
    ▼
Network
    │
    ▼
API
    │
    ▼
Rendering
    │
    ▼
Visible Response
```

Optimizing only API latency ignores much of the actual user experience.

---

## ADR-058 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The first frontend architecture layer establishes:

```text
                         REACT APPLICATION
                                │
             ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             ▼                  ▼                  ▼
           ROUTES            FEATURES          PLATFORM
                                │
             ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             ▼                  ▼                  ▼
          LOCAL STATE      SERVER STATE      GLOBAL STATE
             │                  │                  │
           React           TanStack Query      Redux
             │                  │                  │
             └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                ▼
                           API LAYER
                                │
                                ▼
                           BFF/GATEWAY
                                │
                                ▼
                           BACKEND APIs
```

The first 60 sections establish several non-negotiable rules:

```text
1. Frontend architecture follows domain boundaries.

2. TypeScript is the production baseline.

3. Features expose controlled public interfaces.

4. shared/ does not become a dumping ground.

5. React routes are UX controls, not authorization boundaries.

6. State is classified before selecting a library.

7. Server state does not automatically belong in Redux.

8. URL state belongs in the URL where navigation semantics require it.

9. TanStack Query is preferred for appropriate server state.

10. Redux Toolkit is reserved for genuinely complex global client state.

11. Client validation improves UX; backend validation remains authoritative.

12. Components do not scatter HTTP calls throughout the application.

13. OpenAPI-generated clients should be evaluated.

14. Authentication architecture follows ADR-056.

15. Long-lived sensitive browser credentials are not casually stored
    in localStorage.

16. Frontend environment variables are not secret.

17. Rendering failures are isolated with error boundaries.

18. Large capabilities use deliberate code splitting.

19. Bundle size has measurable budgets.

20. Frontend performance is an architectural requirement,
    not post-release cleanup.
```

**Part 2** should continue from **Section 61 — Core Web Vitals & Performance Architecture**, covering **LCP → INP → CLS → RUM → performance budgets → rendering performance → memoization boundaries → virtualization → image/media optimization → 3D/WebGL performance → worker threads → caching → service workers/PWA → offline behavior → optimistic/offline mutations → WebSocket/SSE frontend integration → reconnect/state synchronization → accessibility/WCAG → keyboard navigation → screen readers → semantic HTML → focus management → accessible forms → responsive/mobile-first design → design tokens → component library → Storybook → MUI/Tailwind boundary → theming → dark mode → internationalization → localization → pluralization → RTL → dates/time zones → frontend observability → error monitoring → source maps → correlation IDs → analytics/privacy → CSP → XSS → DOM sanitization → Trusted Types evaluation → CSRF → clickjacking → dependency/supply-chain security → npm lockfiles → vulnerability scanning → third-party scripts → feature flags → experimentation → testing pyramid → Vitest → React Testing Library → MSW → Playwright → visual regression → accessibility testing → contract testing → frontend CI/CD → artifact immutability → CDN/static assets → hashed filenames → cache busting → rollback → micro-frontends decision framework → Module Federation → independent deployment trade-offs → shared dependencies → team ownership → frontend governance → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise frontend reference architecture.**


# ADR-058 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, React Platform, State Management, Design System, Web Performance & Frontend Security

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Performance Is an Architecture Requirement**.

---

# 61. Core Web Vitals

Mediverse should measure real user experience using Core Web Vitals and supporting frontend telemetry.

The primary dimensions are:

```text
LCP
→ Loading experience

INP
→ Interaction responsiveness

CLS
→ Visual stability
```

Synthetic tests alone are insufficient.

---

# 62. Largest Contentful Paint

LCP measures how quickly important visible content becomes available.

Typical contributors:

```text
Slow server response
Render-blocking resources
Large images
Large JavaScript bundles
Client-only data waterfalls
Fonts
```

Optimize the actual critical rendering path rather than chasing a score blindly.

---

# 63. Interaction to Next Paint

INP measures responsiveness to user interaction.

Poor INP may result from:

```text
Long JavaScript tasks
Heavy React rendering
Large DOM
Complex event handlers
Main-thread computation
Third-party scripts
```

---

# 64. Cumulative Layout Shift

Unexpected layout movement damages usability.

```text
Before:

[ Course title ]

After image loads:

[ IMAGE        ]
[ Course title ]
```

Reserve dimensions for images, video, 3D canvases and dynamically loaded content.

---

# 65. Real User Monitoring

Production performance should be measured from actual sessions.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Performance Events
   │
   ▼
RUM
   │
   ▼
Metrics / Dashboards
```

RUM reveals device/network conditions that laboratory tests cannot fully reproduce.

---

# 66. Performance Budgets

Budgets should cover more than bundle size.

```text
JavaScript transfer
CSS
Images
Fonts
Third-party scripts
LCP
INP
CLS
API latency
```

CI should detect meaningful regressions.

---

# 67. Rendering Performance

Do not assume React rerenders are inherently problematic.

Optimize when measurement demonstrates meaningful cost.

```text
Measure
  │
  ▼
Identify bottleneck
  │
  ▼
Optimize
```

not:

```text
Memoize everything
```

---

# 68. Memoization

`memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` should be used deliberately.

They introduce their own complexity and runtime bookkeeping.

Use them when:

```text
Expensive computation exists
Referential stability matters
Measured rerender cost exists
```

---

# 69. Large Lists

Rendering thousands of DOM nodes simultaneously can degrade performance.

```text
10,000 records
     │
     ▼
Virtualized Window
     │
     ▼
Only visible rows rendered
```

Virtualization should be considered for genuinely large interactive collections.

---

# 70. Image Optimization

Educational imagery may become a major bandwidth cost.

Use:

```text
Appropriate dimensions
Responsive images
Modern formats
Lazy loading
Compression
CDN delivery
```

Do not ship a 5000×5000 anatomical image into a 300-pixel card.

---

# 71. Responsive Images

Browsers should receive appropriately sized assets.

Conceptually:

```html
<img
  srcset="small ... medium ... large ..."
  sizes="..."
>
```

This matters especially for mobile learners.

---

# 72. Video Architecture

Video should normally use specialized delivery rather than application-server file streaming.

```text
Source Video
    │
    ▼
Transcoding
    │
    ▼
Adaptive Streaming
    │
    ▼
CDN
    │
    ▼
Browser
```

Large media belongs in the media architecture established by earlier ADRs.

---

# 73. 3D Module Performance

Mediverse's 3D learning experiences require separate performance budgets.

```text
3D Scene
  │
  ├── Geometry
  ├── Textures
  ├── Materials
  ├── Lighting
  ├── Animation
  └── Physics
```

A visually impressive scene that destroys mobile performance is a failed educational feature.

---

# 74. 3D Asset Optimization

3D assets should be optimized using techniques appropriate to the rendering stack:

```text
Geometry simplification
Texture compression
LOD
Asset streaming
Instancing
Lazy loading
Efficient materials
```

Raw production-model assets should not automatically ship to browsers.

---

# 75. Level of Detail

Different model complexity may be used depending on distance or context.

```text
Far
→ Low detail

Medium
→ Medium detail

Close
→ High detail
```

LOD can substantially reduce GPU load.

---

# 76. WebGL Capability Detection

Do not assume every learner has a powerful GPU.

```text
Device Capability
       │
       ▼
Can support experience?
       │
   ┌───┴───┐
   ▼       ▼
  Yes      No
   │       │
   ▼       ▼
Full 3D   Reduced/Fallback Experience
```

Education must remain accessible when high-end rendering is unavailable.

---

# 77. Progressive 3D Enhancement

Core learning content should not become inaccessible solely because WebGL fails.

```text
Core Educational Content
        │
        ▼
Enhanced 3D Experience
```

3D should enhance learning rather than become an unnecessary availability dependency.

---

# 78. Web Workers

CPU-intensive browser operations may be moved away from the main thread.

```text
UI Thread
   │
   ▼
Worker
   │
   ▼
Heavy computation
```

Candidates may include parsing, transformation or computational workloads.

Workers do not directly manipulate the DOM.

---

# 79. Main Thread Budget

The browser main thread must remain responsive.

Avoid:

```text
Huge synchronous JSON processing
Expensive loops
Large DOM mutations
Heavy 3D calculations
Blocking third-party scripts
```

during critical interaction.

---

# 80. Browser Caching

Static assets should use effective caching.

```text
Hashed Asset
app.a81f3.js
     │
     ▼
Long Cache Lifetime
```

Content hashes permit aggressive immutable caching.

---

# 81. Service Workers

Service workers may enable:

```text
Offline caching
Background capabilities
Network interception
PWA behavior
```

They also introduce cache invalidation and deployment complexity.

Use them only with an explicit offline/PWA requirement.

---

# 82. PWA Decision

Mediverse may benefit from PWA capabilities where learners face inconsistent connectivity.

Potential value:

```text
Installability
Offline reading
Cached learning content
Reduced repeat bandwidth
```

But a PWA is not automatically required merely because Mediverse is a web application.

---

# 83. Offline Architecture

Offline support must define exactly what remains functional.

```text
Offline
 │
 ├── Previously downloaded chapter → YES
 ├── Cached images → MAYBE
 ├── New assessment submission → QUEUE?
 └── Live collaboration → NO
```

"Works offline" is too vague to implement.

---

# 84. Offline Mutations

Queuing state-changing operations offline introduces conflict problems.

```text
Offline Client
      │
      ▼
Mutation
      │
      ▼
Queue
      │
      ▼
Reconnect
      │
      ▼
Server state changed meanwhile?
```

Only workflows with clear reconciliation semantics should support this.

---

# 85. Realtime Frontend Integration

ADR-057 established WebSocket/SSE architecture.

Frontend real-time data should flow through a controlled abstraction.

```text
WebSocket / SSE
      │
      ▼
Realtime Client
      │
      ▼
Domain Event Handler
      │
      ▼
Query Cache / State
      │
      ▼
Components
```

Do not open unrelated socket connections from random components.

---

# 86. Realtime Cache Synchronization

Incoming events may:

```text
Invalidate query
Update cached entity
Append notification
Trigger refetch
```

The strategy depends on domain semantics.

---

# 87. Reconnection State

After reconnection:

```text
Connection Lost
      │
      ▼
Events missed
      │
      ▼
Reconnect
      │
      ▼
Resynchronize authoritative state
```

Do not assume no events occurred during disconnection.

---

# 88. Accessibility

Accessibility is a product requirement, not optional polish.

Mediverse should target an appropriate **WCAG 2.x AA-level** standard for applicable experiences.

---

# 89. Semantic HTML

Prefer native semantic elements.

```html
<button>
<nav>
<main>
<form>
<label>
```

over rebuilding basic semantics from generic `<div>` elements.

Native semantics provide accessibility behavior for free.

---

# 90. Keyboard Navigation

All critical functionality should be operable without a mouse.

Test:

```text
Tab
Shift+Tab
Enter
Space
Escape
Arrow navigation where appropriate
```

---

# 91. Focus Management

Dynamic interfaces must manage focus deliberately.

Examples:

```text
Modal opens
→ Focus moves appropriately

Modal closes
→ Focus returns appropriately

Route changes
→ Page context remains understandable
```

---

# 92. Screen Readers

Interactive controls need meaningful accessible names and relationships.

Do not create:

```html
<div onclick="...">X</div>
```

when a semantic button is appropriate.

---

# 93. ARIA

ARIA should supplement semantic HTML.

Rule:

> Prefer native semantics before adding ARIA.

Incorrect ARIA can make accessibility worse.

---

# 94. Accessible Forms

Forms require:

```text
Labels
Instructions
Error association
Keyboard operation
Focus handling
Required-state communication
```

Color alone must not communicate errors.

---

# 95. Color Contrast

Text and interactive elements should meet required contrast targets.

The design system should encode accessible combinations instead of forcing every developer to calculate them independently.

---

# 96. Reduced Motion

Users may request reduced motion.

```text
prefers-reduced-motion
```

should influence animations where appropriate.

This is particularly relevant to immersive 3D experiences.

---

# 97. Accessibility Testing

Use multiple layers:

```text
Static rules
Automated accessibility tests
Component tests
Browser tests
Manual keyboard testing
Screen-reader validation for critical workflows
```

Automated tools cannot prove full accessibility.

---

# 98. Responsive Architecture

Mediverse should be mobile-first.

```text
Mobile
  │
  ▼
Tablet
  │
  ▼
Desktop
  │
  ▼
Large Display
```

Do not build desktop first and then hide half the interface on phones.

---

# 99. Breakpoints

Breakpoints should follow layout requirements rather than specific device brands.

```text
Content no longer fits
      │
      ▼
Layout changes
```

This is more durable than designing for individual phone models.

---

# 100. Touch Interaction

Interactive targets should be practical for touch input.

Hover-only functionality is unacceptable for essential workflows.

---

# 101. Design System

Mediverse should establish a governed design system.

```text
Design Tokens
      │
      ▼
Primitives
      │
      ▼
Components
      │
      ▼
Patterns
      │
      ▼
Product Features
```

This provides consistency without duplicating UI logic.

---

# 102. Design Tokens

Tokens should represent foundational decisions.

```text
Typography
Spacing
Radius
Elevation
Color
Motion
Breakpoints
```

Feature code should avoid arbitrary repeated values where tokens exist.

---

# 103. Semantic Tokens

Prefer semantic meaning:

```text
color.text.primary
color.surface.error
color.action.primary
```

over application-wide dependencies on raw values such as:

```text
#1976d2
```

Semantic tokens make themes and redesigns easier.

---

# 104. Component Library

Reusable components may include:

```text
Button
Input
Select
Dialog
Card
Table
Tabs
Tooltip
Navigation
Feedback
```

But do not build custom versions of mature primitives merely to claim Mediverse has its own design system.

---

# 105. MUI Boundary

MUI may provide the foundational component layer.

```text
MUI
 │
 ▼
Mediverse Design Components
 │
 ▼
Features
```

Feature code should preferably consume Mediverse-governed abstractions for highly standardized components.

---

# 106. Tailwind Boundary

If Tailwind is retained, its role must be explicit.

A reasonable boundary is:

```text
Tailwind
→ Layout / utility styling

MUI / Design System
→ Complex interactive components
```

Using MUI, Tailwind and arbitrary CSS simultaneously without rules creates visual and maintenance inconsistency.

---

# 107. Styling Governance

Reject:

```text
MUI sx
+
Tailwind
+
CSS Modules
+
Styled Components
+
inline style
+
global CSS
```

all used randomly for identical concerns.

Select a small, documented styling strategy.

---

# 108. Storybook

Storybook should be considered for isolated development and documentation of reusable design-system components.

```text
Component
   │
   ├── Variants
   ├── States
   ├── Accessibility
   └── Documentation
```

It becomes especially valuable as component ownership grows.

---

# 109. Theming

Theme configuration should centrally control:

```text
Colors
Typography
Spacing
Component defaults
Motion
```

Features should not implement independent theme systems.

---

# 110. Dark Mode

Dark mode should be token-driven.

```text
Semantic Token
     │
     ├── Light Theme
     └── Dark Theme
```

Do not implement dark mode as hundreds of conditional component styles.

---

# 111. Internationalization

User-visible strings should be externalizable where multilingual support is required.

```text
Component
   │
   ▼
Translation Key
   │
   ▼
Locale Resource
```

Avoid hardcoding user-facing text throughout components.

---

# 112. Translation Is More Than String Replacement

Languages differ in:

```text
Word length
Grammar
Pluralization
Ordering
Gender
Number formatting
Date formatting
Direction
```

UI layouts must tolerate these differences.

---

# 113. Pluralization

Do not construct translated phrases using naive concatenation.

```text
count + " students"
```

Localization frameworks should handle plural rules.

---

# 114. RTL

If right-to-left languages become supported:

```text
LTR
◄────────────►
RTL
◄────────────►
```

layout, icons, navigation and spacing must be evaluated.

Logical CSS properties can reduce hardcoded directional assumptions.

---

# 115. Date and Time

Store/communicate timestamps using unambiguous formats.

Presentation should consider:

```text
User locale
User timezone
Course timezone
Event timezone
```

Never assume the browser's timezone represents the business timezone for every workflow.

---

# 116. Frontend Observability

Production frontend telemetry should cover:

```text
JavaScript errors
Unhandled promise rejections
API failures
Web Vitals
Route performance
Resource failures
Release version
Device/browser context
```

while respecting privacy constraints.

---

# 117. Error Monitoring

Errors should include enough context to diagnose failures:

```text
Release
Route
Error
Stack
Correlation ID
Relevant feature
```

Avoid capturing unnecessary sensitive data.

---

# 118. Source Maps

Production source maps are valuable for debugging minified errors.

They should be managed so diagnostic systems can use them without unnecessarily exposing source internals publicly.

---

# 119. Correlation IDs

Frontend error reports should include backend correlation/trace identifiers where available.

```text
Browser Error
     │
     ▼
Request ID
     │
     ▼
Gateway
     │
     ▼
Backend Trace
```

This connects user-visible failures with distributed-system diagnostics.

---

# 120. Analytics

Product analytics should answer defined questions.

Examples:

```text
Course completion
Feature adoption
Navigation friction
Assessment abandonment
```

Do not collect every possible interaction merely because analytics tooling permits it.

---

# 121. Privacy-Aware Telemetry

Telemetry must avoid accidental capture of:

```text
Passwords
Tokens
Sensitive form fields
Private learning content
Personal data beyond approved purpose
```

Logging every Redux state transition to production analytics would be reckless.

---

# 122. Content Security Policy

CSP should restrict where executable/browser resources can originate.

Conceptually:

```text
script-src
style-src
img-src
connect-src
frame-src
```

CSP provides defense in depth against classes of content injection.

---

# 123. XSS

Cross-site scripting remains a critical browser threat.

React escapes ordinary rendered strings by default, but unsafe APIs can bypass that protection.

---

# 124. Dangerous HTML

Use of:

```text
dangerouslySetInnerHTML
```

requires explicit justification.

Untrusted HTML must be sanitized using a proven sanitization approach.

Do not write a custom regex HTML sanitizer.

---

# 125. Rich Educational Content

Mediverse may render rich medical content.

The trust boundary should be:

```text
Content Source
     │
     ▼
Validation / Sanitization
     │
     ▼
Approved Renderer
     │
     ▼
Browser
```

CMS/editor content should not automatically be considered safe HTML.

---

# 126. Trusted Types

Trusted Types should be evaluated for high-security browser deployments where the application/browser support model makes it practical.

It can strengthen DOM-XSS defenses but does not replace secure coding.

---

# 127. CSRF

If Mediverse uses cookie-based authentication:

```text
Browser Cookie
     │
     ▼
State-changing API
```

CSRF protections from ADR-056/057 remain required.

Frontend and backend architecture must agree on the mechanism.

---

# 128. Clickjacking

Sensitive Mediverse interfaces should control whether they can be embedded by external sites.

Use appropriate browser security headers/policies.

Do not rely on JavaScript frame-busting hacks.

---

# 129. Dependency Security

The frontend dependency tree is a supply-chain boundary.

```text
Application
   │
   ▼
Direct Dependencies
   │
   ▼
Transitive Dependencies
```

One compromised package can affect the shipped browser application.

---

# 130. Lockfiles

Package lockfiles should be committed and respected by CI.

```text
package.json
     +
lockfile
     │
     ▼
Reproducible Dependency Graph
```

Uncontrolled dependency resolution damages reproducibility.

---

# 131. Dependency Updates

Dependencies should be updated deliberately.

Avoid both extremes:

```text
Never update anything
```

and:

```text
Automatically merge every major upgrade into production
```

Security, compatibility and regression testing must guide updates.

---

# 132. Third-Party Scripts

Every third-party browser script executes inside a high-value trust boundary.

Examples:

```text
Analytics
Chat widgets
Advertising
Monitoring
Payment integrations
```

Minimize them.

Evaluate:

```text
Security
Privacy
Performance
Availability
Business necessity
```

before inclusion.

---

# 133. Feature Flags

Feature flags decouple deployment from release.

```text
Deploy Code
    │
    ▼
Feature OFF
    │
    ▼
Controlled Enablement
```

They can support gradual rollout and emergency disablement.

---

# 134. Flag Types

Differentiate:

```text
Release flags
Experiment flags
Operational flags
Permission/entitlement configuration
```

Do not use frontend feature flags as authorization.

---

# 135. Flag Lifecycle

Temporary flags must have owners and removal dates.

Otherwise:

```text
if flagA
  if flagB
    if !flagC
```

eventually becomes permanent architectural debt.

---

# 136. Frontend Testing Pyramid

A healthy strategy combines:

```text
           E2E
          /   \
     Integration
       /       \
   Component / Unit
```

Do not attempt to prove the entire application using thousands of brittle browser tests.

---

# 137. Vitest

Vitest should be used for fast unit-level testing in the Vite ecosystem where appropriate.

Targets include:

```text
Utilities
Reducers
Hooks
Domain transformations
Validation
```

---

# 138. React Testing Library

Component tests should focus on user-observable behavior.

Prefer:

```text
User clicks Submit
Error message appears
```

over testing internal component implementation details.

---

# 139. MSW

Mock Service Worker should be evaluated for realistic API mocking in frontend tests and development.

```text
Frontend
   │
   ▼
HTTP Request
   │
   ▼
MSW
   │
   ▼
Contract-aligned Response
```

Mocks must remain synchronized with API contracts.

---

# 140. Playwright

Playwright should cover critical end-to-end workflows.

Examples:

```text
Login
Course enrollment
Chapter learning
Assessment submission
Instructor workflow
Critical administration
```

Focus on business-critical journeys.

---

# 141. Visual Regression

Design-system and high-value screens may use screenshot-based regression testing.

This can detect:

```text
Layout breakage
Theme regression
Unexpected component changes
Responsive failures
```

Visual tests require controlled environments to avoid noise.

---

# 142. Accessibility CI

Automated accessibility checks should run against critical components/pages.

They supplement—not replace—manual accessibility validation.

---

# 143. Frontend Contract Testing

Frontend CI should validate compatibility against ADR-057 API contracts.

```text
OpenAPI
   │
   ▼
Generated Types / Client
   │
   ▼
Compile
   │
   ▼
Contract Tests
```

Backend contract changes should fail early when they break frontend assumptions.

---

# 144. Frontend CI/CD

Conceptually:

```text
Commit
  │
  ▼
Lint
  │
  ▼
Type Check
  │
  ▼
Unit / Component Tests
  │
  ▼
Accessibility Checks
  │
  ▼
Build
  │
  ▼
Bundle Budget
  │
  ▼
Security Scan
  │
  ▼
E2E / Smoke
  │
  ▼
Immutable Artifact
  │
  ▼
Deploy
```

The same artifact should move through environments where feasible.

---

# 145. Static Asset Deployment

Production React assets should typically follow:

```text
Build
  │
  ▼
Immutable Static Assets
  │
  ▼
Object/Static Hosting
  │
  ▼
CDN
  │
  ▼
Browser
```

Application servers should not unnecessarily serve large static bundles when dedicated infrastructure exists.

---

# 146. Cache Busting & Rollback

Hashed filenames enable simultaneous old/new assets.

```text
app.a123.js
app.b456.js
```

Deployment must avoid HTML referencing assets that no longer exist.

Rollback should restore a coherent artifact set rather than reconstructing builds manually.

---

# 147. Micro-Frontend Decision

Mediverse should **not adopt micro-frontends by default**.

They become justified when there is a real organizational problem such as:

```text
Multiple autonomous frontend teams
Independent release requirements
Clearly separated domains
Different deployment cadences
```

A large application is not automatically a micro-frontend problem.

---

# 148. Micro-Frontend Trade-Offs

Micro-frontends can provide:

```text
Team autonomy
Independent delivery
Domain ownership
```

but introduce:

```text
Duplicate dependencies
Inconsistent UX
Runtime integration complexity
Routing complexity
Shared-state problems
Version conflicts
Observability complexity
Performance overhead
```

Module Federation or similar technology should only follow an explicit architectural decision.

---

# 149. Frontend Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ JavaScript for large production code where TypeScript is practical
❌ any everywhere
❌ Technical-folder-only architecture at application scale
❌ shared/ as a dumping ground
❌ Arbitrary cross-feature deep imports
❌ 2,000-line page components containing entire domains
❌ Redux for every piece of state
❌ Server responses copied blindly into Redux
❌ Every state value stored globally
❌ Derived values duplicated in state
❌ API calls scattered through random components
❌ Client validation trusted as security
❌ React route guards treated as authorization
❌ Long-lived sensitive tokens casually stored in localStorage
❌ Secrets embedded in Vite environment variables
❌ One global loading spinner for every operation
❌ Memoization everywhere without measurement
❌ Entire application shipped as one giant bundle
❌ Raw high-resolution images sent to tiny displays
❌ Unoptimized 3D assets shipped directly to mobile browsers
❌ 3D rendering made mandatory for basic educational access
❌ Unlimited DOM lists
❌ Service worker introduced without cache lifecycle design
❌ "Offline support" without defined semantics
❌ Socket connections created by random components
❌ Reconnect loops without backoff
❌ Mouse-only interaction
❌ div-based fake buttons
❌ Accessibility postponed until launch
❌ Desktop-only design followed by emergency mobile fixes
❌ MUI + Tailwind + CSS-in-JS + global CSS used randomly
❌ Hardcoded colors instead of design tokens
❌ User-facing strings hardcoded everywhere
❌ Browser timezone assumed to equal business timezone
❌ Sensitive values captured in analytics
❌ Unsanitized HTML rendering
❌ Custom regex HTML sanitizers
❌ Uncontrolled third-party scripts
❌ Feature flags used as authorization
❌ Permanent abandoned feature flags
❌ Testing implementation details instead of behavior
❌ Entire test strategy dependent on E2E
❌ Mutable production frontend artifacts
❌ Micro-frontends introduced because they sound enterprise
```

---

# 150. Decision Outcome & Final Reference Architecture

| Area                        | Decision                                        |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Framework                   | **React**                                       |
| Language                    | **TypeScript**                                  |
| Build platform              | **Vite**                                        |
| Code organization           | Domain/feature-oriented                         |
| Feature interfaces          | Controlled public exports                       |
| Routing                     | React Router                                    |
| Route guards                | UX only                                         |
| Local state                 | React                                           |
| URL state                   | Router/URL                                      |
| Server state                | TanStack Query preferred where appropriate      |
| Global complex client state | Redux Toolkit selectively                       |
| Form architecture           | React Hook Form                                 |
| Runtime schema validation   | Required where appropriate                      |
| API access                  | Feature API layer + shared HTTP client          |
| Generated OpenAPI client    | Preferred/evaluated                             |
| Browser authentication      | ADR-056 governed                                |
| BFF                         | Preferred evaluation for sensitive browser auth |
| Browser secrets             | **Impossible by design — do not embed**         |
| Error isolation             | React Error Boundaries                          |
| Code splitting              | Route/feature based                             |
| 3D modules                  | Lazy-loaded + separately budgeted               |
| Performance                 | Core Web Vitals + RUM                           |
| Large lists                 | Virtualization when needed                      |
| Images                      | Responsive + optimized + CDN                    |
| 3D                          | Progressive enhancement                         |
| PWA                         | Requirement-driven                              |
| Offline                     | Explicit capability model                       |
| Realtime                    | Central client abstraction                      |
| Accessibility               | WCAG 2.x AA target                              |
| Responsive design           | Mobile-first                                    |
| Design system               | Required                                        |
| UI foundation               | MUI                                             |
| Tailwind                    | Controlled utility/layout role                  |
| Storybook                   | Design-system documentation/testing             |
| Theme                       | Token-driven                                    |
| Dark mode                   | Semantic-token based                            |
| i18n                        | Architecture-supported                          |
| Time handling               | Locale + timezone aware                         |
| Frontend observability      | Required                                        |
| Source maps                 | Controlled diagnostic access                    |
| CSP                         | Required defense-in-depth                       |
| Untrusted HTML              | Sanitized                                       |
| Dependency lockfile         | Required                                        |
| Supply-chain scanning       | CI enforced                                     |
| Feature flags               | Lifecycle-governed                              |
| Unit testing                | Vitest                                          |
| Component testing           | React Testing Library                           |
| API mocking                 | MSW                                             |
| E2E                         | Playwright                                      |
| Accessibility CI            | Required                                        |
| Visual regression           | Critical UI/design system                       |
| API contract validation     | Required                                        |
| Artifact                    | Immutable                                       |
| Static deployment           | CDN-oriented                                    |
| Rollback                    | Previous immutable artifact                     |
| Micro-frontends             | **Rejected as default**                         |
| Module Federation           | Only after explicit justification               |
| Status                      | **Accepted**                                    |
| Priority                    | **Critical**                                    |

         ROUTING           DESIGN SYSTEM       FEATURES

            │        Courses      Learning    Assessment       Admin

The frontend has one final invariant:

> **A feature is not production-ready merely because it renders correctly on the developer's machine. It must remain secure, accessible, responsive, observable, contract-compatible, performant on realistic devices, testable, and safely deployable.**
