ADR-059 should cover **mobile platform strategy → native vs React Native vs PWA → shared web/mobile boundaries → React Native architecture → Expo evaluation → TypeScript → navigation → mobile feature modules → API client reuse → authentication → OAuth/OIDC native flows → PKCE → secure token storage → biometric authentication → Keychain/Keystore → certificate/network security → device integrity considerations → local database → SQLite → encrypted storage → offline-first learning → downloadable courses → media downloads → 3D mobile constraints → synchronization engine → dirty tracking → sync queue → conflict detection → conflict resolution → optimistic mutations → idempotency → retry/backoff → delta synchronization → background synchronization → network awareness → push notifications → FCM/APNs → notification permissions → deep links → universal/app links → notification security → mobile state management → caching → image/media optimization → battery/data usage → accessibility → responsive device layouts → tablet experience → localization → mobile analytics → crash reporting → privacy → mobile secrets → API keys → root/jailbreak threat model → screenshot/clipboard considerations → testing → unit/component/E2E → device matrix → performance testing → release signing → Android/iOS builds → CI/CD → Play Store/App Store → staged rollout → feature flags → forced/minimum versions → backward API compatibility → OTA update boundaries → rollback → observability → mobile SLOs → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise mobile/offline architecture.**

# ADR-059 — Enterprise Mobile Architecture, React Native, Offline-First Learning, Synchronization, Push Notifications, Mobile Security & App Delivery

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-059
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-058 established Mediverse's enterprise React web architecture.

ADR-059 establishes the architecture for delivering Mediverse as a **secure, offline-capable, high-performance mobile learning platform across Android and iOS**, while avoiding unnecessary duplication between web and mobile systems.

The governing principle is:

> **Mobile is not a smaller web application. Mobile architecture must explicitly account for unreliable connectivity, device storage, operating-system lifecycle, battery and bandwidth constraints, application-store distribution, device security and long-lived client versions.**

```text
                         MOBILE USER
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌──────────────────┐
                    │ MEDIVERSE MOBILE │
                    │   Android / iOS  │
                    └────────┬─────────┘
                             │
             ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
             ▼               ▼                ▼
           ONLINE          OFFLINE        DEVICE APIs
             │               │                │
             ▼               ▼                ▼
          API/BFF       LOCAL DATABASE      Push
             │               │             Biometrics
             │               │             Storage
             │               │             Deep Links
             │               │
             │         ┌─────┴─────┐
             │         ▼           ▼
             │      CONTENT     SYNC QUEUE
             │       CACHE          │
             │                      │
             └──────────┬───────────┘
                        ▼
                   SYNC ENGINE
                        │
                        ▼
                   API GATEWAY
                        │
                        ▼
                MEDIVERSE SERVICES
```

# 1. Mobile Platform Strategy

Mediverse should distinguish four delivery models:

```text
Responsive Web
PWA
Cross-platform Native
Platform-native Applications
```

These are architectural options, not maturity levels.

A native application should exist only where device/platform capabilities justify its cost.

# 2. PWA vs Native Mobile

ADR-058 already supports progressive web capabilities.

PWA should cover experiences adequately served by:

```text
Browser
Responsive UI
Caching
Basic offline content
Web notifications where supported
```

Native mobile becomes justified when Mediverse requires deeper:

```text
Offline storage
Background synchronization
Push notifications
Secure device credentials
Large media downloads
Device integrations
App-store distribution
Native performance
```

# 3. React Native Decision

React Native should be the preferred native mobile framework for Mediverse.

```text
Android ─┐
         ├── React Native + TypeScript
iOS ─────┘
```

This aligns with the React/TypeScript frontend skill set while still producing native mobile applications.

# 4. React Native Is Not React Web

Shared concepts:

```text
React
TypeScript
Hooks
State patterns
Domain models
API contracts
```

Do not assume sharing:

```text
DOM
CSS
Browser APIs
Every component
Every navigation pattern
```

Trying to force 100% code sharing usually produces poor architecture.

# 5. Shared Code Strategy

Good candidates for sharing:

```text
packages/
├── api-contracts/
├── domain-types/
├── validation/
├── business-rules/
├── telemetry-contracts/
└── utilities/
```

Platform-specific UI should generally remain platform-specific.

# 6. Monorepo Evaluation

A monorepo may simplify sharing between:

```text
Web
Mobile
Shared contracts
Design tokens
Generated API clients
```

Conceptually:

```text
mediverse/
├── apps/
│   ├── web/
│   └── mobile/
└── packages/
    ├── api/
    ├── domain/
    ├── validation/
    └── design-tokens/
```

Use it only with explicit package boundaries.

# 7. Expo

Expo should be evaluated as the default React Native development platform.

It can simplify:

```text
Builds
Device APIs
Push integration
Updates
Native configuration
Development tooling
```

But Expo does not remove the need to understand Android and iOS behavior.

# 8. Expo Escape Hatch

If Mediverse eventually requires unsupported low-level native functionality, the architecture must allow custom native modules or prebuild/native projects.

Do not reject Expo merely because such a possibility exists.

# 9. TypeScript

Mobile production code uses TypeScript under the same strictness philosophy as ADR-058.

```text
API Contract
    │
    ▼
Generated Types
    │
    ▼
Domain Layer
    │
    ▼
Mobile Features
```

# 10. Mobile Application Structure

Prefer domain-oriented organization:

```text
src/
├── app/
├── features/
│   ├── auth/
│   ├── courses/
│   ├── learning/
│   ├── assessments/
│   ├── downloads/
│   ├── notifications/
│   └── profile/
├── shared/
├── storage/
├── sync/
└── infrastructure/
```

# 11. Navigation

Navigation should explicitly model:

```text
Authentication flow
Main application
Course flow
Learning flow
Assessment flow
Profile
Deep-linked destinations
```

Navigation state must not become authorization state.

# 12. Navigation Architecture

Conceptually:

```text
Root Navigator
     │
     ├── Authentication
     │
     └── Authenticated App
            │
            ├── Home
            ├── Courses
            ├── Learning
            └── Profile
```

# 13. Deep Links

Mediverse should support links such as:

```text
mediverse://courses/123
```

and preferably platform-standard HTTPS links where practical.

```text
HTTPS Link
    │
    ▼
Operating System
    │
    ▼
Mediverse App
    │
    ▼
Course 123
```

# 14. Universal/App Links

Prefer verified HTTPS-based application links for externally distributed links.

They provide safer association between domain and installed application than arbitrary custom schemes.

# 15. Deep-Link Authorization

A deep link is navigation input.

It is not permission.

```text
/course/admin/123
        │
        ▼
Authorization still required
```

# 16. API Architecture

Mobile should consume ADR-057 governed APIs.

```text
Mobile
  │
  ▼
API Client
  │
  ▼
BFF / Gateway
  │
  ▼
Services
```

Do not create an unrelated mobile backend unless client-specific requirements justify a mobile BFF.

# 17. Mobile BFF

A mobile BFF may become useful for:

```text
Payload aggregation
Bandwidth reduction
Mobile-specific DTOs
Version compatibility
Authentication/session architecture
```

It must not become the owner of core business logic.

# 18. Generated API Client

OpenAPI-generated TypeScript clients should be evaluated for web/mobile sharing.

```text
OpenAPI
   │
   ▼
Generated Package
   │
   ├── Web
   └── Mobile
```

This can significantly reduce contract drift.

# 19. Mobile API Compatibility

Mobile versions may remain installed for months or years.

Therefore:

```text
Backend Deployment
      │
      X
Assume every client updated today
```

is unacceptable.

Backward compatibility matters more for mobile than rapidly deployed web clients.

# 20. Authentication

Native authentication follows ADR-056.

Preferred architecture:

```text
Mobile App
    │
    ▼
System Browser
    │
    ▼
Identity Provider
    │
    ▼
Authorization Code + PKCE
    │
    ▼
Mobile App
```

# 21. Embedded Login WebViews

OAuth authentication should not casually collect IdP credentials inside arbitrary embedded WebViews.

System/browser-based authorization flows provide stronger trust boundaries and SSO behavior.

# 22. PKCE

Public mobile clients cannot securely hold conventional client secrets.

Therefore Authorization Code + PKCE is required for applicable OAuth native flows.

# 23. Mobile Client Secret

This is not a secret:

```text
client_secret =
"embedded-inside-the-APK"
```

Attackers can extract application binaries.

Public clients must be designed accordingly.

# 24. Token Storage

Sensitive tokens must not be stored in ordinary plaintext application storage.

Use platform-backed secure storage such as:

```text
iOS Keychain
Android Keystore-backed mechanisms
```

through the selected mobile framework.

# 25. Secure Storage Boundary

Use secure storage for:

```text
Refresh tokens
Sensitive credentials
Device-bound secrets
```

Do not put large application databases into Keychain/Keystore.

# 26. Biometric Authentication

Biometrics can protect access to locally stored credentials or sensitive application functionality.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Face/Fingerprint
 │
 ▼
Device Authentication
 │
 ▼
Protected Credential
```

Biometrics do not replace backend identity and authorization.

# 27. Device PIN Fallback

Biometric policy must define whether device credentials may serve as fallback.

This is a security/product decision, not something individual screens should determine.

# 28. Logout

Mobile logout should address:

```text
Application state
Refresh credentials
Secure storage
Cached sensitive data
Server-side session/token state
Push registration
```

Removing only the visible profile is not logout.

# 29. Account Switching

If multiple accounts are supported:

```text
Account A data
      │
      X
Account B session
```

Caches, local databases and downloads must be isolated or cleared correctly.

# 30. Local Storage Classification

Mobile data should be classified before storage.

```text
Ephemeral UI State
Cache
Downloaded Content
Offline Mutable Data
Credentials
Sensitive Personal Data
```

Different categories require different controls.

# 31. Local Database

Structured offline data may use SQLite or an appropriate mobile database abstraction.

```text
Mobile Features
      │
      ▼
Repository
      │
      ▼
Local Database
```

Feature code should not scatter raw SQL throughout screens.

# 32. Repository Boundary

Prefer:

```text
UI
 │
 ▼
Domain/Application
 │
 ▼
Repository
 │
 ├── Local
 │
 └── Remote
```

This allows online/offline behavior without contaminating every component.

# 33. Local Database Schema

The local database is a schema requiring migrations.

```text
App v10
 │
 ▼
Database v5
 │
 ▼
Upgrade
 │
 ▼
Database v6
```

Mobile migrations must be tested across real upgrade paths.

# 34. Encryption at Rest

Sensitive locally stored data should be encrypted where the threat model requires it.

But encryption is not magic if encryption keys are stored insecurely beside the database.

# 35. Offline-First Learning

For learning content, Mediverse should prefer an offline-capable architecture.

```text
Course
  │
  ▼
Download
  │
  ▼
Local Content
  │
  ▼
Learn Offline
  │
  ▼
Progress Recorded Locally
  │
  ▼
Reconnect
  │
  ▼
Synchronize
```

# 36. Offline-First Does Not Mean Everything Offline

Suitable:

```text
Downloaded chapters
Reading
Images
Selected video
Progress capture
Notes
```

Potentially unsuitable:

```text
Live collaboration
Fresh administrative data
Security-sensitive operations
Real-time examinations
```

Offline behavior must be capability-specific.

# 37. Download Manifest

Offline courses should have a manifest.

```text
Course Download
      │
      ├── Metadata
      ├── Chapters
      ├── Images
      ├── Audio
      ├── Video
      └── 3D assets
```

The manifest enables size calculation, versioning and integrity checks.

# 38. Download Size

Before large downloads, show users meaningful size information.

```text
Download Course
~1.8 GB
```

Large medical media downloads without warning are unacceptable on constrained data plans.

# 39. Network-Aware Downloads

Download behavior should consider:

```text
Wi-Fi
Cellular
Roaming
Offline
Battery
User preference
```

Users should be able to restrict large downloads to Wi-Fi.

# 40. Resumable Downloads

Large media downloads should support continuation after interruption where the storage/backend architecture permits it.

```text
500 MB
  │
  X network lost at 340 MB
  │
  ▼
Resume
```

Restarting every large download from zero creates poor mobile behavior.

# 41. Download Integrity

Downloaded assets should be verifiable.

Conceptually:

```text
Manifest Hash
     │
     ▼
Downloaded Asset
     │
     ▼
Integrity Check
```

Corrupted content should not silently enter the offline library.

# 42. Content Versioning

Offline content requires version information.

```text
Course v7 on server
Course v5 on device
```

The client needs policy for:

```text
Keep
Update
Invalidate
Warn
```

# 43. Content Invalidation

Critical corrected educational content may require invalidation.

The architecture must distinguish:

```text
Optional content update
```

from:

```text
Safety/correctness-critical replacement
```

# 44. Media Downloads

Video/audio should not automatically be duplicated inside the database.

Preferred:

```text
Metadata
→ Local DB

Binary media
→ Managed filesystem/cache
```

# 45. Storage Quotas

The application must track storage usage.

```text
Downloaded Courses
      │
      ▼
4.2 GB Used
      │
      ▼
Manage Downloads
```

Users need control over large offline assets.

# 46. Cache Eviction

Caches should have policies such as:

```text
LRU
Age
Storage pressure
Explicit cleanup
```

Downloaded user-requested content should not be treated identically to disposable cache.

# 47. 3D Mobile Architecture

Mobile 3D should have stricter budgets than desktop web.

Consider:

```text
GPU capability
Memory
Thermal load
Battery
Asset size
Frame rate
```

A desktop-quality anatomical model cannot simply be copied into every phone.

# 48. Adaptive 3D Quality

```text
High-End Device
      │
      ▼
High Quality

Mid-range
      │
      ▼
Reduced Quality

Low capability
      │
      ▼
Fallback / 2D
```

Learning access remains more important than maximum graphical fidelity.

# 49. Sync Engine

Offline mutable data requires a centralized synchronization engine.

```text
LOCAL CHANGES
     │
     ▼
SYNC QUEUE
     │
     ▼
CONNECTIVITY
     │
     ▼
REMOTE API
     │
     ▼
ACKNOWLEDGEMENT
     │
     ▼
LOCAL STATE
```

Screens should not independently invent synchronization logic.

# 50. Syncable Entity

Syncable records should contain enough metadata to reason about state.

Conceptually:

```text
entityId
localVersion
serverVersion
updatedAt
syncState
operationId
```

Exact fields depend on domain semantics.

# 51. Dirty Tracking

Local modifications should be explicitly identifiable.

```text
CLEAN
  │
  ▼
User modifies
  │
  ▼
DIRTY
  │
  ▼
Sync succeeds
  │
  ▼
CLEAN
```

# 52. Sync Queue

Pending mutations should enter a durable queue when offline support requires reliability.

```text
Operation 1
Operation 2
Operation 3
```

A transient in-memory array is insufficient if the application may terminate.

# 53. Operation Identity

Each retryable mutation should have a stable operation/idempotency identifier.

```text
operationId = 7f...
```

This allows server-side duplicate detection.

# 54. Mobile Idempotency

Consider:

```text
Submit Progress
     │
     X network dies after server commit
     │
     ▼
Client retries
```

Without idempotency, one logical action may be processed twice.

ADR-057 idempotency requirements apply directly.

# 55. Sync Retry

Retries should use:

```text
Backoff
Jitter
Connectivity awareness
Bounded attempts where appropriate
```

Do not hammer APIs continuously while the device has no usable network.

# 56. Sync State Machine

Conceptually:

```text
PENDING
   │
   ▼
SYNCING
   │
   ├── Success → SYNCED
   │
   ├── Conflict → CONFLICT
   │
   └── Failure → RETRY
```

Explicit states are easier to debug than implicit boolean combinations.

# 57. Conflict

A conflict occurs when local and remote state diverge incompatibly.

```text
Device:
Note version 5 → changed

Server:
Note version 5 → independently changed
```

Blind last-write-wins may destroy user data.

# 58. Conflict Strategy

Conflict policy must be domain-specific.

Possible strategies:

```text
Server wins
Client wins
Last write wins
Field merge
Operation merge
User resolution
Reject and refresh
```

There is no universal correct conflict algorithm.

# 59. Progress Synchronization

Learning progress may often be merged using monotonic/domain rules.

Example:

```text
Device says chapter completed
Server says chapter incomplete
```

The correct rule may differ from ordinary last-write-wins.

Domain semantics should decide.

# 60. Notes Synchronization

User-generated notes are more dangerous to overwrite.

For concurrent edits, Mediverse may require:

```text
Version check
Conflict copy
Merge
User resolution
```

rather than silently deleting one side.

---

## ADR-059 — Part 1 Complete

The first mobile architecture layer is now:

```text
                        MOBILE APPLICATION
                                │
               ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
               ▼                ▼                ▼
             ONLINE          OFFLINE           DEVICE
               │                │                │
               ▼                ▼                ▼
             APIs          LOCAL DATA        Secure APIs
               │                │                │
               │       ┌────────┼────────┐       │
               │       ▼        ▼        ▼       │
               │    Content   Cache    Pending    │
               │                      Mutations   │
               │                         │        │
               └──────────────┬──────────┘        │
                              ▼                   │
                         SYNC ENGINE ◄────────────┘
                              │
              ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
              ▼               ▼                ▼
         IDEMPOTENCY       CONFLICTS         RETRIES
              │               │                │
              └───────────────┼────────────────┘
                              ▼
                         SERVER STATE
```

The first 60 sections establish these rules:

```text
1. Mobile is not treated as a smaller web application.

2. React Native is the preferred native strategy.

3. Expo is evaluated as the default development platform.

4. Web/mobile share domain contracts—not blindly every UI component.

5. Mobile authentication uses standards-based native OAuth + PKCE.

6. Client secrets embedded in applications are not secrets.

7. Sensitive credentials use platform-backed secure storage.

8. Local structured data uses a governed database/repository boundary.

9. Offline learning is a first-class capability.

10. Offline support is capability-specific rather than universal.

11. Large media downloads are resumable and network-aware.

12. Downloaded content is versioned and integrity-aware.

13. 3D quality adapts to device capabilities.

14. Offline mutations flow through a centralized durable sync engine.

15. Retryable operations have stable idempotency identities.

16. Synchronization has explicit state transitions.

17. Conflict resolution follows domain semantics.

18. User data is not silently destroyed through naive
    last-write-wins synchronization.
```

**Part 2** should continue from **Section 61 — Delta Synchronization**, then cover **sync cursors → tombstones/deletions → multi-device synchronization → background sync → OS restrictions → connectivity detection → push notification architecture → FCM/APNs → device tokens → notification preferences → topics → push security → sensitive notification content → deep links → notification deduplication → badge state → local notifications → state management → TanStack Query/mobile caching → Redux boundaries → memory pressure → image/media caching → battery efficiency → bandwidth budgets → accessibility → Dynamic Type/font scaling → screen readers → touch targets → orientation/tablet layouts → localization → RTL → mobile observability → crash reporting → ANR/freeze monitoring → mobile performance → startup time → frame rate → memory → battery → analytics/privacy → mobile application security → secure storage → certificate/TLS considerations → certificate pinning trade-offs → rooted/jailbroken devices → device attestation evaluation → screenshots → clipboard → backups → exported Android components → Android intents → iOS URL handling → WebView security → dependency security → native module supply chain → permissions → least privilege → testing → unit/component/integration → mobile E2E → physical-device testing → device matrix → network-condition testing → offline testing → upgrade/migration testing → release signing → Android signing keys → iOS signing → CI/CD → build artifacts → Play Store/App Store → staged rollout → crash gates → feature flags → remote config → minimum supported version → forced upgrades → API compatibility → OTA update boundaries → rollback → release observability → ownership → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise mobile/offline reference architecture.**



# ADR-059 — Enterprise Mobile Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Notes Synchronization**.

---

# 61. Delta Synchronization

Mobile clients should not repeatedly download complete datasets merely to discover a few changes.

Prefer:

```text
Device
  │
  │ lastSyncCursor = abc123
  ▼
Server
  │
  ▼
Changes since abc123
  │
  ├── Updated entities
  ├── New entities
  └── Deleted entities
```

Delta synchronization reduces bandwidth, processing and battery consumption.

---

# 62. Sync Cursor

The server may issue an opaque synchronization cursor.

```text
GET /sync?cursor=abc123

Response
├── changes[]
└── nextCursor=xyz789
```

Clients must treat cursors as opaque tokens rather than attempting to interpret their internal structure.

---

# 63. Cursor Consistency

A cursor should represent a meaningful server-side synchronization position.

It should not simply be:

```text
client current timestamp
```

when clock differences or concurrent writes can cause missed records.

---

# 64. Sync Pagination

Large synchronization results should be paginated.

```text
cursor=A
   │
   ▼
Page 1
   │
   ▼
continuation=B
   │
   ▼
Page 2
```

The client should advance its durable synchronization checkpoint only according to defined consistency semantics.

---

# 65. Deletions

Delta synchronization must communicate deletions.

Otherwise:

```text
Server deletes Course X

Device never receives Course X again

But local Course X remains forever
```

This creates stale local state.

---

# 66. Tombstones

A deletion may temporarily be represented by a tombstone.

```text
{
   id: "course-123",
   deleted: true,
   version: 17
}
```

Tombstones allow offline clients to learn that previously synchronized records were removed.

---

# 67. Tombstone Retention

Tombstones cannot necessarily be retained forever.

Therefore the synchronization architecture needs a retention policy.

If a device has been offline beyond the supported synchronization window:

```text
Incremental Sync
      │
      X
Cursor expired
      │
      ▼
Full Resynchronization
```

may be required.

---

# 68. Multi-Device Synchronization

A learner may use:

```text
Phone
Tablet
Web
```

against the same account.

The server remains authoritative for shared state.

```text
Phone ──┐
Tablet ─┼──► Server State
Web ────┘
```

Do not design synchronization assuming one user owns one device.

---

# 69. Device Identity

A generated installation/device identifier may help with:

```text
Push registration
Sync diagnostics
Session management
Conflict analysis
```

It must not be treated as proof of user identity.

---

# 70. Background Synchronization

Where OS capabilities permit:

```text
Application Backgrounded
        │
        ▼
OS grants execution window
        │
        ▼
Sync Engine
        │
        ▼
Upload/download limited changes
```

Background execution must be considered opportunistic.

---

# 71. OS Background Restrictions

This assumption is rejected:

```text
Background worker
      =
Runs whenever we want
```

Android and iOS aggressively manage background execution.

Critical workflows must not depend on unrestricted background processing.

---

# 72. Foreground Synchronization

When the application returns to foreground:

```text
App Resume
   │
   ▼
Check freshness
   │
   ▼
Sync if necessary
```

This is an important recovery mechanism when background execution did not occur.

---

# 73. Connectivity Detection

Network APIs can indicate connectivity state.

But:

```text
Connected to Wi-Fi
       ≠
Mediverse API reachable
```

Actual request outcomes remain authoritative.

---

# 74. Network State

Useful states include:

```text
Offline
Wi-Fi
Cellular
Unknown
Expensive connection
```

The application may adapt synchronization and download behavior accordingly.

---

# 75. Push Notification Architecture

Push notifications should use platform push services.

```text
Mediverse
    │
    ▼
Notification Service
    │
    ├───────────────┐
    ▼               ▼
   FCM             APNs
    │               │
    ▼               ▼
 Android           iOS
```

Mediverse should not attempt to maintain persistent connections solely to reinvent platform push delivery.

---

# 76. Push Tokens

Platform push tokens identify application installations/endpoints.

```text
User
 │
 ├── Phone token A
 ├── Tablet token B
 └── Old token C
```

They are mutable infrastructure identifiers, not permanent user IDs.

---

# 77. Push Token Lifecycle

Tokens may:

```text
Rotate
Expire
Become invalid
Change after reinstall
```

The backend must update registrations and remove invalid tokens.

---

# 78. User-to-Device Mapping

Push registration should associate:

```text
User
Installation
Platform
Push token
Application version
Notification preferences
```

where required.

Logout/account switching must update this association correctly.

---

# 79. Notification Preferences

Users should control supported categories such as:

```text
Learning reminders
Course updates
Assessment reminders
Social/activity notifications
Announcements
```

Transactional or mandatory notifications should be classified separately where applicable.

---

# 80. Notification Permission

Push permission should be requested contextually.

Bad:

```text
First app launch
      │
      ▼
Immediately request every permission
```

Better:

```text
User understands feature
      │
      ▼
Explain value
      │
      ▼
Request required permission
```

---

# 81. Push Payload Security

Push payloads should contain the minimum information necessary.

Do not assume push infrastructure or the lock screen is an appropriate place for sensitive data.

Prefer:

```text
"New learning update available"
```

over exposing sensitive educational/account information unnecessarily.

---

# 82. Push Is a Signal

Where freshness matters:

```text
Push
 │
 ▼
Application
 │
 ▼
Fetch authoritative state
```

The push message should not necessarily become the authoritative domain record.

---

# 83. Notification Deep Links

A notification may route to:

```text
Course
Chapter
Assessment
Message
Announcement
```

but destination authorization remains mandatory.

---

# 84. Notification Deduplication

Retries or multiple event paths can produce duplicates.

Use stable notification/event identifiers where necessary.

```text
eventId
   │
   ▼
Already processed?
   │
 ┌─┴─┐
 ▼   ▼
Yes  No
 │    │
Drop Process
```

---

# 85. Local Notifications

The mobile application may schedule local reminders for suitable workflows.

Example:

```text
Study reminder
Downloaded assessment reminder
```

Local notifications should not represent server-authoritative events that require fresh server state.

---

# 86. Badge State

Badge counts require explicit semantics.

```text
Unread notifications?
Unread messages?
Pending tasks?
```

Do not mix unrelated concepts into an unexplained number.

---

# 87. Mobile State Architecture

ADR-058 principles remain applicable:

```text
Local UI State
→ React

Server State
→ TanStack Query where appropriate

Complex Global Client State
→ Redux Toolkit selectively

Persistent Offline State
→ Local database

Navigation State
→ Navigation system
```

---

# 88. Local Database Is Not Redux

This architecture is rejected:

```text
SQLite
  │
  ▼
Copy everything
  │
  ▼
Redux
```

Duplicating large persistent datasets creates synchronization and memory problems.

---

# 89. TanStack Query Mobile

TanStack Query may manage online server-state caching.

It must integrate carefully with:

```text
Connectivity
App foreground/background
Persistent storage
Offline database
Sync engine
```

Do not create two competing authoritative caches.

---

# 90. Memory Pressure

Mobile memory is constrained.

Avoid retaining:

```text
Huge course datasets
Decoded full-resolution images
Multiple 3D scenes
Large video buffers
Unbounded query caches
```

simultaneously.

---

# 91. Image Cache

Images may use a managed cache.

```text
Remote Image
    │
    ▼
Disk Cache
    │
    ▼
Decoded Image
    │
    ▼
Screen
```

Memory and disk caching require separate limits.

---

# 92. Media Cache

Streaming media cache and explicitly downloaded media should be distinguished.

```text
Temporary playback cache
        ≠
User-selected offline download
```

Eviction policies should respect that distinction.

---

# 93. Battery Efficiency

Mobile architecture should minimize:

```text
Continuous polling
Unnecessary GPS
Repeated wakeups
Aggressive background synchronization
Constant socket reconnects
Excessive animation
Unnecessary 3D rendering
```

Battery consumption is an application-quality metric.

---

# 94. Bandwidth Budget

Mediverse should measure:

```text
Cold-start traffic
Normal session traffic
Course download size
Image transfer
Video transfer
Synchronization traffic
```

Mobile bandwidth is not unlimited.

---

# 95. Accessibility

Mobile accessibility remains mandatory.

Support should include:

```text
Screen readers
Dynamic text sizing
Accessible labels
Touch target sizing
Focus order
Contrast
Reduced motion
```

---

# 96. Dynamic Type

Interfaces should tolerate larger system font settings.

This is unacceptable:

```text
Larger font
   │
   ▼
Text clipped
Buttons inaccessible
Navigation broken
```

Layouts should adapt.

---

# 97. Screen Readers

Important elements require meaningful accessibility semantics for technologies such as platform screen readers.

Icon-only controls require accessible labels.

---

# 98. Touch Targets

Interactive elements should provide practical touch areas.

Tiny visual icons should not require pixel-perfect tapping.

---

# 99. Orientation

Do not assume portrait-only unless the product explicitly requires it.

3D anatomical learning and tablet workflows may benefit significantly from landscape layouts.

---

# 100. Tablet Architecture

Tablet should not simply be:

```text
Phone UI stretched to 13 inches
```

Large displays may support:

```text
Master/detail
Split panes
Persistent navigation
Side-by-side learning material
3D + explanation panels
```

---

# 101. Foldables and Variable Windows

Responsive layout decisions should depend on available window dimensions rather than rigid assumptions about device categories.

---

# 102. Localization

Mobile follows the internationalization architecture established in ADR-058.

Support should include:

```text
Translation
Pluralization
Number formatting
Dates
Time zones
RTL
Locale-aware content
```

---

# 103. Mobile Observability

Production mobile telemetry should capture approved signals such as:

```text
Crashes
Unhandled errors
Application hangs
Startup performance
API failures
Sync failures
Release version
Device/OS class
Navigation failures
```

while respecting privacy controls.

---

# 104. Crash Reporting

Crash reports should identify:

```text
App version
Build number
OS version
Device class
Stack trace
Release
Relevant breadcrumbs
```

without unnecessarily collecting sensitive user content.

---

# 105. ANR / Application Hangs

Crash-free statistics alone are insufficient.

An application that freezes for 20 seconds but does not crash still provides a failed experience.

Monitor:

```text
Android ANRs
iOS hangs
Long JS-thread stalls
```

where tooling permits.

---

# 106. Startup Performance

Measure:

```text
Process start
    │
    ▼
Application shell
    │
    ▼
Usable screen
```

Do not initialize every SDK, course cache and analytics subsystem before showing useful UI.

---

# 107. Lazy Initialization

Non-critical capabilities should initialize when needed.

Candidates:

```text
3D engine
Heavy analytics
Rare admin capabilities
Large editors
Optional integrations
```

---

# 108. Frame Rate

Animations, scrolling and 3D interactions should remain responsive on supported devices.

Monitor dropped frames rather than assuming development-machine performance represents production devices.

---

# 109. JavaScript Thread

React Native workloads must avoid monopolizing the JS thread with expensive synchronous processing.

Heavy work should be restructured, deferred or moved to suitable native/background mechanisms where justified.

---

# 110. Memory Monitoring

Memory-heavy workflows require testing:

```text
Large course
+
Video
+
Images
+
3D model
+
Navigation history
```

Memory leaks may cause operating-system termination rather than clean application errors.

---

# 111. Analytics & Privacy

Mobile analytics should have defined purposes.

Collect:

```text
What product decision will this event support?
```

before adding telemetry.

Avoid indiscriminate event collection.

---

# 112. Mobile Secrets

An APK or IPA cannot securely hide static secrets.

Reject:

```text
Secret API key
      │
      ▼
Bundle into app
      │
      ▼
"Nobody will find it"
```

Anything distributed to clients should be treated as extractable.

---

# 113. TLS

All production network communication containing protected application traffic should use HTTPS/TLS.

The mobile client must validate server certificates correctly.

---

# 114. Certificate Pinning

Certificate pinning can reduce some interception risks but introduces operational hazards:

```text
Certificate rotation
Emergency changes
CDN migration
Pin expiration
Application versions unable to update
```

Therefore Mediverse should **not adopt certificate pinning by default**.

Use it only after explicit threat-model justification and with a safe rotation strategy.

---

# 115. Rooted/Jailbroken Devices

Root/jailbreak detection can provide a risk signal.

It is not a reliable security boundary.

```text
Device detection
      │
      ▼
Risk signal
      │
      X
Absolute proof
```

Server-side authorization and security controls remain mandatory.

---

# 116. Device Attestation

Platform attestation mechanisms may be evaluated for high-risk capabilities.

Potential use:

```text
App installation
      │
      ▼
Platform Attestation
      │
      ▼
Risk Engine
```

Attestation should contribute to risk decisions rather than replace authentication.

---

# 117. Screenshots

Sensitive screens may require screenshot/screen-recording restrictions where platform capabilities and threat models justify them.

Do not apply restrictions indiscriminately; they can harm legitimate accessibility and learning workflows.

---

# 118. Clipboard

Sensitive data should not automatically be copied into the system clipboard.

Clipboard contents may be accessible beyond the immediate application context depending on platform behavior.

---

# 119. Application Backups

Sensitive local data must be evaluated against Android/iOS backup behavior.

Data that should not leave the device through platform backup mechanisms must be configured accordingly.

---

# 120. Android Exported Components

Android activities/services/receivers/providers should follow least exposure.

```text
Does another application need access?
        │
   ┌────┴────┐
   ▼         ▼
  Yes        No
   │         │
Explicit   Not exported
control
```

---

# 121. Intent Validation

External Android intents and deep-link parameters are untrusted input.

Validate them before use.

---

# 122. iOS URL Handling

Incoming URLs/universal links should also be treated as untrusted navigation input.

Malformed or unauthorized routes must fail safely.

---

# 123. WebView Security

WebViews should be minimized.

When required:

```text
Trusted origins
Navigation restrictions
Controlled JavaScript
Secure bridge design
No unnecessary file access
```

must be defined.

A WebView JavaScript bridge can become a serious security boundary.

---

# 124. Permissions

Request only permissions required by real features.

```text
Camera
Microphone
Photos
Notifications
Location
```

should each have explicit product justification.

Mediverse should not request location merely because a dependency supports it.

---

# 125. Permission Timing

Permissions should be requested near the feature that needs them.

Context improves user understanding and reduces unnecessary permission denial.

---

# 126. Native Dependency Security

React Native applications include:

```text
npm packages
Native Android dependencies
Native iOS dependencies
Build plugins
Expo/native modules
```

Supply-chain scanning must account for all layers.

---

# 127. Testing Strategy

Mobile quality requires:

```text
Unit tests
Component tests
Integration tests
E2E tests
Offline tests
Migration tests
Real-device tests
Performance tests
```

One emulator is not a mobile testing strategy.

---

# 128. Unit & Component Tests

Test:

```text
Domain transformations
Sync state machines
Conflict rules
Validation
Hooks
UI behavior
```

without requiring full-device execution where unnecessary.

---

# 129. Sync Engine Testing

Synchronization deserves dedicated deterministic tests.

Test scenarios including:

```text
Successful sync
Network failure
Timeout
Duplicate request
Server conflict
Cursor expiration
Partial synchronization
Application termination
Retry
Deletion/tombstone
```

---

# 130. Offline Testing

Explicitly test:

```text
Launch offline
Lose network during operation
Reconnect
Switch Wi-Fi → cellular
Slow connection
High latency
Packet loss
API unavailable
```

Offline-first architecture cannot be validated only on stable office Wi-Fi.

---

# 131. Database Migration Testing

Test upgrades across supported historical versions.

```text
App v8 DB
   │
   ▼
Upgrade directly to v12
```

may be a real user path.

Testing only fresh installs misses migration failures.

---

# 132. Device Matrix

Testing should cover representative:

```text
Low-end Android
Mid-range Android
High-end Android
Supported iPhones
Tablet
Different OS versions
Different screen dimensions
```

The exact matrix should derive from supported-user telemetry.

---

# 133. Physical Devices

Emulators/simulators are valuable but cannot fully reproduce:

```text
GPU behavior
Camera
Biometrics
Battery
Thermal throttling
Real networking
Vendor-specific Android behavior
```

Critical release testing needs physical devices.

---

# 134. Release Signing

Production mobile artifacts must be cryptographically signed.

Signing credentials are high-value production secrets.

They belong in controlled CI/release infrastructure—not developer repositories.

---

# 135. Android Signing Keys

Android signing keys require:

```text
Restricted access
Secure backup
Rotation/recovery planning
CI integration
Auditability
```

Loss or compromise can have severe release consequences.

---

# 136. iOS Signing

iOS certificates/profiles/App Store credentials require equivalent controlled management and automated renewal processes where practical.

---

# 137. Mobile CI/CD

Conceptually:

```text
Commit
  │
  ▼
Lint
  │
  ▼
Type Check
  │
  ▼
Unit / Component Tests
  │
  ▼
Security Scan
  │
  ▼
Build
  │
  ▼
Integration / E2E
  │
  ▼
Signed Artifact
  │
  ▼
Internal Testing
  │
  ▼
Store Release
```

---

# 138. Immutable Builds

The exact signed artifact approved for release should be traceable to:

```text
Source commit
Dependencies
Configuration
Build pipeline
Build number
Release
```

Rebuilding "the same version" later is not equivalent to preserving the original artifact.

---

# 139. Staged Rollout

New versions should use staged/phased rollout where supported.

```text
1%
 │
 ▼
5%
 │
 ▼
25%
 │
 ▼
50%
 │
 ▼
100%
```

Progression depends on health signals, not simply elapsed time.

---

# 140. Release Health Gates

Monitor:

```text
Crash-free sessions
ANRs/hangs
Startup failures
Authentication failures
API errors
Sync failures
Performance regression
```

A release with severe regressions should be halted before reaching all users.

---

# 141. Feature Flags

Feature flags can separate application deployment from feature activation.

```text
App Version
    │
    ▼
Feature Code Present
    │
    ▼
Remote Flag
    │
 ┌──┴──┐
 ▼     ▼
OFF    ON
```

Flags do not replace backend authorization.

---

# 142. Remote Configuration

Remote configuration may control safe operational values such as:

```text
Feature availability
UI configuration
Operational thresholds
Rollout percentages
```

It must not become a mechanism for remotely executing arbitrary code.

---

# 143. Minimum Supported Version

Backend systems should know which mobile versions remain supported.

```text
Current: 12.4
Minimum: 10.2
```

Versions below the minimum may receive an upgrade-required response where necessary.

---

# 144. Forced Upgrade

Forced upgrades should be rare.

Appropriate reasons may include:

```text
Critical security issue
Irreconcilable protocol incompatibility
Dangerously incorrect application behavior
```

Using forced updates for ordinary feature releases creates unnecessary user disruption.

---

# 145. API Compatibility Window

Because store approval and user adoption take time:

```text
Backend N
   │
   ├── Mobile N
   ├── Mobile N-1
   └── Older supported clients
```

must coexist.

Server teams cannot assume coordinated deployment with mobile clients.

---

# 146. OTA Updates

JavaScript/asset OTA updates may be useful where the chosen React Native/Expo architecture supports them.

But OTA updates must respect platform policies and native-runtime compatibility.

```text
JS Update
   │
   ▼
Compatible with installed native runtime?
   │
 ┌─┴─┐
 ▼   ▼
Yes  No
 │    │
OTA  Store binary required
```

---

# 147. Mobile Rollback

Rollback mechanisms depend on failure type.

```text
Feature problem
→ Disable flag

Compatible JS regression
→ OTA rollback where supported

Native binary regression
→ Halt rollout + submit corrected binary

Backend incompatibility
→ Restore compatibility server-side
```

There is no universal instant mobile rollback.

---

# 148. Mobile Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Treating mobile as responsive web inside a wrapper
❌ Forcing 100% web/mobile code sharing
❌ Embedding OAuth client secrets in APK/IPA
❌ Collecting IdP passwords in arbitrary WebViews
❌ Storing refresh tokens in plaintext storage
❌ Biometrics treated as backend authorization
❌ Offline support implemented independently by screens
❌ In-memory-only queues for durable offline mutations
❌ Retryable mutations without idempotency
❌ Last-write-wins used blindly for user-generated content
❌ Full database download on every synchronization
❌ Ignoring remote deletions
❌ Assuming one user has one device
❌ Assuming background tasks always run
❌ Treating network connectivity indicator as API availability
❌ Push tokens treated as permanent user identity
❌ Sensitive information exposed on lock-screen notifications
❌ Push payload treated as authoritative state
❌ Redux used as a copy of the local database
❌ Unlimited query/image/media caches
❌ Desktop 3D assets shipped unchanged to phones
❌ Infinite socket reconnect loops
❌ Polling constantly while backgrounded
❌ Ignoring battery and cellular bandwidth
❌ Phone UI merely stretched onto tablets
❌ Secrets stored in application bundles
❌ Certificate pinning added without rotation planning
❌ Root detection treated as a security boundary
❌ WebViews with unrestricted navigation/bridges
❌ Requesting every permission on first launch
❌ Testing only on one emulator
❌ Testing offline features only with reliable Wi-Fi
❌ Testing only fresh database installations
❌ Signing keys committed to repositories
❌ Rebuilding production artifacts manually
❌ Releasing immediately to 100% of users
❌ Feature flags used as authorization
❌ Forced upgrades for ordinary releases
❌ Backend assuming every mobile client updates immediately
❌ OTA updates crossing incompatible native-runtime boundaries
```

---

```text
                              USER
                               │
                               ▼
                 ┌─────────────────────────┐
```

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                     | Decision                                 |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| Native mobile framework  | **React Native + TypeScript**            |
| Development platform     | **Expo preferred/evaluated**             |
| Responsive web/PWA       | Retained alongside native                |
| Web/mobile sharing       | Contracts/domain logic selectively       |
| 100% UI sharing          | Rejected                                 |
| Mobile structure         | Feature/domain-oriented                  |
| API contracts            | ADR-057 governed                         |
| Generated clients        | Preferred where practical                |
| Authentication           | OAuth/OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE     |
| Embedded client secrets  | Rejected                                 |
| Sensitive token storage  | Keychain/Keystore-backed                 |
| Biometrics               | Local protection / step-up UX            |
| Local structured storage | SQLite/appropriate mobile DB             |
| Offline learning         | **First-class capability**               |
| Binary downloads         | Managed filesystem                       |
| Large downloads          | Network-aware + resumable                |
| Content integrity        | Verified                                 |
| Content versioning       | Required                                 |
| Mobile 3D                | Adaptive quality                         |
| Low-capability devices   | Accessible fallback                      |
| Offline mutations        | Durable sync queue                       |
| Synchronization          | Central sync engine                      |
| Delta sync               | Preferred                                |
| Sync cursor              | Opaque server-controlled                 |
| Deletions                | Tombstones/defined equivalent            |
| Multi-device             | Explicitly supported                     |
| Conflict strategy        | Domain-specific                          |
| Retryable mutations      | Idempotent                               |
| Background execution     | Opportunistic                            |
| Push                     | FCM + APNs                               |
| Push token               | Installation endpoint, not identity      |
| Sensitive push content   | Minimized                                |
| Push payload             | Signal where freshness matters           |
| Deep links               | Verified links preferred                 |
| Mobile server state      | TanStack Query selectively               |
| Persistent state         | Local DB                                 |
| Global client state      | Redux Toolkit selectively                |
| Accessibility            | Required                                 |
| Tablet UX                | Adaptive, not stretched phone UI         |
| Observability            | Crashes + hangs + performance + sync     |
| Certificate pinning      | **Not default**                          |
| Root/jailbreak detection | Risk signal only                         |
| Device attestation       | Selective risk control                   |
| WebViews                 | Minimized/restricted                     |
| Permissions              | Least privilege/contextual               |
| Physical-device testing  | Required                                 |
| Offline/network testing  | Required                                 |
| Migration testing        | Required                                 |
| Release signing          | Controlled CI infrastructure             |
| Production artifacts     | Immutable/traceable                      |
| Distribution             | Play Store + App Store                   |
| Rollout                  | Staged/phased                            |
| Feature flags            | Governed                                 |
| Minimum version          | Supported                                |
| Forced updates           | Exceptional                              |
| API compatibility        | Multiple mobile generations              |
| OTA updates              | Native-runtime compatibility constrained |
| Rollback                 | Layer-specific                           |
| Status                   | **Accepted**                             |
| Priority                 | **Critical**                             |

# ADR-059 — COMPLETE ✅

The critical architecture can now be reduced to one lifecycle:

```text
                         USER ACTION
                              │
                              ▼
                       MOBILE FEATURE
                              │
                              ▼
                         REPOSITORY
                              │
                 ┌────────────┴────────────┐
                 ▼                         ▼
             LOCAL STATE                NETWORK
                 │                         │
                 ▼                         ▼
            IMMEDIATE UX               REMOTE API
                 │                         │
                 ▼                         │
            SYNC QUEUE                     │
                 │                         │
                 └────────────┬────────────┘
                              ▼
                         SYNC ENGINE
                              │
                ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
                ▼             ▼             ▼
           IDEMPOTENCY     CONFLICT      RETRY
                │             │             │
                └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                              ▼
                       SERVER TRUTH
                              │
                              ▼
                         DELTA SYNC
                              │
                              ▼
                         LOCAL STATE
                              │
                              ▼
                       CONSISTENT UX
```

The defining invariant is:

> **The mobile application must continue to provide a coherent learning experience when the network is slow, intermittent or absent, while converging safely toward authoritative server state when connectivity returns.**
