# ADR-060 — Enterprise Cloud & AWS Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-060
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-059 established the mobile and offline architecture.

ADR-060 establishes how Mediverse runs in **AWS as a secure, highly available, observable, recoverable and cost-governed production platform**.

The governing principle is:

> **Cloud architecture must assume infrastructure failure, credential compromise, traffic spikes, deployment mistakes and regional service disruption will eventually occur. The platform must contain the blast radius and recover predictably.**

```text
                         INTERNET / USERS
                                │
                                ▼
                           Route 53
                                │
                                ▼
                         CloudFront + WAF
                                │
                                ▼
                              ALB
                                │
                     ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                     ▼                     ▼
                  AZ-A                    AZ-B
                     │                     │
               ┌─────┴─────┐         ┌─────┴─────┐
               │    EKS    │         │    EKS    │
               └─────┬─────┘         └─────┬─────┘
                     │                     │
                     └──────────┬──────────┘
                                ▼
                       PLATFORM SERVICES
                                │
          ┌────────────┬────────┼────────┬────────────┐
          ▼            ▼        ▼        ▼            ▼
         RDS       ElastiCache  MSK   OpenSearch      S3
      PostgreSQL      Redis    Kafka                  │
          │                                             ▼
          └────────────── KMS / BACKUPS ────────── CloudFront

                   SECURITY / CONTROL PLANE

        Organizations │ IAM │ SCP │ CloudTrail │ Config
        GuardDuty │ Security Hub │ Secrets Manager │ KMS

                     OPERATIONS PLANE

        Terraform │ GitOps │ Observability │ DR │ FinOps
```

# 1. AWS Organization Strategy

Mediverse should not place the entire platform inside one AWS account.

Preferred hierarchy:

```text
AWS Organization
│
├── Security OU
├── Infrastructure OU
├── Non-Production OU
└── Production OU
```

Account boundaries provide stronger blast-radius isolation than naming conventions.

# 2. Account Architecture

A mature baseline should evolve toward:

```text
Management Account
│
├── Security Account
├── Log Archive Account
├── Shared Services Account
├── Development Account
├── Testing/Staging Account
└── Production Account
```

Additional workload accounts should be created when organizational scale warrants them.

# 3. Management Account

The Organizations management account should contain minimal workloads.

It should primarily manage:

```text
Organizations
Account lifecycle
Billing
Organization-wide governance
```

Running application workloads there unnecessarily expands the blast radius of privileged access.

# 4. Security Account

Central security capabilities should be delegated where supported.

```text
Security Account
├── Security Hub
├── GuardDuty administration
├── Security tooling
└── Investigation capabilities
```

Workload administrators should not automatically control security oversight.

# 5. Log Archive Account

Immutable or tightly controlled organization-level logs should be centralized.

```text
AWS Accounts
    │
    ├── CloudTrail
    ├── Security logs
    └── Audit logs
          │
          ▼
   Log Archive Account
```

An attacker compromising a workload account should not easily erase centralized evidence.

# 6. Shared Services Account

Shared infrastructure may include:

```text
CI/CD integrations
Artifact infrastructure
DNS administration
Shared observability
Network services
```

Only genuinely shared capabilities belong here.

# 7. Production Isolation

Production should be isolated from development.

Reject:

```text
One AWS account
├── dev-vpc
├── test-vpc
└── prod-vpc
```

as the long-term enterprise boundary.

Separate accounts provide stronger IAM, quota, billing and blast-radius boundaries.

# 8. AWS Control Tower

AWS Control Tower should be evaluated for establishing and governing the multi-account landing zone.

Its value includes:

```text
Account provisioning
Guardrails
Central governance
Baseline configuration
```

It should not be introduced merely for an "enterprise" label if the platform remains very small.

# 9. Organizational Units

OUs should reflect governance policy rather than application names.

Example:

```text
Root
├── Security
├── Infrastructure
├── Workloads
│   ├── NonProd
│   └── Prod
└── Sandbox
```

# 10. Service Control Policies

SCPs establish maximum account permissions.

Potential guardrails:

```text
Prevent disabling CloudTrail
Restrict unsupported regions
Protect security services
Restrict dangerous account operations
```

SCPs do not grant IAM permissions.

# 11. Region Strategy

Mediverse should initially use a **single primary AWS Region with Multi-AZ architecture** unless business RTO/RPO requirements justify multi-region operation.

Do not confuse:

```text
Multi-AZ
```

with:

```text
Multi-Region
```

They address different failure domains.

# 12. Region Selection

Region selection should consider:

```text
User latency
Data residency
Service availability
Cost
Compliance
Disaster recovery
Operational capability
```

The closest region is not automatically the correct region.

# 13. Availability Zones

Production services should span multiple AZs where the AWS service and workload permit.

```text
Region
├── AZ-A
├── AZ-B
└── AZ-C
```

A single-AZ Kubernetes platform is not highly available.

# 14. Failure Domains

Architecture should explicitly recognize:

```text
Process
Pod
Node
Availability Zone
Region
Account
External dependency
```

Resilience mechanisms should match the failure domain being addressed.

# 15. VPC Architecture

Each major workload environment should have deliberate VPC architecture.

```text
VPC
│
├── Public Subnets
├── Private Application Subnets
└── Isolated/Data Subnets
```

Subnet classification should reflect routing behavior, not naming alone.

# 16. CIDR Planning

CIDR allocation must be planned before VPC proliferation.

Avoid overlapping ranges such as:

```text
Dev  → 10.0.0.0/16
Prod → 10.0.0.0/16
```

if future network connectivity may be required.

# 17. IP Address Management

At sufficient scale, centralized IPAM should govern:

```text
Account
Region
VPC
Subnet
CIDR allocation
```

Ad-hoc CIDR selection becomes painful once environments interconnect.

# 18. Public Subnets

Public subnets should contain only resources requiring direct routing through an Internet Gateway.

Typical examples may include internet-facing load-balancer interfaces and NAT Gateways.

Application nodes do not become public merely because doing so is easier.

# 19. Private Application Subnets

EKS worker nodes and application workloads should normally run in private subnets.

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
ALB
   │
   ▼
Private EKS Workloads
```

# 20. Isolated Data Subnets

Databases and sensitive data infrastructure should normally avoid direct internet routes.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Database Subnet
```

Internet exposure of PostgreSQL is not a production architecture.

# 21. Route Tables

Route tables should explicitly reflect subnet intent.

```text
Public
→ Internet Gateway

Private
→ NAT / VPC endpoints as needed

Isolated
→ Internal routes only
```

# 22. NAT Gateway

Private workloads requiring outbound internet connectivity may use NAT Gateways.

For production HA:

```text
AZ-A Private → NAT-A
AZ-B Private → NAT-B
AZ-C Private → NAT-C
```

Cross-AZ NAT routing should be avoided where availability and cost justify per-AZ NAT.

# 23. NAT Cost

NAT Gateway can become a significant hidden cost.

Traffic such as:

```text
S3
ECR
CloudWatch
AWS APIs
```

should be evaluated for VPC endpoints rather than blindly traversing NAT.

# 24. VPC Endpoints

Gateway/interface endpoints can provide private connectivity to supported AWS services.

```text
Private Workload
      │
      ▼
VPC Endpoint
      │
      ▼
AWS Service
```

Benefits can include:

```text
Reduced NAT traffic
Private routing
Improved security posture
```

Endpoints themselves also have cost and should not be created without reason.

# 25. Security Groups

Security groups should follow least privilege.

Bad:

```text
0.0.0.0/0 → PostgreSQL 5432
```

Preferred:

```text
Application SG
      │
      ▼
Database SG:5432
```

# 26. Network ACLs

NACLs provide subnet-level stateless filtering.

They should not be overused to create an operationally incomprehensible duplicate firewall architecture where security groups already provide the required controls.

# 27. VPC Peering

VPC peering may work for small connectivity topologies.

But:

```text
VPC A ─ VPC B
 │ \      / │
 │  \    /  │
VPC C ─ VPC D
```

does not scale cleanly.

# 28. Transit Gateway

Transit Gateway should be evaluated when many VPCs/accounts require centralized connectivity.

```text
        TGW
      /  |  \
     /   |   \
  VPC-A VPC-B VPC-C
```

Do not deploy it when two isolated VPCs have no connectivity requirement.

# 29. DNS Architecture

DNS should be centrally governed.

```text
Route 53
│
├── Public Hosted Zones
└── Private Hosted Zones
```

Service discovery inside Kubernetes remains a separate layer.

# 30. Route 53

Route 53 should provide public DNS for Mediverse domains and may participate in:

```text
Health checks
Failover
Weighted routing
Latency routing
```

where the architecture requires them.

# 31. TLS Certificates

Public TLS certificates should use managed certificate lifecycle through ACM where supported.

Manual certificate files copied between servers should be eliminated.

# 32. CloudFront

CloudFront should front suitable static/media content.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
CloudFront
 │
 ├── HIT → Edge response
 │
 └── MISS → Origin
```

This is particularly important for Mediverse's images, media and frontend assets.

# 33. CloudFront Origins

Potential origins include:

```text
S3
ALB
Media infrastructure
```

Different content types may require separate cache behaviors.

# 34. Private S3 Origins

S3 buckets used behind CloudFront should not automatically be public.

Preferred:

```text
Internet
   X
S3

Internet
 │
 ▼
CloudFront
 │
 ▼
Controlled S3 Origin
```

# 35. AWS WAF

WAF should protect appropriate internet-facing entry points.

Controls may include:

```text
Managed rule groups
IP/reputation controls
Rate-based rules
Application-specific rules
```

WAF does not replace secure application code.

# 36. DDoS Protection

AWS Shield Standard provides baseline DDoS protection for supported services.

More advanced protection should be driven by threat/risk and business requirements.

# 37. Application Load Balancer

ALB should handle HTTP/HTTPS ingress where appropriate.

```text
Client
 │
 ▼
CloudFront/WAF
 │
 ▼
ALB
 │
 ▼
EKS
```

# 38. Network Load Balancer

NLB should be selected for workloads requiring its Layer-4 characteristics.

Do not use NLB merely because it sounds more performant.

# 39. EKS Decision

Amazon EKS should host Mediverse Kubernetes workloads.

This aligns with the Kubernetes architecture established by previous ADRs while offloading control-plane management to AWS.

# 40. EKS Account Boundary

Production and non-production clusters should reside in their corresponding AWS accounts.

```text
NonProd Account
     │
     ▼
NonProd EKS

Prod Account
     │
     ▼
Prod EKS
```

# 41. Cluster Strategy

Do not create:

```text
One EKS cluster per microservice
```

without exceptional justification.

A cluster is a platform boundary, not a deployment unit for every application.

# 42. Production Cluster HA

EKS application capacity should span AZs.

```text
EKS
├── Nodes AZ-A
├── Nodes AZ-B
└── Nodes AZ-C
```

Workloads should use topology-aware scheduling where availability requires it.

# 43. Managed Node Groups

Managed node groups provide a reasonable baseline for worker capacity.

Separate groups may exist for workloads with materially different requirements.

Examples:

```text
General workloads
Memory-heavy workloads
Compute-heavy workloads
Specialized GPU workloads
```

# 44. Karpenter

Karpenter should be evaluated for dynamic node provisioning and workload-aware capacity management.

Potential benefits:

```text
Faster provisioning
Instance flexibility
Bin packing
Spot integration
```

It adds operational policy that must be tested carefully.

# 45. Cluster Autoscaler

Cluster Autoscaler remains an alternative where its simpler model better matches the environment.

Do not operate overlapping node autoscaling systems without a deliberate architecture.

# 46. Pod Autoscaling

Application scaling may use HPA based on suitable signals.

```text
Traffic
  │
  ▼
Metrics
  │
  ▼
HPA
  │
  ▼
Pod Replicas
```

CPU is not always the correct workload metric.

# 47. Vertical Pod Autoscaling

VPA may assist resource recommendation or selected workloads.

Automatically changing resource requests in production requires careful compatibility with HPA and workload behavior.

# 48. Resource Requests

Production workloads require realistic CPU/memory requests.

Without them, Kubernetes scheduling and autoscaling decisions become unreliable.

# 49. Resource Limits

Limits should be selected deliberately.

Extremely tight limits create:

```text
CPU throttling
OOM kills
Instability
```

while unlimited resource usage damages multi-tenant cluster stability.

# 50. Pod Disruption Budgets

Critical replicated services should define disruption tolerance.

```text
Replicas: 3
PDB:
minimum available: 2
```

PDBs cannot protect against every failure and should not block cluster maintenance indefinitely.

# 51. Topology Spread

Critical replicas should avoid accidental concentration.

```text
Pod 1 → AZ-A
Pod 2 → AZ-B
Pod 3 → AZ-C
```

Topology spread constraints and anti-affinity should be used where appropriate.

# 52. EKS Networking

Pod networking must account for VPC IP consumption.

Large clusters can exhaust subnet address space long before compute capacity is exhausted.

CIDR planning therefore directly affects Kubernetes scalability.

# 53. Kubernetes Network Policies

Namespace boundaries do not automatically prevent pod-to-pod traffic.

Network policy should enforce required east-west restrictions.

```text
Frontend
   │
   ▼
API

Frontend
   X
Database
```

# 54. Kubernetes Ingress

Ingress/Gateway configuration should expose only required workloads.

Internal services should remain internal.

# 55. Gateway API

Kubernetes Gateway API should be evaluated as the platform matures because it provides richer role-oriented traffic management than traditional Ingress abstractions.

Migration should be requirement-driven.

# 56. AWS Load Balancer Controller

AWS-integrated Kubernetes ingress/load-balancer management should be controlled through supported controllers rather than manual load-balancer creation for every deployment.

# 57. ECR

Container images should be stored in Amazon ECR or the approved enterprise registry architecture.

```text
CI
 │
 ▼
Build
 │
 ▼
Scan
 │
 ▼
ECR
 │
 ▼
EKS
```

# 58. Image Immutability

Production deployment should reference immutable image digests or otherwise immutable version identifiers.

Reject:

```text
image: mediverse-api:latest
```

for controlled production releases.

# 59. ECR Scanning

Container images should undergo vulnerability scanning.

A scan result should feed release policy according to severity and exploitability.

# 60. AWS Identity for Pods

Pods should receive AWS permissions through workload identity mechanisms such as EKS Pod Identity or IRSA according to the selected platform standard.

Reject:

```text
Application pod
     │
     ▼
Node's giant IAM role
     │
     ▼
Access to everything
```

Workload identity should follow least privilege.

---

## ADR-060 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The first AWS architecture layer establishes:

```text
                         AWS ORGANIZATION
                                │
               ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
               ▼                ▼                ▼
            SECURITY         NON-PROD          PROD
               │                │                │
               │                ▼                ▼
               │              VPC              VPC
               │                │                │
               │           ┌────┼────┐      ┌────┼────┐
               │           ▼    ▼    ▼      ▼    ▼    ▼
               │          AZ-A AZ-B AZ-C    AZ-A AZ-B AZ-C
               │                │                │
               │                ▼                ▼
               │               EKS              EKS
               │                                  │
               └──────── GOVERNANCE ──────────────┘
```

The first 60 sections establish these non-negotiable rules:

```text
1. Production is isolated by AWS account boundaries.

2. Security and audit evidence are centrally controlled.

3. Multi-AZ is the production baseline.

4. Multi-region is driven by RTO/RPO rather than prestige.

5. Network CIDRs are planned centrally.

6. Application workloads run privately by default.

7. Databases are not internet-facing.

8. NAT architecture is both an availability and cost decision.

9. VPC endpoints are evaluated for private AWS-service traffic.

10. Security groups follow least privilege.

11. Route 53 centrally governs public DNS.

12. CloudFront fronts appropriate static/media delivery.

13. S3 origins are private by default.

14. WAF provides edge defense, not application correctness.

15. EKS is the Kubernetes runtime.

16. Kubernetes workloads span failure domains.

17. Autoscaling occurs at both pod and infrastructure layers
    where justified.

18. Kubernetes scheduling uses realistic resource requests.

19. Pod network/IP capacity is treated as a scalability concern.

20. AWS permissions are assigned to workloads rather than
    inherited from oversized node roles.

21. Container artifacts are immutable and scanned.

22. Cloud infrastructure is designed around blast-radius
    containment rather than a single giant account/VPC.
```

**Part 2** should continue from **Section 61 — IAM & Human Access Architecture**, then cover **IAM Identity Center → federation → break-glass access → least privilege → permission boundaries → workload identity → cross-account roles → KMS → envelope encryption → key policies → rotation → Secrets Manager → Parameter Store → secret rotation → RDS PostgreSQL → Multi-AZ → read replicas → connection management → RDS Proxy → backup/PITR → database encryption → ElastiCache Redis → replication/failover → MSK/Kafka → broker/AZ topology → OpenSearch → S3 → bucket policies → versioning → lifecycle → storage classes → multipart uploads → media architecture → backup architecture → AWS Backup → immutable backups → cross-account/cross-region copies → CloudTrail → AWS Config → GuardDuty → Security Hub → centralized security findings → observability → CloudWatch → Prometheus/Grafana integration → OpenTelemetry → centralized logs → RTO/RPO → disaster-recovery tiers → backup/restore → pilot light → warm standby → active-active → multi-region decision → Route 53 failover → data replication → DR exercises → Terraform architecture → remote state → state locking → account/environment modules → GitOps → infrastructure promotion → drift detection → tagging → cost allocation → budgets → anomaly detection → Savings Plans → Reserved Instances → Spot → Graviton evaluation → NAT/data-transfer costs → S3 lifecycle economics → FinOps → quotas/service limits → capacity planning → operational runbooks → AWS anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise AWS reference architecture.**


# ADR-060 — Enterprise Cloud & AWS Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — AWS Identity for Pods**.

---

# 61. IAM & Human Access Architecture

Human access to AWS should be centralized rather than based on individually created IAM users across accounts.

```text
Human User
    │
    ▼
Corporate Identity Provider
    │
    ▼
IAM Identity Center
    │
    ▼
Permission Set
    │
    ▼
AWS Account / Role
```

Long-lived IAM users should be exceptional.

---

# 62. IAM Identity Center

IAM Identity Center should provide centralized workforce access across Mediverse AWS accounts.

It should govern:

```text
User/group assignment
Account access
Permission sets
Federated sessions
Central access lifecycle
```

---

# 63. Federation

Where an enterprise identity provider exists:

```text
Enterprise IdP
      │
      ▼
IAM Identity Center
      │
      ▼
AWS Accounts
```

should be preferred over maintaining a separate AWS identity lifecycle.

---

# 64. Permission Sets

Access should be based on job responsibilities.

Examples:

```text
Developer
ReadOnly
PlatformEngineer
SecurityAuditor
ProductionOperator
BillingAdministrator
```

Do not create unique permissions manually for every individual.

---

# 65. Least Privilege

Permissions should answer:

```text
Who?
Can perform what action?
Against which resource?
Under what conditions?
```

Avoid:

```text
Action: *
Resource: *
```

except where explicitly justified for tightly controlled administration.

---

# 66. Production Human Access

Routine developer workflows should not require unrestricted production console access.

Preferred:

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
CI/CD / GitOps
   │
   ▼
Production
```

Direct production access should be controlled and auditable.

---

# 67. Break-Glass Access

Emergency privileged access should exist for scenarios where normal identity or deployment paths fail.

```text
Normal Access Fails
       │
       ▼
Break-Glass Procedure
       │
       ▼
Strong Authentication
       │
       ▼
Temporary Privileged Access
       │
       ▼
Audit + Review
```

Break-glass credentials must not become everyday administrator credentials.

---

# 68. Temporary Credentials

Prefer short-lived AWS credentials.

```text
Federation
   │
   ▼
STS
   │
   ▼
Temporary Session
```

Long-lived access keys create unnecessary credential exposure.

---

# 69. Access Keys

Human IAM access keys should be minimized.

Workloads should use IAM roles/workload identity rather than static AWS keys stored in:

```text
GitHub secrets
Kubernetes Secrets
application.yml
developer laptops
```

unless an unavoidable integration requires them.

---

# 70. Cross-Account Roles

Cross-account operations should use explicit IAM roles.

```text
CI Account
    │
    ▼
AssumeRole
    │
    ▼
Production Deployment Role
```

Trust policy and permissions policy should remain independently understandable.

---

# 71. Permission Boundaries

Permission boundaries may be used where delegated IAM creation is necessary.

They constrain the maximum permissions delegated identities can grant.

They do not grant permissions themselves.

---

# 72. IAM Policy Governance

IAM policies should be:

```text
Version controlled
Reviewed
Tested
Least privilege
Traceable to ownership
```

Security-critical permissions should not be manually edited without auditability.

---

# 73. KMS Architecture

AWS KMS should provide centralized cryptographic key management for supported AWS workloads.

```text
Application/Data
      │
      ▼
AWS Service
      │
      ▼
KMS Key
```

Encryption architecture should distinguish AWS-managed and customer-managed keys based on governance requirements.

---

# 74. Envelope Encryption

Large data should not normally be directly encrypted by repeatedly sending entire payloads to KMS.

Conceptually:

```text
KMS Key
   │
   ▼
Data Encryption Key
   │
   ▼
Encrypt Data
```

The encrypted data key can accompany encrypted content.

---

# 75. KMS Key Policies

Key policies are a critical authorization boundary.

A principal having access to an AWS resource does not automatically imply permission to use every KMS key.

---

# 76. Key Separation

Separate keys should be considered when required by:

```text
Environment
Data classification
Administrative boundary
Service ownership
Compliance
Blast radius
```

Do not create one KMS key per object or one universal key for the entire organization.

---

# 77. Key Rotation

Rotation policy should follow key type and governance requirements.

Rotation does not eliminate the need to:

```text
Control key access
Audit usage
Protect key policies
Plan key deletion
```

---

# 78. Key Deletion

KMS key deletion is potentially destructive.

```text
Delete Key
    │
    ▼
Encrypted Data
    │
    X
Cannot decrypt
```

Deletion requires waiting periods, approval and impact analysis.

---

# 79. Secrets Manager

Secrets Manager should be preferred for secrets requiring managed lifecycle capabilities.

Examples:

```text
Database credentials
External API credentials
Rotatable application secrets
```

---

# 80. Parameter Store

Systems Manager Parameter Store may hold non-secret configuration and selected protected parameters where its capabilities are sufficient.

Do not force every configuration value into Secrets Manager.

---

# 81. Secret Separation

```text
Configuration
      ≠
Secret
```

Example:

```text
DATABASE_HOST
→ configuration

DATABASE_PASSWORD
→ secret
```

This distinction improves lifecycle management.

---

# 82. Secret Rotation

Where supported and operationally safe:

```text
Old Secret
    │
    ▼
Generate New
    │
    ▼
Update Dependency
    │
    ▼
Validate
    │
    ▼
Retire Old
```

Applications must tolerate the chosen rotation strategy.

---

# 83. Secrets in Kubernetes

AWS secrets should be integrated into Kubernetes using an approved mechanism rather than manually copying long-lived credentials into manifests.

```text
Secrets Manager
      │
      ▼
Approved Integration
      │
      ▼
Pod
```

Git remains prohibited as secret storage.

---

# 84. RDS PostgreSQL

Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL should remain the primary managed relational database platform for Mediverse where PostgreSQL semantics are required.

```text
EKS Services
     │
     ▼
RDS PostgreSQL
```

Self-hosting PostgreSQL inside EKS is rejected for the primary production relational database unless a future requirement fundamentally changes the trade-off.

---

# 85. RDS Multi-AZ

Production databases should use Multi-AZ deployment where availability requirements demand it.

```text
AZ-A
Primary
   │
   │ synchronous managed replication
   ▼
AZ-B
Standby
```

Multi-AZ primarily improves availability—not read scaling.

---

# 86. Database Failover

Applications must tolerate database failover.

Expect:

```text
Existing connections break
Transient errors occur
Endpoint remains logically stable
New connections required
```

A Multi-AZ checkbox does not make applications failure-proof.

---

# 87. Read Replicas

Read replicas may support:

```text
Read scaling
Analytics-style workloads
Reporting
Selected read-heavy services
```

They introduce replication lag.

Do not use replicas where immediate read-after-write consistency is required unless the application handles the semantics.

---

# 88. Database Connections

Microservices can create a connection explosion.

```text
50 services
×
20 pods
×
20 connections

= 20,000 potential connections
```

Connection pools must be intentionally sized.

---

# 89. RDS Proxy

RDS Proxy should be evaluated where connection pooling/multiplexing provides meaningful benefit.

Potential cases:

```text
Highly elastic workloads
Large numbers of application instances
Connection churn
Serverless workloads
```

It is not automatically required for every Spring Boot service.

---

# 90. PostgreSQL Connection Pools

Application pools such as HikariCP should use bounded configurations based on:

```text
Database capacity
Replica count
Pod count
Workload behavior
Query duration
```

Increasing pool size is not automatically a performance improvement.

---

# 91. Database Encryption

RDS storage encryption should use KMS according to the platform encryption standard.

Encryption in transit should also be enforced for application connections where required.

---

# 92. RDS Backups

Production RDS should enable automated backups and point-in-time recovery according to defined retention requirements.

```text
Database
   │
   ├── Automated Backups
   ├── Transaction Logs
   └── Snapshots
```

---

# 93. Backup Is Not High Availability

These concepts solve different problems:

```text
Multi-AZ
→ Infrastructure availability

Backup
→ Historical recovery

Read Replica
→ Read scaling / selected DR capability
```

None replaces the others.

---

# 94. Backup Restore Testing

A backup that has never been restored is an assumption.

Regular exercises should validate:

```text
Backup exists
Backup is readable
Restore works
Application connects
Data is usable
Recovery time is acceptable
```

---

# 95. ElastiCache Redis

Amazon ElastiCache should host Redis workloads where managed Redis-compatible infrastructure fits Mediverse requirements.

Use cases may include:

```text
Caching
Distributed coordination
Rate-limit state
Ephemeral application data
```

Redis should not become the accidental authoritative database for critical durable business state.

---

# 96. Redis High Availability

Production Redis architecture should use appropriate replication and Multi-AZ failover where required.

Applications must still tolerate transient connection failures during failover.

---

# 97. Redis Cache Failure

Cache architecture should assume Redis can become unavailable.

Where Redis is genuinely a cache:

```text
Redis Down
    │
    ▼
Performance degradation
```

should be preferred over:

```text
Redis Down
    │
    ▼
Entire platform unusable
```

unless the feature fundamentally depends on Redis.

---

# 98. MSK / Kafka

Amazon MSK should be evaluated as the managed Kafka platform where ADR-052 Kafka requirements remain valid.

```text
Producer Services
       │
       ▼
      MSK
       │
       ▼
Consumer Services
```

---

# 99. Kafka AZ Architecture

Kafka brokers should span availability zones.

```text
Broker 1 → AZ-A
Broker 2 → AZ-B
Broker 3 → AZ-C
```

Topic replication must align with failure tolerance.

---

# 100. Kafka Durability

Production topics should define:

```text
Replication factor
min.insync.replicas
Producer acknowledgements
Retention
Partition strategy
```

These settings must align with ADR-052 delivery guarantees.

---

# 101. MSK Connectivity

MSK should remain privately reachable from authorized workloads.

Public Kafka brokers should not be the default architecture.

---

# 102. OpenSearch

Amazon OpenSearch Service should be evaluated for ADR-053 search workloads where its operational model fits.

It should remain a derived/search system.

```text
PostgreSQL
→ authoritative data

Events / indexing
→ OpenSearch

OpenSearch
→ search projection
```

---

# 103. Search Failure

Loss of OpenSearch should not corrupt authoritative business data.

Search may degrade while transactional systems remain available where product requirements allow it.

---

# 104. S3 Architecture

Amazon S3 should provide durable object storage for appropriate content such as:

```text
Images
Documents
Audio
Video source assets
3D assets
Exports
Backups where applicable
Logs
```

Buckets should be purpose-oriented rather than one universal bucket for everything.

---

# 105. S3 Public Access

S3 Block Public Access should remain enabled unless a narrowly justified architecture requires otherwise.

Public delivery should generally occur through controlled mechanisms such as CloudFront.

---

# 106. S3 Bucket Policies

Bucket policies should constrain:

```text
Allowed principals
Allowed actions
Transport security
Expected access paths
Cross-account access
```

Broad wildcard access should be rejected.

---

# 107. S3 Encryption

S3 objects should use appropriate server-side encryption.

Customer-managed KMS keys should be used where access governance requires them.

---

# 108. S3 Versioning

Versioning should be enabled for buckets where accidental overwrite/deletion recovery matters.

```text
Object v1
Object v2
Object v3
```

Versioning increases storage usage, so lifecycle policy must account for old versions.

---

# 109. S3 Lifecycle

Lifecycle rules should move or expire data based on actual access patterns.

Conceptually:

```text
Frequently Accessed
      │
      ▼
Less Frequent
      │
      ▼
Archive
      │
      ▼
Expiration
```

Do not archive data without considering retrieval latency and cost.

---

# 110. Multipart Upload

Large media uploads should use multipart/resumable mechanisms.

```text
Large Video
   │
   ├── Part 1
   ├── Part 2
   ├── Part 3
   └── ...
```

Failed abandoned multipart uploads should be cleaned through lifecycle policy.

---

# 111. Direct Client Upload

Where security requirements permit:

```text
Mobile/Web
    │
    ▼
Request Upload Authorization
    │
    ▼
Backend
    │
    ▼
Short-Lived Upload URL
    │
    ▼
Client ─────────► S3
```

can avoid proxying large binaries through application pods.

Authorization must occur before upload capability is issued.

---

# 112. Media Processing

Uploaded media should follow an asynchronous pipeline.

```text
Upload
  │
  ▼
S3
  │
  ▼
Event
  │
  ▼
Processing
  │
  ├── Validation
  ├── Transcoding
  ├── Optimization
  ├── Metadata
  └── Security checks
        │
        ▼
Published Asset
```

User-uploaded files should not automatically become trusted/public content.

---

# 113. CloudFront Media Delivery

Processed public/authorized media should use CDN delivery where appropriate.

For protected content, signed URLs/cookies or equivalent controlled access mechanisms should be evaluated.

---

# 114. Backup Architecture

Backup policy should classify workloads by recoverability.

```text
Workload
   │
   ▼
RPO / RTO
   │
   ▼
Backup Policy
```

Not every dataset requires identical retention.

---

# 115. AWS Backup

AWS Backup should be evaluated for centralized policy-driven backup of supported resources.

Potential benefits:

```text
Central policy
Cross-account backup
Retention
Vault management
Compliance visibility
```

---

# 116. Backup Isolation

Critical backups should be isolated from workload administrators where practical.

```text
Production Account
      │
      ▼
Cross-Account Backup
      │
      ▼
Backup/Security Account
```

This reduces the blast radius of destructive compromise.

---

# 117. Immutable Backups

Backup Vault Lock or equivalent immutability controls should be evaluated for critical recovery datasets.

The purpose is to resist:

```text
Accidental deletion
Malicious deletion
Ransomware-style destruction
```

---

# 118. Cross-Region Backups

Cross-region copies should be driven by regional disaster requirements.

A backup stored only in the failed region does not satisfy every regional disaster scenario.

---

# 119. CloudTrail

Organization-level CloudTrail should capture supported management activity centrally.

```text
AWS Activity
    │
    ▼
CloudTrail
    │
    ▼
Central Log Archive
```

Security-sensitive trails should be protected from workload administrators.

---

# 120. AWS Config

AWS Config should be evaluated for resource configuration history and compliance checks.

Questions it can help answer include:

```text
Was this bucket public?
When did this security group change?
Which resources violate policy?
```

---

# 121. GuardDuty

GuardDuty should provide managed threat detection across governed accounts.

Findings should enter a centralized security workflow rather than being ignored inside individual accounts.

---

# 122. Security Hub

Security Hub should aggregate supported security findings and posture signals.

```text
GuardDuty
Config
Inspector
Other supported findings
      │
      ▼
Security Hub
      │
      ▼
Triage / Automation
```

A dashboard full of unowned findings is not a security program.

---

# 123. Vulnerability Management

Vulnerability signals may originate from:

```text
Container scanning
Dependency scanning
Host/node scanning
AWS Inspector
Application testing
```

Findings require severity, ownership, remediation SLA and exception processes.

---

# 124. Centralized Observability

AWS telemetry should integrate with the broader Mediverse observability architecture.

```text
Applications
EKS
AWS Services
Databases
Network
     │
     ▼
Metrics / Logs / Traces
     │
     ▼
Central Observability
```

---

# 125. CloudWatch

CloudWatch should collect appropriate AWS-native:

```text
Metrics
Logs
Alarms
Service telemetry
```

It may coexist with Prometheus/Grafana/OpenTelemetry rather than forcing one monitoring system to solve every problem.

---

# 126. OpenTelemetry

Application telemetry should remain vendor-neutral where practical.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
OpenTelemetry
    │
    ├── Metrics
    ├── Traces
    └── Logs/context
```

This reduces unnecessary coupling between application instrumentation and a single backend.

---

# 127. Prometheus & Grafana

Kubernetes/application metrics may continue using Prometheus-compatible collection and Grafana dashboards.

Managed AWS offerings may be evaluated when they reduce operational burden without violating platform requirements.

---

# 128. Log Architecture

Logs should be:

```text
Structured
Timestamped
Environment-aware
Service-aware
Trace-correlated
Retention-governed
```

Do not log secrets merely because centralized logging exists.

---

# 129. Alerting

Alerts should represent actionable conditions.

Bad:

```text
CPU > 50%
```

with no operational meaning.

Better signals include:

```text
SLO burn
Sustained error rate
Critical dependency unavailable
Queue lag beyond threshold
Database capacity risk
```

---

# 130. RTO & RPO

Disaster recovery begins with explicit business requirements.

```text
RTO
→ Maximum acceptable recovery time

RPO
→ Maximum acceptable data loss window
```

Architecture cannot rationally select a DR strategy before these are defined.

---

# 131. DR Tiering

Different services may have different recovery requirements.

Example:

```text
Identity / Core Learning
→ High priority

Transactional database
→ High priority

Recommendation cache
→ Lower priority

Rebuildable search index
→ Lower data-recovery priority
```

Do not assign expensive active-active architecture to every component.

---

# 132. Backup-and-Restore DR

Lowest infrastructure cost:

```text
Primary Region
      │
      X
Regional Failure
      │
      ▼
Provision DR Infrastructure
      │
      ▼
Restore Backups
```

Recovery time is relatively high.

---

# 133. Pilot Light

Critical foundational services remain prepared in the secondary region.

```text
Primary
→ Full capacity

DR
→ Minimal critical foundation
```

During disaster, DR capacity is expanded.

---

# 134. Warm Standby

A reduced but functioning environment runs in the secondary region.

```text
Primary
→ 100%

Secondary
→ Reduced capacity
```

Failover scales the standby environment.

This costs more but reduces recovery time.

---

# 135. Active-Active

Both regions actively serve production traffic.

```text
Users
  │
  ├── Region A
  └── Region B
```

This creates major complexity around:

```text
Data consistency
Routing
State
Messaging
Deployments
Operations
Cost
```

Mediverse should **not adopt active-active multi-region by default**.

---

# 136. Mediverse DR Decision

Initial preferred model:

```text
Primary Region
→ Multi-AZ production

Secondary Region
→ Backup/pilot-light or warm-standby capability
   according to validated RTO/RPO
```

Active-active requires a separate future ADR and business justification.

---

# 137. Route 53 Failover

For multi-region DR:

```text
Route 53
   │
   ├── Primary healthy → Primary Region
   │
   └── Primary failed  → DR Region
```

DNS failover alone does not make the application recoverable.

Data, secrets, images, infrastructure and dependencies must also exist or be recoverable.

---

# 138. DR Data Replication

Each datastore requires its own DR strategy.

```text
PostgreSQL
→ backup / cross-region replica strategy

S3
→ replication / backup

Kafka
→ replication/recovery strategy

Redis
→ usually rebuild or replication depending on role

OpenSearch
→ snapshot/rebuild strategy
```

There is no single "replicate AWS" button.

---

# 139. DR Exercises

Disaster recovery must be tested.

```text
Declare Scenario
      │
      ▼
Recover
      │
      ▼
Measure RTO
      │
      ▼
Measure Data Loss
      │
      ▼
Validate Application
      │
      ▼
Record Gaps
```

A DR document that has never been executed is not evidence of recoverability.

---

# 140. Terraform Architecture

AWS infrastructure should be managed through Terraform according to the established IaC strategy.

Conceptually:

```text
modules/
├── network/
├── eks/
├── rds/
├── redis/
├── kafka/
├── storage/
└── security/

environments/
├── dev/
├── staging/
└── prod/
```

Modules should represent reusable infrastructure capabilities, not hide the entire AWS account behind one enormous module.

---

# 141. Terraform State

Terraform state must be remote, encrypted and access-controlled.

```text
Terraform
    │
    ▼
Remote State Backend
    │
    ├── Encryption
    ├── Locking
    ├── Versioning
    └── Restricted Access
```

State may contain sensitive infrastructure information.

---

# 142. Terraform State Separation

Production and non-production should not share one giant Terraform state.

Prefer boundaries aligned with:

```text
Account
Environment
Platform component
Blast radius
Ownership
```

One corrupted state file should not endanger the entire organization.

---

# 143. Terraform Execution

Production Terraform should run through controlled CI/CD workflows.

```text
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
terraform plan
    │
    ▼
Review
    │
    ▼
Approval
    │
    ▼
terraform apply
```

Routine production infrastructure changes from individual laptops should be minimized.

---

# 144. GitOps Boundary

Terraform and GitOps should have clear ownership.

```text
Terraform
→ AWS infrastructure
→ EKS cluster
→ foundational cloud resources

GitOps
→ Kubernetes applications
→ application configuration
→ platform workloads
```

Do not allow both systems to fight over the same resource.

---

# 145. Drift Detection

Infrastructure drift should be detected.

```text
Desired State
     │
     ▼
Actual AWS State
     │
     ▼
Difference?
```

Emergency manual changes must be reconciled back into IaC.

---

# 146. Tagging & Cost Allocation

Required resource metadata should include appropriate:

```text
Environment
Application
Owner
Cost center/team
Managed-by
Data classification where useful
```

Tagging standards should be enforced automatically where possible.

---

# 147. FinOps Architecture

Cost should be treated as an operational signal.

```text
AWS Usage
   │
   ▼
Cost Allocation
   │
   ▼
Budgets / Anomalies
   │
   ▼
Team Visibility
   │
   ▼
Optimization
```

Cost optimization without ownership usually becomes a periodic cleanup exercise rather than engineering discipline.

Key areas include:

```text
Compute rightsizing
Savings Plans
Reserved capacity where appropriate
Spot workloads
Graviton evaluation
S3 lifecycle
Idle resources
NAT Gateway traffic
Cross-AZ transfer
Cross-region transfer
Log retention
Oversized databases
Unused EBS volumes
Overprovisioned Kubernetes
```

---

# 148. AWS Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Entire enterprise in one AWS account
❌ Production workloads in the Organizations management account
❌ Developers permanently holding AdministratorAccess in production
❌ Long-lived human AWS access keys
❌ Static AWS credentials inside Kubernetes manifests
❌ One giant node IAM role used by every pod
❌ Production databases exposed publicly
❌ 0.0.0.0/0 database security groups
❌ Overlapping VPC CIDRs selected without planning
❌ Public EKS nodes merely for convenience
❌ Every private AWS API call routed through NAT without analysis
❌ VPC endpoints created blindly without cost analysis
❌ One EKS cluster per microservice
❌ latest container tags in production
❌ Kubernetes namespaces treated as network isolation
❌ One universal KMS key for everything
❌ Secrets committed to Git
❌ Secrets treated as normal configuration
❌ Self-hosted primary PostgreSQL in EKS without strong justification
❌ Huge DB connection pools used as a performance fix
❌ Read replicas assumed to be strongly consistent
❌ Redis used as accidental durable system of record
❌ Kafka deployed without replication/failure planning
❌ OpenSearch treated as authoritative data
❌ Public S3 buckets used simply to make CloudFront work
❌ Large uploads proxied unnecessarily through application pods
❌ Backups existing without restore tests
❌ Backups controlled only by the same compromised workload account
❌ CloudTrail logs deletable by ordinary workload administrators
❌ Security Hub deployed with nobody owning findings
❌ Alerting on every metric fluctuation
❌ Multi-AZ described as disaster recovery from region failure
❌ Multi-region active-active introduced without RTO/RPO justification
❌ DNS failover treated as complete disaster recovery
❌ DR documentation never exercised
❌ One Terraform state for the entire organization
❌ Production Terraform routinely applied from laptops
❌ Terraform and GitOps managing the same resources
❌ Manual AWS changes never reconciled into IaC
❌ No cost allocation tags
❌ NAT/data-transfer costs ignored
❌ Kubernetes overprovisioning accepted indefinitely
❌ Cost optimization performed without reliability context
```

---

```text
                              USERS
                                │
                                ▼
                            Route 53
                                │
                                ▼
```

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                     | Decision                               |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| Cloud provider           | **AWS**                                |
| Account model            | **Multi-account**                      |
| Production isolation     | Separate AWS account                   |
| Security account         | Required                               |
| Log archive              | Centralized                            |
| Landing zone             | Control Tower evaluated                |
| Workforce access         | IAM Identity Center                    |
| Human credentials        | Short-lived/federated                  |
| Production admin         | Restricted + auditable                 |
| Break-glass              | Controlled emergency mechanism         |
| Workload AWS access      | EKS Pod Identity / IRSA                |
| Static AWS keys          | Avoided                                |
| Region baseline          | Single primary region                  |
| Availability             | Multi-AZ                               |
| Multi-region             | RTO/RPO-driven                         |
| Network                  | VPC with public/private/data tiers     |
| EKS nodes                | Private                                |
| Databases                | Private                                |
| VPC endpoints            | Cost/security evaluated                |
| Kubernetes               | Amazon EKS                             |
| Worker capacity          | Managed node groups                    |
| Dynamic provisioning     | Karpenter evaluated                    |
| Container registry       | ECR                                    |
| Image deployment         | Immutable                              |
| Primary relational DB    | RDS PostgreSQL                         |
| DB availability          | Multi-AZ                               |
| DB scaling               | Read replicas selectively              |
| Connection proxy         | RDS Proxy selectively                  |
| Cache                    | ElastiCache Redis                      |
| Event streaming          | MSK/Kafka                              |
| Search                   | OpenSearch                             |
| Object storage           | S3                                     |
| CDN                      | CloudFront                             |
| Edge protection          | WAF + AWS DDoS baseline                |
| Encryption               | KMS governed                           |
| Secret storage           | Secrets Manager                        |
| Configuration            | Parameter Store where appropriate      |
| Audit                    | Organization CloudTrail                |
| Threat detection         | GuardDuty                              |
| Security posture         | Security Hub                           |
| Configuration history    | AWS Config                             |
| Observability            | OpenTelemetry + AWS/platform telemetry |
| Backups                  | Policy-driven                          |
| Backup isolation         | Cross-account for critical data        |
| Immutable backup         | Evaluated/required by data class       |
| DR baseline              | Backup/pilot-light or warm standby     |
| Active-active            | **Rejected by default**                |
| DR testing               | Mandatory                              |
| Infrastructure as Code   | Terraform                              |
| Terraform state          | Remote + encrypted + separated         |
| Kubernetes desired state | GitOps                                 |
| Terraform/GitOps overlap | Prohibited                             |
| Drift detection          | Required                               |
| Tagging                  | Mandatory                              |
| FinOps                   | Continuous engineering discipline      |
| Production rollout       | Controlled                             |
| Status                   | **Accepted**                           |
| Priority                 | **Critical**                           |

# ADR-060 — COMPLETE ✅

Mediverse now has a full application-to-cloud path:

```text
USER
 │
 ▼
Route53
 │
 ▼
CloudFront / WAF
 │
 ▼
ALB
 │
 ▼
EKS
 │
 ├───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┐
 ▼               ▼               ▼               ▼
Services       Workers        Realtime        Platform
 │               │               │               │
 └───────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┘
                 ▼
             DATA PLANE
                 │
 ┌───────────────┼───────────────┬───────────────┐
 ▼               ▼               ▼               ▼
RDS             Redis           Kafka           S3
 │               │               │               │
 └───────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┘
                 ▼
          SECURITY / BACKUP
                 │
                 ▼
            RECOVERY
```

The final invariant is:

> **AWS managed services reduce infrastructure operations; they do not eliminate architecture. Availability, security, recoverability and cost still depend on how those services are configured, connected, governed and tested.**
