# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                           | Decision                                 |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| Observability framework        | **OpenTelemetry**                        |
| Application metrics            | Prometheus-compatible                    |
| Visualization                  | Grafana                                  |
| Operational logging            | Loki preferred where suitable            |
| Search-heavy logs              | OpenSearch selectively                   |
| Telemetry signals              | Metrics + logs + traces                  |
| Request monitoring             | RED                                      |
| Resource monitoring            | USE                                      |
| User monitoring                | Business SLIs + RUM + synthetics         |
| Trace propagation              | Required                                 |
| Log/trace correlation          | Required                                 |
| High-cardinality metric labels | Prohibited                               |
| Histogram strategy             | Required for critical latency            |
| Exemplars                      | Preferred                                |
| Kubernetes state               | kube-state-metrics                       |
| Node telemetry                 | Required                                 |
| AWS telemetry                  | Integrated                               |
| RDS monitoring                 | DB + query + connection level            |
| Redis monitoring               | Required                                 |
| Kafka monitoring               | Broker + consumer lag                    |
| Frontend observability         | RUM                                      |
| Mobile observability           | Crash/performance/version telemetry      |
| Logging                        | Structured                               |
| Sensitive logging              | Restricted/redacted                      |
| Log retention                  | Tiered                                   |
| Audit logs                     | Protected                                |
| Alert manager                  | Alertmanager/equivalent                  |
| Paging                         | User-impact/action-driven                |
| Alert deduplication            | Required                                 |
| SLI                            | User-centric                             |
| SLO                            | Required for critical services           |
| Error budgets                  | Required                                 |
| Burn-rate alerts               | Preferred                                |
| Composite journey SLOs         | Supported                                |
| Ownership                      | Mandatory                                |
| On-call                        | Critical services                        |
| Incident severity              | Standardized                             |
| Incident command               | Major incidents                          |
| Runbooks                       | Required for paging alerts               |
| Postmortems                    | Significant incidents                    |
| Corrective actions             | Owned + tracked                          |
| Capacity planning              | Required                                 |
| Load testing                   | Required for critical workloads          |
| Performance baseline           | Maintained                               |
| Chaos engineering              | Controlled/hypothesis-driven             |

| Status                         | **Accepted**                             |

# ADR-063 — COMPLETE ✅

Mediverse now has the full production feedback loop:

```text
BUILD
  │
  ▼
DEPLOY
  │
  ▼
OBSERVE
  │
  ▼
MEASURE USER RELIABILITY
  │
  ▼
SLO / ERROR BUDGET
  │
  ├──────── Healthy ────────► CONTINUE DELIVERY
  │
  └──────── Burning ────────► RELIABILITY WORK
                                   │
                                   ▼
                                INCIDENT
                                   │
                                   ▼
                                RECOVER
                                   │
                                   ▼
                                 LEARN
                                   │
                                   ▼
                                IMPROVE
                                   │
                                   └──────────► BUILD
```

The defining invariant is:

> **A service is not healthy because its pods are running. It is healthy when users can successfully complete the outcomes the service exists to provide, within explicitly defined reliability objectives.**

# ADR-064 — Enterprise Security Architecture

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-064
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-061 established infrastructure/GitOps controls. ADR-062 established software-supply-chain trust. ADR-063 established production observability and SRE.

ADR-064 establishes the security architecture governing the entire Mediverse platform.

> **Security is not a perimeter around Mediverse. It is a property of every identity, request, workload, artifact, data flow, infrastructure resource and operational action.**

```text
                           INTERNET
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌───────────────────┐
                    │  EDGE SECURITY    │
                    │ WAF / DDoS / TLS  │
                    └─────────┬─────────┘
                              ▼
                     IDENTITY & ACCESS
                              │
                              ▼
                    APPLICATION / APIs
                              │
              ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
              ▼               ▼               ▼
          Kubernetes         Data          AWS Services
              │               │               │
              └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                              ▼
                      SECURITY CONTROLS
                              │
          ┌───────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          ▼                   ▼                    ▼
      Prevent              Detect               Respond
          │                   │                    │
          └───────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                              ▼
                       SECURITY GOVERNANCE
```

# 1. Security Objectives

Mediverse security must protect:

```text
Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Authenticity
Accountability
Privacy
```

Security cannot be reduced to confidentiality alone.

# 2. Zero Trust

Mediverse adopts Zero Trust principles.

Core rule:

> **Never grant trust merely because a request originated from an internal network, cluster, account or previously authenticated device.**

Every access decision should be based on verified identity, authorization and relevant context.

# 3. Zero Trust Is Not Zero Access

Zero Trust does not mean forcing every interaction through excessive manual approval.

It means:

```text
Verify explicitly
      +
Least privilege
      +
Assume breach
```

# 4. Defense in Depth

No single security control should be considered sufficient.

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
WAF
   │
   ▼
Authentication
   │
   ▼
Authorization
   │
   ▼
Application Validation
   │
   ▼
Network Controls
   │
   ▼
Workload Identity
   │
   ▼
Data Authorization
   │
   ▼
Encryption
```

Failure of one layer should not immediately expose everything behind it.

# 5. Assume Breach

Architecture should ask:

```text
What happens if this credential is stolen?

What happens if this pod is compromised?

What happens if this developer account is compromised?

What happens if malicious code reaches CI?

What happens if one AWS account is breached?
```

Blast-radius reduction becomes a first-class architectural objective.

# 6. Shared Responsibility

Security responsibilities must be explicit.

```text
AWS
→ underlying cloud infrastructure

Platform Team
→ cloud/Kubernetes/platform controls

Service Teams
→ application security

Security Team
→ policy, assurance, detection, response

Data Owners
→ classification and usage requirements
```

"Security owns security" is rejected.

# 7. Asset Inventory

Mediverse must maintain inventory of critical assets.

Examples:

```text
AWS accounts
EKS clusters
Databases
S3 buckets
Applications
APIs
Repositories
Container images
Secrets
Certificates
Domains
Third-party integrations
```

You cannot reliably secure assets you do not know exist.

# 8. Asset Ownership

Every critical asset requires:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Environment
Data classification
Lifecycle
Security requirements
```

Unowned infrastructure should be investigated and removed or assigned.

# 9. Data Classification

Mediverse should classify data into defined categories.

A practical baseline:

```text
PUBLIC
INTERNAL
CONFIDENTIAL
RESTRICTED
```

# 10. Restricted Data

Restricted classification may include applicable:

```text
Authentication credentials
Private keys
Sensitive personal data
Medical-domain data
Financial information
Security evidence
Highly sensitive business information
```

Exact classification depends on actual Mediverse business use.

# 11. Classification Drives Controls

Classification should influence:

```text
Encryption
Access control
Logging
Retention
Backup
Sharing
Monitoring
Deletion
Incident severity
```

Labeling data "restricted" while treating it identically to public data achieves nothing.

# 12. Data Flow Mapping

Critical data flows should be documented.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
React
 │
 ▼
API
 │
 ▼
Spring Boot
 │
 ├── PostgreSQL
 ├── Redis
 ├── Kafka
 └── S3
```

Security review must understand where sensitive information actually travels.

# 13. Trust Boundaries

Threat models should identify trust-boundary crossings.

```text
Internet
   │
═══╪════════ Trust Boundary
   ▼
AWS Edge
   │
═══╪════════
   ▼
Application
   │
═══╪════════
   ▼
Data Layer
```

Every crossing deserves scrutiny.

# 14. Threat Modeling

Threat modeling should occur for:

```text
New critical systems
Major architecture changes
Authentication flows
Sensitive data processing
External integrations
High-risk features
```

It should happen before deployment, not only after a penetration test finds the design flaw.

# 15. STRIDE

STRIDE may be used as a structured threat-discovery technique.

```text
S → Spoofing
T → Tampering
R → Repudiation
I → Information Disclosure
D → Denial of Service
E → Elevation of Privilege
```

It is a thinking framework, not a compliance checkbox.

# 16. Spoofing

Ask:

```text
Can an attacker impersonate:

User?
Administrator?
Service?
CI pipeline?
AWS workload?
Webhook sender?
```

Identity architecture must provide answers.

# 17. Tampering

Consider unauthorized modification of:

```text
Requests
Database records
Artifacts
Container images
Git repositories
Configuration
Audit evidence
```

Integrity controls differ by asset.

# 18. Repudiation

Sensitive actions should have enough trustworthy audit evidence to establish:

```text
Who
Did what
To which resource
When
From which relevant context
Result
```

# 19. Information Disclosure

Review potential exposure through:

```text
APIs
Logs
Errors
Backups
S3
Metrics
Traces
Database snapshots
Support tooling
```

Observability systems themselves can become data-leak channels.

# 20. Denial of Service

Availability threats include:

```text
Request floods
Expensive queries
Queue flooding
Connection exhaustion
Storage exhaustion
Algorithmic abuse
Dependency exhaustion
```

Autoscaling alone does not solve DoS.

# 21. Elevation of Privilege

Ask whether compromised identities can move from:

```text
User → Admin

Pod → Cluster Admin

Developer → Production

CI → Organization Admin

AWS workload → Account Admin
```

These transitions should be deliberately prevented.

# 22. Attack Trees

Complex threats may use attack trees.

```text
Goal:
Access Restricted Student Data
          │
   ┌──────┼──────────┐
   ▼      ▼          ▼
Steal   Exploit    Compromise
Admin   API auth   Database
```

This helps identify alternative attack paths.

# 23. Abuse Cases

Threat modeling must consider valid functionality used maliciously.

Examples:

```text
Mass account creation
Credential stuffing
Course-content scraping
API enumeration
Spam
Notification abuse
File-upload abuse
Search abuse
```

# 24. Security Requirements

Threat-model outcomes must become actionable requirements.

Bad:

```text
"Improve API security."
```

Better:

```text
Administrative endpoints require MFA-backed privileged identity.

Object authorization must be evaluated server-side.

Uploads are restricted by type and size.

Production S3 buckets prohibit public access.
```

# 25. Identity Architecture

Human and machine identities must remain distinct.

```text
Human Identity
      │
      ├── User
      ├── Administrator
      └── Engineer

Machine Identity
      │
      ├── Service
      ├── CI
      └── Automation
```

Sharing human credentials with machines is rejected.

# 26. Authentication

Authentication proves an identity.

It does not prove that identity may perform a requested operation.

```text
Authentication
     ≠
Authorization
```

# 27. Strong Authentication

Privileged administrative access should require stronger authentication controls than ordinary low-risk operations.

MFA should be required for privileged human access where supported.

# 28. Password Security

If Mediverse stores passwords directly through its identity architecture, passwords should use modern adaptive password hashing.

Never store:

```text
plaintext password

encrypted reversible password

raw SHA-256(password)
```

as password-storage mechanisms.

# 29. Credential Stuffing

Authentication endpoints require defenses against automated reuse of stolen credentials.

Potential controls include:

```text
Rate limiting
Risk detection
MFA
Breached-password controls
Bot defenses
Monitoring
```

# 30. Account Enumeration

Authentication and recovery flows should avoid unnecessary disclosure of whether specific accounts exist.

This must be balanced against user experience and operational requirements.

# 31. Password Reset

Password-reset tokens should be:

```text
Random
Short-lived
Single-use
Securely stored/validated
Invalidated appropriately
```

Reset flows are authentication systems and must be treated accordingly.

# 32. Authorization

Authorization should occur server-side.

Never rely on:

```text
React button hidden
→ therefore user cannot perform operation
```

The backend must enforce access.

# 33. RBAC

Role-Based Access Control is appropriate for broad permissions.

```text
STUDENT
INSTRUCTOR
MODERATOR
ADMIN
```

Roles should not become thousands of ad-hoc permission combinations.

# 34. ABAC

Attribute-Based Access Control may supplement RBAC where access depends on context.

Examples:

```text
Resource owner
Organization
Course
Tenant
Data classification
Relationship
```

# 35. Object-Level Authorization

Every resource operation must consider whether the caller may access that specific object.

```text
GET /users/123/document/789
```

Authentication alone does not authorize access to document `789`.

# 36. IDOR/BOLA

Broken Object Level Authorization is a major API threat.

Never assume an unpredictable UUID is an authorization mechanism.

```text
Resource ID
    ≠
Permission
```

# 37. Least Privilege

Every identity should receive only permissions necessary for its current responsibility.

This applies to:

```text
Users
Administrators
Developers
CI
Pods
AWS services
Databases
```

# 38. Privileged Access

Administrative privileges should be:

```text
Rare
Auditable
Time-bounded where practical
Protected by strong authentication
Separated from normal identities
```

# 39. Break-Glass Access

Emergency privileged access should exist for genuine recovery scenarios.

It must be:

```text
Restricted
Monitored
Audited
Tested
Reviewed after use
```

A break-glass account nobody has tested is not a recovery strategy.

# 40. Machine Identity

Services should authenticate as workloads rather than sharing generic application credentials where platform support exists.

```text
course-service
     │
     ▼
Workload Identity
     │
     ▼
Authorized AWS Resource
```

# 41. EKS Workload Identity

EKS workloads requiring AWS access should use workload-specific AWS identity mechanisms rather than static access keys.

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
Service Account / Workload Identity
 │
 ▼
Scoped IAM Role
```

# 42. Shared AWS Credentials — Rejected

This is rejected:

```text
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY

copied into 30 Kubernetes Secrets
```

Credential rotation and blast radius become unacceptable.

# 43. Service-to-Service Authentication

Internal traffic should not automatically be trusted because both services run inside EKS.

Sensitive service interactions require authenticated identities where risk warrants it.

# 44. mTLS

Mutual TLS may be used where strong workload authentication and transport security are required.

```text
Service A
   │ certificate
   ▼
mTLS
   ▲
   │ certificate
Service B
```

# 45. Service Mesh Evaluation

A service mesh should be introduced only if its benefits justify operational complexity.

Potential capabilities:

```text
mTLS
Workload identity
Traffic policy
Telemetry
Authorization
```

Do not deploy Istio simply because microservices exist.

# 46. Certificate Lifecycle

Certificates require:

```text
Issuance
Validation
Renewal
Rotation
Revocation
Expiration monitoring
```

Manual certificate renewal is an avoidable production outage source.

# 47. API Security

Every API should be treated as an externally attackable interface according to its exposure and trust boundary.

Security must include:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Validation
Rate limits
Abuse controls
Logging
Transport security
```

# 48. OWASP API Risks

API security reviews should explicitly consider relevant OWASP API threat categories, particularly:

```text
Broken object authorization
Broken authentication
Property-level authorization
Resource consumption
Function-level authorization
Sensitive business-flow abuse
SSRF
Security misconfiguration
Unsafe API consumption
Inventory failures
```

# 49. API Inventory

Mediverse must know which APIs exist.

Track:

```text
Owner
Version
Exposure
Authentication model
Data classification
Lifecycle
```

Forgotten APIs become security liabilities.

# 50. API Version Retirement

Deprecated API versions must eventually be removed.

Keeping every historical API forever preserves historical vulnerabilities forever.

# 51. Input Validation

All external input is untrusted.

Validate:

```text
Type
Length
Range
Format
Structure
Allowed values
Business constraints
```

at the server.

# 52. Allowlist Validation

Where practical:

```text
Allow known-valid
```

is stronger than attempting to enumerate every malicious possibility.

# 53. Injection

Applications must use safe APIs for:

```text
SQL
Shell commands
LDAP
Templates
Search queries
```

String concatenation of untrusted input into executable/query contexts is rejected.

# 54. SQL Injection

Use parameterized queries/ORM binding correctly.

Do not construct:

```text
"SELECT ... WHERE email = '" + userInput + "'"
```

# 55. SSRF

Server-side URL fetching must treat URLs as hostile input.

Controls may include:

```text
Allowed destinations
Protocol restrictions
DNS/IP validation
Network egress controls
Metadata-service protection
Redirect validation
```

# 56. Unsafe Deserialization

Do not deserialize arbitrary attacker-controlled objects into powerful runtime types.

Use explicit schemas and restricted data models.

# 57. Mass Assignment

APIs should not blindly bind request objects directly to privileged persistence models.

Example risk:

```json
{
  "name": "User",
  "role": "SUPER_ADMIN"
}
```

when `role` was never supposed to be user-controlled.

# 58. Error Handling

External errors should not expose:

```text
Stack traces
Database credentials
SQL statements
Internal filesystem paths
Secret values
Infrastructure internals
```

Detailed diagnostics belong in protected observability systems.

# 59. Rate Limiting

Rate limiting should exist at appropriate layers.

```text
Edge
 │
 ▼
API
 │
 ▼
Expensive operation
```

Different endpoints may require different limits.

# 60. Resource Consumption Controls

Protect expensive operations through:

```text
Request size limits
Pagination
Timeouts
Concurrency controls
Query limits
Upload limits
Queue limits
```

Rate limits alone are insufficient.

---

## ADR-064 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The security model now begins with:

```text
                       ASSET
                         │
                         ▼
                  CLASSIFICATION
                         │
                         ▼
                   DATA FLOW
                         │
                         ▼
                 TRUST BOUNDARY
                         │
                         ▼
                  THREAT MODEL
                         │
                         ▼
               SECURITY REQUIREMENT
                         │
             ┌───────────┼───────────┐
             ▼           ▼           ▼
          IDENTITY    APPLICATION   PLATFORM
             │           │           │
             └───────────┼───────────┘
                         ▼
                  SECURITY CONTROL
                         │
                         ▼
                    TELEMETRY
                         │
                         ▼
                 DETECT / RESPOND
```

The critical principle is:

> **Authentication is not authorization, internal networking is not trust, encryption is not complete security, and a successful vulnerability scan is not proof that the architecture is secure.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Bot & Abuse Protection**, then cover **session security → JWT architecture and threats → OAuth 2.x/OIDC → token lifecycle → refresh-token rotation → frontend security → CSP → XSS → CSRF → CORS → clickjacking → Spring Security hardening → file-upload security → malware scanning → S3 security → Kubernetes threat model → Pod Security Standards → RBAC → service accounts → NetworkPolicy → admission control → secrets → runtime security → Falco evaluation → container escape → node hardening → EKS control-plane security → AWS Organizations/SCPs → IAM guardrails → KMS/key hierarchy → Secrets Manager → WAF → Shield → GuardDuty → Security Hub → Inspector → CloudTrail → Config → Detective evaluation → encryption at rest/in transit → field-level encryption/tokenization → backup security → privacy-by-design → data minimization → retention/deletion → consent → compliance applicability → HIPAA/GDPR/SOC 2/ISO 27001 evaluation → vulnerability management → penetration testing → bug bounty → security logging/SIEM → SOC → detection engineering → MITRE ATT&CK → security incident response → credential compromise → ransomware → breach response → insider threats → tabletop exercises → risk register → exceptions → security architecture review → Secure SDLC → security champions → security metrics → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise security reference architecture.**

# ADR-064 — Enterprise Security Architecture

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Resource Consumption Controls**.

---

# 61. Bot & Abuse Protection

Not every malicious interaction exploits a software vulnerability.

Legitimate functionality can be automated at abusive scale.

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
Bot / Human?
   │
   ▼
Abuse Detection
   │
   ├── Legitimate → Continue
   │
   └── Suspicious → Challenge / Limit / Block
```

Potential abuse includes:

```text
Credential stuffing
Account creation farms
Content scraping
Enumeration
Spam
Search abuse
Expensive API abuse
Automated uploads
```

---

# 62. Abuse Controls

Controls should be layered:

```text
AWS WAF
   │
   ▼
Rate Limiting
   │
   ▼
Authentication Controls
   │
   ▼
Application-Level Quotas
   │
   ▼
Behavioral Detection
```

IP blocking alone is insufficient against distributed attackers.

---

# 63. Session Security

Browser sessions require explicit lifecycle controls.

Consider:

```text
Creation
Expiration
Idle timeout
Revocation
Logout
Credential changes
Device/session management
```

A session should not remain valid indefinitely simply because authentication succeeded once.

---

# 64. Cookie Security

Where cookies carry authentication/session information, appropriate attributes should include:

```text
Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
```

according to the application architecture.

Sensitive authentication cookies should not be readable by ordinary frontend JavaScript unless the design genuinely requires it.

---

# 65. JWT Architecture

JWTs are signed data structures—not encrypted secret containers by default.

Therefore:

```text
JWT Payload
     ≠
Secret Storage
```

Do not put passwords, secrets or unnecessarily sensitive information inside JWT claims.

---

# 66. JWT Validation

Resource servers must validate appropriate:

```text
Signature
Issuer
Audience
Expiration
Not-before constraints
Algorithm expectations
Required claims
```

Parsing a JWT is not equivalent to authenticating it.

---

# 67. JWT Algorithm Security

The verifier must control which algorithms are acceptable.

Never trust an attacker-controlled token to decide how it should be verified.

---

# 68. JWT Lifetime

Access tokens should normally be relatively short-lived.

```text
Short-lived Access Token
          +
Controlled Refresh Mechanism
```

is preferable to access tokens remaining valid for days or months.

---

# 69. JWT Revocation Limitation

Stateless JWT validation creates a trade-off:

```text
No central lookup
      │
      ▼
Fast validation

but

Issued token
      │
      ▼
Harder immediate revocation
```

Token lifetime and session architecture must account for this.

---

# 70. Refresh Tokens

Refresh tokens represent high-value credentials.

They require stronger protection than ordinary access tokens.

```text
Refresh Token
     │
     ▼
Authorization Server
     │
     ▼
New Access Token
```

---

# 71. Refresh-Token Rotation

Where supported, refresh-token rotation should issue a new refresh token when the previous one is used.

```text
RT1
 │
 ▼
Exchange
 │
 ├── AT2
 └── RT2

RT1 → invalid/reused detection
```

This can improve detection and containment of token theft.

---

# 72. OAuth Architecture

OAuth should be used as an authorization framework—not invented independently inside every Mediverse service.

```text
User
  │
  ▼
Authorization Server
  │
  ▼
Client
  │
  ▼
Access Token
  │
  ▼
Resource Server
```

---

# 73. OpenID Connect

OIDC should provide authentication identity semantics on top of OAuth where applicable.

```text
OAuth
→ delegated authorization

OIDC
→ authentication/identity layer
```

These concepts should not be treated as identical.

---

# 74. Authorization Code + PKCE

Browser/mobile public clients should use modern authorization flows such as Authorization Code with PKCE where appropriate.

Legacy insecure OAuth patterns should not be introduced.

---

# 75. Redirect URI Security

OAuth redirect URIs must be tightly controlled.

Loose wildcard redirects can turn authentication infrastructure into a token-stealing mechanism.

---

# 76. Token Audience

A token issued for one resource should not automatically authorize another unrelated resource.

```text
Token audience:
course-api

       X

admin-api
```

Audience validation reduces token confusion.

---

# 77. Token Scope

OAuth scopes should express meaningful delegated capabilities.

Avoid:

```text
scope=everything
```

for every application.

---

# 78. Frontend Security Boundary

The browser is an untrusted execution environment.

Anything delivered to the browser should be considered visible or modifiable by the user.

Therefore frontend code cannot safely contain:

```text
Database passwords
AWS secret keys
Private API credentials
Signing keys
Server secrets
```

---

# 79. XSS

Cross-Site Scripting can execute attacker-controlled JavaScript in a user's browser context.

Controls include:

```text
Framework escaping
Safe DOM APIs
Input/output handling
CSP
Dependency security
Avoiding dangerous HTML injection
```

---

# 80. React and XSS

React's normal rendering behavior provides useful escaping, but React does not make XSS impossible.

Features such as raw HTML insertion require extreme caution.

Security must not rely on:

> "We use React, therefore XSS cannot happen."

---

# 81. Content Security Policy

CSP should be adopted for web applications where practical.

A strong CSP can restrict:

```text
Script sources
Frame sources
Connections
Images
Objects
Base URI
Form destinations
```

and reduce XSS impact.

---

# 82. CSP Rollout

CSP should often begin with monitoring/reporting and then move toward enforcement.

A policy allowing:

```text
*
unsafe-inline
unsafe-eval
```

provides far less protection than teams sometimes assume.

---

# 83. CSRF

Cookie-authenticated state-changing operations require CSRF consideration because browsers automatically attach cookies.

```text
Victim Browser
      │
      ▼
Malicious Site
      │
      ▼
Authenticated Request
```

SameSite and CSRF-token strategies should match the authentication architecture.

---

# 84. CORS

CORS is a browser-origin access control mechanism.

It is **not** backend authentication.

This is rejected:

```text
CORS allows only mediverse.com
therefore API is secure
```

Non-browser clients are not constrained by browser CORS enforcement.

---

# 85. CORS Policy

Production APIs should use explicit allowed origins rather than unrestricted:

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

when credentials or sensitive operations are involved.

---

# 86. Clickjacking

Web applications should restrict unauthorized framing where appropriate through:

```text
CSP frame-ancestors
```

and/or applicable browser security headers.

---

# 87. Browser Security Headers

Relevant applications should evaluate/enforce appropriate:

```text
Content-Security-Policy
Strict-Transport-Security
X-Content-Type-Options
Referrer-Policy
Permissions-Policy
```

according to application behavior.

---

# 88. Spring Security

Spring Boot services should centralize security using Spring Security rather than implementing authentication filters and authorization logic inconsistently across controllers.

---

# 89. Method Security

Sensitive business operations should receive authorization close to the operation where useful.

```text
HTTP Security
     +
Method/Domain Authorization
```

provides defense in depth.

---

# 90. Security Context

Business logic should derive identity from trusted authentication context.

Do not accept:

```json
{
  "userId": "administrator"
}
```

from a client and assume that represents the authenticated actor.

---

# 91. File Upload Security

Uploads are hostile input.

Validate:

```text
Maximum size
Allowed type
Actual content
Filename handling
Storage location
Authorization
Malware status
```

---

# 92. File Extension Validation

A filename ending in:

```text
.pdf
```

does not prove that the content is a PDF.

Content validation should not rely only on extensions.

---

# 93. Uploaded Filenames

Do not directly trust client filenames as storage paths.

Prevent:

```text
Path traversal
Name collisions
Control characters
Unsafe metadata
```

Generate server-controlled storage identifiers.

---

# 94. Malware Scanning

Where users can upload files later consumed or downloaded by others, malware scanning should be incorporated according to risk.

```text
Upload
  │
  ▼
Quarantine
  │
  ▼
Scan
  │
 ┌┴─────────────┐
 ▼              ▼
Clean        Malicious
 │              │
Release       Reject
```

---

# 95. Upload Quarantine

Unverified uploads should not immediately become publicly accessible.

Quarantine separates ingestion from trusted availability.

---

# 96. S3 Security

Production S3 buckets should default to:

```text
Block public access
Encryption
Least-privilege IAM
Logging/auditing where required
Lifecycle policy
Versioning where justified
```

Public access should be explicit and exceptional.

---

# 97. Presigned URLs

Presigned URLs should be:

```text
Short-lived
Purpose-specific
Permission-scoped
```

They are bearer capabilities and must be protected accordingly.

---

# 98. Kubernetes Threat Model

A compromised pod must not automatically imply:

```text
Pod
 ↓
Node
 ↓
Cluster
 ↓
AWS Account
 ↓
Enterprise
```

Every transition should encounter another security boundary.

---

# 99. Pod Security Standards

Production workloads should generally target Kubernetes Restricted Pod Security Standards where application compatibility permits.

Avoid unnecessary:

```text
privileged: true
hostNetwork
hostPID
hostPath
root execution
dangerous capabilities
```

---

# 100. Container User

Application containers should run as non-root where practical.

```text
runAsNonRoot: true
```

should become the normal expectation rather than an exception.

---

# 101. Linux Capabilities

Containers should drop unnecessary capabilities.

Preferred direction:

```text
Drop ALL
   │
   ▼
Add only specifically required capability
```

---

# 102. Read-Only Filesystem

Applications should use read-only root filesystems where compatible.

Writable locations should be explicitly defined.

---

# 103. Kubernetes RBAC

RBAC permissions should be scoped to:

```text
Required verbs
Required resources
Required namespaces
```

Avoid:

```text
resources: ["*"]
verbs: ["*"]
```

for normal workloads.

---

# 104. Service Accounts

Each workload should use an appropriately scoped service account.

Do not share one privileged service account across unrelated applications.

---

# 105. Service Account Tokens

Workloads that do not require Kubernetes API access should avoid unnecessary service-account token exposure where supported.

---

# 106. NetworkPolicy

Namespaces should adopt default network restrictions where practical.

```text
Pod
 │
 ├── Allowed → Required dependency
 │
 └── Denied  → Everything else
```

Flat pod-to-pod networking should not automatically imply unrestricted communication.

---

# 107. Egress Security

Outbound traffic matters as much as inbound traffic.

A compromised application with unrestricted internet egress can:

```text
Exfiltrate data
Contact command-and-control infrastructure
Download payloads
Attack external systems
```

Egress controls should be risk-based.

---

# 108. Admission Control

ADR-061's policy architecture should enforce important workload constraints before resources enter the cluster.

Examples:

```text
Approved registries
No privileged workloads
Required resource controls
Required security context
Signature verification
Required labels
```

---

# 109. Kubernetes Secrets

Kubernetes Secrets are not automatically a complete secret-management system.

Base64 encoding is not encryption.

Production secret authority remains the architecture defined in ADR-061:

```text
AWS Secrets Manager
       │
       ▼
External Secrets
       │
       ▼
Kubernetes
```

---

# 110. Secret Rotation

Applications should support secret rotation without requiring dangerous manual procedures.

Rotation design must include the consumer lifecycle.

---

# 111. Runtime Security

Preventive controls will not catch everything.

Runtime detection should observe suspicious behavior such as:

```text
Unexpected shell execution
Sensitive file access
Privilege escalation attempts
Unusual process execution
Unexpected network activity
Container escape indicators
```

---

# 112. Falco Evaluation

Falco or an equivalent runtime security technology should be evaluated for Kubernetes runtime threat detection.

It should only be deployed with:

```text
Tuned rules
Alert ownership
Response procedures
Noise control
```

Thousands of ignored Falco alerts provide no security.

---

# 113. Container Escape

Container isolation is not equivalent to a hardened security boundary against every kernel-level attack.

Controls include:

```text
Node patching
Non-root containers
Capability reduction
Seccomp
No privileged mode
Minimal host mounts
Runtime monitoring
```

---

# 114. Seccomp

Production containers should use an appropriate seccomp profile where supported.

Default runtime profiles are preferable to completely unconfined syscall access.

---

# 115. Node Security

EKS worker nodes should be:

```text
Minimal
Patched
Immutable/replaced rather than manually modified
Access-restricted
Monitored
```

Routine SSH administration should not be the operating model.

---

# 116. EKS Control Plane Security

EKS controls should include appropriate:

```text
Endpoint access restrictions
Audit logging
Authentication controls
RBAC
Encryption
Network architecture
Upgrade governance
```

---

# 117. AWS Organizations

Mediverse should use AWS Organizations to establish account-level isolation and centralized governance.

```text
AWS Organization
      │
      ├── Security
      ├── Logging
      ├── Shared Services
      ├── NonProd
      └── Production
```

Account separation reduces blast radius.

---

# 118. Service Control Policies

SCPs should provide organizational guardrails.

Potential restrictions:

```text
Disable security logging
Leave organization
Use prohibited regions
Disable foundational controls
Create disallowed resource classes
```

SCPs are guardrails—not application authorization systems.

---

# 119. IAM

AWS IAM should follow:

```text
Least privilege
Role-based access
Short-lived credentials
Workload identities
Strong human authentication
Auditing
```

Long-lived IAM user access keys should be minimized aggressively.

---

# 120. IAM Permission Boundaries

Permission boundaries may be used where delegated role creation requires a maximum privilege ceiling.

They should not replace well-designed IAM policies.

---

# 121. KMS

AWS KMS should provide centralized cryptographic key management for supported AWS services and application encryption requirements.

```text
Application / AWS Service
          │
          ▼
         KMS
          │
          ▼
Controlled Key Operation
```

---

# 122. Key Hierarchy

Do not use one universal encryption key for everything.

Key separation should consider:

```text
Environment
Data classification
Application/domain
Operational ownership
Blast radius
```

---

# 123. Envelope Encryption

For application-level encryption, envelope encryption should be preferred where appropriate.

```text
KMS Key
   │
   ▼
Data Encryption Key
   │
   ▼
Sensitive Data
```

Large datasets should not be directly encrypted by repeatedly sending every byte to KMS.

---

# 124. Key Rotation

Cryptographic key lifecycle requires:

```text
Creation
Usage
Rotation
Revocation
Deletion controls
Audit
```

Rotation should be tested, not merely configured.

---

# 125. Secrets Manager

AWS Secrets Manager should remain the production authority for appropriate application secrets.

Store:

```text
Database credentials
API credentials
Integration secrets
```

not arbitrary application configuration.

---

# 126. AWS WAF

AWS WAF should protect relevant internet-facing application endpoints.

Controls may include:

```text
Managed rules
Rate-based rules
IP reputation
Request constraints
Application-specific rules
Bot controls where justified
```

---

# 127. AWS Shield

AWS Shield provides DDoS protection capabilities.

Shield Advanced should be evaluated based on:

```text
Business criticality
Exposure
DDoS risk
Cost
Required response capabilities
```

It should not be purchased merely because "enterprise architecture" sounds incomplete without it.

---

# 128. GuardDuty

Amazon GuardDuty should provide threat detection across supported AWS telemetry sources.

Findings must enter an owned response workflow.

Detection without response ownership is security theatre.

---

# 129. Security Hub

AWS Security Hub should aggregate relevant security posture/findings where it improves centralized governance.

Findings should be:

```text
Prioritized
Assigned
Tracked
Remediated
```

not simply accumulated.

---

# 130. Inspector

Amazon Inspector should be used where appropriate for supported workload vulnerability assessment.

It complements—not replaces—the CI scanning controls from ADR-062.

---

# 131. CloudTrail

CloudTrail is foundational audit telemetry.

Security teams should be able to determine:

```text
Who called which AWS API?
When?
From where?
Against what?
Was it successful?
```

Critical audit trails should receive centralized protection.

---

# 132. AWS Config

AWS Config should support configuration/compliance visibility where required.

It complements Terraform drift management because:

```text
Terraform
→ desired infrastructure state

AWS Config
→ observed AWS resource configuration/compliance
```

---

# 133. Detective

Amazon Detective may be evaluated where its investigation capabilities materially improve AWS security investigations.

Do not add investigation products without an operating model to use them.

---

# 134. Encryption in Transit

Sensitive network communication should use modern TLS.

This includes appropriate:

```text
Internet → Edge
Service → Service
Application → Database
Application → AWS service
Administrative access
```

depending on the service capabilities and risk.

---

# 135. Encryption at Rest

Sensitive persistent storage should use encryption.

Examples:

```text
RDS
S3
EBS
Backups
Snapshots
Log stores
Artifact repositories
```

Encryption should be enabled through centrally governed controls.

---

# 136. Field-Level Encryption

Highly sensitive fields may require protection beyond volume/database encryption.

```text
Database
   │
   ├── Normal fields
   │
   └── Sensitive field → application-level encryption
```

Use only where threat model and requirements justify the operational complexity.

---

# 137. Tokenization

Tokenization may replace sensitive identifiers with controlled tokens where systems do not need the original value.

This can reduce sensitive-data exposure across downstream services.

---

# 138. Backup Security

Backups contain the same sensitive information as production systems.

Therefore they require:

```text
Encryption
Access control
Retention
Immutability where appropriate
Auditability
Restore testing
Deletion lifecycle
```

An encrypted production database with publicly exposed backups is not secure.

---

# 139. Privacy by Design

Privacy requirements should influence architecture before data collection begins.

Ask:

```text
Do we need this data?

Why?

For how long?

Who needs access?

Where will it flow?

Can we avoid collecting it?
```

---

# 140. Data Minimization

The safest sensitive data is data Mediverse never collected.

Services should request and persist only information required for legitimate functionality.

---

# 141. Data Retention

Retention policies should define:

```text
Data category
Purpose
Retention duration
Deletion trigger
Legal/compliance constraints
Owner
```

"Keep forever because storage is cheap" is rejected.

---

# 142. Data Deletion

Deletion architecture must account for copies across:

```text
Primary databases
Caches
Search indexes
Object storage
Analytics
Backups
Logs
```

Deleting one PostgreSQL row does not necessarily delete the user's data ecosystem-wide.

---

# 143. Consent and Purpose

Where applicable, data usage should align with the purpose and consent/legal basis under which it was collected.

Consent requirements depend on actual Mediverse jurisdiction and product operation.

They must not be invented from the technology architecture alone.

---

# 144. Compliance Applicability

Framework applicability must be determined from actual business/legal facts.

Mediverse should **not automatically claim**:

```text
HIPAA compliant
GDPR compliant
SOC 2 compliant
ISO 27001 certified
```

simply because security controls exist.

Technical architecture supports compliance; it does not create legal applicability or certification.

---

# 145. Security Assurance Program

The security program should combine:

```text
Secure SDLC
      │
      ├── Threat Modeling
      ├── Code Review
      ├── SAST/SCA
      ├── Supply-Chain Security
      ├── Vulnerability Management
      ├── Penetration Testing
      ├── Cloud Security
      └── Runtime Detection
```

No single scanner replaces this system.

---

# 146. Vulnerability Management

Vulnerabilities require lifecycle governance:

```text
Discover
   │
   ▼
Validate
   │
   ▼
Prioritize
   │
   ▼
Assign
   │
   ▼
Remediate / Mitigate
   │
   ▼
Verify
   │
   ▼
Close
```

Prioritization should consider exploitability, exposure and business impact—not CVSS alone.

---

# 147. Security Operations & Incident Response

Security telemetry should flow into an operational detection/response capability.

```text
CloudTrail ───────┐
GuardDuty ────────┤
WAF ──────────────┤
Application ──────┤
EKS Runtime ──────┤
Identity ─────────┤
                  ▼
             SIEM / Detection
                  │
                  ▼
             Investigation
                  │
            ┌─────┴─────┐
            ▼           ▼
          Benign      Incident
                        │
                        ▼
                    Containment
                        │
                        ▼
                    Eradication
                        │
                        ▼
                     Recovery
                        │
                        ▼
                     Lessons
```

Detection engineering should map important scenarios to attacker behavior frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK where useful.

Incident playbooks should cover at minimum:

```text
Credential compromise
Privileged account compromise
Malicious artifact
Data exposure
Ransomware/extortion scenario
Compromised Kubernetes workload
Compromised CI pipeline
Dependency compromise
Insider misuse
AWS account compromise
```

Tabletop exercises should validate these procedures before a real incident.

---

# 148. Security Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Internal network treated as trusted

❌ Authentication treated as authorization

❌ Frontend authorization treated as security enforcement

❌ UUIDs treated as access control

❌ Shared administrator accounts

❌ Permanent privileged access without justification

❌ AWS access keys copied into Kubernetes Secrets

❌ One IAM role shared by unrelated workloads

❌ Wildcard IAM permissions everywhere

❌ Internal microservice traffic automatically trusted

❌ Service mesh deployed merely because microservices exist

❌ JWT payload treated as secret storage

❌ JWT parsed without complete validation

❌ Multi-day/month access tokens without justification

❌ Refresh tokens handled like ordinary cookies/local data

❌ CORS treated as API authentication

❌ React treated as proof XSS is impossible

❌ CSP containing broad wildcards and unsafe directives called "secure"

❌ Secrets embedded in frontend bundles

❌ User-supplied IDs trusted as authenticated identity

❌ File extension treated as content validation

❌ Uploaded files immediately made public

❌ Client filenames used directly as filesystem/storage paths

❌ Public S3 buckets created by default

❌ Presigned URLs with excessive lifetime

❌ Privileged containers accepted by default

❌ Containers running as root without need

❌ Shared Kubernetes service accounts

❌ Flat unrestricted Kubernetes networking

❌ Kubernetes Secrets confused with a complete secrets-management system

❌ Runtime security generating thousands of ignored alerts

❌ Routine SSH into EKS nodes

❌ One AWS account for the entire enterprise

❌ Long-lived IAM users used for automation

❌ One KMS key used indiscriminately for everything

❌ Encryption at rest treated as complete data security

❌ Production encrypted while backups remain weakly protected

❌ Sensitive data logged for debugging

❌ Collecting data because "we might need it later"

❌ Infinite data retention

❌ User deletion implemented only in one database

❌ Claiming HIPAA/GDPR compliance from architecture diagrams

❌ CVSS score used as the only vulnerability priority

❌ Penetration test performed once per year and called a security program

❌ Security findings accumulated without ownership

❌ GuardDuty/Security Hub enabled without response workflows

❌ Security incidents handled without evidence preservation

❌ "Blameless" used to avoid accountability for security failures

❌ Security exceptions without owner or expiration

❌ Security review performed only immediately before production
```

---
