# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                         | Decision                                        |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Security model               | **Zero Trust + Defense in Depth**               |
| Core assumption              | Assume breach                                   |
| Asset inventory              | Required                                        |
| Asset ownership              | Required                                        |
| Data classification          | Required                                        |
| Data-flow mapping            | Required for critical systems                   |
| Threat modeling              | Required for high-risk changes                  |
| Threat methodology           | STRIDE + abuse-case analysis                    |
| Human authentication         | Strong authentication/MFA for privileged access |
| Authorization                | Server-side                                     |
| Access model                 | RBAC + selective ABAC                           |
| Object authorization         | Mandatory                                       |
| Privilege model              | Least privilege                                 |
| Emergency access             | Audited break-glass                             |
| Machine identity             | Workload identity                               |
| Static AWS keys in workloads | **Rejected**                                    |
| Internal network trust       | **Rejected**                                    |
| Service mTLS                 | Risk-based                                      |
| Service mesh                 | Only if justified                               |
| API inventory                | Required                                        |
| Input validation             | Allowlist-oriented                              |
| Rate limiting                | Layered                                         |
| OAuth/OIDC                   | Standardized identity protocols                 |
| Public-client OAuth          | Authorization Code + PKCE                       |
| JWTs                         | Short-lived, strictly validated                 |
| Refresh tokens               | Protected + rotation preferred                  |
| Frontend secrets             | **Prohibited**                                  |
| CSP                          | Required where practical                        |
| XSS/CSRF                     | Explicitly controlled                           |
| CORS                         | Explicit, not authentication                    |
| Spring Security              | Standard backend security framework             |
| File uploads                 | Validate + quarantine + scan where required     |
| S3                           | Private by default                              |
| Pod security                 | Restricted baseline where compatible            |
| Container user               | Non-root preferred                              |
| Kubernetes RBAC              | Least privilege                                 |
| NetworkPolicy                | Default restriction preferred                   |
| Admission control            | Required                                        |
| Secret authority             | AWS Secrets Manager                             |
| Runtime detection            | Required/evaluated                              |
| Falco                        | Evaluate/adopt with tuned rules                 |
| EKS nodes                    | Hardened/replaceable                            |
| AWS accounts                 | Segmented                                       |
| Organizations/SCP            | Governance baseline                             |
| IAM                          | Short-lived + least privilege                   |
| Encryption keys              | AWS KMS                                         |
| Key separation               | Required                                        |
| Encryption at rest           | Required for sensitive stores                   |
| Encryption in transit        | Required                                        |
| Field encryption             | Risk-based                                      |
| Backup security              | Equivalent to production data                   |
| Privacy model                | Privacy by design                               |
| Data minimization            | Required                                        |
| Retention                    | Explicit                                        |
| Deletion                     | End-to-end                                      |
| Compliance claims            | Evidence/applicability based only               |
| Vulnerability management     | Risk-based lifecycle                            |
| Security telemetry           | Centralized                                     |
| SIEM/SOC                     | Required as organizational scale/risk warrants  |
| Detection engineering        | Required                                        |
| Security incident response   | Required                                        |
| Tabletop exercises           | Required for critical scenarios                 |
| Security exceptions          | Owned + expiring                                |
| Security architecture review | Risk-based                                      |
| Secure SDLC                  | Mandatory                                       |
| Status                       | **Accepted**                                    |
| Priority                     | **Critical**                                    |

# ADR-064 — COMPLETE ✅

The Mediverse security lifecycle is now:

```text
IDENTIFY
   │
   ▼
CLASSIFY
   │
   ▼
THREAT MODEL
   │
   ▼
PREVENT
   │
   ▼
VERIFY
   │
   ▼
DETECT
   │
   ▼
RESPOND
   │
   ▼
RECOVER
   │
   ▼
LEARN
   │
   ▼
IMPROVE
   │
   └──────────────► THREAT MODEL
```

The defining invariant is:

> **No user, service, pod, network, artifact, repository, pipeline or AWS account receives trust merely because of where it exists. Access must be explicitly authenticated, authorized, constrained, observable and revocable.**

## Next — ADR-065

### **ADR-065 — Enterprise Data Architecture, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, OpenSearch, S3, Data Governance, Data Lifecycle, Backup/DR & Data Platform**

ADR-065 should now go deep into the data layer itself: **data architecture principles → operational vs analytical data → system-of-record ownership → database-per-service → shared database anti-pattern → PostgreSQL architecture → schema design → normalization/denormalization → primary/foreign keys → UUID vs sequence IDs → indexes → query planning → transactions → isolation levels → optimistic/pessimistic locking → connection pooling/HikariCP → PgBouncer evaluation → read replicas → partitioning → PostgreSQL extensions → RDS/Aurora PostgreSQL decision → Multi-AZ → backups/PITR → Redis architecture → cache-aside → TTL → invalidation → cache stampede → distributed locking → session storage → Redis HA → Kafka domain events → topic design → partition keys → ordering → consumer groups → delivery semantics → idempotency → retries → DLQs → schema evolution → Schema Registry → transactional outbox → CDC/Debezium evaluation → event replay → OpenSearch indexing → search synchronization → index lifecycle → S3 object architecture → presigned uploads → lifecycle/tiering → data ownership → data contracts → lineage → metadata → quality → retention → archival → deletion → privacy integration → encryption → backup architecture → RPO/RTO → restore testing → regional disaster recovery → data migration → zero-downtime schema evolution → analytics platform boundary → lake/lakehouse evaluation → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise data reference architecture.**

# ADR-065 — Enterprise Data Architecture & Data Platform

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-065
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-064 established how Mediverse protects identities, workloads and sensitive information.

ADR-065 establishes how Mediverse **owns, stores, queries, caches, searches, streams, protects, retains, restores and eventually deletes data**.

> **A technology should own data because its consistency, access and lifecycle characteristics fit the workload—not because the technology is fashionable or already installed.**

```text id="7p4jcv"
                           MEDIVERSE
                               │
                               ▼
                         DOMAIN SERVICES
                               │
             ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
             ▼                 ▼                 ▼
        TRANSACTIONAL        EVENTS           OBJECTS
             │                 │                 │
             ▼                 ▼                 ▼
        PostgreSQL           Kafka              S3
             │                 │
             ├───────┐         │
             ▼       ▼         ▼
           Redis  OpenSearch  Consumers
             │       │
             └───────┼─────────────────┐
                     ▼                 ▼
                Derived State      Analytics
                     │
                     ▼
              DATA GOVERNANCE
                     │
        ┌────────────┼────────────┐
        ▼            ▼            ▼
      Quality      Lineage      Lifecycle
                                   │
                                   ▼
                             Backup / DR
```

# 1. Data Architecture Principles

Mediverse data architecture should optimize for:

```text id="dbctfx"
Correctness
Ownership
Availability
Durability
Performance
Security
Recoverability
Traceability
Lifecycle governance
```

No single database should be expected to optimize every dimension.

# 2. Polyglot Persistence

Mediverse adopts controlled polyglot persistence.

```text id="zd20ck"
PostgreSQL
→ transactional relational state

Redis
→ transient/cache state

Kafka
→ durable event streams

OpenSearch
→ search/read projections

S3
→ object/blob storage
```

Polyglot persistence is useful only when each technology has a clear responsibility.

# 3. Database Proliferation

Using multiple data technologies introduces:

```text id="8b8z7m"
Operational complexity
Backup complexity
Security complexity
Consistency challenges
Developer learning cost
Monitoring requirements
```

A new datastore requires architectural justification.

# 4. Operational vs Analytical Data

Operational systems and analytical systems have different workloads.

```text id="yhr02j"
OLTP
→ transactions
→ low latency
→ current operational state

Analytics
→ aggregation
→ historical analysis
→ large scans
```

Large analytical queries should not routinely compete with production transactions.

# 5. System of Record

Every important data entity should have an authoritative owner.

Example:

```text id="1nmzwj"
User Service
     │
     ▼
User Database
     │
     ▼
SYSTEM OF RECORD
```

Redis, Kafka and OpenSearch copies do not automatically become authoritative.

# 6. Derived State

Derived stores should be reconstructable where practical.

```text id="g3x1dx"
PostgreSQL
     │
     ▼
Domain Event
     │
     ├── Redis
     └── OpenSearch
```

If OpenSearch is lost, Mediverse should not lose authoritative course data.

# 7. Data Ownership

A service owns its domain data and is responsible for:

```text id="b3z43e"
Schema
Integrity
Access
Migration
Retention
Events
Recovery
```

Ownership should be explicit.

# 8. Database per Service

For independently deployable microservices, logical database ownership should follow service/domain boundaries.

```text id="ulz6n2"
Course Service ─────► Course Data

User Service ───────► User Data

Assessment Service ─► Assessment Data
```

This does not necessarily require a separate physical RDS instance for every microservice.

# 9. Logical vs Physical Isolation

Isolation can exist at several levels:

```text id="drayb2"
RDS instance
   │
Database
   │
Schema
   │
Table
```

The correct level depends on:

```text id="2xnxpm"
Scale
Security
Failure isolation
Cost
Operational maturity
```

# 10. Shared Database Anti-Pattern

This architecture is rejected:

```text id="2o31ca"
Service A ─┐
Service B ─┼──► Same tables
Service C ─┘
```

where every service directly manipulates every other service's tables.

That creates hidden runtime and deployment coupling.

# 11. Cross-Service Data Access

A service requiring another domain's data should normally use:

```text id="0if5mg"
API
Event
Materialized projection
```

rather than direct SQL into another service's private schema.

# 12. Data Contract

Cross-domain data sharing requires a contract.

Contracts should define:

```text id="eh9ilq"
Meaning
Schema
Ownership
Compatibility
Nullability
Lifecycle
```

Data contracts apply to APIs and events.

# 13. PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL should remain Mediverse's primary relational OLTP database.

Appropriate workloads include:

```text id="w6mup4"
Users
Courses
Enrollments
Assessments
Permissions
Transactions
Metadata
Workflow state
```

# 14. PostgreSQL Schema Design

Schema design should start from domain invariants, not ORM convenience.

```text id="h6v0ik"
Domain Rule
    │
    ▼
Data Model
    │
    ▼
Constraints
    │
    ▼
Application Mapping
```

The database should enforce important integrity rules where appropriate.

# 15. Normalization

Transactional schemas should generally begin normalized enough to avoid unnecessary duplication and update anomalies.

```text id="vzgig4"
Student
Course
Enrollment
```

should represent separate concepts rather than repeatedly embedding entire student/course records.

# 16. Denormalization

Denormalization is justified when measurement demonstrates a meaningful read/performance requirement.

It introduces synchronization complexity.

Do not denormalize merely because joins "sound slow."

# 17. Primary Keys

Every important relational entity should have a stable primary key.

Primary-key choice should consider:

```text id="8fxnax"
Uniqueness
Index locality
Exposure
Generation model
Distribution
Storage
```

# 18. Sequence IDs

PostgreSQL-generated numeric identifiers provide:

```text id="kwfek8"
Compact indexes
Good locality
Simple generation
```

but expose predictable identifiers if used externally.

Predictability itself is not an authorization vulnerability if authorization is implemented correctly.

# 19. UUIDs

UUIDs are useful for distributed generation and opaque external identifiers.

They cost more index/storage space than compact integers.

UUIDs should not be chosen because someone believes:

```text id="6tm4m4"
UUID = secure
```

Authorization remains mandatory.

# 20. UUID Strategy

If UUIDs are heavily indexed at scale, time-ordered UUID approaches may improve index locality compared with purely random identifiers where ecosystem support and requirements justify them.

# 21. Foreign Keys

Foreign keys should enforce important relational integrity inside an owned relational boundary.

```text id="67snvc"
Enrollment.course_id
       │
       ▼
Course.id
```

# 22. Cross-Service Foreign Keys

Foreign keys should not create database-level coupling between independently owned microservice domains.

Distributed boundaries require application/event contracts instead.

# 23. Constraints

Use database constraints for invariants such as:

```text id="bcrl3j"
NOT NULL
UNIQUE
CHECK
FOREIGN KEY
```

where appropriate.

Application validation alone cannot protect against every writer or race condition.

# 24. Index Architecture

Indexes should exist because query patterns require them.

Every index introduces:

```text id="r1dp8h"
Storage
Write amplification
Maintenance
Vacuum overhead
Memory pressure
```

More indexes are not automatically better.

# 25. Composite Indexes

Column order matters.

```text id="ocn20x"
INDEX (course_id, status)
```

is not universally equivalent to:

```text id="2tvr3w"
INDEX (status, course_id)
```

Index design must follow query predicates and selectivity.

# 26. Unused Indexes

Unused/redundant indexes should be identified and removed carefully.

Keeping indexes forever because "they may help someday" imposes permanent write cost.

# 27. Query Planning

Production query performance should be investigated using PostgreSQL planning tools such as:

```text id="nq8cqg"
EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
```

with appropriate caution.

Guessing that an ORM-generated query is efficient is insufficient.

# 28. Sequential Scans

A sequential scan is not automatically bad.

For small tables or queries selecting much of a table, it may be optimal.

Performance tuning based on simplistic rules produces bad databases.

# 29. N+1 Queries

ORM-based services must actively detect N+1 query patterns.

```text id="l0y0q4"
1 query
   +
100 child queries
```

can destroy performance while each individual query looks harmless.

# 30. Fetch Strategy

JPA relationships should not be made globally eager merely to eliminate LazyInitializationException.

That trades one problem for uncontrolled query loading.

Fetch requirements should be explicit per use case.

# 31. Transactions

Transactions protect related state transitions.

```text id="cjhkqp"
BEGIN
  update A
  insert B
  update C
COMMIT
```

Either the intended unit succeeds or fails according to transaction semantics.

# 32. Transaction Boundary

Transaction boundaries should follow business operations.

A transaction should not remain open across slow external API calls without strong justification.

# 33. ACID

PostgreSQL provides strong transactional guarantees:

```text id="kprcmh"
Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability
```

but application architecture must still use transactions correctly.

# 34. Isolation Levels

Isolation levels trade concurrency against anomaly prevention.

Relevant PostgreSQL levels include:

```text id="2n9cd4"
READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ
SERIALIZABLE
```

Higher isolation is not automatically better.

# 35. Read Committed

PostgreSQL's common default is appropriate for many operations.

Business logic must understand that repeated queries inside a transaction may observe changed committed data.

# 36. Serializable

Serializable transactions provide stronger guarantees but can require transaction retries.

Use when the invariant genuinely requires it.

Do not set every transaction to Serializable by default.

# 37. Lost Updates

Concurrent modifications require explicit handling.

Example:

```text id="1zb0aa"
Request A reads version 5
Request B reads version 5

A updates
B updates

Whose change wins?
```

The architecture must answer.

# 38. Optimistic Locking

Optimistic locking should be preferred for many low-contention business entities.

```text id="lwluxn"
version = 7

UPDATE ...
WHERE id = ?
AND version = 7
```

If zero rows update, a concurrent modification occurred.

# 39. Pessimistic Locking

Pessimistic locking may be justified for highly contended critical operations.

It introduces:

```text id="7h03kj"
Blocking
Deadlocks
Reduced concurrency
```

and should be used deliberately.

# 40. Deadlocks

Deadlocks are expected possibilities in concurrent transactional systems.

Applications should:

```text id="ytfy9g"
Detect
Log
Retry safe operations
Use consistent lock ordering
Keep transactions short
```

# 41. Connection Pooling

Spring Boot services should use bounded connection pools such as HikariCP.

```text id="xvjs67"
Application Threads
       │
       ▼
     HikariCP
       │
       ▼
   PostgreSQL
```

# 42. Pool Size

Connection pool size should not be calculated as:

```text id="dxxgzu"
100 connections
×
50 pods
=
5000 database connections
```

without considering database capacity.

Horizontal scaling can destroy a database through connection multiplication.

# 43. Connection Budget

The platform should maintain a database connection budget.

```text id="1sztqb"
Database max connections
          │
          ├── Application pools
          ├── Administration
          ├── Migrations
          └── Safety reserve
```

# 44. PgBouncer

PgBouncer should be evaluated when large numbers of application connections create material PostgreSQL overhead.

```text id="o7jqjg"
Applications
     │
     ▼
PgBouncer
     │
     ▼
PostgreSQL
```

It is not mandatory merely because PostgreSQL exists.

# 45. Pooling Semantics

Transaction-level pooling can conflict with assumptions about session-level database state.

Applications must be validated before adopting it.

# 46. Timeouts

Database access should define bounded:

```text id="rwd3j9"
Connection timeout
Statement timeout
Transaction timeout
Lock timeout
```

where appropriate.

Infinite waits turn dependency degradation into thread exhaustion.

# 47. Long Transactions

Long-running transactions can interfere with:

```text id="os6pu8"
Vacuum
Locking
Storage cleanup
Replication
Concurrency
```

They should be observable.

# 48. PostgreSQL Vacuum

MVCC creates dead tuples that require vacuuming.

Autovacuum is essential production infrastructure, not optional database housekeeping.

# 49. Table Bloat

High-update workloads should monitor:

```text id="g9db28"
Dead tuples
Vacuum behavior
Index bloat
Table growth
```

before performance degradation becomes severe.

# 50. Partitioning

Partitioning should be introduced for specific scale/maintenance requirements.

Potential dimensions:

```text id="i9jmvf"
Time
Tenant
Lifecycle category
```

Partitioning small tables adds complexity without meaningful benefit.

# 51. Read Replicas

Read replicas may offload appropriate read workloads.

```text id="4u04w6"
Primary
   │
   ├── Writes
   │
   └────► Replica
             │
             ▼
            Reads
```

# 52. Replica Lag

Read replicas are not guaranteed to be immediately current.

Applications requiring read-after-write consistency should not blindly route those reads to asynchronous replicas.

# 53. RDS vs Aurora PostgreSQL

Mediverse should default to **Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL** unless Aurora PostgreSQL's scaling, availability or operational characteristics solve a demonstrated requirement.

Aurora should not be selected simply because it is the more sophisticated AWS offering.

# 54. RDS Multi-AZ

Critical production PostgreSQL workloads should use appropriate Multi-AZ architecture.

```text id="2rgexs"
Primary
   │
   ▼
Synchronous Standby
```

depending on the selected RDS deployment model.

# 55. Multi-AZ Is Not Backup

High availability and backup solve different failures.

```text id="l6o02f"
Multi-AZ
→ infrastructure availability

Backup/PITR
→ data recovery
```

A bad `DELETE` can replicate perfectly to the standby.

# 56. Automated Backups

Production databases should use automated backups and point-in-time recovery according to required recovery objectives.

# 57. PITR

Point-in-time recovery should allow restoration to a point before a destructive event within configured retention.

```text id="4ivfwj"
12:00 Healthy
12:17 Bad operation
12:30 Incident discovered

Restore target
→ before 12:17
```

# 58. Backup Verification

A backup is not proven until restore is tested.

```text id="fvdvqe"
Backup succeeded
      ≠
Recovery succeeded
```

# 59. Database Encryption

Production databases containing sensitive data should use encryption at rest and TLS in transit according to ADR-064.

# 60. PostgreSQL Observability

ADR-063's database telemetry should cover:

```text id="sw4q3u"
Connections
Transactions
Locks
Slow queries
IO
CPU
Memory
Vacuum
Replication
Storage
Query latency
```

Database health cannot be reduced to CPU percentage.

---

## ADR-065 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The authoritative-data architecture now follows:

```text id="3qsd9c"
                       DOMAIN
                         │
                         ▼
                     SERVICE
                         │
                         ▼
                  SYSTEM OF RECORD
                         │
                         ▼
                    PostgreSQL
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ▼              ▼              ▼
        Events          Cache         Search
          │              │              │
          ▼              ▼              ▼
        Kafka           Redis        OpenSearch
          │              │              │
          └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                         ▼
                    DERIVED STATE
```

The critical rule is:

> **PostgreSQL should own transactional truth. Redis should accelerate access, Kafka should distribute durable facts/events, OpenSearch should provide search projections, and S3 should own objects. None of those secondary technologies should accidentally become the authoritative source merely because an application happens to read from them.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Redis Architecture**, then cover **cache-aside → TTL → invalidation → cache stampede → stale data → negative caching → distributed locking → Redis sessions → Redis HA → Kafka architecture → domain events → topic design → partitions → keys → ordering → consumer groups → offset management → at-least-once semantics → idempotency → retries → DLQ → poison messages → schema evolution → Schema Registry → transactional outbox → CDC/Debezium → event replay → event retention → OpenSearch architecture → indexing → synchronization → mappings → shards/replicas → search relevance → index aliases → reindexing → ILM → S3 object architecture → object keys → multipart upload → presigned URLs → versioning → lifecycle/tiering → event integration → data contracts → lineage → metadata/catalog → data quality → retention → archival → deletion → encryption → backup strategy → RPO/RTO → restore testing → cross-region DR → data migration → zero-downtime schema evolution → analytics boundary → lake/lakehouse evaluation → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise data reference architecture.**


# ADR-065 — Enterprise Data Architecture & Data Platform

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — PostgreSQL Observability**.

---

# 61. Redis Architecture

Redis should provide **fast, transient or reconstructable state**, not become an accidental system of record.

```text
Application
     │
     ├──────────────► PostgreSQL
     │                 AUTHORITATIVE
     │
     ▼
   Redis
     │
     ▼
ACCELERATION /
TRANSIENT STATE
```

Appropriate uses include:

```text
Caching
Session state
Rate-limit counters
Short-lived coordination
Derived lookup data
```

---

# 62. Cache-Aside Pattern

Cache-aside should be the default caching model for many application reads.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Redis lookup
   │
 ┌─┴───────────┐
 ▼             ▼
HIT           MISS
 │             │
 ▼             ▼
Return      PostgreSQL
               │
               ▼
          Populate Redis
               │
               ▼
             Return
```

The application remains aware that PostgreSQL owns the truth.

---

# 63. Cache TTL

Cached entries should normally have bounded lifetimes.

```text
Cache Entry
    │
    ▼
   TTL
    │
    ▼
Expiration
```

TTL provides a recovery mechanism when explicit invalidation fails.

---

# 64. TTL Selection

TTL must follow data semantics.

```text
Rarely changing reference data
→ longer TTL

Frequently changing state
→ shorter TTL

Security-sensitive authorization state
→ carefully bounded TTL
```

There is no universal "best Redis TTL."

---

# 65. Cache Invalidation

When authoritative data changes, stale cache must be considered explicitly.

Strategies include:

```text
Delete-on-write
Update-on-write
Event-driven invalidation
TTL expiration
```

Invalidation behavior is part of application correctness.

---

# 66. Cache Invalidation Race

Consider:

```text
Request A
→ reads old DB value

Request B
→ updates DB
→ invalidates cache

Request A
→ writes old value into cache
```

Naive cache-aside implementations can reintroduce stale state.

High-value data requires concurrency-aware design.

---

# 67. Stale Data

Some workflows can tolerate temporary staleness.

Others cannot.

```text
Course description
→ probably tolerates short staleness

Authorization revocation
→ much less tolerance

Financial/critical transactional state
→ usually inappropriate for casual caching
```

Consistency requirements must drive cache design.

---

# 68. Cache Stampede

When a popular cache entry expires:

```text
                Cache expires
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
       ▼             ▼             ▼
    Request       Request       Request
       │             │             │
       └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                     ▼
                 Database
```

Thousands of requests may hit PostgreSQL simultaneously.

---

# 69. Stampede Mitigation

Possible strategies include:

```text
TTL jitter
Request coalescing
Single-flight loading
Controlled locking
Background refresh
Stale-while-revalidate
```

The strategy should match traffic characteristics.

---

# 70. TTL Jitter

If millions of keys receive identical TTLs, they may expire simultaneously.

Introduce bounded randomization where appropriate.

```text
Base TTL = 3600 sec

Actual:
3300–3900 sec
```

This spreads regeneration load.

---

# 71. Negative Caching

Repeated misses may also be cached temporarily.

Example:

```text
GET course/999999
      │
      ▼
Not Found
      │
      ▼
Short negative cache
```

This prevents repeated expensive lookups for nonexistent resources.

Negative TTLs should generally be short.

---

# 72. Redis Memory

Redis memory must be treated as bounded infrastructure.

Monitor:

```text
Used memory
Fragmentation
Evictions
Key count
Largest keys
TTL distribution
```

"Redis is fast" does not mean "Redis has infinite RAM."

---

# 73. Eviction Policies

Eviction policy must match workload semantics.

A cache can tolerate eviction.

A supposedly durable state store may not.

This is another reason not to casually use Redis as authoritative storage.

---

# 74. Large Redis Values

Avoid turning Redis into:

```text
key
 ↓
20 MB JSON document
```

without strong justification.

Large values increase:

```text
Network cost
Serialization cost
Memory pressure
Latency
Replication cost
```

---

# 75. Distributed Locking

Redis-based distributed locks may be appropriate for limited coordination scenarios.

But a lock does not magically make a distributed workflow correct.

Correctness must consider:

```text
Lock expiration
Process pauses
Network partitions
Retry behavior
Fencing
Duplicate execution
```

---

# 76. Lock Expiration

Every distributed lock should have bounded lifetime.

Otherwise a crashed lock owner can block progress indefinitely.

---

# 77. Fencing Tokens

For critical distributed coordination, fencing/version tokens may be needed so an expired lock holder cannot later modify state.

```text
Worker A → token 41
Worker B → token 42

Storage accepts only newest valid token.
```

---

# 78. Redis Session Storage

Redis may store server-managed session state where the authentication architecture requires centralized sessions.

```text
Browser
   │ session ID
   ▼
Application
   │
   ▼
Redis Session
```

Session TTL must match security/session policy from ADR-064.

---

# 79. Session Failure Strategy

If Redis sessions are critical:

```text
Redis unavailable
      │
      ▼
Authentication/session impact
```

must be explicitly designed.

Redis availability then becomes part of authentication availability.

---

# 80. Redis High Availability

Critical Redis workloads should use appropriate managed HA architecture such as ElastiCache replication/failover capabilities.

Applications must handle failover and transient connection errors.

---

# 81. Redis Persistence

Persistence configuration depends on Redis's role.

If Redis stores only reconstructable cache:

```text
Data loss
→ acceptable/rebuild
```

If Redis contains important transient state, recovery requirements become stronger.

---

# 82. Redis Key Design

Keys should be predictable and namespaced.

Example:

```text
course:v1:details:1234
```

rather than unrelated arbitrary naming conventions.

Avoid putting sensitive raw data unnecessarily into key names.

---

# 83. Kafka Architecture

Kafka should provide Mediverse's durable event-streaming backbone.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
 Kafka Topic
   │
   ├────────► Consumer A
   ├────────► Consumer B
   └────────► Consumer C
```

Kafka enables independent consumers to react to domain events.

---

# 84. Domain Events

Domain events represent facts that have already occurred.

Good:

```text
StudentEnrolled
CoursePublished
AssessmentSubmitted
PaymentCompleted
```

Poor event naming:

```text
ProcessStudent
DoCourseThing
HandlePayment
```

Events should describe facts rather than vague commands.

---

# 85. Event Ownership

The service owning the domain fact should normally own publication of its event.

```text
Enrollment Service
      │
      ▼
StudentEnrolled
```

Consumers must not redefine the producer's domain semantics.

---

# 86. Event Payload

Events should contain enough information to support intended consumers without becoming uncontrolled copies of entire database rows.

Design explicitly:

```text
eventId
eventType
eventVersion
occurredAt
aggregateId
payload
metadata
```

---

# 87. Event ID

Every event should have a stable unique identifier where consumers require deduplication or traceability.

```text
event_id
```

is distinct from:

```text
trace_id
```

One identifies the business/event record; the other identifies distributed execution.

---

# 88. Kafka Topic Design

Topics should represent meaningful event streams.

Avoid both extremes:

```text
One topic for everything
```

and:

```text
One topic for every tiny event
```

Topic boundaries should consider ownership, retention, security, throughput and consumer patterns.

---

# 89. Topic Naming

Mediverse should standardize topic naming.

Example conceptual structure:

```text
<domain>.<entity/event-family>.v<major>
```

Exact naming conventions should be centrally documented.

---

# 90. Kafka Partitions

Partitions provide parallelism and ordering boundaries.

```text
Topic
 ├── Partition 0
 ├── Partition 1
 └── Partition 2
```

More partitions increase concurrency but also operational overhead.

---

# 91. Partition Key

Events requiring ordering for the same entity should use a stable key.

Example:

```text
key = enrollmentId
```

Then events for the same enrollment normally map to the same partition.

---

# 92. Ordering Guarantee

Kafka ordering exists **within a partition**, not globally across an entire topic.

Architecture must never assume universal topic ordering unless the topic effectively has one partition—which limits scalability.

---

# 93. Hot Partitions

Poor partition-key selection can produce:

```text
Partition 0 → 90% traffic
Partition 1 → 5%
Partition 2 → 5%
```

This destroys expected parallelism.

Partition distribution should be observable.

---

# 94. Consumer Groups

Consumer groups provide scalable competing consumption.

```text
Topic Partitions
   │
   ▼
Consumer Group
 ┌────┼────┐
 ▼    ▼    ▼
C1   C2   C3
```

Each partition is assigned to one consumer in a group at a time.

---

# 95. Consumer Scaling

Adding consumers beyond the number of available partitions does not increase processing parallelism for that consumer group.

```text
3 partitions
10 consumers

→ up to 3 actively consuming partition assignments
```

Partition strategy therefore affects future scalability.

---

# 96. Offset Management

Offsets represent consumer progress.

Commit semantics must correspond to processing semantics.

Dangerous:

```text
Read
 ↓
Commit
 ↓
Process
 ↓
Crash
```

The message may appear consumed despite incomplete work.

---

# 97. At-Least-Once Processing

Mediverse should assume **at-least-once delivery** for most Kafka business processing unless a stronger architecture is explicitly demonstrated.

Therefore:

```text
Message may be processed
more than once.
```

Consumers must be designed accordingly.

---

# 98. Idempotent Consumers

A repeated event should not create repeated business effects.

Example:

```text
PaymentCompleted event
arrives twice

      X

Two enrollments
```

Consumers should use:

```text
event IDs
business uniqueness constraints
idempotency records
state/version checks
```

as appropriate.

---

# 99. Exactly-Once Claims

"Exactly once" should not be claimed casually.

Kafka transaction semantics can provide strong guarantees within supported boundaries, but end-to-end systems involving:

```text
Kafka
PostgreSQL
External APIs
Email
Payment providers
```

still require careful idempotency and transactional design.

---

# 100. Retry Strategy

Transient failures should retry with bounded policy.

```text
Attempt
  │
  ▼
Failure
  │
  ▼
Backoff
  │
  ▼
Retry
```

Infinite immediate retries can amplify outages.

---

# 101. Retry Topics

For asynchronous processing, delayed/retry topics may isolate temporarily failing messages from healthy traffic.

```text
Main Topic
    │
    ▼
Consumer
    │
  Failure
    ▼
Retry Topic
    │
    ▼
Retry Consumer
```

---

# 102. Dead-Letter Queue

Messages that repeatedly fail may move to a DLQ.

```text
Message
  │
  ▼
Retries exhausted
  │
  ▼
DLQ
```

A DLQ is not a garbage bin.

It requires ownership, monitoring and remediation.

---

# 103. Poison Messages

A malformed or logically invalid message must not block an entire partition indefinitely.

Consumers need controlled handling for poison messages.

---

# 104. Kafka Consumer Lag

Consumer lag is a first-class operational signal.

```text
Producer
  │ 1000 msg/s
  ▼
Kafka
  │
  ▼ 600 msg/s
Consumer

Lag ↑
```

A consumer can be "running" while being operationally broken.

---

# 105. Event Schema

Events require explicit schemas.

Schema design should define:

```text
Field names
Types
Required fields
Optional fields
Semantic meaning
Compatibility rules
```

---

# 106. Schema Registry

A Schema Registry should be used where structured Kafka contracts require centralized schema governance.

Potential serialization choices include:

```text
Avro
Protobuf
JSON Schema
```

Selection should be standardized rather than varied arbitrarily by service.

---

# 107. Schema Evolution

Event schemas must evolve compatibly.

Prefer:

```text
Add optional field
```

over:

```text
Rename/remove required field
without migration
```

because old and new producers/consumers frequently coexist.

---

# 108. Event Versioning

Versioning should be deliberate.

Do not create:

```text
EventV2
EventV3
EventV4
```

for every minor additive change.

Major semantic incompatibility may justify explicit version changes.

---

# 109. Transactional Outbox

The transactional outbox pattern should be used when a service must atomically persist database state and guarantee eventual event publication.

Without it:

```text
DB COMMIT
   │
   ▼
Publish Kafka
   │
   X crash

Database changed
Event missing
```

---

# 110. Outbox Architecture

```text
Application Transaction
        │
        ├── Update Domain Table
        │
        └── Insert Outbox Record
                 │
               COMMIT
                 │
                 ▼
          Outbox Publisher
                 │
                 ▼
               Kafka
```

Database state and event intent are committed atomically.

---

# 111. Outbox Consumers Still Need Idempotency

Transactional outbox solves producer-side dual-write risk.

It does **not** eliminate duplicate delivery downstream.

Consumers remain idempotent.

---

# 112. CDC

Change Data Capture may publish database changes without application polling.

```text
PostgreSQL WAL
      │
      ▼
CDC
      │
      ▼
Kafka
```

CDC is useful when database change streams are genuinely required.

---

# 113. Debezium Evaluation

Debezium should be evaluated as the preferred CDC technology when PostgreSQL-to-Kafka CDC is required.

It should not be deployed merely because Kafka exists.

---

# 114. CDC vs Domain Events

Raw CDC changes and domain events are not identical.

```text
CDC:
row column changed

Domain Event:
StudentEnrollmentCancelled
```

Domain events express business meaning.

CDC expresses storage changes.

Do not confuse them.

---

# 115. Event Replay

Kafka retention enables event replay where consumer design supports it.

```text
Existing Topic
     │
     ▼
Reset/new consumer
     │
     ▼
Rebuild Projection
```

Replay capability is valuable for rebuilding derived stores.

---

# 116. Replay Safety

Before replaying events, verify:

```text
Idempotency
External side effects
Schema compatibility
Processing capacity
Ordering assumptions
```

Replaying `SendEmail` behavior accidentally to five million historical events is not recovery.

---

# 117. Kafka Retention

Retention should follow event purpose.

```text
Operational transient events
→ shorter

Rebuild-critical event streams
→ longer

Regulated/sensitive events
→ policy-driven
```

Kafka should not become infinite archival storage by accident.

---

# 118. OpenSearch Architecture

OpenSearch should provide search-oriented projections.

```text
PostgreSQL
     │
     ▼
Event / CDC
     │
     ▼
Indexer
     │
     ▼
OpenSearch
     │
     ▼
Search API
```

OpenSearch should not normally own transactional truth.

---

# 119. Search Synchronization

Synchronization must tolerate temporary divergence.

```text
PostgreSQL updated
       │
       ▼
Event
       │
       ▼
OpenSearch updated later
```

Search is therefore commonly eventually consistent.

Product behavior must acknowledge that.

---

# 120. Search Document Design

Search documents should be optimized for retrieval.

Denormalization is normal here.

Example:

```text
Course Search Document

courseId
title
description
instructorName
category
tags
language
rating
```

This is a projection, not the normalized OLTP model.

---

# 121. OpenSearch Mapping

Field mappings must be explicit for important production indexes.

Incorrect dynamic mapping can create:

```text
Wrong field types
Mapping explosion
Poor relevance
High memory use
```

---

# 122. Search Text Fields

Distinguish:

```text
text
→ analyzed full-text search

keyword
→ exact match/filter/aggregation
```

Using the wrong type produces poor search behavior.

---

# 123. OpenSearch Shards

Shard count should follow actual index size and workload.

Too many tiny shards waste resources.

Too few oversized shards limit scalability and recovery.

---

# 124. OpenSearch Replicas

Replicas provide read capacity and availability.

They do not replace authoritative-data backup/reconstruction strategy.

---

# 125. Search Relevance

Search quality requires deliberate relevance design.

Potential signals:

```text
Text relevance
Field boosting
Popularity
Recency
User context where permitted
```

A technically healthy OpenSearch cluster can still provide terrible search results.

---

# 126. Index Aliases

Applications should access logical aliases where useful.

```text
courses-search
      │
      ▼
courses-v17
```

This supports safer index replacement.

---

# 127. Zero-Downtime Reindexing

```text
courses-v17
     │
     ├──── application reads alias
     │
Build
     ▼
courses-v18
     │
     ▼
Validate
     │
     ▼
Switch Alias
```

Avoid destructive in-place migrations when safer replacement is possible.

---

# 128. Index Lifecycle

Index lifecycle policies should manage:

```text
Retention
Rollover
Tiering
Deletion
```

for time-oriented data where appropriate.

---

# 129. S3 Object Architecture

S3 should own durable object/blob data such as appropriate:

```text
Uploaded learning assets
Images
Documents
Video objects
Exports
Backups
Data-lake objects
```

depending on domain requirements.

---

# 130. Object Key Design

S3 keys should be server-controlled and structured.

Example:

```text
courses/{courseId}/assets/{generatedObjectId}
```

Do not use raw client filenames as authoritative keys.

---

# 131. Object Metadata

Relational metadata and binary objects should usually remain separated.

```text
PostgreSQL
→ object ID
→ owner
→ type
→ state
→ authorization

S3
→ actual bytes
```

This allows relational authorization without storing large binaries in PostgreSQL.

---

# 132. Multipart Upload

Large files should use multipart upload where appropriate.

```text
Client
  │
  ├── Part 1
  ├── Part 2
  ├── Part 3
  │
  ▼
S3 CompleteMultipartUpload
```

This improves resilience and throughput for large objects.

---

# 133. Presigned Upload

Clients may upload directly to S3 using tightly scoped presigned URLs.

```text
Client
   │
   ▼
Mediverse API
   │ authorization
   ▼
Presigned URL
   │
   ▼
S3
```

The API remains responsible for authorization before granting upload capability.

---

# 134. Upload Completion

Receiving an object in S3 does not automatically mean it is trusted.

```text
Upload
  │
  ▼
QUARANTINE
  │
  ▼
Validation / Malware Scan
  │
 ┌┴───────────┐
 ▼            ▼
Approved    Rejected
```

This inherits ADR-064.

---

# 135. S3 Versioning

Versioning should be enabled where accidental overwrite/deletion recovery requirements justify it.

Versioning increases storage usage and requires lifecycle management.

---

# 136. S3 Lifecycle

Lifecycle rules should transition objects based on access and retention requirements.

```text
Frequent access
      │
      ▼
Less frequent
      │
      ▼
Archive
      │
      ▼
Deletion
```

Storage tiering must not violate retrieval or compliance requirements.

---

# 137. S3 Events

S3 object events may trigger asynchronous workflows.

Example:

```text
Object Uploaded
      │
      ▼
Event
      │
      ▼
Scanner / Processor
      │
      ▼
Metadata Update
```

Consumers must remain idempotent.

---

# 138. Data Lineage

Critical data should have traceable lineage.

```text
Source
  │
  ▼
Transformation
  │
  ▼
Derived Dataset
  │
  ▼
Consumer
```

Teams should be able to answer:

> Where did this data come from, and what transformed it?

---

# 139. Metadata & Catalog

As the data estate grows, Mediverse should maintain metadata describing:

```text
Dataset
Owner
Description
Classification
Schema
Source
Consumers
Retention
Quality expectations
```

A formal data catalog becomes justified as scale increases.

---

# 140. Data Quality

Critical datasets should define measurable quality dimensions.

Examples:

```text
Completeness
Validity
Uniqueness
Consistency
Freshness
Accuracy where measurable
```

A pipeline completing successfully does not prove its data is correct.

---

# 141. Data Retention & Archival

Retention policy from ADR-064 must be implemented technically across every relevant data technology.

```text
PostgreSQL
Redis
Kafka
OpenSearch
S3
Analytics
Backups
```

Each system requires an explicit lifecycle.

---

# 142. End-to-End Deletion

Deletion workflows must propagate across authoritative and derived stores.

```text
Deletion Request
       │
       ▼
System of Record
       │
       ├── Redis invalidation
       ├── OpenSearch removal
       ├── S3 deletion
       ├── Analytics handling
       └── Event/lifecycle processing
```

Retention/legal requirements may modify exact behavior.

---

# 143. RPO & RTO

Every critical data service must define:

```text
RPO
Recovery Point Objective

→ How much data loss is acceptable?

RTO
Recovery Time Objective

→ How long can recovery take?
```

Without explicit RPO/RTO, "we have backups" is incomplete.

---

# 144. Restore Testing

Recovery must be exercised.

```text
Backup
   │
   ▼
Restore
   │
   ▼
Integrity Validation
   │
   ▼
Application Validation
   │
   ▼
Measured RPO/RTO
```

Only then is the recovery design proven.

---

# 145. Regional Disaster Recovery

Cross-region DR should be driven by business RTO/RPO—not architecture aesthetics.

Potential strategies:

```text
Backup and Restore

Pilot Light

Warm Standby

Active/Passive

Active/Active
```

Each increases cost and complexity.

Mediverse should not adopt active-active databases across regions unless requirements justify the consistency and operational burden.

---

# 146. Database Migration

Schema migration should be automated and version-controlled.

For Spring Boot services, Flyway or Liquibase should be standardized rather than allowing uncontrolled manual production SQL.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Migration
 │
 ▼
Validated Delivery Pipeline
 │
 ▼
Database
```

---

# 147. Zero-Downtime Schema Evolution

Use **expand → migrate → contract** for incompatible schema changes.

```text
1. EXPAND

Old App ───► old_column
New App ───► old_column + new_column

2. MIGRATE

Backfill / transition data

3. SWITCH

New App ───► new_column

4. CONTRACT

Remove old_column
```

Application and schema changes should tolerate mixed versions during rolling deployments.

---

# 148. Data Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ One database treated as the datastore for every problem
❌ New datastore introduced because it is fashionable
❌ Every microservice directly modifying shared tables
❌ Cross-service joins into private schemas
❌ Redis becoming accidental authoritative storage
❌ Cache entries without lifecycle
❌ Same TTL applied blindly to every data type
❌ Authorization state cached indefinitely
❌ Cache stampedes ignored
❌ Redis distributed locks assumed to solve distributed correctness
❌ Unlimited Redis memory assumptions
❌ Kafka events named as vague implementation commands
❌ Events containing complete database dumps
❌ Partition keys chosen without distribution analysis
❌ Global Kafka ordering assumed
❌ More consumers added than partitions and expected to increase throughput
❌ Offsets committed before unsafe processing
❌ Duplicate delivery ignored
❌ "Exactly once" claimed across arbitrary external systems
❌ Infinite immediate retries
❌ DLQ created without ownership
❌ Schema changes breaking existing consumers
❌ CDC confused with domain events
❌ Event replay executed without side-effect analysis
❌ Kafka used as permanent archive by accident
❌ OpenSearch treated as transactional truth
❌ Dynamic mappings allowed to grow without control
❌ Search relevance ignored because cluster health is green
❌ Hundreds of tiny OpenSearch shards
❌ S3 client filenames used directly as trusted object keys
❌ Uploaded objects trusted immediately
❌ Binary files stored in PostgreSQL without reason
❌ S3 versioning enabled without lifecycle controls
❌ Data copied into analytics without ownership/classification
❌ Pipeline success treated as data-quality proof
❌ Retention implemented in PostgreSQL but forgotten in Kafka/OpenSearch/S3
❌ User deletion implemented only in one datastore
❌ Backups created but never restored
❌ RPO/RTO left undefined
❌ Multi-AZ confused with backup
❌ Active-active multi-region architecture selected for prestige
❌ Manual production schema edits
❌ Breaking database migration deployed with application simultaneously
```

---
