# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                        |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Primary OLTP               | **PostgreSQL**                                  |
| AWS relational default     | **RDS PostgreSQL**                              |
| Aurora PostgreSQL          | Requirement-driven evaluation                   |
| Service data ownership     | Mandatory                                       |
| Database-per-service       | Logical ownership                               |
| Shared-table microservices | **Rejected**                                    |
| Schema design              | Domain/invariant driven                         |
| Referential integrity      | DB constraints within domain boundary           |
| IDs                        | Sequence/UUID based on requirements             |
| Indexing                   | Query-driven                                    |
| ORM fetch strategy         | Explicit                                        |
| Transaction boundaries     | Business-operation aligned                      |
| Default isolation          | Workload-driven                                 |
| Optimistic locking         | Preferred for normal low-contention concurrency |
| Pessimistic locking        | Selective                                       |
| Connection pool            | HikariCP                                        |
| Connection budget          | Required                                        |
| PgBouncer                  | Scale-driven evaluation                         |
| Multi-AZ                   | Critical production DBs                         |
| PITR                       | Required                                        |
| Restore testing            | Required                                        |
| Cache                      | **Redis**                                       |
| Cache model                | Cache-aside default                             |
| Cache TTL                  | Mandatory/bounded                               |
| Cache invalidation         | Explicit                                        |
| Stampede protection        | Required for high-volume keys                   |
| Redis as authoritative DB  | Generally **rejected**                          |
| Sessions                   | Redis where architecture requires               |
| Event backbone             | **Kafka**                                       |
| Event model                | Domain facts                                    |
| Delivery assumption        | At least once                                   |
| Consumers                  | Idempotent                                      |
| Ordering                   | Partition scoped                                |
| Retry                      | Bounded/backoff                                 |
| DLQ                        | Owned + monitored                               |
| Event schemas              | Governed                                        |
| Schema Registry            | Required where structured contracts justify it  |
| Dual-write solution        | **Transactional Outbox**                        |
| CDC                        | Requirement-driven                              |
| CDC technology             | Debezium preferred evaluation                   |
| Search                     | **OpenSearch**                                  |
| OpenSearch role            | Derived search projection                       |
| Search consistency         | Eventual                                        |
| Reindexing                 | Alias-based replacement                         |
| Object storage             | **Amazon S3**                                   |
| Upload model               | Authorized presigned upload                     |
| Upload security            | Quarantine + validation/scanning                |
| Data lineage               | Required for critical data                      |
| Data quality               | Measured                                        |
| Retention                  | Technology-wide                                 |
| Deletion                   | End-to-end                                      |
| RPO/RTO                    | Defined per critical data service               |
| DR                         | Requirement-driven                              |
| Schema migration           | Version-controlled automation                   |
| Zero-downtime migration    | Expand → migrate → contract                     |
| Analytics                  | Separated from production OLTP                  |
| Lake/lakehouse             | Scale/use-case driven                           |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                                    |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                                    |

# ADR-065 — COMPLETE ✅

Mediverse now has a defined data lifecycle:

```text
CREATE
   │
   ▼
VALIDATE
   │
   ▼
TRANSACT
   │
   ▼
STORE AUTHORITATIVELY
   │
   ├────────► CACHE
   │
   ├────────► EVENT
   │
   ├────────► SEARCH
   │
   └────────► ANALYTICS
                  │
                  ▼
               GOVERN
                  │
                  ▼
                RETAIN
                  │
                  ▼
                ARCHIVE
                  │
                  ▼
                DELETE

while independently:

AUTHORITATIVE DATA
        │
        ▼
      BACKUP
        │
        ▼
       PITR
        │
        ▼
   RESTORE TEST
        │
        ▼
        DR
```

The defining invariant is:

> **Every important piece of data has one authoritative owner, explicit consistency semantics, a controlled lifecycle and a tested recovery path. Caches, search indexes and event projections may disappear and be rebuilt without changing what Mediverse considers true.**

## Next — ADR-066

### **ADR-066 — Enterprise Resilience, High Availability, Disaster Recovery, Business Continuity & Failure Engineering**

ADR-065 defined data-specific recovery, but the next ADR should move one level higher and define **whole-platform survival**: failure taxonomy → reliability boundaries → blast-radius architecture → graceful degradation → timeout budgets → retries/backoff/jitter → retry amplification → circuit breakers → bulkheads → load shedding → backpressure → rate limiting → queue buffering → idempotency → dependency failure → partial failure → fallback strategy → Kubernetes self-healing → readiness/liveness/startup probes → PDB → topology spread → anti-affinity → node/AZ failure → EKS availability → ALB failure behavior → RDS failover → Redis failover → Kafka broker/partition failure → OpenSearch node failure → S3 dependency behavior → DNS failure → external SaaS failure → regional AWS outage → multi-AZ baseline → multi-region decision framework → active/passive vs warm standby vs active/active → Route 53 failover → data replication constraints → consistency during DR → RPO/RTO hierarchy → dependency recovery order → DR runbooks → restore orchestration → failover/failback → backup isolation/immutability → ransomware recovery → business continuity → degraded operating modes → crisis communications → chaos experiments → fault injection → game days → resilience scorecards → dependency maps → resilience testing in CI/CD → capacity during failure → operational readiness → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise resilience/DR reference architecture.**

# ADR-066 — Enterprise Resilience, High Availability, Disaster Recovery & Failure Engineering

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-066
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-063 defined how Mediverse detects and responds to production reliability problems.

ADR-065 defined how authoritative data is protected and recovered.

ADR-066 defines how the **entire Mediverse platform behaves when infrastructure, applications, dependencies, availability zones, data systems or regions fail**.

> **Resilience is not preventing every failure. It is controlling how failures propagate, preserving critical capabilities, and restoring normal operation within explicit recovery objectives.**

```text
                           USERS
                             │
                             ▼
                       GLOBAL ENTRY
                             │
                             ▼
                       AWS REGION
                             │
              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
              ▼              ▼              ▼
             AZ-A           AZ-B           AZ-C
              │              │              │
              └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                             ▼
                         EKS / ALB
                             │
                  ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                  ▼          ▼          ▼
              Services     Kafka      Data
                  │          │          │
                  └──────────┼──────────┘
                             ▼
                    RESILIENCE CONTROLS
                             │
        ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
        ▼                    ▼                    ▼
      Prevent              Contain              Recover
        │                    │                    │
        └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                             ▼
                      BUSINESS CONTINUITY
```

# 1. Resilience Objectives

Mediverse resilience architecture must optimize for:

```text
Availability
Fault containment
Recoverability
Data durability
Predictable degradation
Operational simplicity
Controlled blast radius
```

Perfect availability is not a realistic engineering objective.

# 2. Reliability vs Resilience

Reliability asks:

```text
How consistently does the system work?
```

Resilience asks:

```text
What happens when it does not?
```

A reliable architecture still requires failure engineering.

# 3. High Availability vs Disaster Recovery

These solve different problems.

```text
High Availability
→ continue operating through expected localized failures

Disaster Recovery
→ restore service after severe disruption
```

Multi-AZ does not eliminate the need for DR.

# 4. Failure Is Normal

Distributed systems experience:

```text
Process crashes
Pod failures
Node failures
Network loss
Latency spikes
Database failovers
Dependency outages
AZ failures
Bad deployments
Human mistakes
Regional failures
```

Architecture must assume these occur.

# 5. Failure Taxonomy

Mediverse should classify failures by scope:

```text
Component
Process
Pod
Node
Service
Dependency
Availability Zone
Region
Control plane
Data
Security
Organization/operations
```

Response strategy depends on scope.

# 6. Transient Failures

Transient failures may disappear quickly.

Examples:

```text
Temporary network timeout
Short DB failover
Brief DNS issue
Temporary throttling
```

These may justify controlled retries.

# 7. Persistent Failures

Persistent failures require different treatment.

```text
Database unavailable
Broken deployment
Expired certificate
Invalid configuration
Deleted resource
```

Retrying forever does not repair persistent failure.

# 8. Partial Failure

Distributed systems frequently experience partial failure.

```text
Service A
   │
   ├── Service B ✓
   ├── Redis ✓
   ├── Kafka ✗
   └── RDS ✓
```

The architecture must define what Service A should still provide.

# 9. Correlated Failure

Redundancy only helps when redundant components do not fail together.

```text
Replica A ─┐
Replica B ─┼── Same Node
Replica C ─┘
```

provides poor protection against node failure.

# 10. Blast Radius

Every architecture decision should ask:

> If this component fails or is compromised, how much of Mediverse fails with it?

Blast radius should be minimized.

# 11. Failure Domains

AWS availability zones, Kubernetes nodes, namespaces, accounts and regions provide different failure/isolation boundaries.

Workloads should intentionally use these boundaries.

# 12. Criticality Classification

Not every Mediverse capability requires identical resilience.

Example:

```text
Tier 0
Authentication / critical platform dependencies

Tier 1
Core learning workflows

Tier 2
Search / notifications / secondary workflows

Tier 3
Noncritical analytics / background processing
```

Exact tiers should be defined by business impact.

# 13. Critical User Journeys

Resilience should prioritize user outcomes such as:

```text
Authenticate
Open course
Consume lesson
Submit assessment
Persist progress
```

over preserving every secondary feature.

# 14. Graceful Degradation

When dependencies fail, services should preserve safe functionality where possible.

```text
Search unavailable
      │
      ▼
Course browsing still available
```

rather than:

```text
Search unavailable
      │
      ▼
Entire application unavailable
```

# 15. Degraded Modes

Potential degraded operation:

```text
Recommendations unavailable
→ show normal catalogue

Redis unavailable
→ selected reads fall back to DB

Notification system unavailable
→ core transaction continues + notification delayed

Analytics unavailable
→ operational application continues
```

Fallback must be safe.

# 16. Unsafe Degradation

Never degrade by bypassing correctness or security.

Rejected:

```text
Authorization service unavailable
        │
        ▼
Allow everyone
```

Security-sensitive failure should normally fail closed.

# 17. Dependency Classification

Dependencies should be classified:

```text
Hard dependency
→ operation cannot safely succeed without it

Soft dependency
→ operation can continue with reduced capability

Asynchronous dependency
→ operation can queue/defer work
```

# 18. Dependency Map

Critical services should maintain dependency maps.

```text
Course Service
     │
     ├── RDS        HARD
     ├── Redis      SOFT
     ├── Kafka      ASYNC/HARD depending operation
     └── OpenSearch SOFT
```

This improves incident and DR reasoning.

# 19. Timeout Architecture

Every remote call should normally have a bounded timeout.

```text
Caller
  │
  ▼
Dependency
  │
  X
```

Without a timeout, the caller may wait until its own resources are exhausted.

# 20. Timeout Budget

Timeouts should derive from the end-to-end latency budget.

Example:

```text
User budget = 2 seconds

API gateway     100 ms
Service A       400 ms
Service B       500 ms
Database        300 ms
Safety margin   700 ms
```

Independent arbitrary five-second timeouts across every hop are dangerous.

# 21. Nested Timeout Rule

Downstream timeouts should normally fit inside upstream deadlines.

```text
Client deadline
     │
     ▼
Service A timeout
     │
     ▼
Service B timeout
```

Otherwise upstream may abandon work while downstream continues consuming resources.

# 22. Deadline Propagation

Where practical, request deadlines should propagate through service calls.

This prevents downstream systems from performing work whose result can no longer be used.

# 23. Retry Architecture

Retries should be used only for failures likely to be transient and operations safe to retry.

```text
Attempt
   │
   X
   ▼
Backoff
   │
   ▼
Retry
```

# 24. Retry Safety

Before retrying ask:

```text
Is operation idempotent?
Could previous attempt have succeeded?
Can duplication create business damage?
```

A network timeout does not prove the server failed to execute the operation.

# 25. Retry Amplification

Retries can turn a small outage into a major one.

```text
10,000 requests
× 3 retries
=
30,000 attempts
```

If several service layers independently retry, amplification becomes much worse.

# 26. Retry Ownership

Retries should be deliberately owned by the most appropriate layer.

Do not blindly configure:

```text
Ingress retries
+
Service retries
+
SDK retries
+
Database retries
```

for the same failure.

# 27. Exponential Backoff

Retries should commonly use increasing delays.

```text
100 ms
200 ms
400 ms
800 ms
...
```

This reduces pressure on a recovering dependency.

# 28. Jitter

Clients should randomize retry timing.

Without jitter:

```text
10,000 clients fail
        │
        ▼
wait 1 second
        │
        ▼
10,000 retry simultaneously
```

creating a retry storm.

# 29. Retry Limits

Retries must be bounded by:

```text
Attempt count
Deadline
Total elapsed time
```

Infinite retries are rejected.

# 30. Circuit Breaker

Circuit breakers should protect callers from repeatedly invoking unhealthy dependencies.

```text
CLOSED
  │ failures
  ▼
OPEN
  │ cooldown
  ▼
HALF-OPEN
  │ test
  ├── success → CLOSED
  └── failure → OPEN
```

# 31. Circuit Breaker Purpose

A circuit breaker protects:

```text
Caller resources
Dependency recovery
Overall system stability
```

It does not repair the failed dependency.

# 32. Circuit Breaker Scope

Circuit breakers should be scoped by meaningful dependency boundaries.

One unhealthy downstream operation should not unnecessarily disable unrelated operations.

# 33. Resilience4j

For Spring Boot services, Resilience4j should be preferred where application-level:

```text
Timeout
Retry
Circuit breaker
Bulkhead
Rate limiter
```

patterns are required.

Configuration should be dependency-specific rather than copied globally.

# 34. Bulkheads

Bulkheads prevent one workload from consuming all resources.

```text
Service
   │
   ├── Course calls pool
   ├── Search calls pool
   └── Notification calls pool
```

If notification calls hang, course processing retains capacity.

# 35. Thread-Pool Isolation

Critical downstream calls may require bounded concurrency or separate execution resources.

Unlimited worker/thread creation is not resilience.

# 36. Connection-Pool Bulkhead

Database and HTTP connection pools naturally act as resource boundaries.

Their size must be bounded and observable.

# 37. Load Shedding

When a system exceeds safe capacity, deliberately rejecting work may preserve core service.

```text
Incoming load
      │
      ▼
Capacity threshold
   ┌──┴──┐
   ▼     ▼
Accept  Reject
```

Serving 80% successfully may be preferable to timing out 100%.

# 38. Load Shedding Priority

Critical operations may receive priority over secondary work.

Example:

```text
Assessment submission
→ preserve

Recommendation refresh
→ shed
```

# 39. Backpressure

Producers should not overwhelm slower consumers indefinitely.

```text
Producer
  │
  ▼
Buffer
  │
  ▼
Consumer
```

When consumption falls behind, the architecture must:

```text
Slow producers
Buffer safely
Reject work
Scale consumers
```

rather than allow unbounded growth.

# 40. Queue Buffering

Kafka can absorb temporary downstream slowdown.

But queues move pressure in time—they do not eliminate it.

A consumer processing 500 events/sec cannot permanently survive a producer generating 5,000/sec.

# 41. Queue Capacity

Monitor:

```text
Lag
Retention
Processing rate
Oldest message age
Disk capacity
```

Queue depth alone is insufficient.

# 42. Idempotency

Retry and recovery architecture depends heavily on idempotency.

```text
Same logical request
      │
      ├── Attempt 1
      ├── Attempt 2
      └── Attempt 3

Result
→ one business effect
```

# 43. Idempotency Keys

Externally retryable mutation APIs may support idempotency keys where duplicate execution is dangerous.

Example:

```text
POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: <unique-operation-id>
```

The server must persist/validate semantics correctly.

# 44. Fallback Strategy

Fallbacks must provide meaningful, safe behavior.

Useful:

```text
Recommendation engine unavailable
→ show popular courses
```

Bad:

```text
Database unavailable
→ fabricate successful enrollment
```

# 45. Cached Fallback

Previously cached data may provide temporary degraded reads.

The UI should avoid presenting stale information as current when freshness matters.

# 46. Static Fallback

Some informational content can fall back to static/default responses.

This should never conceal critical transactional failure.

# 47. Dependency Failure Budget

Services should understand how dependency reliability affects their SLO.

```text
Service SLO
   │
   ├── Own failures
   ├── DB failures
   ├── Kafka failures
   └── External dependency failures
```

Dependencies do not excuse user-visible failure.

# 48. External SaaS Failure

Third-party dependencies should have:

```text
Timeouts
Retries where safe
Circuit breakers
Fallbacks
Monitoring
Contracted expectations
Exit/recovery strategy
```

where critical.

# 49. Kubernetes Self-Healing

Kubernetes should automatically replace failed workload instances.

```text
Pod failure
   │
   ▼
Controller detects
   │
   ▼
Replacement pod
```

This protects against process/pod failure—not every application failure.

# 50. Liveness Probe

Liveness determines whether a container should be restarted.

Use it only when restart can reasonably recover the failure.

# 51. Liveness Anti-Pattern

Do not make liveness depend directly on every downstream dependency.

```text
Database briefly unavailable
      │
      ▼
All application liveness fails
      │
      ▼
All pods restart
```

This turns a database incident into an application restart storm.

# 52. Readiness Probe

Readiness determines whether the pod should receive traffic.

```text
Ready
→ endpoint receives traffic

Not Ready
→ removed from service routing
```

# 53. Startup Probe

Slow-starting services should use startup probes where needed so liveness checks do not kill them before initialization completes.

# 54. Probe Independence

Use:

```text
Startup
→ can application finish starting?

Readiness
→ can application serve useful traffic?

Liveness
→ is process irrecoverably unhealthy?
```

These are different questions.

# 55. Pod Disruption Budget

Critical replicated services should use PDBs where appropriate to limit simultaneous voluntary disruption.

```text
replicas = 6
minAvailable = 4
```

can prevent maintenance from removing too much capacity at once.

# 56. PDB Limitation

PDBs do not protect against every involuntary failure.

They are not an HA mechanism by themselves.

# 57. Replica Count

Critical services should normally have multiple replicas.

```text
replicas: 1
```

is a deliberate single-instance failure risk.

# 58. Topology Spread

Replicas should spread across appropriate topology domains.

```text
AZ-A        AZ-B        AZ-C
 │           │           │
Pod A       Pod B       Pod C
```

where infrastructure capacity supports it.

# 59. Pod Anti-Affinity

Anti-affinity may prevent important replicas from concentrating on one node.

Hard constraints should be used carefully because they can also make scheduling impossible.

# 60. Capacity for Failure

Normal operation should leave enough capacity to survive expected failure.

If three AZs each run at almost 100%:

```text
AZ-A 99%
AZ-B 99%
AZ-C 99%
```

losing one AZ cannot be absorbed by the remaining two.

---

## ADR-066 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The resilience foundation is now:

```text
                    USER REQUEST
                         │
                         ▼
                    TIME BUDGET
                         │
                         ▼
                      SERVICE
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ▼              ▼              ▼
       Timeout          Retry         Bulkhead
          │              │              │
          │          Backoff/Jitter     │
          │              │              │
          └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                         ▼
                   Circuit Breaker
                         │
                    ┌────┴────┐
                    ▼         ▼
                 Healthy    Failed
                    │         │
                    ▼         ▼
                 Normal    Fallback /
                           Degraded
                              │
                              ▼
                         User Outcome
```

The defining rule is:

> **A resilient service does not merely restart after failure. It bounds waiting, bounds retries, isolates resource exhaustion, prevents cascading failure, preserves safe functionality where possible and exposes failure clearly when correctness cannot be maintained.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Node Failure**, then cover **AZ failure → EKS architecture → autoscaling under failure → ALB behavior → DNS → RDS failover → connection recovery → Redis failover → Kafka broker/partition failure → OpenSearch failure → S3 failure → external dependency isolation → multi-AZ baseline → regional failure → multi-region decision framework → backup/restore → pilot light → warm standby → active/passive → active/active → Route 53 failover → health checks → DNS TTL → data replication → consistency during DR → RPO/RTO hierarchy → dependency recovery order → DR orchestration → failover → failback → backup isolation/immutability → ransomware recovery → business continuity → crisis management → degraded operating modes → resilience testing → chaos engineering → AWS Fault Injection Service → game days → resilience scorecards → resilience testing in CI/CD → capacity under failure → operational readiness → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise resilience/DR reference architecture.**

# ADR-066 — Enterprise Resilience, High Availability, Disaster Recovery & Failure Engineering

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Capacity for Failure**.

---

# 61. Node Failure

Kubernetes nodes must be treated as disposable infrastructure.

```text
Node Failure
     │
     ▼
Pods become unavailable
     │
     ▼
Kubernetes reschedules
     │
     ▼
Healthy nodes
```

Applications must not depend on local node state for durable business data.

---

# 62. Node Replacement

Failed/unhealthy nodes should normally be replaced rather than manually repaired.

```text
Immutable infrastructure
        >
SSH + manual repair
```

This aligns with ADR-061.

---

# 63. Node Drain

Planned maintenance should use controlled draining.

```text
Node
 │
 ▼
Cordon
 │
 ▼
Drain
 │
 ▼
PDB evaluation
 │
 ▼
Pods rescheduled
```

Maintenance procedures should verify remaining capacity before disruption.

---

# 64. Availability-Zone Failure

Production architecture should assume an entire AZ can become unavailable.

```text
             Region
                │
      ┌─────────┼─────────┐
      ▼         ▼         ▼
     AZ-A      AZ-B      AZ-C
      X         │         │
                ▼         ▼
             Continue Operation
```

Critical workloads should not depend on one AZ.

---

# 65. AZ-Aware Scheduling

Application replicas should be distributed across availability zones.

The architecture should prevent accidental concentration caused by:

```text
Insufficient nodes
Poor scheduling constraints
Capacity imbalance
Single-AZ node groups
Persistent-volume topology
```

---

# 66. AZ Failure Capacity

The remaining AZs must have enough capacity to absorb critical workloads.

For three AZs, planning should consider:

```text
Normal:
A + B + C

Failure:
B + C
```

not only normal-state efficiency.

---

# 67. Cluster Autoscaler During Failure

Autoscaling may provision replacement capacity after failure.

But autoscaling is not instantaneous.

Therefore:

```text
Spare capacity
      +
Autoscaling
```

is stronger than relying exclusively on emergency provisioning.

---

# 68. Karpenter

Karpenter may provide dynamic EKS node provisioning where adopted by ADR-061.

Failure architecture must consider:

```text
Instance availability
AZ capacity
Instance-family diversity
Provisioning latency
AWS API dependencies
Disruption policies
```

---

# 69. Instance Diversification

Critical workloads should avoid unnecessary dependence on one EC2 instance type.

Flexible node requirements improve recovery during regional capacity constraints.

---

# 70. Spot Instances

Spot capacity should primarily host interruption-tolerant workloads.

Critical capacity must not depend entirely on Spot.

```text
Critical baseline
→ On-Demand

Elastic/fault-tolerant capacity
→ Spot where appropriate
```

---

# 71. EKS Control Plane

EKS provides a managed Kubernetes control plane, but workloads must still tolerate temporary Kubernetes API unavailability.

Existing application traffic should not require continuous control-plane access to function.

---

# 72. Control-Plane Dependency

Applications should not unnecessarily make business requests depend on live Kubernetes API access.

```text
User Request
     │
     X
kubectl/Kubernetes API
```

should not be a normal application dependency.

---

# 73. ALB Architecture

Internet-facing traffic should use redundant AWS-managed load-balancing capabilities.

```text
Internet
   │
   ▼
  ALB
   │
 ┌─┼───────────────┐
 ▼ ▼               ▼
AZ-A              AZ-B              AZ-C
```

Backends must expose meaningful health signals.

---

# 74. Load-Balancer Health

ALB target health should align with application readiness.

A process being alive does not necessarily mean it can safely receive traffic.

---

# 75. Deregistration Draining

During deployment or termination, existing connections should receive appropriate time to complete where protocol/workload permits.

```text
Pod termination
      │
      ▼
Stop new traffic
      │
      ▼
Drain requests
      │
      ▼
Terminate
```

---

# 76. Graceful Shutdown

Spring Boot applications should support graceful shutdown.

Shutdown sequence should coordinate:

```text
Readiness removal
Request draining
Consumer shutdown
Background work
Connection closure
Process exit
```

---

# 77. Termination Grace Period

Kubernetes termination grace periods must reflect actual shutdown requirements.

Too short:

```text
Request processing
      │
      X SIGKILL
```

Too long can unnecessarily delay deployments/recovery.

---

# 78. DNS Resilience

DNS is a critical dependency.

Architecture should consider:

```text
Resolver availability
Caching
TTL
Failover records
Propagation delay
Application DNS caching
```

DNS changes are not instantaneous global switches.

---

# 79. DNS TTL

TTL determines a trade-off:

```text
Short TTL
→ faster endpoint change
→ more DNS queries

Long TTL
→ better caching
→ slower failover
```

TTL should match failover requirements.

---

# 80. Application DNS Caching

JVM/application DNS caching behavior must be understood.

A 30-second Route 53 TTL is useless for rapid failover if the application retains an obsolete address much longer.

---

# 81. RDS Failure

Applications must expect database connection loss during RDS failover.

```text
Application
     │
     X
Primary DB
     │
     ▼
Failover
     │
     ▼
New Primary
```

Existing connections may become invalid.

---

# 82. Database Connection Recovery

Connection pools should discard broken connections and establish new ones after failover.

Applications must not require restart merely because the database endpoint changed behind DNS.

---

# 83. Transaction Failure During Failover

A transaction interrupted by database failover may have uncertain outcome.

Applications must not assume:

```text
connection lost
=
transaction definitely failed
```

Idempotency and reconciliation may be required.

---

# 84. RDS Multi-AZ

Critical relational workloads should use Multi-AZ deployment as the primary HA mechanism.

This protects against infrastructure failure but not:

```text
Bad DELETE
Schema corruption
Application bug
Malicious modification
Logical data corruption
```

Those require recovery mechanisms.

---

# 85. Read Replica Failure

Loss of a read replica should degrade read capacity rather than destroy write availability.

Applications should have routing/fallback behavior appropriate to consistency requirements.

---

# 86. Redis Failure

Redis failure should be evaluated according to Redis's role.

For cache:

```text
Redis unavailable
      │
      ▼
Controlled fallback
      │
      ▼
PostgreSQL
```

But this can create a database traffic surge.

---

# 87. Cache Failure Storm

If Redis disappears:

```text
100k cached requests
       │
       ▼
PostgreSQL
```

may overload the authoritative database.

Fallback therefore requires:

```text
Rate limiting
Load shedding
Request coalescing
Database capacity protection
```

---

# 88. Redis Failover

Managed Redis replication/failover should be used for critical Redis workloads.

Clients must tolerate:

```text
Connection reset
Endpoint transition
Temporary errors
Replica promotion
```

---

# 89. Kafka Broker Failure

Kafka should tolerate individual broker failures when replication is configured correctly.

```text
Partition
   │
   ├── Leader Broker A  X
   ├── Replica Broker B
   └── Replica Broker C

             │
             ▼
       New leader elected
```

---

# 90. Kafka Replication

Critical topics should use appropriate replication factors across failure domains.

A replication factor of three is useful only if replicas are actually distributed appropriately.

---

# 91. Kafka In-Sync Replicas

Producer durability settings should consider:

```text
acks
min.insync.replicas
replication factor
```

These determine the trade-off between availability and durability during broker failures.

---

# 92. Kafka Consumer Recovery

Consumers must survive:

```text
Broker restart
Partition reassignment
Rebalancing
Transient network loss
Consumer restart
```

without corrupting business state.

---

# 93. Kafka Backlog Recovery

After consumer outage:

```text
Producer continues
       │
       ▼
Kafka backlog
       │
       ▼
Consumer restored
       │
       ▼
Catch-up
```

Capacity must support recovery faster than ongoing production.

Otherwise backlog never disappears.

---

# 94. OpenSearch Failure

Search should be treated as a secondary capability where possible.

```text
OpenSearch unavailable
       │
       ▼
Search degraded
       │
       ▼
Core transactional workflows continue
```

This prevents search failure from becoming platform failure.

---

# 95. OpenSearch Replica Recovery

Production search indexes should use appropriate replicas and multi-AZ placement.

Shard recovery capacity must be considered during node failure.

---

# 96. Search Rebuild

Because OpenSearch is derived state:

```text
Catastrophic Search Loss
        │
        ▼
Authoritative Data / Events
        │
        ▼
Reindex
        │
        ▼
Search Restored
```

Rebuild procedures must be tested.

---

# 97. S3 Failure Behavior

Applications should handle S3 failures explicitly.

For noncritical media:

```text
Object unavailable
→ placeholder / retry later
```

For critical upload:

```text
Storage unavailable
→ operation fails safely
```

Never report durable upload success before durability is established.

---

# 98. Asynchronous Dependency Isolation

Nonessential external side effects should be moved out of synchronous request paths where possible.

```text
Enrollment
    │
    ▼
DB Commit
    │
    ▼
Event
    │
    ├── Email
    ├── Analytics
    └── Notification
```

Email-provider failure should not roll back a valid enrollment.

---

# 99. Multi-AZ Baseline

Mediverse production should use multi-AZ architecture as its standard HA baseline for critical components.

```text
               REGION
                  │
       ┌──────────┼──────────┐
       ▼          ▼          ▼
      AZ-A       AZ-B       AZ-C
       │          │          │
       └──────────┼──────────┘
                  ▼
             APPLICATION
                  │
                  ▼
             DATA SERVICES
```

---

# 100. Multi-Region Is Not Default

Multi-region architecture is substantially more difficult than multi-AZ.

It introduces:

```text
Data replication
Consistency problems
Failover orchestration
DNS complexity
Higher cost
Operational duplication
Testing requirements
Security duplication
```

Mediverse should not adopt it without business justification.

---

# 101. Regional Failure

Regional DR begins with a scenario:

```text
Primary AWS Region
       X
       │
       ▼
Can Mediverse recover elsewhere?
```

The answer depends on RTO/RPO.

---

# 102. Multi-Region Decision Framework

Adoption should consider:

```text
Required RTO
Required RPO
Revenue/business impact
Regulatory requirements
Regional outage tolerance
Operational maturity
Data consistency requirements
Cost
```

---

# 103. Backup and Restore Strategy

Lowest-complexity regional DR:

```text
Primary Region
      │
      ▼
Cross-Region Backup
      │
      ▼
Disaster
      │
      ▼
Provision Secondary
      │
      ▼
Restore
```

Cost is relatively low.

RTO is relatively high.

---

# 104. Pilot Light

Pilot light maintains critical foundational components in the DR region.

```text
DR Region

Data replication ✓
Core infrastructure ✓
Full compute scale ✗
```

During disaster, compute capacity is expanded.

---

# 105. Warm Standby

Warm standby maintains a reduced but functioning secondary environment.

```text
Primary
100% capacity

Secondary
20–40% capacity
```

During failover, secondary capacity scales up.

---

# 106. Active/Passive

One region serves traffic while another is prepared to take over.

```text
Region A
 ACTIVE

Region B
 PASSIVE
```

This simplifies write consistency compared with active/active.

---

# 107. Active/Active

Both regions simultaneously serve production traffic.

```text
          USERS
            │
      ┌─────┴─────┐
      ▼           ▼
 Region A       Region B
 ACTIVE         ACTIVE
```

This is the most complex option.

---

# 108. Active/Active Warning

Active/active requires explicit answers for:

```text
Where are writes accepted?
How are conflicts resolved?
How is identity synchronized?
How is Kafka coordinated?
How is cache consistency handled?
What happens during network partition?
```

If these answers do not exist, the architecture is not truly active/active.

---

# 109. Recommended Mediverse DR Direction

Until business requirements prove otherwise:

```text
Production HA
→ Multi-AZ

Regional DR
→ Backup/Restore initially

Evolution
→ Pilot Light / Warm Standby
   when RTO requires it
```

Active/active is rejected as the default.

---

# 110. Route 53 Failover

For regional active/passive DR, Route 53 may direct users toward the healthy region.

```text
               Route 53
                  │
          ┌───────┴───────┐
          ▼               ▼
      Primary          Secondary
       Region            Region
```

Health checks must represent actual service readiness.

---

# 111. Health-Check Design

A DR health check should not declare a region healthy merely because one load balancer returns HTTP 200.

It should reflect critical dependencies sufficiently to determine whether the region can serve the intended journey.

---

# 112. False Failover

Over-sensitive health checks can cause unnecessary regional failover.

Failover itself carries risk.

Therefore:

```text
Temporary degradation
≠
automatic regional disaster
```

---

# 113. Failover Automation

Automation should be used where it reduces recovery time safely.

But destructive/high-risk decisions may require controlled human approval depending on architecture and maturity.

"Fully automatic" is not automatically superior.

---

# 114. Data Replication

Regional DR requires independent replication decisions for:

```text
PostgreSQL
S3
Kafka
Redis
OpenSearch
Secrets
Container images
Configuration
Infrastructure state
```

There is no single "replicate region" switch.

---

# 115. Authoritative vs Derived DR

Prioritize authoritative state.

```text
PostgreSQL
S3 authoritative objects
Secrets/configuration
        │
        ▼
      RECOVER
        │
        ▼
Kafka/projections as required
        │
        ▼
Redis/OpenSearch rebuild
```

Derived systems may often be reconstructed.

---

# 116. Consistency During DR

Regional failover can create:

```text
Replication lag
Lost recent writes
Duplicate processing
Out-of-order events
Stale caches
```

Applications must operate according to declared RPO and consistency semantics.

---

# 117. Split Brain

A severe risk is both regions believing they are primary writers.

```text
Region A ── writes
      X network
Region B ── writes
```

Without conflict strategy, data diverges.

Single-writer DR is simpler and preferred unless active/active is explicitly justified.

---

# 118. RPO Hierarchy

Recovery Point Objectives should be defined by business capability/data class.

Example:

```text
Tier 0 transactional data
→ very low acceptable loss

Tier 1 learning progress
→ low acceptable loss

Derived search indexes
→ reconstructable

Cache
→ zero recovery requirement
```

Exact numbers require business agreement.

---

# 119. RTO Hierarchy

Recovery Time Objectives should similarly vary.

```text
Authentication
→ fastest

Core learning
→ fast

Search
→ slower acceptable

Analytics
→ substantially slower acceptable
```

Do not assign identical RTOs to every component.

---

# 120. Dependency Recovery Order

Recovery should follow dependencies.

```text
1. AWS/network foundation
        │
2. Identity/secrets
        │
3. Authoritative databases
        │
4. Messaging
        │
5. Core services
        │
6. Edge/API
        │
7. Search/cache
        │
8. Secondary systems
```

Starting frontend pods before the database exists achieves little.

---

# 121. DR Runbook

Every critical system requires executable recovery documentation.

A runbook should contain:

```text
Trigger conditions
Roles
Dependencies
Commands/automation
Validation
Decision points
Rollback/failback
Communication
Evidence
```

---

# 122. Recovery Orchestration

Infrastructure-as-code and GitOps should reconstruct environments rather than relying on manual recreation.

```text
Terraform
   │
   ▼
AWS Infrastructure
   │
   ▼
EKS
   │
   ▼
Argo CD
   │
   ▼
Applications
```

ADR-061 becomes a DR dependency.

---

# 123. DR Infrastructure Drift

The secondary region must not exist only as outdated Terraform that has never successfully deployed.

Recovery code must be exercised.

---

# 124. Failover Procedure

A controlled regional failover may conceptually follow:

```text
Declare disaster
      │
      ▼
Freeze/confirm primary writes
      │
      ▼
Validate replicated data
      │
      ▼
Promote secondary data systems
      │
      ▼
Start/scale workloads
      │
      ▼
Validate critical journeys
      │
      ▼
Shift traffic
      │
      ▼
Monitor
```

Exact steps depend on selected technologies.

---

# 125. Failback

Returning to the original region can be harder than failing over.

```text
Secondary now contains newer writes
          │
          ▼
Original region restored
          │
          ▼
How does data return?
```

Failback must be designed before the first disaster.

---

# 126. Failback Strategy

Failback should consider:

```text
Data synchronization
Write freeze requirements
DNS transition
Validation
Rollback
Customer impact
```

Never improvise this during recovery.

---

# 127. Backup Isolation

Backups should be protected from the same administrative failure that destroys production.

Potential controls:

```text
Separate account
Restricted IAM
Independent encryption controls
Cross-region copies
Retention controls
```

---

# 128. Immutable Backups

Critical recovery data should use immutability mechanisms where justified.

The objective:

```text
Compromised production admin
          │
          X
Cannot immediately destroy
all recovery points
```

---

# 129. Backup Deletion Protection

Backup deletion should require stronger controls than ordinary application data modification.

A ransomware attacker should not be able to erase both production and recovery with one credential.

---

# 130. Ransomware Recovery

Recovery architecture should assume:

```text
Production compromised
Credentials compromised
Some backups targeted
Configuration potentially malicious
```

Recovery therefore requires trusted recovery points and clean infrastructure—not merely restarting existing servers.

---

# 131. Clean-Room Recovery

Severe security incidents may require:

```text
Trusted IaC
   │
   ▼
Clean AWS environment
   │
   ▼
Trusted artifacts
   │
   ▼
Verified backup
   │
   ▼
Restore
```

rather than reusing compromised infrastructure.

---

# 132. Business Continuity

DR restores technology.

Business continuity answers:

> How does the organization continue critical operations while technology is degraded or unavailable?

This requires coordination beyond engineering.

---

# 133. Business Impact Analysis

Critical capabilities should undergo BIA to determine:

```text
Maximum tolerable downtime
Business impact
Data-loss tolerance
Dependencies
Manual alternatives
Recovery priority
```

Technical RTO/RPO should follow business requirements.

---

# 134. Crisis Roles

Major incidents should establish explicit roles such as:

```text
Incident Commander
Technical Lead
Security Lead
Communications Lead
Business Representative
Scribe
```

One person should not attempt to perform every function.

---

# 135. Crisis Communication

Communication plans should define:

```text
Internal stakeholders
Leadership
Support
Customers/users
Vendors
Regulators where applicable
```

including who is authorized to communicate.

---

# 136. Status Communication

During major outages, updates should communicate:

```text
Known impact
Current mitigation
What is unknown
Next update time
```

Avoid unsupported recovery estimates.

---

# 137. Degraded Business Modes

Mediverse should identify operations that can continue during partial outages.

Example:

```text
Search unavailable
→ direct course navigation

Recommendation unavailable
→ default catalogue

Analytics unavailable
→ no user-facing impact

Notification unavailable
→ queue and deliver later
```

---

# 138. Chaos Engineering

Chaos engineering should validate resilience assumptions through controlled failure.

```text
Hypothesis
    │
    ▼
Inject Failure
    │
    ▼
Observe
    │
    ▼
Compare Expected vs Actual
    │
    ▼
Improve
```

Randomly breaking production without a hypothesis is not chaos engineering.

---

# 139. Chaos Preconditions

Before production chaos experiments:

```text
Observability exists
Rollback exists
Blast radius is bounded
Owners are present
Steady-state metric is defined
Experiment has stop conditions
```

---

# 140. AWS Fault Injection Service

AWS Fault Injection Service should be evaluated for controlled experiments such as:

```text
EC2 interruption
Network impairment
Resource stress
Selected AWS service faults
```

where supported and useful.

---

# 141. Kubernetes Failure Experiments

Game days should test scenarios including:

```text
Kill pod
Kill node
Drain node
Lose AZ capacity
Break DNS
Increase latency
Block dependency
Terminate consumer
Force DB failover
Disable Redis
```

in controlled environments.

---

# 142. Game Days

Regular game days should validate cross-team operational readiness.

A successful game day is not one where nothing fails.

It is one where assumptions are tested and weaknesses are discovered safely.

---

# 143. DR Exercises

At least periodically, teams should execute realistic recovery exercises:

```text
Backup restore
Regional infrastructure creation
Database recovery
Application deployment
Traffic failover
Critical journey validation
Failback
```

Paper runbooks alone are insufficient.

---

# 144. Resilience in CI/CD

Some failure properties should be continuously tested.

Examples:

```text
Timeout behavior
Retry limits
Idempotency
Dependency unavailability
Graceful shutdown
Startup/readiness behavior
Schema compatibility
```

Not every resilience test requires production chaos.

---

# 145. Capacity Testing

Load tests should evaluate:

```text
Normal capacity
Peak capacity
One-pod loss
One-node loss
One-AZ loss
Dependency slowdown
Recovery catch-up
```

Testing only healthy steady state gives misleading capacity numbers.

---

# 146. Resilience Scorecard

Critical services should maintain a scorecard covering:

```text
SLO defined?
Timeouts configured?
Retries bounded?
Circuit breaker?
Bulkhead?
Graceful degradation?
Multi-replica?
Multi-AZ?
PDB?
RPO/RTO?
Backup?
Restore tested?
DR runbook?
Chaos tested?
Owner?
```

This converts resilience from architectural rhetoric into measurable engineering work.

---

# 147. Operational Readiness Review

Before a critical service reaches production, verify:

```text
Failure modes understood
Dependencies documented
SLOs established
Alerts operational
Capacity known
Runbooks available
Backup/recovery proven
Security controls operational
Deployment rollback tested
Ownership established
```

Production should not be the first resilience test.

---

# 148. Resilience Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "Kubernetes makes us highly available"

❌ Single replica for critical services

❌ All replicas scheduled on one node/AZ

❌ 100% normal-state infrastructure utilization

❌ Critical workloads entirely dependent on Spot

❌ Durable state stored on pod/node filesystem

❌ Liveness probe checking every downstream dependency

❌ Readiness and liveness treated identically

❌ No graceful shutdown

❌ Arbitrary five-minute termination periods

❌ Remote calls without timeouts

❌ Every layer independently retrying

❌ Infinite retries

❌ Retry without idempotency analysis

❌ Retry storms without jitter

❌ Circuit breaker configured globally with identical settings

❌ Unlimited thread pools

❌ Unlimited connection pools

❌ Queue buffering treated as infinite capacity

❌ Kafka backlog ignored because brokers are healthy

❌ Fallback that violates security/correctness

❌ Redis outage allowed to DDoS PostgreSQL

❌ Database failover assumed transparent to active transactions

❌ Multi-AZ treated as backup

❌ Read replicas treated as immediately consistent

❌ OpenSearch failure allowed to break transactional APIs

❌ Email/SaaS dependency placed directly inside critical transaction

❌ Multi-region adopted for prestige

❌ Active/active claimed without conflict-resolution design

❌ Route 53 treated as instantaneous failover

❌ DR health check based only on load-balancer HTTP 200

❌ Automatic regional failover on every temporary error

❌ RPO/RTO defined by engineers without business input

❌ Same RPO/RTO assigned to every system

❌ Recovery order undefined

❌ DR runbook never executed

❌ Secondary infrastructure existing only as untested Terraform

❌ Failover designed but failback ignored

❌ Backups accessible through same compromised credentials

❌ Backups never restored

❌ Backup success treated as recovery proof

❌ Ransomware recovery assuming production credentials remain trusted

❌ Chaos engineering performed without bounded blast radius

❌ Game day judged successful because nothing broke

❌ Capacity testing only under healthy conditions

❌ Production used as first failure test
```

---
