# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                         | Decision                                    |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Resilience model             | **Failure-aware + defense in depth**        |
| Production HA baseline       | **Multi-AZ**                                |
| Critical service replicas    | Multiple                                    |
| Pod distribution             | AZ/node aware                               |
| Critical capacity            | Failure-capable                             |
| Spot                         | Supplemental/fault-tolerant workloads       |
| Node model                   | Replaceable/immutable                       |
| Application state on nodes   | **Rejected**                                |
| Startup probe                | Workload-driven                             |
| Readiness                    | Traffic eligibility                         |
| Liveness                     | Restart-worthy failure only                 |
| PDB                          | Critical workloads where appropriate        |
| Graceful shutdown            | Required                                    |
| Remote-call timeout          | Required                                    |
| Deadline propagation         | Preferred                                   |
| Retries                      | Bounded + safe                              |
| Retry backoff                | Exponential                                 |
| Retry jitter                 | Required at scale                           |
| Retry ownership              | Explicit                                    |
| Circuit breaker              | Dependency-specific                         |
| Spring implementation        | Resilience4j preferred                      |
| Bulkheads                    | Critical dependency isolation               |
| Load shedding                | Required where overload threatens stability |
| Backpressure                 | Explicit                                    |
| Idempotency                  | Required for retryable side effects         |
| Hard dependency failure      | Fail safely                                 |
| Soft dependency failure      | Graceful degradation                        |
| Async side effects           | Decoupled                                   |
| Redis outage                 | Controlled DB fallback                      |
| Kafka failure                | Replication + idempotent recovery           |
| OpenSearch                   | Degradable/rebuildable                      |
| RDS                          | Multi-AZ + recovery                         |
| Multi-AZ                     | **HA, not DR backup**                       |
| Regional DR                  | Requirement-driven                          |
| Initial DR                   | **Backup/Restore**                          |
| Evolution                    | Pilot Light / Warm Standby                  |
| Active/passive               | Preferred before active/active              |
| Active/active                | Exceptional                                 |
| DNS failover                 | Route 53 where required                     |
| DR health                    | Critical-journey aware                      |
| Split brain                  | Must be prevented                           |
| RPO                          | Business/data-tier specific                 |
| RTO                          | Business/service-tier specific              |
| Recovery order               | Dependency-driven                           |
| IaC/GitOps recovery          | Required                                    |
| Failover runbook             | Required                                    |
| Failback runbook             | Required                                    |
| Backup isolation             | Required                                    |
| Immutable recovery points    | Critical data where justified               |
| Ransomware recovery          | Clean recovery architecture                 |
| Business continuity          | Required                                    |
| Chaos engineering            | Controlled/hypothesis-driven                |
| Game days                    | Required for critical platform              |
| DR exercises                 | Periodic                                    |
| Failure testing              | CI/CD where practical                       |
| Capacity testing             | Includes degraded scenarios                 |
| Resilience scorecards        | Required for critical services              |
| Operational readiness review | Required                                    |
| Status                       | **Accepted**                                |
| Priority                     | **Critical**                                |

# ADR-066 — COMPLETE ✅

The complete resilience lifecycle is now:

```text
DESIGN FOR FAILURE
       │
       ▼
IDENTIFY FAILURE DOMAIN
       │
       ▼
BOUND TIME
       │
       ▼
BOUND RESOURCES
       │
       ▼
ISOLATE
       │
       ▼
RETRY SAFELY
       │
       ▼
DEGRADE GRACEFULLY
       │
       ▼
FAIL OVER
       │
       ▼
RECOVER
       │
       ▼
VALIDATE
       │
       ▼
FAIL BACK
       │
       ▼
TEST FAILURE
       │
       ▼
LEARN
       │
       └──────────────► DESIGN FOR FAILURE
```

The defining invariant is:

> **No individual pod, node, availability zone, cache, search cluster, broker, third-party service or other non-authoritative component should be capable of unnecessarily taking down the entire Mediverse platform. Severe failures must have explicit recovery paths governed by measurable RPO/RTO objectives and proven through real restore and failure exercises.**

## Next — ADR-067

### **ADR-067 — Enterprise Application Architecture & Spring Boot Microservices Engineering Standard**

With infrastructure, supply chain, observability, security, data and resilience foundations established, ADR-067 should finally standardize how Mediverse services themselves are engineered: **modular monolith vs microservices decision → bounded contexts → Domain-Driven Design → service boundaries → aggregate design → package architecture → hexagonal/clean architecture → ports and adapters → domain/application/infrastructure separation → Spring Boot baseline → Java version → Maven multi-module strategy → dependency governance → configuration → profiles → typed configuration → REST API standards → URI/resource modeling → HTTP semantics → status codes → request/response DTOs → validation → Problem Details/RFC 9457 → pagination → filtering → sorting → API versioning → OpenAPI → API-first vs code-first → controllers → application services → domain services → repositories → JPA boundaries → transaction design → MapStruct evaluation → Lombok policy → exception architecture → structured logging → correlation → Micrometer instrumentation → security integration → OAuth/OIDC resource server → method authorization → outbound HTTP clients → RestClient/WebClient decision → timeout/retry integration → Kafka producers/consumers → outbox integration → idempotency → scheduled jobs → async execution → virtual threads evaluation → concurrency → caching → feature flags → database migrations → testing pyramid → JUnit 5 → Mockito → AssertJ → Testcontainers → WireMock → contract testing → architecture tests/ArchUnit → mutation testing evaluation → performance testing → service templates → golden paths → backward compatibility → deprecation → production readiness → microservice anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise application reference architecture.**



# ADR-067 — Enterprise Application Architecture & Spring Boot Microservices Engineering Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-067
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-061 through ADR-066 established the infrastructure, supply-chain, observability, security, data and resilience foundations.

ADR-067 defines **how Mediverse application services are designed, structured, implemented, tested and evolved**.

> **A microservice is not a Spring Boot project with its own Dockerfile. It is an independently evolvable business capability with explicit ownership, contracts, data boundaries and operational responsibility.**

```text
                         MEDIVERSE
                             │
                             ▼
                      BUSINESS DOMAIN
                             │
                             ▼
                     BOUNDED CONTEXTS
                             │
            ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
            ▼                ▼                ▼
         Identity          Learning       Assessment
            │                │                │
            ▼                ▼                ▼
        Application      Application      Application
         Service           Service           Service
            │                │                │
            └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                             ▼
                    ENGINEERING STANDARD
                             │
       ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
       ▼                     ▼                     ▼
   Architecture             APIs                 Events
       │                     │                     │
       ▼                     ▼                     ▼
    Spring Boot           REST/OIDC              Kafka
       │                     │                     │
       └─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┘
                             ▼
                      PRODUCTION READY
```

# 1. Architecture Objective

Mediverse application architecture should optimize for:

```text
Business alignment
Maintainability
Testability
Independent evolution
Explicit dependencies
Security
Observability
Resilience
Operational ownership
```

Not maximum service count.

# 2. Microservices Are Not the Goal

The goal is not:

```text
100 services
```

The goal is:

```text
Clear business boundaries
        +
Independent change
        +
Controlled coupling
```

A badly decomposed microservice system is worse than a well-structured monolith.

# 3. Modular Monolith First

A new capability should not automatically become an independent service.

A modular monolith may be preferable when:

```text
Domain boundaries are uncertain
Team is small
Independent scaling is unnecessary
Deployment independence provides little value
Operational maturity is limited
```

# 4. Microservice Extraction

Extract a service when there is a meaningful reason such as:

```text
Independent lifecycle
Independent scaling
Strong domain boundary
Different availability requirement
Security isolation
Team ownership
Technology/runtime requirement
```

"Microservices are enterprise architecture" is rejected.

# 5. Domain-Driven Design

Mediverse should use DDD concepts where they clarify complex business domains.

```text
Business Domain
      │
      ▼
Subdomain
      │
      ▼
Bounded Context
      │
      ▼
Domain Model
```

DDD is not permission to create unnecessary abstraction around simple CRUD.

# 6. Bounded Context

A bounded context establishes a boundary within which domain terminology and models have consistent meaning.

Example:

```text
LEARNING CONTEXT

Course
Lesson
Module
Progress
Enrollment
```

# 7. Context Boundaries

Different contexts may represent the same real-world concept differently.

```text
Identity Context
Student → identity/profile

Learning Context
Student → learner/enrollment relationship

Assessment Context
Student → assessment candidate
```

Trying to create one universal enterprise `Student` object creates coupling.

# 8. Ubiquitous Language

Code should reflect business terminology.

Prefer:

```java
enrollStudent()
publishCourse()
submitAssessment()
```

over vague operations such as:

```java
processData()
handleItem()
executeOperation()
```

# 9. Service Boundary

A service should represent a cohesive capability.

Bad:

```text
StudentNameService
StudentEmailService
StudentAddressService
```

This is distributed object decomposition, not useful microservices.

# 10. Service Ownership

Every service requires:

```text
Owning team
Repository/module
Domain responsibility
Data ownership
API ownership
SLO
Runbook
On-call responsibility
```

An unowned microservice becomes operational debt.

# 11. Aggregate

DDD aggregates define transactional consistency boundaries.

```text
Course Aggregate
      │
      ├── Course
      ├── Modules
      └── Lessons
```

Only if those entities genuinely belong inside the same consistency boundary.

# 12. Aggregate Size

Large aggregates increase:

```text
Transaction scope
Lock contention
Object loading
Concurrency conflicts
```

Aggregates should protect invariants, not mirror entire database graphs.

# 13. Aggregate Root

External domain operations should normally interact through the aggregate root.

```text
Application Service
       │
       ▼
    Course
       │
       ▼
    Lesson
```

rather than allowing arbitrary mutation of internal aggregate state.

# 14. Domain Invariants

Business invariants belong close to the domain.

Example:

```text
Published course
cannot contain
zero publishable lessons.
```

Do not spread the same rule independently across controllers, frontend and database scripts.

# 15. Entity

An entity has identity across time.

```text
Course
Enrollment
Assessment
```

Identity matters even when attributes change.

# 16. Value Object

Value objects represent descriptive concepts without independent identity.

Examples may include:

```text
EmailAddress
Money
DateRange
CourseCode
```

Value objects should normally be immutable.

# 17. Domain Service

A domain service is appropriate when important domain logic does not naturally belong to one entity/value object.

Do not create a `SomethingService` for every class.

# 18. Application Service

Application services orchestrate use cases.

```text
Controller
    │
    ▼
Application Service
    │
    ├── Domain
    ├── Repository
    └── Event Port
```

They should not become thousand-line containers for every business rule.

# 19. Hexagonal Architecture

Mediverse services should use ports-and-adapters principles for sufficiently complex services.

```text
                    INBOUND
                       │
                       ▼
                  REST / Kafka
                       │
                       ▼
                ┌─────────────┐
                │ APPLICATION │
                └──────┬──────┘
                       ▼
                   DOMAIN
                       │
                ┌──────┴──────┐
                ▼             ▼
           Repository      Event Port
                │             │
                ▼             ▼
              JPA           Kafka
```

# 20. Dependency Direction

Core business logic should not depend directly on infrastructure details.

Preferred:

```text
Infrastructure
      │
      ▼
Application
      │
      ▼
Domain
```

Dependencies point inward.

# 21. Ports

Ports define capabilities required or exposed by the application.

Examples:

```text
CourseRepository
PaymentGateway
EventPublisher
ObjectStorage
```

They should model useful capabilities rather than mechanically wrapping every library call.

# 22. Adapters

Adapters implement ports using technologies.

```text
CourseRepository
      │
      ▼
JpaCourseRepositoryAdapter
```

or:

```text
ObjectStorage
      │
      ▼
S3ObjectStorageAdapter
```

# 23. Architecture Complexity

Not every CRUD service requires seven abstraction layers.

For simple services:

```text
Controller
   │
Service
   │
Repository
```

may be sufficient.

Architecture must scale with domain complexity.

# 24. Package Structure

Prefer feature/domain-oriented structure over purely technical global folders.

Weak:

```text
controller/
service/
repository/
entity/
dto/
```

for a large application.

Better:

```text
course/
enrollment/
assessment/
identity/
```

with internal layers where required.

# 25. Example Service Structure

```text
course-service/
│
├── course/
│   ├── domain/
│   │   ├── Course.java
│   │   ├── CourseId.java
│   │   └── CourseRepository.java
│   │
│   ├── application/
│   │   ├── CreateCourseUseCase.java
│   │   └── PublishCourseUseCase.java
│   │
│   ├── inbound/
│   │   ├── rest/
│   │   └── kafka/
│   │
│   └── outbound/
│       ├── persistence/
│       └── messaging/
│
├── shared/
└── CourseApplication.java
```

# 26. Java Baseline

Mediverse should standardize on a supported modern Java LTS release.

For new development, the baseline should be centrally governed rather than allowing services to independently select Java versions.

# 27. Spring Boot Baseline

Spring Boot versions should be centrally governed and upgraded systematically.

Avoid:

```text
Service A → arbitrary Boot version
Service B → another
Service C → unsupported release
```

Version fragmentation increases security and operational cost.

# 28. Dependency Governance

Common dependency versions should be controlled through:

```text
Spring dependency management
Internal BOM where justified
Automated dependency updates
ADR-062 vulnerability policy
```

# 29. Maven

Maven should remain the standard Java build system unless a future ADR explicitly changes it.

Builds must be reproducible and CI-friendly.

# 30. Maven Modules

Multi-module Maven projects are appropriate when modules are released and evolved together.

Do not create a giant Maven reactor containing independently deployed services merely to "share code."

# 31. Shared Libraries

Shared libraries should be small and stable.

Good candidates:

```text
Observability conventions
Security integration
Common test utilities
Platform client conventions
```

Bad candidate:

```text
shared-domain-everything.jar
```

# 32. Shared Domain Models

Services should not share persistence/domain entity JARs.

```text
user-domain.jar
     │
 ┌───┼───┐
 ▼   ▼   ▼
A    B    C
```

creates compile-time distributed coupling.

# 33. Configuration

Application configuration should be externalized.

```text
Application artifact
      +
Environment configuration
```

The same artifact should move between environments where practical.

# 34. Spring Profiles

Profiles may select environment-specific behavior sparingly.

Avoid turning profiles into entirely different applications.

# 35. Typed Configuration

Prefer typed configuration:

```java
@ConfigurationProperties
```

over hundreds of scattered:

```java
@Value("${...}")
```

expressions.

# 36. Configuration Validation

Required configuration should fail fast during startup.

A service should not discover three hours later that a required endpoint was missing.

# 37. Secrets

Secrets must follow ADR-064.

Never store secrets in:

```text
application.yml
Git
Dockerfile
Frontend bundle
Plain CI variables without governance
```

# 38. REST API Philosophy

REST APIs should model resources and business capabilities consistently.

```text
/api/courses
/api/courses/{courseId}
/api/courses/{courseId}/modules
```

Avoid RPC disguised as arbitrary URLs everywhere.

# 39. HTTP GET

GET should retrieve state and remain safe from business mutation.

Rejected:

```text
GET /deleteCourse?id=123
```

# 40. POST

POST should generally create resources or execute non-idempotent commands where resource modeling requires it.

# 41. PUT

PUT should represent idempotent replacement/update semantics where appropriate.

Repeated identical requests should produce equivalent intended state.

# 42. PATCH

PATCH should represent partial modification when the API requires it.

Patch semantics must be explicitly defined.

# 43. DELETE

DELETE should represent resource deletion/deactivation according to domain lifecycle.

Physical deletion is not always implied.

# 44. HTTP Status Codes

Use meaningful status codes.

```text
200 → successful response
201 → created
202 → accepted asynchronous work
204 → success without response body
400 → malformed/invalid request
401 → unauthenticated
403 → authenticated but forbidden
404 → resource unavailable/not found
409 → state/conflict
422 → semantic validation where adopted
429 → rate limited
500 → unexpected server failure
503 → temporarily unavailable
```

Do not return `200 OK` for every outcome.

# 45. 401 vs 403

```text
401
→ authentication missing/invalid

403
→ identity known but not authorized
```

These should not be used interchangeably.

# 46. Request DTOs

External API models should not bind directly to persistence entities.

```text
HTTP JSON
   │
   ▼
Request DTO
   │
   ▼
Application Command
   │
   ▼
Domain
```

# 47. Response DTOs

Responses should expose deliberate API contracts.

Do not serialize JPA entities directly.

That can leak:

```text
Internal fields
Relationships
Lazy-loading behavior
Persistence structure
Sensitive properties
```

# 48. Validation

Use Bean Validation for structural validation where appropriate.

Examples:

```java
@NotBlank
@Size
@Email
@Positive
```

Business invariants still belong in the domain/application layer.

# 49. Validation Layers

```text
Request validation
→ structural correctness

Domain validation
→ business correctness

Database constraints
→ persistence integrity
```

These complement one another.

# 50. Error Contract

Mediverse APIs should use a standardized error representation.

RFC 9457 Problem Details should be preferred where compatible.

Conceptually:

```json
{
  "type": "...",
  "title": "Course not found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "...",
  "instance": "...",
  "code": "COURSE_NOT_FOUND"
}
```

# 51. Internal Error Leakage

External errors must not expose:

```text
Java stack traces
SQL
Database names
Secrets
Internal hostnames
Implementation internals
```

Detailed diagnostics remain in protected logs.

# 52. Exception Architecture

Exceptions should be translated centrally.

```text
Domain/Application Exception
          │
          ▼
@ControllerAdvice
          │
          ▼
Problem Details
```

Avoid duplicated `try/catch` blocks in every controller.

# 53. Pagination

Collection endpoints expected to grow should support pagination.

```text
GET /courses?page=0&size=20
```

or cursor-based pagination where scale/consistency requirements justify it.

# 54. Page Size

Servers should enforce maximum page sizes.

Rejected:

```text
GET /courses?size=999999999
```

# 55. Offset Pagination

Offset/page pagination is simple and appropriate for many administrative and moderate-size datasets.

Large/high-change datasets may experience performance and consistency issues.

# 56. Cursor Pagination

Cursor/keyset pagination should be considered for large continuously changing datasets.

```text
GET /feed?after=<cursor>
```

It avoids increasingly expensive deep offsets.

# 57. Filtering

Filtering parameters should be explicit and validated.

Avoid exposing arbitrary database query construction through request parameters.

# 58. Sorting

Allowed sort fields should be controlled.

```text
?sort=createdAt,desc
```

should not become unrestricted SQL-field exposure.

# 59. API Versioning

Version APIs only when compatibility requirements demand it.

Potential strategy:

```text
/api/v1/courses
```

Major versions should represent meaningful contract incompatibility.

# 60. Backward Compatibility

Existing clients should not break because a service casually changed:

```text
Field name
Field type
Required property
Enum meaning
Status semantics
```

Contract evolution must be deliberate.

---

## ADR-067 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The application architecture now follows:

```text
                   BUSINESS CAPABILITY
                          │
                          ▼
                   BOUNDED CONTEXT
                          │
                          ▼
                       SERVICE
                          │
            ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
            ▼             ▼             ▼
         INBOUND      APPLICATION     DOMAIN
            │             │             │
            │             └──────┬──────┘
            │                    ▼
            │                 PORTS
            │                    │
            └────────────────────┼───────────────┐
                                 ▼               ▼
                            PostgreSQL          Kafka
                                 │               │
                                 ├──── Redis     │
                                 └──── S3        │
                                                 ▼
                                           Other Services
```

The critical rule is:

> **Service boundaries follow business ownership and consistency boundaries—not controllers, database tables or organizational enthusiasm for microservices. Domain logic remains independent of transport and infrastructure wherever complexity justifies that separation, while simple services remain simple.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — OpenAPI & API Contract Governance**, then cover **API-first vs code-first → API documentation → deprecation → controller design → command/query separation → CQRS evaluation → application services → repositories → JPA entity boundaries → transaction management → DTO mapping → MapStruct → Lombok policy → outbound HTTP clients → RestClient vs WebClient → timeout/retry integration → OAuth/OIDC resource server → method authorization → Kafka producers → Kafka consumers → transactional outbox → idempotency → scheduled jobs → async execution → Java virtual threads → concurrency → caching → feature flags → Flyway → structured logging → correlation IDs → Micrometer → tracing → health endpoints → Actuator security → testing pyramid → JUnit 5 → Mockito → AssertJ → Spring slice tests → Testcontainers → WireMock → contract testing → ArchUnit → mutation testing → performance testing → service templates/golden paths → backward compatibility → production readiness → microservice anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise Spring Boot application reference architecture.**


# ADR-067 — Enterprise Application Architecture & Spring Boot Microservices Engineering Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Backward Compatibility**.

---

# 61. OpenAPI Contract Governance

Every externally consumed REST API should expose an OpenAPI specification.

```text
Spring Boot Service
       │
       ▼
    OpenAPI
       │
       ├── Paths
       ├── Schemas
       ├── Security
       ├── Errors
       └── Examples
```

OpenAPI is an API contract, not merely Swagger UI documentation.

---

# 62. API-First vs Code-First

Mediverse should not force one approach onto every service.

```text
API-first
→ useful for externally coordinated contracts

Code-first
→ efficient for team-owned/internal APIs
```

The important requirement is that implementation and published contract remain synchronized.

---

# 63. API-First

API-first should be preferred when:

```text
Frontend/backend teams work independently
External consumers exist
Multiple services depend on contract
SDK generation is required
Contract review is important
```

Design occurs before implementation.

---

# 64. Code-First

Code-first may remain appropriate for simpler internal services.

```text
Controller / DTO
       │
       ▼
Generated OpenAPI
       │
       ▼
Contract validation
```

Generated specifications must still be reviewed.

---

# 65. API Contract CI

CI should detect unintended contract changes.

```text
Previous OpenAPI
       │
       ▼
Compatibility Check
       ▲
       │
New OpenAPI
```

Breaking changes should fail or require explicit approval according to governance.

---

# 66. API Documentation

Documentation should explain more than endpoints.

Include:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Rate limits
Pagination
Errors
Idempotency
Examples
Deprecation
Versioning
```

---

# 67. API Deprecation

Deprecated APIs require an explicit migration path.

```text
v1
 │
 ├── Deprecated
 │
 ▼
Migration Window
 │
 ▼
v2
 │
 ▼
v1 Removal
```

Removal dates must reflect consumer commitments.

---

# 68. Controller Responsibility

Controllers should remain thin.

```text
HTTP
 │
 ▼
Controller
 │
 ▼
Application Service
```

Controllers handle transport concerns—not core business workflows.

---

# 69. Fat Controller Anti-Pattern

Rejected:

```text
Controller
 ├── authorization logic
 ├── SQL
 ├── business rules
 ├── Kafka publishing
 ├── mapping
 └── transaction orchestration
```

This destroys separation and testability.

---

# 70. Command/Query Separation

Application use cases should distinguish state-changing commands from queries conceptually.

```text
Command
→ changes state

Query
→ reads state
```

This does not require a full CQRS architecture.

---

# 71. CQRS Evaluation

Full CQRS should be introduced only when read and write requirements genuinely diverge.

```text
Commands
   │
   ▼
Write Model

Queries
   │
   ▼
Read Model
```

CQRS adds synchronization and operational complexity.

---

# 72. CQRS Anti-Pattern

Do not create:

```text
CommandBus
QueryBus
20 handlers
15 abstractions
```

around five CRUD endpoints merely because CQRS is fashionable.

---

# 73. Application Use Cases

Application services should expose business-oriented operations.

Prefer:

```java
publishCourse()
enrollLearner()
submitAssessment()
```

rather than generic:

```java
save()
update()
process()
```

where meaningful domain semantics exist.

---

# 74. Repository Boundary

Repositories should model domain persistence needs.

```text
Domain
   │
   ▼
CourseRepository
   │
   ▼
Persistence Adapter
   │
   ▼
JPA
```

Domain code should not require knowledge of Hibernate internals.

---

# 75. Spring Data JPA

Spring Data JPA should remain the standard relational persistence abstraction for normal Mediverse services.

Native SQL or specialized access is allowed when measurement or query complexity justifies it.

---

# 76. JPA Entity Boundary

Persistence entities should remain inside the owning service.

Never expose them as:

```text
REST contracts
Kafka contracts
Shared-library contracts
Cross-service domain models
```

---

# 77. JPA Relationships

Relationships should be modeled conservatively.

A large object graph such as:

```text
Course
 └── Modules
      └── Lessons
           └── Resources
                └── Progress
```

should not automatically become a deeply navigable JPA graph.

---

# 78. Lazy Loading

Lazy loading should generally remain the default for potentially expensive relationships.

Required data should be fetched explicitly within valid transaction boundaries.

---

# 79. Open Session in View

Mediverse APIs should generally avoid depending on Open Session in View.

```text
Controller serialization
        │
        X
hidden DB query
```

Database access should be explicit in application/persistence layers.

---

# 80. Transaction Management

Transactions should normally begin at application-service/use-case boundaries.

```text
Controller
    │
    ▼
@Transactional
Application Use Case
    │
    ▼
Repositories
```

---

# 81. Transaction Scope

Transactions should be short.

Do not routinely perform:

```text
BEGIN
 ↓
Database update
 ↓
Call external API
 ↓
Wait 10 seconds
 ↓
Kafka request
 ↓
COMMIT
```

External operations should not hold database transactions open unnecessarily.

---

# 82. Read-Only Transactions

Read-only transaction hints may be used where useful.

They do not replace query optimization or correct database architecture.

---

# 83. Transaction Propagation

Spring transaction propagation should be used deliberately.

`REQUIRES_NEW` should not become a convenient mechanism for hiding poor transaction design.

---

# 84. DTO Mapping

Mapping between:

```text
API DTO
Application model
Domain model
Persistence model
```

should remain explicit enough that boundaries are visible.

---

# 85. MapStruct

MapStruct should be preferred for repetitive compile-time DTO mapping where manual mapping becomes noisy.

It provides:

```text
Compile-time generation
Type safety
Low runtime overhead
Explicit mapping configuration
```

---

# 86. Mapping Warning

Do not map every layer into an identical object merely to claim architectural purity.

If three objects contain identical fields and provide no meaningful boundary, reconsider the design.

---

# 87. Lombok Policy

Lombok may be used selectively for boilerplate reduction.

Acceptable examples:

```text
@Getter
@Builder
@RequiredArgsConstructor
```

Use cautiously on domain/JPA models.

---

# 88. Lombok @Data

`@Data` should generally be avoided on JPA entities.

Generated:

```text
equals()
hashCode()
toString()
setters
```

can interact badly with entity identity, lazy relationships and mutable state.

---

# 89. Constructor Injection

Dependencies should use constructor injection.

Preferred:

```java
public CourseService(CourseRepository repository) {
    this.repository = repository;
}
```

Field injection should be avoided.

---

# 90. Outbound HTTP Client

Spring services requiring synchronous HTTP calls should standardize on supported Spring HTTP clients rather than introducing arbitrary client libraries per service.

---

# 91. RestClient

For modern Spring Boot synchronous request/response workloads, `RestClient` should be preferred over legacy `RestTemplate` for new code.

```text
Service
  │
  ▼
RestClient
  │
  ▼
Remote API
```

---

# 92. WebClient

`WebClient` should be used when reactive/non-blocking behavior is actually required.

Using WebClient does not automatically make an application scalable.

---

# 93. RestTemplate

Existing `RestTemplate` applications may continue during controlled migration, but new services should not select it as the default.

---

# 94. HTTP Client Configuration

Every outbound client should explicitly define:

```text
Connection timeout
Request/read timeout
Connection pool
TLS
Authentication
Observability
Retry behavior
```

Defaults should not be trusted blindly.

---

# 95. Resilience Integration

Outbound calls should follow ADR-066.

```text
RestClient
    │
    ▼
Timeout
    │
    ▼
Bulkhead
    │
    ▼
Retry where safe
    │
    ▼
Circuit Breaker
```

Do not blindly apply every resilience pattern to every endpoint.

---

# 96. OAuth2 Resource Server

Protected Spring Boot APIs should normally operate as OAuth2/OIDC resource servers according to ADR-064.

```text
Access Token
     │
     ▼
Spring Security
     │
     ▼
JWT validation
     │
     ▼
SecurityContext
```

---

# 97. Token Validation

Services should validate:

```text
Signature
Issuer
Audience where required
Expiration
Relevant claims
```

A token being syntactically valid is insufficient.

---

# 98. Authorization

Authorization should exist close to protected operations.

```text
Authenticated Identity
        │
        ▼
Role / Scope / Permission
        │
        ▼
Business Authorization
        │
        ▼
Operation
```

---

# 99. Method Security

Spring method authorization may protect application-service operations.

Example:

```java
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('course:publish')")
```

But complex business authorization should not become unreadable SpEL expressions.

---

# 100. Ownership Authorization

Resource ownership must be validated.

```text
User has COURSE_EDIT
        │
        ▼
Does user have permission
for THIS course?
```

Global roles alone may not answer this.

---

# 101. Kafka Producer

Kafka producers should publish governed domain events.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Outbox
    │
    ▼
Publisher
    │
    ▼
Kafka
```

Direct publishing is acceptable only where dual-write consistency is irrelevant.

---

# 102. Producer Configuration

Production producer settings should explicitly consider:

```text
acks
Retries
Delivery timeout
Compression
Batching
Idempotence
Serialization
```

Configuration must follow durability and latency requirements.

---

# 103. Kafka Consumer

Consumers should implement a clear pipeline.

```text
Deserialize
    │
    ▼
Validate
    │
    ▼
Idempotency
    │
    ▼
Business Processing
    │
    ▼
Commit
```

---

# 104. Consumer Idempotency

Consumers must assume duplicate delivery unless stronger guarantees are proven.

Use appropriate:

```text
eventId
unique constraint
processed-event record
aggregate version
business key
```

---

# 105. Consumer Transactions

Database writes and offset handling require deliberate semantics.

Do not acknowledge a message before critical processing is safely completed.

---

# 106. Poison Events

Invalid messages should follow ADR-065 retry/DLQ policy.

A single bad message must not indefinitely block a partition.

---

# 107. Transactional Outbox

Business state and event intent should be persisted atomically.

```text
@Transactional
     │
     ├── Domain state
     └── Outbox event
             │
           COMMIT
             │
             ▼
          Publisher
             │
             ▼
            Kafka
```

---

# 108. Outbox Cleanup

Published outbox records require controlled lifecycle management.

Without cleanup:

```text
outbox
  │
  ▼
millions
  │
  ▼
billions
```

eventually becomes an operational problem.

---

# 109. Scheduled Jobs

Scheduled jobs should be used for inherently scheduled work—not as a substitute for proper event architecture.

Examples:

```text
Periodic cleanup
Retention enforcement
Scheduled publication
Reconciliation
```

---

# 110. Distributed Scheduling

In a multi-replica service:

```text
Pod A ─ scheduled job
Pod B ─ scheduled job
Pod C ─ scheduled job
```

may execute the same task three times.

Jobs must be:

```text
Idempotent
Leader-controlled
Externally scheduled
or appropriately locked
```

depending on semantics.

---

# 111. Kubernetes CronJob

Platform-level scheduled tasks should consider Kubernetes CronJobs when execution is naturally independent of a continuously running service.

---

# 112. Async Execution

Spring `@Async` should be used carefully.

It does not create durable asynchronous processing.

```text
Application crashes
      │
      ▼
In-memory async task
      X
```

Durable business work belongs in durable queues/events.

---

# 113. Executor Governance

Thread pools must be bounded.

Rejected:

```text
unlimited queue
+
unlimited workload
```

which simply converts overload into memory exhaustion and latency.

---

# 114. Virtual Threads

Java virtual threads should be evaluated for high-concurrency blocking-I/O services where the selected Java/Spring stack supports them appropriately.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Virtual Thread
   │
   ▼
Blocking I/O
```

They can reduce thread-management cost.

---

# 115. Virtual Threads Are Not Magic

Virtual threads do not increase:

```text
Database connections
CPU
Kafka partitions
Remote API capacity
Memory
```

A service can create 100,000 virtual threads and still have only 50 database connections.

Backpressure remains necessary.

---

# 116. Concurrency Safety

Singleton Spring beans may be accessed concurrently.

Mutable request-specific state must not be stored in singleton service fields.

---

# 117. Caching

Application caching should follow ADR-065.

```text
Application
   │
   ▼
Redis
   │ miss
   ▼
PostgreSQL
```

Cache behavior is part of application correctness.

---

# 118. Spring Cache Abstraction

Spring Cache may be used where its abstraction matches requirements.

Do not hide complex invalidation semantics behind annotations if correctness becomes unclear.

---

# 119. Feature Flags

Feature flags should separate deployment from release where useful.

```text
Deploy code
    │
    ▼
Flag OFF
    │
    ▼
Controlled enablement
```

---

# 120. Feature Flag Lifecycle

Flags require:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Default
Expiration/removal plan
Observability
```

Permanent forgotten flags create combinatorial complexity.

---

# 121. Database Migration

Flyway should be the default relational schema migration tool unless a service has an approved reason to use Liquibase.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Flyway Migration
 │
 ▼
Deployment
 │
 ▼
PostgreSQL
```

---

# 122. Migration Immutability

Applied migration files should not normally be edited.

Create a new migration.

Changing history destroys reproducibility between environments.

---

# 123. Zero-Downtime Migration

Follow ADR-065:

```text
EXPAND
   │
   ▼
DEPLOY COMPATIBLE CODE
   │
   ▼
BACKFILL
   │
   ▼
SWITCH
   │
   ▼
CONTRACT
```

Database and application versions must tolerate rolling deployment overlap.

---

# 124. Structured Logging

Application logs should be machine-readable in production.

Example conceptual fields:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "...",
  "level": "INFO",
  "service": "course-service",
  "traceId": "...",
  "message": "Course published",
  "courseId": "..."
}
```

Follow ADR-063 for observability governance.

---

# 125. Logging Policy

Do not log:

```text
Passwords
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
Secrets
Sensitive request bodies
Sensitive medical/personal information without explicit approved need
```

Security rules from ADR-064 apply.

---

# 126. Correlation and Trace Context

Services should propagate standard trace context across:

```text
HTTP
Kafka
Async workflows
```

Do not invent unrelated proprietary correlation mechanisms without need.

---

# 127. Micrometer

Spring Boot services should use Micrometer-based instrumentation for application metrics and tracing integration.

Common metrics include:

```text
Request latency
Request count
Error rate
JVM
Connection pools
Kafka
Cache
Business metrics
```

---

# 128. Business Metrics

Technical metrics alone are insufficient.

Useful business signals may include:

```text
Enrollments completed
Assessment submissions
Course publication failures
Upload processing failures
```

Avoid high-cardinality identifiers as metric labels.

---

# 129. Spring Boot Actuator

Actuator should provide operational endpoints required by the platform.

Typical endpoints:

```text
health
info
metrics
prometheus
```

Exposure should be explicitly configured.

---

# 130. Actuator Security

Do not expose all Actuator endpoints publicly.

Sensitive operational endpoints require network/security controls.

---

# 131. Health Indicators

Health should distinguish application state from dependency state.

Readiness may depend on hard dependencies.

Liveness should not restart applications merely because an external dependency is temporarily unavailable.

---

# 132. Testing Strategy

Mediverse adopts a layered testing strategy.

```text
              /\
             /  \
            / E2E\
           /------\
          /Contract\
         /----------\
        /Integration \
       /--------------\
      /   Unit Tests   \
     /__________________\
```

The objective is confidence—not maximizing one test category.

---

# 133. JUnit 5

JUnit 5 should remain the standard Java test framework.

Tests should describe behavior rather than implementation trivia.

---

# 134. AssertJ

AssertJ should be preferred for expressive assertions where useful.

Tests should remain readable enough that failures explain what behavior broke.

---

# 135. Mockito

Mockito should isolate collaborators in focused unit tests.

Do not mock everything.

A test containing:

```text
15 mocks
```

often signals excessive coupling or a test operating at the wrong level.

---

# 136. Spring Slice Tests

Use focused Spring tests where appropriate:

```text
@WebMvcTest
@DataJpaTest
@JsonTest
```

instead of booting the entire application for every test.

---

# 137. Testcontainers

Integration tests requiring infrastructure should prefer Testcontainers for realistic dependencies.

```text
JUnit
  │
  ├── PostgreSQL container
  ├── Kafka container
  └── Redis container
```

where justified.

This reduces divergence from production behavior compared with simplistic substitutes.

---

# 138. H2 Warning

H2 should not be relied upon as proof that PostgreSQL-specific persistence behavior works.

Differences exist in:

```text
SQL
Types
Locking
Sequences
Constraints
Query behavior
```

PostgreSQL integration tests should use PostgreSQL.

---

# 139. WireMock

WireMock or equivalent should simulate external HTTP dependencies for integration tests.

Tests should cover:

```text
Success
Timeout
5xx
Malformed response
Slow response
Retry behavior
```

not only happy paths.

---

# 140. Contract Testing

Consumer/provider contract testing should be considered when independently deployed services have important API dependencies.

```text
Consumer expectation
       │
       ▼
Contract
       │
       ▼
Provider verification
```

This detects integration breakage before deployment.

---

# 141. ArchUnit

ArchUnit should enforce important architectural boundaries where useful.

Examples:

```text
Domain must not depend on controller
Domain must not depend on JPA adapter
Controllers must not access repositories directly
```

Architecture rules become executable.

---

# 142. Mutation Testing

Mutation testing should be evaluated for high-value domain logic.

It asks:

> Would the test suite detect deliberately introduced logic defects?

Do not require it indiscriminately across trivial code.

---

# 143. Performance Testing

Critical APIs should have explicit performance tests.

Measure:

```text
Latency
Throughput
Error rate
Resource consumption
Database load
Connection saturation
```

under realistic concurrency.

---

# 144. Golden Path

The platform team should provide a standard Spring Boot service template.

```text
New Service
    │
    ▼
Golden Path Template
    │
    ├── Security
    ├── Observability
    ├── Testing
    ├── Docker
    ├── Kubernetes
    ├── CI/CD
    ├── OpenAPI
    └── Resilience
```

Teams should not rebuild platform plumbing for every service.

---

# 145. Template Governance

A service template should accelerate teams without permanently locking them to outdated dependencies.

Templates require:

```text
Versioning
Upgrade guidance
Ownership
Security maintenance
Documentation
```

---

# 146. Production Readiness

Before production, each service should prove:

```text
Owner identified
API/event contracts documented
Authorization implemented
Database migrations tested
Observability operational
Timeouts configured
Retries bounded
Health probes correct
Resources defined
SLO established
Runbook available
Rollback tested
Backup/recovery addressed
Load characteristics understood
```

---

# 147. Service Evolution

Services must evolve without assuming synchronized deployment of every consumer.

```text
Producer v2
   │
   ├── Consumer v1
   └── Consumer v2
```

Compatibility windows are normal in distributed systems.

---

# 148. Microservice Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Microservices because "enterprise systems use microservices"
❌ Service per database table
❌ Service per entity
❌ Distributed monolith
❌ Shared database tables across service boundaries
❌ Shared JPA entity libraries
❌ Synchronous calls through five services for simple operations
❌ Circular service dependencies
❌ Universal enterprise domain object
❌ DDD abstractions around trivial CRUD
❌ Huge aggregates
❌ Business logic in controllers
❌ Controllers accessing repositories directly
❌ JPA entities serialized as APIs
❌ EAGER relationships everywhere
❌ Open Session in View hiding database access
❌ Transactions around external network calls
❌ Arbitrary REQUIRES_NEW usage
❌ @Data on every JPA entity
❌ Field injection
❌ RestTemplate selected for new applications without reason
❌ WebClient used only because "reactive is faster"
❌ HTTP calls without bounded timeouts
❌ Retry annotations copied onto every client
❌ Huge authorization expressions
❌ Kafka events published before database commit
❌ Consumers assuming exactly-once processing
❌ In-memory @Async used for durable business work
❌ Scheduled jobs duplicated across every replica
❌ Unbounded executors
❌ Virtual threads treated as infinite capacity
❌ Cache annotations hiding incorrect invalidation
❌ Permanent feature flags
❌ Editing already-applied Flyway migrations
❌ Breaking schema changes during rolling deployment
❌ Secrets/PII dumped into logs
❌ Public unrestricted Actuator endpoints
❌ H2 used as proof of PostgreSQL compatibility
❌ Mock-heavy tests with no integration coverage
❌ Full Spring context started for every unit test
❌ E2E tests used as the entire test strategy
❌ No contract compatibility checks
❌ New service built from scratch with different conventions
❌ Shared libraries becoming a distributed monolith
❌ Services deployed independently but unable to evolve independently
```

---
