# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                                |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| Architecture strategy      | Business-capability driven                              |
| Microservices              | Requirement-driven, not default                         |
| Early architecture         | Modular monolith acceptable/preferred where appropriate |
| Domain modeling            | DDD where complexity justifies it                       |
| Service boundary           | Bounded context/capability                              |
| Aggregate                  | Transactional invariant boundary                        |
| Architecture style         | Hexagonal/ports-and-adapters for complex services       |
| Simple CRUD                | Keep simple                                             |
| Package strategy           | Feature/domain oriented                                 |
| Java                       | Centrally governed modern LTS                           |
| Spring Boot                | Centrally governed supported release                    |
| Build                      | Maven                                                   |
| Shared entity libraries    | **Rejected**                                            |
| Configuration              | Externalized + typed                                    |
| Secrets                    | ADR-064                                                 |
| REST                       | Resource/business-capability oriented                   |
| DTOs                       | Required at external boundaries                         |
| JPA entity exposure        | **Rejected**                                            |
| Validation                 | Request + domain + DB                                   |
| Error standard             | RFC 9457 Problem Details                                |
| Pagination                 | Required for growing collections                        |
| API versioning             | Compatibility-driven                                    |
| OpenAPI                    | Required for consumed APIs                              |
| API-first                  | Contract-heavy APIs                                     |
| Code-first                 | Acceptable for simpler internal APIs                    |
| Contract compatibility CI  | Required                                                |
| Controllers                | Thin                                                    |
| CQRS                       | Requirement-driven                                      |
| Persistence                | Spring Data JPA                                         |
| OSIV dependence            | Generally **rejected**                                  |
| Transaction boundary       | Application use case                                    |
| Mapping                    | Explicit                                                |
| MapStruct                  | Preferred when mapping complexity warrants              |
| Lombok                     | Selective                                               |
| `@Data` on JPA             | Generally **rejected**                                  |
| DI                         | Constructor injection                                   |
| Synchronous HTTP           | RestClient preferred                                    |
| Reactive HTTP              | WebClient where genuinely required                      |
| RestTemplate               | Legacy/migration only                                   |
| Resilience                 | ADR-066                                                 |
| Authentication             | OAuth2/OIDC                                             |
| Authorization              | Scope/role + resource/business authorization            |
| Messaging                  | Kafka                                                   |
| Event delivery             | At least once assumption                                |
| Consumers                  | Idempotent                                              |
| Dual writes                | Transactional outbox                                    |
| Scheduled work             | Explicit distributed semantics                          |
| Durable async              | Kafka/queue, not `@Async`                               |
| Virtual threads            | Workload-driven evaluation                              |
| Cache                      | Redis / ADR-065                                         |
| Feature flags              | Governed + temporary                                    |
| DB migrations              | Flyway default                                          |
| Migration strategy         | Expand → migrate → contract                             |
| Logging                    | Structured                                              |
| Metrics/tracing            | Micrometer                                              |
| Operations endpoints       | Actuator                                                |
| Unit testing               | JUnit 5                                                 |
| Assertions                 | AssertJ                                                 |
| Mocking                    | Mockito selectively                                     |
| Slice tests                | Preferred where applicable                              |
| Integration infrastructure | Testcontainers                                          |
| PostgreSQL testing         | Real PostgreSQL                                         |
| HTTP dependency simulation | WireMock                                                |
| Contract testing           | Important independent-service boundaries                |
| Architecture enforcement   | ArchUnit                                                |
| Mutation testing           | Critical domain logic evaluation                        |
| Performance testing        | Critical APIs                                           |
| Service creation           | Golden-path template                                    |
| Production readiness       | Mandatory review                                        |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                                            |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                                            |

# ADR-067 — COMPLETE ✅

The application engineering lifecycle is now:

```text
BUSINESS CAPABILITY
        │
        ▼
BOUNDED CONTEXT
        │
        ▼
SERVICE BOUNDARY
        │
        ▼
DOMAIN MODEL
        │
        ▼
APPLICATION USE CASE
        │
        ▼
PORTS
        │
        ▼
ADAPTERS
        │
        ▼
CONTRACTS
        │
        ▼
SECURITY
        │
        ▼
RESILIENCE
        │
        ▼
OBSERVABILITY
        │
        ▼
TESTING
        │
        ▼
DELIVERY
        │
        ▼
PRODUCTION
        │
        ▼
MEASURE
        │
        ▼
EVOLVE
```

The defining invariant is:

> **A Mediverse service owns a cohesive business capability, its contracts and its data. Business logic is protected from infrastructure concerns, cross-service coupling is explicit, distributed failure is assumed, and independent deployment must correspond to genuine independent evolution.**

## Next — ADR-068

### **ADR-068 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, React Engineering & Web Platform Standard**

The backend/platform foundation is now sufficiently defined. ADR-068 should establish the browser/application layer: **React architecture → TypeScript baseline → Vite/build strategy → SPA vs SSR/SSG decision → Next.js evaluation → frontend bounded contexts → feature-based organization → component architecture → design system → Storybook → accessibility/WCAG → responsive/mobile-first architecture → routing → React Router → layouts → server state vs client state → TanStack Query → Redux Toolkit decision → local state → Context boundaries → forms → React Hook Form → Zod → API client generation from OpenAPI → authentication/OIDC → BFF evaluation → token storage → CSRF/XSS/CSP → authorization UX → error handling → Problem Details integration → loading/empty/error states → optimistic updates → caching → pagination/infinite scrolling → file upload → presigned S3 flows → WebSocket/SSE → real-time updates → 3D/WebGL architecture for Mediverse educational modules → Three.js/React Three Fiber → asset streaming → performance budgets → code splitting → lazy loading → Core Web Vitals → image/media optimization → PWA/offline evaluation → internationalization → accessibility testing → Vitest → React Testing Library → MSW → Playwright → visual regression → frontend observability → OpenTelemetry/RUM → feature flags → environment configuration → frontend security → dependency governance → npm/pnpm decision → CI/CD → static asset delivery → CloudFront → S3 → cache invalidation → deployment strategies → micro-frontends evaluation → frontend anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise web reference architecture.**

# ADR-068 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, React Engineering & Web Platform Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-068
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-067 established the backend application engineering standard.

ADR-068 defines how Mediverse builds the **browser-facing application platform**: React architecture, TypeScript, state management, API integration, authentication, accessibility, responsive design, educational 3D experiences, frontend security, performance, testing and delivery.

> **The frontend is not a collection of pages consuming APIs. It is an independently engineered application platform with its own architecture, security boundaries, performance budgets, accessibility requirements and operational lifecycle.**

```text id="ux1m8a"
                              USER
                               │
                               ▼
                         CLOUDFRONT / CDN
                               │
                               ▼
                        MEDIVERSE WEB APP
                               │
                 ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
                 ▼             ▼             ▼
               ROUTING        UI/UX         SECURITY
                 │             │             │
                 └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                               ▼
                       FEATURE MODULES
                               │
             ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
             ▼                 ▼                 ▼
         Server State      Client State       Forms
             │                 │                 │
             └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                               ▼
                          API LAYER
                               │
                ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
                ▼              ▼              ▼
               REST           SSE/WS          S3
                │
                ▼
                         MEDIVERSE APIs

                    + EDUCATIONAL ENGINE
                               │
                               ▼
                       React Three Fiber
                               │
                               ▼
                          Three.js/WebGL
```

# 1. Frontend Architecture Objective

Mediverse frontend architecture should optimize for:

```text id="5t3d1z"
Maintainability
Accessibility
Performance
Security
Testability
Consistency
Developer productivity
Mobile usability
Observability
Independent evolution
```

Not maximum framework complexity.

# 2. React Baseline

React should remain Mediverse's primary web UI library.

React is responsible primarily for:

```text id="n09iwd"
Component composition
Rendering
Interaction
Local UI state
Application UI lifecycle
```

React should not become the solution to every frontend concern.

# 3. TypeScript

Production Mediverse frontend code should use TypeScript.

```text id="f6q60e"
JavaScript
    │
    ▼
TypeScript
    │
    ├── Static checking
    ├── Better refactoring
    ├── API modeling
    └── IDE support
```

New production application code should not default to plain JavaScript.

# 4. Strict TypeScript

TypeScript strictness should be enabled progressively and treated as the target baseline.

Avoid:

```text id="aq0m5w"
any
any
any
```

merely to silence compiler errors.

`any` transfers type errors from compile time back into production runtime.

# 5. Type Boundaries

External data must still be validated at runtime.

```text id="fl1nyv"
API JSON
   │
   X
TypeScript interface
```

TypeScript does not validate network responses.

Runtime validation remains useful at untrusted boundaries.

# 6. Build Tool

Vite should remain the default build/development tooling for the Mediverse SPA architecture.

```text id="ef1s0k"
Source
  │
  ▼
Vite
  │
  ├── Development server
  ├── TypeScript
  ├── Bundling
  └── Production assets
```

# 7. SPA Architecture

A Single Page Application remains appropriate for authenticated Mediverse learning workflows.

Examples:

```text id="hp33qa"
Dashboard
Course learning
Assessment
Student progress
Admin workflows
Interactive 3D modules
```

These are application experiences rather than primarily static documents.

# 8. SPA Limitation

SPA should not be treated as universally superior.

Potential disadvantages include:

```text id="c2pvs4"
Initial JavaScript cost
SEO limitations
Client rendering dependency
Complex loading states
Browser resource usage
```

# 9. SSR/SSG

Server-side rendering or static generation should be evaluated for:

```text id="fw8h0f"
Public landing pages
Marketing pages
Public course catalogue
SEO-sensitive content
Documentation
Public educational resources
```

# 10. Next.js Evaluation

Next.js should be evaluated if Mediverse develops a substantial SEO/public-content surface requiring:

```text id="rmj9t4"
SSR
SSG
Streaming
Server Components
Integrated routing
Server-side web capabilities
```

Do not migrate the authenticated application merely because Next.js is popular.

# 11. Rendering Decision

Mediverse may therefore evolve toward:

```text id="16ikst"
mediverse.com
→ SSR/SSG public experience

app.mediverse.com
→ React application experience
```

if product requirements justify separation.

# 12. Feature-Oriented Architecture

Frontend source structure should follow business features rather than global technical folders.

Weak at scale:

```text id="5ml1mq"
components/
hooks/
services/
pages/
utils/
```

Better:

```text id="b2rbbn"
features/
 ├── courses/
 ├── learning/
 ├── assessment/
 ├── identity/
 └── progress/
```

# 13. Feature Boundary

A feature may contain:

```text id="vhl2j7"
features/course/
│
├── api/
├── components/
├── hooks/
├── model/
├── pages/
├── schemas/
├── tests/
└── index.ts
```

Internal structure should scale with actual complexity.

# 14. Shared Layer

Shared code should contain genuinely cross-cutting capabilities.

```text id="6g6z0k"
shared/
 ├── api/
 ├── auth/
 ├── components/
 ├── design-system/
 ├── observability/
 └── utilities/
```

Do not move code into `shared` merely because two files currently use it.

# 15. Feature Encapsulation

Features should expose deliberate public interfaces.

```text id="pgg4y3"
features/course/index.ts
```

can prevent consumers from depending on arbitrary feature internals.

# 16. Circular Dependencies

Feature architecture should prevent:

```text id="f55cz5"
Course
  ↓
Assessment
  ↓
Progress
  ↓
Course
```

Circular dependencies indicate unclear boundaries.

# 17. Component Architecture

Components should be separated conceptually into:

```text id="h0ceyk"
Design-system primitives
Reusable domain components
Feature components
Page composition
```

Not every component belongs in a global component library.

# 18. Design System

Mediverse should establish a reusable design system.

```text id="e2o8jc"
Design Tokens
     │
     ▼
Primitives
     │
     ▼
Components
     │
     ▼
Patterns
     │
     ▼
Application UI
```

# 19. Design Tokens

Visual decisions should use tokens for:

```text id="zv7qk1"
Typography
Spacing
Borders
Radius
Elevation
Breakpoints
Motion
Semantic colors
```

rather than arbitrary values repeated throughout the codebase.

# 20. UI Library Strategy

A component library such as MUI may accelerate development, but Mediverse should wrap/customize it through the design system where long-term consistency requires it.

Application code should not become inseparably coupled to vendor-specific styling everywhere.

# 21. Tailwind

Tailwind CSS may be used where it improves implementation speed and consistency.

But mixing:

```text id="0e1hkr"
MUI
+
Tailwind
+
CSS Modules
+
styled-components
+
random inline CSS
```

without governance creates a styling architecture mess.

One primary styling strategy should dominate.

# 22. Storybook

Reusable UI components should be developed/documented through Storybook where its maintenance cost is justified.

```text id="jj0o5k"
Component
   │
   ├── Default
   ├── Loading
   ├── Error
   ├── Disabled
   └── Accessibility states
```

# 23. Accessibility

Accessibility is a product requirement, not final-stage QA.

Mediverse should target an appropriate WCAG 2.2 conformance level, with **AA as the normal baseline** for user-facing interfaces.

# 24. Semantic HTML

Prefer native semantic elements.

```html id="mujzxn"
<button>
<nav>
<main>
<form>
<label>
```

over recreating semantics using clickable `<div>` elements.

# 25. Keyboard Accessibility

All important workflows must be usable without a mouse.

This includes:

```text id="uqjgg1"
Navigation
Forms
Dialogs
Menus
Assessments
Media controls
Interactive learning controls
```

# 26. Focus Management

Dynamic interfaces must manage focus deliberately.

Opening a modal, changing routes or displaying validation errors should not leave keyboard/screen-reader users lost.

# 27. ARIA

ARIA should supplement missing semantics.

It should not replace correct HTML unnecessarily.

> **No ARIA is better than incorrect ARIA.**

# 28. Contrast

Text and interactive controls must meet defined contrast requirements.

Brand design does not override accessibility.

# 29. Motion Accessibility

Animations and 3D experiences should respect reduced-motion preferences where applicable.

```text id="pbf4nb"
prefers-reduced-motion
```

should influence nonessential animation.

# 30. 3D Accessibility

A 3D anatomical learning experience cannot be the only way to access required educational information.

Provide equivalent:

```text id="1h3f77"
Text
Labels
Images/diagrams
Structured descriptions
Keyboard-accessible controls
```

where applicable.

# 31. Responsive Architecture

Mediverse should be mobile-first.

```text id="0a13pf"
Mobile
  │
  ▼
Tablet
  │
  ▼
Desktop
  │
  ▼
Large display
```

Layouts should progressively enhance rather than shrink desktop interfaces until they barely fit.

# 32. Breakpoints

Breakpoints should follow layout needs, not specific device models.

Avoid:

```text id="w79o9n"
iPhone breakpoint
Samsung breakpoint
Pixel breakpoint
```

Device catalogs change continuously.

# 33. Touch Targets

Interactive controls must remain usable on touch devices.

Tiny desktop-style click targets are unacceptable for mobile learning workflows.

# 34. Routing

React Router should remain the default router for the SPA architecture.

```text id="8gk1yx"
/
├── /courses
├── /courses/:courseId
├── /learn/:courseId
├── /assessments
└── /profile
```

# 35. Route Ownership

Routes should map cleanly to feature/page boundaries.

Avoid one massive routing file containing application-specific implementation logic.

# 36. Nested Layouts

Use nested layouts for shared UI structures such as:

```text id="hvgjd8"
Application shell
Student dashboard
Admin console
Course learning workspace
```

# 37. Route-Level Code Splitting

Large feature routes should be lazy loaded.

```text id="l8lgm7"
Initial App
   │
   ├── Core
   └── Current Route

Later
   │
   ▼
Load Assessment Module
```

Users should not download the entire Mediverse application before viewing the login screen.

# 38. Route Protection

Protected routes may improve UX, but frontend route guards are not authorization controls.

```text id="fy9lnf"
Frontend guard
→ UX

Backend authorization
→ Security
```

# 39. State Classification

Before choosing a state library, classify state.

```text id="97d8po"
Server state
Client application state
URL state
Form state
Local component state
Authentication state
```

Treating all state identically creates unnecessary complexity.

# 40. Server State

Remote backend state should be treated differently from local UI state.

Examples:

```text id="97dnmq"
Courses
Enrollments
Assessments
Progress
Search results
```

This state has:

```text id="hdyl4p"
Caching
Freshness
Refetching
Mutation
Synchronization
```

concerns.

# 41. TanStack Query

TanStack Query should be preferred for REST/server-state management.

```text id="m9y99d"
Component
    │
    ▼
TanStack Query
    │
    ├── Cache
    ├── Deduplication
    ├── Refetch
    ├── Mutation
    └── Invalidation
    │
    ▼
API Client
```

# 42. Redux Toolkit

Redux Toolkit should be used only for meaningful global client-side application state that cannot be handled cleanly by:

```text id="h7q3yf"
Server-state library
URL
Context
Local state
```

Do not put every API response into Redux.

# 43. Redux Decision

Good Redux candidates may include complex:

```text id="4s4xug"
Cross-feature workflows
Client-side editing state
Global application coordination
Long-lived UI workflows
```

Not ordinary server fetching.

# 44. Local State

Use React local state for state owned by one component/subtree.

```text id="0jldii"
Modal open?
Selected tab?
Temporary UI toggle?
```

does not require Redux.

# 45. URL State

State users should be able to:

```text id="9xj8hk"
Bookmark
Share
Navigate back/forward
Refresh
```

often belongs in the URL.

Examples:

```text id="q6cj3j"
Search query
Page
Filters
Sort
Selected course tab
```

# 46. Context

React Context is appropriate for low-frequency cross-tree concerns.

Examples:

```text id="3k05ab"
Theme
Locale
Authentication context
```

It should not automatically replace a state-management architecture.

# 47. Forms

Forms should use a consistent form architecture.

React Hook Form should be preferred for complex forms.

```text id="8r5r68"
Form
 │
 ▼
React Hook Form
 │
 ▼
Validation Schema
 │
 ▼
API Mutation
```

# 48. Zod

Zod should be preferred where runtime TypeScript-friendly schema validation provides value.

```text id="yrcchj"
Input
  │
  ▼
Zod Schema
  │
  ├── valid
  └── errors
```

# 49. Client Validation

Client validation improves UX.

It is not a security boundary.

Every important rule must still be validated by the backend.

# 50. Validation UX

Validation errors should be:

```text id="15ps33"
Specific
Associated with fields
Keyboard accessible
Screen-reader accessible
Actionable
```

"Invalid input" is usually poor UX.

# 51. API Layer

Components should not scatter raw HTTP calls throughout the UI.

Preferred:

```text id="o45syw"
Component
   │
   ▼
Feature Hook
   │
   ▼
API Client
   │
   ▼
Backend
```

# 52. OpenAPI Client Generation

Generated TypeScript API clients should be evaluated/preferred for stable OpenAPI-governed APIs.

```text id="gfl1m0"
Spring Boot
    │
    ▼
OpenAPI
    │
    ▼
Client Generation
    │
    ▼
TypeScript Client
```

This reduces contract duplication.

# 53. Generated Client Boundary

Generated code should normally sit behind a thin application-facing API layer.

Do not spread generator-specific types throughout every UI component.

# 54. Problem Details

Frontend error handling should understand the ADR-067 Problem Details contract.

```text id="11qh82"
HTTP failure
    │
    ▼
Problem Details
    │
    ▼
Error Mapper
    │
    ▼
User-facing state
```

# 55. Error Classification

The frontend should distinguish:

```text id="y3wjs7"
Validation error
Authentication error
Authorization error
Not found
Conflict
Rate limiting
Dependency outage
Unexpected failure
Network failure
```

A generic "Something went wrong" should be the last fallback.

# 56. Loading State

Every asynchronous experience should define:

```text id="spueui"
Loading
Success
Empty
Error
Refreshing
```

rather than assuming data immediately exists.

# 57. Skeletons

Skeleton interfaces may improve perceived loading for predictable layouts.

Do not use misleading skeletons for operations where progress cannot be meaningfully predicted.

# 58. Empty State

Empty data is not necessarily an error.

```text id="9ng57r"
0 enrolled courses
```

should produce a useful empty-state experience, not a blank screen.

# 59. Optimistic Updates

Optimistic UI should be used only where rollback semantics are clear.

```text id="9fn95m"
User action
    │
    ▼
Update UI immediately
    │
    ▼
API request
   ┌┴─────────┐
   ▼          ▼
Success     Failure
             │
             ▼
           Rollback
```

# 60. Optimistic Update Safety

Do not optimistically claim success for high-risk operations where backend acceptance is uncertain or irreversible.

Examples requiring caution:

```text id="85k4my"
Assessment final submission
Payments
Security changes
Critical enrollment operations
```

---

## ADR-068 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The frontend architecture now follows:

```text id="hs1zpx"
                         USER
                           │
                           ▼
                        ROUTER
                           │
                           ▼
                     FEATURE PAGE
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
           LOCAL UI      FORM       SERVER STATE
              │            │            │
              │       React Hook       │
              │          Form          │
              │            │            │
              │           Zod      TanStack Query
              │            │            │
              └────────────┼────────────┘
                           ▼
                       API LAYER
                           │
                           ▼
                    GENERATED CLIENT
                           │
                           ▼
                      REST / OIDC
                           │
                           ▼
                    MEDIVERSE APIs
```

For Mediverse specifically, there is another critical boundary:

```text id="r3dmky"
                 LEARNING EXPERIENCE
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ▼              ▼              ▼
        TEXT          DIAGRAMS          3D
          │              │              │
          └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                         ▼
                 SAME LEARNING GOAL
```

The defining rule is:

> **React owns presentation and interaction—not the entire application state universe. Server state, form state, URL state, local UI state and global client state are different problems and should use different tools.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Authentication & OIDC Browser Architecture**, then cover **Authorization Code + PKCE → BFF evaluation → token storage → refresh strategy → cookies → CSRF → XSS → CSP → authorization UX → session expiry → TanStack Query caching → invalidation → pagination/infinite scrolling → prefetching → offline behavior → file uploads → S3 presigned URLs → upload progress → large/multipart uploads → media delivery → video architecture → SSE/WebSocket → real-time state → Three.js → React Three Fiber → Drei → anatomical/physiology 3D architecture → GLTF/GLB → Draco/Meshopt → texture optimization → progressive 3D loading → LOD → Web Workers → WebGL capability fallback → 3D accessibility → performance budgets → Core Web Vitals → bundle budgets → code splitting → tree shaking → image optimization → font optimization → service workers/PWA → internationalization → Marathi/English and future language architecture → RTL readiness → accessibility testing → Vitest → React Testing Library → MSW → Playwright → visual regression → frontend observability/RUM → Web Vitals telemetry → error boundaries → source maps → privacy-safe telemetry → feature flags → environment configuration → npm vs pnpm → dependency governance → frontend supply chain → CI/CD → S3/CloudFront deployment → cache-control → immutable assets → SPA routing → cache invalidation → rollback → micro-frontends evaluation → frontend anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise web reference architecture.**


# ADR-068 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, React Engineering & Web Platform Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Optimistic Update Safety**.

---

# 61. Authentication & OIDC Browser Architecture

Mediverse browser authentication should use standards-based OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Mediverse Web
   │
   ▼
Identity Provider
   │
   ▼
Authentication
   │
   ▼
Mediverse APIs
```

The frontend must not implement its own password/token protocol.

---

# 62. Authorization Code + PKCE

For browser-based public clients using OAuth directly, **Authorization Code Flow with PKCE** should be the baseline.

```text
Browser
   │
   ├── code_challenge
   ▼
Identity Provider
   │
   ▼
Authorization Code
   │
   ▼
Browser
   │
   ├── code_verifier
   ▼
Token Endpoint
```

Implicit Flow should not be used for new Mediverse applications.

---

# 63. PKCE Purpose

PKCE protects authorization-code exchange by binding the authorization request to the client that initiated it.

An intercepted authorization code alone should therefore be insufficient for token exchange.

---

# 64. BFF Evaluation

A **Backend for Frontend (BFF)** should be evaluated for the main authenticated Mediverse web application.

```text
Browser
   │
   │ Secure session cookie
   ▼
BFF
   │
   │ OAuth tokens
   ▼
Mediverse APIs
```

This can keep OAuth tokens outside browser JavaScript.

---

# 65. BFF Benefits

A BFF can provide:

```text
Token isolation
HttpOnly session cookies
API aggregation
Browser-specific contracts
Centralized CSRF protection
Simpler browser authentication
```

It also adds another deployable runtime and must therefore solve a real requirement.

---

# 66. BFF Is Not an API Gateway

These responsibilities should not be confused.

```text
BFF
→ frontend-specific backend behavior

API Gateway
→ platform/API ingress concerns
```

They may coexist.

---

# 67. Token Storage

Long-lived authentication tokens should not casually be stored in:

```text
localStorage
sessionStorage
IndexedDB
```

because JavaScript-accessible storage is exposed to successful XSS.

---

# 68. HttpOnly Cookies

When BFF/session architecture is adopted, session cookies should normally use appropriate:

```text
HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite
```

settings.

`HttpOnly` prevents ordinary JavaScript from directly reading the cookie.

---

# 69. Cookie Limitation

Cookies improve token isolation but introduce CSRF considerations because browsers attach cookies automatically.

Security architecture therefore changes rather than disappears.

---

# 70. CSRF

State-changing cookie-authenticated requests require appropriate CSRF defenses.

Potential controls include:

```text
SameSite policy
CSRF tokens
Origin validation
Request-method discipline
```

according to architecture.

---

# 71. XSS

XSS remains one of the most important browser threats.

Primary controls include:

```text
React escaping
Avoiding unsafe HTML injection
Input/output handling
CSP
Dependency governance
No arbitrary script execution
```

---

# 72. dangerouslySetInnerHTML

Use of:

```text
dangerouslySetInnerHTML
```

must be exceptional.

If rich HTML is required, content must pass through an approved sanitization architecture.

---

# 73. Content Security Policy

Mediverse should deploy a restrictive CSP.

Conceptually:

```text
default-src 'self'
script-src ...
style-src ...
img-src ...
connect-src ...
frame-src ...
object-src 'none'
```

Exact directives depend on production integrations.

---

# 74. CSP Rollout

For complex existing applications, CSP may first be deployed in report-only mode to identify legitimate dependencies before enforcement.

The target remains enforcement—not permanent report-only operation.

---

# 75. Third-Party Scripts

Every third-party browser script increases:

```text
Supply-chain risk
Privacy exposure
Performance cost
CSP complexity
Failure dependencies
```

Third-party JavaScript requires explicit justification.

---

# 76. Frontend Authorization UX

The UI may hide or disable actions the current user cannot perform.

```text
Permission
    │
    ▼
UI Capability
```

But this is usability—not security enforcement.

---

# 77. Backend Authorization Remains Mandatory

An attacker can bypass the React application and call APIs directly.

Therefore:

```text
Frontend permission check
        ≠
Authorization boundary
```

ADR-064 and ADR-067 remain authoritative.

---

# 78. Session Expiration

Expired authentication should produce controlled behavior.

```text
API
 │
 ▼
401
 │
 ▼
Auth handler
 │
 ▼
Renew session if valid
or
Re-authenticate
```

Do not create infinite token-refresh loops.

---

# 79. Concurrent Authentication Failure

If 50 API calls simultaneously receive authentication failure, the frontend should avoid initiating 50 independent refresh operations.

Authentication renewal should be coordinated.

---

# 80. Logout

Logout should clear application authentication state and invalidate server-side sessions/tokens where the selected architecture supports it.

Sensitive cached user-specific state should also be cleared.

---

# 81. TanStack Query Cache

Server-state cache policy should reflect data semantics.

```text
Query
 │
 ├── fresh
 │
 ├── stale
 │
 └── garbage collected
```

Do not assign identical freshness settings to every API.

---

# 82. Query Keys

Query keys should be deterministic and structured.

Example:

```text
['courses', courseId]
['courses', { category, page }]
```

Poor key design causes invalidation and cache-consistency bugs.

---

# 83. Cache Invalidation

After mutations, invalidate only relevant queries where practical.

```text
Update Course
     │
     ▼
Mutation Success
     │
     ├── course/{id}
     └── affected course lists
```

Globally invalidating every query wastes network and server capacity.

---

# 84. Prefetching

Likely next data may be prefetched when evidence shows UX benefit.

Examples:

```text
Next lesson
Course details
Adjacent page
```

Do not prefetch half the application speculatively.

---

# 85. Pagination

Frontend pagination must match backend semantics.

For stable administrative lists:

```text
page + size
```

may be sufficient.

For feeds/large changing datasets:

```text
cursor
```

may be preferable.

---

# 86. Infinite Scrolling

Infinite scrolling should be used only where the interaction model benefits from it.

It is often poor for:

```text
Administrative tables
Precise navigation
Accessibility-heavy workflows
Content users need to relocate
```

Pagination may be superior.

---

# 87. Offline Behavior

The frontend should explicitly distinguish:

```text
Online
Offline
Poor connection
Backend unavailable
```

rather than presenting every network failure as the same generic error.

---

# 88. File Upload Architecture

Large uploads should avoid unnecessarily passing file bytes through application servers.

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Mediverse API
   │ authorize
   ▼
Presigned Upload
   │
   ▼
S3
```

---

# 89. Upload Workflow

Recommended flow:

```text
1. Select file
       │
2. Client validation
       │
3. Request upload authorization
       │
4. Receive presigned destination
       │
5. Upload to S3
       │
6. Confirm completion
       │
7. Server-side validation/scanning
       │
8. Asset becomes available
```

Client validation does not replace server validation.

---

# 90. Upload Progress

Large uploads should provide meaningful progress.

```text
Uploading
████████░░ 80%
```

But the UI must distinguish:

```text
Upload completed
```

from:

```text
Asset validated and ready
```

---

# 91. Multipart Upload

Large educational videos and 3D assets should use multipart upload where appropriate.

This enables:

```text
Chunking
Retry of failed parts
Better large-file resilience
Potential resume behavior
```

---

# 92. Abandoned Multipart Uploads

Incomplete multipart uploads consume storage.

S3 lifecycle policies should clean abandoned uploads according to ADR-065.

---

# 93. Media Delivery

Public/authorized static media should normally be delivered through CDN architecture rather than Spring Boot streaming every byte.

```text
S3
 │
 ▼
CloudFront
 │
 ▼
Browser
```

---

# 94. Private Media

Private course assets require authorization-aware delivery.

Potential architecture:

```text
Browser
   │
   ▼
Authorization API
   │
   ▼
Signed URL / Cookie
   │
   ▼
CloudFront
   │
   ▼
S3
```

---

# 95. Video Architecture

Large educational video should use streaming-oriented delivery rather than treating every video as a giant downloadable object.

Adaptive streaming should be evaluated for serious production video workloads.

---

# 96. Real-Time Architecture

Real-time communication should be requirement-driven.

Options include:

```text
Polling
Long polling
SSE
WebSocket
```

Do not choose WebSockets merely because the feature is described as "real time."

---

# 97. Server-Sent Events

SSE is appropriate for primarily server-to-browser streams such as:

```text
Processing status
Notifications
Progress updates
AI generation status
```

where full bidirectional communication is unnecessary.

---

# 98. WebSockets

WebSockets should be used when persistent bidirectional communication is genuinely required.

Examples may include:

```text
Collaborative interaction
Live classroom features
Interactive presence
Bidirectional real-time sessions
```

---

# 99. Reconnection

Real-time clients must handle:

```text
Disconnect
Reconnect
Duplicate event
Missed event
Session expiration
Network change
```

A WebSocket connection should never be assumed permanent.

---

# 100. Real-Time State Reconciliation

After reconnect:

```text
Reconnect
   │
   ▼
Fetch authoritative state
   │
   ▼
Apply subsequent events
```

may be safer than assuming every event was received.

---

# 101. 3D Learning Architecture

Mediverse's 3D educational modules should be treated as a specialized rendering subsystem.

```text
React Application
       │
       ▼
React Three Fiber
       │
       ▼
Three.js
       │
       ▼
WebGL / GPU
       │
       ▼
3D Educational Scene
```

3D should remain isolated from ordinary application concerns.

---

# 102. React Three Fiber

React Three Fiber should be preferred for integrating Three.js scenes into the React application when React lifecycle/composition provides value.

Raw Three.js remains appropriate for lower-level capabilities when necessary.

---

# 103. Drei

`@react-three/drei` may provide reusable helpers for:

```text
Controls
Loaders
Environment
Text
Camera utilities
Performance helpers
```

Use helpers deliberately rather than treating Drei as the architecture.

---

# 104. 3D Feature Boundary

A 3D physiology module should have its own feature boundary.

```text
features/anatomy3d/
│
├── components/
├── scenes/
├── models/
├── interactions/
├── loaders/
├── annotations/
├── educational-content/
└── tests/
```

Do not scatter WebGL logic throughout ordinary React pages.

---

# 105. 3D Asset Format

**glTF/GLB** should be the default runtime delivery format for 3D web assets.

It supports web-oriented:

```text
Meshes
Materials
Textures
Animations
Scene hierarchy
```

---

# 106. Source vs Runtime Assets

Production runtime assets should be distinguished from authoring assets.

```text
Blender / Source
      │
      ▼
Optimization Pipeline
      │
      ▼
GLB Runtime Asset
      │
      ▼
CDN
```

Do not ship raw authoring assets directly to users.

---

# 107. Geometry Optimization

Models should be optimized for browser rendering.

Consider:

```text
Polygon count
Draw calls
Material count
Mesh count
Texture size
Animation complexity
```

A beautiful 4-million-polygon organ model that freezes mid-range phones is a failed web asset.

---

# 108. Draco and Meshopt

Geometry compression such as Draco or Meshopt should be evaluated according to asset characteristics.

Compression trades:

```text
Smaller transfer
        vs
Client decode cost
```

Measure on target devices.

---

# 109. Texture Optimization

Textures frequently dominate 3D payload size.

Optimize:

```text
Resolution
Compression
Texture count
Mipmaps
Color channels
Reuse
```

Modern GPU-friendly compressed texture formats should be evaluated.

---

# 110. Progressive 3D Loading

Users should not wait for an entire complex anatomical scene before receiving useful feedback.

```text
UI shell
   │
   ▼
Essential model
   │
   ▼
Annotations
   │
   ▼
High-detail assets
```

Progressive loading improves perceived performance.

---

# 111. Level of Detail

Complex scenes should evaluate LOD.

```text
Far
→ low-detail model

Near
→ higher-detail model
```

Rendering detail users cannot perceive wastes GPU resources.

---

# 112. Frustum Culling

Objects outside the visible camera region should not consume unnecessary rendering work where engine capabilities permit optimization.

Scene design should support efficient culling.

---

# 113. Draw Calls

3D performance is not determined only by polygon count.

Excessive:

```text
Objects
Materials
State changes
Draw calls
```

can severely reduce performance.

---

# 114. Instancing

Repeated objects should use GPU instancing where appropriate.

Example:

```text
Thousands of repeated structures
        │
        ▼
Instanced rendering
```

instead of thousands of independent draw calls.

---

# 115. Web Workers

CPU-heavy operations that do not require DOM access should be evaluated for Web Workers.

Examples:

```text
Data parsing
Complex calculations
Asset processing
Some simulation work
```

This can protect main-thread responsiveness.

---

# 116. Main Thread

The browser main thread is a finite resource shared by:

```text
React
Layout
Input
JavaScript
3D orchestration
Animation
```

Long tasks directly damage UX.

---

# 117. WebGL Capability Detection

The application should detect unsupported or severely constrained rendering environments.

```text
3D supported
     │
   ┌─┴─────┐
   ▼       ▼
  Yes      No
   │       │
   ▼       ▼
3D Mode  Accessible
         fallback
```

---

# 118. 3D Fallback

Fallbacks may include:

```text
2D anatomical diagrams
Images
Video
Interactive labelled illustrations
Structured text
```

Educational access must not depend entirely on GPU capability.

---

# 119. Educational Annotations

3D scenes should connect visual structures to learning content.

```text
3D Structure
    │
    ▼
Annotation
    │
    ├── Name
    ├── Description
    ├── Function
    ├── Clinical relevance
    └── Audio where appropriate
```

3D without instructional design is decoration.

---

# 120. Performance Budgets

Mediverse should define explicit frontend performance budgets.

Budgets should cover:

```text
Initial JavaScript
Route chunks
Images
Fonts
3D assets
Long tasks
Core Web Vitals
```

Exact thresholds should be measured against target devices and network conditions.

---

# 121. Core Web Vitals

Frontend performance monitoring should track current user-centric web performance metrics, including applicable Core Web Vitals.

These metrics should be collected from real users where privacy requirements permit.

---

# 122. Bundle Budget

CI should detect abnormal bundle growth.

```text
Build
 │
 ▼
Bundle Analysis
 │
 ├── within budget → pass
 └── excessive     → review/fail
```

Bundle size should not silently grow forever.

---

# 123. Tree Shaking

Libraries should be imported in ways that allow unused code elimination.

A 20 KB requirement should not introduce a 2 MB dependency bundle without scrutiny.

---

# 124. Dynamic Imports

Heavy features should load on demand.

```text
Student Dashboard
      │
      X
No need to load
3D anatomy engine immediately
```

The 3D runtime should be loaded when needed.

---

# 125. Image Optimization

Images should use appropriate:

```text
Dimensions
Compression
Responsive variants
Lazy loading
Modern formats
```

Serving desktop-resolution images to every mobile device wastes bandwidth.

---

# 126. Font Optimization

Fonts should be deliberately governed.

Avoid downloading numerous:

```text
Families
Weights
Styles
Scripts
```

that most users never need.

Use appropriate preload/subsetting/self-hosting strategies where justified.

---

# 127. PWA Evaluation

PWA capabilities should be requirement-driven.

Useful possibilities:

```text
Installability
Offline shell
Cached educational resources
Background capabilities where supported
```

But "make it a PWA" is not itself a product requirement.

---

# 128. Service Worker Risk

Service workers introduce another cache/lifecycle layer.

Poor update logic can leave users running stale application code after deployment.

Versioning and invalidation must be deliberate.

---

# 129. Offline Learning

If offline learning becomes a product requirement, architecture must explicitly solve:

```text
Content download
Storage quotas
Content versioning
Progress recording
Synchronization
Conflicts
Security
Expiry
Logout cleanup
```

This is substantially more complex than caching HTML.

---

# 130. Internationalization

User-facing strings should not be permanently embedded throughout components.

```text
Component
   │
   ▼
Translation Key
   │
   ▼
Locale Resource
```

The architecture should support future language expansion.

---

# 131. English and Marathi

Where Mediverse supports English and Marathi, educational terminology requires curated translations rather than blind machine substitution.

Medical meaning must remain authoritative.

---

# 132. Locale Formatting

Localization includes:

```text
Dates
Times
Numbers
Units
Pluralization
Relative time
```

not only translated strings.

---

# 133. RTL Readiness

Even if initial languages are LTR, shared design-system components should avoid assumptions that make future RTL support unnecessarily difficult.

Prefer logical layout concepts where practical.

---

# 134. Frontend Testing Strategy

Mediverse should use layered frontend testing.

```text
             /\
            /E2E\
           /----\
          /Visual\
         /------\
        /Integration\
       /----------\
      / Component  \
     /--------------\
    /   Unit Tests   \
   /__________________\
```

Tests should protect user behavior rather than implementation details.

---

# 135. Vitest

Vitest should be the default unit/component test runner for the Vite frontend unless future tooling requirements justify change.

---

# 136. React Testing Library

React Testing Library should test components from the user's perspective.

Prefer:

```text
Find button by accessible role
Click
Observe outcome
```

over testing internal component state.

---

# 137. MSW

Mock Service Worker should be preferred for realistic API mocking in frontend tests where appropriate.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
HTTP request
    │
    ▼
MSW
    │
    ▼
Controlled response
```

This tests the API boundary more realistically than mocking every hook.

---

# 138. Playwright

Playwright should be the primary browser E2E framework.

Critical journeys should include:

```text
Login
Course discovery
Enrollment
Lesson consumption
Assessment submission
File upload
Permission boundaries
```

---

# 139. Accessibility Testing

Automated accessibility testing should be integrated into component and/or browser testing.

Automation cannot prove full accessibility.

Manual keyboard and assistive-technology testing remains necessary for critical experiences.

---

# 140. Visual Regression

Visual regression testing should be used selectively for:

```text
Design-system components
Critical layouts
Complex learning visualizations
```

Do not create thousands of unstable screenshots with no ownership.

---

# 141. Error Boundaries

React Error Boundaries should isolate rendering failures where appropriate.

```text
3D Module crashes
       │
       ▼
Local Error Boundary
       │
       ▼
Rest of course remains usable
```

One component failure should not unnecessarily blank the whole application.

---

# 142. Frontend Observability

Production frontend telemetry should capture appropriate:

```text
JavaScript errors
Failed requests
Performance
Core Web Vitals
Route transitions
Feature failures
3D initialization failures
```

while respecting privacy requirements.

---

# 143. Source Maps

Production source maps may be made available securely to approved observability tooling.

They should not expose sensitive source/configuration unnecessarily.

---

# 144. Environment Configuration

Frontend builds must assume all shipped browser configuration is publicly inspectable.

Therefore:

```text
VITE_API_URL
→ acceptable configuration

VITE_DATABASE_PASSWORD
→ catastrophic design error
```

There are no secret frontend environment variables once bundled into browser code.

---

# 145. Package Management & Supply Chain

Mediverse should standardize one Node package-management workflow.

npm is acceptable; pnpm should be evaluated if workspace efficiency and strict dependency handling provide measurable value.

Regardless of tool:

```text
Lockfile
Reproducible install
Dependency scanning
Controlled upgrades
Registry governance
```

are required.

---

# 146. Frontend CI/CD

Frontend CI should execute approximately:

```text
Checkout
   │
   ▼
Locked Dependency Install
   │
   ▼
Type Check
   │
   ▼
Lint
   │
   ▼
Unit / Component Tests
   │
   ▼
Build
   │
   ▼
Bundle Budget
   │
   ▼
Security Checks
   │
   ▼
E2E / Required Quality Gates
   │
   ▼
Deploy Artifact
```

Build once; promote immutable artifacts where deployment architecture permits.

---

# 147. S3 + CloudFront Deployment

For SPA/static deployment:

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
CI
 │
 ▼
Vite Build
 │
 ▼
Immutable Assets
 │
 ▼
S3
 │
 ▼
CloudFront
 │
 ▼
Users
```

Hashed assets should receive long-lived caching.

The HTML shell should use a shorter caching strategy so deployments can reference new asset hashes.

---

# 148. Frontend Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Plain JavaScript for new production application code without reason
❌ TypeScript with pervasive any
❌ Assuming TypeScript validates API data
❌ React state used for every state category
❌ Every API response copied into Redux
❌ Global Context used as a high-frequency state database
❌ One enormous components/ directory
❌ Circular feature dependencies
❌ Everything moved into shared/
❌ Business logic scattered through JSX
❌ Raw fetch/Axios calls in every component
❌ Hand-maintained duplicate API types when generated contracts are viable
❌ Client validation treated as security
❌ Frontend route guards treated as authorization
❌ OAuth tokens casually persisted in localStorage
❌ dangerouslySetInnerHTML with untrusted content
❌ Third-party scripts added without security/performance review
❌ CSP permanently disabled because integrations are inconvenient
❌ Every error displayed as "Something went wrong"
❌ Blank screens during loading
❌ Empty results treated as errors
❌ Optimistic success for irreversible operations
❌ Infinite scrolling everywhere
❌ Cache invalidation by refreshing the whole application
❌ Uploading multi-GB video through Spring Boot without reason
❌ Declaring S3 upload complete before security processing completes
❌ Spring Boot used as a static-media streaming server
❌ WebSockets selected for simple status updates
❌ Reconnect logic assuming no events were missed
❌ Raw unoptimized Blender assets shipped to browsers
❌ Multi-million-polygon models shipped to mobile devices
❌ 8K textures everywhere
❌ Loading Three.js on the login page
❌ 3D as the only representation of required educational content
❌ 3D visual spectacle without learning purpose
❌ No reduced-motion support
❌ Device-specific responsive breakpoints
❌ Clickable divs replacing buttons
❌ ARIA used instead of semantic HTML
❌ Accessibility postponed until release
❌ Bundle size allowed to grow without budgets
❌ Service worker caching without update strategy
❌ "Offline support" implemented as cache everything
❌ Strings hardcoded throughout UI
❌ Machine translation trusted for authoritative medical terminology
❌ Tests coupled to implementation details
❌ E2E tests used for every behavior
❌ Screenshot tests created without ownership
❌ Browser telemetry collecting sensitive content
❌ Secrets placed in VITE_* variables
❌ npm install without lockfile discipline in CI
❌ CDN invalidation used for every hashed asset
❌ Micro-frontends introduced because microservices exist
```

---

# 149. Final Mediverse Enterprise Web Reference Architecture

```text
                               USER
                                │
                                ▼
                         DNS / CLOUDFRONT
                                │
                ┌───────────────┴───────────────┐
                ▼                               ▼
           HTML SHELL                     STATIC ASSETS
                │                               │
                │                          JS / CSS / Fonts
                │                          Images / GLB
                │                               │
```

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                      | Decision                                       |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Primary frontend          | **React**                                      |
| Language                  | **TypeScript**                                 |
| Type safety               | Strict target                                  |
| Build tooling             | **Vite**                                       |
| Authenticated application | SPA                                            |
| Public SEO content        | SSR/SSG evaluation                             |
| Next.js                   | Requirement-driven                             |
| Source architecture       | Feature-oriented                               |
| Shared code               | Controlled                                     |
| UI architecture           | Design system                                  |
| Component documentation   | Storybook where justified                      |
| Styling                   | One governed primary strategy                  |
| Accessibility             | **WCAG 2.2 AA baseline**                       |
| Responsive model          | Mobile-first                                   |
| Routing                   | React Router                                   |
| Route loading             | Code split/lazy                                |
| Backend authorization     | Mandatory                                      |
| Server state              | **TanStack Query**                             |
| Global client state       | Redux Toolkit only when justified              |
| Local state               | React                                          |
| URL state                 | Router/search params                           |
| Forms                     | **React Hook Form**                            |
| Runtime schemas           | **Zod**                                        |
| API contracts             | OpenAPI                                        |
| API client                | Generated where viable                         |
| Errors                    | Problem Details aware                          |
| Authentication            | OIDC/OAuth                                     |
| Browser OAuth             | Authorization Code + PKCE                      |
| BFF                       | Preferred evaluation for authenticated app     |
| Token storage             | Avoid casual browser persistence               |
| Cookies                   | Secure + HttpOnly where BFF/session model used |
| CSRF                      | Explicit controls                              |
| XSS                       | Defense in depth                               |
| CSP                       | Required production control                    |
| Uploads                   | Presigned S3                                   |
| Large uploads             | Multipart                                      |
| Media                     | S3 + CloudFront                                |
| Real-time                 | Requirement-driven                             |
| SSE                       | Server→client streaming                        |
| WebSocket                 | Bidirectional use cases                        |
| 3D framework              | **Three.js + React Three Fiber**               |
| 3D runtime format         | **GLTF/GLB**                                   |
| 3D compression            | Draco/Meshopt evaluation                       |
| 3D performance            | LOD + progressive loading + optimization       |
| 3D fallback               | Mandatory                                      |

| Core Web Vitals           | Monitored                                      |
| Heavy features            | Dynamic imports                                |
| PWA                       | Requirement-driven                             |
| Offline learning          | Dedicated architecture if required             |
| Internationalization      | Built-in architectural capability              |
| Medical translation       | Curated/validated                              |
| Unit/component tests      | Vitest + RTL                                   |
| API mocking               | MSW                                            |
| Browser E2E               | Playwright                                     |
| Accessibility testing     | Automated + manual                             |

| Secrets in browser        | **Impossible/rejected**                        |

| Frontend deployment       | S3 + CloudFront                                |
| Static assets             | Immutable/hash cached                          |

# ADR-068 — COMPLETE ✅

The complete frontend lifecycle is now:

```text
USER NEED
   │
   ▼
ACCESSIBLE UX
   │
   ▼
FEATURE BOUNDARY
   │
   ▼
ROUTE
   │
   ▼
COMPONENTS
   │
   ├────────► LOCAL STATE
   │
   ├────────► URL STATE
   │
   ├────────► FORM STATE
   │
   └────────► SERVER STATE
                    │
                    ▼
                 API LAYER
                    │
                    ▼
               AUTHORIZATION
                    │
                    ▼
                 BACKEND
                    │
                    ▼
                 RESPONSE
                    │
                    ▼
                USER STATE
                    │
                    ▼
              OBSERVABILITY
                    │
                    ▼
                 MEASURE
                    │
                    ▼
```
