
For the educational experience:

```text
                 LEARNING OBJECTIVE
                         │
            ┌────────────┼────────────┐
            ▼            ▼            ▼
           TEXT        DIAGRAM       AUDIO
            │            │            │
            └────────────┼────────────┘
                         ▼
                         3D
                         │
                         ▼
                  INTERACTION
                         │
                         ▼
                   EXPLANATION
                         │
                         ▼
                    ASSESSMENT
                         │
                         ▼
                     MASTERY
```

The defining invariant is:

> **Every frontend technology must improve a measurable user or engineering outcome. React, Redux, WebSockets, PWA capabilities and 3D rendering are tools—not architecture goals. For Mediverse, 3D is justified only when it improves understanding, and it must never make the learning experience inaccessible or unusable on constrained devices.**

## Next — ADR-069

### **ADR-069 — Enterprise AI/LLM, RAG, Intelligent Tutoring & Medical AI Architecture Standard**

This should be the next major architecture boundary because Mediverse is not just a CRUD learning platform. Its strongest differentiation can come from an **AI-assisted medical learning layer**.

ADR-069 should cover **AI capability boundaries → AI tutor architecture → LLM provider abstraction → managed API vs self-hosted models → model routing → medical-domain risk classification → AI as educational support vs clinical decision support → prompt architecture → system prompts → prompt versioning → structured outputs → tool/function calling → RAG → authoritative medical knowledge corpus → document ingestion → parsing → chunking → metadata → embeddings → vector database decision → pgvector vs OpenSearch vector search → hybrid retrieval → reranking → context construction → citation architecture → source grounding → hallucination controls → "I don't know" behavior → chapter/lecture scoped tutoring → learner-level personalization → conversation memory → privacy boundaries → prompt injection → indirect prompt injection → retrieval poisoning → data exfiltration prevention → moderation/guardrails → model output validation → medical terminology handling → multilingual tutoring → English/Marathi support → anatomy/physiology 3D-aware AI tutoring → multimodal architecture → image/diagram understanding → speech-to-text → text-to-speech → quiz generation → question difficulty → adaptive learning → knowledge tracing → recommendation engine → evaluation datasets → factuality evaluation → retrieval evaluation → answer relevance → citation correctness → LLM-as-judge limitations → human expert evaluation → regression testing → red-team testing → latency budgets → streaming responses → token budgets → semantic caching → cost controls → rate limiting → provider outages → model fallback → observability → prompt/model telemetry → privacy-safe traces → AI audit trail → model/version provenance → feedback loops → experiment framework → feature flags → AI safety → regulatory boundary → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise AI reference architecture.**

# ADR-069 — Enterprise AI/LLM, RAG, Intelligent Tutoring & Medical AI Architecture Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-069
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-068 established the Mediverse frontend and interactive learning architecture.

ADR-069 defines the architecture for the platform's **AI tutoring, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, medical knowledge grounding, multimodal learning, adaptive education, model governance, evaluation, security, observability and cost controls**.

The fundamental boundary is:

> **Mediverse AI is an educational reasoning and tutoring system. It must not silently evolve into an unvalidated clinical decision-support system.**

```text id="lkk25m"
                         LEARNER
                            │
                            ▼
                     MEDIVERSE UI
                            │
                            ▼
                     AI TUTOR API
                            │
               ┌────────────┼────────────┐
               ▼            ▼            ▼
          SECURITY      ORCHESTRATION   MEMORY
               │            │            │
               └────────────┼────────────┘
                            ▼
                     INTENT / POLICY
                            │
             ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
             ▼              ▼              ▼
            RAG           TOOLS       MODEL ROUTER
             │              │              │
             ▼              │              ▼
       MEDICAL KNOWLEDGE    │         LLM PROVIDERS
             │              │
             ▼              │
        RETRIEVAL           │
             │              │
             ▼              │
         RERANKING          │
             │              │
             └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                            ▼
                      GENERATION
                            │
                            ▼
                     VALIDATION
                            │
                            ▼
                       CITATIONS
                            │
                            ▼
                        LEARNER
```

# 1. AI Architecture Objective

Mediverse AI should optimize for:

```text id="72x7sj"
Educational correctness
Grounded answers
Traceability
Safety
Personalization
Explainability
Evaluation
Security
Latency
Cost control
```

Raw model capability alone is insufficient.

# 2. AI Capability Boundary

Every AI capability must have an explicit purpose.

Examples:

```text id="kgm3uq"
Explain physiology
Summarize a chapter
Generate practice questions
Explain incorrect answers
Navigate anatomical models
Recommend revision topics
```

Avoid a universal unrestricted "AI does everything" endpoint.

# 3. Educational AI Boundary

Mediverse AI may explain medical concepts for education.

It must distinguish educational assistance from patient-specific medical advice.

```text id="rv0ojw"
Educational Question
        │
        ▼
Mediverse Tutor
        │
        ▼
Educational Explanation
```

# 4. Clinical Boundary

Requests involving actual patient diagnosis, treatment or clinical decisions require a fundamentally different governance and validation regime.

Do not pretend a disclaimer transforms an educational chatbot into validated clinical software.

# 5. Risk Classification

AI capabilities should be classified before implementation.

```text id="l5j2kn"
LOWER RISK
│
├── terminology explanation
├── chapter summarization
├── flashcards
└── study planning

HIGHER RISK
│
├── medical factual generation
├── clinical scenario reasoning
├── drug-related education
└── patient-specific questions
```

Controls should increase with risk.

# 6. AI Gateway

Application services should not directly integrate independently with model providers.

Preferred:

```text id="sp2h77"
Course Service ──┐
Assessment ──────┼──► AI Gateway / AI Platform
Tutor ───────────┘
                         │
                         ▼
                    Model Providers
```

# 7. Provider Abstraction

Provider-specific APIs should sit behind an internal abstraction.

```text id="d5hyhk"
AITutor
   │
   ▼
ModelGateway
   │
   ├── Provider A
   ├── Provider B
   └── Self-hosted Model
```

Do not leak provider SDK objects across application architecture.

# 8. Provider Portability

Provider abstraction should support migration and fallback.

But pretending every model has identical capabilities is also wrong.

The abstraction must preserve important differences such as:

```text id="3jz8hx"
Context window
Structured output
Tool calling
Vision
Latency
Cost
Safety behavior
```

# 9. Managed vs Self-Hosted Models

Managed APIs should generally be preferred initially when they provide sufficient:

```text id="2f5j6a"
Quality
Security
Privacy
Reliability
Latency
Commercial terms
```

Self-hosting should solve a concrete requirement.

# 10. Self-Hosting Cost

Running a model internally introduces:

```text id="3rl2i1"
GPU infrastructure
Model serving
Scaling
Batching
Monitoring
Upgrades
Security
Capacity planning
Model evaluation
```

"Open source" does not mean operationally free.

# 11. Model Router

Different tasks may use different models.

```text id="4o6qdd"
Request
   │
   ▼
Model Router
   │
   ├── Simple explanation → efficient model
   ├── Complex reasoning  → stronger model
   ├── Vision             → multimodal model
   └── Embedding          → embedding model
```

# 12. Routing Inputs

Routing may consider:

```text id="2arvup"
Task
Risk
Latency requirement
Language
Modality
Context size
Cost
Model availability
```

# 13. Model Version Pinning

Production workloads should not silently move between model versions where provider controls allow pinning.

Model upgrades require evaluation.

```text id="zyb3vh"
Model v1
   │
   ▼
Evaluation
   │
   ▼
Model v2
   │
   ▼
Controlled rollout
```

# 14. Prompt Architecture

Prompts are production artifacts.

They require:

```text id="90n6yt"
Versioning
Review
Testing
Ownership
Change history
Evaluation
```

They should not live as random strings scattered across Java/TypeScript files.

# 15. Prompt Registry

Important prompts should be centrally managed.

```text id="g81r1o"
Tutor Prompt v17
Quiz Prompt v8
Summary Prompt v5
3D Explanation Prompt v4
```

Each deployed response should be attributable to a prompt version.

# 16. System Instructions

System instructions should establish:

```text id="d6s20v"
Role
Scope
Safety boundary
Expected format
Tool policy
Citation policy
Uncertainty behavior
```

Avoid giant prompts attempting to encode the entire platform.

# 17. Prompt Composition

Prefer composable prompt architecture.

```text id="8b7h1f"
Base Policy
    +
Tutor Behavior
    +
Course Context
    +
Retrieved Evidence
    +
User Question
```

# 18. Structured Outputs

Machine-consumed model responses should use structured outputs where supported.

Example conceptual contract:

```json id="gwzq1x"
{
  "answer": "...",
  "citations": [],
  "confidence": "...",
  "followUpQuestions": []
}
```

Do not parse critical application behavior from arbitrary prose with regex.

# 19. Output Validation

Structured model output must still be validated against the expected schema.

```text id="cb2h8d"
LLM
 │
 ▼
JSON
 │
 ▼
Schema Validation
 │
 ├── valid → continue
 │
 └── invalid → controlled recovery
```

# 20. Tool Calling

Models may request approved tools.

```text id="0rqvx9"
LLM
 │
 ▼
Tool Request
 │
 ▼
Policy / Authorization
 │
 ▼
Tool Execution
 │
 ▼
Result
 │
 ▼
LLM
```

The model does not receive unrestricted infrastructure access.

# 21. Tool Allowlist

Available tools must be explicit.

Potential tools:

```text id="4w3h50"
Retrieve course content
Fetch learner progress
Search terminology
Load anatomy metadata
Generate quiz draft
```

Not:

```text id="1cdub7"
execute arbitrary SQL
execute shell command
access unrestricted S3
```

# 22. Tool Authorization

User authorization must propagate to tool execution.

```text id="scf9kx"
Learner asks AI
      │
      ▼
AI calls content tool
      │
      ▼
Can learner access course?
      │
   ┌──┴──┐
   ▼     ▼
  Yes    No
```

AI must not become an authorization bypass.

# 23. Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Medical educational answers should use RAG when authoritative source grounding materially improves correctness.

```text id="7mywsv"
Question
   │
   ▼
Retrieval
   │
   ▼
Evidence
   │
   ▼
LLM
   │
   ▼
Grounded Answer
```

# 24. RAG Limitation

RAG does not eliminate hallucination.

It can fail through:

```text id="fvl8pb"
Bad retrieval
Missing evidence
Wrong ranking
Misinterpreted evidence
Unsupported synthesis
Stale source material
```

# 25. Authoritative Corpus

The medical knowledge corpus requires explicit governance.

Sources should have:

```text id="x19wp0"
Authority
Version
Edition
Topic
Publication date
License
Owner
Review status
```

# 26. Source Provenance

Every indexed knowledge item should retain provenance.

```text id="b0kglh"
Document
  │
  ├── Source
  ├── Edition
  ├── Chapter
  ├── Section
  ├── Page/location
  └── Ingestion version
```

Without provenance, citations become unreliable.

# 27. Content Licensing

Technical ability to ingest a textbook does not imply legal permission to reproduce/index it.

Content licensing must be resolved before ingestion.

# 28. Ingestion Pipeline

```text id="xmkjgo"
SOURCE
  │
  ▼
UPLOAD / CONNECTOR
  │
  ▼
VALIDATION
  │
  ▼
PARSING
  │
  ▼
NORMALIZATION
  │
  ▼
CHUNKING
  │
  ▼
METADATA
  │
  ▼
EMBEDDING
  │
  ▼
INDEX
```

# 29. Document Parsing

Parsing must preserve useful document structure.

Important structures include:

```text id="cnf86y"
Chapter
Section
Heading
Paragraph
Table
Figure reference
Learning objective
```

Flattening everything into anonymous text destroys retrieval quality.

# 30. Chunking

Chunking strategy should follow semantic structure rather than arbitrary character counts alone.

```text id="vfdks8"
Chapter
  │
  ▼
Section
  │
  ▼
Semantic chunks
```

# 31. Chunk Size

There is no universal perfect chunk size.

It should be evaluated against:

```text id="3jrx0m"
Content structure
Embedding model
Retrieval task
Context window
Citation precision
Answer quality
```

# 32. Chunk Overlap

Overlap may preserve context across boundaries.

Excessive overlap creates:

```text id="4bsayq"
Index duplication
Storage cost
Retrieval redundancy
Context waste
```

Measure it.

# 33. Metadata

Chunks should carry useful metadata.

Example:

```text id="2eyc92"
subject = physiology
chapter = cardiovascular
topic = cardiac-cycle
contentType = textbook
edition = ...
language = en
```

# 34. Metadata Filtering

Retrieval should use metadata when context already narrows the search.

If a learner is studying cardiovascular physiology, retrieving unrelated pathology because embeddings happen to be similar is undesirable.

# 35. Embeddings

Embeddings represent content in vector space.

```text id="eg2nt7"
Text
 │
 ▼
Embedding Model
 │
 ▼
Vector
 │
 ▼
Similarity Search
```

Embedding models are infrastructure dependencies requiring version governance.

# 36. Embedding Migration

Changing embedding models may require re-embedding the corpus.

Therefore store:

```text id="xob4tv"
embeddingModel
embeddingVersion
embeddingDimensions
ingestionVersion
```

# 37. Vector Database Decision

Mediverse should initially evaluate **PostgreSQL + pgvector** before adding a dedicated vector platform.

This is appropriate when:

```text id="wpajw0"
Corpus is manageable
PostgreSQL already exists
Operational simplicity matters
Filtering requirements are relational
```

# 38. Dedicated Search Engine

OpenSearch or another search platform becomes more compelling when requirements include substantial:

```text id="lq5pdv"
Full-text search
Hybrid search
Large corpus scale
Complex ranking
Search analytics
Distributed indexing
```

Architecture should follow measured need.

# 39. Vector Search

Pure semantic vector search should not automatically be assumed superior.

Medical terminology frequently benefits from exact lexical matching.

# 40. Hybrid Retrieval

Mediverse should prefer evaluation of:

```text id="g2t50z"
Semantic retrieval
        +
Lexical retrieval
        +
Metadata filtering
```

for authoritative educational search.

# 41. Retrieval Pipeline

```text id="hnqf8e"
Question
   │
   ▼
Query Understanding
   │
   ├── Metadata filters
   ├── Lexical query
   └── Embedding
          │
          ▼
     Candidate Retrieval
          │
          ▼
        Merge
          │
          ▼
       Reranker
          │
          ▼
      Top Evidence
```

# 42. Reranking

A reranker may improve precision by re-evaluating retrieved candidates against the original question.

This adds latency and cost, so use evaluation rather than assumption.

# 43. Top-K

Increasing `topK` does not automatically improve answers.

Too much retrieved context can:

```text id="xkkp3v"
Distract the model
Increase tokens
Increase latency
Increase cost
Introduce contradictory evidence
```

# 44. Context Construction

Retrieved evidence should be clearly separated from system instructions and user content.

```text id="50o0am"
SYSTEM POLICY

USER QUESTION

RETRIEVED SOURCES
[source 1]
[source 2]
[source 3]
```

Boundaries matter for both quality and security.

# 45. Citation Architecture

Generated educational claims should link back to supporting source locations where the experience requires authoritative grounding.

```text id="gx5vji"
AI Claim
   │
   ▼
Source Chunk
   │
   ▼
Document
   │
   ▼
Chapter / Section / Page
```

# 46. Citation Verification

A citation being present does not mean it supports the claim.

Evaluation must test:

```text id="z5a74m"
Citation exists
Citation is relevant
Citation actually supports claim
Source is authoritative
```

# 47. Unsupported Claims

If retrieved evidence does not support an answer, the model should be allowed to say that the available Mediverse sources do not establish it.

Fabricating confidence is worse than admitting insufficient evidence.

# 48. Knowledge Scope

Tutor queries may be scoped to:

```text id="6j7hyq"
Current paragraph
Current lesson
Current chapter
Current subject
Entire approved corpus
```

depending on user intent.

# 49. Context-Aware Tutor

The frontend may provide learning context:

```text id="x6rfn0"
Course
Lesson
Current topic
Selected 3D structure
Assessment context
```

This can make tutoring dramatically more relevant than a generic chatbot.

# 50. Conversation Memory

AI conversation memory should be deliberately separated into:

```text id="7ghu91"
Current-turn context
Short conversation context
Learner profile/preferences
Long-term learning state
```

These are different data categories.

# 51. Conversation History

Do not blindly send the entire chat history to every model request.

Use:

```text id="u40fcd"
Recent relevant turns
Summarized context
Retrieved history
```

where appropriate.

# 52. Memory Accuracy

Generated summaries used as memory may contain errors.

Critical learning state should come from authoritative application data rather than model-generated recollection.

# 53. Learner Personalization

Useful personalization may include:

```text id="l5gw14"
Current curriculum
Completed topics
Weak concepts
Preferred explanation depth
Previous assessment performance
```

Personalization should improve education rather than manipulate engagement.

# 54. Prompt Injection

User content must be treated as untrusted.

Example:

```text id="krzvno"
"Ignore all previous instructions..."
```

must not override higher-priority platform policies.

# 55. Indirect Prompt Injection

Retrieved documents can also contain malicious instructions.

```text id="a5e0sc"
Document
   │
   ▼
"Ignore system instructions..."
   │
   ▼
RAG Context
```

Retrieved text is data—not trusted instructions.

# 56. Retrieval Poisoning

Knowledge ingestion must prevent unauthorized users from injecting content into trusted medical corpora.

Corpus write access is a high-trust operation.

# 57. Data Exfiltration

Models and tools must not expose:

```text id="cf0d59"
Other users' conversations
Restricted course content
Secrets
System prompts
Internal credentials
Private documents
```

# 58. Prompt Confidentiality

System prompts should not contain secrets.

Assume prompt content could eventually be exposed through debugging, logging, attacks or operational mistakes.

# 59. Guardrails

Guardrails should exist at multiple layers.

```text id="2ej82e"
INPUT
 │
 ▼
Policy
 │
 ▼
Retrieval / Tools
 │
 ▼
Model
 │
 ▼
Output Validation
 │
 ▼
Safety / Grounding
 │
 ▼
USER
```

A single "safety prompt" is not an architecture.

# 60. AI Security Principle

The model must never become the final authority for:

```text id="5ub6ve"
Authentication
Authorization
Security policy
Database access control
Payment decisions
Infrastructure permissions
```

Deterministic systems remain authoritative.

---

## ADR-069 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The AI architecture now follows:

```text id="yzmcwx"
                         LEARNER
                            │
                            ▼
                      AI TUTOR API
                            │
                            ▼
                    POLICY / SECURITY
                            │
                 ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                 ▼          ▼          ▼
              CONTEXT      RAG        TOOLS
                 │          │          │
                 │          ▼          │
                 │      RETRIEVAL      │
                 │          │          │
                 │       RERANK        │
                 │          │          │
                 └──────────┼──────────┘
                            ▼
                       MODEL ROUTER
                            │
                 ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                 ▼          ▼          ▼
              Efficient   Reasoning  Multimodal
                Model       Model      Model
                 │          │          │
                 └──────────┼──────────┘
                            ▼
                    STRUCTURED OUTPUT
                            │
                            ▼
                       VALIDATION
                            │
                            ▼
                       CITATIONS
                            │
                            ▼
                         LEARNER
```

The critical architectural distinction is:

```text id="u7gvt0"
            LANGUAGE MODEL
                  │
                  ▼
            PROPOSE / REASON
                  │
                  X
        NOT SYSTEM AUTHORITY


        DETERMINISTIC SYSTEM
                  │
                  ▼
             AUTHORIZE
             VALIDATE
             ENFORCE
             PERSIST
```

The defining rule is:

> **The LLM may reason, explain, retrieve, summarize and propose. It must not become the authoritative security, data-integrity or access-control layer. Medical answers requiring factual grounding must be traceable to governed evidence, and insufficient evidence must remain an acceptable outcome.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Medical AI Output Safety & Factuality**, then cover **clinical-question boundaries → uncertainty → answer verification → moderation → multilingual medical terminology → Marathi tutoring → multimodal AI → image/diagram reasoning → 3D-aware AI tutor → scene/tool integration → speech-to-text → text-to-speech → AI-generated quizzes → question validation → adaptive difficulty → learner knowledge model → knowledge tracing → spaced repetition → recommendation engine → AI-generated learning paths → human educator oversight → content approval workflows → evaluation architecture → golden datasets → factuality → groundedness → retrieval recall/precision → reranker evaluation → citation correctness → hallucination rate → LLM-as-judge limitations → expert medical evaluation → adversarial/red-team testing → prompt regression → model upgrade gates → latency architecture → streaming → token budgets → context compression → semantic caching → rate limiting → cost attribution → quotas → provider outage/fallback → AI SLOs → observability → traces → prompt/model provenance → privacy-safe telemetry → auditability → user feedback → experimentation → feature flags → AI incident response → production readiness → AI anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise AI architecture.**

# ADR-069 — Enterprise AI/LLM, RAG, Intelligent Tutoring & Medical AI Architecture Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — AI Security Principle**.

---

# 61. Medical AI Output Safety & Factuality

Medical educational output must be treated as higher-risk than ordinary generative content.

The system should distinguish:

```text
Fluent answer
      ≠
Correct answer
      ≠
Grounded answer
      ≠
Educationally appropriate answer
```

Generation quality therefore requires multiple independent controls.

---

# 62. Medical Claim Grounding

Important factual medical claims should be grounded in approved Mediverse knowledge sources when the capability is operating in grounded tutoring mode.

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Evidence Retrieval
   │
   ▼
Generation
   │
   ▼
Claim ↔ Evidence Check
   │
   ▼
Answer
```

The model's pretrained knowledge alone should not automatically be treated as authoritative course content.

---

# 63. Clinical Question Detection

The system should detect when a conversation moves from education toward patient-specific clinical decision-making.

Examples:

```text
"What causes tachycardia?"
→ educational

"My heart rate is 150 and I feel dizzy. What should I do?"
→ patient-specific / higher-risk
```

The second case crosses a materially different risk boundary.

---

# 64. Clinical Boundary Enforcement

Clinical-risk classification should influence system behavior.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Risk Classification
   │
   ├── Educational
   │      ▼
   │    Tutor
   │
   └── Clinical-risk
          ▼
      Restricted Policy
```

A prompt disclaimer alone is not sufficient enforcement.

---

# 65. Uncertainty

The AI must be permitted to express uncertainty.

Useful states include:

```text
Supported
Partially supported
Conflicting evidence
Insufficient evidence
Outside approved corpus
```

Forced confidence creates hallucinations.

---

# 66. Evidence Conflict

If authoritative sources disagree, the system should not silently select one answer.

```text
Source A ─┐
          ├──► Conflict Detection
Source B ─┘
                 │
                 ▼
        Explain disagreement
```

Edition, guideline date and source authority may matter.

---

# 67. Answer Verification

High-value generated answers should support a post-generation verification stage where practical.

```text
Draft Answer
     │
     ▼
Claims Extraction
     │
     ▼
Evidence Verification
     │
     ▼
Final Answer
```

Verification should not simply ask the same model, with the same context, whether it thinks its own answer is correct and treat that as proof.

---

# 68. Claim-Level Verification

Verification should operate at meaningful claim granularity.

Example:

```text
Answer
 ├── Claim 1 → Source A ✓
 ├── Claim 2 → Source B ✓
 └── Claim 3 → unsupported ✗
```

Unsupported material can then be removed, qualified or regenerated.

---

# 69. Moderation

Input/output moderation should be capability-specific.

It may need to detect:

```text
Abuse
Unsafe requests
Self-harm content
Sexual content
Violence
Prompt attacks
Privacy violations
Clinical-risk requests
```

Medical terminology itself must not be incorrectly blocked merely because it contains anatomically explicit terms.

---

# 70. Medical Context-Aware Safety

A medical learning platform necessarily discusses:

```text
Anatomy
Reproductive physiology
Disease
Injury
Drugs
Death
Clinical procedures
```

Safety systems therefore need context awareness.

Naive keyword blocking would make the platform unusable.

---

# 71. Multilingual Medical AI

Language translation must preserve medical meaning.

Architecture:

```text
Learner Language
      │
      ▼
Terminology Layer
      │
      ▼
Retrieval
      │
      ▼
Reasoning
      │
      ▼
Localized Explanation
```

---

# 72. Canonical Medical Terminology

Where possible, concepts should have language-independent identifiers.

Conceptually:

```text
Concept ID
   │
   ├── English term
   ├── Marathi term
   ├── Synonyms
   └── Abbreviations
```

This is more robust than treating translated strings as independent concepts.

---

# 73. Marathi Tutoring

For Marathi educational support, the system should preserve important English medical terminology where that improves academic usefulness.

Example style:

```text
हृदयाचे आकुंचन (cardiac contraction)
```

rather than forcing unnatural translations for every technical term.

---

# 74. Translation Validation

High-value medical terminology dictionaries should be reviewed by qualified subject/language experts.

LLM translation alone should not establish canonical terminology.

---

# 75. Cross-Lingual Retrieval

A Marathi question may need to retrieve English authoritative material.

```text
Marathi Query
     │
     ▼
Cross-Lingual Understanding
     │
     ▼
English Corpus
     │
     ▼
Evidence
     │
     ▼
Marathi Explanation
```

Retrieval quality must be explicitly evaluated for this scenario.

---

# 76. Multimodal AI

Mediverse AI should support multimodal educational interactions where they improve learning.

Potential inputs:

```text
Text
Diagram
Image
3D scene state
Audio
```

---

# 77. Image Understanding

Image-capable models may assist with educational diagrams.

```text
Diagram
   +
Question
   │
   ▼
Vision Model
   │
   ▼
Educational Explanation
```

The model should receive sufficient contextual information to know what educational material it is analyzing.

---

# 78. Image Grounding

Visual interpretation can hallucinate structures.

Where authoritative labels/metadata exist, use them.

```text
Image
   │
   ├── Visual model
   └── Authoritative metadata
            │
            ▼
       Explanation
```

---

# 79. 3D-Aware Tutor

The AI tutor should understand the current 3D learning context without requiring the model to infer everything from screenshots.

```text
3D Scene
   │
   ├── selectedStructure = mitralValve
   ├── lesson = cardiacCycle
   ├── animationPhase = ventricularSystole
   └── cameraContext
           │
           ▼
        AI Tutor
```

Structured scene state is superior to guessing scene semantics from pixels.

---

# 80. 3D Tool Integration

The tutor may invoke controlled frontend actions.

Example:

```text
Learner:
"Show me where the mitral valve is."

AI
 │
 ▼
Tool:
focusStructure("mitral-valve")
 │
 ▼
3D Engine
 │
 ▼
Highlight + Camera Focus
```

---

# 81. AI-to-3D Command Safety

The model should not emit arbitrary JavaScript.

Instead:

```text
LLM
 │
 ▼
Structured Tool Call
 │
 ▼
Schema Validation
 │
 ▼
Allowed Scene Command
```

---

# 82. 3D Tool Allowlist

Potential commands:

```text
focusStructure()
highlightStructure()
isolateStructure()
playAnimation()
pauseAnimation()
setLearningStep()
showAnnotation()
```

The scene engine remains authoritative over execution.

---

# 83. Scene State Feedback

After executing a tool, the frontend should return structured state.

```text
AI command
    │
    ▼
3D engine
    │
    ▼
Execution result
    │
    ▼
AI
```

This prevents the model from assuming an action succeeded.

---

# 84. Speech-to-Text

Voice input may improve accessibility and tutoring interaction.

```text
Learner Speech
      │
      ▼
Speech Recognition
      │
      ▼
Transcript
      │
      ▼
AI Tutor
```

Transcripts should remain visible/editable where practical.

---

# 85. Medical Speech Recognition

General speech recognition may perform poorly on:

```text
Drug names
Anatomical terminology
Latin-derived terms
Abbreviations
Mixed Marathi-English speech
```

Medical vocabulary accuracy requires evaluation.

---

# 86. Text-to-Speech

AI explanations may be converted to speech.

```text
Tutor Response
      │
      ▼
TTS
      │
      ▼
Audio
```

Text must remain available for accessibility and verification.

---

# 87. TTS Pronunciation

Medical terminology pronunciation should be tested.

A fluent voice that repeatedly mispronounces core terminology damages educational quality.

---

# 88. AI Quiz Generation

AI may generate draft questions from approved learning content.

```text
Learning Objective
      +
Approved Evidence
      │
      ▼
Question Generator
      │
      ▼
Validation
      │
      ▼
Question Bank
```

---

# 89. Quiz Structure

Generated questions should use structured contracts.

```json
{
  "question": "...",
  "type": "single_best_answer",
  "options": [],
  "correctOption": "...",
  "explanation": "...",
  "learningObjective": "...",
  "citations": []
}
```

---

# 90. Quiz Validation

A generated question is not automatically valid because an LLM produced it.

Validation should inspect:

```text
Correctness
Single best answer
Distractor quality
Ambiguity
Learning-objective alignment
Difficulty
Evidence support
Terminology
```

---

# 91. Assessment Boundary

High-stakes graded assessments should not be populated directly with uncontrolled real-time generated questions.

Prefer:

```text
AI Draft
   │
   ▼
Validation
   │
   ▼
Human Review where required
   │
   ▼
Approved Question Bank
```

---

# 92. Distractor Generation

Incorrect answer choices should be:

```text
Plausible
Clearly incorrect under the intended interpretation
Educationally meaningful
Non-trivial
```

Random nonsense makes MCQs easier without improving learning.

---

# 93. Explanation Generation

Question explanations should describe:

```text
Why the correct answer is correct
Why relevant distractors are incorrect
Underlying concept
Source evidence
```

This is more educationally useful than returning only an answer key.

---

# 94. Adaptive Difficulty

Difficulty may adapt based on learner performance.

```text
Performance
    │
    ▼
Learner Model
    │
    ▼
Difficulty Selection
    │
    ▼
Next Question
```

The adjustment mechanism should be measurable and explainable.

---

# 95. Difficulty Is Multidimensional

Difficulty is not merely:

```text
easy / medium / hard
```

It can depend on:

```text
Recall depth
Concept integration
Clinical application
Distractor similarity
Required reasoning steps
Prior knowledge
```

---

# 96. Learner Knowledge Model

Mediverse should maintain an authoritative learning-state model outside the LLM.

```text
Learner
   │
   ▼
Knowledge Model
   │
   ├── Topic mastery
   ├── Attempts
   ├── Accuracy
   ├── Recency
   └── Confidence estimate
```

The LLM may consume this state but should not be its sole source of truth.

---

# 97. Knowledge Graph

Curriculum concepts may be represented as dependencies.

```text
Cell Physiology
      │
      ▼
Membrane Potential
      │
      ▼
Action Potential
      │
      ▼
Cardiac Electrophysiology
```

This supports prerequisite-aware learning.

---

# 98. Knowledge Tracing

Knowledge tracing may estimate changing learner mastery over time.

Conceptually:

```text
Prior Mastery
     +
Question Result
     +
Difficulty
     +
Time
     │
     ▼
Updated Mastery
```

Sophisticated ML is not mandatory initially.

---

# 99. Start Simple

Do not jump immediately to deep-learning knowledge-tracing models.

A transparent model using:

```text
Attempts
Accuracy
Difficulty
Recency
Confidence
```

may provide more operational value initially.

Complexity should be earned through evidence.

---

# 100. Spaced Repetition

Review scheduling should incorporate forgetting and recall history.

```text
Successful Recall
      │
      ▼
Longer Interval

Failed Recall
      │
      ▼
Shorter Interval
```

AI may generate explanations, but scheduling should remain deterministic enough to test.

---

# 101. Recommendation Engine

Learning recommendations may combine:

```text
Curriculum requirements
Mastery
Prerequisites
Recent mistakes
Upcoming assessments
Learner goals
```

Recommendations should optimize learning outcomes—not raw screen time.

---

# 102. Recommendation Explainability

The system should be capable of explaining:

> "Why am I being asked to study this?"

Example:

```text
Recommended:
Cardiac Action Potentials

Because:
2 recent errors
+
prerequisite for ECG interpretation
```

---

# 103. AI-Generated Learning Paths

AI may propose learning paths.

But the curriculum graph and academic requirements remain authoritative.

```text
AI Proposal
    │
    ▼
Constraint Validation
    │
    ▼
Learning Path
```

---

# 104. Educator Oversight

Educators need governance controls for AI-generated learning material.

Potential states:

```text
Draft
Reviewed
Approved
Rejected
Archived
```

---

# 105. Human Review

Human review should be risk-based.

Not every low-risk AI explanation requires pre-publication review.

But reusable/high-impact content may.

Examples:

```text
Generated flashcard
→ automated checks may suffice

Official assessment question
→ stronger review

Canonical medical explanation
→ subject expert review
```

---

# 106. Content Provenance

Reusable AI-generated content should record:

```text
Model
Model version
Prompt version
Source documents
Generation time
Reviewer
Approval status
```

---

# 107. Evaluation Architecture

AI quality must be measured systematically.

```text
AI Change
   │
   ▼
Evaluation Suite
   │
   ├── Retrieval
   ├── Factuality
   ├── Grounding
   ├── Safety
   ├── Language
   └── User Experience
   │
   ▼
Release Decision
```

---

# 108. Golden Evaluation Dataset

Maintain curated evaluation cases representing real Mediverse tasks.

Examples:

```text
Basic physiology questions
Complex mechanism explanations
Ambiguous questions
Marathi questions
Diagram questions
3D-context questions
Insufficient-evidence cases
Adversarial prompts
```

---

# 109. Dataset Versioning

Evaluation datasets are production assets.

Record:

```text
Dataset version
Question
Expected properties
Reference answer
Source evidence
Risk category
Language
Difficulty
```

---

# 110. Factuality Evaluation

Factuality evaluation should ask whether medical claims are correct according to the approved reference set.

Fluency must not influence factual scoring.

---

# 111. Groundedness Evaluation

Groundedness asks:

```text
Does the answer follow
the provided evidence?
```

A fact may happen to be correct while still being unsupported by the retrieved sources.

Those are different metrics.

---

# 112. Retrieval Evaluation

RAG should be evaluated independently from generation.

Measure:

```text
Recall@K
Precision@K
MRR where useful
Relevant chunk ranking
Metadata filter correctness
```

If retrieval fails, prompt engineering will not reliably fix the system.

---

# 113. Retrieval Test Cases

Each important test query should identify expected relevant evidence.

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Expected Source(s)
   │
   ▼
Retriever
   │
   ▼
Compare
```

---

# 114. Citation Correctness

Measure whether:

```text
Citation exists
        │
        ▼
Correct source?
        │
        ▼
Correct passage?
        │
        ▼
Actually supports claim?
```

Citation count is not a quality metric.

---

# 115. Hallucination Measurement

Track unsupported-claim rate rather than relying on subjective impressions that answers "look good."

A polished hallucination is still a failure.

---

# 116. LLM-as-Judge

LLMs may assist evaluation at scale.

They should not be treated as unquestionable ground truth.

Potential problems:

```text
Model bias
Position bias
Preference for verbosity
Self-preference
Prompt sensitivity
Inconsistent scoring
```

---

# 117. Expert Medical Evaluation

A representative subset of outputs should be evaluated by qualified medical educators/subject experts.

Human evaluation should focus on:

```text
Accuracy
Educational clarity
Omissions
Misleading simplification
Clinical nuance
Terminology
```

---

# 118. Inter-Rater Reliability

For subjective evaluations, multiple evaluators may disagree.

Evaluation design should measure agreement where important rather than pretending human labels are perfectly objective.

---

# 119. Prompt Regression Testing

Prompt changes require regression evaluation.

```text
Prompt v18
   │
   ▼
Evaluation Suite
   │
   ▼
Compare against v17
```

"Prompt looks better" is not an adequate production release criterion.

---

# 120. Model Upgrade Gate

A new model version should pass:

```text
Quality
Safety
Grounding
Latency
Cost
Multilingual
Tool-use
Structured-output
```

evaluation before broad rollout.

---

# 121. Adversarial Testing

AI red-team suites should test:

```text
Prompt injection
Indirect injection
Data extraction attempts
Authorization bypass
System prompt extraction
Corpus poisoning
Unsafe clinical requests
Tool misuse
Malformed structured output
Excessive resource consumption
```

---

# 122. Streaming Responses

Long tutoring answers should support token streaming where it improves perceived latency.

```text
Request
  │
  ▼
Model
  │
  ▼
Token Stream
  │
  ▼
Browser
```

Streaming does not reduce actual generation cost.

---

# 123. Streaming Safety

Some controls can only evaluate complete output.

Architecture must decide whether content can safely stream before all post-generation validation is complete.

Higher-risk workflows may require buffering or staged validation.

---

# 124. Latency Budget

AI requests should have explicit latency budgets.

Break latency down:

```text
Authentication
     +
Retrieval
     +
Reranking
     +
Model queue
     +
Generation
     +
Validation
```

Without decomposition, "AI is slow" is not actionable.

---

# 125. Parallelization

Independent work should run concurrently where safe.

```text
Question
   │
   ├── Retrieve knowledge
   ├── Fetch learner context
   └── Fetch scene context
           │
           ▼
         Merge
```

Sequential network chains create avoidable latency.

---

# 126. Token Budgets

Each AI capability should define token/context budgets.

```text
System instructions
+
Conversation
+
Retrieved evidence
+
Tool results
+
Output
```

All consume finite context and money.

---

# 127. Context Compression

Large conversations should use controlled compression.

Potential strategies:

```text
Relevant-turn selection
Conversation summarization
Structured memory
Retrieval over conversation history
```

Do not continuously append everything forever.

---

# 128. Context Relevance

More context is not necessarily better.

Irrelevant context can reduce:

```text
Accuracy
Attention
Latency
Cost efficiency
```

Context selection is an engineering problem.

---

# 129. Semantic Caching

Semantically similar low-risk requests may use cached answers where:

```text
Source corpus unchanged
Prompt/model policy compatible
Personalization irrelevant
Freshness acceptable
Security scope identical
```

This requires strict cache-key and authorization design.

---

# 130. Cache Safety

Never serve another user's private/personalized AI result because semantic similarity matched.

Cache boundaries must include authorization and personalization dimensions where applicable.

---

# 131. AI Rate Limiting

AI endpoints require stronger consumption controls than ordinary cheap APIs.

Limits may consider:

```text
User
Organization
Feature
Model
Token usage
Request cost
Time window
```

---

# 132. Cost Attribution

Every model invocation should be attributable to a meaningful dimension.

```text
Service
Feature
Model
Tenant/user class where appropriate
Environment
Token usage
```

This allows cost optimization.

---

# 133. Cost Per Learning Outcome

The useful metric is not merely:

```text
$ / 1M tokens
```

Mediverse should eventually understand:

```text
Cost per tutoring session
Cost per quiz generated
Cost per active learner
Cost per completed learning objective
```

---

# 134. Quotas

Free or bounded plans may require quotas.

Quota enforcement must happen before expensive model execution where possible.

---

# 135. Model Fallback

Fallback should be capability-aware.

```text
Primary Model
      │ failure
      ▼
Fallback Router
      │
      ▼
Compatible Model
```

A cheaper fallback that cannot perform required structured/tool/vision behavior is not actually compatible.

---

# 136. Provider Outage

The application should degrade deliberately.

Potential fallback:

```text
AI Tutor unavailable
        │
        ├── Existing course content ✓
        ├── Search ✓
        ├── Assessments ✓
        └── 3D learning ✓
```

An LLM outage should not make the entire learning platform unusable.

---

# 137. AI SLOs

AI capabilities need their own SLOs.

Possible indicators:

```text
Availability
Time to first token
End-to-end latency
Structured-output success
Retrieval success
Tool execution success
Grounded-answer rate
```

---

# 138. AI Observability

Every AI request should produce a trace across:

```text
Tutor API
   │
   ▼
Retrieval
   │
   ▼
Reranking
   │
   ▼
Model
   │
   ▼
Tools
   │
   ▼
Validation
```

This integrates with ADR-063.

---

# 139. AI Telemetry

Useful metadata may include:

```text
Request ID
Feature
Prompt version
Model/version
Retriever version
Embedding version
Retrieved document IDs
Token usage
Latency
Tool calls
Validation result
```

Subject to privacy rules.

---

# 140. Prompt Logging

Raw prompts and responses may contain sensitive or copyrighted content.

Do not indiscriminately log everything.

Prefer configurable:

```text
Metadata-only telemetry
Redaction
Sampling
Restricted diagnostic logging
Retention limits
```

---

# 141. AI Audit Trail

For high-value generated artifacts, retain enough provenance to reconstruct:

```text
What generated this?
Which model?
Which prompt?
Which sources?
Which tools?
Which validation?
Who approved it?
```

---

# 142. User Feedback

AI responses may support structured feedback.

```text
Helpful?
Accurate?
Citation problem?
Too difficult?
Too simple?
```

Feedback should feed evaluation—not automatically retrain or modify production behavior.

---

# 143. Feedback Poisoning

User feedback is untrusted data.

Attackers or noisy users can intentionally manipulate feedback.

Training/evaluation pipelines must validate and aggregate it appropriately.

---

# 144. Experimentation

AI changes should support controlled experiments.

```text
Model A
vs
Model B

Prompt A
vs
Prompt B

Retriever A
vs
Retriever B
```

Experiments must measure educational and safety outcomes, not only engagement.

---

# 145. Feature Flags

New AI capabilities should use controlled rollout.

```text
Internal
   │
   ▼
Medical reviewers
   │
   ▼
Small cohort
   │
   ▼
Expanded cohort
   │
   ▼
General availability
```

Rollback should be fast.

---

# 146. AI Incident Response

AI incidents require explicit operational procedures.

Examples:

```text
Systematic factual errors
Unsafe outputs
Data exposure
Prompt injection exploitation
Broken citations
Model-provider regression
Runaway costs
Retrieval corruption
```

Response may include:

```text
Disable feature
Switch model
Rollback prompt
Disable corpus
Block tool
Invalidate cache
Preserve evidence
Investigate
```

---

# 147. Production Readiness

Before an AI capability reaches production it should demonstrate:

```text
✓ Defined educational purpose
✓ Risk classification
✓ Approved data sources
✓ Source licensing understood
✓ Prompt versioned
✓ Model version governed
✓ Authorization enforced
✓ Prompt injection tested
✓ Retrieval evaluated
✓ Grounding evaluated
✓ Factuality evaluated
✓ Citation correctness evaluated
✓ Multilingual evaluation where relevant
✓ Medical expert review where required
✓ Latency budget
✓ Token/cost budget
✓ Rate limits
✓ Fallback behavior
✓ Observability
✓ Auditability
✓ Privacy review
✓ Incident runbook
✓ Feature flag / kill switch
```

---

# 148. AI Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "Add ChatGPT" treated as an architecture
❌ One unrestricted AI endpoint for everything
❌ LLM used as authorization engine
❌ LLM allowed to execute arbitrary SQL
❌ LLM allowed to execute arbitrary JavaScript
❌ Provider SDK spread across every microservice
❌ Provider abstraction pretending all models are identical
❌ Model versions changing silently
❌ Prompts scattered as string literals
❌ Prompt changes deployed without evaluation
❌ Secrets embedded in system prompts
❌ Free-form text parsed with regex when schemas are available
❌ Tool calls executed without authorization
❌ RAG treated as hallucination elimination
❌ Entire textbook flattened into arbitrary chunks
❌ No source provenance
❌ Copyrighted content ingested without licensing review
❌ Vector search assumed superior to lexical search
❌ topK increased until answers "look better"
❌ Entire corpus dumped into model context
❌ Citations generated without verifying support
❌ Citation count treated as correctness
❌ Model pretrained knowledge treated as canonical curriculum
❌ Model forced to answer when evidence is missing
❌ Entire conversation resent forever
❌ Model-generated memory treated as authoritative learner state
❌ Retrieved documents trusted as instructions
❌ User-uploaded content inserted into trusted corpus automatically
❌ System prompts assumed secret
❌ One safety prompt treated as security
❌ Medical terminology blocked by naive moderation
❌ Machine translation trusted as canonical medical terminology
❌ Marathi queries evaluated only in English
❌ Screenshots used when structured 3D scene state exists
❌ AI emits arbitrary Three.js code
❌ AI assumes a 3D tool call succeeded
❌ Speech recognition deployed without medical vocabulary testing
❌ AI-generated questions directly inserted into high-stakes exams
❌ Incorrect MCQ distractors generated as obvious nonsense
❌ LLM owns learner mastery state
❌ Deep ML knowledge tracing introduced before basic measurement
❌ Recommendation engine optimizes screen time instead of learning
❌ LLM-as-judge treated as objective ground truth
❌ No medical expert evaluation
❌ Fluent answers mistaken for factual answers
❌ Prompt/model upgrades without regression gates
❌ Streaming unsafe content before applicable validation
❌ Unlimited token budgets
❌ Every query sent to the most expensive model
❌ Semantic cache leaking personalized responses
❌ No AI-specific rate limiting
❌ No cost attribution
❌ Provider outage breaks the whole platform
❌ Raw prompts/responses logged indefinitely
❌ User feedback automatically treated as training truth
❌ Experiments optimize engagement while ignoring correctness
❌ No feature kill switch
❌ No AI incident response process
```

# 150. Decision Outcome

| Area                      | Decision                                                         |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| AI role                   | Educational assistance                                           |
| Clinical decision support | Outside default Mediverse AI boundary                            |
| AI integration            | Central governed AI platform/gateway                             |
| Provider coupling         | Abstracted                                                       |
| Managed models            | Initial preference where requirements permit                     |
| Self-hosting              | Requirement-driven                                               |
| Model routing             | Capability/risk/cost aware                                       |
| Model upgrades            | Evaluated + controlled                                           |
| Prompts                   | Versioned production artifacts                                   |
| Structured output         | Preferred for machine consumption                                |
| Tool calling              | Allowlisted + authorized                                         |
| Arbitrary tool execution  | **Rejected**                                                     |
| RAG                       | Primary grounding mechanism where authoritative evidence matters |
| Knowledge sources         | Governed + licensed                                              |
| Provenance                | Mandatory                                                        |
| Chunking                  | Semantic/structure-aware                                         |
| Embeddings                | Version governed                                                 |
| Initial vector store      | **PostgreSQL + pgvector evaluation/preference**                  |
| Dedicated search          | Scale/search-requirement driven                                  |
| Retrieval                 | Hybrid evaluation                                                |
| Reranking                 | Evaluation-driven                                                |
| Citations                 | Claim-support oriented                                           |
| Unsupported answers       | Uncertainty permitted                                            |
| Conversation memory       | Scoped and controlled                                            |
| Learner state             | Deterministic application data                                   |
| Prompt injection          | Untrusted-input model                                            |
| Retrieved documents       | Data, not instructions                                           |
| AI authorization          | Never authoritative                                              |
| Medical safety            | Risk-based                                                       |
| Multilingual              | First-class architecture                                         |
| Marathi                   | Medical terminology-aware                                        |
| Multimodal                | Supported where educationally useful                             |
| 3D tutor                  | Structured scene-aware                                           |
| AI→3D commands            | Schema-controlled tools                                          |
| Speech                    | STT/TTS evaluation                                               |
| Quiz generation           | Draft + validation                                               |
| High-stakes assessments   | Controlled/approved question bank                                |
| Adaptive learning         | Learner-model driven                                             |
| Knowledge tracing         | Start interpretable/simple                                       |
| Spaced repetition         | Deterministic core                                               |
| Recommendations           | Learning-outcome optimized                                       |
| Human oversight           | Risk-based                                                       |
| AI provenance             | Required for reusable/high-value artifacts                       |
| Evaluation datasets       | Versioned                                                        |
| Retrieval evaluation      | Independent                                                      |
| Factuality                | Explicit metric                                                  |
| Groundedness              | Explicit metric                                                  |
| Citation correctness      | Explicit metric                                                  |
| LLM-as-judge              | Supporting tool only                                             |
| Expert medical review     | Required where risk warrants                                     |
| Prompt regression         | Required                                                         |
| Model upgrade gates       | Required                                                         |
| Red teaming               | Required                                                         |
| Streaming                 | UX/risk driven                                                   |
| Token budgets             | Per capability                                                   |
| Semantic caching          | Low-risk + authorization-safe only                               |
| Rate limiting             | AI-specific                                                      |
| Cost attribution          | Required                                                         |

# ADR-069 — COMPLETE ✅

The complete AI lifecycle is now:

```text
AUTHORITATIVE KNOWLEDGE
          │
          ▼
      INGESTION
          │
          ▼
      RETRIEVAL
          │
          ▼
       EVIDENCE
          │
          ▼
   CONTEXT + POLICY
          │
          ▼
     MODEL ROUTING
          │
          ▼
      GENERATION
          │
          ▼
      VALIDATION
          │
          ▼
      GROUNDING
          │
          ▼
      CITATIONS
          │
          ▼
       LEARNER
          │
          ▼
       FEEDBACK
          │
          ▼
      EVALUATION
          │
          ▼
       IMPROVE
```

And its trust architecture is:

```text
                     LLM
                      │
                      ▼
              REASON / PROPOSE
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        ▼             ▼             ▼
     Explain       Retrieve       Suggest
        │             │             │
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      ▼
                VALIDATED OUTPUT


              AUTHORITATIVE SYSTEMS
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        ▼             ▼             ▼
      Identity       Data        Curriculum
        │             │             │
        ├──────── Authorization ─────┤
        │             │             │
        ├──────── Persistence ───────┤
        │             │             │
        └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                      ▼
                   ENFORCE
```

The defining invariant is:

> **Mediverse AI may generate explanations, recommendations, questions and actions, but authoritative knowledge, identity, authorization, learner state, curriculum constraints and data integrity remain outside the model. Every high-value AI output must be attributable to a model, prompt, evidence set and validation path, and the system must be capable of refusing to manufacture certainty when authoritative evidence is insufficient.**

## Next — ADR-070

### **ADR-070 — Enterprise Testing, Quality Engineering, Verification & Release Confidence Standard**

ADR-070 should now unify the testing fragments scattered across the previous ADRs into one enforceable quality architecture: **quality ownership → test strategy → risk-based testing → test pyramid vs testing trophy → unit/component/integration/contract/E2E boundaries → Java/Spring Boot testing → JUnit 5 → AssertJ → Mockito → Testcontainers → PostgreSQL/Kafka/Redis integration → frontend Vitest/RTL/MSW → Playwright → API contract testing → OpenAPI compatibility → Kafka schema compatibility → database migration testing → infrastructure/Terraform testing → Kubernetes/Helm validation → policy-as-code testing → security testing → SAST/SCA/DAST → container/IaC scanning → authentication/authorization tests → performance/load/stress/soak testing → resilience/chaos testing → backup/restore verification → disaster-recovery exercises → observability testing → accessibility testing → visual regression → 3D/WebGL testing → AI/RAG evaluation integration → test data management → synthetic data → environment strategy → ephemeral environments → test isolation → flaky-test governance → coverage policy → mutation testing → quality gates → release evidence → progressive delivery verification → production smoke tests → canary analysis → rollback verification → defect escape metrics → DORA/quality metrics → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise quality engineering reference architecture.**


# ADR-070 — Enterprise Testing, Quality Engineering, Verification & Release Confidence Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-070
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-069 established the AI/LLM, RAG, intelligent tutoring, evaluation and medical-AI governance architecture.

ADR-070 establishes how Mediverse proves that changes are safe to release through **automated testing, integration verification, contract testing, infrastructure validation, security testing, performance engineering, resilience testing, accessibility verification, AI evaluation and production validation**.

> **Passing tests is not the objective. The objective is obtaining sufficient evidence that a change is safe to release.**

```text
                         CODE CHANGE
                              │
                              ▼
                     STATIC VERIFICATION
                              │
                              ▼
                         UNIT TESTS
                              │
                              ▼
                   COMPONENT / INTEGRATION
                              │
                              ▼
                     CONTRACT VERIFICATION
                              │
                              ▼
                      SYSTEM / E2E TESTS
                              │
                              ▼
                  SECURITY / PERFORMANCE
                              │
                              ▼
                 INFRASTRUCTURE VALIDATION
                              │
                              ▼
                      RELEASE EVIDENCE
                              │
                              ▼
                    PROGRESSIVE DELIVERY
                              │
                              ▼
                   PRODUCTION VALIDATION
                              │
                        ┌─────┴─────┐
                        ▼           ▼
                      HEALTHY     FAILURE
                        │           │
                        ▼           ▼
                     PROMOTE      ROLLBACK
```

# 1. Quality Engineering Objective

Mediverse quality engineering should optimize for:

```text
Correctness
Release confidence
Fast feedback
Security
Reliability
Accessibility
Performance
Reproducibility
Observability
Low defect escape rate
```

Testing volume alone is not a quality metric.

# 2. Quality Ownership

Quality belongs to the engineering team.

```text
Developer
   +
QA / QE
   +
Security
   +
SRE
   +
Product
   +
Domain Expert
```

A separate QA team cannot compensate for poor engineering discipline upstream.

# 3. Shift Left and Right

Quality verification should occur both:

```text
                 SOFTWARE LIFECYCLE

Requirements
     │
Development
     │
CI
     │
Staging
     │
Production
     │
Operations

◄──── SHIFT LEFT

                         SHIFT RIGHT ────►
```

Production telemetry complements pre-production testing.

It does not replace it.

# 4. Risk-Based Testing

Testing depth should follow risk.

```text
Low Risk Change
     │
     ▼
Focused Verification

Critical Change
     │
     ▼
Broader Verification
     │
     ├── Integration
     ├── Security
     ├── Performance
     ├── Resilience
     └── Production safeguards
```

# 5. Critical Areas

Higher verification should apply to:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Assessment grading
Payments if introduced
Database migrations
Medical educational content
AI-generated medical information
Data privacy
Infrastructure changes
Backup/recovery
```

# 6. Test Portfolio

Mediverse should use multiple test layers.

```text
               ┌───────────────┐
               │     E2E       │
               ├───────────────┤
               │   Contract    │
               ├───────────────┤
               │ Integration   │
               ├───────────────┤
               │ Component     │
               ├───────────────┤
               │     Unit      │
               └───────────────┘
```

No single layer provides sufficient confidence.

# 7. Test Pyramid

The test pyramid remains useful as a cost heuristic:

```text
             /\
            /E2E\
           /----\
          / INT  \
         /--------\
        /   UNIT   \
       /____________\
```

But exact ratios should not become dogma.

# 8. Testing Trophy

Frontend-heavy systems may benefit from stronger integration/component coverage.

The actual principle is:

> Put the most tests where they provide the best confidence-to-cost ratio.

# 9. Unit Tests

Unit tests should validate isolated business logic.

Good candidates:

```text
Calculations
Validation rules
Domain policies
State transitions
Mapping
Scoring logic
Utility algorithms
```

# 10. Unit Test Characteristics

Good unit tests should generally be:

```text
Fast
Deterministic
Independent
Readable
Focused
```

# 11. Java Testing Baseline

Spring Boot services should standardize on:

```text
JUnit 5
AssertJ
Mockito
Spring Boot Test
Testcontainers
```

where appropriate.

# 12. JUnit 5

JUnit 5 should be the default Java testing framework.

Tests should describe behavior rather than implementation trivia.

```java
@Test
void shouldRejectEnrollmentWhenCourseIsClosed() {
    // arrange
    // act
    // assert
}
```

# 13. AssertJ

AssertJ should be preferred for expressive assertions where it improves readability.

Assertions should communicate intent clearly.

# 14. Mockito

Mockito should isolate dependencies when true unit isolation provides value.

Do not mock every object simply because mocking is possible.

# 15. Over-Mocking

This is weak:

```text
Controller mock
   ↓
Service mock
   ↓
Repository mock
   ↓
Mapper mock
   ↓
Everything passes
```

while the real application fails when components interact.

# 16. Behavior vs Implementation

Tests should avoid asserting internal method calls unless those interactions represent meaningful behavior.

Refactoring implementation should not unnecessarily destroy the test suite.

# 17. Spring Slice Tests

Use focused Spring tests where appropriate.

Examples:

```text
@WebMvcTest
@DataJpaTest
@JsonTest
```

These provide more realistic framework behavior without always starting the complete application.

# 18. Full Spring Integration Tests

Use:

```text
@SpringBootTest
```

where complete Spring wiring is genuinely part of what must be verified.

Do not make every test a full application boot.

# 19. Integration Tests

Integration tests verify real boundaries.

```text
Application
    │
    ├── PostgreSQL
    ├── Redis
    ├── Kafka
    ├── S3-compatible service
    └── External API stub
```

# 20. Testcontainers

Testcontainers should be preferred for important infrastructure integration tests.

```text
JUnit
  │
  ▼
Testcontainers
  │
  ├── PostgreSQL
  ├── Kafka
  └── Redis
```

This provides substantially stronger confidence than replacing infrastructure with mocks.

# 21. PostgreSQL Integration

Repository/database tests should use PostgreSQL when production behavior depends on PostgreSQL.

Using H2 to prove PostgreSQL-specific behavior is unreliable.

Differences can include:

```text
SQL dialect
JSONB
Sequences
Indexes
Constraints
Transactions
Locking
Extensions
```

# 22. H2 Boundary

H2 may remain useful for narrow lightweight tests.

It should not be considered a production-equivalent PostgreSQL substitute.

# 23. Database Constraints

Integration tests should verify important database-enforced invariants.

```text
Unique constraints
Foreign keys
NOT NULL
Check constraints
Optimistic locking
```

Application validation alone is insufficient.

# 24. Transaction Testing

Tests should cover relevant transactional behavior:

```text
Commit
Rollback
Concurrent modification
Partial failure
Isolation assumptions
```

especially for critical workflows.

# 25. Kafka Integration

Kafka-based services should verify actual producer/consumer behavior.

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Kafka Testcontainer
   │
   ▼
Consumer
```

# 26. Event Tests

Event testing should validate:

```text
Topic
Key
Headers
Schema
Payload
Consumer behavior
Retry behavior
Idempotency
```

# 27. Redis Integration

Redis tests should verify behaviors that depend on real Redis semantics.

Examples:

```text
TTL
Atomic operations
Locks where used
Cache invalidation
Serialization
```

# 28. External API Testing

Third-party APIs should not be called unpredictably from ordinary CI tests.

Use controlled stubs/mocks such as:

```text
WireMock
MockWebServer
MSW for browser tests
```

# 29. Contract Testing

Distributed services require explicit contract verification.

```text
Consumer
    │
    ▼
Contract
    │
    ▼
Provider
```

Unit tests on both sides do not prove compatibility.

# 30. OpenAPI Contract

REST APIs should verify implementation compatibility with approved OpenAPI contracts.

Changes should detect:

```text
Removed endpoint
Removed field
Changed type
Changed required field
Changed status semantics
```

# 31. Breaking API Changes

CI should identify backward-incompatible API changes before deployment.

```text
OpenAPI v1
    │
    ▼
Diff
    │
    ▼
OpenAPI v2
    │
 ┌──┴───┐
 ▼      ▼
Safe   Breaking
```

# 32. Consumer-Driven Contracts

Consumer-driven contract testing may be used where service coupling and release independence justify it.

It should solve real compatibility problems, not become ceremony.

# 33. Kafka Schema Compatibility

Event schemas require compatibility verification.

Depending on serialization:

```text
Avro
JSON Schema
Protobuf
```

schema evolution rules must be tested.

# 34. Event Evolution

Consumers should tolerate approved compatible evolution.

Avoid assuming every producer and consumer deploy simultaneously.

# 35. Database Migration Testing

Every schema migration should be tested against realistic previous schema state.

```text
Production-like Schema N
          │
          ▼
Migration N+1
          │
          ▼
Application N+1
```

# 36. Flyway Verification

Flyway migrations should execute automatically in CI integration environments.

Test:

```text
Clean initialization
Upgrade from previous version
Constraint changes
Data migration
Application compatibility
```

# 37. Migration Rollback Reality

Not every database migration is safely reversible.

The release architecture should distinguish:

```text
Application rollback
        vs
Database rollback
```

They are not the same problem.

# 38. Expand-and-Contract Testing

Zero/low-downtime migrations should test compatibility across deployment versions.

```text
Expand schema
     │
Old + New App
     │
Migrate
     │
Remove old usage
     │
Contract schema
```

# 39. Frontend Testing

ADR-068 frontend tests should integrate into the central quality strategy.

```text
Vitest
React Testing Library
MSW
Playwright
Accessibility tests
Visual regression
```

# 40. Component Tests

Components should be tested through visible user behavior.

```text
Render
  │
  ▼
Interact
  │
  ▼
Observe accessible output
```

# 41. Frontend API Mocking

MSW should simulate API boundaries rather than mocking every internal hook.

This allows more realistic:

```text
Loading
Success
Validation errors
401
403
404
429
500
Network failure
```

testing.

# 42. Browser E2E

Playwright should verify critical complete user journeys.

Examples:

```text
Login
Course enrollment
Lesson navigation
Assessment
Progress update
File upload
3D module launch
Logout
```

# 43. E2E Scope

E2E tests should focus on high-value workflows.

Do not reproduce every unit test through a browser.

E2E suites are slower and more fragile.

# 44. Authentication E2E

Authentication tests should cover:

```text
Valid login
Invalid credentials
Expired session
Logout
Protected route
Session renewal
```

# 45. Authorization Testing

Authorization requires explicit negative testing.

```text
Student → student resource ✓
Student → admin resource ✗
User A → User B private resource ✗
```

Testing only successful access is insufficient.

# 46. IDOR/BOLA Testing

APIs must test attempts to access another user's resource by manipulating identifiers.

Frontend hiding does not count as protection.

# 47. Role Matrix

Critical permissions should have a testable matrix.

```text
              Student  Educator  Admin
View course      ✓        ✓       ✓
Edit course      ✗        ✓       ✓
Manage users     ✗        ✗       ✓
```

# 48. Security Testing Layers

Security testing should include:

```text
SAST
SCA
Secret scanning
Container scanning
IaC scanning
DAST
Authorization tests
Dependency governance
Manual penetration testing where warranted
```

# 49. SAST

Static application security testing should run during CI.

Findings must be severity-triaged rather than blindly ignored.

# 50. Software Composition Analysis

Dependencies should be scanned for known vulnerabilities.

```text
pom.xml
package-lock.json
Container packages
```

all form part of the software supply chain.

# 51. Secret Scanning

Repositories and CI should detect accidental credentials such as:

```text
API keys
Private keys
Passwords
Cloud credentials
Tokens
```

Secrets should not enter Git history.

# 52. Container Scanning

Built container images should be scanned before promotion.

The artifact actually deployed matters more than only scanning source dependencies.

# 53. IaC Security

Terraform and Kubernetes configuration should undergo security/policy checks.

Examples:

```text
Public storage
Overly permissive IAM
Privileged containers
Missing resource limits
Unsafe network exposure
```

# 54. DAST

Dynamic security testing should target running environments where it provides value.

It complements rather than replaces secure development and static analysis.

# 55. Penetration Testing

Independent penetration testing should be performed based on:

```text
Risk
Release significance
Compliance
External exposure
Architecture changes
```

Automated scanners are not substitutes for skilled adversarial testing.

# 56. Performance Testing

Performance testing should establish whether the system satisfies defined SLOs under expected load.

```text
Load
 │
 ▼
System
 │
 ▼
Latency / Throughput / Errors / Saturation
```

# 57. Performance Baseline

Before optimization, establish baseline measurements.

Without baselines, claims such as "this release is faster" are speculation.

# 58. Load Testing

Load tests should model realistic expected usage.

Examples:

```text
Concurrent learners
Course browsing
Assessment submissions
Video metadata requests
AI tutoring requests
```

# 59. Stress Testing

Stress testing deliberately exceeds expected capacity.

Goal:

```text
Where does it break?
How does it break?
Can it recover?
```

# 60. Soak Testing

Soak tests run sustained load over longer periods to expose:

```text
Memory leaks
Connection leaks
Resource exhaustion
Queue buildup
Cache growth
Performance degradation
```
