## ADR-070 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The quality architecture now follows:

```text
                         CHANGE
                            │
                            ▼
                      STATIC CHECKS
                            │
                            ▼
                         UNIT
                            │
                            ▼
                       COMPONENT
                            │
                            ▼
                      INTEGRATION
                            │
            ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
            ▼               ▼               ▼
        PostgreSQL         Kafka           Redis
            │               │               │
            └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                            ▼
                        CONTRACTS
                            │
                  ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                  ▼                   ▼
               OpenAPI             Events
                  │                   │
                  └─────────┬─────────┘
                            ▼
                           E2E
                            │
                            ▼
              SECURITY / PERFORMANCE
                            │
                            ▼
                     RELEASE EVIDENCE
```

The defining principle so far is:

> **Mocks prove assumptions. Integration tests prove integrations. Contract tests prove compatibility. E2E tests prove selected user journeys. None of them alone proves system quality.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Performance Test Architecture**, then cover **k6/Gatling → workload modeling → latency percentiles → throughput → saturation → performance regression gates → AI load testing → WebSocket/SSE testing → 3D/WebGL performance → resilience testing → fault injection → chaos engineering → dependency failure → Kafka failure → Redis failure → PostgreSQL failover → timeout/retry/circuit-breaker verification → Kubernetes disruption → backup verification → restore tests → disaster-recovery exercises → RPO/RTO validation → observability testing → alert testing → synthetic monitoring → accessibility → visual regression → browser/device matrix → 3D educational verification → AI/RAG evaluation gates → test data → synthetic data → privacy → environment strategy → ephemeral environments → deterministic tests → flaky-test governance → quarantine policy → coverage → mutation testing → CI parallelization → quality gates → release evidence → canary verification → production smoke tests → rollback testing → defect metrics → DORA + quality metrics → anti-patterns → final enterprise quality engineering reference architecture.**


# ADR-070 — Enterprise Testing, Quality Engineering, Verification & Release Confidence Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Soak Testing**.

---

# 61. Performance Test Architecture

Performance testing should model the complete request path.

```text
Virtual Users
     │
     ▼
Ingress / CDN
     │
     ▼
API Gateway
     │
     ▼
Application
     │
 ┌───┼───────────┐
 ▼   ▼           ▼
DB  Redis       Kafka
 │
 ▼
Dependencies
```

Testing a controller in isolation does not establish system capacity.

# 62. Load-Testing Tooling

Mediverse should standardize primarily on **k6** for API/platform load testing.

Gatling remains reasonable where JVM-native simulation or advanced workload modeling provides a concrete advantage.

Tool proliferation should be avoided.

# 63. Workload Modeling

Tests should reproduce realistic behavior rather than simply hammering one endpoint.

```text
1000 Learners
      │
      ├── 40% course browsing
      ├── 25% lesson activity
      ├── 15% assessments
      ├── 10% progress APIs
      └── 10% AI tutoring
```

Production telemetry should eventually inform these distributions.

# 64. Arrival Rate vs Concurrent Users

Performance tests should distinguish:

```text
Concurrent users
        ≠
Requests per second
```

A user may remain active while generating very few requests.

Workload models should therefore reflect actual traffic patterns.

# 65. Latency Percentiles

Average latency is insufficient.

Track at minimum useful percentiles such as:

```text
p50
p90
p95
p99
```

A healthy average can conceal a severe tail-latency problem.

# 66. Throughput

Capacity analysis should measure:

```text
Requests/sec
Transactions/sec
Events/sec
Messages/sec
Bytes/sec
```

according to subsystem.

# 67. Saturation

Performance tests must correlate latency with infrastructure saturation.

Observe:

```text
CPU
Memory
GC
Thread pools
DB connections
Kafka lag
Redis latency
Disk I/O
Network
```

# 68. Bottleneck Identification

When latency rises:

```text
Latency ↑
   │
   ├── CPU saturated?
   ├── DB pool exhausted?
   ├── locks?
   ├── dependency latency?
   ├── GC?
   ├── queue buildup?
   └── network?
```

Do not respond by blindly adding replicas.

# 69. Performance Regression Gates

Important services should maintain baseline performance results.

```text
Baseline
   │
   ▼
New Build
   │
   ▼
Comparison
   │
 ┌─┴────────┐
 ▼          ▼
Within     Regression
Budget       │
             ▼
           Review
```

# 70. Performance Gate Stability

Performance gates should run in sufficiently controlled environments.

Tiny latency differences from noisy shared infrastructure should not fail builds arbitrarily.

# 71. Database Performance Testing

Performance verification should include realistic:

```text
Dataset sizes
Indexes
Query patterns
Pagination
Concurrency
Connection pools
```

A query tested against 20 rows tells little about production behavior against millions.

# 72. N+1 Regression Testing

Critical ORM workflows should detect accidental N+1 behavior.

```text
GET /courses
     │
     ▼
1 course query
+
500 child queries
```

may pass functional tests while failing operationally.

# 73. Cache Performance

Caching tests should verify:

```text
Hit rate
Miss behavior
Stampede behavior
TTL
Invalidation
Dependency fallback
```

A cache is not automatically a performance improvement.

# 74. AI Performance Testing

AI workloads require separate modeling.

Measure:

```text
Time to first token
Tokens/sec
Total response time
Retrieval latency
Reranking latency
Tool latency
Provider throttling
Concurrent streams
```

# 75. AI Cost Under Load

AI load testing should estimate financial capacity as well as technical capacity.

```text
100 requests/sec
        │
        ▼
Token consumption
        │
        ▼
Model cost
        │
        ▼
Daily / Monthly projection
```

A technically scalable architecture can still be financially unsustainable.

# 76. SSE Testing

SSE testing should verify:

```text
Concurrent connections
Reconnect
Last-event behavior
Proxy timeout
Idle timeout
Authentication expiry
Resource consumption
```

# 77. WebSocket Testing

WebSocket workloads should test:

```text
Connection establishment
Concurrent connections
Message rate
Broadcast/fan-out
Disconnect
Reconnect
Backpressure
Node termination
```

# 78. Frontend Performance Testing

Browser performance tests should measure real rendering behavior.

```text
Network
  │
  ▼
JS Download
  │
  ▼
Parse / Execute
  │
  ▼
React Render
  │
  ▼
Interactive UI
```

Backend latency alone does not describe user experience.

# 79. 3D Performance Testing

Mediverse 3D modules require device-aware benchmarks.

Measure:

```text
Asset download
Decode time
Scene initialization
Frame rate
Frame time
Memory
GPU pressure
Interaction responsiveness
```

# 80. 3D Device Matrix

Test at least representative:

```text
Low/mid-range mobile
Modern mobile
Integrated-GPU laptop
Desktop
```

Optimizing only on developer workstations is unacceptable.

# 81. Frame-Time Budget

3D performance should reason primarily in frame time.

Approximately:

```text
60 FPS → ~16.7 ms/frame
30 FPS → ~33.3 ms/frame
```

Actual target depends on experience/device capability.

# 82. Graceful 3D Degradation

Tests should verify that constrained devices can reduce:

```text
Model detail
Texture quality
Effects
Animation complexity
```

or fall back to non-3D learning experiences.

# 83. Resilience Testing

Functional success under healthy conditions is insufficient.

Mediverse must verify behavior when dependencies fail.

```text
Application
    │
    ├── DB failure
    ├── Redis failure
    ├── Kafka failure
    ├── AI provider failure
    └── network latency
```

# 84. Fault Injection

Controlled fault injection may simulate:

```text
Latency
Connection failure
Timeout
HTTP errors
Pod termination
Resource pressure
Dependency unavailability
```

# 85. Chaos Engineering

Chaos engineering should be introduced only after basic resilience engineering exists.

Randomly killing infrastructure without hypotheses, observability and safeguards is not useful chaos engineering.

# 86. Chaos Hypothesis

A valid experiment starts with:

> "If dependency X fails, user capability Y should continue within boundary Z."

Then deliberately test it.

# 87. PostgreSQL Failure

Test application behavior during:

```text
Connection loss
Restart
Failover
Connection exhaustion
Slow queries
Deadlocks
```

where architecture supports those conditions.

# 88. Redis Failure

If Redis is unavailable, determine explicitly whether each capability should:

```text
Fail closed
Fail open
Use database fallback
Return degraded response
```

Do not discover this behavior during production incidents.

# 89. Kafka Failure

Test:

```text
Broker unavailable
Producer timeout
Consumer restart
Lag accumulation
Duplicate delivery
Retry
DLQ
Poison messages
```

# 90. Retry Verification

Retries must be tested against transient and permanent failures.

```text
Transient
   │
   ▼
Retry
   │
   ▼
Success

Permanent
   │
   ▼
Bounded retries
   │
   ▼
Fail
```

Infinite retry loops are failures.

# 91. Retry Storm Testing

During dependency outage:

```text
10,000 requests
      ×
3 retries
      =
30,000 dependency attempts
```

Retry policies can amplify incidents.

Load/resilience testing should expose this.

# 92. Timeout Testing

Every remote dependency should have defined timeout behavior.

Tests should verify:

```text
Connect timeout
Read timeout
Request timeout
End-to-end deadline
```

where relevant.

# 93. Circuit Breaker Verification

If circuit breakers are used, verify:

```text
Closed
   │
Failures
   ▼
Open
   │
Cooldown
   ▼
Half-open
   │
Recovery
   ▼
Closed
```

# 94. Kubernetes Disruption

Test application behavior during:

```text
Pod restart
Rolling deployment
Node drain
Replica loss
Autoscaling
Readiness failure
```

# 95. Pod Termination

Graceful shutdown tests should verify:

```text
SIGTERM
   │
   ▼
Stop accepting work
   │
   ▼
Finish/transfer work
   │
   ▼
Close resources
   │
   ▼
Exit
```

# 96. Backup Verification

A successful backup job does not prove recoverability.

```text
Backup created
      ≠
Backup restorable
```

Restore verification is mandatory.

# 97. Restore Testing

Regularly restore backups into isolated environments and verify:

```text
Database starts
Schema valid
Data readable
Application connects
Critical workflows operate
```

# 98. Backup Integrity

Tests should detect:

```text
Corruption
Missing objects
Incomplete backup
Wrong encryption keys
Permission failures
```

# 99. Disaster-Recovery Exercises

DR procedures should be exercised rather than merely documented.

```text
Primary unavailable
       │
       ▼
Declare disaster
       │
       ▼
Restore / fail over
       │
       ▼
Validate
       │
       ▼
Resume service
```

# 100. RPO Verification

Recovery Point Objective must be measured against actual recovery behavior.

If RPO is 15 minutes but restoration loses four hours of data, the architecture failed regardless of documentation.

# 101. RTO Verification

Recovery Time Objective should be measured from realistic disaster declaration to usable service restoration.

Automation that technically restores a database but requires six hours of manual debugging does not satisfy a one-hour RTO.

# 102. Observability Testing

Observability must itself be tested.

Verify that failures produce useful:

```text
Logs
Metrics
Traces
Events
Alerts
```

# 103. Trace Verification

Critical workflows should verify trace propagation across:

```text
Ingress
  │
  ▼
Service A
  │
  ▼
Kafka
  │
  ▼
Service B
  │
  ▼
Database
```

where tracing architecture supports it.

# 104. Alert Testing

Alerts should be deliberately triggered in controlled environments.

An alert rule that has never fired is an unverified assumption.

# 105. Alert Quality

Test for:

```text
Detection
Correct severity
Useful context
Routing
Deduplication
Recovery notification
```

# 106. Synthetic Monitoring

Production synthetic tests should periodically verify critical safe workflows.

Examples:

```text
Landing page
Authentication endpoint health
Course catalogue
Read-only API
```

Avoid synthetic tests that create uncontrolled production data.

# 107. Production Smoke Tests

Immediately after deployment, verify a small set of critical capabilities.

```text
Deployment
    │
    ▼
Smoke Tests
    │
 ┌──┴──┐
 ▼     ▼
Pass   Fail
 │      │
 ▼      ▼
Continue Rollback
```

# 108. Accessibility Testing

Accessibility quality requires:

```text
Static analysis
Component automation
Browser automation
Keyboard testing
Screen-reader testing
Human review
```

No single scanner proves WCAG compliance.

# 109. Automated Accessibility

Automated tools should detect common problems such as:

```text
Missing labels
Invalid ARIA
Contrast issues
Heading problems
Form accessibility
```

within their technical limitations.

# 110. Keyboard Verification

Critical workflows must be tested using keyboard-only interaction.

Especially:

```text
Navigation
Dialogs
Forms
Assessment
Media controls
3D controls/fallback
```

# 111. Screen-Reader Verification

Critical learning experiences should receive manual assistive-technology testing.

Automated DOM checks cannot prove understandable screen-reader behavior.

# 112. Visual Regression

Visual regression should protect stable high-value UI surfaces.

```text
Baseline Screenshot
        │
        ▼
New Screenshot
        │
        ▼
Diff
```

Differences require interpretation, not automatic panic.

# 113. Browser Matrix

Mediverse should define supported browser versions explicitly.

Testing should focus on supported browsers rather than attempting every browser ever released.

# 114. Device Matrix

Device testing should be risk-based.

Cover representative:

```text
Viewport sizes
Touch input
Pixel densities
Performance classes
Mobile browsers
Desktop browsers
```

# 115. 3D Educational Verification

3D testing must validate more than rendering.

Verify:

```text
Correct anatomical structure
Correct label
Correct animation
Correct interaction
Correct learning explanation
Correct fallback
```

A technically beautiful but anatomically incorrect model is a critical defect.

# 116. AI/RAG Quality Gates

ADR-069 evaluation should become part of release verification.

```text
AI Change
   │
   ▼
Golden Dataset
   │
   ├── Retrieval
   ├── Factuality
   ├── Grounding
   ├── Citation correctness
   ├── Safety
   └── Multilingual
   │
   ▼
Quality Gate
```

# 117. AI Regression

Model or prompt changes should be compared against the currently approved baseline.

A new model being newer or more expensive does not establish superiority.

# 118. AI Nondeterminism

AI tests must account for probabilistic output.

Avoid assertions such as:

```text
response ==
exact giant paragraph
```

Prefer evaluating:

```text
Required facts
Forbidden claims
Schema
Evidence
Safety
Semantic criteria
```

# 119. RAG Retrieval Tests

Retrieval should be testable without generation.

```text
Query
   │
   ▼
Retriever
   │
   ▼
Top-K
   │
   ▼
Expected evidence present?
```

This isolates retrieval failures from model failures.

# 120. Medical Expert Gate

High-risk reusable medical educational content should support subject-matter expert approval where ADR-069 requires it.

Automated tests cannot establish every medical nuance.

# 121. Test Data Management

Test data should be:

```text
Controlled
Repeatable
Representative
Non-sensitive
Versionable where useful
Easy to reset
```

# 122. Production Data

Copying raw production data into lower environments should not be the default testing strategy.

It introduces privacy and security risk.

# 123. Synthetic Data

Synthetic data should model realistic:

```text
Users
Courses
Assessments
Progress
Relationships
Edge cases
Scale
```

without reproducing sensitive user information.

# 124. Seed Data

Deterministic seed datasets should support integration and E2E environments.

Tests should know their starting state.

# 125. Test Isolation

Tests should not depend on execution order.

```text
Test A
   X
must not create state
required by Test B
```

Each test should own or reliably initialize required state.

# 126. Environment Strategy

Testing should span:

```text
Developer environment
      │
      ▼
CI isolated dependencies
      │
      ▼
Ephemeral integration environment
      │
      ▼
Shared staging where required
      │
      ▼
Production verification
```

# 127. Ephemeral Environments

Pull requests may receive short-lived environments when the cost is justified.

```text
Pull Request
     │
     ▼
Namespace / Environment
     │
     ▼
Deploy
     │
     ▼
Integration / E2E
     │
     ▼
Destroy
```

# 128. Shared Environment Problem

Shared QA environments commonly create:

```text
Data collisions
Unknown configuration
Test interference
Manual mutation
Flaky failures
```

Ephemeral environments reduce—but do not automatically eliminate—these problems.

# 129. Environment Parity

Lower environments should match production behavior where differences matter.

Not necessarily production scale.

Prioritize parity for:

```text
Database engine
Runtime
Container
Configuration model
Networking behavior
Security controls
Deployment mechanism
```

# 130. Flaky-Test Governance

A flaky test is a defect.

```text
Same code
Same test
Different result
```

destroys trust in CI.

# 131. Flaky-Test Tracking

Track:

```text
Test
Failure frequency
Owner
First observed
Root cause
Resolution
```

Do not normalize repeated reruns until green.

# 132. Quarantine Policy

Temporary quarantine may prevent one flaky test from blocking all engineering.

But quarantine requires:

```text
Owner
Ticket
Reason
Expiry
```

Otherwise quarantine becomes a graveyard.

# 133. Deterministic Testing

Control sources of nondeterminism:

```text
Time
Randomness
Network
Concurrency
External APIs
Shared state
Locale
Timezone
```

where possible.

# 134. Code Coverage

Coverage is a diagnostic metric—not proof of correctness.

```text
100% line coverage
        ≠
100% behavior correctness
```

# 135. Coverage Policy

Coverage thresholds may prevent catastrophic testing decline.

They should not incentivize meaningless assertions purely to increase percentages.

# 136. Mutation Testing

Mutation testing should be evaluated for high-value domain logic.

```text
Original:
score >= 50

Mutation:
score > 50
```

If tests still pass, the suite may not meaningfully protect that behavior.

# 137. CI Parallelization

Independent test stages should run concurrently where infrastructure allows.

```text
                 BUILD
                   │
       ┌───────────┼───────────┐
       ▼           ▼           ▼
     Unit       Security     Frontend
       │           │           │
       ▼           ▼           ▼
 Integration   IaC Scan      Browser
       └───────────┼───────────┘
                   ▼
                GATE
```

Fast feedback matters.

# 138. Test Selection

Large repositories may use change-aware test selection.

However, incorrect dependency analysis can skip necessary tests.

Critical release pipelines should retain broader verification stages.

# 139. Quality Gates

A production candidate should satisfy defined gates such as:

```text
✓ Compilation
✓ Static analysis
✓ Unit tests
✓ Integration tests
✓ Contract compatibility
✓ Security policy
✓ Migration validation
✓ Required E2E
✓ Performance thresholds where applicable
✓ Accessibility requirements
✓ AI evaluation where applicable
✓ Artifact integrity
```

# 140. Release Evidence

Each release should produce machine-readable evidence.

```text
Release
  │
  ├── Commit SHA
  ├── Artifact digest
  ├── Test results
  ├── Security results
  ├── Contract results
  ├── Migration status
  └── Deployment verification
```

# 141. Progressive Delivery Verification

Release confidence continues after CI.

```text
Artifact
   │
   ▼
Small Cohort
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
 ┌─┴─────────┐
 ▼           ▼
Healthy    Regression
 │           │
 ▼           ▼
Expand     Rollback
```

# 142. Canary Analysis

Canary evaluation should compare meaningful signals.

Examples:

```text
Error rate
Latency
Saturation
Business failures
Authentication failures
AI failures
```

A pod merely being `Running` is not sufficient.

# 143. Rollback Testing

Rollback procedures must themselves be tested.

```text
Deploy N+1
    │
    ▼
Failure
    │
    ▼
Rollback N
    │
    ▼
Validate
```

Do not assume Helm rollback automatically solves database or event-contract incompatibility.

# 144. Defect Escape Metrics

Track defects discovered after release.

Classify by:

```text
Severity
Subsystem
Root cause
Detection gap
Test layer that should have caught it
```

The objective is improving the quality system, not assigning blame.

# 145. DORA + Quality Metrics

Delivery metrics should be interpreted together.

Useful measures include:

```text
Deployment frequency
Lead time for changes
Change failure rate
Failed deployment recovery time
```

alongside:

```text
Escaped defects
Flaky tests
Rollback frequency
SLO violations
Security findings
Performance regressions
```

Optimizing deployment frequency alone can produce fast delivery of bad software.

# 146. Quality Feedback Loop

```text
PRODUCTION INCIDENT
        │
        ▼
ROOT CAUSE
        │
        ▼
WHY WASN'T IT DETECTED?
        │
        ▼
ADD / IMPROVE CONTROL
        │
        ▼
TEST / MONITOR / POLICY
        │
        ▼
PREVENT RECURRENCE
```

Every significant escaped defect should improve the engineering system.

# 147. Release Confidence Model

Release confidence should be evidence-based.

```text
                RELEASE CONFIDENCE
                        │
       ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
       ▼                ▼                ▼
   CORRECTNESS       SECURITY        RELIABILITY
       │                │                │
       ├──────── PERFORMANCE ────────────┤
       │                │                │
       ├─────── ACCESSIBILITY ───────────┤
       │                │                │
       ├──────── COMPATIBILITY ──────────┤
       │                │                │
       └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                        ▼
                 RELEASE DECISION
```

# 148. Quality Engineering Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "QA owns quality"
❌ Testing only after development completes
❌ Test count treated as quality
❌ 100% coverage treated as correctness
❌ Everything mocked
❌ Every test boots the full Spring application
❌ H2 treated as PostgreSQL
❌ Unit tests used to claim integration works
❌ No database constraint tests
❌ No transaction/concurrency testing
❌ Kafka mocked everywhere
❌ REST services released without contract compatibility checks
❌ Breaking OpenAPI changes discovered by consumers in production
❌ Event schema changes deployed without compatibility validation
❌ Database migrations tested only on empty databases
❌ Assuming application rollback means database rollback
❌ E2E tests used for every behavior
❌ Authorization tests checking only allowed paths
❌ Frontend route guards treated as security tests
❌ Security scanning postponed until release
❌ Vulnerability scanners treated as penetration tests
❌ Load tests hitting one endpoint unrealistically
❌ Average latency used as primary performance metric
❌ Performance testing against tiny datasets
❌ Adding replicas before identifying bottlenecks
❌ AI performance measured only by total latency
❌ Ignoring AI cost under load
❌ WebSockets tested only with one connection
❌ 3D tested only on high-end developer machines
❌ FPS ignored while optimizing 3D
❌ Chaos engineering before basic resilience
❌ Random pod killing without hypotheses
❌ Infinite retries
❌ Retry amplification ignored
❌ No dependency timeout tests
❌ Backup success treated as recovery proof
❌ DR documentation never exercised
❌ RPO/RTO existing only in PowerPoint
❌ Observability assumed to work without tests
❌ Alerts never deliberately triggered
❌ Automated accessibility scanner treated as WCAG certification
❌ 3D visual correctness assumed to imply anatomical correctness
❌ AI tests asserting exact generated paragraphs
❌ RAG evaluated only end-to-end
❌ LLM output fluency treated as medical correctness
❌ Raw production user data copied into QA
❌ Tests dependent on execution order
❌ Shared QA environment manually mutated forever
❌ Flaky tests rerun until green
❌ Quarantined tests with no owner or expiry
❌ Coverage increased using meaningless assertions
❌ Sequential CI when independent stages can parallelize
❌ Every test executed on every keystroke regardless of cost
❌ Production release based only on CI green status
❌ Canary judged only by Kubernetes pod health
❌ Rollback process never tested
❌ Deployment frequency optimized while quality collapses
❌ Escaped defects fixed without improving prevention/detection
```

The governing invariant is:

> **A green pipeline is evidence, not proof. Release confidence comes from independent layers of verification covering correctness, contracts, security, performance, resilience, accessibility, infrastructure and production behavior. Tests that do not protect a meaningful failure mode are maintenance cost, not quality engineering.**

## Next — ADR-071

### **ADR-071 — Enterprise Developer Platform, Internal Developer Portal, Golden Paths & Engineering Productivity Standard**

This is the logical next architecture boundary because ADR-001 through ADR-070 have now created a large set of standards. Without a developer platform, engineers would have to understand and manually implement all of them for every service.

ADR-071 should define **platform engineering principles → developer experience → Internal Developer Platform → Backstage evaluation → software catalog → ownership model → service metadata → templates/scaffolding → golden paths → Spring Boot service template → React application template → Kafka consumer/producer template → AI service template → repository bootstrap → GitHub standards → CODEOWNERS → branch protection → CI reusable workflows → Jenkins/shared libraries where retained → build conventions → Maven parent/BOM → npm workspace conventions → Dockerfile standards → Kubernetes workload templates → Helm library charts → Argo CD application templates → Terraform modules → AWS account/environment provisioning → secrets integration → database provisioning → Kafka topic provisioning → DNS/certificate automation → observability-by-default → dashboards/alerts/traces → security-by-default → SAST/SCA/SBOM/signing → policy-as-code → developer self-service → environment creation → ephemeral environments → preview environments → developer local stack → Docker Compose/Testcontainers → dev containers evaluation → service documentation → TechDocs → API catalog → OpenAPI/AsyncAPI discoverability → dependency graph → scorecards → production-readiness checks → platform APIs → platform CLI → paved roads vs mandatory controls → exception process → platform SLOs → developer productivity measurement → DORA → SPACE framework → cognitive load → platform adoption → platform versioning → migration strategy → platform team operating model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse Internal Developer Platform reference architecture.**

# ADR-071 — Enterprise Developer Platform, Internal Developer Portal, Golden Paths & Engineering Productivity Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-071
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-070 established the enterprise quality engineering and release confidence architecture.

ADR-071 establishes the **Internal Developer Platform (IDP)** that enables engineers to build Mediverse services **consistently, securely, and quickly** without requiring every engineer to manually understand and implement every architectural standard from ADR-001 through ADR-070.

> **The platform exists to reduce cognitive load, standardize engineering practices, and accelerate delivery—not to centralize power or create bureaucracy.**

```text
                         ENGINEER
                             │
                             ▼
                  INTERNAL DEVELOPER PORTAL
                             │
      ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
      ▼                      ▼                      ▼
 Service Catalog        Templates          Documentation
      │                      │                      │
      └──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┘
                             ▼
                    PLATFORM SELF-SERVICE
                             │
      ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
      ▼                      ▼                      ▼
 Infrastructure        CI/CD            Observability
      │                      │                      │
      └──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┘
                             ▼
                      DEPLOYED SERVICE
```

---

# 1. Developer Platform Objective

The platform should optimize for:

```text
Fast onboarding
Low cognitive load
Consistency
Self-service
Security by default
Observability by default
Quality by default
Developer productivity
Platform reliability
```

The objective is **making the correct path the easiest path**.

---

# 2. Platform Engineering Philosophy

Platform Engineering is **building products for developers**.

Its customers are:

```text
Backend Engineers
Frontend Engineers
DevOps Engineers
QA Engineers
Data Engineers
AI Engineers
SREs
```

---

# 3. Internal Developer Platform (IDP)

The IDP becomes the single entry point for engineering.

Capabilities include:

```text
Create service
Create environment
Browse APIs
View documentation
Deploy
Observe
Request infrastructure
Manage ownership
```

---

# 4. Golden Path

A Golden Path is:

> The recommended, well-supported way to build a service.

It should include:

```text
Architecture
Libraries
CI
Deployment
Monitoring
Security
Documentation
```

---

# 5. Paved Roads

Golden Paths should be:

```text
Simple
Opinionated
Documented
Supported
Automated
```

Engineers should rarely need to start from an empty repository.

---

# 6. Platform Boundaries

The platform owns:

```text
Templates
CI standards
Infrastructure modules
Deployment automation
Observability tooling
Security defaults
```

Application teams own:

```text
Business logic
Domain models
Features
Product behavior
```

---

# 7. Developer Experience (DX)

DX is an architectural concern.

Poor DX results in:

```text
Shadow tooling
Manual work
Architecture drift
Inconsistent implementations
Higher defect rates
```

---

# 8. Measure Developer Experience

Potential indicators:

```text
Time to first commit
Time to production
Service creation time
PR cycle time
Deployment success
Developer satisfaction
```

---

# 9. Backstage Evaluation

An Internal Developer Portal such as **Backstage** should be evaluated.

Potential capabilities:

```text
Software catalog
Templates
TechDocs
Ownership
API catalog
Scorecards
Plugins
```

Backstage is a platform—not the platform strategy itself.

---

# 10. Software Catalog

Every production system should exist in the catalog.

Metadata:

```text
Owner
Repository
Environment
Dependencies
Lifecycle
Criticality
Documentation
```

---

# 11. Ownership Model

Every service must have exactly one accountable owning team.

Avoid:

```text
Owner:
"Everyone"
```

---

# 12. Service Metadata

Every service should declare:

```yaml
service:
  name:
  owner:
  lifecycle:
  language:
  repository:
  api:
  documentation:
```

Metadata enables automation.

---

# 13. Service Templates

Developers should scaffold services instead of cloning old repositories.

Templates may include:

```text
Spring Boot Service
React App
Kafka Consumer
Kafka Producer
AI Service
Worker
Gateway
```

---

# 14. Spring Boot Template

Default template includes:

```text
Spring Boot
Health checks
Metrics
Tracing
Security
OpenAPI
Dockerfile
Helm
CI
Tests
```

---

# 15. React Template

Default React template includes:

```text
React
Vite
TypeScript
MUI
Testing
Accessibility
Routing
State management
```

---

# 16. AI Service Template

AI services should automatically include:

```text
Prompt registry
Evaluation hooks
Tracing
Rate limiting
Model abstraction
Policy enforcement
```

---

# 17. Repository Bootstrap

Repository creation should automatically generate:

```text
README
Architecture docs
CODEOWNERS
LICENSE
ADR folder
GitHub Actions/Jenkins config
Issue templates
Pull request template
```

---

# 18. CODEOWNERS

Critical paths require explicit ownership.

```text
/security/
  Security Team

/platform/
  Platform Team

/services/auth/
  Identity Team
```

---

# 19. Branch Protection

Protected branches require:

```text
Reviews
Passing CI
Signed commits if required
No force push
Status checks
```

---

# 20. Reusable CI

CI logic should be centralized.

Avoid copying identical YAML into hundreds of repositories.

---

## ADR-071 — Part 1 Complete (Sections 1–20)

The platform architecture now establishes:

```text
Developer
     │
     ▼
 Internal Developer Portal
     │
     ▼
 Golden Paths
     │
     ▼
 Templates
     │
     ▼
 Automated Standards
     │
     ▼
 Production Services
```

The governing principle is:

> **Developers should spend their time solving business problems, not repeatedly rebuilding infrastructure, CI pipelines, security controls, observability, or deployment logic that the platform can provide consistently.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 21 — Repository Standards & Build Conventions**, then cover **Maven parent/BOM → Gradle conventions → npm workspaces → Dockerfile standards → Kubernetes templates → Helm library charts → Argo CD templates → Terraform modules → AWS provisioning → secrets management → database/Kafka provisioning → observability-by-default → security-by-default → TechDocs → API catalog → dependency graph → scorecards → self-service environments → preview environments → local developer stack → Dev Containers → platform CLI → policy enforcement → exception process → platform SLOs → DORA/SPACE metrics → cognitive load → platform adoption → versioning → operating model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse Internal Developer Platform reference architecture.**


# ADR-071 — Enterprise Developer Platform, Internal Developer Portal, Golden Paths & Engineering Productivity Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 21–100

Continuing directly from **Section 20 — Reusable CI**.

---

# 21. Repository Standards & Build Conventions

Repositories should follow predictable conventions.

```text
repository/
│
├── src/
├── tests/
├── docs/
├── deploy/
├── scripts/
├── Dockerfile
├── README.md
├── CODEOWNERS
└── build configuration
```

Standardization reduces unnecessary cognitive load and enables platform automation.

---

# 22. Repository Types

The platform should recognize explicit repository archetypes.

```text
backend-service
frontend-application
worker
AI-service
infrastructure
shared-library
documentation
```

Each archetype may receive different golden-path capabilities.

---

# 23. Build Reproducibility

The same source revision should produce functionally equivalent artifacts regardless of developer workstation.

```text
Source
  +
Locked Dependencies
  +
Controlled Toolchain
       │
       ▼
Reproducible Build
```

"Works on my machine" is not an acceptable deployment model.

---

# 24. Java Build Standard

Mediverse should standardize the primary Java build path instead of casually supporting Maven and Gradle equally.

Given the existing Spring Boot ecosystem, **Maven should remain the default Mediverse backend build standard** unless a concrete project requirement justifies Gradle.

---

# 25. Maven Parent

A Mediverse parent POM should centralize common configuration.

```text
mediverse-parent
      │
      ├── Java version
      ├── compiler
      ├── testing plugins
      ├── code quality
      ├── dependency policy
      └── build defaults
```

Application repositories inherit rather than duplicate these settings.

---

# 26. Maven BOM

Dependency versions should be centrally governed where practical.

```text
Mediverse BOM
     │
     ├── Spring ecosystem
     ├── observability
     ├── testing
     ├── security
     └── internal libraries
```

Spring Boot's own dependency management should remain authoritative where appropriate rather than unnecessarily overriding every transitive version.

---

# 27. Maven Wrapper

Repositories should include:

```text
mvnw
mvnw.cmd
.mvn/
```

CI should use the wrapper rather than depending on whatever Maven happens to exist on an agent.

---

# 28. Gradle Convention

Gradle may be supported for justified workloads.

If used, conventions should live in shared convention plugins rather than copied `build.gradle` fragments.

Supporting two build systems has a real platform-maintenance cost.

---

# 29. Node Package Management

Frontend projects should standardize package-manager behavior.

The platform should avoid a mixture of:

```text
npm
yarn
pnpm
```

without justification.

Lockfiles are mandatory.

---

# 30. Frontend Build Reproducibility

CI should use deterministic installation.

Conceptually:

```text
package.json
     +
lockfile
     │
     ▼
Deterministic Install
     │
     ▼
Vite Build
```

Dependency updates should be intentional.

---

# 31. Monorepo vs Polyrepo

The IDP must support repository strategy without pretending one topology solves every organizational problem.

```text
MONOREPO
   │
   ├── easier atomic changes
   ├── shared tooling
   └── potentially larger CI complexity

POLYREPO
   │
   ├── ownership isolation
   ├── independent lifecycle
   └── duplicated coordination risk
```

Mediverse should choose topology by bounded context and team ownership rather than trend.

---

# 32. Dockerfile Standard

Production Dockerfiles should come from maintained patterns.

Typical Spring Boot flow:

```text
Source
   │
   ▼
Build Stage
   │
   ▼
Application Artifact
   │
   ▼
Minimal Runtime Image
```

---

# 33. Multi-Stage Builds

Build dependencies should not automatically enter runtime images.

```dockerfile
FROM build-image AS build
# compile

FROM runtime-image
# copy only required runtime artifact
```

This reduces attack surface and image size.

---

# 34. Container Runtime Standard

Production containers should normally:

```text
Run non-root
Use minimal base image
Expose only required ports
Use explicit resource expectations
Support graceful shutdown
Expose health endpoints
Avoid embedded secrets
```

---

# 35. Container Image Metadata

Images should carry traceable metadata.

```text
Commit SHA
Build ID
Version
Repository
Creation timestamp
```

The deployed image must be traceable back to source.

---

# 36. Immutable Image Promotion

Do not rebuild source separately for each environment.

Preferred:

```text
BUILD ONCE
    │
    ▼
IMAGE DIGEST
    │
    ├── Dev
    ├── UAT
    ├── Staging
    └── Production
```

Configuration changes; the artifact does not.

---

# 37. Kubernetes Workload Template

The platform should provide supported Kubernetes workload templates.

Defaults should include:

```text
Deployment
Service
Config
ServiceAccount
Probes
Resources
Security Context
Pod Disruption configuration where needed
Observability metadata
```

---

# 38. Resource Defaults

Every workload should declare resource requests.

Limits should follow measured workload behavior and cluster policy.

Missing resource configuration makes scheduling and capacity planning unreliable.

---

# 39. Health Probe Defaults

Golden paths should provide:

```text
startupProbe
readinessProbe
livenessProbe
```

where appropriate.

These probes represent different failure questions and should not be blindly configured identically.

---

# 40. Kubernetes Security Defaults

Templates should enforce or strongly default:

```text
runAsNonRoot
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
readOnlyRootFilesystem where compatible
capability reduction
seccomp
service-account isolation
```

---

# 41. Helm Standardization

Application teams should not repeatedly recreate identical Helm boilerplate.

Use:

```text
Mediverse Helm Library
        │
        ▼
Service Chart
        │
        ▼
Environment Values
```

---

# 42. Helm Library Charts

Reusable chart logic may cover:

```text
Deployment
Service
Ingress
Probes
Resources
Security context
Autoscaling
Observability
```

Application charts supply workload-specific configuration.

---

# 43. Helm Versioning

Library chart versions must be explicit.

A central chart update must not silently mutate hundreds of production deployments.

---

# 44. Argo CD Application Templates

GitOps onboarding should be generated automatically.

```text
Service
   │
   ▼
Environment Definition
   │
   ▼
Argo CD Application
   │
   ▼
Kubernetes
```

---

# 45. GitOps Ownership

Git should remain the desired-state authority for deployment configuration.

The portal may create or modify desired state through controlled workflows.

It should not become a hidden configuration database competing with Git.

---

# 46. Terraform Module Strategy

Infrastructure should use curated modules.

```text
Platform Module
      │
      ├── Networking
      ├── Database
      ├── IAM
      ├── Storage
      ├── Kubernetes
      └── Observability
```

---

# 47. Module Abstraction

Modules should hide irrelevant complexity without hiding important operational choices.

Bad abstraction:

```text
createEverything = true
```

Good abstraction exposes meaningful supported decisions.

---

# 48. Terraform Module Versioning

Modules require semantic/versioned release management.

```text
module v1
   │
   ▼
module v2
   │
   ▼
Explicit Upgrade
```

Automatic breaking upgrades are unacceptable.

---

# 49. Infrastructure Provisioning

Self-service infrastructure should follow:

```text
Developer Request
       │
       ▼
Platform API
       │
       ▼
Policy Validation
       │
       ▼
Git / Terraform
       │
       ▼
Cloud Infrastructure
```

---

# 50. AWS Provisioning

The platform may provide controlled workflows for:

```text
S3
RDS
ElastiCache
MSK where applicable
IAM roles
DNS
Certificates
Queues/topics
```

The developer should request capability, not manually construct unrestricted infrastructure.

---

# 51. Environment Model

Environment types should be explicit.

```text
Local
Development
Preview
UAT
Staging
Production
```

Not every service necessarily requires every environment.

---

# 52. Environment Provisioning

Environment creation should become declarative.

```yaml
environment:
  name: uat1
  service: course-service
  size: small
  database: postgres
  redis: true
```

The platform translates intent into approved infrastructure.

---

# 53. Preview Environments

Pull requests may receive temporary environments.

```text
PR #481
   │
   ▼
Preview Namespace
   │
   ├── application
   ├── configuration
   └── test dependencies
```

These should expire automatically.

---

# 54. Environment TTL

Temporary resources need TTL policies.

Otherwise self-service becomes:

```text
Create
Create
Create
Create
...
Never Delete
```

and cloud cost grows indefinitely.

---

# 55. Namespace Provisioning

Kubernetes namespace creation should automatically apply:

```text
ResourceQuota
LimitRange
RBAC
NetworkPolicy
Labels
Observability
Cost metadata
```

---

# 56. Database Self-Service

Applications may request databases through supported platform workflows.

```text
Service
   │
   ▼
Database Request
   │
   ▼
Policy
   │
   ▼
Provision PostgreSQL
   │
   ▼
Credentials via Secret System
```

---

# 57. Database Ownership

A database instance/schema must have explicit:

```text
Owner
Environment
Backup policy
Retention
Criticality
Data classification
```

---

# 58. Kafka Self-Service

Teams should be able to request approved Kafka resources.

Example declaration:

```yaml
topic:
  name: learning.progress.updated
  partitions: 6
  retention: 7d
  owner: learning-platform
```

---

# 59. Kafka Governance

Topic provisioning should validate:

```text
Naming
Ownership
Retention
Partitions
Schema strategy
ACLs
Environment
```

Unlimited developer-created topics without governance create operational debt.

---

# 60. DNS Automation

Service exposure should automate DNS where appropriate.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Ingress
    │
    ▼
DNS
```

Manual DNS tickets should not be the normal path.

---

# 61. Certificate Automation

TLS certificate provisioning and renewal should be automated.

```text
DNS / Ingress
      │
      ▼
Certificate Controller
      │
      ▼
TLS Certificate
```

Human calendar reminders for certificate renewal are an operational failure mode.

---

# 62. Secrets Integration

The platform should integrate applications with the enterprise secret-management architecture.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Workload Identity
    │
    ▼
Secret Manager
```

Developers should not manually distribute production credentials.

---

# 63. Secret Injection

Preferred mechanisms should minimize long-lived static credentials.

Possible patterns include:

```text
Workload identity
External Secrets integration
Short-lived credentials
Dynamic credentials
```

depending on infrastructure.

---

# 64. Observability by Default

Every golden-path backend should automatically receive:

```text
Structured logging
Metrics
Distributed tracing
Health endpoints
Correlation IDs
Standard dashboards
Baseline alerts
```

Observability should not be a post-production task.

---

# 65. Standard Telemetry

Platform conventions should standardize metadata such as:

```text
service.name
service.version
environment
team
trace_id
deployment
```

Without common dimensions, cross-service observability becomes chaotic.

---

# 66. Dashboard Provisioning

Creating a service should provision baseline dashboards.

```text
Service
   │
   ▼
Dashboard
   │
   ├── Request rate
   ├── Error rate
   ├── Latency
   ├── CPU
   ├── Memory
   └── Dependencies
```

---

# 67. Alert Defaults

Golden paths should provide baseline operational alerts.

Teams then add domain-specific alerts.

Avoid hundreds of noisy generic alerts that nobody owns.

---

# 68. SLO Integration

Production services should declare relevant service objectives.

```yaml
slo:
  availability: 99.9
  latencyP95Ms: 500
```

The platform can generate monitoring configuration from supported declarations.

---

# 69. Security by Default

A newly generated service should start secure.

Not:

```text
Generate insecure service
       │
       ▼
Security review six months later
```

---

# 70. Security Golden Path

Templates should automatically integrate:

```text
Authentication hooks
Authorization patterns
SAST
SCA
Secret scanning
Container scanning
SBOM
Image signing
IaC scanning
```

---

# 71. SBOM Generation

Every production artifact should support a Software Bill of Materials.

```text
Artifact
   │
   ▼
SBOM
   │
   ├── libraries
   ├── versions
   └── packages
```

This improves vulnerability response and supply-chain visibility.

---

# 72. Artifact Signing

Release artifacts/images should be signed where the supply-chain architecture requires it.

Deployment policy can verify provenance before execution.

---

# 73. Policy as Code

Platform requirements should be machine-enforceable where practical.

Examples:

```text
No privileged containers
Required ownership metadata
Approved registries
Required resource requests
No public database exposure
Signed production artifacts
```

---

# 74. Policy Enforcement Layers

Policies may execute at:

```text
IDE / local
      │
      ▼
Pull Request
      │
      ▼
CI
      │
      ▼
GitOps
      │
      ▼
Admission Control
```

Earlier feedback is generally cheaper.

---

# 75. Mandatory Controls vs Paved Roads

Not every platform recommendation should be mandatory.

Distinguish:

```text
MANDATORY
Security / compliance / critical reliability

RECOMMENDED
Golden-path conventions

OPTIONAL
Team-specific choices
```

Otherwise the platform becomes unnecessarily restrictive.

---

# 76. Exception Process

Teams need a controlled escape hatch.

```text
Exception Request
       │
       ▼
Reason
       │
       ▼
Risk Assessment
       │
       ▼
Approval / Rejection
       │
       ▼
Expiry
```

Permanent undocumented exceptions create architecture fragmentation.

---

# 77. Documentation as Code

Service documentation should live close to engineering workflows and support version control.

Documentation should evolve with the system.

---

# 78. TechDocs

If Backstage is adopted, TechDocs should be evaluated for:

```text
Architecture
Operations
Runbooks
Development
Troubleshooting
Ownership
```

The portal should make documentation discoverable.

---

# 79. Documentation Template

Every service should include:

```text
Purpose
Architecture
Local setup
API
Dependencies
Configuration
Deployment
Observability
Runbook
Ownership
```

---

# 80. API Catalog

REST APIs should be discoverable centrally.

```text
Software Catalog
      │
      ▼
API Catalog
      │
      ├── OpenAPI
      ├── owner
      ├── consumers
      └── lifecycle
```

---

# 81. Event Catalog

Kafka/event-driven interfaces require equivalent discoverability.

```text
Event
  │
  ├── Producer
  ├── Consumers
  ├── Schema
  ├── Owner
  └── Compatibility
```

AsyncAPI may be evaluated where it improves this workflow.

---

# 82. Dependency Graph

The platform should derive system relationships.

```text
Frontend
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ├── Course Service ──► PostgreSQL
   ├── Progress Service ─► Kafka
   └── Tutor Service ───► AI Platform
```

This is useful during incidents and change analysis.

---

# 83. Service Scorecards

Scorecards can expose platform adoption and production readiness.

Possible checks:

```text
✓ Owner defined
✓ Documentation exists
✓ SLO defined
✓ Security scans enabled
✓ Tests enabled
✓ Runbook exists
✓ Resource limits configured
✓ SBOM generated
```

---

# 84. Scorecard Warning

Scorecards should not become meaningless compliance gamification.

A service receiving "100/100" does not prove it is reliable.

Measure controls that matter.

---

# 85. Production Readiness Check

Before first production deployment, the platform should verify minimum readiness.

```text
Ownership
Security
Observability
SLO
Capacity
Backups where relevant
Runbook
Deployment strategy
Rollback
Dependencies
```

---

# 86. Developer Self-Service

High-frequency engineering requests should not require ticket queues.

Examples:

```text
Create service
Create preview environment
Provision database
Create Kafka topic
Request DNS
View logs
View metrics
Rotate development secret
```

---

# 87. Self-Service Guardrails

Self-service does not mean unrestricted access.

```text
Developer Intent
      │
      ▼
Platform Policy
      │
 ┌────┴────┐
 ▼         ▼
Allowed   Rejected
 │
 ▼
Automated Provisioning
```

---

# 88. Platform API

The IDP should expose stable platform capabilities through APIs.

The portal is a client of those APIs.

This prevents architecture from becoming:

```text
Backstage Plugin
      │
      ▼
Thousands of lines
of hidden infrastructure logic
```

---

# 89. Platform CLI

A CLI may complement the portal.

Example conceptual commands:

```text
mediverse service create
mediverse env create
mediverse service status
mediverse logs
mediverse doctor
```

CLI and portal should invoke the same underlying platform capabilities.

---

# 90. Local Developer Experience

A developer should be able to move from:

```text
git clone
```

to a functioning local environment with minimal undocumented manual work.

---

# 91. Local Stack

Local development may use:

```text
Application
PostgreSQL
Redis
Kafka where required
Mock external services
```

through Docker Compose and/or Testcontainers depending on use case.

---

# 92. Docker Compose Boundary

Docker Compose is useful for developer environments.

It should not become a second manually maintained production architecture.

Production truth remains Kubernetes/GitOps.

---

# 93. Testcontainers for Development

Testcontainers can support local integration workflows without requiring developers to permanently run every dependency.

This aligns developer and CI integration behavior.

---

# 94. Dev Containers Evaluation

Dev Containers may be evaluated where environment consistency materially improves onboarding.

They are especially useful when teams repeatedly struggle with:

```text
JDK versions
Node versions
CLI dependencies
Native tooling
```

But they add their own maintenance cost and should not be mandatory without benefit.

---

# 95. Developer Bootstrap

Target experience:

```text
Clone Repository
      │
      ▼
Run Bootstrap
      │
      ▼
Dependencies Ready
      │
      ▼
Application Running
      │
      ▼
Tests Passing
```

Onboarding documentation should not require 40 manual environment steps.

---

# 96. Platform SLOs

The platform itself is production infrastructure for engineers.

It therefore requires SLOs.

Potential indicators:

```text
Service creation success
Environment provisioning success
CI availability
Deployment success
Portal availability
Provisioning latency
```

---

# 97. Platform Reliability

If the IDP fails, existing production workloads should normally continue running.

```text
IDP outage
   │
   X
   └── must not terminate production applications
```

Control-plane availability and workload availability should be decoupled.

---

# 98. Platform Observability

Platform workflows should be traceable.

```text
Developer Request
       │
       ▼
Portal
       │
       ▼
Platform API
       │
       ▼
Git / CI / Terraform
       │
       ▼
Cloud / Kubernetes
```

Failures should identify the actual broken stage.

---

# 99. Platform Auditability

Sensitive actions should record:

```text
Actor
Action
Resource
Environment
Time
Result
Approval where required
```

Self-service must remain accountable.

---

# 100. Developer Productivity

Platform success should not be measured by:

```text
Number of templates
Number of plugins
Lines of platform code
Number of portal pages
```

It should be measured by whether engineering becomes safer and easier.

---

## ADR-071 — Part 2 Complete

**Sections 21–100 completed.**

The platform now has four major planes:

```text
                         ENGINEER
                            │
                            ▼
                  ┌───────────────────┐
                  │ DEVELOPER PORTAL  │
                  │      + CLI        │
                  └─────────┬─────────┘
                            │
             ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
             ▼              ▼              ▼
        CATALOG         GOLDEN PATHS    SELF-SERVICE
             │              │              │
             │              ▼              │
             │          TEMPLATES           │
             │              │              │
             └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                            ▼
                      PLATFORM APIs
                            │
       ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
       ▼                    ▼                    ▼
   SOFTWARE              DELIVERY          INFRASTRUCTURE
       │                    │                    │
       ├─ Maven/BOM         ├─ CI                ├─ Terraform
       ├─ React/Vite        ├─ Registry          ├─ AWS
       ├─ Docker            ├─ GitOps            ├─ Kubernetes
       └─ Templates         └─ Argo CD           └─ Data services
                            │
                            ▼
                    PLATFORM CONTROLS
                            │
       ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
       ▼                    ▼                    ▼
    SECURITY          OBSERVABILITY          QUALITY
       │                    │                    │
       ├─ SAST              ├─ Logs             ├─ Tests
       ├─ SCA               ├─ Metrics          ├─ Contracts
       ├─ SBOM              ├─ Traces           ├─ Scans
       ├─ Signing           ├─ SLOs             └─ Gates
       └─ Policy            └─ Alerts
                            │
                            ▼
                       PRODUCTION
```

The critical platform rule is:

> **The portal is not the platform. Backstage is not the platform. Kubernetes is not the platform. Terraform is not the platform. The platform is the integrated product that exposes safe, supported engineering capabilities through stable interfaces and golden paths.**

# ADR-071 — Enterprise Developer Platform, Internal Developer Portal, Golden Paths & Engineering Productivity Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 101–150

Continuing directly from **Section 100 — Developer Productivity**.

---

# 101. DORA & Engineering Productivity Measurement

Platform effectiveness should be evaluated using delivery outcomes rather than platform activity.

Core DORA-oriented measures include:

```text
Deployment Frequency
Lead Time for Changes
Change Failure Rate
Failed Deployment Recovery Time
```

The platform should improve these metrics without incentivizing teams to game them.

---

# 102. Metrics Must Be Interpreted Together

Optimizing one metric independently can create destructive incentives.

```text
Deployment Frequency ↑
        │
        X
does not automatically mean
        │
        ▼
Engineering Productivity ↑
```

If change failure rate simultaneously increases, delivery capability may actually be deteriorating.

---

# 103. SPACE Framework

Developer productivity should also consider the broader SPACE dimensions:

```text
S → Satisfaction & well-being
P → Performance
A → Activity
C → Communication & collaboration
E → Efficiency & flow
```

No single metric accurately represents developer productivity.

---

# 104. Activity Metrics

Metrics such as:

```text
Commits
Pull requests
Lines of code
Tickets closed
Hours online
```

must not be used as individual productivity scores.

They measure activity—not engineering value.

---

# 105. Cognitive Load

One of the IDP's primary responsibilities is reducing unnecessary cognitive load.

Without a platform:

```text
Developer
   │
   ├── Spring configuration
   ├── Maven configuration
   ├── Docker
   ├── Kubernetes
   ├── Helm
   ├── Terraform
   ├── IAM
   ├── Argo CD
   ├── Prometheus
   ├── OpenTelemetry
   ├── security scanners
   ├── CI
   └── cloud networking
```

With a good platform:

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
"I need a production-ready
Spring Boot service."
   │
   ▼
Golden Path
```

Abstraction should remove repetitive infrastructure decisions without hiding operationally important behavior.

---

# 106. Cognitive Load Categories

Platform design should distinguish:

```text
Intrinsic Load
    │
    └── complexity inherent to business/domain problem

Extraneous Load
    │
    └── unnecessary tooling/process complexity

Germane Load
    │
    └── knowledge useful for solving the problem
```

The platform should primarily attack **extraneous cognitive load**.

---

# 107. Developer Surveys

Quantitative telemetry cannot measure every developer experience problem.

Periodic surveys should evaluate:

```text
Onboarding difficulty
CI frustration
Environment reliability
Documentation quality
Platform discoverability
Deployment confidence
Tooling satisfaction
```

---

# 108. Platform Adoption

Track adoption by capability.

```text
Spring Golden Path       85%
Observability Defaults   92%
Platform CI              78%
Self-Service DB          61%
Preview Environments     43%
```

Low adoption should trigger investigation—not immediate enforcement.

---

# 109. Adoption Diagnosis

Low adoption may mean:

```text
Poor documentation
Missing capability
Bad UX
Migration cost
Performance problems
Platform unreliability
Golden path too restrictive
Teams unaware of capability
```

Do not automatically conclude that developers are "resisting standards."

---

# 110. Golden-Path Adoption

Golden-path usage should be observable.

The important question is:

> Are teams voluntarily choosing the paved road because it is genuinely easier?

Mandatory adoption can conceal a bad developer experience.

---

# 111. Platform Product Analytics

The IDP should understand usage such as:

```text
Service creations
Environment requests
Provisioning failures
Template usage
CLI usage
Portal usage
Documentation searches
Failed workflows
```

Telemetry should respect privacy and should not become developer surveillance.

---

# 112. Time to First Production

A useful platform metric is:

```text
Repository Created
       │
       ▼
First Working Commit
       │
       ▼
First Successful CI
       │
       ▼
First Non-Prod Deployment
       │
       ▼
First Production Deployment
```

Measure where time is actually being lost.

---

# 113. PR Cycle Time

PR cycle time may reveal friction across:

```text
CI duration
Review delay
Environment availability
Test instability
Security approval
Deployment process
```

The platform should target systemic bottlenecks.

---

# 114. CI Feedback Time

Developers should receive high-value feedback quickly.

Preferred progression:

```text
SECONDS
 └── formatting / linting

MINUTES
 └── unit / component / security

LATER
 └── integration / E2E / expensive verification
```

Do not force developers to wait 45 minutes to discover a formatting error.

---

# 115. Environment Provisioning Time

Self-service environments should have measurable provisioning objectives.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Provisioning
   │
   ▼
Ready
```

If "self-service" takes two hours, developer experience remains poor.

---

# 116. Developer Toil

Track repetitive work that can reasonably be automated.

Examples:

```text
Manual certificate requests
Manual namespace creation
Repeated pipeline setup
Manual dashboard setup
Secret rotation tickets
Manual DNS changes
Environment cleanup
```

High-frequency toil should feed the platform roadmap.

---

# 117. Platform Team Topology

The platform team should own the internal platform as a product.

```text
APPLICATION TEAMS
       │
       ▼
 PLATFORM TEAM
       │
       ├── Developer Platform
       ├── Golden Paths
       ├── Platform APIs
       ├── Self-Service
       └── Shared Capabilities
```

It should not become a ticket-processing infrastructure team.

---

# 118. Platform-as-Product

The platform requires:

```text
Users
User research
Roadmap
Prioritization
Documentation
Support
SLOs
Versioning
Feedback
```

Internal software still needs product management.

---

# 119. Platform Product Manager

At sufficient organizational scale, a platform product-management function should coordinate:

```text
Developer needs
Platform priorities
Adoption
Roadmap
Success metrics
Cross-team requirements
```

The role should not dictate architecture independently of engineering.

---

# 120. Platform Roadmap

Platform investment should prioritize high-frequency/high-friction engineering problems.

Conceptually:

```text
                     HIGH FREQUENCY

                          │
              Automate    │    PRIORITIZE
                          │
LOW FRICTION ─────────────┼──────────── HIGH FRICTION
                          │
                Ignore    │    Investigate
                          │
```

Do not build features merely because they make impressive portal demos.

---

# 121. Support Model

Platform support should have explicit channels.

```text
Documentation
     │
     ▼
Self-Service Diagnostics
     │
     ▼
Developer Community
     │
     ▼
Platform Support
     │
     ▼
Incident Escalation
```

---

# 122. Platform Doctor

The CLI should provide diagnostic capability where practical.

Conceptually:

```text
mediverse doctor
```

could validate:

```text
Git credentials
Cloud identity
Kubernetes connectivity
Required CLI versions
Repository metadata
Platform connectivity
Local container runtime
```

Diagnostics should identify actionable failures.

---

# 123. Documentation Ownership

Every platform capability requires an explicit documentation owner.

```text
Platform Feature
      │
      ├── Code Owner
      ├── Operational Owner
      └── Documentation Owner
```

Documentation without ownership becomes stale quickly.

---

# 124. Platform Versioning

Platform capabilities require controlled versioning.

Versioned surfaces include:

```text
Templates
Maven parent
BOM
Helm libraries
Terraform modules
CI workflows
Platform APIs
CLI
```

---

# 125. Backward Compatibility

Platform upgrades should minimize forced synchronized migrations.

```text
Platform v1
     │
     ├── Service A
     ├── Service B
     └── Service C

Platform v2 released

Services migrate
independently where possible.
```

---

# 126. Template Versioning

A generated repository must record which template/version created it.

Example:

```yaml
platform:
  template: spring-service
  version: 4.2.0
```

Otherwise the platform cannot reliably understand repository lineage.

---

# 127. Template Upgrade Problem

Scaffolding solves repository creation.

It does **not** solve future upgrades.

```text
Template v1
    │
    ▼
Generate Service
    │
    ▼
Service evolves independently
    │
    X
Template v2 cannot simply
overwrite repository
```

Upgrade strategy must therefore be designed separately.

---

# 128. Automated Template Evolution

Where possible, common behavior should live in versioned shared components rather than copied template code.

Examples:

```text
Maven parent
BOM
Shared CI workflows
Helm library
Terraform modules
Internal libraries
```

This reduces mass-copy migration requirements.

---

# 129. Dependency Automation

Dependency-update automation should propose controlled upgrades.

```text
Dependency Update
      │
      ▼
Automated PR
      │
      ▼
CI / Security / Tests
      │
      ▼
Review
```

Blind automatic production upgrades are inappropriate for critical dependencies.

---

# 130. Service Migration Campaigns

Major platform upgrades may require structured migration campaigns.

```text
Identify affected services
          │
          ▼
Provide migration tooling
          │
          ▼
Automated PRs
          │
          ▼
Team validation
          │
          ▼
Track completion
```

Manual wiki instructions for hundreds of repositories do not scale.

---

# 131. Deprecation Policy

Platform capabilities should have lifecycle states.

```text
Experimental
    │
    ▼
Supported
    │
    ▼
Deprecated
    │
    ▼
End of Support
    │
    ▼
Removed
```

Transitions require communication and migration paths.

---

# 132. Breaking Platform Changes

Breaking changes require:

```text
Impact analysis
Migration guide
Compatibility window
Automation where practical
Explicit deadline
Support
```

Platform teams should not unexpectedly break application teams through central updates.

---

# 133. Federated Platform Contribution

Application teams should be able to contribute improvements.

```text
Application Team
      │
      ▼
Platform Contribution
      │
      ▼
Review
      │
      ▼
Reusable Capability
```

This prevents the platform team from becoming the sole bottleneck.

---

# 134. InnerSource

Shared platform components may use an InnerSource model.

Required controls include:

```text
Contribution guidelines
Maintainers
CODEOWNERS
Review policy
Testing
Release process
```

"Everyone can edit everything" is not InnerSource governance.

---

# 135. Plugin Governance

Portal plugins introduce code, dependencies and privileges.

Every plugin should have:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Security review
Dependency policy
Permission scope
Maintenance plan
```

---

# 136. Backstage Plugin Security

If Backstage is adopted, plugins must not automatically receive broad infrastructure access.

```text
Backstage Plugin
       │
       ▼
Platform API
       │
       ▼
Authorization
       │
       ▼
Capability
```

Prefer this over:

```text
Plugin
   │
   ▼
Administrator Cloud Credentials
```

---

# 137. Platform API Lifecycle

Platform APIs should follow explicit lifecycle management.

```text
Design
  │
  ▼
Review
  │
  ▼
Version
  │
  ▼
Release
  │
  ▼
Observe
  │
  ▼
Deprecate
```

The internal nature of an API does not justify careless breaking changes.

---

# 138. Platform Security Threat Model

The IDP is security-sensitive because it may influence:

```text
Source repositories
CI/CD
Cloud infrastructure
Kubernetes
Secrets
DNS
Databases
Production deployments
```

Compromise can have organization-wide blast radius.

---

# 139. Platform Identity

Platform actions should use strong identity.

```text
Human
  │
  ▼
Enterprise Identity

Workload
  │
  ▼
Workload Identity
```

Long-lived shared administrative credentials should be eliminated where possible.

---

# 140. Privileged Operations

High-risk operations may require stronger controls.

Examples:

```text
Production database deletion
Production environment destruction
IAM privilege escalation
Secret-system administration
Critical DNS modification
```

Controls may include:

```text
Explicit authorization
Approval
Step-up authentication
Audit logging
Break-glass procedures
```

according to risk.

---

# 141. Platform Disaster Recovery

The platform requires recovery planning for critical state such as:

```text
Catalog metadata
Platform configuration
Git repositories
Artifact metadata
Terraform state
Secrets infrastructure
CI configuration
```

But the IDP should avoid becoming the only copy of authoritative desired state.

---

# 142. Platform Control-Plane Failure

Architecture should support:

```text
Portal unavailable
       │
       ▼
Existing production workloads
       │
       ▼
CONTINUE RUNNING
```

Where possible, GitOps reconciliation and existing runtime services should not depend continuously on portal availability.

---

# 143. FinOps Integration

Self-service infrastructure must expose cost implications.

```text
Developer Request
       │
       ▼
Estimated Cost
       │
       ▼
Policy / Budget
       │
       ▼
Provision
       │
       ▼
Actual Cost Attribution
```

"Self-service" without cost controls can become self-service cloud waste.

---

# 144. Cost Attribution

Platform-created resources should automatically receive attribution metadata.

Examples:

```text
team
service
environment
cost-center
owner
lifecycle
```

Cost allocation should not depend on manually reconstructing ownership months later.

---

# 145. Platform Capacity Planning

The platform must plan capacity for shared systems such as:

```text
CI runners
Artifact registry
Kubernetes
Observability
Kafka
Shared databases where applicable
Build caches
```

A successful developer platform can create its own scaling bottlenecks.

---

# 146. CI Runner Strategy

CI runners should be segmented by workload and trust level where necessary.

```text
CI Control Plane
      │
      ├── Standard Builds
      ├── Integration Tests
      ├── Privileged/Special Builds
      └── Production Deployment
```

Untrusted pull-request workloads should not automatically share privileged execution environments.

---

# 147. Build Caching

CI should use safe caching for:

```text
Maven dependencies
Node dependencies
Build outputs where deterministic
Container layers
```

Cache keys must prevent stale or incompatible artifacts from contaminating builds.

---

# 148. Architecture Conformance

The platform should automatically detect important architectural drift.

Examples:

```text
Missing ownership
Unsupported Java version
Deprecated parent POM
Old Helm library
Missing security scan
Missing SLO
Privileged container
Unsupported API version
```

Conformance should distinguish:

```text
Violation
Warning
Recommendation
```

rather than treating every deviation as equally severe.

---

# 149. Platform Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Calling Kubernetes the "developer platform"
❌ Calling Backstage alone the "developer platform"
❌ Portal-first architecture without stable platform APIs
❌ Building a portal before understanding developer problems
❌ Platform team acting as ticket queue
❌ Every service starting from an empty repository
❌ Copying old repositories as templates
❌ Supporting Maven and Gradle equally without need
❌ Uncontrolled dependency versions
❌ CI depending on random agent tool versions
❌ Dockerfiles handcrafted differently for every service
❌ Rebuilding artifacts separately per environment
❌ Kubernetes workloads without resource expectations
❌ Helm boilerplate copied across hundreds of repositories
❌ Central Helm updates silently modifying all services
❌ Terraform modules exposing hundreds of irrelevant inputs
❌ Breaking Terraform module updates automatically consumed
❌ Portal becoming a competing desired-state database
❌ Production infrastructure provisioned manually by default
❌ Self-service without guardrails
❌ Temporary environments without TTL
❌ Databases without owners
❌ Kafka topics without ownership/schema governance
❌ Manual certificate renewal
❌ Production secrets manually distributed
❌ Observability added after incidents
❌ Security added after service creation
❌ Policy enforced only at production admission
❌ Every recommendation made mandatory
❌ No exception mechanism
❌ Permanent architecture exceptions
❌ Documentation with no owner
❌ API/event interfaces undiscoverable
❌ Scorecards used as meaningless gamification
❌ Ticket-based provisioning for routine resources
❌ Portal plugins containing hidden infrastructure logic
❌ CLI and portal implementing different business rules
❌ Developer onboarding requiring dozens of undocumented steps
❌ IDP outage breaking running production workloads
❌ Platform telemetry used for developer surveillance
❌ Commit count treated as productivity
❌ Lines of code treated as productivity
❌ Low platform adoption blamed automatically on developers
❌ Optimizing DORA metrics individually
❌ Platform roadmap driven by impressive demos
❌ Template generation with no upgrade strategy
❌ Shared configuration copied instead of versioned
❌ Breaking platform changes without migration tooling
❌ Platform team as sole contribution bottleneck
❌ Backstage plugins with administrator cloud credentials
❌ Long-lived shared platform credentials
❌ Production destructive actions without stronger controls
❌ Self-service infrastructure without FinOps visibility
❌ Untrusted CI workloads sharing privileged runners
❌ Architecture conformance treating warnings and critical violations identically
```

                      │

The defining invariant is:

> **The Mediverse platform must remove accidental complexity without removing necessary engineering understanding. Golden paths should encode proven defaults, mandatory controls should enforce genuine organizational risks, self-service should eliminate routine ticket queues, and every abstraction must retain an escape path for legitimate requirements. Platform success is measured by safer, faster, lower-friction software delivery—not by how much platform technology has been built.**
