# Next — ADR-072

## **ADR-072 — Enterprise Architecture Governance, Standards Enforcement, Technical Debt & Evolution Standard**

With **71 ADRs**, Mediverse now has the opposite problem from where it started: architecture is no longer under-specified. It risks becoming **over-specified and impossible for engineers to navigate**.

ADR-072 should therefore establish the governance system that keeps all previous ADRs usable rather than turning them into a documentation graveyard.

It should cover **architecture governance philosophy → Architecture Decision Record lifecycle → ADR taxonomy → numbering/indexing → proposed/accepted/deprecated/superseded states → decision ownership → decision scope → mandatory vs recommended standards → Architecture Review Board boundaries → lightweight vs heavyweight review → automated conformance → fitness functions → policy-as-code → repository/service scorecards → exception requests → risk acceptance → exception expiry → waivers → architecture drift → drift detection → technical debt taxonomy → debt registry → intentional vs accidental debt → debt interest → prioritization → remediation budgets → dependency debt → infrastructure debt → security debt → data debt → observability debt → test debt → AI debt → architectural runway → evolutionary architecture → changeability → reversible vs irreversible decisions → experimentation → RFC process → proof-of-concepts → technology radar → emerging technology evaluation → build-vs-buy framework → vendor lock-in evaluation → deprecation → migration programs → strangler pattern → legacy modernization → service retirement → data migration → architecture documentation freshness → C4 synchronization → ADR dependency graph → governance metrics → decision lead time → exception rate → drift rate → debt trends → architecture effectiveness → governance anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise architecture governance operating model.**

# ADR-072 — Enterprise Architecture Governance, Standards Enforcement, Technical Debt & Evolution Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-072
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-071 established the Internal Developer Platform, golden paths, platform APIs, self-service engineering capabilities, and developer productivity model.

ADR-072 establishes the governance mechanism that keeps the growing Mediverse architecture **coherent without turning architecture into bureaucracy**.

> **Architecture governance exists to control consequential risk and preserve system evolvability—not to require architects to approve every engineering decision.**

```text
                    BUSINESS / ENGINEERING CHANGE
                               │
                               ▼
                        DECISION REQUIRED?
                               │
                    ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                    ▼                     ▼
                   NO                    YES
                    │                     │
             Golden Path            CLASSIFY DECISION
                    │                     │
                    │          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                    │          ▼          ▼          ▼
                    │      LOCAL      CROSS-CUTTING  STRATEGIC
                    │          │          │          │
                    │          ▼          ▼          ▼
                    │       TEAM ADR     RFC       EAB REVIEW
                    │          │          │          │
                    └──────────┴──────────┼──────────┘
                                         ▼
                                   IMPLEMENTATION
                                         │
                                         ▼
                              AUTOMATED CONFORMANCE
                                         │
                              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                              ▼                     ▼
                           COMPLIANT              DRIFT
                              │                     │
                              ▼                     ▼
                           OPERATE          EXCEPTION / FIX
                              │                     │
                              └──────────┬──────────┘
                                         ▼
                                      LEARN
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                EVOLVE ARCHITECTURE
```

# 1. Governance Objective

Architecture governance should optimize for:

```text
Consistency
Risk control
Decision clarity
Autonomy
Traceability
Changeability
Security
Maintainability
Evolvability
Low bureaucracy
```

Governance that slows every decision is defective governance.

# 2. Governance Philosophy

Mediverse adopts:

```text
Central principles
        +
Distributed decisions
        +
Automated enforcement
        +
Explicit exceptions
```

Centralized approval of every technical choice does not scale.

# 3. Governance vs Control

Governance answers:

```text
What constraints matter?
Why do they matter?
Who owns them?
How are they verified?
How can exceptions occur?
```

It should not dictate every implementation detail.

# 4. Decision Locality

Decisions should be made at the lowest responsible level.

```text
Local implementation decision
        │
        ▼
Application Team

Cross-service decision
        │
        ▼
Architecture Collaboration

Enterprise-impact decision
        │
        ▼
EAB
```

# 5. Architecture Decision Classification

Mediverse decisions should be classified approximately as:

```text
LEVEL 1 — Local
Implementation detail

LEVEL 2 — Service
Service architecture

LEVEL 3 — Cross-Cutting
Multiple teams/services

LEVEL 4 — Strategic
Enterprise/platform/security/data
```

Governance effort increases with blast radius.

# 6. ADR Purpose

An ADR records:

```text
Context
Decision
Alternatives
Consequences
Constraints
Ownership
Status
```

An ADR is a decision record—not a generic technical tutorial.

# 7. ADR Creation Threshold

Create an ADR when a decision is:

```text
Architecturally significant
Difficult to reverse
Cross-cutting
Security-sensitive
Operationally significant
Expensive
Likely to be questioned later
```

Do not create ADRs for trivial implementation choices.

# 8. ADR Taxonomy

With a large architecture corpus, ADRs should be categorized.

```text
Architecture
├── Foundation
├── Application
├── Data
├── Integration
├── Security
├── Cloud
├── Platform
├── Observability
├── AI
├── Quality
└── Governance
```

# 9. ADR Index

A machine-readable index should exist.

Example:

```yaml
- id: ADR-071
  title: Internal Developer Platform
  status: accepted
  owner: platform
  domain: platform
```

This enables discovery and automated tooling.

# 10. ADR Status Model

Use explicit lifecycle states.

```text
PROPOSED
   │
   ▼
ACCEPTED
   │
   ├──────────────► DEPRECATED
   │
   ▼
SUPERSEDED
```

`Rejected` may also be recorded when preserving the reasoning has value.

# 11. Proposed

`Proposed` means:

> The decision is under active consideration and is not yet an architectural standard.

Implementation should not treat proposals as mandatory policy.

# 12. Accepted

`Accepted` means the decision represents the current approved architecture within its declared scope.

# 13. Deprecated

Deprecated decisions remain visible for historical context but should not be selected for new implementations.

# 14. Superseded

A superseded ADR must identify its replacement.

```text
ADR-024
   │
   ▼
Superseded by
   │
   ▼
ADR-081
```

Do not rewrite history by deleting the old ADR.

# 15. ADR Immutability Principle

Once accepted, the original decision history should generally remain understandable.

Minor corrections are acceptable.

Material decision changes should normally produce a new ADR or explicit revision history rather than silently rewriting architecture history.

# 16. Decision Ownership

Every ADR should identify an accountable owner.

Examples:

```text
Platform
Security
Data
Identity
AI
Frontend
SRE
```

An owner is responsible for maintaining the decision—not personally implementing every consumer.

# 17. Decision Scope

Every ADR should state scope explicitly.

```text
Enterprise-wide
Platform-wide
Domain-specific
Service-specific
Environment-specific
```

Without scope, teams cannot determine applicability.

# 18. Decision Dependencies

ADRs should reference decisions they depend upon.

```text
ADR-071
   │
   ├── ADR-070 Quality
   ├── Security ADRs
   ├── Kubernetes ADRs
   └── GitOps ADRs
```

# 19. ADR Dependency Graph

At Mediverse scale, decision relationships should become machine-discoverable.

```text
ADR-069 AI
   │
   ▼
ADR-070 Quality
   │
   ▼
ADR-071 Platform
   │
   ▼
ADR-072 Governance
```

This makes impact analysis possible.

# 20. Standard Strength

Architecture requirements must distinguish:

```text
MUST
SHOULD
MAY
```

Using "must" everywhere destroys meaningful prioritization.

# 21. Mandatory Standards

`MUST` should be reserved primarily for:

```text
Security boundaries
Compliance
Data protection
Critical reliability
Compatibility
Enterprise invariants
```

Violation requires an approved exception.

# 22. Recommended Standards

`SHOULD` means the default architecture is strongly recommended but legitimate alternatives may exist.

Deviation should have a technical reason.

# 23. Optional Guidance

`MAY` represents supported options rather than requirements.

It should not later be enforced as though it were mandatory.

# 24. Architecture Review Board Boundary

The EAB should focus on high-impact decisions.

```text
EAB
 │
 ├── Enterprise standards
 ├── Major platform changes
 ├── Cross-domain architecture
 ├── Critical technology adoption
 └── High-risk exceptions
```

It should not review ordinary controller implementations.

# 25. Lightweight Review

Most architecture decisions should use lightweight asynchronous review.

```text
Proposal
   │
   ▼
ADR / RFC
   │
   ▼
Relevant Owners
   │
   ▼
Decision
```

Meetings should not be the default governance mechanism.

# 26. Heavyweight Review

Deeper review is justified for decisions involving:

```text
Large financial commitment
Irreversible migration
Sensitive data
Critical security
Major vendor dependency
Enterprise-wide platform change
High operational blast radius
```

# 27. Architecture RFC

Before major decisions become ADRs, an RFC may capture exploration.

```text
Problem
  │
  ▼
RFC
  │
  ├── Alternatives
  ├── Evidence
  ├── Prototype
  └── Feedback
  │
  ▼
ADR
```

RFC explores.

ADR records the decision.

# 28. Proof of Concept

A PoC should answer a specific uncertainty.

Bad:

```text
"Let's try technology X."
```

Better:

```text
"Can X sustain 10k concurrent streams
while meeting our p95 latency and
operational requirements?"
```

# 29. PoC Exit Criteria

Before beginning a PoC define:

```text
Hypothesis
Success criteria
Failure criteria
Timebox
Owner
Decision to be informed
```

Otherwise prototypes become undeclared production systems.

# 30. Automated Conformance

Architecture standards should be automatically verified where practical.

```text
ADR
 │
 ▼
Machine-Enforceable Rule
 │
 ▼
CI / Platform / Admission
```

Documentation alone is a weak enforcement mechanism.

# 31. Architecture Fitness Functions

Evolutionary architecture should use fitness functions to continuously test important properties.

Examples:

```text
No forbidden dependency
API compatibility maintained
No privileged containers
Latency budget respected
Service ownership exists
Critical data encrypted
```

# 32. Structural Fitness Functions

Architecture tests can enforce dependency boundaries.

Example:

```text
Controller
   │
   ▼
Application
   │
   ▼
Domain

Infrastructure
   │
   X
must not leak into prohibited layers
```

Tools such as architecture tests may automate this for Java codebases.

# 33. Runtime Fitness Functions

Some architecture characteristics require runtime verification.

Examples:

```text
Availability
Latency
Resilience
Recovery
Scalability
```

These connect ADR-072 back to ADR-070.

# 34. Policy as Code

Machine-enforceable governance should use policy where appropriate.

Examples:

```text
Kubernetes policy
Terraform policy
IAM policy
CI rules
Repository policy
Artifact policy
```

# 35. Enforcement Placement

Apply controls as early as practical.

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
Local Validation
   │
   ▼
PR
   │
   ▼
CI
   │
   ▼
GitOps
   │
   ▼
Admission
   │
   ▼
Runtime Detection
```

# 36. Preventive vs Detective Controls

Not every rule must block deployment.

```text
Preventive
    │
    └── Stop dangerous state

Detective
    │
    └── Identify drift/problem

Advisory
    │
    └── Recommend improvement
```

# 37. Architecture Scorecards

ADR-071 scorecards should expose relevant conformance.

```text
Service
  │
  ├── Owner ✓
  ├── Supported runtime ✓
  ├── SLO ✓
  ├── Security scanning ✓
  ├── Backup ✗
  └── Deprecated dependency ⚠
```

# 38. Scorecard Severity

Findings should distinguish:

```text
Critical violation
Policy violation
Technical debt
Warning
Recommendation
```

A missing optional README section should not be treated like a publicly exposed production database.

# 39. Architecture Drift

Architecture drift occurs when implementation diverges from approved architecture.

```text
Approved State
      │
      ▼
Implementation Changes
      │
      ▼
Different Actual State
```

Drift may be intentional or accidental.

# 40. Drift Detection

Detect drift through:

```text
CI
Repository scanning
Cloud configuration
Kubernetes state
Dependency analysis
Runtime topology
Catalog metadata
```

# 41. Drift Response

Drift should result in one of:

```text
Fix implementation
Update architecture
Approve temporary exception
Replace obsolete standard
```

Blindly forcing implementation back to an outdated ADR is not good governance.

# 42. Exception Mechanism

Architecture must support legitimate exceptions.

```text
STANDARD
   │
   ▼
Constraint prevents compliance
   │
   ▼
Exception Request
```

Without an escape mechanism, teams either stop delivering or bypass governance secretly.

# 43. Exception Record

Each exception should contain:

```text
Standard violated
Reason
Scope
Risk
Compensating controls
Owner
Approver
Expiration
Remediation plan
```

# 44. Risk Acceptance

An exception is a risk decision.

The person accepting the exception must have authority appropriate to the risk.

Developers should not silently accept enterprise security risk on behalf of the organization.

# 45. Exception Expiry

Exceptions should normally expire.

```text
Approved
   │
   ▼
Temporary Period
   │
   ▼
Review
 ┌─┴─────────────┐
 ▼               ▼
Close          Renew
```

# 46. Exception Renewal

Renewal must not be automatic.

Re-evaluate:

```text
Risk
Reason
Alternative
Remediation progress
Business need
```

# 47. Exception Metrics

Track:

```text
Open exceptions
Expired exceptions
Repeated exceptions
Average lifetime
Standards causing most exceptions
```

A standard generating constant exceptions may itself be defective.

# 48. Technical Debt Definition

Technical debt is a future cost created by a current technical compromise or deficiency.

Not every imperfect implementation is technical debt.

# 49. Debt Taxonomy

Mediverse should classify debt.

```text
Technical Debt
├── Architecture
├── Code
├── Dependency
├── Infrastructure
├── Security
├── Data
├── Testing
├── Observability
├── Documentation
└── AI
```

# 50. Intentional Debt

Intentional debt may be acceptable.

Example:

```text
"We will use a temporary synchronous
integration to meet the pilot deadline
and migrate to the event architecture
before production scale."
```

The problem is not the compromise.

The problem is forgetting it.

# 51. Accidental Debt

Accidental debt emerges through:

```text
Poor design
Missing knowledge
Unplanned coupling
Repeated shortcuts
Architecture drift
Neglected upgrades
```

It still requires explicit management once discovered.

# 52. Debt Registry

Significant debt should be recorded.

```yaml
debt:
  id: TD-104
  owner: learning-team
  category: dependency
  severity: high
  remediationTarget: 2026-Q4
```

Do not create bureaucracy for every TODO comment.

# 53. Debt Ownership

Every registered debt item needs an owner.

```text
Debt without owner
      =
Debt nobody will fix
```

# 54. Debt Interest

Debt has "interest" when it continuously increases delivery or operational cost.

Examples:

```text
Every feature requires workaround
Every deployment requires manual step
Every incident involves same weak component
Every upgrade becomes harder
```

High-interest debt deserves priority.

# 55. Debt Principal vs Interest

Think separately about:

```text
Principal
   │
   └── Cost to remove debt

Interest
   │
   └── Ongoing cost of keeping debt
```

A large remediation cost may still be justified if recurring interest is worse.

# 56. Debt Prioritization

Prioritize using:

```text
Risk
Interest
Business impact
Change frequency
Incident contribution
Security exposure
Remediation cost
Strategic importance
```

"Oldest debt first" is usually simplistic.

# 57. Debt Budget

Teams should reserve capacity for meaningful engineering health.

A rigid universal percentage such as "20% forever" is unnecessary.

Investment should follow actual debt risk and interest.

# 58. Dependency Debt

Dependency debt includes:

```text
Unsupported Java
Unsupported Spring Boot
Deprecated libraries
Vulnerable packages
Old PostgreSQL
Old Kubernetes APIs
```

# 59. Dependency Lifecycle

The platform should identify:

```text
Current
Behind
Deprecated
Unsupported
Vulnerable
```

and automate upgrades where practical.

# 60. Infrastructure Debt

Infrastructure debt includes:

```text
Manual provisioning
Snowflake servers
Old Terraform
Unsupported Kubernetes resources
Unowned cloud resources
Missing automation
```

## ADR-072 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The governance model now becomes:

```text
                        ARCHITECTURE INTENT
                                │
                                ▼
                              ADR
                                │
             ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             ▼                  ▼                  ▼
          STANDARD          GUIDANCE          FITNESS
             │                  │              FUNCTIONS
             │                  │                  │
             └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                ▼
                           IMPLEMENTATION
                                │
                                ▼
                       AUTOMATED CONFORMANCE
                                │
                     ┌──────────┴──────────┐
                     ▼                     ▼
                 COMPLIANT               DRIFT
                     │                     │
                     │           ┌─────────┼─────────┐
                     │           ▼         ▼         ▼
                     │          FIX    EXCEPTION   ADR CHANGE
                     │           │         │         │
                     └───────────┴─────────┼─────────┘
                                           ▼
                                    TECHNICAL DEBT
                                           │
                                           ▼
                                      PRIORITIZE
                                           │
                                           ▼
                                        EVOLVE
```

The most important governance rule so far is:

> **An ADR is not automatically correct forever because it was once accepted. Governance must protect architectural intent while retaining the ability to challenge, supersede, or retire decisions when evidence changes.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Security, Data, Testing, Observability & AI Debt**, then cover **debt remediation economics → debt trends → architectural runway → evolutionary architecture → changeability → reversible vs irreversible decisions → experimentation → technology radar → emerging technology evaluation → build-vs-buy → vendor lock-in → technology lifecycle → deprecation → migration programs → strangler modernization → legacy retirement → service retirement → data migration governance → architecture documentation freshness → C4 synchronization → ADR discovery/search → architecture knowledge graph → governance automation → architecture metrics → decision lead time → exception rate → drift rate → debt trends → governance effectiveness → team autonomy → architecture community of practice → governance operating model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise architecture governance reference architecture and ADR-072 decision outcome.**

# ADR-072 — Enterprise Architecture Governance, Standards Enforcement, Technical Debt & Evolution Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Infrastructure Debt**.

---

# 61. Security Debt

Security debt includes known weaknesses intentionally or accidentally left unresolved.

```text
Security Debt
     │
     ├── Unsupported crypto
     ├── Excessive IAM permissions
     ├── Long-lived credentials
     ├── Missing authorization controls
     ├── Unpatched dependencies
     └── Legacy authentication
```

Security debt must be risk-ranked rather than treated like ordinary refactoring backlog.

# 62. Security Debt Escalation

Critical security debt may override ordinary product prioritization.

```text
Finding
   │
   ▼
Risk Assessment
   │
   ├── Low ─────► Backlog
   ├── Medium ──► Planned remediation
   ├── High ────► Priority remediation
   └── Critical ► Immediate action
```

# 63. Data Debt

Data debt includes:

```text
Poor data quality
Unknown ownership
Duplicate sources of truth
Missing lineage
Weak schemas
Uncontrolled PII
Inconsistent identifiers
Unmaintained migrations
```

Data debt frequently survives application rewrites because the underlying data remains.

# 64. Schema Debt

Examples include:

```text
Ambiguous columns
Missing constraints
Incorrect data types
Unbounded JSON usage
Duplicated fields
Legacy nullable fields
```

Database schema quality is part of architecture quality.

# 65. Testing Debt

Testing debt includes:

```text
Missing critical tests
Flaky tests
Slow pipelines
Over-mocking
Weak integration coverage
Missing contract tests
Unmaintained E2E suites
```

High test count does not imply low testing debt.

# 66. Observability Debt

Observability debt includes:

```text
Unstructured logs
Missing metrics
Missing traces
Unknown service ownership
No SLOs
No useful dashboards
No actionable alerts
```

It often becomes visible only during incidents—when remediation is most expensive.

# 67. Documentation Debt

Documentation debt exists when operational or architectural knowledge diverges from reality.

```text
Documentation
      │
      X
Actual System
```

Stale documentation can be worse than absent documentation because it creates false confidence.

# 68. AI Debt

AI systems introduce additional debt categories.

```text
AI Debt
 ├── Prompt debt
 ├── Model-version debt
 ├── Evaluation debt
 ├── Dataset debt
 ├── Retrieval debt
 ├── Embedding debt
 ├── Safety-policy debt
 └── Observability debt
```

# 69. Prompt Debt

Prompts should not evolve into unexplained production strings.

Significant prompts need:

```text
Version
Owner
Purpose
Evaluation
Model compatibility
Change history
```

# 70. Evaluation Debt

AI capabilities without maintained evaluation datasets accumulate evaluation debt.

Without regression evidence:

```text
Prompt Change
     +
Model Change
     +
RAG Change
     =
Unknown Quality Change
```

# 71. Retrieval Debt

RAG systems can accumulate:

```text
Stale embeddings
Obsolete documents
Duplicate chunks
Weak metadata
Bad chunking
Poor retrieval configuration
```

A stronger LLM does not automatically repair poor retrieval architecture.

# 72. Debt Remediation Economics

Debt should be treated as an economic decision.

```text
Cost of Remediation
       vs
Expected Cost of Retention
```

Retention cost includes delivery friction, incidents, risk, operational toil and future migration difficulty.

# 73. Remediate vs Retain

Immediate remediation is justified when:

```text
Risk is unacceptable
Interest is high
Change frequency is high
Security exposure is serious
Migration window is closing
Dependency reaches EOL
```

Some low-interest debt can rationally remain.

# 74. Debt Trend

Track debt direction, not merely total count.

```text
Debt
 ^
 |          /
 |        /
 |      /
 |_____/____________> Time

BAD: debt accumulating faster
than remediation.
```

# 75. Debt Aging

Age can be useful but should not dominate prioritization.

A two-week-old critical security weakness may matter more than a three-year-old harmless code smell.

# 76. Debt Hotspots

Combine debt with change frequency.

```text
HIGH CHANGE + HIGH DEBT
        │
        ▼
Priority Hotspot

LOW CHANGE + LOW RISK
        │
        ▼
Potentially Leave Alone
```

# 77. Architectural Runway

Architecture should provide enough runway for foreseeable product development.

```text
Current Capability
       │
       ▼
Near-Term Product Needs
       │
       ▼
Architectural Runway
```

Do not build five years of speculative infrastructure.

# 78. Runway Planning

Runway should be based on evidence such as:

```text
Product roadmap
Capacity projections
Compliance deadlines
Dependency EOL
Known scaling limits
Upcoming integrations
```

# 79. Evolutionary Architecture

Mediverse should favor architectures capable of controlled change.

```text
Architecture N
      │
      ▼
Small Safe Change
      │
      ▼
Architecture N+1
```

Evolution is preferable to repeated large rewrites.

# 80. Changeability

Important architecture qualities include:

```text
Replaceability
Deployability
Testability
Observability
Modularity
Compatibility
Reversibility
```

A system that works today but cannot safely change is accumulating strategic risk.

# 81. Reversible Decisions

Many decisions are relatively reversible.

Examples:

```text
Internal library
UI component library
Logging format
Local implementation pattern
```

These generally deserve lighter governance.

# 82. Irreversible Decisions

Some decisions have high reversal cost.

Examples:

```text
Public API contract
Persistent data model
Major cloud commitment
Identity architecture
Organization-wide platform
Large vendor contract
```

These deserve stronger evidence and review.

# 83. Two-Way vs One-Way Doors

Use the heuristic:

```text
TWO-WAY DOOR
Change cheaply
    │
    ▼
Decide quickly

ONE-WAY DOOR
Expensive reversal
    │
    ▼
Investigate deeply
```

Do not apply heavyweight governance to every two-way-door decision.

# 84. Experimentation

Uncertainty should often be resolved through controlled experimentation rather than argument.

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Hypothesis
   │
   ▼
Experiment
   │
   ▼
Evidence
   │
   ▼
Decision
```

# 85. Experiment Boundaries

Experiments need:

```text
Scope
Owner
Timebox
Success criteria
Cost boundary
Security boundary
Cleanup plan
```

Otherwise experiments become permanent shadow architecture.

# 86. Technology Radar

Mediverse should maintain a technology radar.

Suggested categories:

```text
ADOPT
TRIAL
ASSESS
HOLD
```

# 87. Adopt

`ADOPT` means:

> Technology is approved and supported for appropriate production use.

It does not mean every team must use it.

# 88. Trial

`TRIAL` means:

> Technology has demonstrated potential and may be used in controlled production contexts with appropriate ownership.

# 89. Assess

`ASSESS` means:

> Technology is being investigated but should not yet become a production dependency without explicit approval.

# 90. Hold

`HOLD` means:

> Avoid for new development.

Reasons may include:

```text
Security
Operational complexity
Poor ecosystem
Strategic mismatch
Licensing
Cost
Better replacement
End of life
```

# 91. Technology Evaluation

Emerging technology should be evaluated against concrete criteria.

```text
Functional fit
Security
Reliability
Performance
Operability
Ecosystem
Skills
Cost
Licensing
Exit strategy
Integration
Maturity
```

# 92. Hype Resistance

Architecture should reject:

```text
Technology is popular
        ↓
Therefore Mediverse needs it
```

Technology adoption requires a problem worth solving.

# 93. Build-vs-Buy Framework

Evaluate:

```text
Strategic differentiation
Requirements fit
Build cost
Operating cost
Vendor cost
Integration
Security
Compliance
Customization
Exit cost
```

# 94. Build When

Building is more defensible when capability:

```text
Creates strategic differentiation
Requires unusual domain behavior
Needs deep integration
Cannot be safely sourced externally
```

# 95. Buy When

Buying is more defensible when capability is commodity and mature external solutions provide better economics.

Examples may include generic infrastructure capabilities rather than core educational differentiation.

# 96. Hidden Build Cost

Building includes:

```text
Development
Testing
Security
Documentation
Operations
Upgrades
On-call
Compliance
Maintenance
```

"Open source" and "free to download" do not mean free to operate.

# 97. Hidden Buy Cost

Buying includes:

```text
Subscription
Integration
Migration
Training
Customization
Vendor management
Exit cost
Data portability
```

# 98. Vendor Lock-In

Vendor dependence is not automatically bad.

The relevant question is:

> Does the value received justify the switching cost and strategic risk?

# 99. Lock-In Assessment

Evaluate:

```text
Proprietary APIs
Data gravity
Contract restrictions
Migration complexity
Skills dependency
Operational coupling
Pricing leverage
```

# 100. Exit Strategy

Critical vendor decisions should document:

```text
Export mechanism
Data format
Replacement options
Migration estimate
Contract termination
Fallback strategy
```

Not every vendor requires an elaborate exit implementation, but critical dependencies require an understood path.

# 101. Technology Lifecycle

Technologies should move through controlled lifecycle states.

```text
Assess
  │
  ▼
Trial
  │
  ▼
Adopt
  │
  ▼
Maintain
  │
  ▼
Deprecate
  │
  ▼
Retire
```

# 102. Deprecation Trigger

Triggers include:

```text
Vendor EOL
Security risk
Unsupported runtime
Low adoption
Better standard
Operational burden
Strategic change
```

# 103. Deprecation Is Not Removal

Deprecation means:

```text
No new adoption
Migration planning
Support window
Replacement guidance
```

Immediate removal may be unsafe.

# 104. Migration Program

Large migrations require programmatic management.

```text
Inventory
   │
   ▼
Classify
   │
   ▼
Prioritize
   │
   ▼
Automate
   │
   ▼
Migrate
   │
   ▼
Validate
   │
   ▼
Retire
```

# 105. Migration Inventory

Before migration, identify:

```text
Systems
Owners
Dependencies
Data
Traffic
Criticality
Versions
Consumers
```

Migrating what you have not inventoried is guesswork.

# 106. Migration Waves

Large migrations should usually occur in waves.

```text
Pilot
  │
  ▼
Low-Risk Cohort
  │
  ▼
General Migration
  │
  ▼
Complex Exceptions
  │
  ▼
Retirement
```

# 107. Automated Migration

Where repetitive changes exist, provide:

```text
Codemods
Automated PRs
Configuration transforms
Migration scripts
Validation tools
```

Humans should review meaningful changes, not manually repeat mechanical edits hundreds of times.

# 108. Strangler Modernization

Legacy systems should often be replaced incrementally.

```text
                 ROUTER
                /      \
               ▼        ▼
          LEGACY      NEW
             │          │
             └────┬─────┘
                  │
        Capability moves gradually
                  │
                  ▼
              NEW SYSTEM
```

# 109. Strangler Boundary

Choose seams such as:

```text
API
Domain capability
Workflow
User segment
Event
Data ownership
```

A poor boundary can create more coupling than the legacy architecture.

# 110. Big-Bang Rewrite

Mediverse should treat complete rewrites skeptically.

They frequently underestimate:

```text
Hidden behavior
Edge cases
Migration
Operational knowledge
Integration complexity
Timeline
```

A rewrite may still be justified, but requires strong evidence.

# 111. Legacy Stabilization

Before modernization, it may be rational to add:

```text
Tests
Observability
API façade
Dependency mapping
Data validation
```

to the legacy system.

Understanding the existing system reduces migration risk.

# 112. Service Retirement

Creating services is easy.

Deleting them is part of architecture.

```text
Candidate Service
      │
      ▼
No Consumers?
      │
      ▼
No Required Data?
      │
      ▼
Traffic Removed
      │
      ▼
Archive
      │
      ▼
Delete
```

# 113. Retirement Checklist

Verify:

```text
Consumers removed
Traffic zero
Jobs disabled
Topics handled
DNS removed
Secrets removed
Infrastructure destroyed
Alerts removed
Documentation updated
Ownership closed
```

# 114. Zombie Services

A service with no known owner and uncertain consumers should be treated as architectural risk.

Do not leave it running forever because nobody is confident enough to delete it.

# 115. Data Migration Governance

Data migration requires explicit controls around:

```text
Source
Target
Mapping
Validation
Consistency
Rollback
Privacy
Retention
Audit
```

# 116. Migration Validation

Validate:

```text
Record counts
Constraints
Relationships
Checksums where useful
Business invariants
Sample correctness
Application behavior
```

Record count alone does not prove semantic correctness.

# 117. Dual Write Risk

Dual writing introduces consistency risk.

```text
Application
   ├────► Old DB
   └────► New DB
```

One write may succeed while the other fails.

Prefer architectures that explicitly handle consistency rather than assuming dual writes are atomic.

# 118. Backfill

Large backfills should be:

```text
Restartable
Observable
Rate-limited
Idempotent where possible
Auditable
```

They must not unexpectedly destroy production capacity.

# 119. Data Cutover

Cutover plans should define:

```text
Preconditions
Traffic switch
Validation
Rollback window
Ownership
Communication
```

# 120. Architecture Documentation Freshness

Architecture documentation needs lifecycle management.

```text
System Changes
      │
      ▼
Docs Updated?
   ┌──┴──┐
   ▼     ▼
 Yes     No
          │
          ▼
      Documentation Drift
```

# 121. Documentation Freshness Metadata

Important documents should include:

```text
Owner
Last reviewed
Scope
Status
Related ADRs
```

# 122. C4 Synchronization

C4 diagrams should reflect significant architecture changes.

```text
ADR
 │
 ▼
Implementation
 │
 ▼
C4 Model
```

Architecture diagrams that describe a system from two years ago should not be treated as authoritative.

# 123. Documentation Source of Truth

Avoid maintaining the same architecture facts manually in five places.

Prefer generating views from structured metadata where feasible.

# 124. ADR Discovery

With 72+ decisions, plain folder browsing becomes insufficient.

Engineers should be able to search by:

```text
Technology
Domain
Service
Owner
Status
Requirement strength
Related ADR
```

# 125. Architecture Knowledge Graph

Structured architecture metadata may create relationships such as:

```text
TEAM
 │ owns
 ▼
SERVICE
 │ implements
 ▼
ADR
 │ depends on
 ▼
PLATFORM
 │ deployed to
 ▼
KUBERNETES
```

This can support impact analysis and discovery.

# 126. Knowledge Graph Boundary

Do not build a complex graph platform merely because the concept is attractive.

Start from concrete discovery and impact-analysis problems.

# 127. Governance Automation

The ideal path is:

```text
Architecture Decision
        │
        ▼
Structured Metadata
        │
        ▼
Policy / Fitness Function
        │
        ▼
Platform Enforcement
        │
        ▼
Evidence
```

This turns architecture from static documentation into executable governance.

# 128. Decision Lead Time

Measure time from significant proposal to decision.

```text
RFC Open
   │
   ▼
Review
   │
   ▼
Decision
```

Long lead time may indicate governance bottlenecks.

# 129. Review SLA

Architecture review should have service expectations.

Teams cannot wait indefinitely for governance responses.

Urgency and decision risk should determine response targets.

# 130. Exception Rate

Track exceptions by standard.

```text
Standard A → 2 exceptions
Standard B → 37 exceptions
```

Standard B deserves investigation.

# 131. Drift Rate

Track meaningful drift over time.

```text
New violations
Resolved violations
Outstanding violations
Age
Severity
```

Raw violation count alone can mislead as the system grows.

# 132. Debt Trend Metrics

Track by:

```text
Category
Severity
Owner
Age
Interest
Creation rate
Remediation rate
```

# 133. Governance Effectiveness

Good governance should result in:

```text
Fewer preventable incidents
Lower architecture drift
Faster safe decisions
Reduced unsupported technology
Controlled exceptions
Improved migration readiness
Higher standard adoption
```

# 134. Governance Cost

Governance itself has cost.

Measure:

```text
Review waiting time
Manual approvals
Exception processing
Required meetings
Documentation burden
Developer friction
```

A control whose cost exceeds the risk reduction should be challenged.

# 135. Team Autonomy

Teams should retain autonomy inside architectural guardrails.

```text
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│      ENTERPRISE GUARDRAILS  │
│                             │
│   ┌─────────────────────┐   │
│   │   TEAM AUTONOMY     │   │
│   │                     │   │
│   │ Implementation      │   │
│   │ Local design        │   │
│   │ Experimentation     │   │
│   └─────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

# 136. Autonomy Requires Accountability

Teams choosing local solutions remain responsible for:

```text
Security
Reliability
Operability
Cost
Compatibility
Supportability
```

Autonomy is not exemption from engineering outcomes.

# 137. Architecture Community of Practice

A cross-team community should share:

```text
Patterns
Failures
Experiments
Migration lessons
New technologies
Architecture proposals
```

Architecture knowledge should not exist only inside the EAB.

# 138. Architecture Office Hours

Optional office hours can provide early feedback before teams invest heavily in questionable designs.

This is more useful than discovering architectural problems at final approval.

# 139. Architecture Champions

Larger teams may nominate architecture champions.

```text
EAB
 │
 ▼
Architecture Community
 │
 ▼
Team Champions
 │
 ▼
Engineering Teams
```

They facilitate communication rather than acting as local architecture police.

# 140. Governance Operating Model

```text
                   ENTERPRISE ARCHITECTURE BOARD
                              │
                 Strategic Standards / Risk
                              │
              ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
              ▼               ▼               ▼
          PLATFORM         SECURITY         DATA/AI
              │               │               │
              └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                              ▼
                 ARCHITECTURE COMMUNITY
                              │
                              ▼
                      ENGINEERING TEAMS
                              │
                              ▼
                    LOCAL DECISION MAKING
```

# 141. Governance Feedback Loop

```text
STANDARD
   │
   ▼
IMPLEMENT
   │
   ▼
MEASURE
   │
   ▼
INCIDENTS / EXCEPTIONS / FRICTION
   │
   ▼
LEARN
   │
   ▼
CHANGE STANDARD
   │
   └────────────► IMPLEMENT
```

Governance itself must evolve.

# 142. Architecture Health Review

Periodic reviews should focus on trends rather than manually inspecting every service.

Review:

```text
Critical debt
Unsupported technology
Architecture drift
Exception hotspots
Major migrations
Security risk
Reliability trends
Platform adoption
```

# 143. Governance Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Every technical decision requiring EAB approval
❌ Architects becoming implementation gatekeepers
❌ Architecture review only through meetings
❌ ADR for every minor coding choice
❌ ADRs without scope or owners
❌ Accepted ADRs silently rewritten
❌ Superseded ADRs deleted
❌ "Must" used for every recommendation
❌ Architecture documents treated as eternally correct
❌ Policies enforced only through documentation
❌ Standards with no machine-verifiable controls where feasible
❌ Every violation blocking production regardless of severity
❌ Drift automatically assumed to mean implementation is wrong
❌ Exceptions handled through private messages
❌ Permanent exceptions without review
❌ Security exceptions approved by unauthorized individuals
❌ Technical debt reduced to TODO count
❌ Every imperfection registered as formal debt
❌ Debt prioritized only by age
❌ Fixed universal debt percentage regardless of risk
❌ Unsupported dependencies ignored until emergency migration
❌ AI prompts changed without versioning/evaluation
❌ RAG debt assumed solvable by larger models
❌ Architecture built years ahead of demonstrated need
❌ Heavy review for reversible decisions
❌ Experiments without timeboxes or cleanup
❌ PoCs quietly becoming production systems
❌ Technology adopted because competitors use it
❌ Technology radar treated as a popularity chart
❌ Open source assumed to have zero cost
❌ SaaS assumed cheaper without exit-cost analysis
❌ Vendor lock-in automatically treated as unacceptable
❌ Critical vendor dependency without exit understanding
❌ Deprecated technology immediately removed without migration window
❌ Migration programs without inventories
❌ Hundreds of identical migrations performed manually
❌ Big-bang rewrite assumed easier than incremental modernization
❌ Legacy system rewritten before its hidden behavior is understood
❌ Services created forever but never retired
❌ Zombie services with unknown ownership
❌ Data migration validated only by row counts
❌ Unsafe dual writes assumed consistent
❌ Backfills with no throttling or restartability
❌ Architecture diagrams never updated
❌ Same architecture metadata manually duplicated everywhere
❌ Building a knowledge graph without a concrete use case
❌ Architecture review with indefinite response times
❌ Governance success measured by number of reviews
❌ Governance cost ignored
❌ Team autonomy without accountability
❌ Central architects disconnected from engineering reality
```

# 144. Architecture Governance Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — REACTIVE
Architecture knowledge lives in people.

LEVEL 2 — DOCUMENTED
Standards and ADRs exist.

LEVEL 3 — STANDARDIZED
Golden paths and explicit governance exist.

LEVEL 4 — AUTOMATED
Policies and fitness functions enforce key standards.

LEVEL 5 — EVOLUTIONARY
Architecture continuously adapts using operational evidence.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4 with selective Level 5 capabilities**, not pursue maturity for its own sake.

# 145. Architecture Decision Flow

```text
                     NEW DECISION
                          │
                          ▼
                 ARCHITECTURALLY
                  SIGNIFICANT?
                   ┌──────┴──────┐
                   ▼             ▼
                  NO            YES
                   │             │
                   ▼             ▼
              TEAM DECISION    REVERSIBLE?
                              ┌──┴───┐
                              ▼      ▼
                             YES     NO
                              │      │
                              ▼      ▼
                           LIGHT    DEEPER
                           REVIEW   REVIEW
                              │      │
                              └──┬───┘
                                 ▼
                              ADR/RFC
                                 │
                                 ▼
                              DECISION
                                 │
                                 ▼
                           IMPLEMENTATION
                                 │
                                 ▼
                         FITNESS FUNCTIONS
                                 │
                         ┌───────┴───────┐
                         ▼               ▼
                      PASS             DRIFT
                         │               │
                         ▼        ┌──────┼──────┐
                      OPERATE     ▼      ▼      ▼
                                FIX   EXCEPT  EVOLVE
```

# 146. Technical Debt Operating Model

```text
                     DISCOVER DEBT
                           │
                           ▼
                        CLASSIFY
                           │
             ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
             ▼             ▼             ▼
          RISK          INTEREST       COST
             │             │             │
             └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                           ▼
                       PRIORITIZE
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
          REMEDIATE       ACCEPT       DEFER
              │            │            │
              ▼            ▼            ▼
           VERIFY      DOCUMENT      REASSESS
              │            │            │
              └────────────┼────────────┘
                           ▼
                         TREND
```

# 147. Evolution Model

```text
BUSINESS NEED
     │
     ▼
ARCHITECTURAL PRESSURE
     │
     ▼
EXPERIMENT / RFC
     │
     ▼
EVIDENCE
     │
     ▼
ADR
     │
     ▼
GOLDEN PATH / STANDARD
     │
     ▼
AUTOMATED CONFORMANCE
     │
     ▼
PRODUCTION
     │
     ▼
OBSERVABILITY
     │
     ▼
REAL-WORLD EVIDENCE
     │
     └──────────────► ARCHITECTURAL EVOLUTION
```
