# 150. Governing Invariant

The final ADR-072 architecture can be reduced to one feedback system:

```text
             INTENT
               │
               ▼
            DECISION
               │
               ▼
            STANDARD
               │
               ▼
          GOLDEN PATH
               │
               ▼
         IMPLEMENTATION
               │
               ▼
          CONFORMANCE
               │
               ▼
           PRODUCTION
               │
               ▼
            EVIDENCE
               │
      ┌────────┼────────┐
      ▼        ▼        ▼
    DRIFT     DEBT   EXCEPTIONS
      │        │        │
      └────────┼────────┘
               ▼
             LEARN
               │
               ▼
             EVOLVE
               │
               └────────────► INTENT
```

> **Architecture governance must preserve intent without freezing implementation. Standards exist because they reduce meaningful organizational risk, not because consistency is inherently valuable. Teams should be autonomous inside explicit guardrails, exceptions should be visible and temporary, technical debt should be managed economically, and production evidence must be allowed to prove that an existing architectural decision needs to change.**

# ADR-072 — COMPLETE ✅

## Next — ADR-073

### **ADR-073 — Enterprise FinOps, Cloud Cost Governance, Capacity Economics & Unit Economics Standard**

This is the logical next boundary because the existing architecture now contains **Kubernetes, AWS infrastructure, PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, observability, CI runners, preview environments, 3D asset delivery and especially AI/LLM workloads**. Without cost architecture, technically correct self-service can create financially unsustainable infrastructure.

ADR-073 should define **FinOps principles → cost ownership → tagging/allocation → showback/chargeback → budgets → forecasting → anomaly detection → cloud unit economics → cost per active learner → cost per course session → cost per assessment → cost per AI tutoring session → cost per 1K AI interactions → token economics → model routing economics → RAG economics → embedding/indexing costs → vector database costs → GPU economics → 3D asset/CDN economics → Kubernetes cost allocation → requests vs actual usage → idle capacity → bin packing → autoscaling economics → Spot/On-Demand/Reserved capacity → RDS sizing → storage lifecycle → Kafka economics → Redis economics → observability cardinality and retention cost → log cost controls → CI/CD cost → ephemeral environment TTL economics → network egress → multi-region cost → DR economics → performance-vs-cost trade-offs → sustainability/resource efficiency → cost-aware architecture reviews → FinOps policy-as-code → cost estimation in developer self-service → cost guardrails → anomaly response → forecasting → optimization backlog → FinOps metrics → anti-patterns → final Mediverse cloud economics reference architecture.**



# ADR-073 — Enterprise FinOps, Cloud Cost Governance, Capacity Economics & Unit Economics Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-073
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Primary Stakeholders:** Platform Engineering, SRE, Cloud Infrastructure, Finance/FinOps, Engineering Teams, AI Platform, Data Platform

ADR-072 established architecture governance, technical-debt management, evolutionary architecture, conformance, exceptions, and evidence-driven architectural change.

ADR-073 establishes the economic control plane for Mediverse.

The objective is not simply:

```text
"Reduce AWS bill."
```

The objective is:

> **Make infrastructure economics visible, attributable, predictable, and optimizable while preserving reliability, security, performance, and developer productivity.**

A cheap architecture that cannot meet its SLOs is not efficient.

An architecture meeting its SLOs at 5× the necessary cost is not efficient either.

```text
                     PRODUCT DEMAND
                           │
                           ▼
                       WORKLOAD
                           │
                           ▼
                   PLATFORM / CLOUD
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
       COMPUTE            DATA              AI
          │                │                │
          └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                           ▼
                         COST
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          ▼                ▼                ▼
      ALLOCATION       UNIT COST       FORECASTING
          │                │                │
          └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                           ▼
                      OPTIMIZATION
                           │
                           ▼
                  ARCHITECTURE FEEDBACK
```

---

# 1. FinOps Objective

Mediverse FinOps should optimize simultaneously for:

```text
Business Value
Cost Efficiency
Reliability
Performance
Security
Scalability
Developer Productivity
Financial Predictability
```

Cost optimization in isolation is explicitly rejected.

---

# 2. FinOps Is an Engineering Concern

Cloud economics cannot belong exclusively to Finance.

```text
Finance
   +
Engineering
   +
Platform
   +
Product
   +
Architecture
       │
       ▼
    FinOps
```

Engineers make architectural decisions that directly create cloud costs.

---

# 3. FinOps Operating Loop

Mediverse adopts:

```text
INFORM
   │
   ▼
OPTIMIZE
   │
   ▼
OPERATE
   │
   ▼
MEASURE
   │
   └──────────► INFORM
```

Cost management must be continuous.

---

# 4. Cost Ownership

Every meaningful cloud resource must have an accountable owner.

Required attribution should include:

```text
Team
Service
Environment
Product/domain
Cost center where applicable
Lifecycle
```

Unowned infrastructure is financial and operational debt.

---

# 5. Resource Tagging Standard

Cloud resources should receive standardized metadata automatically.

Conceptually:

```yaml
tags:
  service: course-service
  team: learning-platform
  environment: production
  product: mediverse
  managed-by: terraform
```

Manual tagging should not be the primary control.

---

# 6. Kubernetes Cost Attribution

Kubernetes introduces shared-resource complexity.

```text
EKS Cluster
    │
    ├── Namespace A
    │      ├── Service A
    │      └── Service B
    │
    ├── Namespace B
    │      └── Service C
    │
    └── Platform workloads
```

Cost allocation therefore requires workload-level metadata rather than only AWS account-level billing.

---

# 7. Shared Cost Allocation

Shared costs may include:

```text
Cluster control plane
Ingress
Observability
Shared Kafka
Shared Redis
Networking
Platform tooling
Security tooling
CI infrastructure
```

These costs should be classified explicitly rather than arbitrarily assigned to one service.

---

# 8. Direct vs Shared Cost

```text
DIRECT COST
    │
    └── Clearly attributable to workload

SHARED COST
    │
    └── Supports multiple workloads

ENTERPRISE COST
    │
    └── Organization-wide capability
```

The allocation method should be transparent.

---

# 9. Showback

Initial FinOps maturity should emphasize **showback**.

```text
Team
 │
 ▼
"You consumed ₹X / $X
this month."
```

Visibility alone often changes engineering behavior.

---

# 10. Chargeback

Chargeback may be introduced only when organizational maturity justifies it.

Poorly designed chargeback can incentivize teams to optimize local budgets while damaging global architecture.

Therefore:

> **Showback first. Chargeback only with clear organizational value.**

---

# 11. Cost Dashboard

Engineering teams should see:

```text
Current spend
Spend trend
Forecast
Budget
Major cost drivers
Anomalies
Unit economics
Optimization opportunities
```

Cost information hidden exclusively inside Finance reports is too late for engineering decisions.

---

# 12. Budget Model

Budgets should exist at useful scopes.

```text
Organization
    │
    ├── Platform
    ├── Product Domain
    │      ├── Service
    │      └── Environment
    └── AI Platform
```

Budget does not automatically mean a hard technical limit.

---

# 13. Budget Thresholds

Typical thresholds may trigger:

```text
50%  → informational
75%  → forecast review
90%  → warning
100% → escalation
```

Actual thresholds should depend on workload characteristics.

---

# 14. Budget Guardrail Warning

Do not automatically terminate production infrastructure because a budget threshold was crossed.

```text
Budget exceeded
      │
      X
      └── Kill production
```

That would convert a financial issue into an availability incident.

---

# 15. Forecasting

Forecast future spend using:

```text
Historical usage
Growth rate
Product roadmap
Traffic projections
Seasonality
New infrastructure
AI adoption
Regional expansion
```

---

# 16. Forecast vs Budget

```text
ACTUAL
   │
   ▼
FORECAST
   │
   ▼
BUDGET
```

The useful signal is not merely today's spend.

It is whether projected spend is moving outside expected economic boundaries.

---

# 17. Cost Anomaly Detection

Mediverse should detect abnormal cost changes.

```text
Normal:
₹10k → ₹11k → ₹10.5k → ₹11.2k

Anomaly:
₹11.2k → ₹47k
```

Detection should happen quickly enough to prevent prolonged waste.

---

# 18. Cost Anomaly Context

An anomaly alert should include:

```text
Service
Team
Environment
Resource type
Previous baseline
Current spend
Change percentage
Likely driver
```

"Your AWS bill increased" is not actionable.

---

# 19. Cost Anomaly Response

```text
ANOMALY
   │
   ▼
IDENTIFY OWNER
   │
   ▼
VALIDATE DEMAND
   │
   ├── Legitimate growth
   ├── Incident
   ├── Misconfiguration
   └── Waste
   │
   ▼
ACTION
```

Not every cost increase is waste.

---

# 20. Unit Economics

Total cloud spend is insufficient for understanding efficiency.

Mediverse should measure cost relative to business activity.

```text
Infrastructure Cost
        │
        ▼
Business Activity
        │
        ▼
UNIT COST
```

---

# 21. Cost per Active Learner

Conceptually:

```text
Monthly Platform Cost
─────────────────────
Monthly Active Learners
```

This helps distinguish healthy business growth from infrastructure inefficiency.

---

# 22. Cost per Learning Session

For appropriate workloads:

```text
Learning Infrastructure Cost
────────────────────────────
Completed Learning Sessions
```

---

# 23. Cost per Assessment

Assessment infrastructure may measure:

```text
Assessment Platform Cost
────────────────────────
Assessments Completed
```

This becomes particularly important when AI-assisted evaluation is introduced.

---

# 24. Cost per AI Tutoring Session

AI economics should be separated from generic application infrastructure.

```text
LLM
+
Embedding
+
Vector Retrieval
+
Supporting Compute
+
Observability
────────────────────
AI Tutoring Sessions
```

---

# 25. Cost per 1,000 AI Interactions

A normalized AI metric may be:

```text
Total AI Variable Cost
──────────────────────
AI Requests / 1,000
```

But request count alone can mislead because prompt and output sizes vary substantially.

---

# 26. Token Economics

For token-priced models:

```text
AI Cost
  =
Input Tokens × Input Price
  +
Output Tokens × Output Price
  +
Additional Provider Costs
```

The platform should record token consumption at useful attribution levels.

---

# 27. AI Cost Attribution

Track AI consumption by:

```text
Feature
Model
Team
Environment
User cohort where privacy permits
Request type
Token usage
```

Do not create uncontrolled high-cardinality observability labels from user identifiers.

---

# 28. AI Model Economics

Model selection must consider more than benchmark quality.

```text
                 MODEL SELECTION

             Quality
               /\
              /  \
             /    \
            /      \
       Cost ─────── Latency
```

The most capable model should not automatically process every request.

---

# 29. Model Routing Economics

Mediverse should support policy-driven model routing.

```text
AI Request
    │
    ▼
Complexity / Risk Classification
    │
 ┌──┼─────────────────────┐
 ▼  ▼                     ▼
Small Model          Standard Model
                          │
                          ▼
                     Premium Model
```

Escalate model capability when the task requires it.

---

# 30. Model Routing Principle

Preferred strategy:

> **Use the least expensive model that reliably satisfies the required quality, safety, and latency target.**

"Always cheapest" is wrong.

"Always strongest" is also wrong.

---

# 31. AI Quality-Cost Frontier

AI evaluation should produce a quality/cost relationship.

```text
Quality
  ^
  |                         ● Premium
  |                 ● Standard
  |          ● Small
  |
  +--------------------------------> Cost
```

The goal is to operate on an acceptable frontier rather than maximize one dimension blindly.

---

# 32. Prompt Economics

Poor prompts can directly create cost.

Examples:

```text
Unnecessary system context
Repeated instructions
Huge conversation histories
Redundant RAG chunks
Excessive requested output
```

Prompt optimization is therefore both a quality and FinOps concern.

---

# 33. Context Window Management

Do not continually send entire conversation history when the task does not require it.

Possible strategies:

```text
Truncation
Summarization
Relevant-history retrieval
Structured memory
Context caching where supported
```

Each strategy must preserve required semantic correctness.

---

# 34. Output Token Control

Applications should specify sensible output limits.

Unlimited generation can create:

```text
Higher latency
Higher cost
Poor UX
Abuse exposure
```

---

# 35. AI Response Caching

Cache deterministic or reusable AI results only where semantically and privacy appropriate.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Cache?
 ┌─┴──────┐
 ▼        ▼
Hit      Miss
 │        │
 ▼        ▼
Return   Model
```

Caching personalized or sensitive responses requires additional caution.

---

# 36. Semantic Cache

Semantic caching may reduce repeated LLM execution for sufficiently equivalent queries.

However:

```text
Similar text
    ≠
Always equivalent intent
```

Incorrect semantic cache hits can damage correctness.

---

# 37. RAG Economics

RAG cost includes more than LLM inference.

```text
Documents
   │
   ▼
Chunking
   │
   ▼
Embedding
   │
   ▼
Vector Storage
   │
   ▼
Retrieval
   │
   ▼
Prompt Tokens
   │
   ▼
Generation
```

---

# 38. Embedding Economics

Embedding cost depends on:

```text
Corpus size
Chunk count
Chunk size
Embedding model
Re-index frequency
Change rate
```

Re-embedding an entire corpus for every small content change is wasteful.

---

# 39. Incremental Indexing

Prefer:

```text
Changed Document
      │
      ▼
Identify Changed Chunks
      │
      ▼
Re-Embed Only Changes
```

when supported by the retrieval architecture.

---

# 40. Chunking Economics

Tiny chunks can create:

```text
More embeddings
More vectors
More metadata
More retrieval candidates
```

Huge chunks can create:

```text
Poor retrieval precision
Larger prompts
Higher token cost
```

Chunking is simultaneously a quality and cost decision.

---

# 41. Vector Database Economics

Evaluate:

```text
Vector count
Dimensions
Replication
Index type
Query volume
Latency
Storage
Backups
Managed-service premium
```

Do not select vector infrastructure solely from benchmark popularity.

---

# 42. RAG Retrieval Budget

AI workflows should define bounded retrieval behavior.

Example:

```text
Query
  │
  ▼
Retrieve top K
  │
  ▼
Rerank
  │
  ▼
Send only useful context
```

Blindly injecting 50 chunks into every prompt is economically and semantically weak.

---

# 43. GPU Economics

If Mediverse eventually hosts models, GPU economics require separate governance.

```text
GPU Cost
   │
   ├── Purchase / rental
   ├── Utilization
   ├── Idle capacity
   ├── Memory
   ├── Batch efficiency
   └── Energy
```

---

# 44. GPU Utilization

An expensive GPU at low utilization can be worse economically than managed inference.

```text
GPU allocated 24h
      │
      ▼
Used 2h
      │
      ▼
Poor utilization
```

---

# 45. Managed API vs Self-Hosted AI

Evaluate:

```text
Request volume
Model requirements
Data constraints
Latency
GPU utilization
Engineering effort
Operational maturity
Provider pricing
```

Self-hosting is not automatically cheaper.

---

# 46. Break-Even Analysis

At sufficient stable volume:

```text
Managed API Cost
        vs
GPU + Platform + Engineering + Operations
```

may justify self-hosting.

The full operational cost must be included.

---

# 47. Kubernetes Economics

Kubernetes cost should be understood as:

```text
Node capacity
+
Control plane
+
Storage
+
Networking
+
Shared platform workloads
+
Operational overhead
```

Not simply pod CPU cost.

---

# 48. Requests vs Actual Usage

For every workload:

```text
CPU Request ──► 2 cores
Actual CPU  ──► 0.2 cores
```

Persistent gaps indicate potential over-requesting.

---

# 49. Memory Requests

Memory requires caution because insufficient allocation may cause:

```text
OOMKill
Restart loops
Latency
Availability degradation
```

Rightsizing must use measured behavior.

---

# 50. Resource Rightsizing

Use:

```text
Historical utilization
Percentiles
Traffic patterns
GC behavior
Burst requirements
SLOs
Failure behavior
```

Do not simply set Kubernetes requests equal to observed average usage.

---

# 51. Resource Limits

Limits should be configured according to workload behavior rather than copied blindly.

CPU throttling and memory termination have different consequences.

---

# 52. Idle Capacity

Measure:

```text
Provisioned Capacity
       -
Used Capacity
       =
Idle Capacity
```

Some idle capacity is deliberate reliability headroom.

Zero idle capacity is not a valid universal target.

---

# 53. Bin Packing

Efficient scheduling should reduce fragmented unused node capacity.

```text
BAD

Node A [50%]
Node B [40%]
Node C [30%]

BETTER

Node A [85%]
Node B [75%]
Node C removed
```

subject to availability and scheduling constraints.

---

# 54. Node Pools

Separate pools may exist for:

```text
General workloads
Memory-intensive workloads
Compute workloads
AI/GPU
System workloads
Spot-compatible workloads
```

Too many specialized pools can themselves reduce utilization.

---

# 55. Cluster Autoscaling

Node capacity should respond to workload demand where appropriate.

```text
Demand ↑
   │
   ▼
Pods Pending
   │
   ▼
Nodes Scale Out

Demand ↓
   │
   ▼
Consolidation
   │
   ▼
Nodes Scale In
```

---

# 56. HPA Economics

Horizontal scaling should use meaningful signals.

```text
CPU
Memory where appropriate
Request rate
Queue depth
Custom metrics
```

Scaling on a poorly correlated metric can increase cost without improving performance.

---

# 57. Scaling Boundaries

Every autoscaled workload should define:

```text
Minimum
Maximum
Scaling metric
Target
Cooldown/stabilization
```

Unlimited scaling can convert an application bug or attack into an uncontrolled bill.

---

# 58. Cost-Aware Autoscaling

Autoscaling policy should consider:

```text
SLO
Demand
Capacity
Cost
```

but must not sacrifice critical availability merely to meet a cost target.

---

# 59. Spot Capacity

Spot/preemptible capacity can reduce compute cost for interruption-tolerant workloads.

Good candidates may include:

```text
CI builds
Batch jobs
Stateless workers
Recomputable processing
Non-critical environments
```

---

# 60. Poor Spot Candidates

Avoid relying exclusively on interruptible capacity for workloads that cannot tolerate disruption.

Examples may include critical singleton workloads without failover or stateful systems lacking interruption handling.

---

## ADR-073 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The emerging FinOps control system is:

```text
                         PRODUCT DEMAND
                               │
                               ▼
                            TRAFFIC
                               │
                               ▼
                           WORKLOADS
                               │
          ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          ▼                    ▼                    ▼
       KUBERNETES             DATA                  AI
          │                    │                    │
          └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                               ▼
                          CLOUD USAGE
                               │
                               ▼
                              COST
                               │
          ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          ▼                    ▼                    ▼
      ATTRIBUTION          FORECAST             ANOMALY
          │                    │                    │
          └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                               ▼
                         UNIT ECONOMICS
                               │
          ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          ▼                    ▼                    ▼
     Cost/Learner       Cost/Session        Cost/AI Request
          │                    │                    │
          └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                               ▼
                          OPTIMIZATION
                               │
          ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
          ▼                    ▼                    ▼
      RIGHTSIZING          SCALING            MODEL ROUTING
          │                    │                    │
          └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                               ▼
                         SLO VALIDATION
                               │
                               ▼
                       ARCHITECTURE FEEDBACK
```

The critical distinction is:

> **FinOps does not ask "How do we make this as cheap as possible?" It asks "What is the minimum sustainable cost required to deliver the required business value, security, reliability, performance, and engineering velocity?"**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — On-Demand, Reserved & Commitment Economics**, then cover **Savings Plans/commitments → workload predictability → RDS/PostgreSQL economics → read replicas → storage classes → backup economics → Redis economics → Kafka/MSK economics → S3 lifecycle → CDN and 3D asset economics → image/video delivery → network egress → NAT cost → cross-AZ traffic → observability economics → metrics cardinality → log-volume governance → trace sampling → retention tiers → CI/CD economics → runner utilization → build caching → artifact storage → preview environment economics → TTL enforcement → development/UAT shutdown schedules → multi-region economics → DR cost → RTO/RPO economics → capacity forecasting → performance-cost frontier → cost-aware architecture reviews → developer self-service cost estimation → FinOps policy-as-code → cost guardrails → optimization backlog → sustainability/resource efficiency → FinOps maturity model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse cloud economics reference architecture and ADR-073 decision outcome.**

# ADR-073 — Enterprise FinOps, Cloud Cost Governance, Capacity Economics & Unit Economics Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Poor Spot Candidates**.

---

# 61. On-Demand Capacity

On-Demand capacity provides maximum flexibility but generally carries a higher unit price than committed capacity.

Best suited for:

```text
Unknown demand
New workloads
Short-lived workloads
Burst capacity
Migration periods
Uncertain architecture
```

Do not purchase long-term commitments merely because a workload currently exists.

---

# 62. Commitment Economics

Stable baseline workloads may benefit from commitment-based pricing.

Conceptually:

```text
Total Demand
     │
     │                 /\      Burst
     │       /\       /  \
     │──────/──\─────/────\────
     │==========================
     │     Stable Baseline
     └──────────────────────────► Time

Stable baseline → Commitment candidate
Variable demand → Flexible capacity
```

---

# 63. Savings Plans / Reserved Capacity

Commitments should be based on measured baseline utilization.

Avoid:

```text
Forecast says we may need 100
        │
        ▼
Commit to 100 immediately
```

Prefer:

```text
Measured stable baseline
        │
        ▼
Conservative commitment
        │
        ▼
Flexible capacity for remainder
```

---

# 64. Commitment Coverage

Track:

```text
Eligible Spend
Committed Spend
Commitment Coverage
Commitment Utilization
Effective Savings
```

High coverage with poor utilization is not optimization.

---

# 65. Commitment Utilization

If committed capacity is purchased but unused:

```text
Discounted Resource
       +
No Utilization
       =
Waste
```

Discount percentage is irrelevant if the resource was unnecessary.

---

# 66. Commitment Laddering

Large commitments should be introduced progressively where uncertainty exists.

```text
Observed Baseline
      │
      ▼
Commitment 1
      │
      ▼
Observe Growth
      │
      ▼
Commitment 2
```

This reduces forecasting risk.

---

# 67. Workload Predictability

Classify workloads:

```text
Predictable
Seasonal
Bursty
Batch
Event-driven
Experimental
```

Capacity strategy should differ by class.

---

# 68. Seasonal Demand

Mediverse may experience predictable educational peaks:

```text
Exam periods
Course launches
Academic deadlines
Live learning events
```

Capacity forecasts should incorporate these patterns rather than extrapolating simple monthly averages.

---

# 69. PostgreSQL Economics

Database cost includes:

```text
Compute
Storage
IO
Backups
Replication
Network
Licensing where applicable
Operations
```

Database optimization must consider workload behavior, not instance price alone.

---

# 70. Database Rightsizing

Measure:

```text
CPU
Memory
Connections
IOPS
Storage growth
Query latency
Cache hit ratio
Replication behavior
```

before changing database capacity.

---

# 71. Oversized Database

A common failure pattern:

```text
Performance Incident
      │
      ▼
Increase DB Size
      │
      ▼
Incident disappears
      │
      ▼
Never investigate query
      │
      ▼
Permanent Cost Increase
```

Scaling hardware can hide application or query defects.

---

# 72. Query Optimization Economics

Before scaling vertically, investigate:

```text
Slow queries
Missing indexes
N+1 queries
Poor joins
Excessive result sets
Connection misuse
Unnecessary database calls
```

A ₹0 query optimization can outperform a permanent infrastructure upgrade.

---

# 73. Read Replica Economics

Read replicas should solve measured problems.

```text
Primary
  │
  ├── Writes
  │
  └── Read Replica
          │
          └── Read-heavy workload
```

Replicas increase:

```text
Compute cost
Storage cost
Replication cost
Operational complexity
```

They are not free scaling.

---

# 74. Database Connection Economics

Uncontrolled connection pools can force larger database infrastructure.

```text
50 Pods
 ×
50 Connections
 =
2,500 Potential Connections
```

Connection-pool sizing is therefore an infrastructure economics concern.

---

# 75. Database Autoscaling Caution

Database capacity is harder to scale elastically than stateless application workloads.

Capacity planning must account for:

```text
Connection behavior
Cache warming
Replication
Storage
Failover
Resize duration
```

---

# 76. Storage Economics

Storage cost depends on more than capacity.

```text
Storage Cost
    =
Capacity
+
IO
+
Requests
+
Replication
+
Backup
+
Retrieval
```

---

# 77. Storage Classification

Data should be classified by access pattern.

```text
HOT
 │
 ▼
Frequently accessed

WARM
 │
 ▼
Occasionally accessed

COLD
 │
 ▼
Rarely accessed

ARCHIVE
 │
 ▼
Retention only
```

---

# 78. Storage Lifecycle

Lifecycle automation should move eligible data between appropriate tiers.

```text
HOT
 │
 ▼
WARM
 │
 ▼
COLD
 │
 ▼
ARCHIVE
 │
 ▼
DELETE
```

subject to retention requirements.

---

# 79. S3 Lifecycle

Potential candidates include:

```text
Old application exports
Historical reports
Archived learning assets
Old logs
Backup artifacts
Unused asset versions
```

Lifecycle rules must respect compliance and recovery requirements.

---

# 80. Orphaned Object Cleanup

Object storage can accumulate:

```text
Abandoned multipart uploads
Old generated assets
Unused versions
Temporary exports
Expired preview assets
```

These should have explicit cleanup policies.

---

# 81. Backup Economics

Backups have value because they reduce recovery risk.

Optimization should consider:

```text
Retention
Frequency
Replication
Storage tier
Restore requirement
Compliance
```

Deleting backups simply to reduce storage cost is not FinOps.

---

# 82. RPO Economics

Lower RPO generally requires more protection.

```text
Lower acceptable data loss
          │
          ▼
More frequent replication / backup
          │
          ▼
Higher Cost
```

Business criticality must justify the target.

---

# 83. RTO Economics

Lower RTO often requires:

```text
Warm capacity
Replication
Automation
Standby infrastructure
Pre-provisioned dependencies
```

which increases cost.

---

# 84. Redis Economics

Redis cost is primarily memory economics.

Track:

```text
Dataset size
Memory utilization
TTL behavior
Eviction
Replication
Persistence
Hit rate
```

---

# 85. Cache Value

Caching is economically useful when:

```text
Cost avoided by cache hits
        >
Cost of operating cache
```

Adding Redis to every service by default is not optimization.

---

# 86. Cache TTL Economics

Excessively long TTLs may waste memory.

Excessively short TTLs may eliminate useful cache benefits.

TTL should reflect:

```text
Freshness requirements
Request frequency
Recomputation cost
Memory pressure
```

---

# 87. Cache Hit Ratio

A large expensive cache with a very low hit ratio should be challenged.

```text
Cache Requests: 1,000,000
Hits:             50,000

Hit Ratio = 5%
```

The workload may not justify the cache.

---

# 88. Kafka Economics

Kafka cost includes:

```text
Broker compute
Storage
Replication
Network
Partitions
Retention
Observability
Operations
```

Topic creation is not economically free.

---

# 89. Kafka Partition Economics

Excessive partitions increase:

```text
Broker overhead
Metadata
File handles
Replication work
Operational complexity
```

Partition count should reflect throughput and parallelism requirements.

---

# 90. Kafka Retention Economics

```text
High throughput
      ×
Long retention
      ×
Replication factor
      =
Large storage requirement
```

Retention should be driven by business and recovery requirements.

---

# 91. Event Payload Economics

Large Kafka messages increase:

```text
Network
Storage
Replication
Consumer processing
```

Events should carry appropriate domain information without becoming uncontrolled document transport.

---

# 92. 3D Asset Economics

Mediverse's immersive content can create substantial delivery cost.

```text
3D Model
Textures
Audio
Animation
Video
       │
       ▼
Asset Size
       │
       ▼
CDN / Network Cost
```

Asset optimization is therefore part of application architecture.

---

# 93. 3D Model Optimization

Consider:

```text
Mesh simplification
LOD
Geometry compression
Texture compression
Texture resizing
Lazy loading
Asset reuse
```

without damaging required visual quality.

---

# 94. Level of Detail

LOD can reduce rendering and transfer requirements.

```text
Near Camera
   │
   ▼
High Detail

Medium Distance
   │
   ▼
Medium Detail

Far Distance
   │
   ▼
Low Detail
```

---

# 95. Asset Compression

Large uncompressed 3D assets should not be distributed casually.

Compression strategy should consider browser/device compatibility and decompression cost.

---

# 96. Texture Economics

A visually simple scene can still become expensive if every asset carries oversized textures.

Track:

```text
Resolution
Compression
Format
Mipmaps
Reuse
Device target
```

---

# 97. CDN Architecture

Static learning assets should generally be delivered through CDN/cache infrastructure rather than repeatedly from application servers.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
CDN Edge
 │
 ├── HIT ─────► Asset
 │
 └── MISS
      │
      ▼
    Origin
```

---

# 98. CDN Cache Hit Ratio

Higher useful cache hit ratios reduce origin load and often reduce latency.

But cache policies must preserve content correctness and invalidation behavior.

---

# 99. Immutable Asset Versioning

Prefer content/version-based asset URLs.

```text
model-v17.glb
```

or equivalent immutable identifiers.

This enables long-lived caching without ambiguous invalidation.

---

# 100. Video Economics

Video delivery may dominate network cost.

Control through:

```text
Adaptive bitrate
Appropriate resolution
Compression
CDN
Caching
Device-aware playback
```

Do not send 4K media to a device displaying a small embedded educational panel unless needed.

---

# 101. Network Egress

Cloud network transfer can become a major cost driver.

Track:

```text
Internet egress
Cross-region traffic
Cross-AZ traffic
NAT traffic
CDN origin traffic
Inter-service traffic
```

---

# 102. Data Gravity

Large datasets should not move repeatedly without reason.

```text
DATA
 │
 └── 50 TB

Repeated cross-region transfer
        │
        ▼
High cost + latency
```

Move computation closer to data where architecture permits.

---

# 103. Cross-AZ Traffic

High-frequency service communication across availability zones can create material transfer cost.

Do not eliminate multi-AZ resilience merely to avoid that cost.

Instead understand and optimize unnecessary traffic.

---

# 104. Cross-Region Traffic

Cross-region architectures should explicitly justify:

```text
Replication
User latency
DR
Regulation
Availability
```

because cross-region data movement has both cost and complexity.

---

# 105. NAT Economics

NAT infrastructure can become a hidden cost center when workloads generate substantial outbound traffic.

Analyze:

```text
Traffic source
Destination
Volume
Need for internet path
Private endpoint availability
```

---

# 106. Private Endpoints

Private/service endpoints may reduce NAT dependence for suitable cloud services.

But endpoint costs themselves must be included.

"Private" does not mean "free."

---

# 107. Chatty Microservices

Architecture can create network cost.

```text
Request
  │
  ▼
Service A
  │
  ▼
Service B
  │
  ▼
Service C
  │
  ▼
Service D
```

Thousands of unnecessary remote calls affect both latency and cost.

---

# 108. Observability Economics

Observability has a non-trivial cost.

```text
Logs
Metrics
Traces
Profiles
Events
        │
        ▼
Ingestion
Storage
Indexing
Query
Retention
```

More telemetry is not automatically better observability.

---

# 109. Logging Economics

Logging cost roughly follows:

```text
Event Volume
   ×
Event Size
   ×
Retention
   ×
Indexing Cost
```

Debug-level production logging should not remain enabled indiscriminately.

---

# 110. Structured Logging

Structured logging improves queryability but does not remove the need for volume control.

Avoid repeatedly logging enormous payloads.

---

# 111. Sensitive Logging

Sensitive information should not be logged merely because storage is available.

This is both:

```text
Security risk
Privacy risk
Compliance risk
Cost waste
```

---

# 112. Log Retention Tiers

Different logs may require different retention.

```text
Operational logs
Security/audit logs
Debug logs
Compliance logs
```

Retention must follow purpose rather than one global number.

---

# 113. Metrics Cardinality

High-cardinality labels can cause explosive monitoring cost.

Dangerous examples include:

```text
user_id
request_id
session_id
email
random identifiers
```

These generally belong in logs/traces rather than metric labels.

---

# 114. Metric Value Review

A metric should exist because someone uses it for:

```text
SLO
Alerting
Capacity
Debugging
Product understanding
```

Unused metrics should be candidates for removal.

---

# 115. Trace Economics

Recording every span for every request indefinitely can become expensive.

Tracing strategy should consider:

```text
Traffic
Incident needs
Criticality
Sampling
Retention
Span volume
```

---

# 116. Trace Sampling

Possible strategies:

```text
Head sampling
Tail sampling
Error-biased sampling
Latency-biased sampling
Adaptive sampling
```

Sampling must preserve useful incident evidence.

---

# 117. Error Trace Retention

High-value traces such as:

```text
Errors
Very slow requests
Critical transactions
```

may deserve higher retention probability than routine successful traffic.

---

# 118. CI/CD Economics

CI consumes:

```text
Runner compute
Storage
Network
Artifact storage
Security scanning
Test environments
Engineering waiting time
```

A slow pipeline has both cloud cost and developer productivity cost.

---

# 119. Runner Utilization

Track:

```text
Busy time
Idle time
Queue time
Job duration
Runner type
Cost per build
```

---

# 120. Ephemeral CI Runners

Ephemeral runners can improve isolation and elasticity.

```text
Job
 │
 ▼
Create Runner
 │
 ▼
Execute
 │
 ▼
Destroy Runner
```

Startup latency and image-pull cost must still be considered.

---

# 121. Build Caching Economics

Effective caching reduces:

```text
Compilation time
Dependency downloads
Container builds
Runner consumption
Developer waiting
```

But caches require storage and invalidation discipline.

---

# 122. Test Economics

Tests have different cost/value profiles.

```text
Unit
  │ cheap / fast

Integration
  │ moderate

E2E
  │ expensive / slower
```

Do not repeatedly execute every expensive test when a cheaper signal can safely determine that it is unnecessary.

---

# 123. Artifact Economics

Registries accumulate:

```text
Container images
Maven artifacts
npm packages
SBOMs
Build outputs
```

Retention policies are required.

---

# 124. Image Retention

Do not delete:

```text
Currently deployed images
Rollback candidates
Required audit artifacts
```

But thousands of obsolete unreferenced development images need not live forever.

---

# 125. Preview Environment Economics

Preview environments create enormous DX value but can create uncontrolled cost.

```text
PR Open
   │
   ▼
Environment Created
   │
   ▼
PR Closed
   │
   ▼
Environment Destroyed
```

Destruction must be automated.

---

# 126. Preview TTL

Every temporary environment should have:

```text
Owner
Creation time
Expiry
Associated PR/task
Cleanup controller
```

No owner + no TTL = predictable waste.

---

# 127. Development Environment Scheduling

Non-production environments that are unused overnight/weekends may be candidates for scheduled scale-down.

Only apply this when it does not disrupt required testing or geographically distributed teams.

---

# 128. UAT Economics

Do not assume UAT must duplicate full production capacity continuously.

UAT should reproduce relevant architecture and behavior while capacity can often be smaller.

---

# 129. Production Parity

Production parity means:

```text
Architecture / configuration behavior
```

not necessarily:

```text
Identical expensive capacity
```

---

# 130. Multi-Region Economics

Multi-region architecture can approximately duplicate major infrastructure categories.

```text
Region A
   +
Region B
   +
Replication
   +
Networking
   +
Operations
```

This must be justified by availability, latency, regulatory, or recovery requirements.

---

# 131. DR Economics

Disaster recovery strategy should align cost with business requirement.

```text
Backup & Restore
      ↓
Pilot Light
      ↓
Warm Standby
      ↓
Active/Passive
      ↓
Active/Active

Increasing readiness
Increasing cost
```

---

# 132. RTO/RPO Cost Frontier

```text
Cost
 ^
 |                         ● Active/Active
 |                 ● Warm Standby
 |          ● Pilot Light
 |    ● Backup/Restore
 |
 +------------------------------------>
              Recovery Capability
```

The strongest DR architecture is not automatically the correct architecture.

---

# 133. Capacity Forecasting

Forecast capacity for:

```text
CPU
Memory
Database
Storage
Kafka
Network
AI tokens
Vector storage
GPU
Observability
CI
```

---

# 134. Capacity Headroom

Production systems require deliberate headroom.

```text
Expected Peak
     +
Failure Headroom
     +
Growth Headroom
     =
Required Capacity
```

100% utilization is not a healthy target.

---

# 135. Performance-Cost Frontier

Every major workload has a trade-off curve.

```text
Performance
    ^
    |                       ●
    |                 ●
    |            ●
    |       ●
    |  ●
    +----------------------------> Cost
```

Beyond some point, large cost increases produce tiny performance improvements.

Architecture should identify that point.

---

# 136. Cost-Aware Architecture Review

Significant ADRs should answer:

```text
What are the major cost drivers?
How does cost scale with traffic?
What is fixed vs variable?
What happens at 10× demand?
What creates egress?
What requires replication?
What are expected unit economics?
What is the exit cost?
```

---

# 137. Developer Self-Service Cost Estimation

ADR-071 self-service workflows should expose estimated economics before provisioning.

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
"Create PostgreSQL"
   │
   ▼
Configuration
   │
   ▼
Estimated Monthly Cost
   │
   ▼
Policy
   │
   ▼
Provision
```

---

# 138. Cost Guardrails

Examples:

```text
Maximum preview environment size
Maximum default DB class
Maximum non-prod retention
Required TTL
GPU approval threshold
High-cost resource approval
```

Guardrails should target material risk rather than create approval bureaucracy for trivial resources.

---

# 139. FinOps Policy as Code

Where practical:

```text
Infrastructure Request
       │
       ▼
Cost Policy
       │
 ┌─────┴─────┐
 ▼           ▼
Allow      Review
```

Examples may include:

```text
Missing cost tags
Oversized non-prod resources
No TTL
Unexpected public egress
Unapproved GPU class
```

---

# 140. Optimization Backlog

Optimization opportunities should be managed like engineering work.

```text
Opportunity
    │
    ▼
Expected Saving
    │
    +
Engineering Cost
    │
    +
Risk
    │
    ▼
Priority
```

Do not spend ₹500,000 of engineering effort to save ₹20,000 annually.

---

# 141. Optimization ROI

Conceptually:

```text
Annual Savings - Implementation Cost - Added Operating Cost
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Implementation Investment
```

Precise financial methodology may vary, but opportunity cost must be considered.

---

# 142. Sustainability & Resource Efficiency

Resource efficiency often aligns with both FinOps and environmental efficiency.

Examples:

```text
Higher utilization
Reduced idle compute
Efficient storage
Reduced unnecessary transfer
Appropriate model selection
Efficient software
```

Do not use sustainability claims as justification for compromising required reliability.

---

# 143. FinOps Metrics

Mediverse should track a focused set of metrics:

```text
Total cloud spend
Forecast accuracy
Budget variance
Cost attribution coverage
Idle resource cost
Commitment utilization
Cost anomalies
Cost per active learner
Cost per learning session
Cost per AI interaction
Kubernetes utilization efficiency
Observability cost
Non-prod cost
Optimization savings
```

---

# 144. FinOps Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — REACTIVE
Bills reviewed after they arrive.

LEVEL 2 — VISIBLE
Costs attributed and dashboards available.

LEVEL 3 — CONTROLLED
Budgets, anomalies and guardrails exist.

LEVEL 4 — OPTIMIZED
Unit economics and automated optimization drive decisions.

LEVEL 5 — ECONOMIC ARCHITECTURE
Cost becomes a continuous architectural fitness dimension.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, with selective Level 5 capabilities where economics materially affect architecture.

---

# 145. FinOps Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "Cloud cost belongs to Finance"
❌ Optimizing only total monthly spend
❌ Cloud resources without owners
❌ Manual tagging as primary attribution
❌ Shared costs hidden or arbitrarily allocated
❌ Chargeback before teams have trustworthy showback
❌ Killing production because budget crossed 100%
❌ Cost alerts without owner/context
❌ Treating every cost increase as waste
❌ Ignoring unit economics
❌ Using request count alone for AI economics
❌ Sending every AI request to the strongest model
❌ Sending every AI request to the cheapest model
❌ Unlimited AI output tokens
❌ Entire conversation history sent blindly to LLMs
❌ Re-embedding entire corpus after tiny changes
❌ Huge RAG context injected without relevance
❌ Self-hosted AI assumed cheaper than APIs
❌ GPU allocation without utilization measurement
❌ Kubernetes requests copied blindly
❌ Rightsizing to average utilization
❌ Zero headroom as optimization target
❌ Autoscaling without maximum boundaries
❌ Stateful critical workloads forced entirely onto Spot
❌ Commitments purchased from optimistic forecasts
❌ Discount percentage treated as savings despite low utilization
❌ Database scaling used to hide bad queries
❌ Read replicas added without measured need
❌ Unlimited application connection pools
❌ Storage retained forever
❌ Backups deleted purely for cost reduction
❌ Redis added to every service by default
❌ Huge caches with poor hit ratios
❌ Kafka partitions created "just in case"
❌ Infinite Kafka retention without requirement
❌ Unoptimized 3D assets delivered directly from application servers
❌ 4K media delivered where lower resolution satisfies UX
❌ Cross-region traffic ignored
❌ NAT cost ignored
❌ Chatty microservices treated as financially free
❌ Debug logs permanently enabled in production
❌ User IDs used as metric labels
❌ Every trace retained forever
❌ CI cost measured without developer waiting time
❌ Build caching ignored
❌ Artifact registries with infinite retention
❌ Preview environments without TTL
❌ Non-production infrastructure running permanently without need
❌ Production parity interpreted as identical capacity
❌ Multi-region deployed because "enterprise systems should have it"
❌ Active/active DR without business justification
❌ 100% infrastructure utilization targeted
❌ Architecture reviews ignoring economics
❌ Self-service hiding cost from developers
❌ Every expensive resource requiring the same approval process
❌ Cost optimization without ROI analysis
❌ Spending more engineering money than optimization can reasonably save
```

---

# 146. FinOps Decision Flow

```text
                    NEW RESOURCE / CHANGE
                             │
                             ▼
                      BUSINESS NEED
                             │
                             ▼
                       COST ESTIMATE
                             │
               ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
               ▼             ▼             ▼
             FIXED        VARIABLE       SHARED
               │             │             │
               └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                             ▼
                        UNIT ECONOMICS
                             │
                             ▼
                         GUARDRAILS
                             │
                    ┌────────┴────────┐
                    ▼                 ▼
                  PASS              REVIEW
                    │                 │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             ▼
                          DEPLOY
                             │
                             ▼
                          MEASURE
                             │
              ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
              ▼              ▼              ▼
          UTILIZATION       COST         SLO/QUALITY
              │              │              │
              └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                             ▼
                         OPTIMIZE
```

---

# 147. Cost Feedback Architecture

```text
AWS Billing / Usage
        │
        ├──────── Kubernetes Allocation
        ├──────── AI Usage
        ├──────── Database Usage
        ├──────── Network Usage
        └──────── Platform Usage
        │
        ▼
   COST DATA MODEL
        │
        ├── Team
        ├── Service
        ├── Environment
        ├── Product
        └── Capability
        │
        ▼
   FINOPS ANALYTICS
        │
   ┌────┼─────┬────────┐
   ▼    ▼     ▼        ▼
Budget Unit  Forecast Anomaly
       Cost
   │    │     │        │
   └────┴─────┼────────┘
              ▼
       ENGINEERING ACTION
              │
       ┌──────┼───────┐
       ▼      ▼       ▼
   Rightsize Scale  Redesign
       │      │       │
       └──────┼───────┘
              ▼
       ARCHITECTURE FEEDBACK
```

---

# 148. FinOps Governance Integration

ADR-073 integrates directly with the preceding architecture:

```text
ADR-071
Developer Platform
      │
      ▼
Self-Service Cost Visibility
      │
      ▼
ADR-072
Architecture Governance
      │
      ▼
Cost-Aware Decisions
      │
      ▼
ADR-073
FinOps
      │
      ▼
Economic Evidence
      │
      └──────────────► Architecture Evolution
```

FinOps therefore becomes an architectural feedback mechanism rather than a monthly billing exercise.

---

# 149. ADR-073 Decision Outcome

| Area                          | Decision                                   |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| FinOps ownership              | Engineering + Platform + Product + Finance |

| Sustainability                | Resource-efficiency aligned                |

| Status                        | **Accepted**                               |
| Priority                      | **Critical**                               |
