# ADR-073 — COMPLETE ✅

The governing invariant is:

> **Mediverse must optimize unit economics rather than blindly minimize infrastructure spend. Every meaningful cost must be attributable, every major architecture decision must understand how its cost scales, self-service must expose economic consequences, and optimization must never silently violate security, reliability, performance, or quality requirements.**

The architecture now closes an important loop:

```text
Business Value
     │
     ▼
Architecture
     │
     ▼
Infrastructure
     │
     ▼
Consumption
     │
     ▼
Cost
     │
     ▼
Unit Economics
     │
     ▼
Optimization
     │
     ▼
SLO / Quality Validation
     │
     └──────────────► Architecture
```

## Next — ADR-074

### **ADR-074 — Enterprise Sustainability Engineering, Green Software, Carbon-Aware Computing & Resource Efficiency Standard**

ADR-073 establishes the economic dimension. ADR-074 should avoid becoming vague ESG documentation and instead establish measurable engineering controls around **software carbon intensity → energy/resource efficiency → compute utilization → embodied vs operational carbon → cloud-region carbon intensity → carbon-aware workload scheduling → temporal shifting of batch/AI jobs → spatial workload placement → renewable-energy considerations → Kubernetes efficiency → idle-resource elimination → CPU/memory efficiency → autoscaling → serverless economics/energy trade-offs → data-storage footprint → retention → network/data-transfer efficiency → CDN → 3D asset efficiency → frontend performance → device energy usage → AI inference energy → model-size selection → GPU utilization → RAG efficiency → embedding lifecycle → training/fine-tuning economics → observability footprint → CI/CD energy → developer environments → sustainable architecture fitness functions → carbon telemetry → SCI measurement → sustainability SLOs/guardrails → FinOps integration → sustainability-aware architecture reviews → greenwashing controls → sustainability maturity model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse sustainable-computing reference architecture.**

# ADR-074 — Enterprise Sustainability Engineering, Green Software, Carbon-Aware Computing & Resource Efficiency Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-074
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** High
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Primary Stakeholders:** Platform Engineering, SRE, FinOps, Cloud Infrastructure, AI Platform, Data Platform, Application Engineering

ADR-073 established the economic control plane for Mediverse.

ADR-074 extends that model to **resource and environmental efficiency**, but with an important constraint:

> **Sustainability engineering must be measurable engineering—not environmental branding attached to ordinary cost optimization.**

```text
                    PRODUCT DEMAND
                          │
                          ▼
                       SOFTWARE
                          │
                          ▼
                     COMPUTATION
                          │
          ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
          ▼               ▼               ▼
       COMPUTE          STORAGE         NETWORK
          │               │               │
          └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                          ▼
                    ENERGY / RESOURCE
                       CONSUMPTION
                          │
             ┌────────────┼────────────┐
             ▼            ▼            ▼
         EFFICIENCY     CARBON       COST
             │            │            │
             └────────────┼────────────┘
                          ▼
                   ARCHITECTURE SIGNAL
```

# 1. Sustainability Objective

Mediverse should reduce unnecessary:

```text
Compute
Memory
Storage
Network transfer
Energy consumption
Hardware demand
AI inference
GPU allocation
Data retention
```

while preserving required:

```text
Security
Reliability
Performance
Accessibility
Correctness
User experience
```

---

# 2. Sustainability Is Not Minimum Consumption

The target is not:

```text
Resource Consumption → 0
```

The target is:

```text
Useful Business / Learning Outcome
──────────────────────────────────
Required Resource Consumption
```

Efficiency must be evaluated relative to delivered value.

---

# 3. Green Software Principles

The engineering model focuses on three major levers:

```text
ENERGY EFFICIENCY
       │
       ├── Do more useful work per energy unit

HARDWARE EFFICIENCY
       │
       ├── Increase useful hardware utilization

CARBON AWARENESS
       │
       └── Where/when possible, execute work
           using lower-carbon electricity
```

---

# 4. Sustainability Hierarchy

Prefer optimization in this order where practical:

```text
Avoid unnecessary work
        │
        ▼
Reduce work
        │
        ▼
Reuse/cache results
        │
        ▼
Improve utilization
        │
        ▼
Move flexible work
        │
        ▼
Use cleaner execution
```

Avoiding computation is generally stronger than making unnecessary computation slightly more efficient.

---

# 5. Measure Before Optimizing

Mediverse rejects optimization based purely on intuition.

Measure:

```text
CPU time
Memory
Requests
Storage
Network
GPU utilization
AI tokens
Asset size
Build time
Idle capacity
```

before making substantial optimization decisions.

---

# 6. Software Carbon Intensity

A useful conceptual model is:

```text
SCI = ((E × I) + M) / R
```

where:

```text
E = Energy consumed
I = Carbon intensity of electricity
M = Embodied emissions allocated to software
R = Functional unit
```

The functional unit matters.

---

# 7. Functional Unit

Potential Mediverse functional units include:

```text
Per active learner
Per learning session
Per assessment
Per 1,000 API requests
Per AI tutoring session
Per course completed
```

Raw emissions without a functional denominator provide limited architectural insight.

---

# 8. Carbon Absolute vs Intensity Metrics

Track both where meaningful:

```text
ABSOLUTE
Total resource/carbon footprint

INTENSITY
Resource/carbon footprint per useful unit
```

A growing platform can improve efficiency while total consumption still rises.

---

# 9. Carbon Data Quality

Carbon estimates inherently contain uncertainty.

Therefore reports should identify:

```text
Measured data
Provider estimates
Modeled estimates
Assumptions
Unknowns
```

False precision should be avoided.

---

# 10. Greenwashing Control

Mediverse must not claim environmental improvement merely because:

```text
Cloud bill decreased
CPU decreased
A provider advertises renewable energy
A workload moved regions
```

A sustainability claim requires evidence relevant to the claim.

---

# 11. FinOps Relationship

FinOps and sustainability frequently align.

```text
Idle Compute ↓
      │
      ├── Cost ↓
      └── Resource Waste ↓
```

But they are not identical.

---

# 12. Cost vs Carbon

A cheaper region or instance is not necessarily lower carbon.

Likewise, lower-carbon execution may not always be cheaper.

Architecture should expose the trade-off where material.

---

# 13. Workload Classification

Classify workloads according to flexibility:

```text
Latency-critical
Interactive
Background
Batch
Deferrable
Interruptible
Location-flexible
AI inference
AI training
```

Carbon-aware scheduling is primarily useful for flexible workloads.

---

# 14. Temporal Flexibility

Some work can move in time.

```text
Job Ready
   │
   ▼
Must run immediately?
   │
 ┌─┴─────┐
 ▼       ▼
YES      NO
 │        │
Run      Schedule into
now      suitable window
```

---

# 15. Carbon-Aware Scheduling

Where trustworthy carbon-intensity information exists:

```text
Flexible Job
     │
     ▼
Allowed Window
     │
     ▼
Carbon Signal
     │
     ▼
Execution Time
```

Cost, deadlines and capacity remain constraints.

---

# 16. Temporal Shifting Candidates

Potential candidates include:

```text
Batch analytics
Search re-indexing
Embedding refresh
Report generation
Non-urgent media processing
Backfills
Some CI workloads
AI evaluation
Model training/fine-tuning
```

---

# 17. Poor Temporal-Shifting Candidates

Do not delay:

```text
Interactive requests
Security-critical processing
Incident response
Time-sensitive notifications
Critical database operations
SLO-bound synchronous workflows
```

merely to obtain a lower-carbon execution window.

---

# 18. Spatial Flexibility

Some workloads may be movable between execution locations.

```text
Workload
   │
   ▼
Permitted Regions
   │
   ▼
Compare
 ├── Latency
 ├── Regulation
 ├── Data gravity
 ├── Carbon
 ├── Cost
 └── Capacity
```

---

# 19. Region Selection

Cloud-region selection must not optimize carbon alone.

Consider:

```text
Data residency
Latency
Availability
Service availability
Network transfer
Cost
Carbon intensity
Disaster recovery
```

---

# 20. Data Gravity Constraint

Moving 20 TB of data to execute a small lower-carbon computation may be counterproductive.

```text
Carbon-aware compute placement
           │
           X
Massive unnecessary transfer
```

Location decisions require end-to-end analysis.

---

# 21. Kubernetes Sustainability

Kubernetes efficiency depends heavily on:

```text
Resource requests
Node utilization
Autoscaling
Bin packing
Node selection
Idle capacity
Workload scheduling
```

ADR-073 FinOps telemetry should therefore be reused.

---

# 22. CPU Request Efficiency

Persistent pattern:

```text
Requested CPU: 4 cores
Used CPU:      0.3 cores
```

may indicate waste.

But rightsizing must preserve burst and SLO requirements.

---

# 23. Memory Efficiency

Memory optimization must account for:

```text
JVM heap
Off-heap memory
OS memory
Cache
Traffic peaks
GC behavior
OOM risk
```

Average memory utilization alone is insufficient.

---

# 24. JVM Efficiency

For Spring Boot workloads, tune using measured evidence around:

```text
Heap sizing
GC behavior
Startup requirements
Container limits
Object allocation
Thread pools
Connection pools
```

Do not perform speculative JVM tuning merely to appear efficient.

---

# 25. Idle Kubernetes Capacity

Track:

```text
Allocated capacity
Requested capacity
Actual usage
Required resilience headroom
```

The difference after required headroom is a candidate efficiency opportunity.

---

# 26. Cluster Consolidation

Where availability constraints permit:

```text
Before

Node A 40%
Node B 35%
Node C 20%
Node D 15%

After consolidation

Node A 75%
Node B 70%
Node C removed
Node D removed
```

This can improve both economics and resource efficiency.

---

# 27. Reliability Headroom

Sustainability must not target maximum utilization.

```text
Useful Utilization
       +
Failure Headroom
       +
Burst Headroom
       =
Healthy Capacity
```

100% utilization creates fragile systems.

---

# 28. Autoscaling

Elastic infrastructure should remove capacity when demand disappears.

```text
Demand ↓
   │
   ▼
Pods ↓
   │
   ▼
Nodes consolidated
   │
   ▼
Resources released
```

Autoscaling without effective scale-down is incomplete.

---

# 29. Scale-to-Zero

Suitable workloads may scale to zero.

Candidates can include:

```text
Development services
Preview environments
Rarely used internal tools
Event-driven workers
Some batch processors
```

---

# 30. Scale-to-Zero Trade-Off

Scale-to-zero can introduce:

```text
Cold starts
Cache loss
Startup latency
Dependency reconnection
```

Do not use it where user experience or SLOs make those costs unacceptable.

---

# 31. Non-Production Efficiency

Non-production environments often contain the largest obvious idle-resource opportunity.

```text
DEV
UAT
Preview
Sandbox
Experiment
```

should have lifecycle policies.

---

# 32. Environment TTL

Temporary infrastructure must have:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Created timestamp
Expiry
Cleanup mechanism
```

This reinforces ADR-071 and ADR-073.

---

# 33. Scheduled Non-Production Capacity

Where teams do not require 24×7 availability:

```text
Working Window
     │
     ▼
Normal Capacity

Unused Window
     │
     ▼
Reduced / Zero Capacity
```

Globally distributed teams require different schedules.

---

# 34. Serverless Efficiency

Serverless can improve utilization for:

```text
Bursty
Intermittent
Event-driven
Low-duty-cycle
```

workloads.

But serverless is not inherently sustainable.

---

# 35. Serverless Trade-Offs

Evaluate:

```text
Invocation overhead
Cold starts
Provider implementation
Execution duration
Memory configuration
Request volume
Data transfer
Always-on alternatives
```

---

# 36. Storage Footprint

Storage sustainability requires control over:

```text
Data creation
Duplication
Replication
Retention
Backups
Derived datasets
Temporary data
Logs
Media
```

---

# 37. Data Minimization

Do not store data without a purpose.

```text
Collect
  │
  ▼
Need?
 ┌┴────┐
 ▼     ▼
Yes    No
 │      │
Store  Don't collect
```

This benefits privacy, security, cost and resource efficiency simultaneously.

---

# 38. Duplicate Data

Duplicate datasets may be justified for:

```text
Performance
Availability
Analytics
Recovery
```

but accidental duplication should be identified.

---

# 39. Retention

Every major data category should have an explicit retention policy.

```text
Operational data
Analytics
Audit
Logs
AI datasets
Embeddings
Backups
Media
Temporary exports
```

"Forever" is not a default retention policy.

---

# 40. Cold Storage

Rarely accessed retained data should use appropriate storage classes where supported.

This reduces active infrastructure requirements while preserving legitimate retention.

---

# 41. Deletion Is Architecture

Data lifecycle must include:

```text
CREATE
  │
  ▼
USE
  │
  ▼
ARCHIVE
  │
  ▼
DELETE
```

Systems designed only for data creation inevitably accumulate waste.

---

# 42. Network Efficiency

Network resource consumption can be reduced by:

```text
Caching
Compression
Batching
CDN
Payload optimization
Avoiding unnecessary calls
Data locality
```

---

# 43. API Payload Efficiency

Avoid returning:

```text
Entire object graph
Huge unused fields
Repeated metadata
Unbounded collections
```

when the consumer needs a small subset.

---

# 44. Pagination

Large collections should use appropriate pagination or streaming.

```text
GET /courses
     │
     X
Return 2 million records
```

is both poor application design and poor resource efficiency.

---

# 45. Compression

Compress appropriate network payloads where the CPU/network trade-off is beneficial.

Compression is not free; it exchanges computation for reduced transfer.

---

# 46. Chatty Architecture

Avoid unnecessary service communication.

```text
One User Action
      │
      ▼
Service A
      │
      ├── 50 calls B
      ├── 70 calls C
      └── 30 calls D
```

Architectural coupling can manifest as energy, cost and latency waste.

---

# 47. CDN Efficiency

Static content should exploit caching and edge delivery where appropriate.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Nearest Edge
 │
 ├── HIT → Return
 │
 └── MISS → Origin
```

---

# 48. Frontend Sustainability

Frontend engineering affects:

```text
Network usage
CPU usage
Memory
Battery
Rendering
Device lifetime pressure
```

Sustainability does not stop at the cloud boundary.

---

# 49. JavaScript Budget

Frontend bundles should have measurable budgets.

Monitor:

```text
Initial JS
Route-level JS
Unused code
Third-party libraries
Compression
```

---

# 50. Code Splitting

React applications should avoid downloading every capability during initial load.

```text
Initial Application
       │
       ├── Core
       │
       └── Lazy Route
              │
              ▼
        Load when needed
```

---

# 51. Third-Party Frontend Cost

Every third-party SDK can add:

```text
Download size
Execution
Network calls
Tracking
Memory
Security exposure
```

Dependencies should justify their cost.

---

# 52. Rendering Efficiency

Avoid unnecessary:

```text
Re-renders
DOM updates
Continuous animations
Expensive calculations
Background polling
```

especially on lower-powered devices.

---

# 53. Polling vs Events

Aggressive polling can generate unnecessary work.

```text
Client
 │
 ├── request every second
 ├── request every second
 ├── request every second
 └── ...
```

Where appropriate, event-driven or adaptive approaches may reduce wasted requests.

---

# 54. Device Diversity

Mediverse must account for users with:

```text
Low-end phones
Older laptops
Limited memory
Slow networks
Battery constraints
```

Efficient software improves accessibility and reach as well as sustainability.

---

# 55. 3D Sustainability

3D experiences require explicit resource budgets.

Track:

```text
Model polygons
Textures
Shaders
Animations
Asset size
Draw calls
Memory
GPU load
```

---

# 56. 3D Progressive Loading

Prefer:

```text
Critical Scene
      │
      ▼
Visible Assets
      │
      ▼
Nearby Assets
      │
      ▼
Optional Detail
```

rather than loading the entire museum/world immediately.

---

# 57. 3D Level of Detail

Use appropriate LOD.

```text
Close
 │
 ▼
Detailed Mesh

Far
 │
 ▼
Simplified Mesh
```

Rendering invisible detail wastes GPU resources.

---

# 58. Texture Budgets

Textures should be sized according to actual display requirements.

A 4K texture used on a tiny distant object is usually waste.

---

# 59. Frame Rate Strategy

Maximum frame rate is not always necessary.

For appropriate educational scenes:

```text
Visual Requirement
       │
       ▼
Required FPS
```

should determine rendering targets.

Do not sacrifice usability or interaction quality merely to reduce GPU work.

---

# 60. Hidden 3D Work

Pause or reduce expensive rendering when:

```text
Tab hidden
Scene not visible
User inactive
Component off-screen
```

where behavior permits.

---

## ADR-074 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The emerging sustainability architecture is:

```text
                       USER / BUSINESS VALUE
                                │
                                ▼
                             WORKLOAD
                                │
             ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             ▼                  ▼                  ▼
         APPLICATION           DATA                AI
             │                  │                  │
             └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                ▼
                        RESOURCE DEMAND
                                │
       ┌────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┐
       ▼                        ▼                        ▼
    COMPUTE                  STORAGE                  NETWORK
       │                        │                        │
       └────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┘
                                ▼
                          ENERGY / HARDWARE
                                │
                   ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                   ▼            ▼            ▼
                CARBON       FINANCIAL    PERFORMANCE
                   │            │            │
                   └────────────┼────────────┘
                                ▼
                         FITNESS DECISION
                                │
              ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
              ▼                 ▼                 ▼
            AVOID             REDUCE            SHIFT
              │                 │                 │
              ├─ unnecessary    ├─ compute        ├─ time
              │  work           ├─ storage        └─ location
              │                 └─ network
              └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                                ▼
                         VERIFY SLO / UX
                                │
                                ▼
                         MEASURE AGAIN
```

The critical rule is:

> **The cleanest computation is often the computation the system did not need to perform. Sustainability therefore starts with eliminating unnecessary work before attempting sophisticated carbon-aware scheduling.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — AI/LLM Sustainability**, covering **AI inference efficiency → model-size economics → model routing → token efficiency → context-window control → RAG efficiency → embedding lifecycle → vector storage → caching → batching → quantization → GPU utilization → training/fine-tuning → AI quality-energy frontier → observability footprint → log/metric/trace sustainability → CI/CD resource consumption → build caching → test selection → developer environments → database/query efficiency → Redis/Kafka efficiency → resilience-vs-resource trade-offs → multi-region footprint → DR → embodied carbon → hardware lifetime → carbon telemetry → carbon-aware platform APIs → sustainability metadata → developer portal integration → sustainability fitness functions → architecture reviews → sustainability budgets → SCI reporting → FinOps integration → optimization prioritization → governance → sustainability maturity model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse sustainable-computing reference architecture and ADR-074 decision outcome.**


# ADR-074 — Enterprise Sustainability Engineering, Green Software, Carbon-Aware Computing & Resource Efficiency Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Hidden 3D Work**.

---

# 61. AI/LLM Sustainability

AI introduces a distinct resource-consumption profile.

```text
AI Capability
     │
     ├── Prompt processing
     ├── Inference
     ├── Retrieval
     ├── Embeddings
     ├── Vector search
     ├── Evaluation
     └── Training / fine-tuning
             │
             ▼
       COMPUTE / ENERGY
```

AI features must therefore justify not only their functional value but also their computational intensity.

---

# 62. AI Value per Computation

The goal is not to minimize AI usage indiscriminately.

Measure useful outcome relative to resource consumption.

```text
Learning Value
────────────────
AI Resource Cost
```

A more expensive inference may be justified when it materially improves an important educational outcome.

---

# 63. Model Size

Larger models generally require greater computational resources.

Therefore:

```text
Task Complexity
      │
      ▼
Required Capability
      │
      ▼
Appropriate Model
```

not:

```text
Every Request
      │
      ▼
Largest Available Model
```

---

# 64. Model Routing

ADR-073's economic model-routing strategy also becomes a sustainability control.

```text
Request
   │
   ▼
Classify
   │
   ├── Simple ─────► Small Model
   ├── Standard ───► Standard Model
   └── Complex ────► High-Capability Model
```

Routing must preserve required quality and safety.

---

# 65. AI Quality-Efficiency Frontier

Model selection should evaluate:

```text
Quality
Latency
Cost
Energy/resource intensity
Safety
```

Conceptually:

```text
Quality
  ^
  |                         ● Large
  |                  ● Medium
  |           ● Small
  |
  +--------------------------------> Resource Use
```

The largest model is justified only when the additional capability matters.

---

# 66. Token Efficiency

Unnecessary tokens create unnecessary computation.

Potential waste includes:

```text
Repeated system instructions
Irrelevant conversation history
Redundant RAG context
Verbose tool outputs
Unnecessary generated text
```

---

# 67. Context Window Governance

Context should contain what the model actually needs.

```text
Available Context
      │
      ▼
Relevance Selection
      │
      ▼
Required Context
      │
      ▼
Model
```

Large context windows should not become an excuse for poor context management.

---

# 68. Conversation Compression

Long-running AI sessions may use:

```text
Recent messages
       +
Structured state
       +
Relevant retrieved history
       +
Summarized older context
```

instead of replaying the entire history indefinitely.

---

# 69. Output Efficiency

Generated responses should be bounded according to product requirements.

```text
Task
 │
 ▼
Required Information
 │
 ▼
Appropriate Output Budget
```

Generating 4,000 tokens where 300 satisfy the learning objective wastes latency and computation.

---

# 70. RAG Efficiency

RAG should retrieve the minimum context required to achieve the target answer quality.

```text
Query
  │
  ▼
Candidate Retrieval
  │
  ▼
Reranking
  │
  ▼
Relevant Context
  │
  ▼
LLM
```

---

# 71. Retrieval Top-K

Large `top-k` values should not be selected blindly.

Increasing retrieval count can increase:

```text
Vector work
Reranking work
Prompt size
Inference work
Latency
```

while potentially reducing answer quality through irrelevant context.

---

# 72. Chunk Efficiency

Chunking should balance:

```text
Retrieval precision
Embedding count
Storage
Prompt size
Semantic completeness
```

Neither extremely small nor extremely large chunks are universally optimal.

---

# 73. Embedding Lifecycle

Embeddings require lifecycle management.

```text
Document Created
      │
      ▼
Embed
      │
      ▼
Document Changed
      │
      ▼
Re-embed Changed Content
      │
      ▼
Document Deleted
      │
      ▼
Delete Embeddings
```

Deleted source content should not leave permanent orphaned vectors.

---

# 74. Incremental Embedding

Prefer changed-content processing over full-corpus re-embedding where technically appropriate.

```text
1 changed chapter
       │
       X
Re-embed 5 million chunks
```

is obvious computational waste.

---

# 75. Vector Storage Efficiency

Track:

```text
Vector count
Dimensions
Indexes
Replicas
Metadata
Retention
Unused collections
```

Vector databases require the same lifecycle discipline as other persistent systems.

---

# 76. AI Caching

Reusable AI results may be cached when correctness, personalization and privacy permit.

```text
Request
  │
  ▼
Reusable Result?
  │
 ┌┴───────┐
 ▼        ▼
YES       NO
 │         │
Cache     Infer
```

---

# 77. Cache Correctness

Sustainability cannot justify stale or incorrect AI output.

Cache keys and invalidation may need to incorporate:

```text
Model version
Prompt version
Knowledge version
User context
Policy version
```

depending on the feature.

---

# 78. AI Batching

Suitable asynchronous AI workloads may batch requests to improve hardware utilization.

Candidates include:

```text
Embedding generation
Offline evaluation
Content classification
Bulk summarization
Dataset processing
```

Interactive tutoring requests generally have different latency constraints.

---

# 79. Quantization

Self-hosted models may use quantization when evaluation demonstrates acceptable quality.

```text
Model
 │
 ▼
Reduced Precision
 │
 ├── Memory ↓
 ├── Compute ↓
 └── Possible Quality Change
```

Quality regression must be measured rather than assumed absent.

---

# 80. GPU Utilization

GPU allocation should expose:

```text
GPU utilization
Memory utilization
Queue depth
Batch efficiency
Idle time
Throughput
```

Expensive accelerators sitting idle represent both financial and resource inefficiency.

---

# 81. GPU Sharing

Where workload isolation and technology permit, GPU sharing may improve utilization.

However, sharing must not introduce unacceptable:

```text
Performance interference
Security risk
Memory contention
Operational complexity
```

---

# 82. GPU Scale-Down

Elastic AI infrastructure should release GPU capacity when sustained demand disappears where architecture permits.

Permanent GPU allocation for occasional experimentation is rejected.

---

# 83. Training vs Fine-Tuning

Before training or fine-tuning, ask whether the problem can be solved through:

```text
Prompting
RAG
Tools
Structured workflows
Smaller adaptation
Existing model
```

Training is not the default solution to every AI product requirement.

---

# 84. Fine-Tuning Justification

Fine-tuning should define:

```text
Quality target
Baseline
Dataset
Expected improvement
Training cost
Inference impact
Evaluation
Lifecycle
```

Without measurable benefit, repeated training cycles are waste.

---

# 85. Experiment Tracking

AI experiments should record enough metadata to avoid repeating failed expensive experiments.

```text
Model
Dataset
Parameters
Prompt
Evaluation
Resource usage
Outcome
```

---

# 86. AI Evaluation Efficiency

Evaluation suites should be representative.

Running every expensive model against every historical example on every tiny change may be unnecessary.

Use layered evaluation:

```text
Small smoke set
      │
      ▼
Regression set
      │
      ▼
Full evaluation
      │
      ▼
Specialized / safety evaluation
```

according to change risk.

---

# 87. Observability Footprint

Observability itself consumes infrastructure.

```text
Application
   │
   ├── Logs
   ├── Metrics
   └── Traces
        │
        ▼
 Collection
 Processing
 Storage
 Query
```

Telemetry must provide operational value.

---

# 88. Log Efficiency

Avoid:

```text
Duplicate logs
Huge payload logging
Permanent debug logging
Repeated stack traces
High-frequency useless events
```

Logging less is acceptable when the removed data had no operational value.

---

# 89. Metric Efficiency

Metrics should use bounded dimensions.

```text
GOOD
service
endpoint
status_class

DANGEROUS
user_id
request_id
email
session_id
```

Unbounded cardinality wastes resources and can destabilize monitoring systems.

---

# 90. Trace Efficiency

Tracing strategy should preserve useful evidence while controlling volume.

Use appropriate:

```text
Sampling
Tail-based retention
Error prioritization
Latency prioritization
Service-specific policies
```

---

# 91. Telemetry Retention

Different telemetry classes require different retention.

```text
High-value audit
      │
      ▼
Longer retention

Temporary debugging
      │
      ▼
Short retention
```

One universal retention period is rejected.

---

# 92. CI/CD Sustainability

Software delivery consumes:

```text
Runner CPU
Memory
Storage
Network
Test infrastructure
Container builds
Security scans
```

Pipeline efficiency is therefore part of sustainable engineering.

---

# 93. Build Caching

Reuse safe deterministic build work.

Examples:

```text
Maven dependencies
Node dependencies
Container layers
Compilation outputs where safe
```

Avoid repeatedly downloading and rebuilding identical inputs.

---

# 94. Incremental Builds

Where tooling supports trustworthy incremental execution:

```text
Changed Code
     │
     ▼
Affected Build Work
```

should be preferred over rebuilding unrelated components.

---

# 95. Test Selection

Testing strategy should maximize defect-detection value per execution cost.

```text
Change
  │
  ▼
Risk Analysis
  │
  ▼
Required Tests
```

This does not justify skipping critical regression or security verification.

---

# 96. Flaky Tests

Flaky tests waste:

```text
Runner resources
Developer time
Repeated execution
Investigation effort
```

Flakiness is therefore quality debt, productivity debt, cost debt and sustainability debt simultaneously.

---

# 97. CI Retry Governance

Blind retry loops are rejected.

```text
Test Failed
   │
   ▼
Retry 10 times
```

can conceal defects while multiplying compute.

Retries should exist only for understood transient failure modes.

---

# 98. Developer Environments

Local and remote development environments should avoid permanently allocated unused infrastructure.

Potential controls:

```text
Auto-stop
Hibernate
TTL
Scale-down
Shared services
On-demand startup
```

---

# 99. Remote Development

Cloud development environments should expose utilization and lifecycle.

```text
Developer starts workspace
        │
        ▼
Workspace active
        │
        ▼
Idle threshold
        │
        ▼
Suspend
```

---

# 100. Database Efficiency

Database sustainability starts with application behavior.

```text
Application
   │
   ├── Query design
   ├── Indexing
   ├── Connection usage
   ├── Result size
   └── Transaction design
```

Hardware scaling should not substitute for basic database engineering.

---

# 101. Query Efficiency

Measure:

```text
Execution time
Rows scanned
Rows returned
IO
CPU
Locking
Frequency
```

A query executed one million times deserves different attention from an equally slow query executed once per month.

---

# 102. Index Efficiency

Indexes trade:

```text
Read Performance ↑
        vs
Storage ↑
Write Work ↑
Maintenance ↑
```

Unused or redundant indexes should be detectable.

---

# 103. N+1 Query Waste

```text
1 request
   │
   ├── Query 1
   ├── Query 2
   ├── Query 3
   ├── ...
   └── Query 500
```

can waste application, database and network resources.

N+1 problems should be detected during performance engineering.

---

# 104. Connection Pool Efficiency

Oversized pools can increase:

```text
Database memory
Connection overhead
Contention
Infrastructure requirements
```

Pool size should be based on measured concurrency rather than arbitrary defaults.

---

# 105. Redis Efficiency

Redis should have a measurable purpose.

```text
Cache
Session
Rate limiting
Coordination
```

Do not introduce an always-on Redis cluster merely because a framework makes it convenient.

---

# 106. Redis Memory Lifecycle

Use:

```text
TTL
Eviction policy
Memory monitoring
Key-size monitoring
Unused-key cleanup
```

where appropriate.

---

# 107. Kafka Efficiency

Kafka sustainability depends on:

```text
Partition count
Replication
Retention
Message size
Compression
Traffic
Consumer behavior
```

---

# 108. Event Compression

Compression can reduce storage and network use for suitable event workloads.

But compression introduces CPU cost.

The correct configuration depends on the workload.

---

# 109. Kafka Retention

Retain events according to business and recovery requirements.

```text
High Throughput
      ×
Long Retention
      ×
Replication
```

can create substantial resource demand.

---

# 110. Dead Consumers

Unused consumers, abandoned consumer groups and obsolete topics should be discoverable and removed through controlled lifecycle management.

---

# 111. Resilience Resource Trade-Off

Reliability often requires redundancy.

```text
Replica 1
Replica 2
Replica 3
```

uses more resources than a singleton.

This is not automatically waste.

---

# 112. Sustainability vs Reliability

Never optimize:

```text
3 replicas → 1 replica
```

without evaluating:

```text
Availability
Failure tolerance
Maintenance
Traffic
Recovery
```

Required resilience has legitimate resource cost.

---

# 113. Redundancy Right-Sizing

The goal is:

```text
Minimum redundancy
that satisfies
required reliability
```

not maximum redundancy everywhere.

---

# 114. Multi-AZ Footprint

Multi-AZ infrastructure may be required for availability.

Optimize unnecessary replication and traffic without eliminating required fault tolerance.

---

# 115. Multi-Region Footprint

Multi-region architectures multiply:

```text
Compute
Storage
Replication
Network
Operational systems
```

They therefore require explicit business justification.

---

# 116. Disaster Recovery Sustainability

DR strategy should align with required RTO/RPO.

```text
Backup/Restore
      │
Pilot Light
      │
Warm Standby
      │
Active/Passive
      │
Active/Active

Resource requirement ↑
```

Do not maintain active/active infrastructure merely for architectural prestige.

---

# 117. Recovery Testing

An apparently efficient backup-only DR architecture that cannot actually recover is not sustainable engineering.

Recovery capability must be tested.

---

# 118. Embodied Carbon

Software ultimately runs on physical hardware whose manufacturing has environmental impact.

Conceptually:

```text
Hardware Footprint
       =
Operational Energy
       +
Embodied Impact
```

Exact allocation may be difficult in public cloud environments.

---

# 119. Hardware Efficiency

Higher useful utilization can reduce the amount of hardware capacity required to deliver equivalent work.

```text
10 poorly utilized servers
          │
          ▼
5 efficiently utilized servers
```

may reduce both operational and embodied resource demand, subject to resilience requirements.

---

# 120. Hardware Lifetime

Software requirements can indirectly shorten device/server usefulness.

Avoid unnecessary:

```text
Memory inflation
CPU inflation
GPU requirements
Bundle growth
Asset growth
```

that provide little user value.

This is especially important for student devices.

---

# 121. Backward Device Support

Efficient Mediverse applications should remain usable on reasonable older hardware where product requirements permit.

This improves both accessibility and device longevity.

---

# 122. Carbon Telemetry

Where reliable data is available, the platform may ingest:

```text
Cloud usage
Energy estimates
Region carbon intensity
Resource utilization
Functional workload volume
```

to derive sustainability metrics.

---

# 123. Carbon Data Pipeline

```text
Cloud / Platform Usage
          │
          ▼
Resource Consumption
          │
          +
Carbon Intensity
          │
          ▼
Estimated Emissions
          │
          +
Functional Units
          │
          ▼
SCI / Intensity Metrics
```

---

# 124. Carbon Signal Reliability

Carbon-aware automation should account for data:

```text
Freshness
Geographic resolution
Temporal resolution
Methodology
Availability
Confidence
```

Do not move production workloads based on unreliable signals.

---

# 125. Sustainability Metadata

Workloads may declare characteristics such as:

```yaml
sustainability:
  workloadClass: batch
  deferrable: true
  maxDelay: 6h
  locationFlexible: false
```

This enables platform-level scheduling decisions.

---

# 126. Carbon-Aware Platform API

Conceptually:

```text
submit-job
    │
    ├── deadline
    ├── region constraints
    ├── resource requirements
    └── carbon flexibility
          │
          ▼
      Scheduler
```

The application should not implement carbon-scheduling logic independently.

---

# 127. Developer Portal Integration

ADR-071's portal should expose useful sustainability information alongside cost.

Example:

```text
Service: ai-tutor

CPU efficiency        78%
Idle capacity         12%
AI tokens/session     4,200
Estimated SCI trend   ↓ 9%
Storage growth        ↑ 14%
```

Avoid meaningless green badges.

---

# 128. Sustainability Scorecard

Potential checks:

```text
✓ Resource requests reviewed
✓ Temporary environments have TTL
✓ Storage lifecycle configured
✓ Observability cardinality controlled
⚠ AI token/session increasing
✗ Orphaned preview environments
```

---

# 129. Sustainability Fitness Functions

Machine-verifiable examples include:

```text
Temporary environment MUST have TTL
Non-prod GPU MUST have owner
Container MUST define resource requests
Large static assets MUST meet delivery budget
Logs MUST respect retention policy
```

Not every sustainability objective can be enforced automatically.

---

# 130. Resource Budgets

Teams may define budgets for:

```text
Frontend bundle size
3D asset size
API payload
AI tokens
Build duration
Storage growth
Log ingestion
```

These are engineering budgets, not merely financial budgets.

---

# 131. Budget Regression

Example:

```text
Frontend JS budget = 500 KB

PR result = 740 KB
```

The pipeline should surface the regression.

Whether it blocks deployment depends on policy severity.

---

# 132. AI Token Budget

AI capabilities should establish expected token envelopes.

```text
Feature
  │
  ├── Expected input
  ├── Expected output
  ├── RAG context
  └── Maximum
```

Unexpected growth becomes observable.

---

# 133. Architecture Review

Significant ADRs should answer:

```text
What work is performed?
What can be avoided?
What is always-on?
What scales with demand?
What data is retained?
What network movement occurs?
What accelerator resources are required?
Can work shift in time/location?
What is the reliability trade-off?
```

---

# 134. Sustainability Review Scope

Heavy sustainability review should be reserved for material workloads such as:

```text
Large AI systems
Large-scale data processing
High-bandwidth media
3D delivery
Multi-region systems
GPU infrastructure
High-volume telemetry
```

Do not create bureaucracy for trivial application changes.

---

# 135. Sustainability Optimization Backlog

Opportunities should include:

```text
Resource saving
Estimated carbon/resource impact
Financial saving
Engineering cost
Reliability risk
User impact
Confidence
```

---

# 136. Optimization Priority

Prioritize high-impact, low-risk opportunities first.

```text
                     HIGH IMPACT
                         │
             PLAN        │      PRIORITIZE
                         │
HIGH EFFORT ─────────────┼──────────── LOW EFFORT
                         │
             AVOID       │      QUICK WIN
                         │
```

Impact estimates should not pretend to be more precise than available data allows.

---

# 137. FinOps Integration

ADR-073 and ADR-074 should share telemetry.

```text
Resource Usage
     │
     ├────► COST
     │       ADR-073
     │
     └────► RESOURCE/CARBON
             ADR-074
```

Separate duplicate measurement systems would create unnecessary complexity.

---

# 138. Joint Optimization

Prefer improvements that simultaneously reduce:

```text
Cost
Resource use
Latency
Operational complexity
```

Examples may include:

```text
Removing unused infrastructure
Query optimization
Asset compression
Build caching
Rightsizing
```

These are high-value engineering improvements.

---

# 139. Trade-Off Governance

When goals conflict:

```text
Security
Reliability
Performance
Accessibility
Cost
Sustainability
```

the trade-off should be explicit.

Sustainability does not automatically outrank safety or reliability.

---

# 140. Sustainability Governance

Ownership should be distributed.

```text
Enterprise Architecture
        │
        ├── Principles
        │
Platform Engineering
        │
        ├── Controls / telemetry
        │
FinOps
        │
        ├── Shared economics
        │
Engineering Teams
        │
        └── Workload efficiency
```

A central sustainability team cannot optimize application code it does not own.

---

# 141. Sustainability Metrics

Mediverse should prefer a focused set:

```text
SCI / functional-unit trend where measurable
Compute utilization
Idle-resource rate
Storage growth
Network transfer
AI tokens/session
GPU utilization
Observability ingestion
Frontend transfer size
3D asset transfer
CI compute time
Temporary-resource waste
```

---

# 142. Metric Interpretation

Metrics must be interpreted alongside product demand.

Example:

```text
Total AI compute ↑ 50%
AI tutoring sessions ↑ 200%
```

may represent improved efficiency rather than deterioration.

Intensity metrics prevent simplistic conclusions.

---

# 143. Sustainability Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — UNAWARE
Resource consumption largely invisible.

LEVEL 2 — VISIBLE
Major workloads and waste measured.

LEVEL 3 — EFFICIENT
Rightsizing, lifecycle and resource budgets standardized.

LEVEL 4 — OPTIMIZED
Sustainability integrated into platform and architecture.

LEVEL 5 — CARBON-AWARE
Flexible workloads respond intelligently to reliable carbon signals.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, adopting Level 5 selectively where it provides measurable benefit.

---

# 144. Sustainability Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Calling ordinary cost reduction "green" without evidence
❌ Carbon claims with false precision
❌ Optimizing carbon while violating security
❌ Optimizing carbon while violating SLOs
❌ Assuming cheaper automatically means greener
❌ Assuming cloud automatically means sustainable
❌ Moving workloads without considering data transfer
❌ Carbon-aware scheduling for latency-critical requests
❌ Maximum Kubernetes utilization as target
❌ Removing resilience headroom
❌ Oversized Kubernetes requests left indefinitely
❌ Non-production infrastructure running forever
❌ Temporary environments without TTL
❌ Serverless automatically considered sustainable
❌ Data retained forever
❌ Duplicate datasets without purpose
❌ Huge API payloads
❌ Unbounded API collections
❌ Aggressive polling without need
❌ Massive frontend bundles
❌ Third-party scripts without value review
❌ Entire 3D worlds downloaded at startup
❌ 4K textures on tiny objects
❌ Rendering hidden scenes continuously
❌ Largest LLM used for every task
❌ Huge context windows filled because capacity exists
❌ Excessive RAG top-k
❌ Full corpus re-embedded after tiny changes
❌ Orphaned vectors retained forever
❌ GPUs permanently allocated to occasional experiments
❌ Fine-tuning without measurable quality objective
❌ Repeating AI experiments without tracking results
❌ Every AI evaluation executed for every trivial change
❌ Unlimited observability ingestion
❌ High-cardinality metric labels
❌ Debug telemetry retained indefinitely
❌ CI repeatedly rebuilding identical dependencies
❌ Blind test retries
❌ Cloud developer workspaces never suspended
❌ Scaling databases instead of fixing obvious query defects
❌ Redis introduced without measurable value
❌ Kafka retention set indefinitely by default
❌ Reliability redundancy classified automatically as waste
❌ Active/active multi-region architecture without requirement
❌ Sustainability scorecards reduced to green badges
❌ Sustainability review required for every tiny code change
❌ Separate FinOps and sustainability telemetry stacks collecting identical data
```

---

# 145. Sustainability Decision Flow

```text
                    NEW WORKLOAD / CHANGE
                             │
                             ▼
                        USER VALUE?
                             │
                             ▼
                      REQUIRED WORK?
                        ┌────┴────┐
                        ▼         ▼
                       NO        YES
                        │         │
                      REMOVE      ▼
                           MINIMIZE WORK
                                 │
                                 ▼
                         RESOURCE PROFILE
                                 │
               ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
               ▼                 ▼                 ▼
            COMPUTE           STORAGE           NETWORK
               │                 │                 │
               └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                                 ▼
                           FLEXIBILITY?
                                 │
                  ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
                  ▼              ▼              ▼
                TIME          LOCATION        NONE
                  │              │              │
                  └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                                 ▼
                         OPTIMIZED EXECUTION
                                 │
                                 ▼
                     SLO / SECURITY / UX CHECK
                                 │
                         ┌───────┴───────┐
                         ▼               ▼
                       PASS             FAIL
                         │               │
                         ▼               ▼
                       RUN            REDESIGN
                         │
                         ▼
                       MEASURE
                         │
                         └────────────► IMPROVE
```

---

```text
                 └────────────┼────────────┘

                       RESOURCE SIGNAL
```

```text
                                │
               ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
               ▼                ▼                ▼
             FINOPS       SUSTAINABILITY     RELIABILITY
            ADR-073          ADR-074             SLO

                       ARCHITECTURE EVIDENCE
```

---

# 148. Final Mediverse Sustainable Computing Reference Architecture

```text
                              MEDIVERSE USERS
                                     │
                                     ▼
                                USER VALUE
                                     │
```
