# 150. Governing Invariant

The entire ADR reduces to:

```text
                        USER VALUE
                            │
                            ▼
                      REQUIRED WORK
                            │
                            ▼
                 CAN WORK BE AVOIDED?
                     ┌──────┴──────┐
                     ▼             ▼
                    YES            NO
                     │             │
                   REMOVE          ▼
                            CAN IT BE REDUCED?
                              ┌────┴────┐
                              ▼         ▼
                             YES        NO
                              │         │
                           OPTIMIZE      ▼
                                  CAN IT BE SHIFTED?
                                    ┌───┴───┐
                                    ▼       ▼
                                   YES      NO
                                    │       │
                                  SHIFT     RUN
                                    │       │
                                    └───┬───┘
                                        ▼
                                VERIFY QUALITY
                                        │
                     ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
                     ▼                  ▼                  ▼
                  SECURITY          RELIABILITY            UX
                     │                  │                  │
                     └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                                        ▼
                                     MEASURE
                                        │
                                        ▼
                                     IMPROVE
```

> **Mediverse will not treat sustainability as a branding exercise or pursue lower resource consumption at the expense of security, reliability, accessibility or learning quality. The architecture must first eliminate unnecessary computation, then reduce unavoidable work, improve hardware utilization, and only then apply temporal or spatial carbon-aware execution where trustworthy signals and workload flexibility make it technically justified.**

# ADR-074 — COMPLETE ✅

## Next — ADR-075

### **ADR-075 — Enterprise Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery, Cyber Resilience & Operational Resilience Standard**

This should now close a major gap across the previous architecture.

ADR-075 should define **business impact analysis → critical business services → service tiering → dependency criticality → maximum tolerable downtime → RTO → RPO → recovery tiers → failure-domain analysis → AZ failure → region failure → Kubernetes cluster loss → database corruption → PostgreSQL PITR → Redis loss → Kafka recovery → object-storage recovery → search/vector-index rebuild → AI provider outage → third-party SaaS outage → DNS/CDN failure → identity-provider failure → secrets/KMS failure → GitHub/SCM outage → CI/CD outage → Argo CD/GitOps failure → Terraform-state loss → observability outage → ransomware/cyber recovery → immutable backups → backup isolation → credential compromise → clean-room recovery → break-glass access → recovery runbooks → dependency startup order → degraded operating modes → read-only mode → AI-disabled mode → feature shedding → data reconciliation → failover/failback → disaster declaration → incident command → communication → recovery exercises → tabletop testing → restore testing → chaos engineering integration → multi-region decision framework → DR economics → regulatory evidence → recovery metrics → resilience scorecards → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise operational-resilience reference architecture.**

# ADR-075 — Enterprise Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery, Cyber Resilience & Operational Resilience Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-075
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Primary Stakeholders:** SRE, Platform Engineering, Security Engineering, Cloud Infrastructure, Database Engineering, Product Engineering, Incident Management, Business Continuity, FinOps

ADR-074 established sustainability and resource-efficiency governance.

ADR-075 establishes how Mediverse continues operating—or recovers safely—when infrastructure, software, data, cloud regions, dependencies, credentials, or operational systems fail.

The fundamental distinction is:

> **High availability reduces the probability and impact of disruption. Disaster recovery determines what happens after disruption exceeds the system's normal fault-tolerance boundary.**

```text
                     BUSINESS SERVICE
                           │
                           ▼
                    CRITICALITY MODEL
                           │
             ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
             ▼             ▼             ▼
            MTD           RTO           RPO
             │             │             │
             └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                           ▼
                     RECOVERY DESIGN
                           │
        ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
        ▼                  ▼                  ▼
   AVAILABILITY          BACKUP              DR
        │                  │                  │
        └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                           ▼
                     FAILURE OCCURS
                           │
                           ▼
                  CONTAIN → RECOVER
                           │
                           ▼
                       VALIDATE
                           │
                           ▼
                       FAILBACK
                           │
                           ▼
                        LEARN
```

# 1. Operational Resilience Objective

Mediverse must be capable of:

```text
Withstanding expected failures
Detecting major disruption
Containing blast radius
Continuing critical capabilities
Recovering data
Recovering infrastructure
Recovering dependencies
Operating in degraded modes
Restoring normal service
Validating integrity
Learning from recovery
```

---

# 2. Resilience Is a Business Property

Infrastructure availability alone does not define resilience.

```text
Infrastructure UP
      │
      ▼
Application UP
      │
      ▼
Critical workflow broken
      │
      ▼
Business service DOWN
```

Therefore resilience targets begin with business capabilities.

---

# 3. Critical Business Services

Mediverse should maintain an explicit catalogue of critical services such as:

```text
Authentication
Course access
Learning content delivery
Assessment
Progress persistence
Administrative operations
AI tutoring
Notifications
Reporting
```

Not all capabilities require identical recovery objectives.

---

# 4. Business Impact Analysis

Each important capability requires a Business Impact Analysis.

Evaluate:

```text
User impact
Financial impact
Academic impact
Data impact
Security impact
Compliance impact
Reputation
Operational dependency
Duration sensitivity
```

---

# 5. Maximum Tolerable Downtime

MTD represents the longest disruption the business can tolerate before consequences become unacceptable.

```text
Failure
  │
  ├─────────────── MTD ───────────────►
  │
  ▼
Impact grows with time
```

RTO must fit within this boundary.

---

# 6. Recovery Time Objective

```text
RTO =
Target duration between disruption
and restoration of required capability
```

RTO is a design requirement—not a number invented after the architecture exists.

---

# 7. Recovery Point Objective

```text
RPO =
Maximum acceptable amount
of data loss measured in time
```

Example:

```text
RPO = 15 minutes

Disaster at 14:00
        │
        ▼
Recovery may legitimately restore
state as old as 13:45
```

---

# 8. RTO and RPO Are Different

```text
RPO → How much data can we lose?

RTO → How long can service remain unavailable?
```

Confusing them leads to incorrect DR architecture.

---

# 9. Recovery Objectives Must Be Realistic

This combination:

```text
RTO = 30 seconds
RPO = 0
Cost = minimal
Architecture = simple
```

is generally contradictory.

Aggressive recovery objectives require engineering and infrastructure investment.

---

# 10. Recovery Service Tiers

Mediverse adopts service recovery tiers.

```text
TIER 0
Critical platform foundations

TIER 1
Critical user/business capabilities

TIER 2
Important capabilities

TIER 3
Non-critical / deferrable capabilities
```

---

# 11. Tier 0

Potential Tier 0 capabilities include:

```text
DNS
Identity foundations
Secrets/KMS
Core networking
Kubernetes control foundations
Primary data recovery capability
Recovery access
```

Exact classification must follow BIA.

---

# 12. Tier 1

Potential examples:

```text
Authentication
Course access
Critical learning APIs
Assessment submission
Progress persistence
```

These generally receive stronger recovery targets.

---

# 13. Tier 2

Examples may include:

```text
Search
Notifications
Analytics
Recommendations
Non-critical administration
```

They may recover after core learning capabilities.

---

# 14. Tier 3

Examples may include:

```text
Historical reporting
Optional personalization
Background analytics
Experimental features
```

These should not delay recovery of critical services.

---

# 15. Dependency Criticality

A Tier 1 service depending synchronously on a Tier 3 dependency can accidentally inherit Tier 3 resilience.

```text
Tier 1 Service
     │
     ▼
Tier 3 Dependency
     │
     ▼
Effective resilience weakened
```

Dependency criticality must therefore be mapped.

---

# 16. Dependency Graph

Maintain recovery-aware dependency relationships.

```text
User
 │
 ▼
Frontend
 │
 ▼
Identity
 │
 ▼
API
 ├── PostgreSQL
 ├── Redis
 ├── Kafka
 ├── Object Storage
 └── AI Provider
```

Recovery order follows dependency reality.

---

# 17. Failure Domains

Architecture must reason explicitly about:

```text
Process
Pod
Node
Availability Zone
Cluster
Region
Cloud service
Cloud account
Identity plane
Control plane
External provider
Human/operator
Data integrity
```

---

# 18. Failure Scope

Recovery strategy depends on scope.

```text
Pod failure
   │
   ▼
Normal Kubernetes recovery

Region failure
   │
   ▼
Disaster recovery

Database corruption
   │
   ▼
Data recovery

Credential compromise
   │
   ▼
Cyber recovery
```

Not every incident is a disaster.

---

# 19. High Availability vs DR

```text
NORMAL FAILURE
     │
     ▼
High Availability
     │
     ▼
Automatic Recovery

CATASTROPHIC FAILURE
     │
     ▼
Disaster Recovery
     │
     ▼
Controlled Recovery
```

Both are required where justified.

---

# 20. Recovery Strategies

Common strategies:

```text
Recreate
Restore
Failover
Rebuild
Rehydrate
Reconcile
Degrade
Isolate
```

A service may require several.

---

# 21. Availability Zone Failure

Production workloads should tolerate expected AZ failures where required by their service tier.

Potential mechanisms:

```text
Multiple replicas
Topology spread
Multi-AZ data services
Load balancing
Pod disruption controls
Capacity headroom
```

---

# 22. Hidden AZ Dependency

Running application pods across three AZs does not create AZ resilience if the database exists in one AZ.

```text
App: Multi-AZ
DB:  Single-AZ
       │
       ▼
Overall service:
Single-AZ dependency
```

Resilience is limited by the weakest critical dependency.

---

# 23. Kubernetes Node Failure

Expected node failure should normally be handled automatically.

```text
Node Lost
   │
   ▼
Pods unavailable
   │
   ▼
Scheduler
   │
   ▼
Replacement placement
```

This is HA—not DR.

---

# 24. Kubernetes Cluster Loss

Cluster destruction requires a stronger recovery capability.

Recovery should not depend on manually remembering how the cluster was configured.

```text
Cluster Lost
    │
    ▼
Infrastructure as Code
    │
    ▼
Cluster Recreated
    │
    ▼
Platform Bootstrap
    │
    ▼
GitOps Reconciliation
```

---

# 25. Rebuildable Infrastructure

Infrastructure should be reconstructable from controlled sources:

```text
Terraform
Helm
GitOps manifests
Configuration repositories
Secrets recovery process
Container registry
Artifact repositories
```

Manual console state is recovery debt.

---

# 26. Cluster State Classification

Not all Kubernetes state should be treated equally.

```text
DECLARATIVE STATE
      │
      └── Recreate from Git/IaC

PERSISTENT BUSINESS STATE
      │
      └── Recover from data systems/backups

EPHEMERAL STATE
      │
      └── Discard/recreate
```

---

# 27. GitOps Recovery

GitOps provides substantial recovery value.

```text
New Cluster
    │
    ▼
Bootstrap Argo CD
    │
    ▼
Connect Git
    │
    ▼
Reconcile Desired State
```

But Git itself becomes a recovery dependency.

---

# 28. Git Repository Recovery

Critical repositories require protection against:

```text
Accidental deletion
Malicious deletion
Provider outage
Credential compromise
Repository corruption
```

Recovery must not assume the primary SCM is always available.

---

# 29. CI/CD Outage

Application runtime should not collapse merely because Jenkins/GitHub Actions or equivalent CI is unavailable.

```text
CI DOWN
  │
  X
Production runtime continues
```

Deployment capability may be degraded, but serving capability should remain independent.

---

# 30. Argo CD Outage

GitOps control-plane failure should generally affect deployment/reconciliation—not immediately terminate running workloads.

Recovery procedures must exist for:

```text
Argo CD loss
Argo CD state corruption
Credential loss
Repository connectivity failure
```

---

# 31. Terraform State Criticality

Terraform state may contain essential infrastructure mapping.

Protect using:

```text
Remote backend
Versioning
Encryption
Access control
Locking
Backup/recovery
Auditability
```

---

# 32. Terraform State Loss

Recovery must distinguish:

```text
Infrastructure exists
State lost
```

from:

```text
Infrastructure lost
State exists
```

These require different procedures.

---

# 33. Database Resilience

PostgreSQL recovery must address:

```text
Instance failure
AZ failure
Storage failure
Logical corruption
Accidental deletion
Bad migration
Region failure
Credential compromise
```

Replication alone does not solve all of them.

---

# 34. Replication Is Not Backup

```text
DELETE FROM important_table;
          │
          ▼
Primary
          │
          ▼
Replica
          │
          ▼
Deletion replicated
```

Replication improves availability.

Backup/PITR protects recoverability.

---

# 35. PostgreSQL Point-in-Time Recovery

PITR should permit recovery to an appropriate point before corruption or destructive change.

```text
13:00 ───── 13:20 ───── 13:40 ───── 14:00
               │
               ▼
         Bad migration

Recovery target:
13:19:xx
```

---

# 36. Database Restore Testing

A backup that has never been restored is an assumption.

Required cycle:

```text
Backup
  │
  ▼
Restore
  │
  ▼
Integrity validation
  │
  ▼
Application validation
  │
  ▼
Evidence
```

---

# 37. Database Recovery Integrity

Successful database startup does not prove successful recovery.

Validate:

```text
Schema
Critical tables
Referential integrity
Recent transactions
Application queries
Migration compatibility
Business invariants
```

---

# 38. Bad Migration Recovery

Database migrations can create disasters without infrastructure failure.

Recovery strategy may involve:

```text
Forward fix
Rollback where safe
PITR
Data repair
Application rollback
Traffic isolation
```

Migration design must account for recoverability.

---

# 39. Redis Recovery

Redis recovery depends on its role.

```text
CACHE
  │
  └── Rebuild acceptable

SESSION STORE
  │
  └── User/session impact

CRITICAL STATE
  │
  └── Stronger persistence required
```

Do not apply one recovery policy to every Redis use case.

---

# 40. Cache Loss

If Redis is only a cache:

```text
Redis Lost
   │
   ▼
Cache Misses
   │
   ▼
Repopulate
```

The primary concern becomes load amplification against backing systems.

---

# 41. Cache Stampede During Recovery

After cache loss:

```text
Thousands of clients
        │
        ▼
Empty Cache
        │
        ▼
Database
        │
        ▼
OVERLOAD
```

Recovery should include controlled warming, rate limiting or request coalescing where required.

---

# 42. Kafka Recovery

Kafka recovery must consider:

```text
Broker failure
AZ failure
Cluster failure
Topic deletion
Retention loss
Consumer state
Producer replay
Message duplication
Ordering
```

---

# 43. Event Replay

Event-driven systems should understand whether events can be replayed safely.

```text
Replay
  │
  ▼
Consumer
  │
  ▼
Idempotent?
 ┌┴────┐
 ▼     ▼
YES    NO
 │      │
Safe   Duplicate side effects
```

Idempotency becomes a recovery capability.

---

# 44. Consumer Offset Recovery

Kafka data may exist while consumer progress is lost or corrupted.

Recovery procedures must account for:

```text
Offset reset
Replay boundary
Duplicate processing
Missing processing
Business reconciliation
```

---

# 45. Object Storage Recovery

Object storage strategy should consider:

```text
Versioning
Replication
Deletion protection
Lifecycle
Backup
Integrity
Metadata
```

particularly for irreplaceable learning content.

---

# 46. Accidental Object Deletion

Versioning can reduce recovery complexity.

```text
Object v1
   │
Object v2
   │
Delete marker
   │
   ▼
Recover previous version
```

where supported.

---

# 47. Search Recovery

Search indexes should generally be treated as derived state when authoritative source data exists.

```text
PostgreSQL / Source
        │
        ▼
Re-index
        │
        ▼
Search Engine
```

Do not create unnecessarily complex backup architectures for fully reproducible indexes.

---

# 48. Vector Index Recovery

Likewise:

```text
Authoritative Documents
       +
Embedding Configuration
       +
Model Version
       │
       ▼
Rebuild Vector Index
```

may be preferable to treating the vector store as irreplaceable state.

---

# 49. Vector Recovery Time

Rebuildability does not mean recovery is instantaneous.

For millions of vectors:

```text
Re-embedding
+
Index construction
+
Validation
=
Potentially long RTO
```

Recovery strategy must account for scale.

---

# 50. AI Provider Failure

Mediverse must assume external AI providers can fail.

```text
AI Request
   │
   ▼
Provider unavailable
   │
   ├── Retry?
   ├── Alternate model?
   ├── Alternate provider?
   └── AI-disabled mode?
```

---

# 51. AI Is Not Necessarily Tier 0

If core learning can continue without AI:

```text
AI unavailable
      │
      ▼
Traditional learning continues
```

This may be preferable to expensive multi-provider AI failover.

Criticality must follow business need rather than AI enthusiasm.

---

# 52. AI Provider Failover

Multi-provider failover introduces:

```text
Prompt compatibility
Model behavior differences
Safety differences
Tool differences
Latency differences
Cost differences
Data-processing differences
```

It should not be implemented casually.

---

# 53. AI-Degraded Mode

Potential degraded behavior:

```text
AI Tutor unavailable

Courses           ✓
Assessments       ✓
Progress          ✓
Search            ✓
AI Tutor          ✗
```

A partial service can be more resilient than an all-or-nothing platform.

---

# 54. Third-Party SaaS Failure

Catalogue external dependencies such as:

```text
Identity
Email
SMS
Payment
AI
Analytics
SCM
Monitoring
CDN
```

and define failure behavior for critical ones.

---

# 55. Dependency Timeout

External calls require bounded timeouts.

```text
Request
  │
  ▼
Third party hangs
  │
  X
Thread waits forever
```

Unbounded dependency waiting can propagate outages.

---

# 56. Retry Discipline

Retries must be:

```text
Bounded
Backed off
Jittered
Idempotency-aware
Failure-aware
```

Unlimited retry storms make incidents worse.

---

# 57. Circuit Breaking

```text
Dependency failing
       │
       ▼
Failure threshold
       │
       ▼
Circuit open
       │
       ▼
Stop unnecessary pressure
```

Circuit breakers are useful where failure modes justify them.

---

# 58. DNS Failure

DNS is often an underestimated Tier 0 dependency.

Recovery planning should include:

```text
Provider outage
Bad DNS deployment
Zone deletion
Credential compromise
TTL behavior
Secondary/recovery procedures
```

---

# 59. CDN Failure

Static content delivery should have defined behavior if CDN service becomes unavailable.

Options may include:

```text
Alternate CDN
Origin fallback
Reduced content mode
Static emergency site
```

depending on criticality.

---

# 60. Identity Provider Failure

Identity outages can block the entire application even while every application service remains healthy.

```text
Users
  │
  ▼
Identity Provider ✗
  │
  X
Application
```

Identity therefore requires explicit continuity architecture.

---

## ADR-075 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The emerging operational-resilience model is:

```text
                         BUSINESS SERVICE
                                │
                                ▼
                         BUSINESS IMPACT
                                │
                  ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
                  ▼             ▼             ▼
                 MTD           RTO           RPO
                  │             │             │
                  └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                                ▼
                          SERVICE TIER
                                │
                                ▼
                       DEPENDENCY GRAPH
                                │
      ┌─────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┐
      ▼                         ▼                         ▼
 INFRASTRUCTURE               DATA                  EXTERNAL
      │                         │                         │
      ├─ Node                   ├─ PostgreSQL             ├─ Identity
      ├─ AZ                     ├─ Redis                  ├─ AI
      ├─ Cluster                ├─ Kafka                  ├─ DNS/CDN
      └─ Region                 ├─ Objects                └─ SaaS
                                └─ Vector/Search
      │                         │                         │
      └─────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┘
                                ▼
                           FAILURE EVENT
                                │
                  ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
                  ▼             ▼             ▼
               CONTAIN       DEGRADE       RECOVER
                  │             │             │
                  └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                                ▼
                       DATA/STATE VALIDATION
                                │
                                ▼
                         SERVICE RESTORATION
                                │
                                ▼
                             FAILBACK
                                │
                                ▼
                       RECOVERY EVIDENCE
                                │
                                ▼
                    ARCHITECTURE IMPROVEMENT
```

The critical rule is:

> **A recovery plan is not evidence of recoverability. Mediverse considers a capability recoverable only when the required infrastructure, data, credentials, dependencies, procedures and people can actually restore it within its agreed recovery objectives under tested conditions.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Identity Continuity & Emergency Authentication**, then cover **secrets/KMS failure → break-glass access → credential compromise → observability outage → region loss → multi-region DR models → backup/restore → pilot light → warm standby → active/passive → active/active → DR economics → immutable backups → backup isolation → ransomware → cyber recovery → clean-room recovery → trusted artifacts → dependency startup order → recovery orchestration → degraded operating modes → read-only mode → feature shedding → traffic management → disaster declaration → incident command → communication → data reconciliation → failover validation → failback → split-brain prevention → recovery runbooks → automation → restore drills → tabletop exercises → game days → chaos engineering integration → regulatory evidence → recovery metrics → resilience scorecards → operational-resilience fitness functions → governance → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise operational-resilience reference architecture and ADR-075 decision outcome.**

# ADR-075 — Enterprise Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery, Cyber Resilience & Operational Resilience Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Identity Provider Failure**.

---

# 61. Identity Continuity

Identity is part of the recovery control plane.

```text
Application healthy
Database healthy
Kubernetes healthy
Network healthy
        │
        ▼
Identity unavailable
        │
        ▼
Users cannot authenticate
        │
        ▼
Business service unavailable
```

Identity continuity must therefore be designed according to business criticality.

---

# 62. Emergency Authentication

Recovery personnel must retain a controlled path into critical infrastructure when normal identity systems are unavailable.

```text
Normal Access
     │
     ▼
Enterprise IdP
     │
     X
Unavailable
     │
     ▼
Break-Glass Path
```

This path must not become an everyday authentication shortcut.

---

# 63. Break-Glass Accounts

Break-glass access should be:

```text
Rarely used
Strongly protected
Independent of failed identity dependencies
Audited
Alerted
Periodically tested
Credential-rotated
Time-bounded where possible
```

A break-glass account whose credentials nobody can retrieve during an emergency provides no resilience.

---

# 64. Break-Glass Governance

Use should trigger immediate security visibility.

```text
Break-Glass Login
       │
       ├── Alert
       ├── Audit
       ├── Incident record
       ├── Session monitoring
       └── Post-use credential rotation
```

---

# 65. Secrets Management Failure

Applications may depend on secrets infrastructure for:

```text
Database credentials
API credentials
TLS material
Signing keys
Service credentials
Third-party tokens
```

Loss of the secrets control plane must have defined runtime and recovery behavior.

---

# 66. Runtime Secret Independence

Where technically safe, an already-running application should not necessarily fail instantly because the secret-management control plane becomes temporarily unavailable.

```text
Secrets Manager unavailable
          │
          ├── Existing workload continues
          │
          └── New workload may fail startup
```

The exact behavior depends on credential rotation and security requirements.

---

# 67. KMS Failure

Encryption creates a critical recovery dependency.

```text
Backup exists
   │
   ▼
Encryption Key unavailable
   │
   ▼
Backup unusable
```

Backing up encrypted data without protecting recovery access to the required keys is incomplete.

---

# 68. Key Recovery

Critical encryption keys require appropriately protected recovery mechanisms consistent with the security architecture.

Recovery must consider:

```text
Deletion
Disablement
Permission loss
Account compromise
Region loss
Operator error
```

---

# 69. Credential Compromise

A disaster can be caused by security compromise rather than infrastructure destruction.

```text
Credential Compromised
        │
        ▼
Contain
        │
        ▼
Revoke
        │
        ▼
Rotate
        │
        ▼
Assess Impact
        │
        ▼
Recover Trusted State
```

---

# 70. Credential Rotation During Recovery

Recovery procedures should identify dependent credentials rather than rotate randomly.

```text
Compromised Root
      │
      ▼
Dependency Graph
      │
      ├── Cloud credentials
      ├── Database credentials
      ├── Git credentials
      ├── CI/CD credentials
      ├── Registry credentials
      └── Third-party tokens
```

---

# 71. Observability Outage

Monitoring infrastructure itself can fail.

```text
Production
   │
   ▼
Observability ✗
   │
   ▼
System state uncertain
```

Absence of alerts during a monitoring outage does not mean the platform is healthy.

---

# 72. Monitoring the Monitoring

Critical observability components should have independent health signals where justified.

```text
Prometheus
Grafana
Log platform
Alerting
      │
      ▼
External / independent health check
```

---

# 73. Observability Degraded Mode

During telemetry failure, operators may rely temporarily on:

```text
Cloud-native health
Kubernetes status
Load-balancer health
Synthetic probes
Application health endpoints
Database health
Direct logs
```

Recovery runbooks should identify these alternate signals.

---

# 74. Region Failure

Region loss is materially different from an AZ failure.

```text
REGION A
   │
   X
Unavailable
   │
   ▼
Can critical Mediverse capabilities
operate elsewhere?
```

The answer must be determined before the incident.

---

# 75. Multi-Region Is Not Automatically Required

Mediverse rejects:

```text
"Enterprise platform"
       │
       ▼
"Therefore active-active multi-region"
```

Multi-region architecture must be justified by:

```text
BIA
RTO
RPO
Availability requirement
Regulation
User geography
DR economics
```

---

# 76. DR Strategy Spectrum

```text
Backup & Restore
       │
       ▼
Pilot Light
       │
       ▼
Warm Standby
       │
       ▼
Active / Passive
       │
       ▼
Active / Active
```

Moving downward generally increases readiness, complexity and cost.

---

# 77. Backup-and-Restore DR

```text
PRIMARY REGION
     │
     ▼
Backups
     │
     ▼
Protected Storage

Disaster
     │
     ▼
Create Infrastructure
     │
     ▼
Restore Data
     │
     ▼
Start Services
```

Suitable where longer RTO is acceptable.

---

# 78. Pilot-Light DR

Maintain only essential foundations in the recovery region.

```text
Recovery Region

Networking       ✓
Critical data    ✓
Core security    ✓
Minimal platform ✓
Full compute     ✗
```

During disaster, remaining capacity is provisioned.

---

# 79. Warm Standby

```text
Primary Region
   │
   ▼
Full Production Capacity

Recovery Region
   │
   ▼
Reduced Running Capacity
```

During failover:

```text
Scale recovery region
        │
        ▼
Redirect traffic
```

This reduces RTO at increased steady-state cost.

---

# 80. Active/Passive

A passive environment is maintained ready for promotion.

```text
Region A
 ACTIVE
   │
   ├──── replication ────► Region B
   │                       PASSIVE
```

Failover procedures must address data consistency and traffic switching.

---

# 81. Active/Active

```text
Users
  │
  ├────────► Region A
  │
  └────────► Region B
```

Both regions serve production traffic.

This introduces difficult problems around:

```text
Data consistency
Conflict resolution
Routing
Sessions
Replication
Split brain
Operational complexity
Testing
```

---

# 82. DR Economics

Recovery architecture should satisfy:

```text
Required Recovery Capability
────────────────────────────
Sustainable Cost + Complexity
```

The strongest possible DR architecture is not automatically the correct one.

---

# 83. Recovery Cost Curve

```text
Cost
 ^
 |                         ● Active/Active
 |                  ● Active/Passive
 |             ● Warm Standby
 |        ● Pilot Light
 |   ● Backup/Restore
 |
 +--------------------------------------> Recovery Speed
```

ADR-073 FinOps governance applies directly.

---

# 84. Data Replication Strategy

Replication should define:

```text
Source
Target
Direction
Latency
Consistency
Failure behavior
Recovery authority
```

"Replicated" alone is insufficient documentation.

---

# 85. Synchronous Replication

Synchronous replication can reduce data loss but may increase:

```text
Write latency
Failure coupling
Network dependency
```

It must match actual RPO requirements.

---

# 86. Asynchronous Replication

Asynchronous replication can reduce runtime coupling but introduces a replication gap.

```text
Primary
  │
  ├── Transaction T1
  ├── Transaction T2
  ├── Transaction T3
  │
  X Disaster
  │
Replica has only T1/T2
```

The potential gap must fit the agreed RPO.

---

# 87. Backup Strategy

Critical data should define:

```text
Backup frequency
Retention
Encryption
Isolation
Immutability
Location
Restore procedure
Validation
Ownership
```

A backup job returning `SUCCESS` proves only that the job completed.

---

# 88. Immutable Backups

Critical backups should be protected against modification/deletion for an appropriate period where supported.

```text
Attacker
   │
   ├── Encrypt production
   └── Delete backups
             │
             X
        Immutable Copy
```

This is particularly important for cyber recovery.

---

# 89. Backup Isolation

Backup access should not share unrestricted administrative paths with production.

```text
Production Admin Compromised
            │
            X
     Backup Security Boundary
            │
            ▼
      Recovery Copy Survives
```

---

# 90. Backup Account Separation

For sufficiently critical workloads, backups may require stronger isolation through separate:

```text
Accounts
Credentials
Roles
Policies
Administrative boundaries
```

according to the threat model.

---

# 91. Backup Geographic Diversity

A regional disaster should not destroy both production and its only recovery copy.

Backup placement must match the disaster scenarios the architecture claims to survive.

---

# 92. Backup Retention

Retention should support:

```text
Operational recovery
Delayed corruption discovery
Security incidents
Compliance
Forensics
```

while ADR-073 and ADR-074 govern unnecessary storage.

---

# 93. Ransomware Recovery

Ransomware changes the recovery problem.

```text
Normal DR:
Infrastructure failed

Cyber DR:
Infrastructure may exist
but cannot be trusted
```

Recovery must restore **trusted state**, not merely available state.

---

# 94. Cyber Recovery

Cyber recovery requires determining:

```text
What was compromised?
When did compromise begin?
Which identities are trusted?
Which artifacts are trusted?
Which backups are clean?
Which infrastructure can be reused?
```

---

# 95. Clean-Room Recovery

For severe compromise:

```text
Compromised Environment
          │
          X
    Security Boundary
          │
          ▼
      CLEAN ROOM
          │
          ├── Trusted identity
          ├── Trusted tooling
          ├── Trusted artifacts
          ├── Clean backups
          └── Controlled networking
```

Recovery should not automatically reuse potentially compromised control planes.

---

# 96. Trusted Recovery Artifacts

Critical recovery inputs include:

```text
Source repositories
Container images
Helm charts
Terraform modules
OS/base images
Dependencies
Backups
SBOMs
Signatures
Configuration
```

Recovery requires confidence in their provenance.

---

# 97. Artifact Integrity

Where ADR security controls provide signatures or attestations:

```text
Artifact
   │
   ▼
Verify provenance
   │
 ┌─┴──────┐
 ▼        ▼
Valid   Unknown
 │        │
Use     Investigate
```

Unknown provenance should not silently enter clean-room recovery.

---

# 98. Recovery Dependency Order

Systems cannot be restored randomly.

Example:

```text
1. Network / DNS foundations
        │
2. Identity / KMS / Secrets
        │
3. Kubernetes / Platform
        │
4. Databases / Persistent State
        │
5. Messaging / Cache
        │
6. Core Application Services
        │
7. Frontend
        │
8. Secondary Capabilities
        │
9. AI / Analytics
```

Actual order must follow the dependency graph.

---

# 99. Recovery Orchestration

Recovery should combine automation and explicit gates.

```text
Automated Step
      │
      ▼
Validation
      │
      ▼
Next Step
      │
      ▼
Validation
```

Blind automation can rapidly reproduce corruption or misconfiguration.

---

# 100. Degraded Operating Modes

Resilience is not binary.

```text
100% Capability
      │
      ▼
Core Capability
      │
      ▼
Read-Only Capability
      │
      ▼
Emergency Information
      │
      ▼
Unavailable
```

Mediverse should intentionally design useful intermediate states.

---

# 101. Read-Only Mode

If writes cannot be safely accepted:

```text
Courses              ✓
Existing content      ✓
Historical progress   ✓

New progress writes   ✗
Assessment submission ✗
Administrative writes ✗
```

A clearly communicated read-only mode may be safer than accepting writes that cannot be preserved.

---

# 102. AI-Disabled Mode

AI should be removable from the critical request path where business requirements allow.

```text
Core Learning
      │
      ├── Course access ✓
      ├── Assessment ✓
      ├── Progress ✓
      └── AI Tutor ✗
```

This prevents an AI-provider outage from unnecessarily becoming a platform outage.

---

# 103. Feature Shedding

During extreme load or partial failure:

```text
Critical
  ├── Authentication
  ├── Course access
  └── Assessment

Optional
  ├── Recommendations
  ├── Analytics
  ├── Rich personalization
  └── AI enrichment
```

Optional work may be disabled to preserve critical capacity.

---

# 104. Graceful Degradation

Applications should define fallback behavior for dependencies.

```text
Recommendation Service ✗
        │
        ▼
Course page still loads
without recommendations
```

A non-critical dependency should not automatically become a critical failure.

---

# 105. Traffic Management

Recovery may require:

```text
DNS changes
Global load balancing
CDN configuration
Ingress changes
Traffic weighting
Maintenance responses
```

Traffic control must itself be recoverable.

---

# 106. Failover

Failover means transferring service responsibility to a recovery environment.

```text
PRIMARY
   │
   X
   │
   ▼
FAILOVER
   │
   ▼
RECOVERY
```

It must not be treated as simply changing DNS.

---

# 107. Failover Preconditions

Before failover, establish where possible:

```text
Failure scope
Data state
Replication state
Recovery environment health
Dependency health
Traffic readiness
Security status
```

---

# 108. Split-Brain Risk

A dangerous scenario:

```text
Region A
accepting writes
     │
     │
     X Network partition
     │
     │
Region B
also accepting writes
```

Both sides may believe they are authoritative.

---

# 109. Single-Writer Authority

Where the data model requires a single writer, failover must explicitly transfer authority.

```text
Writer A
   │
   ▼
Fence A
   │
   ▼
Promote B
   │
   ▼
Writer B
```

Promotion without fencing can corrupt state.

---

# 110. Data Reconciliation

After partial failures, data may diverge.

Recovery may require:

```text
Compare
Detect missing transactions
Detect duplicates
Resolve conflicts
Replay events
Repair derived state
Validate business invariants
```

---

# 111. Idempotent Recovery

Recovery workflows should be safely repeatable where possible.

```text
Run recovery step
       │
       X interrupted
       │
       ▼
Run again safely
```

Idempotency reduces operator fear and recovery complexity.

---

# 112. Failover Validation

After failover, verify more than HTTP `200`.

Validate:

```text
Authentication
Critical reads
Critical writes
Database integrity
Messaging
Object access
User workflows
Security controls
Observability
Capacity
```

---

# 113. Synthetic Recovery Transactions

Controlled synthetic transactions can validate end-to-end capability.

```text
Synthetic User
     │
     ▼
Login
     │
     ▼
Open Course
     │
     ▼
Perform Test Operation
     │
     ▼
Validate Persistence
```

---

# 114. Failback

Failback is a separate operation.

```text
Recovery Region
      │
      ▼
Stable
      │
      ▼
Original Region Restored
      │
      ▼
Synchronize
      │
      ▼
Validate
      │
      ▼
Controlled Failback
```

Never assume returning home is easier than failing over.

---

# 115. Failback Criteria

Failback should require:

```text
Root cause addressed
Original environment trusted
Data synchronized
Dependencies healthy
Capacity ready
Security validated
Rollback path available
```

---

# 116. Disaster Declaration

A major outage does not automatically require DR activation.

Decision authority should be explicit.

```text
Incident
   │
   ▼
Assess
   │
   ▼
Normal recovery viable?
 ┌─┴─────┐
 ▼       ▼
YES      NO
 │        │
Continue  Consider disaster declaration
```

---

# 117. Disaster Declaration Authority

Roles should define who can authorize:

```text
Region failover
Emergency access
Recovery environment activation
Data restoration
Traffic migration
Failback
```

Ambiguity during crisis increases downtime.

---

# 118. Incident Command

Major recovery requires clear command structure.

```text
Incident Commander
        │
        ├── Technical Recovery
        ├── Security
        ├── Communications
        ├── Business/Product
        └── Vendor Coordination
```

One person should not attempt to execute every role.

---

# 119. Recovery Communication

Communication should cover:

```text
What happened
Known impact
Current operating mode
Recovery progress
User actions if any
Next update
```

Do not publish speculative root causes during active recovery.

---

# 120. Internal Communication

Engineering communication should distinguish:

```text
Facts
Hypotheses
Decisions
Actions
Owners
Timestamps
```

This reduces confusion during long-running incidents.

---

# 121. Recovery Runbooks

Critical services require executable recovery documentation.

A runbook should contain:

```text
Trigger
Prerequisites
Access requirements
Commands/actions
Expected output
Validation
Rollback
Escalation
Owner
```

---

# 122. Runbook Quality

This is not sufficient:

```text
"Restore PostgreSQL."
```

A useful runbook answers:

```text
From which backup?
To where?
Using which credentials?
What recovery point?
How is integrity checked?
Who approves promotion?
```

---

# 123. Runbook Versioning

Runbooks should be:

```text
Version controlled
Reviewed
Tested
Updated after exercises/incidents
Accessible during primary-tool outage
```

A runbook stored only inside the failed system is poorly designed.

---

# 124. Recovery Automation

Automate deterministic repetitive operations.

Candidates:

```text
Infrastructure provisioning
Cluster bootstrap
Backup restoration
DNS preparation
Validation probes
Configuration reconciliation
```

---

# 125. Human Gates

Retain human approval around high-risk irreversible operations such as:

```text
Promoting database authority
Destroying corrupted environments
Changing global traffic
Executing destructive restoration
Failback
```

where risk warrants it.

---

# 126. Restore Drills

Restore testing must occur before a disaster.

```text
Select Backup
     │
     ▼
Restore
     │
     ▼
Start Application
     │
     ▼
Validate
     │
     ▼
Measure Recovery Time
```

---

# 127. Tabletop Exercises

Tabletops test decision-making without necessarily disrupting infrastructure.

Scenario:

```text
"Primary AWS region unavailable.
Identity provider degraded.
Last confirmed replication point:
7 minutes ago."
```

Teams then execute the decision process.

---

# 128. Game Days

Game days test operational behavior using controlled technical failure.

Potential scenarios:

```text
Node loss
AZ loss
Database failover
Redis loss
Kafka broker loss
AI provider outage
DNS misconfiguration
Observability failure
```

---

# 129. Chaos Engineering Integration

Chaos engineering validates assumptions about expected failures.

```text
Hypothesis
   │
   ▼
Controlled Failure
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
   ▼
Verify SLO / Recovery
   │
   ▼
Improve
```

Chaos is not random destruction.

---

# 130. DR Exercises vs Chaos Engineering

```text
CHAOS ENGINEERING
Tests resilience to controlled failure.

DR EXERCISE
Tests recovery after normal resilience
boundaries are exceeded.
```

Both are needed for different questions.

---

# 131. Recovery Exercise Scope

Exercises should eventually test combinations.

Real disasters rarely respect architecture diagrams.

Example:

```text
Region outage
    +
Expired recovery credential
    +
Delayed replication
    +
Monitoring degradation
```

Single-failure tests alone create false confidence.

---

# 132. Exercise Safety

Exercises require:

```text
Scope
Abort criteria
Owner
Communication
Blast-radius controls
Rollback
Observation
```

Testing resilience should not casually create a real disaster.

---

# 133. Recovery Evidence

Every material exercise should record:

```text
Scenario
Expected behavior
Actual behavior
RTO achieved
RPO achieved
Failures
Manual steps
Unexpected dependencies
Follow-up actions
```

---

# 134. Recovery Metrics

Mediverse should track:

```text
Restore success rate
Restore duration
Failover duration
Failback duration
Backup success
Backup age
Recovery-point gap
Runbook success
Exercise frequency
RTO compliance
RPO compliance
```

---

# 135. Recovery Time Measurement

Do not stop the clock when infrastructure boots.

```text
Disaster
   │
   ▼
Infrastructure restored
   │
   X
Not necessarily recovered
   │
   ▼
Critical business capability validated
   │
   ▼
RTO achieved
```

Business capability restoration is the meaningful endpoint.

---

# 136. Recovery Scorecard

Example:

| Capability     | Tier | RTO | RPO | Last Restore Test | Result                 |
| -------------- | ---: | --: | --: | ----------------- | ---------------------- |
| Authentication |    1 | 30m | N/A | Current quarter   | PASS                   |
| Course API     |    1 |  1h | 15m | Current quarter   | PASS                   |
| Progress DB    |    1 |  1h |  5m | Current quarter   | PASS                   |
| AI Tutor       |    2 |  4h | N/A | Current quarter   | DEGRADED MODE VERIFIED |
| Analytics      |    3 | 24h | 12h | Current half      | PASS                   |

Targets shown here are illustrative; actual values must come from BIA.

---

# 137. Operational-Resilience Fitness Functions

Machine-verifiable controls may include:

```text
Critical DB MUST have tested backup
Critical service MUST declare recovery tier
Tier 1 service MUST declare RTO/RPO
Temporary DR credentials MUST expire
Critical backups MUST meet maximum-age policy
Recovery repository MUST be accessible
Critical workloads MUST satisfy topology policy
```

---

# 138. Recovery Readiness Gate

A Tier 1 service should not be considered production-ready merely because its deployment succeeds.

```text
Deployment Ready
      +
Monitoring Ready
      +
Security Ready
      +
Recovery Ready
      =
Production Ready
```

---

# 139. Architecture Review Integration

Significant architecture reviews should ask:

```text
What happens if this dependency disappears?
What state can be rebuilt?
What state must be restored?
What is the failure domain?
What is the RTO?
What is the RPO?
How is recovery tested?
What happens during partial recovery?
How is failback performed?
```

---

# 140. DR Change Management

Changes affecting:

```text
Replication
Backups
DNS
Identity
KMS
Database topology
Regions
Recovery automation
Network routing
```

should evaluate impact on recovery capability.

---

# 141. Cyber-Resilience Integration

Operational resilience and cybersecurity intersect at:

```text
Identity
Backups
Artifact integrity
Secrets
Supply chain
Recovery access
Forensics
Clean-room recovery
```

Security architecture that prevents attacks but cannot recover from one is incomplete.

---

# 142. FinOps Integration

ADR-073 applies to DR decisions.

Track:

```text
Steady-state DR cost
Recovery capacity cost
Replication cost
Backup cost
Exercise cost
Expected downtime exposure
```

The cheapest DR architecture may create unacceptable business risk.

---

# 143. Sustainability Integration

ADR-074 applies as well.

Idle standby capacity should be justified by recovery objectives.

```text
Recovery requirement
      │
      ▼
Required standby capacity
```

Not:

```text
"More replicas feel safer."
```

---

# 144. Operational Resilience Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — BACKUP EXISTS
Recovery largely assumed.

LEVEL 2 — DOCUMENTED
RTO/RPO and runbooks exist.

LEVEL 3 — TESTED
Restores and failovers exercised.

LEVEL 4 — ENGINEERED
Recovery integrated into platform,
architecture and delivery.

LEVEL 5 — ADAPTIVE
Recovery is continuously validated,
measured and improved.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, progressing selected Tier 0/1 capabilities toward Level 5.

---

# 145. Operational Resilience Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "We have backups, therefore we have DR"
❌ Replication treated as backup
❌ Backup success treated as restore proof
❌ RTO/RPO invented by infrastructure teams
❌ Every service assigned identical recovery targets
❌ Active/active because it looks enterprise-grade
❌ Multi-region without BIA justification
❌ Application multi-AZ while critical DB remains single-AZ
❌ Recovery dependent on manual console knowledge
❌ Terraform state without recovery protection
❌ GitOps recovery assuming Git can never fail
❌ Runtime depending on CI availability
❌ Search indexes treated as irreplaceable when reproducible
❌ Redis cache treated like authoritative data
❌ Kafka replay without idempotency
❌ AI outage causing complete learning-platform outage unnecessarily
❌ Unlimited retries during dependency failure
❌ DNS omitted from dependency analysis
❌ Identity omitted from DR
❌ Break-glass credentials never tested
❌ Backups encrypted with unrecoverable keys
❌ Production admins able to delete every recovery copy
❌ Backups stored only in the failed region
❌ Cyber recovery performed inside an untrusted control plane
❌ Unsigned/unverified artifacts used in clean-room recovery
❌ Services restored in arbitrary order
❌ Recovery automation without validation gates
❌ DR architecture with no degraded mode
❌ Read-only capability never designed
❌ Optional features consuming resources during critical recovery
❌ Failover treated as a DNS change
❌ Both regions accepting conflicting writes
❌ Failback performed immediately after infrastructure returns
❌ Disaster declaration authority undefined
❌ One engineer acting as commander, operator and communicator
❌ Runbooks stored only in the unavailable platform
❌ Runbooks consisting of vague statements
❌ Recovery exercises never performed
❌ Chaos engineering confused with random failure injection
❌ RTO measured only until servers start
❌ Recovery findings not converted into engineering work
```

---

# 149. ADR-075 Decision Outcome

| Area                       | Decision                                  |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Resilience basis           | Business capability                       |
| BIA                        | Required for critical capabilities        |
| MTD                        | Defined where applicable                  |
| RTO/RPO                    | Business-driven                           |
| Recovery tiers             | Tier 0–3                                  |
| Dependency mapping         | Mandatory for critical services           |
| HA vs DR                   | Explicitly separated                      |
| AZ failure                 | HA where tier requires                    |
| Cluster loss               | IaC + GitOps rebuild                      |
| Manual cloud configuration | Recovery debt                             |
| Git repositories           | Recovery protected                        |
| CI outage                  | Runtime independent                       |
| Terraform state            | Protected and recoverable                 |
| PostgreSQL                 | Backup + PITR + restore tests             |
| Replication                | Not considered backup                     |
| Redis                      | Recovery based on role                    |
| Kafka                      | Replay/idempotency aware                  |
| Object storage             | Version/lifecycle/recovery governed       |
| Search                     | Rebuildable where derived                 |
| Vector indexes             | Rebuildable where appropriate             |
| AI outage                  | Degraded mode preferred where possible    |
| Third-party dependencies   | Failure behavior defined                  |
| DNS                        | Critical dependency                       |
| Identity                   | Explicit continuity requirement           |
| Break-glass                | Protected, audited, tested                |
| Secrets/KMS                | Recovery dependency                       |
| Observability outage       | Alternate signals required                |
| Multi-region               | BIA/RTO/RPO justified                     |
| DR strategy                | Tier-specific                             |
| Active/active              | Exceptional, not default                  |
| Immutable backups          | Critical-data requirement where justified |
| Backup isolation           | Required for cyber resilience             |
| Cyber recovery             | Trusted-state recovery                    |
| Clean room                 | Severe compromise scenario                |
| Artifact integrity         | Verified                                  |
| Recovery ordering          | Dependency driven                         |
| Degraded modes             | Explicitly designed                       |
| Read-only mode             | Supported where useful                    |
| Feature shedding           | Supported                                 |
| Split brain                | Explicitly prevented                      |
| Failover                   | Controlled and validated                  |
| Failback                   | Separate controlled operation             |
| Disaster declaration       | Authority defined                         |
| Incident command           | Required                                  |
| Runbooks                   | Executable and tested                     |
| Restore drills             | Required                                  |
| Tabletop exercises         | Required                                  |
| Game days                  | Required for critical systems             |
| Chaos integration          | Controlled                                |
| Recovery evidence          | Retained                                  |
| Fitness functions          | Automated where meaningful                |
| FinOps integration         | Required                                  |
| Sustainability integration | Required                                  |
| Maturity target            | Level 4; Tier 0/1 toward Level 5          |
| Status                     | **Accepted**                              |
| Priority                   | **Critical**                              |
