# ADR-075 — COMPLETE ✅

The governing invariant is:

> **Mediverse will not claim resilience because replicas, backups, multi-AZ infrastructure or DR documents exist. A critical capability is considered recoverable only when its infrastructure, authoritative data, identities, encryption keys, artifacts, dependencies, operational procedures and human decision paths have been demonstrated to restore the required business service within its agreed RTO and RPO.**

The architecture now closes the recovery loop:

```text
BUSINESS CRITICALITY
        │
        ▼
    RTO / RPO
        │
        ▼
RESILIENCE DESIGN
        │
        ▼
    FAILURE
        │
        ▼
   CONTAINMENT
        │
        ▼
TRUST ASSESSMENT
        │
        ▼
    RECOVERY
        │
        ▼
   VALIDATION
        │
        ▼
   FAILBACK
        │
        ▼
    EXERCISE
        │
        ▼
    EVIDENCE
        │
        ▼
ARCHITECTURE IMPROVEMENT
        │
        └──────────────► RESILIENCE DESIGN
```

## Next — ADR-076

### **ADR-076 — Enterprise Data Governance, Data Architecture, Data Quality, Lineage, Metadata & Data Lifecycle Standard**

This should establish the missing **enterprise data control plane** across Mediverse: **data domains → ownership → data products → authoritative sources → system of record → operational vs analytical data → data classification → schemas → canonical models → metadata catalogue → business glossary → lineage → provenance → data contracts → schema evolution → data-quality dimensions → validation → reconciliation → duplicate detection → master/reference data → identifiers → PostgreSQL governance → Kafka/event-data governance → Redis/cache-data rules → Elasticsearch/search indexes → vector databases → embeddings → AI/RAG knowledge provenance → object storage → lake/lakehouse decisions → ETL/ELT → CDC → batch/stream processing → retention → archival → deletion → legal hold → privacy integration → residency → encryption → access governance → masking/tokenization → synthetic data → production-data restrictions in non-prod → backup lifecycle → data observability → freshness/completeness monitoring → lineage-aware incident analysis → data SLAs/SLOs → data-product scorecards → data governance policy-as-code → architecture fitness functions → FinOps/storage economics → sustainability → DR/data recovery integration → anti-patterns → maturity model → final Mediverse enterprise data-governance reference architecture.**

# ADR-076 — Enterprise Data Governance, Data Architecture, Data Quality, Lineage, Metadata & Data Lifecycle Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-076
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Primary Stakeholders:** Data Platform, Application Engineering, AI Platform, Security, Privacy, SRE, Database Engineering, Analytics, Platform Engineering, FinOps

ADR-075 established how Mediverse protects and recovers critical business capabilities and their data.

ADR-076 establishes something different:

> **How Mediverse determines what data means, who owns it, which system is authoritative, whether it can be trusted, where it came from, where it flows, how long it exists, and how applications, analytics and AI are permitted to use it.**

```text
                    BUSINESS CAPABILITY
                            │
                            ▼
                        DATA DOMAIN
                            │
              ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
              ▼             ▼             ▼
           OWNER         STEWARD       PRODUCER
              │             │             │
              └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                            ▼
                       DATA PRODUCT
                            │
              ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
              ▼             ▼             ▼
          CONTRACT       METADATA       QUALITY
              │             │             │
              └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                            ▼
                    AUTHORITATIVE DATA
                            │
          ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
          ▼                 ▼                 ▼
      OPERATIONAL        ANALYTICAL          AI
          │                 │                 │
          └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                            ▼
                   GOVERNED LIFECYCLE
                            │
       CREATE → USE → SHARE → RETAIN → ARCHIVE → DELETE
```

# 1. Data Governance Objective

Mediverse data must be:

```text
Owned
Defined
Classified
Discoverable
Traceable
Trustworthy
Secure
Interoperable
Recoverable
Lifecycle-managed
Cost-aware
AI-ready where appropriate
```

Data governance is not merely database administration.

---

# 2. Data Is an Enterprise Asset

Application boundaries must not obscure data responsibility.

```text
Application A
Application B
Application C
      │
      ▼
Shared Business Meaning
      │
      ▼
Enterprise Data
```

Ownership follows the business meaning of data, not whichever team happens to operate its current database.

---

# 3. Data Governance Operating Model

Governance is distributed.

```text
Enterprise Data Governance
          │
          ├── Standards
          ├── Classification
          └── Enterprise policy
                    │
          Domain Ownership
                    │
          ├── Meaning
          ├── Quality
          └── Access expectations
                    │
          Platform Engineering
                    │
          ├── Catalogue
          ├── Lineage
          └── Controls
                    │
          Engineering Teams
                    │
          └── Implementation
```

A central committee cannot maintain the semantics of every domain.

---

# 4. Data Domains

Mediverse should organize important data around business domains.

Potential domains include:

```text
Identity
Learner
Educator
Course
Curriculum
Content
Enrollment
Assessment
Progress
Certification
Communication
AI Learning
Billing
Operations
```

Domain boundaries must reflect actual business ownership rather than arbitrary database grouping.

---

# 5. Domain Ownership

Every governed data domain requires an accountable owner.

The owner is responsible for:

```text
Meaning
Authoritative definitions
Quality expectations
Access expectations
Lifecycle requirements
Major contract changes
```

Technical teams may implement controls, but they do not automatically own business semantics.

---

# 6. Data Stewardship

A data steward supports operational governance.

```text
DATA OWNER
    │
    ├── Accountability
    │
DATA STEWARD
    │
    ├── Definitions
    ├── Quality
    ├── Metadata
    └── Governance coordination
```

Owner and steward responsibilities should not be confused.

---

# 7. Data Producers

A producer creates or changes governed data.

Examples:

```text
Enrollment Service
Assessment Service
Progress Service
Content Management
AI Pipeline
External Import
```

Producers must honor the relevant data contract.

---

# 8. Data Consumers

Consumers include:

```text
Applications
Analytics
Reporting
Search
AI/RAG
Notifications
External integrations
```

Consumers should not infer undocumented semantics from implementation details.

---

# 9. Data Products

Important shared datasets should be treated as products.

A data product should expose:

```text
Purpose
Owner
Schema
Semantics
Quality
Access mechanism
SLO
Lineage
Classification
Lifecycle
```

---

# 10. Data Product Is Not Just a Table

```text
TABLE
  │
  X
DATA PRODUCT
```

A data product combines usable data with its operational and semantic contract.

---

# 11. Authoritative Source

For important business facts, Mediverse must identify an authoritative source.

Example:

```text
Learner Enrollment Status

Enrollment Service DB
        │
        ▼
AUTHORITATIVE

Analytics Warehouse
Search Index
Redis Cache
        │
        ▼
DERIVED
```

---

# 12. System of Record

A System of Record maintains the authoritative state for a defined business concept.

This designation must be explicit.

```text
Concept
   │
   ▼
System of Record
   │
   ├── Events
   ├── Replicas
   ├── Search
   ├── Analytics
   └── AI
```

Derived copies do not become authoritative merely because they are easier to query.

---

# 13. Multiple Sources of Truth

Mediverse rejects uncontrolled situations where:

```text
Service A says learner = ACTIVE
Service B says learner = SUSPENDED
Spreadsheet says learner = PENDING
```

without defined authority and reconciliation.

---

# 14. Operational Data

Operational data supports live application workflows.

Characteristics may include:

```text
Transactional
Low-latency
Current
Consistency-sensitive
Application-owned
```

PostgreSQL will commonly serve this role.

---

# 15. Analytical Data

Analytical data serves:

```text
Reporting
Trends
Aggregation
BI
Research
Product analytics
```

It should not silently become the transactional authority.

---

# 16. Operational vs Analytical Separation

```text
APPLICATION
     │
     ▼
OPERATIONAL STORE
     │
     ├── CDC
     ├── Events
     └── ETL/ELT
            │
            ▼
      ANALYTICAL PLATFORM
```

Heavy analytics should not unnecessarily destabilize transactional systems.

---

# 17. Derived Data

Examples:

```text
Search indexes
Materialized views
Caches
Analytics tables
Embeddings
Recommendations
Feature vectors
```

Derived state should identify its authoritative upstream source.

---

# 18. Rebuildability Classification

Each derived dataset should declare whether it is:

```text
Fully rebuildable
Partially rebuildable
Non-rebuildable
```

This directly affects ADR-075 recovery design.

---

# 19. Data Classification

Every significant dataset should have a classification.

Conceptually:

```text
PUBLIC
INTERNAL
CONFIDENTIAL
RESTRICTED
```

Exact labels must align with Mediverse security/privacy standards.

---

# 20. Classification Drives Controls

Classification should influence:

```text
Access
Encryption
Logging
Sharing
Retention
Masking
Backup
Non-production use
AI use
```

Classification without control consequences is decorative governance.

---

# 21. Schema Governance

Important data interfaces require explicit schemas.

Examples:

```text
Database schemas
REST payloads
Kafka events
Files
Analytics tables
Vector metadata
```

---

# 22. Schema Ownership

Every governed schema should have:

```text
Owner
Version
Purpose
Compatibility policy
Change process
```

Anonymous schemas become long-term integration debt.

---

# 23. Canonical Models

Canonical models may be useful for stable enterprise concepts.

Example:

```text
Learner
Course
Assessment
Enrollment
```

But Mediverse rejects a single giant universal canonical model for every internal service.

---

# 24. Bounded Context Semantics

The same word can legitimately mean different things in different domains.

```text
"User"

Identity Domain
      ≠
Learning Domain
      ≠
Billing Domain
```

Governance should clarify semantic differences rather than forcing artificial uniformity.

---

# 25. Business Glossary

Mediverse should maintain definitions for critical business terms.

Example:

```text
Enrollment
Active Learner
Course Completion
Assessment Attempt
Pass
Certification
Learning Session
```

Definitions should be understandable outside implementation code.

---

# 26. Metadata

Metadata should answer:

```text
What is this?
Who owns it?
Where is it?
What does it contain?
How is it classified?
Where did it come from?
Who consumes it?
How fresh is it?
Can it be trusted?
```

---

# 27. Metadata Catalogue

The enterprise catalogue should provide discovery across:

```text
Databases
Tables
Topics
Events
Object datasets
Analytics
Search indexes
Vector collections
AI knowledge sources
```

---

# 28. Technical Metadata

Examples:

```text
Schema
Column type
Topic
Partition
Database
Storage location
Format
Size
Update timestamp
```

---

# 29. Business Metadata

Examples:

```text
Business definition
Owner
Steward
Purpose
Criticality
Quality expectation
Classification
```

Technical metadata alone cannot explain meaning.

---

# 30. Operational Metadata

Examples:

```text
Freshness
Pipeline status
Quality status
Volume
Last successful load
Incident state
SLO compliance
```

This connects governance to real operation.

---

# 31. Data Lineage

Lineage describes movement and transformation.

```text
PostgreSQL
    │
    ▼
CDC
    │
    ▼
Kafka
    │
    ▼
Transformation
    │
    ▼
Analytics
    │
    ▼
Dashboard
```

---

# 32. Column-Level Lineage

For high-value data, lineage may need to explain:

```text
source.date_of_birth
        │
        ▼
calculate_age()
        │
        ▼
analytics.age_group
```

rather than merely saying Database A feeds Database B.

---

# 33. Lineage Value

Lineage supports:

```text
Impact analysis
Incident response
Privacy requests
Quality debugging
Schema changes
AI provenance
Audit
Recovery
```

---

# 34. Change Impact Analysis

Before changing a governed field:

```text
Schema Change
     │
     ▼
Lineage Graph
     │
     ├── API
     ├── Kafka consumer
     ├── Analytics
     ├── Dashboard
     └── AI pipeline
```

This reduces invisible downstream breakage.

---

# 35. Data Provenance

Provenance answers:

```text
Where did this data originate?
Who produced it?
When?
Using which process?
Using which version?
```

This becomes especially important for AI knowledge.

---

# 36. Data Contracts

A data contract defines expectations between producer and consumers.

Potential contract:

```yaml
dataset: assessment-result
owner: assessment-domain
version: 3

quality:
  attemptId:
    required: true
  score:
    min: 0
    max: 100

freshness:
  target: 5m
```

The exact implementation may vary.

---

# 37. Contract Scope

Contracts may govern:

```text
Schema
Semantics
Nullability
Quality
Freshness
Compatibility
Ownership
Classification
SLO
```

---

# 38. Producer Responsibility

The producer must not silently redefine shared fields.

Example:

```text
score = percentage

becomes

score = raw_points
```

without contract evolution.

That is a breaking semantic change even if the database type remains `INTEGER`.

---

# 39. Consumer Responsibility

Consumers must not depend on undocumented behavior.

```text
"Field currently happens to be null only rarely"
```

is not a contract.

---

# 40. Schema Evolution

Changes should be classified:

```text
Backward compatible
Forward compatible
Breaking
Semantic breaking
```

Semantic compatibility matters as much as syntactic compatibility.

---

# 41. Additive Changes

Adding optional fields is commonly safer than removing or redefining existing fields.

But compatibility must still be verified against real consumers.

---

# 42. Breaking Changes

Breaking changes require:

```text
Version strategy
Consumer migration
Transition period
Observability
Retirement plan
```

---

# 43. Event Schema Governance

Kafka events require particular discipline because stored historical events may outlive application deployments.

```text
Producer v1
Producer v2
Producer v3
      │
      ▼
Historical Event Log
```

Consumers may encounter multiple schema generations.

---

# 44. Event Meaning

An event should describe a meaningful fact.

```text
EnrollmentCreated
AssessmentSubmitted
CourseCompleted
```

rather than exposing arbitrary database internals as the enterprise event model.

---

# 45. Event Immutability

Published historical events should generally represent immutable facts.

Corrections should normally be represented through new events rather than rewriting history where event semantics require auditability.

---

# 46. Data Quality

Data quality is multidimensional.

Mediverse should evaluate:

```text
Accuracy
Completeness
Consistency
Validity
Uniqueness
Timeliness
Integrity
```

---

# 47. Accuracy

Accuracy asks:

> Does the stored value correctly represent the real-world or business fact it claims to represent?

A syntactically valid value can still be inaccurate.

---

# 48. Completeness

Example:

```text
Required learner records: 100,000
Complete records:          98,400

Completeness = 98.4%
```

The acceptable threshold depends on the use case.

---

# 49. Consistency

Consistency asks whether related representations agree.

```text
Enrollment DB: ACTIVE
Analytics:     ACTIVE
Search:        SUSPENDED
```

The disagreement requires investigation according to freshness and authority rules.

---

# 50. Validity

Validity tests rules such as:

```text
score ∈ [0,100]
courseId exists
completionDate >= enrollmentDate
email conforms to expected format
```

---

# 51. Uniqueness

Identifiers expected to be unique should not produce duplicates.

Examples:

```text
Assessment attempt ID
Enrollment ID
Course ID
Event ID
```

---

# 52. Timeliness

Correct data delivered too late can still be poor-quality data.

```text
Expected freshness = 5 minutes
Actual freshness   = 7 hours
```

This is a data-quality incident.

---

# 53. Referential Integrity

Where applicable:

```text
Enrollment.course_id
        │
        ▼
Course.id
```

must remain valid.

Distributed architectures may require application-level or asynchronous integrity controls where database foreign keys cannot span systems.

---

# 54. Quality Rules

Quality rules should be:

```text
Explicit
Measurable
Owned
Automatable where possible
Severity-aware
```

---

# 55. Quality at Ingestion

Reject or quarantine invalid data as early as practical.

```text
Incoming Data
      │
      ▼
Validation
  ┌───┴───┐
  ▼       ▼
PASS     FAIL
  │       │
Store   Reject/Quarantine
```

---

# 56. Quality at Transformation

Every transformation can introduce defects.

Therefore critical pipelines should validate:

```text
Input
Transformation
Output
```

rather than trusting successful execution alone.

---

# 57. Quarantine

Bad data should not always be discarded.

```text
Invalid Input
      │
      ▼
Quarantine
      │
      ├── Reason
      ├── Source
      ├── Timestamp
      └── Replay path
```

where business requirements justify recovery.

---

# 58. Reconciliation

Reconciliation compares expected and actual state across boundaries.

Example:

```text
Assessment submissions: 10,000
Kafka events:           10,000
Analytics records:       9,998
```

The two missing records require investigation.

---

# 59. Duplicate Detection

Distributed retries may create duplicates.

```text
Producer
   │
   ├── Event X
   │
   X timeout
   │
   └── Retry Event X
```

Stable identifiers and idempotent consumers help control duplication.

---

# 60. Master and Reference Data

Some shared data requires stronger governance.

Examples:

```text
Country codes
Languages
Academic classifications
Course categories
Institution identifiers
Status codes
```

Reference data should not diverge independently across dozens of services.

---

## ADR-076 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The emerging enterprise data control plane is:

```text
                           BUSINESS
                              │
                              ▼
                         DATA DOMAIN
                              │
               ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
               ▼              ▼              ▼
             OWNER          STEWARD       PRODUCER
               │              │              │
               └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                              ▼
                         DATA PRODUCT
                              │
        ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
        ▼                     ▼                     ▼
     CONTRACT              METADATA              QUALITY
        │                     │                     │
        └─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┘
                              ▼
                    AUTHORITATIVE SOURCE
                              │
            ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
            ▼                 ▼                 ▼
        OPERATIONAL        ANALYTICAL         DERIVED
            │                 │                 │
            └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                              ▼
                           LINEAGE
                              │
                              ▼
                         CONSUMPTION
               ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
               ▼              ▼              ▼
          APPLICATION      ANALYTICS          AI
               │              │              │
               └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                              ▼
                     GOVERNED LIFECYCLE
                              │
                              ▼
              CREATE → RETAIN → ARCHIVE → DELETE
```

The critical rule is:

> **A database containing data does not make that database an authoritative source, and a pipeline successfully moving data does not make the resulting data trustworthy. Mediverse requires ownership, semantics, contracts, lineage, quality evidence and lifecycle governance around important data.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Enterprise Identifier Strategy**, then cover **natural vs surrogate identifiers → globally unique IDs → master/reference-data governance → PostgreSQL governance → database/schema ownership → cross-service database access → CDC → transactional outbox → Kafka governance → event lineage → Redis/cache authority → Elasticsearch/search lifecycle → object-storage governance → lake/lakehouse decision framework → ETL/ELT → batch/stream processing → late/out-of-order data → vector databases → embedding provenance → RAG knowledge governance → AI training/evaluation datasets → synthetic data → production data in non-production → masking/tokenization → access governance → row/column controls → residency → encryption → retention → archival → deletion → legal hold → backup lifecycle → data observability → freshness/volume/schema anomalies → data incidents → data SLOs → data-product scorecards → policy-as-code → fitness functions → FinOps/storage economics → sustainability → DR integration → maturity model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise data-governance reference architecture and ADR-076 decision outcome.**

# ADR-076 — Enterprise Data Governance, Data Architecture, Data Quality, Lineage, Metadata & Data Lifecycle Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Master and Reference Data**.

---

# 61. Enterprise Identifier Strategy

Identifiers must be stable, unambiguous and appropriate to their domain.

```text
Business Entity
      │
      ▼
Stable Identifier
      │
      ├── APIs
      ├── Events
      ├── Databases
      ├── Analytics
      └── AI/Data Products
```

Changing a display name, email address or other mutable business attribute must not unexpectedly change entity identity.

---

# 62. Natural vs Surrogate Identifiers

Natural identifiers originate from business attributes.

Examples:

```text
email
registration_number
external_course_code
```

Surrogate identifiers are system-generated.

```text
learner_id
course_id
assessment_id
```

Mutable business attributes should generally not become permanent technical identity.

---

# 63. Globally Unique Identifiers

Distributed systems may benefit from identifiers that can be generated independently.

Possible approaches include:

```text
UUID
ULID
Provider-generated identifiers
Domain-specific identifiers
```

The choice should consider:

```text
Uniqueness
Ordering
Storage
Index behavior
Exposure
Interoperability
```

No identifier format is universally superior.

---

# 64. Identifier Immutability

Once externally referenced, identifiers should normally remain stable.

```text
Learner ID
    │
    ├── Enrollment
    ├── Progress
    ├── Assessment
    ├── Events
    └── Analytics
```

Reassigning identifiers can corrupt lineage and reconciliation.

---

# 65. External Identifiers

External identifiers should be distinguished from internal identity.

```text
Mediverse Learner ID
        │
        ├── University ID
        ├── LMS ID
        └── Identity Provider ID
```

Mappings require explicit ownership.

---

# 66. Reference Data Governance

Shared reference datasets should define:

```text
Owner
Authoritative source
Allowed values
Version
Effective dates
Change process
Consumers
```

Hard-coded copies across services create uncontrolled divergence.

---

# 67. PostgreSQL Governance

PostgreSQL remains an important operational system of record for Mediverse.

Governance must cover:

```text
Database ownership
Schema ownership
Migration ownership
Access
Indexing
Retention
Backup
Classification
Observability
```

---

# 68. Database Ownership

Every production database must have an accountable owning service/team.

```text
progress-db
     │
     ▼
Progress Domain
```

"Shared database owned by everyone" usually means owned by nobody.

---

# 69. Schema Ownership

Schemas should correspond to clear ownership boundaries where practical.

A service must not modify another service's schema simply because network connectivity exists.

---

# 70. Cross-Service Database Access

Mediverse rejects routine direct database coupling:

```text
Service A
   │
   └──────── SQL ───────► Service B Database
```

Prefer:

```text
Service A
   │
   ├── API
   └── Event
         │
         ▼
     Service B
```

Exceptions require architectural justification.

---

# 71. Why Direct Database Coupling Is Dangerous

It bypasses:

```text
Domain rules
API contracts
Authorization logic
Compatibility boundaries
Observability
Ownership
```

and makes independent evolution substantially harder.

---

# 72. Database Migration Governance

Schema migrations require:

```text
Versioning
Review
Backward compatibility
Deployment sequencing
Rollback/forward-fix strategy
Observability
Recovery awareness
```

ADR-075 applies to destructive migration failure.

---

# 73. Expand-and-Contract Migration

Prefer staged migration for breaking schema evolution.

```text
EXPAND
  │
  ├── Add new structure
  │
  ▼
MIGRATE
  │
  ├── Applications transition
  │
  ▼
CONTRACT
  │
  └── Remove obsolete structure
```

This reduces deployment coupling.

---

# 74. Change Data Capture

CDC can propagate operational changes without repeatedly querying entire tables.

```text
PostgreSQL
    │
    ▼
Transaction Log
    │
    ▼
CDC
    │
    ▼
Kafka / Data Platform
```

CDC is infrastructure, not business semantics by itself.

---

# 75. CDC Governance

CDC pipelines must define:

```text
Source
Captured tables
Schema evolution
Ordering
Replay
Retention
Sensitive fields
Consumers
Failure handling
```

Blindly publishing every database column is rejected.

---

# 76. Transactional Outbox

Where reliable state change plus event publication is required:

```text
Business Transaction
       │
       ├── Update Domain State
       └── Insert Outbox Event
                │
                ▼
             COMMIT
                │
                ▼
          Event Publisher
                │
                ▼
              Kafka
```

This avoids unsafe dual-write patterns.

---

# 77. Dual-Write Anti-Pattern

```text
Update PostgreSQL ✓
Publish Kafka Event ✗
```

can leave inconsistent systems.

Likewise:

```text
Publish Event ✓
Database Commit ✗
```

can publish facts that never became authoritative state.

---

# 78. Kafka Data Governance

Kafka topics are governed data interfaces.

Each important topic should define:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Schema
Classification
Retention
Partition strategy
Consumers
Compatibility
SLO
```

---

# 79. Topic Naming

Topic names should communicate domain and purpose rather than implementation accident.

Conceptually:

```text
assessment.submitted
enrollment.changed
course.completed
```

Naming conventions should be standardized platform-wide.

---

# 80. Event Lineage

Lineage should follow events through downstream processing.

```text
Assessment DB
      │
      ▼
AssessmentSubmitted
      │
      ▼
Kafka
      │
      ├── Progress Processor
      ├── Analytics
      └── Notification
```

This makes downstream impact visible.

---

# 81. Event Retention

Kafka retention should reflect:

```text
Replay requirements
Recovery
Audit needs
Consumer lag
Storage economics
Compliance
```

Infinite retention is not a default.

---

# 82. Event Replay Governance

Before replay:

```text
Replay Window
     │
     ▼
Affected Consumers
     │
     ▼
Idempotency
     │
     ▼
Side Effects
     │
     ▼
Approval / Execution
```

Replay is a controlled data operation.

---

# 83. Redis Data Authority

Redis should normally contain:

```text
Cached
Ephemeral
Derived
Short-lived coordination state
```

rather than irreplaceable authoritative business data.

---

# 84. Cache Provenance

A cache entry should conceptually have an upstream authority.

```text
PostgreSQL
    │
    ▼
Application
    │
    ▼
Redis
```

When Redis and PostgreSQL disagree, authority must already be known.

---

# 85. Cache Lifecycle

Cache governance should define:

```text
TTL
Invalidation
Eviction
Maximum size
Serialization version
Sensitive-data rules
```

---

# 86. Elasticsearch/Search Governance

Search indexes are generally derived data products.

```text
Authoritative Data
       │
       ▼
Index Pipeline
       │
       ▼
Elasticsearch
       │
       ▼
Search API
```

The source of truth remains upstream.

---

# 87. Search Schema

Search mappings require governance around:

```text
Field types
Analyzers
Language
Index versions
Aliases
Sensitive fields
Re-index strategy
```

---

# 88. Reindexing

Large schema changes may require:

```text
Index v1
   │
   ▼
Create Index v2
   │
   ▼
Backfill
   │
   ▼
Validate
   │
   ▼
Switch Alias
   │
   ▼
Retire v1
```

This enables controlled migration.

---

# 89. Object Storage Governance

Object storage may contain:

```text
Course media
Documents
Exports
Datasets
Backups
AI knowledge sources
3D assets
```

Each object class requires ownership and lifecycle policy.

---

# 90. Object Metadata

Important objects should carry or be associated with metadata such as:

```text
Owner
Classification
Content type
Created time
Source
Retention class
Checksum
Version
```

---

# 91. Data Lake Decision

Mediverse should not create a data lake merely because large organizations commonly have one.

A lake is justified when requirements exist for:

```text
Large-scale analytics
Raw historical data
Multiple analytical consumers
ML datasets
Cross-domain analysis
```

---

# 92. Data Lakehouse Decision

A lakehouse architecture may be considered when Mediverse requires combined:

```text
Object storage economics
Table semantics
Schema management
Transactional capabilities
Analytical interoperability
```

It is not automatically superior to a warehouse or simpler analytical platform.

---

# 93. Data Swamp Prevention

```text
DATA LAKE
   │
   ▼
No ownership
No catalogue
No quality
No lifecycle
No semantics
   │
   ▼
DATA SWAMP
```

Cheap storage does not justify uncontrolled accumulation.

---

# 94. ETL vs ELT

Both patterns are permitted.

```text
ETL

Extract → Transform → Load

ELT

Extract → Load → Transform
```

Selection depends on:

```text
Platform capability
Security
Data volume
Latency
Transformation complexity
Governance
```

---

# 95. Batch Processing

Batch workloads should define:

```text
Input
Schedule
Expected volume
Freshness
Retry behavior
Idempotency
Output
SLO
```

A batch job completing successfully does not prove its output is correct.

---

# 96. Stream Processing

Streaming systems should define:

```text
Ordering
Event time
Processing time
Windows
State
Checkpoints
Late events
Duplicates
Recovery
```

---

# 97. Event Time vs Processing Time

```text
Event occurred: 10:00
Event received: 10:07
Event processed: 10:08
```

These timestamps represent different concepts and must not be conflated.

---

# 98. Late Data

Streaming pipelines should explicitly define how late events are handled.

Possible strategies:

```text
Accept within window
Update previous result
Route to correction stream
Quarantine
Reject
```

---

# 99. Out-of-Order Events

```text
Expected:
A → B → C

Received:
A → C → B
```

Consumers requiring ordering must define how this is resolved.

---

# 100. Data Pipeline Idempotency

Reprocessing the same input should not accidentally multiply business results.

```text
Input X
  │
  ├── Process
  │
  X failure
  │
  └── Process again
```

Idempotency is both a data-quality and recovery property.

---

# 101. Vector Database Governance

Vector stores require governance equivalent to other enterprise data platforms.

Track:

```text
Collection owner
Source corpus
Embedding model
Dimensions
Metadata schema
Classification
Retention
Index configuration
```

---

# 102. Embedding Provenance

Every governed embedding set should be traceable to:

```text
Source document
Source version
Chunking strategy
Embedding model
Model version
Creation time
Pipeline version
```

---

# 103. Embeddings Are Derived Data

Conceptually:

```text
Source Content
     │
     ▼
Chunking
     │
     ▼
Embedding Model
     │
     ▼
Vectors
```

The vector is not the authoritative source document.

---

# 104. Embedding Model Change

Changing embedding models may invalidate compatibility with existing vectors.

```text
Embedding Model A
       │
       ▼
Vector Space A

Embedding Model B
       │
       ▼
Vector Space B
```

Mixing incompatible embeddings without deliberate design is rejected.

---

# 105. RAG Knowledge Governance

RAG introduces a governed knowledge pipeline.

```text
Knowledge Source
      │
      ▼
Validation
      │
      ▼
Classification
      │
      ▼
Chunking
      │
      ▼
Embedding
      │
      ▼
Retrieval
      │
      ▼
LLM
```

---

# 106. RAG Source Authority

The system must know whether retrieved content is:

```text
Authoritative
Approved
Draft
Historical
User-generated
External
```

Retrieval relevance does not prove authority.

---

# 107. RAG Freshness

Knowledge sources should expose:

```text
Published time
Effective time
Last updated
Version
Expiry where applicable
```

Stale content can produce confidently wrong AI responses.

---

# 108. RAG Deletion Propagation

```text
Source deleted
      │
      ▼
Chunk deleted
      │
      ▼
Embedding deleted
      │
      ▼
Search/vector index updated
      │
      ▼
Cache invalidated
```

Deletion must propagate through derived AI systems.

---

# 109. AI Dataset Governance

Datasets used for:

```text
Training
Fine-tuning
Evaluation
RAG
Prompt testing
Safety testing
```

require ownership, provenance and permitted-use metadata.

---

# 110. AI Dataset Versioning

An experiment should identify exactly which dataset version was used.

```text
Model Version
      +
Dataset Version
      +
Configuration
      =
Reproducible Evaluation
```

---

# 111. AI Evaluation Data Separation

Evaluation datasets should be protected from accidental contamination by training/fine-tuning data where the evaluation methodology requires independence.

Otherwise reported quality can become misleading.

---

# 112. Synthetic Data

Synthetic data may be used for:

```text
Development
Testing
Performance testing
Demonstrations
AI experimentation
```

where it adequately represents required characteristics.

---

# 113. Synthetic Does Not Mean Safe Automatically

Synthetic datasets should be assessed for:

```text
Re-identification risk
Source leakage
Realistic distributions
Bias
Coverage
Utility
```

A copied production record with the name changed is not genuinely synthetic.

---

# 114. Production Data in Non-Production

Default:

```text
Production Sensitive Data
          │
          X
     DEV / TEST
```

unless an explicitly approved and controlled requirement exists.

---

# 115. Non-Production Data Controls

Prefer:

```text
Synthetic data
Masked datasets
Tokenized datasets
Purpose-built fixtures
```

over unrestricted production clones.

---

# 116. Data Masking

Masking should remove or transform sensitive values while preserving required testing utility.

```text
Original
ganesh@example.com

Masked
user_18492@example.test
```

Masking rules must consider relationships between fields.

---

# 117. Tokenization

Tokenization may replace sensitive values with controlled tokens.

```text
Sensitive Value
      │
      ▼
Tokenization Service
      │
      ▼
Opaque Token
```

The token vault becomes a security-critical dependency.

---

# 118. Access Governance

Data access must follow:

```text
Identity
Purpose
Role
Classification
Least privilege
Auditability
```

Database connectivity alone does not authorize unrestricted data use.

---

# 119. Row-Level Controls

Where justified, access may be restricted by row.

Example:

```text
Educator A
    │
    ▼
Students assigned to A
```

rather than all learners in the platform.

---

# 120. Column-Level Controls

Sensitive attributes may require stronger access than ordinary fields.

```text
Course title       → normal authorized access
Sensitive identity → restricted access
```

Controls should follow classification.

---

# 121. Data Residency

Some data may be constrained to approved geographic locations.

Residency requirements must propagate to:

```text
Primary database
Replicas
Backups
Analytics
Logs
Search
AI providers
Vector stores
```

Moving only the primary database is insufficient.

---

# 122. Data Sovereignty Dependency

Before using an external processor:

```text
Dataset
   │
   ▼
Classification
   │
   ▼
Residency Requirement
   │
   ▼
Provider / Region Eligibility
```

This is especially important for AI and analytics services.

---

# 123. Encryption at Rest

Sensitive persistent data should use appropriate encryption.

This includes where applicable:

```text
Databases
Object storage
Backups
Analytics
Search
Vector stores
```

Encryption keys themselves require ADR-075 recovery planning.

---

# 124. Encryption in Transit

Data moving across:

```text
Client → Platform
Service → Service
Platform → Database
Platform → External Provider
Region → Region
```

should use appropriate transport protection.

---

# 125. Retention Governance

Retention must be explicit by data category.

```text
Dataset
   │
   ▼
Purpose
   │
   ▼
Retention Requirement
   │
   ▼
Archive / Delete
```

"Keep everything indefinitely" is rejected.

---

# 126. Retention Metadata

Important datasets should identify:

```text
Retention class
Retention start event
Retention duration
Deletion action
Archive requirement
Legal hold behavior
```

---

# 127. Archival

Archival is appropriate when data must remain available but no longer requires expensive operational storage.

```text
HOT
 │
 ▼
WARM
 │
 ▼
COLD / ARCHIVE
 │
 ▼
DELETE
```

---

# 128. Deletion

Deletion must propagate through relevant copies.

```text
Authoritative DB
      │
      ├── Cache
      ├── Search
      ├── Analytics
      ├── Object storage
      ├── Vector DB
      └── Derived datasets
```

A deletion API that removes one row while leaving five governed copies is incomplete.

---

# 129. Deletion Verification

For critical deletion workflows:

```text
Deletion Requested
       │
       ▼
Delete
       │
       ▼
Propagation
       │
       ▼
Verification
       │
       ▼
Evidence
```

---

# 130. Legal Hold

Where legally applicable, legal hold can override ordinary deletion schedules.

```text
Normal Retention Expired
        │
        ▼
Legal Hold Active?
    ┌───┴───┐
    ▼       ▼
   YES      NO
    │        │
Retain     Delete
```

Legal requirements must be defined by appropriate legal/privacy authority, not guessed by engineering.

---

# 131. Backup Lifecycle

Backups are copies of governed data and therefore inherit relevant:

```text
Classification
Encryption
Residency
Retention
Access
Deletion constraints
```

Backup systems are not outside data governance.

---

# 132. Backup vs Deletion

Immediate removal of an individual record from immutable backups may be technically impossible or conflict with recovery requirements.

Therefore deletion architecture must explicitly define backup handling rather than pretending backup copies do not exist.

---

# 133. Data Observability

Data systems require operational visibility across:

```text
Freshness
Volume
Schema
Quality
Distribution
Pipeline health
Lineage
```

Application infrastructure monitoring alone is insufficient.

---

# 134. Freshness Monitoring

```text
Expected update:
every 5 minutes

Last successful update:
47 minutes ago
```

should generate a meaningful data-health signal.

---

# 135. Volume Anomalies

Detect unexpected:

```text
Record count drops
Record explosions
Missing partitions
Empty batches
Unusual event rates
```

according to expected behavior.

---

# 136. Schema Anomalies

Detect unexpected:

```text
Column removal
Type changes
Nullability changes
Unknown event versions
Unexpected fields
```

before they silently corrupt downstream systems.

---

# 137. Distribution Anomalies

Some failures preserve schema and row counts while corrupting values.

Example:

```text
Typical score mean: 72
Current score mean: 3
```

Distribution monitoring can expose these failures.

---

# 138. Data Incidents

A data incident may occur even when infrastructure is fully healthy.

Examples:

```text
Stale analytics
Missing events
Incorrect transformation
Duplicate records
Broken lineage
Corrupted embeddings
Wrong reference data
```

Data incidents require ownership and incident processes.

---

# 139. Lineage-Aware Incident Analysis

```text
Bad Source Data
      │
      ▼
Lineage Graph
      │
      ├── Analytics
      ├── Search
      ├── Recommendations
      └── AI/RAG
```

Lineage allows responders to identify affected consumers quickly.

---

# 140. Data SLOs

Critical data products may define SLOs for:

```text
Freshness
Completeness
Availability
Quality
Delivery latency
```

Example:

```text
99.9% of progress events
available analytically
within 10 minutes
```

Targets must follow actual product requirements.

---

# 141. Data Product Scorecard

Example:

| Dimension          | Status |
| ------------------ | ------ |
| Owner              | ✓      |
| Contract           | ✓      |
| Classification     | ✓      |
| Lineage            | ✓      |
| Freshness SLO      | ✓      |
| Quality rules      | ✓      |
| Retention          | ✓      |
| Recovery tested    | ✓      |
| Consumer inventory | ⚠      |
| Cost allocation    | ✓      |

A scorecard exposes governance debt rather than hiding it in documentation.

---

# 142. Data Policy as Code

Machine-verifiable rules should be automated where useful.

Examples:

```text
Restricted dataset MUST have owner
Production dataset MUST declare classification
Kafka topic MUST declare retention
Data product MUST declare authoritative source
Temporary dataset MUST have expiry
AI vector collection MUST identify embedding model
```

---

# 143. Data Fitness Functions

Architecture pipelines may validate:

```text
Schema compatibility
Required metadata
Retention configuration
Sensitive-data controls
Quality thresholds
Lineage registration
Recovery requirements
```

Governance should move left without turning every change into bureaucracy.

---

# 144. FinOps and Storage Economics

ADR-073 applies throughout the data lifecycle.

Track:

```text
Database storage
Replicas
Backups
Kafka retention
Object storage
Analytics
Search indexes
Vector indexes
Data transfer
```

Data without lifecycle governance becomes permanent cost.

---

# 145. Sustainability Integration

ADR-074 applies equally.

Prefer eliminating:

```text
Unused copies
Obsolete datasets
Unnecessary replication
Repeated full processing
Orphaned vectors
Infinite telemetry/data retention
```

before optimizing the infrastructure storing them.

---

# 146. Disaster Recovery Integration

ADR-075 and ADR-076 must share state classification.

```text
AUTHORITATIVE
     │
     └── Backup / replication / PITR

DERIVED
     │
     └── Rebuild where feasible

EPHEMERAL
     │
     └── Recreate / discard
```

Recovery investment should follow data value and rebuildability.

---

# 147. Data Governance Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — FRAGMENTED

Data exists across systems with
unclear ownership and semantics.


LEVEL 2 — CATALOGUED

Important data is classified,
owned and discoverable.


LEVEL 3 — GOVERNED

Contracts, quality, lifecycle
and lineage are standardized.


LEVEL 4 — PRODUCTIZED

Data products expose measurable
quality, SLOs and platform controls.


LEVEL 5 — INTELLIGENT

Governance is increasingly automated,
lineage-aware and integrated into
applications, analytics and AI.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, selectively adopting Level 5 capabilities where automation produces real operational value.

---

# 148. Data Governance Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "The database is the documentation"
❌ Tables without owners
❌ Shared databases owned by everyone
❌ Multiple uncontrolled sources of truth
❌ Analytics systems treated as transactional authority
❌ Search indexes treated as authoritative state
❌ Redis caches treated as authoritative business records
❌ Vector databases treated as original knowledge
❌ Direct cross-service database coupling by default
❌ Breaking migrations without transition strategy
❌ Database CDC exposed as enterprise semantics automatically
❌ Database + Kafka unsafe dual writes
❌ Kafka topics without owners
❌ Events without schemas
❌ Events exposing arbitrary database internals
❌ Semantic changes hidden behind compatible data types
❌ Infinite Kafka retention by default
❌ Replay without idempotency analysis
❌ Data lakes without ownership/catalogue/lifecycle
❌ ETL success treated as data-quality proof
❌ Streaming without late-event strategy
❌ Streaming without duplicate strategy
❌ Embeddings without source provenance
❌ Mixing incompatible embedding spaces
❌ RAG retrieval treated as proof of authority
❌ Deleted documents remaining indefinitely in vector stores
❌ AI datasets without versions
❌ Evaluation data contaminated by training data
❌ Production databases cloned freely into development
❌ Calling lightly modified production records "synthetic"
❌ Sensitive data available because network connectivity exists
❌ Residency applied only to the primary database
❌ Backups excluded from classification governance
❌ Retention = forever
❌ Deletion only from the primary table
❌ Legal requirements invented by engineers
❌ Quality defined only as "pipeline succeeded"
❌ Monitoring only infrastructure and ignoring data freshness
❌ Schema monitoring without semantic governance
❌ Data incidents without owners
❌ Lineage existing only as a static architecture diagram
❌ Governance requiring manual approval for every trivial dataset
❌ Policy documents without automated controls where automation is practical
❌ Storage optimization while retaining useless data forever
```

---

| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| Governance model                  | Federated ownership + central standards        |
| Data organization                 | Business domains                               |

| Data steward                      | Required for governed critical domains         |
| Data products                     | Standard for important shared datasets         |
| Authoritative source              | Explicit                                       |
| System of record                  | Explicit by business concept                   |
| Operational/analytical separation | Preferred                                      |
| Derived data                      | Upstream authority required                    |
| Classification                    | Mandatory for significant data                 |
| Schema ownership                  | Explicit                                       |
| Canonical models                  | Selective, not universal                       |
| Business glossary                 | Required for critical concepts                 |
| Metadata catalogue                | Enterprise capability                          |
| Lineage                           | Required for critical data flows               |
| Column lineage                    | Risk/value based                               |
| Provenance                        | Required where material                        |
| Data contracts                    | Required for important shared interfaces       |
| Semantic compatibility            | Governed                                       |
| Event schemas                     | Governed                                       |
| Quality dimensions                | Multi-dimensional                              |
| Quality validation                | Automated where practical                      |
| Quarantine                        | Supported                                      |
| Reconciliation                    | Required where consistency matters             |
| Identifier strategy               | Domain-governed                                |
| PostgreSQL ownership              | Service/domain aligned                         |

| Object storage                    | Lifecycle governed                             |
| Data lake                         | Requirement-driven                             |
| Lakehouse                         | Requirement-driven                             |
| Batch/stream                      | Explicit semantics                             |
| Late/out-of-order data            | Explicitly handled                             |
| Vector DB                         | Governed                                       |
| Embedding provenance              | Required                                       |
| RAG source authority              | Required                                       |
| AI datasets                       | Versioned and provenance-aware                 |
| Synthetic data                    | Preferred for non-prod where suitable          |
| Production data in non-prod       | Restricted by default                          |
| Access                            | Least privilege + purpose                      |
| Residency                         | End-to-end                                     |
| Encryption                        | Classification driven                          |
| Retention                         | Explicit                                       |
| Archival                          | Lifecycle based                                |
| Deletion                          | Propagated and verifiable                      |
| Legal hold                        | Overrides ordinary deletion where applicable   |
| Backups                           | Governed data copies                           |
| Data observability                | Required for critical products                 |
| Data SLOs                         | Required where business-critical               |
| Policy-as-code                    | Preferred where measurable                     |
| FinOps                            | Integrated                                     |
| Sustainability                    | Integrated                                     |
| DR                                | Authority/rebuildability aligned               |
| Maturity target                   | Level 4                                        |
| Status                            | **Accepted**                                   |
| Priority                          | **Critical**                                   |
