# ADR-076 — COMPLETE ✅

The governing invariant is:

> **Mediverse will not treat data as trustworthy merely because it exists in a database, event stream, warehouse, search index or vector store. Important data must have explicit business meaning, accountable ownership, an authoritative source, governed contracts, traceable provenance and lineage, measurable quality, controlled access, and a defined lifecycle from creation through verified deletion.**

The complete data control loop becomes:

```text
BUSINESS MEANING
      │
      ▼
   OWNERSHIP
      │
      ▼
AUTHORITATIVE SOURCE
      │
      ▼
   CONTRACT
      │
      ▼
   PRODUCE
      │
      ▼
  VALIDATE
      │
      ▼
 DISTRIBUTE
      │
      ▼
   LINEAGE
      │
      ▼
   CONSUME
      │
      ├────► Applications
      ├────► Analytics
      ├────► Search
      └────► AI
      │
      ▼
   OBSERVE
      │
      ▼
QUALITY / SLO
      │
      ▼
   RETAIN
      │
      ▼
ARCHIVE / DELETE
      │
      ▼
   EVIDENCE
      │
      └──────────────► GOVERNANCE
```

## Next — ADR-077

### **ADR-077 — Enterprise AI Governance, Responsible AI, LLMOps, Model Risk & AI Safety Standard**

ADR-076 now gives Mediverse the governed data foundation that AI needs. ADR-077 should establish the **AI control plane** across the entire platform: **AI capability classification → use-case intake → AI risk tiering → prohibited/restricted use cases → human oversight → model inventory → provider/model approval → build-vs-buy → model cards → system cards → model provenance → versioning → prompt governance → system-prompt ownership → prompt injection → jailbreak resistance → input/output controls → PII/data leakage → provider data-processing rules → model routing → fallback models → hallucination management → grounded generation → RAG governance integration → citation/provenance → tool/function calling → agent permissions → least agency → autonomous-action boundaries → human-in-the-loop → high-impact decisions → confidence/uncertainty → structured outputs → content safety → bias/fairness evaluation → accessibility → multilingual behavior → model evaluation framework → golden datasets → regression testing → adversarial testing → red teaming → AI security → supply-chain risk → model/prompt deployment → LLMOps → shadow/canary rollout → online evaluation → drift → quality monitoring → token/cost telemetry → ADR-073 FinOps integration → ADR-074 sustainability integration → ADR-075 AI continuity → ADR-076 data governance → AI observability → audit trails → incident response → kill switches → rollback → third-party AI governance → open-source model governance → self-hosted GPU/model serving → fine-tuning governance → training-data provenance → synthetic data → embedding-model governance → vector/RAG lifecycle → AI experimentation → research-to-production gates → AI policy-as-code → AI fitness functions → developer golden paths → AI scorecards → governance operating model → maturity model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise Responsible-AI/LLMOps reference architecture and ADR-077 decision outcome.**

# ADR-077 — Enterprise AI Governance, Responsible AI, LLMOps, Model Risk & AI Safety Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-077
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Primary Stakeholders:** AI Platform Engineering, Application Engineering, Security, Privacy, Data Governance, SRE, Product, Clinical/Academic Governance, Platform Engineering, FinOps

ADR-076 established the governed data foundation required for trustworthy AI.

ADR-077 establishes how Mediverse is permitted to **design, acquire, build, evaluate, deploy, operate, monitor, secure and retire AI capabilities**.

The core principle is:

> **An AI model producing plausible output is not evidence that an AI system is safe, reliable or production-ready.**

```text
                       AI USE CASE
                           │
                           ▼
                      RISK ASSESSMENT
                           │
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ▼            ▼            ▼
            DATA         MODEL        ACTION
             RISK          RISK         RISK
              │            │            │
              └────────────┼────────────┘
                           ▼
                     CONTROL PROFILE
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ▼                   ▼                   ▼
    SECURITY           EVALUATION          OVERSIGHT
       │                   │                   │
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ▼
                       AI SYSTEM
                           │
             ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
             ▼             ▼             ▼
            LLM           RAG           AGENT
             │             │             │
             └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                           ▼
                    CONTROLLED RELEASE
                           │
                           ▼
                 OBSERVE → EVALUATE
                           │
                           ▼
               CONTINUE / DEGRADE / KILL
```

# 1. AI Governance Objective

Mediverse AI systems must be:

```text
Purpose-defined
Risk-classified
Data-governed
Secure
Evaluated
Traceable
Observable
Cost-controlled
Human-governed
Recoverable
Reversible
```

AI governance applies to the **complete AI system**, not only the foundation model.

---

# 2. AI System Boundary

An AI system may include:

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
System Prompt
    │
    ▼
Retrieved Context
    │
    ▼
LLM
    │
    ▼
Tools / APIs
    │
    ▼
Post-processing
    │
    ▼
User Experience
```

Evaluating only the model while ignoring these components is insufficient.

---

# 3. AI Capability Inventory

Every production AI capability must be registered.

The inventory should identify:

```text
Use case
Business owner
Technical owner
Risk tier
Model/provider
Data categories
RAG sources
Tools
Deployment status
Evaluation status
```

Unknown AI systems become unmanaged enterprise risk.

---

# 4. AI Use-Case Intake

AI implementation begins with a use case—not a model.

```text
Business Problem
      │
      ▼
Can deterministic software solve it?
   ┌──┴──┐
   ▼     ▼
  YES    NO
   │      │
Use it   Evaluate AI
```

Mediverse rejects adding LLMs where conventional software is more reliable and economical.

---

# 5. AI Risk Classification

AI capabilities should be classified according to consequences.

Conceptually:

```text
TIER 0 — Minimal
TIER 1 — Low
TIER 2 — Moderate
TIER 3 — High
TIER 4 — Critical / Restricted
```

Controls increase with risk.

---

# 6. Risk Dimensions

Classification should consider:

```text
User harm
Academic impact
Medical/clinical impact
Privacy
Security
Autonomy
Financial impact
Scale
Reversibility
Data sensitivity
Model uncertainty
```

---

# 7. Low-Risk AI

Potential examples:

```text
Course summarization
Formatting assistance
Internal tagging
Content classification
Search query rewriting
```

provided the specific implementation does not introduce higher-risk consequences.

---

# 8. Moderate-Risk AI

Potential examples:

```text
Personalized study recommendations
AI tutoring
Question generation
Assessment feedback
Learning-plan generation
```

These require stronger evaluation because users may rely on their correctness.

---

# 9. High-Risk AI

Potential high-impact capabilities include AI influencing:

```text
Academic progression
Formal assessment
Clinical interpretation
Safety-critical recommendations
Access decisions
```

These require substantially stronger controls and human governance.

---

# 10. Risk Is Use-Case Specific

The same model may have different risk levels.

```text
LLM
 │
 ├── Rewrite heading
 │      LOW
 │
 ├── Explain physiology
 │      MODERATE
 │
 └── Make clinical decision
        HIGH/RESTRICTED
```

Model identity alone does not determine system risk.

---

# 11. Prohibited AI Uses

Mediverse should explicitly define uses that AI must not perform autonomously.

Examples may include:

```text
Unreviewed high-impact decisions
Unbounded privileged actions
Security-control bypass
Undisclosed manipulation
Use of prohibited data
Unsupported clinical authority
```

Exact prohibitions must align with applicable governance and regulation.

---

# 12. Human Accountability

AI never becomes the accountable business owner.

```text
AI Recommendation
       │
       ▼
Human / Governed Process
       │
       ▼
Accountable Decision
```

Responsibility cannot be delegated to a model.

---

# 13. Human-in-the-Loop

Human review is required where consequences justify it.

```text
AI Output
   │
   ▼
Human Review
 ┌─┴────┐
 ▼      ▼
Approve Reject
```

But adding a meaningless "Approve" button does not constitute meaningful oversight.

---

# 14. Human-on-the-Loop

Some systems may operate automatically while humans supervise and can intervene.

```text
AI System
    │
    ▼
Automated Operation
    │
    ▼
Monitoring
    │
    ▼
Human Intervention
```

Appropriate only when risk and reversibility permit.

---

# 15. Human-out-of-the-Loop

Fully autonomous AI should be limited to sufficiently low-risk, bounded and reversible actions.

Autonomy must be explicitly authorized rather than accidentally emerging from tool access.

---

# 16. Model Inventory

Every production model dependency should identify:

```text
Provider
Model
Version
Purpose
Owner
Risk tier
Deployment
Evaluation
Fallback
Retirement state
```

---

# 17. Model Approval

A model should not become production-approved because a developer successfully called its API.

Approval should evaluate:

```text
Capability
Security
Privacy
Data processing
Quality
Latency
Availability
Cost
Safety
Operational support
```

---

# 18. Build vs Buy

Mediverse may use:

```text
Hosted proprietary models
Hosted open models
Self-hosted models
Fine-tuned models
Specialized ML models
```

Selection must be requirement-driven.

---

# 19. Model Selection

Do not default to the largest available model.

```text
Required Quality
      +
Latency
      +
Safety
      +
Context
      +
Cost
      +
Availability
      =
Model Selection
```

---

# 20. Model Cards

Where available or internally maintained, model documentation should capture:

```text
Intended use
Known limitations
Evaluation
Safety considerations
Data considerations
Version
```

---

# 21. AI System Cards

Mediverse should additionally document the complete application-level AI system.

```text
MODEL CARD
    │
    ▼
Model characteristics

SYSTEM CARD
    │
    ▼
How Mediverse actually uses it
```

System-level risk cannot be inferred from model documentation alone.

---

# 22. Model Provenance

Mediverse must know where deployed models originate.

For self-hosted models:

```text
Source
License
Version
Weights
Checksum
Configuration
Dependencies
```

must be traceable.

---

# 23. Model Versioning

Model changes can change application behavior even when application code remains identical.

```text
Application v12
     │
     ▼
Model v1
     │
     ▼
Model v2
     │
     ▼
Different behavior
```

Model version changes therefore require controlled release.

---

# 24. Provider Alias Risk

Using a provider alias such as:

```text
latest
default
recommended
```

may allow behavior to change without Mediverse deployment.

Where reproducibility matters, pinning/version governance is preferred where provider capabilities permit it.

---

# 25. Prompt Governance

Prompts are production logic.

Treat important prompts like code:

```text
Version
Owner
Review
Testing
Deployment
Rollback
```

---

# 26. System Prompt Ownership

Every important system prompt should have an owner.

Uncontrolled prompt changes can alter:

```text
Behavior
Safety
Tone
Tool usage
Output format
Data handling
```

---

# 27. Prompt Repository

Production prompts should be maintained in controlled configuration/source systems rather than copied across application code and dashboards.

---

# 28. Prompt Versioning

Telemetry should make it possible to associate an AI response with:

```text
Application version
Prompt version
Model version
RAG version
Configuration version
```

This is essential for debugging regressions.

---

# 29. Prompt Injection

RAG and agentic systems must assume external text may contain malicious instructions.

```text
Document
   │
   ▼
"Ignore previous instructions..."
   │
   ▼
Retriever
   │
   ▼
LLM
```

Retrieved data must not automatically acquire system-level authority.

---

# 30. Instruction Hierarchy

Systems should distinguish:

```text
Trusted system instructions
        │
Developer/application controls
        │
User instructions
        │
Retrieved/untrusted content
```

Untrusted content should be treated as data, not privileged instructions.

---

# 31. Jailbreak Resistance

Mediverse should evaluate whether users can induce the system to bypass intended controls.

Testing should cover:

```text
Instruction override
Role manipulation
Encoding tricks
Multi-turn attacks
Context poisoning
Tool manipulation
```

according to system risk.

---

# 32. Input Controls

Inputs may require:

```text
Size limits
File validation
Classification
Malware controls
PII handling
Prompt-injection defenses
Rate limits
```

depending on the capability.

---

# 33. Output Controls

AI output may require:

```text
Schema validation
Safety filtering
Grounding checks
Citation checks
Policy checks
Business-rule validation
```

before reaching users or downstream systems.

---

# 34. Structured Output

When AI feeds software:

```text
Free-form prose
      │
      X
Business operation
```

is often unsafe.

Prefer validated structured output where appropriate:

```json
{
  "courseId": "C102",
  "action": "recommend",
  "confidence": 0.82
}
```

---

# 35. Deterministic Validation

Never ask an LLM to enforce a rule that conventional code can enforce reliably.

```text
LLM proposes action
       │
       ▼
Deterministic validator
       │
   ┌───┴───┐
   ▼       ▼
 ACCEPT   REJECT
```

---

# 36. Sensitive Data Exposure

Prompts may contain governed data.

Before external transmission:

```text
Data
 │
 ▼
Classification
 │
 ▼
Provider permitted?
 │
 ├── YES → controlled processing
 └── NO  → block/redact/local alternative
```

ADR-076 controls apply.

---

# 37. Provider Data Processing

For external AI providers, governance must understand:

```text
Retention
Training use
Logging
Region
Subprocessors
Security
Deletion
Contractual controls
```

Provider assumptions must not be guessed.

---

# 38. Data Minimization

Send only data required for the AI task.

```text
Complete learner record
          │
          X
Question needs only course topic
```

More context is not automatically better.

---

# 39. PII Redaction

Where appropriate:

```text
Prompt
  │
  ▼
PII Detection
  │
  ▼
Redaction / Tokenization
  │
  ▼
Model
```

But redaction must not be assumed perfect.

---

# 40. Model Routing

Mediverse may route requests according to:

```text
Risk
Task
Latency
Cost
Context size
Availability
Quality
Data restrictions
```

---

# 41. Model Router

```text
AI Request
    │
    ▼
Policy Router
    │
 ┌──┼───────────┐
 ▼  ▼           ▼
Small Model   Large Model   Self-hosted
```

Routing rules are governed application logic.

---

# 42. Fallback Models

Fallback should not mean:

```text
Primary fails
    │
    ▼
Send everything to any available model
```

Fallback models must satisfy the request's security and data-processing requirements.

---

# 43. Behavioral Fallback

A secondary model may produce materially different output.

Therefore fallback requires evaluation of:

```text
Quality
Safety
Prompt compatibility
Tool compatibility
Structured output
```

---

# 44. No-AI Fallback

Sometimes the correct fallback is:

```text
AI unavailable
      │
      ▼
Disable AI feature
      │
      ▼
Core learning continues
```

ADR-075 governs continuity.

---

# 45. Hallucination Risk

LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims.

Mediverse must not treat linguistic confidence as factual confidence.

---

# 46. Grounded Generation

Where factual correctness matters:

```text
User Question
      │
      ▼
Retrieve Trusted Sources
      │
      ▼
Generate from Context
      │
      ▼
Validate / Cite
```

Grounding reduces but does not eliminate hallucination.

---

# 47. Source Authority

RAG must respect ADR-076 authority metadata.

```text
Retrieved Document
      │
      ▼
Relevant?
      │
      ▼
Authoritative?
```

These are different questions.

---

# 48. Citation Provenance

Where AI provides source-backed answers, citations should be traceable to actual retrieved evidence.

The system must avoid fabricated source references.

---

# 49. Retrieval Quality

RAG evaluation must test:

```text
Recall
Precision
Ranking
Freshness
Authority
Chunk quality
Metadata filtering
```

Evaluating only final LLM prose hides retrieval failures.

---

# 50. Context Quality

More retrieved chunks can decrease quality.

```text
Relevant Context
      +
Irrelevant Context
      +
Conflicting Context
      =
Potentially worse answer
```

Context-window size is not a quality strategy.

---

# 51. Tool Calling

An LLM may request tools such as:

```text
Search
Database query
Calendar
Email
Learning APIs
Administrative APIs
```

The model's request is not authorization.

---

# 52. Tool Authorization

```text
LLM proposes tool call
        │
        ▼
Policy / Authorization
        │
    ┌───┴───┐
    ▼       ▼
 ALLOW     DENY
```

Authorization must be enforced outside the model.

---

# 53. Least Agency

Agents receive the minimum capability necessary.

```text
Read course catalogue
        ✓

Delete course
        ✗

Change learner grade
        ✗
```

unless explicitly required and governed.

---

# 54. Agent Permission Boundaries

Agent permissions should be constrained by:

```text
User identity
Agent identity
Task
Tool
Resource
Scope
Time
Risk
```

---

# 55. User Authorization Propagation

An AI agent acting for a user must not silently gain more authority than the user.

```text
User permissions
       │
       ▼
Agent effective permissions
       │
       ≤
User permissions
```

Additional service-level restrictions may further reduce authority.

---

# 56. Confirmation Before Consequence

High-impact actions should require explicit confirmation or human approval where appropriate.

```text
AI proposes:
"Submit assessment?"
       │
       ▼
User confirms
       │
       ▼
Execute
```

---

# 57. Reversible Actions

Prefer reversible operations when AI acts autonomously.

```text
Draft
Preview
Stage
Recommend
Queue
```

before:

```text
Delete
Publish
Submit
Approve
Revoke
```

---

# 58. Agent Loop Limits

Autonomous loops require bounds.

```text
Maximum steps
Maximum runtime
Maximum tokens
Maximum cost
Maximum tool calls
```

An agent must not reason-and-act indefinitely.

---

# 59. Agent Memory

Agent memory introduces persistent data governance.

Memory requires:

```text
Purpose
Scope
Retention
User visibility
Deletion
Classification
Access
```

ADR-076 applies.

---

# 60. Agent Identity

Production agents should have distinguishable machine identity.

```text
Human User
     │
     ▼
AI Agent
     │
     ▼
Tool
```

Audit trails should show both the initiating human/context and executing agent where applicable.

---

## ADR-077 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The emerging AI governance model is:

```text
                         AI USE CASE
                              │
                              ▼
                        RISK TIERING
                              │
           ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
           ▼                  ▼                  ▼
          DATA              MODEL             ACTION
           │                  │                  │
           └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                              ▼
                       GOVERNANCE PROFILE
                              │
      ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
      ▼                       ▼                       ▼
    PROMPT                   RAG                    AGENT
      │                       │                       │
      ├─ Version              ├─ Authority             ├─ Identity
      ├─ Injection            ├─ Provenance            ├─ Tools
      ├─ Inputs               ├─ Freshness             ├─ Permissions
      └─ Outputs              └─ Retrieval             └─ Limits
      │                       │                       │
      └───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┘
                              ▼
                           MODEL
                              │
                 ┌────────────┼────────────┐
                 ▼            ▼            ▼
              QUALITY       SAFETY       COST
                 │            │            │
                 └────────────┼────────────┘
                              ▼
                       CONTROLLED ACTION
                              │
                              ▼
                        HUMAN OVERSIGHT
                              │
                              ▼
                         AUDITABILITY
```

The governing principle emerging from Sections 1–60 is:

> **Mediverse treats LLM output as untrusted probabilistic output until the surrounding system establishes the required level of grounding, validation, authorization and human oversight. A model may propose; deterministic controls and accountable actors decide what the system is permitted to do.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — AI Evaluation Framework**, then cover **evaluation dimensions → golden datasets → offline evaluation → task-specific metrics → LLM-as-judge limitations → human evaluation → hallucination/groundedness testing → RAG evaluation → agent evaluation → tool-use testing → regression suites → adversarial testing → red teaming → bias/fairness → multilingual evaluation → accessibility → uncertainty → confidence → calibration → content safety → AI security → model supply chain → open-source models → self-hosting → GPU/model-serving governance → fine-tuning → training-data provenance → model/prompt release management → research-to-production gates → shadow deployment → canary rollout → A/B testing → online evaluation → drift → AI observability → token/cost telemetry → latency → quality monitoring → feedback loops → audit trails → AI incident response → kill switches → rollback → provider outage → model deprecation → LLMOps → model/prompt registry → reproducibility → AI FinOps → sustainability → DR integration → data-governance integration → policy-as-code → fitness functions → developer golden paths → AI scorecards → governance operating model → maturity model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise AI/LLMOps reference architecture and ADR-077 decision outcome.**

# ADR-077 — Enterprise AI Governance, Responsible AI, LLMOps, Model Risk & AI Safety Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing from **Section 60 — Agent Identity**.

---

# 61. AI Evaluation Framework

No AI capability reaches production merely because its outputs "look good."

Evaluation must answer:

```text
Does it solve the intended task?
        │
        ├── Correctly?
        ├── Reliably?
        ├── Safely?
        ├── Fairly?
        ├── Within latency targets?
        ├── Within cost limits?
        └── Under adversarial conditions?
```

Evaluation requirements scale with the AI risk tier.

---

# 62. Evaluation Dimensions

Mediverse AI evaluation should consider:

```text
Task Quality
Groundedness
Factuality
Safety
Robustness
Consistency
Latency
Cost
Accessibility
Fairness
Tool Accuracy
Retrieval Quality
User Experience
```

A single aggregate score is insufficient for important systems.

---

# 63. Task-Specific Metrics

Metrics must reflect the actual task.

```text
Classification
    └── Precision / Recall / F1

Retrieval
    └── Recall@K / Precision@K / ranking

Generation
    └── Groundedness / correctness / relevance

Agent
    └── Task success / tool correctness / policy compliance
```

Using the wrong metric can make a bad system appear good.

---

# 64. Golden Evaluation Datasets

Critical AI capabilities should maintain representative evaluation datasets.

```text
Golden Dataset
      │
      ├── Normal cases
      ├── Difficult cases
      ├── Edge cases
      ├── Safety cases
      ├── Adversarial cases
      └── Historical regressions
```

---

# 65. Golden Dataset Governance

ADR-076 applies.

Evaluation datasets require:

```text
Owner
Version
Provenance
Classification
Expected outputs/criteria
Coverage
Retention
```

A random spreadsheet of prompts is not an enterprise evaluation framework.

---

# 66. Evaluation Dataset Independence

Where methodology requires independent evaluation:

```text
Training / Tuning Data
          │
          X
    Golden Evaluation
```

Contamination can produce misleading performance results.

---

# 67. Offline Evaluation

Before deployment:

```text
Candidate AI System
        │
        ▼
Evaluation Suite
        │
        ▼
Quality + Safety + Cost
        │
        ▼
Release Gate
```

Offline evaluation becomes part of AI CI/CD.

---

# 68. Evaluation Baselines

New versions should be compared against:

```text
Current production version
Previous approved version
Deterministic baseline
Human baseline where meaningful
```

A model improvement claim requires a meaningful reference point.

---

# 69. Regression Testing

Changes to any of these can cause AI regressions:

```text
Model
Prompt
RAG corpus
Chunking
Embedding model
Retriever
Tool definitions
Temperature
Context policy
Post-processing
```

Therefore AI regression testing must cover the system, not just the model.

---

# 70. LLM-as-Judge

LLMs may assist evaluation, especially at scale.

But:

```text
LLM judges LLM
      │
      ▼
Potential bias
Position bias
Model preference
Prompt sensitivity
Inconsistency
```

LLM-as-judge results must not automatically be treated as ground truth.

---

# 71. Human Evaluation

Human evaluation remains important for:

```text
Nuance
Pedagogical usefulness
Domain correctness
Ambiguous cases
Safety
User experience
```

especially for higher-risk educational and medical content.

---

# 72. Human Evaluator Guidance

Evaluators require explicit rubrics.

```text
Bad:

"Is this response good?"

Better:

Accuracy
Relevance
Groundedness
Completeness
Safety
Clarity
```

Otherwise evaluator disagreement becomes meaningless noise.

---

# 73. Inter-Rater Agreement

For subjective evaluations, Mediverse should measure evaluator consistency where appropriate.

Large disagreement may indicate:

```text
Poor rubric
Ambiguous task
Insufficient expertise
Subjective requirement
```

rather than merely "bad evaluators."

---

# 74. Hallucination Evaluation

Test whether generated claims are:

```text
Supported
Unsupported
Contradicted
Unverifiable
```

according to the task's evidence requirements.

---

# 75. Groundedness Evaluation

For RAG:

```text
Generated Claim
      │
      ▼
Retrieved Evidence
      │
 ┌────┼────┐
 ▼    ▼    ▼
Yes Partial No
```

A relevant document does not guarantee that every generated claim is grounded in it.

---

# 76. Retrieval Evaluation

RAG evaluation should separate:

```text
RETRIEVAL FAILURE

Correct evidence never retrieved

from

GENERATION FAILURE

Correct evidence retrieved
but model answered incorrectly
```

Without this separation, teams optimize the wrong component.

---

# 77. RAG Evaluation Pipeline

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Expected Evidence
   │
   ▼
Retriever
   │
   ├── Recall@K
   ├── Ranking
   ├── Authority
   └── Freshness
          │
          ▼
         LLM
          │
          ├── Correctness
          ├── Groundedness
          └── Citation accuracy
```

---

# 78. Agent Evaluation

Agents require more than answer-quality testing.

Evaluate:

```text
Task completion
Planning behavior
Tool selection
Argument correctness
Authorization compliance
Step count
Recovery behavior
Cost
Side effects
```

---

# 79. Tool-Use Testing

For each tool:

```text
Should tool be called?
        │
        ▼
Correct tool?
        │
        ▼
Correct arguments?
        │
        ▼
Authorized?
        │
        ▼
Result interpreted correctly?
```

---

# 80. Agent Failure Scenarios

Test:

```text
Tool timeout
Tool returns malformed data
Permission denied
Partial success
Duplicate response
Network failure
Conflicting tool results
Malicious tool output
```

Agents must not assume tool success.

---

# 81. Adversarial Testing

AI systems should be tested against intentional attempts to cause failure.

Examples:

```text
Prompt injection
Jailbreak
Context poisoning
Data extraction
Tool abuse
Role confusion
Malformed inputs
Resource exhaustion
```

---

# 82. AI Red Teaming

Higher-risk capabilities require structured red-team exercises.

```text
Threat Model
     │
     ▼
Attack Scenarios
     │
     ▼
Execute
     │
     ▼
Observe Failure
     │
     ▼
Mitigate
     │
     ▼
Retest
```

---

# 83. Red-Team Findings

Findings should enter normal engineering governance:

```text
Finding
   │
   ▼
Severity
   │
   ▼
Owner
   │
   ▼
Remediation
   │
   ▼
Verification
```

A red-team report sitting in a document repository provides little protection.

---

# 84. Bias and Fairness Evaluation

Where user impact warrants it, evaluate whether system quality materially differs across relevant populations or contexts.

Metrics must be selected according to the use case.

Fairness cannot be reduced to one universal number.

---

# 85. Multilingual Evaluation

Mediverse must not assume:

```text
English quality
      =
Marathi quality
      =
Hindi quality
      =
Other language quality
```

Each supported language requires representative evaluation where AI behavior matters.

---

# 86. Translation Risk

AI-generated translation can alter:

```text
Meaning
Terminology
Medical concepts
Assessment intent
Safety information
```

Critical educational content may require domain-aware validation.

---

# 87. Accessibility Evaluation

AI-generated interfaces/content should be assessed for compatibility with accessibility requirements.

AI should not create a second, less-accessible user experience.

---

# 88. Uncertainty

Probabilistic systems inherently contain uncertainty.

The application should not convert uncertainty into false certainty through UI design.

```text
Model uncertain
      │
      ▼
UI displays:
"Definitely correct"
      │
      ▼
Bad system design
```

---

# 89. Confidence Scores

Raw model probabilities or self-reported confidence must not automatically be interpreted as calibrated real-world confidence.

Calibration must be demonstrated where confidence drives decisions.

---

# 90. Abstention

AI systems should be capable of declining when evidence or confidence is inadequate.

```text
Question
   │
   ▼
Sufficient evidence?
 ┌─┴─────┐
 ▼       ▼
YES      NO
 │        │
Answer   Abstain / escalate
```

A forced answer is often worse than no answer.

---

# 91. Content Safety

Safety controls may cover:

```text
Harmful instructions
Harassment
Sexual content
Self-harm
Violence
Illegal activity
Sensitive content
```

according to product requirements and applicable policies.

Safety controls must be tested, not merely configured.

---

# 92. Safety Layering

Do not rely on one safety mechanism.

```text
Input Controls
      │
      ▼
System Instructions
      │
      ▼
Model Safety
      │
      ▼
Output Controls
      │
      ▼
Application Rules
```

Defense in depth applies to AI.

---

# 93. AI Security Threat Model

AI threat modeling should include:

```text
Prompt injection
Model extraction
Data exfiltration
Training-data leakage
RAG poisoning
Tool abuse
Supply-chain compromise
Credential exposure
Denial-of-wallet
Resource exhaustion
```

---

# 94. Denial-of-Wallet

AI introduces a failure mode where attackers may generate excessive cost.

```text
Attacker
   │
   ▼
Expensive Requests
   │
   ▼
Tokens / GPUs / Tools
   │
   ▼
Cost Explosion
```

Rate limits and budgets become security controls as well as FinOps controls.

---

# 95. AI Supply Chain

The AI supply chain may include:

```text
Models
Tokenizers
Libraries
Containers
CUDA/runtime
Prompt packages
Embedding models
Datasets
Evaluation frameworks
```

Each dependency introduces provenance and vulnerability considerations.

---

# 96. Open-Source Model Governance

Before adopting an open-source/open-weight model, evaluate:

```text
License
Source
Provenance
Model card
Security
Known limitations
Runtime requirements
Maintenance
Community/support
```

"Free weights" does not mean free operationally or legally.

---

# 97. Model Artifact Integrity

Self-hosted model artifacts should be verified before deployment.

```text
Approved Model
     │
     ▼
Checksum / Signature
     │
     ▼
Verification
     │
     ▼
Deployment
```

---

# 98. Self-Hosted Model Governance

Self-hosting transfers responsibility to Mediverse for:

```text
Capacity
GPU infrastructure
Scaling
Patching
Security
Availability
Serving
Monitoring
Model lifecycle
```

It should not be selected solely to avoid API charges.

---

# 99. GPU Capacity Governance

GPU workloads should define:

```text
Model size
Memory requirements
Concurrency
Batching
Latency
Utilization
Scaling
Recovery
Cost
```

Idle GPU capacity can become substantial waste.

---

# 100. Model Serving

The serving layer should expose operational signals such as:

```text
Request rate
Queue depth
Time to first token
Generation latency
Tokens/sec
GPU utilization
Errors
OOM events
```

---

# 101. Fine-Tuning Governance

Fine-tuning requires explicit justification.

```text
Problem
   │
   ├── Prompt engineering enough?
   ├── RAG enough?
   ├── Tooling enough?
   │
   ▼
Fine-tuning justified?
```

Fine-tuning is not the default solution to every quality problem.

---

# 102. Training-Data Provenance

Fine-tuning datasets must identify:

```text
Origin
Ownership
License/permission
Classification
Processing
Version
Quality
```

ADR-076 governs the dataset.

---

# 103. Fine-Tuning Reproducibility

Record:

```text
Base model
Dataset version
Hyperparameters
Training code
Environment
Random seed where relevant
Resulting artifact
Evaluation results
```

---

# 104. Fine-Tuned Model Evaluation

A successful training job is not evidence of improvement.

```text
Base Model
     │
     ▼
Baseline Evaluation

Fine-Tuned Model
     │
     ▼
Same Evaluation
     │
     ▼
Compare
```

Safety regressions must be evaluated alongside quality improvements.

---

# 105. Research-to-Production Boundary

Experimentation environments may move quickly.

Production cannot inherit that looseness automatically.

```text
Research
   │
   ▼
Candidate
   │
   ▼
Evaluation
   │
   ▼
Security Review
   │
   ▼
Governance Gate
   │
   ▼
Production
```

---

# 106. Production Readiness Gate

Production AI requires, according to risk:

```text
Owner
Risk classification
Approved model
Approved data use
Evaluation evidence
Security controls
Observability
Cost limits
Rollback
Incident process
```

---

# 107. AI Release Unit

The actual AI release unit may be:

```text
Application version
+
Model version
+
Prompt version
+
Retriever version
+
Embedding version
+
Knowledge version
+
Tool configuration
```

This combination defines behavior.

---

# 108. Shadow Deployment

Candidate AI may receive production-like requests without controlling user-visible behavior.

```text
Request
   │
   ├────► Production AI ───► User
   │
   └────► Candidate AI ────► Evaluation
```

Sensitive-data policies still apply.

---

# 109. Canary Deployment

```text
Traffic
  │
  ├── 95% Current
  └──  5% Candidate
```

Observe quality, safety, latency and cost before expansion.

---

# 110. AI A/B Testing

A/B tests should have:

```text
Hypothesis
Success metric
Guardrail metrics
Population definition
Duration
Stopping criteria
```

User experimentation must respect applicable privacy and product governance.

---

# 111. Online Evaluation

Production evaluation should monitor real-world behavior that offline datasets may miss.

Signals may include:

```text
User corrections
Abandonment
Regeneration
Escalation
Tool failures
Citation failures
Safety events
```

---

# 112. Feedback Is Not Ground Truth

```text
Thumbs Up
```

does not necessarily mean:

```text
Factually Correct
```

User feedback is one signal among several.

---

# 113. Model Drift

AI quality may change because of:

```text
User behavior
Data distribution
Knowledge corpus
Provider model changes
Prompt changes
Tool changes
External world changes
```

Drift monitoring should therefore be system-aware.

---

# 114. Knowledge Drift

For educational knowledge:

```text
Source changes
      │
      ▼
RAG corpus stale
      │
      ▼
AI answers stale
```

ADR-076 freshness controls must propagate into AI observability.

---

# 115. AI Observability

AI telemetry should include appropriate:

```text
Request metadata
Model
Prompt version
Token usage
Latency
Retrieval
Tool calls
Errors
Safety events
Evaluation signals
Cost
```

without violating privacy/data-minimization requirements.

---

# 116. AI Trace

A trace may conceptually show:

```text
User Request
     │
     ▼
Prompt Build
     │
     ▼
Retrieval
     │
     ▼
Model Call
     │
     ▼
Tool Call
     │
     ▼
Model Call
     │
     ▼
Response
```

This is essential for debugging agentic systems.

---

# 117. Sensitive Trace Data

AI observability can accidentally become a secondary sensitive-data store.

Logs/traces must therefore apply:

```text
Redaction
Classification
Access controls
Retention
Encryption
```

ADR-076 applies.

---

# 118. Token Telemetry

Track:

```text
Input tokens
Output tokens
Cached tokens where relevant
Context utilization
Tokens by model
Tokens by capability
```

This supports performance and cost analysis.

---

# 119. AI Cost Attribution

ADR-073 requires attribution where practical.

```text
AI Cost
  │
  ├── Product
  ├── Feature
  ├── Environment
  ├── Model
  └── Tenant/use case
```

Without attribution, optimization becomes guesswork.

---

# 120. AI Unit Economics

Useful metrics may include:

```text
Cost per tutoring session
Cost per generated assessment
Cost per successful agent task
Cost per 1,000 AI interactions
```

Raw monthly API cost is insufficient.

---

# 121. Latency Budget

AI requests should define latency budgets.

```text
Total UX Budget
      │
      ├── Retrieval
      ├── Model queue
      ├── Time to first token
      ├── Generation
      └── Tools
```

Optimize the bottleneck rather than blindly switching models.

---

# 122. Quality–Latency–Cost Triangle

```text
                 QUALITY
                   /\
                  /  \
                 /    \
                /      \
               /________\
            COST       LATENCY
```

Model selection and routing require explicit trade-offs.

---

# 123. AI Incident Definition

AI incidents may include:

```text
Unsafe outputs
Systematic hallucinations
Data leakage
Prompt injection
Unauthorized tool actions
Severe quality regression
Unexpected provider behavior
Runaway cost
RAG poisoning
```

Infrastructure can remain perfectly healthy during an AI incident.

---

# 124. AI Incident Response

```text
Detect
  │
  ▼
Assess
  │
  ▼
Contain
  │
  ▼
Disable / Degrade / Rollback
  │
  ▼
Investigate
  │
  ▼
Correct
  │
  ▼
Re-evaluate
```

---

# 125. AI Kill Switch

Critical AI capabilities require a fast path to disable risky behavior.

```text
AI Feature
   │
   ▼
Kill Switch
 ┌─┴─────┐
 ▼       ▼
ON      OFF
```

This should not require an emergency code deployment where avoidable.

---

# 126. Granular Kill Switches

Prefer disabling:

```text
Specific model
Specific tool
Specific agent
Specific feature
Specific tenant
Specific data source
```

rather than unnecessarily shutting down the entire platform.

---

# 127. AI Rollback

Rollback may require restoring:

```text
Model
Prompt
Retriever
Embedding model
Knowledge index
Tool definitions
Routing configuration
```

Application-code rollback alone may not restore previous AI behavior.

---

# 128. Provider Outage

ADR-075 governs continuity.

Possible behavior:

```text
Primary AI unavailable
        │
        ├── Approved fallback
        ├── Smaller/local model
        └── AI-disabled mode
```

Selection depends on risk and data restrictions.

---

# 129. Provider Model Deprecation

Providers may retire models.

Therefore Mediverse needs:

```text
Deprecation monitoring
Replacement evaluation
Migration plan
Regression testing
Cutover
Rollback where possible
```

Do not wait until the provider's shutdown date.

---

# 130. LLMOps Control Plane

```text
                        LLMOps
                          │
       ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
       ▼                  ▼                  ▼
     BUILD              RELEASE            OPERATE
       │                  │                  │
       ├─ Prompts          ├─ Evaluation      ├─ Traces
       ├─ RAG              ├─ Approval        ├─ Quality
       ├─ Models           ├─ Canary          ├─ Safety
       └─ Agents           └─ Rollback        └─ Cost
```

---

# 131. Model and Prompt Registry

Mediverse should maintain discoverable records of production:

```text
Models
Prompts
Embedding models
RAG configurations
Agent configurations
Evaluation results
```

---

# 132. Reproducibility

For a material AI response or regression investigation, teams should be able to determine as far as technically possible:

```text
Which model?
Which prompt?
Which context?
Which retrieval configuration?
Which knowledge version?
Which tools?
Which application version?
```

Perfect output reproducibility may not always be possible with external probabilistic services, but configuration provenance is still mandatory.

---

# 133. Developer Golden Path

Platform engineering should provide reusable AI patterns for:

```text
Model access
Authentication
RAG
Prompt registry
Evaluation
Tracing
Cost telemetry
Safety controls
Tool authorization
Deployment
```

This reduces teams building incompatible AI infrastructure independently.

---

# 134. AI Policy as Code

Machine-verifiable rules may include:

```text
Production AI MUST have owner
Production AI MUST declare risk tier
External model MUST be approved
Agent tool MUST declare authorization
AI capability MUST have evaluation suite
High-risk AI MUST have oversight
Production prompt MUST be versioned
AI feature MUST declare fallback behavior
```

---

# 135. AI Fitness Functions

Architecture pipelines can verify:

```text
Evaluation thresholds
Prompt version presence
Approved model list
Data-policy compatibility
Token limits
Agent step limits
Tool allowlists
Kill-switch configuration
Observability
```

# 137. AI FinOps Integration

ADR-073 applies directly.

Optimization hierarchy:

```text
Remove unnecessary AI call
        │
        ▼
Reduce context
        │
        ▼
Cache safely
        │
        ▼
Use smaller suitable model
        │
        ▼
Batch where appropriate
        │
        ▼
Optimize infrastructure
```

Do not start with GPU tuning when the application makes unnecessary model calls.

---

# 138. AI Sustainability Integration

ADR-074 applies.

Efficiency strategies include:

```text
Right-size models
Reduce redundant generation
Reduce unnecessary context
Cache appropriate outputs
Batch workloads
Avoid idle GPU capacity
Retire unused models/indexes
```

Quality and safety requirements remain primary constraints.

---

# 139. AI Disaster-Recovery Integration

ADR-075 governs:

```text
Provider outage
Model-serving outage
Vector DB loss
Embedding-index recovery
Prompt registry loss
AI configuration loss
GPU cluster loss
```

Core learning should remain available without AI where the business model permits.

---

# 140. Data-Governance Integration

ADR-076 governs:

```text
Training data
Evaluation data
Prompt data
RAG sources
Embeddings
Agent memory
AI logs
Feedback
Generated artifacts
```

AI does not create an exemption from enterprise data governance.

# 141. AI Governance Operating Model

```text
Enterprise Architecture
        │
        ├── Standards
        │
AI Governance
        │
        ├── Risk
        ├── Policy
        └── Approval
        │
Domain/Product
        │
        ├── Business accountability
        │
AI Platform

        └── Observability
        │
Engineering
        │
```

Governance should be federated rather than centralized into a bottleneck.

---

# 142. Risk-Based Governance

Do not require the same approval process for:

```text
AI-generated UI label
```

and:

```text
AI-generated high-impact learner decision
```

Over-governance of trivial AI encourages teams to bypass governance entirely.

---

# 143. AI Governance Maturity

```text
LEVEL 1 — EXPERIMENTAL

Teams independently call models.


LEVEL 2 — INVENTORIED

Models and AI capabilities are known.


LEVEL 3 — CONTROLLED

Risk, evaluation, security and
release standards exist.


LEVEL 4 — PLATFORMIZED

LLMOps, evaluation, observability
and policy controls are standardized.


LEVEL 5 — CONTINUOUSLY ASSURED

Production behavior continuously feeds
evaluation, risk and governance.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, selectively progressing high-value capabilities toward Level 5.

---

# 144. AI Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ "Use AI because the product needs AI"
❌ Using LLMs for deterministic rules
❌ Largest model by default
❌ API availability treated as model approval
❌ Model-only evaluation
❌ Prompts stored as uncontrolled strings
❌ Production prompts changed without versioning
❌ Provider "latest" aliases without change awareness
❌ Retrieved text treated as trusted instructions
❌ RAG relevance treated as authority
❌ More context assumed to mean better answers
❌ Hallucination solved by adding RAG and doing no evaluation
❌ Fabricated citations
❌ Tool request treated as authorization
❌ Agent permissions exceeding user permissions
❌ Unbounded agent loops
❌ Permanent agent memory without lifecycle governance
❌ AI self-reported confidence treated as calibrated confidence
❌ Forced answers when evidence is inadequate
❌ One safety filter treated as sufficient
❌ Red-team findings without remediation
❌ English evaluation assumed to cover every language
❌ LLM-as-judge treated as unquestionable ground truth
❌ Fine-tuning before defining the actual problem
❌ Successful fine-tuning job treated as improvement
❌ Open-weight models assumed to be free
❌ Self-hosting assumed cheaper
❌ GPU clusters without utilization governance
❌ Production release without golden evaluation
❌ Application rollback assumed to roll back AI behavior
❌ User thumbs-up treated as factual correctness
❌ Logging complete prompts regardless of sensitivity
❌ No token/cost attribution
❌ No kill switch
❌ Fallback to an unapproved provider
❌ AI provider outage taking down core learning unnecessarily
❌ AI governance applied only before launch
```

```text
                           ▼
                        ADR-074
                    SUSTAINABILITY
                           │
                           ▼

```

Therefore:

```text
AI quality without data governance
            = unreliable knowledge

AI without resilience
            = fragile capability

AI without FinOps
            = uncontrolled economics

AI without sustainability
            = unnecessary resource consumption

AI without evolutionary governance
            = architecture drift
```
