# ADR-077 — COMPLETE ✅

The governing invariant is:

> **Mediverse will never treat an AI model as an authority, authorization mechanism, deterministic policy engine, or accountable decision-maker. AI outputs are probabilistic and potentially wrong. Production trust must come from the surrounding architecture: governed data, evidence, evaluation, deterministic validation, least-privilege authorization, human accountability, observability, controlled release, reversibility and continuous assurance.**

The complete AI lifecycle becomes:

```text
BUSINESS PROBLEM
      │
      ▼
AI JUSTIFIED?
      │
      ▼
RISK CLASSIFY
      │
      ▼
DESIGN
      │
      ├── Model
      ├── Prompt
      ├── RAG
      └── Agent
      │
      ▼
SECURE
      │
      ▼
EVALUATE
      │
      ▼
APPROVE
      │
      ▼
SHADOW
      │
      ▼
CANARY
      │
      ▼
PRODUCTION
      │
      ▼
OBSERVE
      │
      ├── Quality
      ├── Safety
      ├── Security
      ├── Latency
      └── Cost
      │
      ▼
CONTINUOUS EVALUATION
      │
   ┌──┴─────────────┐
   ▼                ▼
HEALTHY          UNACCEPTABLE
   │                │
CONTINUE      DEGRADE / ROLLBACK
                    │
                    ▼
                KILL SWITCH
                    │
                    ▼
                INVESTIGATE
                    │
                    ▼
                 IMPROVE
                    │
                    └──────────────► DESIGN
```

## Next — ADR-078

### **ADR-078 — Enterprise Developer Platform, Internal Developer Platform, Platform Engineering & Golden Path Standard**

The architecture now has extensive governance, but there is a growing risk: **developers could be forced to manually understand and implement dozens of ADRs for every service. That does not scale.**

ADR-078 should turn these architectural decisions into a usable **Internal Developer Platform (IDP)** and paved roads covering **platform-as-a-product → developer personas → developer journey → service catalogue → service templates → Backstage/developer portal decision → software catalog → ownership metadata → service creation → Spring Boot golden path → React golden path → Python/AI service golden path → repository templates → standardized project structure → local development → Dev Containers → Docker → buildpacks vs Dockerfiles → CI templates → Jenkins/GitHub Actions abstraction → artifact publishing → Nexus → SonarQube → SBOM → signing → deployment manifests → Helm abstraction → GitOps onboarding → Argo CD → environment provisioning → namespaces → secrets → databases → Kafka topics → Redis → object storage → DNS → certificates → observability-by-default → OpenTelemetry → dashboards → alerts → SLO templates → security controls → policy-as-code → self-service infrastructure → Terraform modules → Crossplane/operator decision → ephemeral environments → preview environments → developer sandbox → production promotion → progressive delivery → feature flags → rollback → service scorecards → TechDocs → ADR discovery → API catalogue → event catalogue → data-product catalogue → AI capability catalogue → dependency visualization → ownership → on-call integration → cost visibility → sustainability visibility → DORA metrics → developer-experience metrics → platform SLOs → platform API → CLI → portal → GitOps interfaces → guardrails vs gates → escape hatches → platform versioning → migration → deprecation → platform teams → product management → adoption → golden-path compliance → platform maturity model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse Internal Developer Platform reference architecture and ADR-078 decision outcome.**



# ADR-078 — Enterprise Developer Platform, Internal Developer Platform, Platform Engineering & Golden Path Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-078
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Primary Stakeholders:** Platform Engineering, Application Engineering, DevOps, SRE, Security, Data Platform, AI Platform, Enterprise Architecture, FinOps, Developer Experience

ADR-077 established the enterprise AI governance and LLMOps control plane.

ADR-078 addresses the scalability problem created by the architecture itself:

> **If every Mediverse developer must manually understand and correctly implement dozens of architecture, security, observability, Kubernetes, GitOps, data, AI, resilience and FinOps standards, the architecture has failed to become an engineering platform.**

The solution is not more documentation.

The solution is to encode the preferred architecture into **paved roads, reusable capabilities and self-service workflows**.

```text
                    DEVELOPER INTENT
                           │
                           ▼
                 DEVELOPER PLATFORM
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ▼                   ▼                   ▼
     PORTAL               CLI                API
       │                   │                   │
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ▼
                      GOLDEN PATH
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ▼                   ▼                   ▼
    APPLICATION       INFRASTRUCTURE       GOVERNANCE
       │                   │                   │
       ├─ Repository       ├─ Namespace        ├─ Security
       ├─ CI/CD            ├─ Database         ├─ Observability
       ├─ Container        ├─ Kafka            ├─ Compliance
       ├─ Helm             ├─ Redis            ├─ FinOps
       └─ GitOps           └─ Storage          └─ Resilience
                           │
                           ▼
                     RUNNING SERVICE
                           │
                           ▼
                    SERVICE CATALOGUE
                           │
                           ▼
                    OPERATE & EVOLVE
```

# 1. Platform Engineering Objective

Mediverse platform engineering exists to reduce unnecessary cognitive load for product teams.

Developers should primarily think about:

```text
Business capability
Domain logic
API design
Data semantics
User experience
Testing
```

rather than repeatedly solving:

```text
Kubernetes boilerplate
CI pipeline construction
Helm conventions
Observability wiring
Security defaults
Artifact publication
GitOps configuration
Infrastructure provisioning
```

---

# 2. Platform as a Product

The platform must be operated as an internal product.

```text
Platform Team
     │
     ▼
Platform Product
     │
     ▼
Internal Customers
     │
     ▼
Engineering Teams
```

This requires:

```text
Product ownership
Roadmap
User research
Documentation
Support
SLOs
Telemetry
Adoption metrics
Feedback
Lifecycle management
```

---

# 3. Platform Is Not a Ticket Queue

This is rejected:

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
ServiceNow/Jira Ticket
    │
    ▼
Platform Team
    │
    ▼
Manual Terraform
    │
    ▼
Wait 5 Days
```

Prefer:

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Self-Service Request
    │
    ▼
Policy Validation
    │
    ▼
Automated Provisioning
    │
    ▼
Minutes
```

---

# 4. Internal Developer Platform

The IDP provides a coherent interface over underlying engineering capabilities.

```text
                     IDP
                      │
       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
       ▼              ▼              ▼
     Portal           CLI            API
       │              │              │
       └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                      ▼
               Platform Services
                      │
       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
       ▼              ▼              ▼
     GitHub         Jenkins      Kubernetes
       │              │              │
     Nexus         SonarQube       Argo CD
       │              │              │
   Terraform      Observability    Cloud
```

The IDP does not replace these systems.

It provides a usable abstraction over them.

---

# 5. Cognitive Load

Platform engineering should reduce **extraneous cognitive load**, not eliminate useful engineering knowledge.

Developers still need to understand:

```text
Containers
Networking
Kubernetes concepts
Observability
Security
Distributed systems
```

But they should not repeatedly reconstruct organizational conventions.

---

# 6. Abstraction Boundary

Bad abstraction:

```text
Developer clicks "Deploy"
and has no idea what exists.
```

Bad platform:

```text
Developer must write
700 lines of Kubernetes YAML.
```

Preferred:

```text
Developer declares intent
        │
        ▼
Platform generates/controls complexity
        │
        ▼
Underlying implementation remains inspectable
```

---

# 7. Developer Personas

The platform should recognize different consumers.

```text
Backend Developer
Frontend Developer
AI Engineer
Data Engineer
DevOps Engineer
SRE
Platform Engineer
Security Engineer
```

One workflow will not satisfy every persona.

---

# 8. Developer Journey

A typical service journey becomes:

```text
Discover
   │
   ▼
Create
   │
   ▼
Develop
   │
   ▼
Test
   │
   ▼
Deploy
   │
   ▼
Observe
   │
   ▼
Operate
   │
   ▼
Evolve
   │
   ▼
Retire
```

The platform should support the complete lifecycle.

---

# 9. Platform Capability Model

The platform should expose capabilities rather than raw infrastructure.

Examples:

```text
"Create PostgreSQL database"

instead of

"Create RDS subnet groups,
security groups, parameter groups,
secrets and monitoring manually."
```

---

# 10. Golden Paths

A golden path is the recommended implementation route.

```text
Developer Requirement
        │
        ▼
Golden Path
        │
        ▼
Secure + Observable +
Deployable + Governed Service
```

Golden paths should make the correct path easier than the incorrect path.

---

# 11. Golden Path Is Not Mandatory Architecture

Golden paths are defaults.

They are not intended to eliminate legitimate architectural variation.

```text
80–90% common path
       │
       ▼
Golden Path

Exceptional requirement
       │
       ▼
Reviewed Escape Hatch
```

---

# 12. Guardrails vs Gates

Prefer:

```text
GUARDRAIL

"Here is the safe automated path."
```

over excessive:

```text
GATE

"Open ticket and wait for approval."
```

Hard gates remain justified for genuinely high-risk actions.

---

# 13. Service Catalogue

Every production service should be discoverable.

The catalogue should answer:

```text
What is this service?
Who owns it?
Where is the repository?
Where is it deployed?
Which APIs does it expose?
Which databases does it own?
Which events does it publish?
What depends on it?
Where are its dashboards?
Who is on call?
```

---

# 14. Catalogue Metadata

Conceptually:

```yaml
service:
  name: assessment-service
  owner: assessment-team
  lifecycle: production
  type: spring-boot

system:
  domain: assessment

links:
  repository: ...
  dashboard: ...
  runbook: ...

dependencies:
  database: assessment-db
  topics:
    - assessment.submitted
```

Metadata format should be standardized.

---

# 15. Ownership Metadata

Production components without owners are unacceptable.

```text
Component
    │
    ▼
Team
    │
    ▼
Contact
    │
    ▼
Operational Responsibility
```

---

# 16. System Model

Catalogue hierarchy may conceptually use:

```text
DOMAIN
   │
   ▼
SYSTEM
   │
   ▼
COMPONENT
   │
   ▼
RESOURCE
```

Example:

```text
Learning Domain
      │
      ▼
Assessment System
      │
      ▼
Assessment Service
      │
      ├── PostgreSQL
      └── Kafka Topics
```

---

# 17. Service Creation

Creating a production service should become a platform workflow.

```text
Create Service
     │
     ▼
Select Template
     │
     ▼
Enter Metadata
     │
     ▼
Generate Repository
     │
     ▼
Provision CI/CD
     │
     ▼
Register Catalogue
     │
     ▼
Create GitOps Configuration
```

---

# 18. Software Templates

Templates should encode approved architecture.

Potential templates:

```text
Spring Boot REST Service
Spring Boot Kafka Worker
React Application
Python API
AI/RAG Service
Batch Worker
Scheduled Job
```

---

# 19. Template Responsibilities

A template may provide:

```text
Repository structure
Build configuration
Testing
Containerization
Health endpoints
Observability
Security defaults
CI
Helm
GitOps
Documentation
Ownership metadata
```

---

# 20. Template Versioning

Templates evolve.

Therefore generated applications must record template provenance where useful.

```text
service-template
      │
      ├── v1
      ├── v2
      └── v3
```

Otherwise hundreds of generated services silently diverge.

---

# 21. Template Updates

Scaffolding once is insufficient.

The platform needs mechanisms to help existing services adopt improvements.

Possible approaches:

```text
Automated PRs
Codemods
Dependency bots
Shared libraries
Central CI templates
Helm library charts
Policy enforcement
```

---

# 22. Spring Boot Golden Path

The standard backend path should provide:

```text
Spring Boot
    │
    ├── Java baseline
    ├── Maven/Gradle standard
    ├── Spring Security
    ├── OpenAPI
    ├── Actuator
    ├── OpenTelemetry
    ├── Structured logging
    ├── Testing
    ├── Docker
    ├── Helm
    └── GitOps
```

---

# 23. Spring Boot Repository Structure

Conceptually:

```text
assessment-service/
├── src/
├── pom.xml
├── Dockerfile
├── helm/
├── docs/
├── catalog-info.yaml
├── CODEOWNERS
├── README.md
└── architecture/
```

Exact layout may evolve through platform standards.

---

# 24. React Golden Path

The frontend path should provide:

```text
React + Vite
     │
     ├── Routing
     ├── API client
     ├── Authentication integration
     ├── Error handling
     ├── Observability
     ├── Testing
     ├── Accessibility baseline
     ├── Container/build
     └── Deployment
```

---

# 25. AI Service Golden Path

ADR-077 controls should be embedded.

```text
AI Service Template
      │
      ├── Approved model gateway
      ├── Prompt registry
      ├── RAG integration
      ├── Evaluation
      ├── Tracing
      ├── Token telemetry
      ├── Safety controls
      ├── Kill switch
      └── AI catalogue registration
```

---

# 26. Python Service Golden Path

Python services should standardize:

```text
Runtime version
Dependency management
Testing
Linting
Security scanning
OpenTelemetry
Container
Health endpoints
Deployment
```

rather than each team creating its own runtime conventions.

---

# 27. Repository Creation

Repositories should automatically receive appropriate:

```text
Branch protection
CODEOWNERS
Security scanning
CI
Dependency management
README
Documentation
Ownership metadata
```

---

# 28. Repository Standards

Repositories should make important information obvious:

```text
How do I build?
How do I test?
How do I run locally?
How do I deploy?
Who owns this?
Where are the docs?
```

A developer should not need tribal knowledge to answer these.

---

# 29. Local Development

Golden paths must work locally.

```text
git clone
   │
   ▼
documented bootstrap
   │
   ▼
dependencies available
   │
   ▼
application running
```

Local development that requires two days of manual setup is a platform failure.

---

# 30. Developer Environment

The platform may standardize:

```text
JDK
Node.js
Python
Docker
kubectl
Helm
Terraform
Cloud CLI
```

while avoiding unnecessarily rigid workstation control.

---

# 31. Dev Containers

Dev Containers may be supported where they materially improve:

```text
Environment consistency
Onboarding
Toolchain management
Reproducibility
```

They should remain a tool, not become mandatory complexity without demonstrated value.

---

# 32. Local Dependency Strategy

Services may need:

```text
PostgreSQL
Redis
Kafka
Object storage emulator
Mock external services
```

The platform should provide documented lightweight local patterns.

---

# 33. Docker Standards

Container standards should define:

```text
Base images
Non-root execution
Image metadata
Health behavior
Signal handling
Resource awareness
Vulnerability management
```

---

# 34. Dockerfile vs Buildpacks

Mediverse should support both where justified.

```text
Standard application
      │
      ▼
Buildpack / standardized build

Special runtime requirement
      │
      ▼
Reviewed Dockerfile
```

The decision should be driven by control and developer experience, not fashion.

---

# 35. Base Image Governance

Approved base images should be:

```text
Minimal
Patched
Scanned
Versioned
Traceable
```

Teams should not independently select arbitrary internet images for production.

---

# 36. CI Golden Path

CI should be reusable rather than duplicated.

```text
Commit
   │
   ▼
Compile
   │
   ▼
Unit Test
   │
   ▼
Static Analysis
   │
   ▼
Security Scan
   │
   ▼
Package
   │
   ▼
Container
   │
   ▼
SBOM
   │
   ▼
Sign
   │
   ▼
Publish
```

---

# 37. Central CI Templates

Whether Jenkins or another CI system executes the pipeline, common logic should live in maintained reusable templates.

```text
100 repositories
      │
      X
100 independently copied pipelines
```

---

# 38. Jenkins Integration

If Jenkins remains part of the Mediverse toolchain, the platform should abstract repetitive pipeline construction.

```text
Repository
    │
    ▼
Shared Pipeline Library
    │
    ▼
Jenkins
```

Product teams should configure intent rather than rewrite pipeline internals.

---

# 39. GitHub Actions Integration

Where GitHub Actions is used, reusable workflows should provide equivalent organizational controls.

The platform architecture should avoid unnecessarily coupling golden paths to one CI implementation.

---

# 40. Artifact Management

Build outputs must enter governed repositories.

```text
Build
 │
 ▼
Artifact
 │
 ▼
Nexus / Registry
 │
 ▼
Deployment
```

Production should not rebuild arbitrary source during deployment.

---

# 41. Nexus Integration

Nexus should support governed storage for appropriate:

```text
Maven artifacts
npm packages
Container artifacts
Internal packages
```

with lifecycle and access controls.

---

# 42. SonarQube Integration

Static analysis should be integrated automatically.

```text
Pull Request
     │
     ▼
SonarQube
     │
     ▼
Quality/Security Signals
```

Teams should not manually configure basic analysis for every repository.

---

# 43. Software Bill of Materials

Build pipelines should generate SBOMs where required by security standards.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Dependencies
    │
    ▼
SBOM
```

This supports supply-chain visibility.

---

# 44. Artifact Signing

Production artifacts should support provenance and signing controls according to security requirements.

```text
Build
 │
 ▼
Artifact
 │
 ▼
Sign
 │
 ▼
Verify
 │
 ▼
Deploy
```

---

# 45. Immutable Artifact Promotion

Prefer:

```text
Build Once
    │
    ▼
Test
    │
    ▼
Promote Same Artifact
    │
    ▼
Production
```

rather than rebuilding separately for each environment.

---

# 46. Deployment Abstraction

Developers should declare deployment requirements.

Example:

```yaml
service:
  replicas: 3
  port: 8080

resources:
  profile: medium

database:
  postgres: true

observability:
  tier: standard
```

The platform translates intent into implementation.

---

# 47. Kubernetes Golden Path

Platform defaults should handle:

```text
Deployment
Service
Ingress/Gateway
Resources
Probes
Security context
Autoscaling
Network controls
Observability
Configuration
Secrets integration
```

---

# 48. Raw Kubernetes YAML

Raw manifests remain inspectable, but ordinary teams should not need to hand-author every resource.

```text
Application intent
      │
      ▼
Platform abstraction
      │
      ▼
Helm / Kubernetes
```

---

# 49. Helm Golden Path

Helm remains an implementation mechanism for Kubernetes packaging.

The platform should provide:

```text
Base chart
Library chart
Standard values
Validation
Versioning
Upgrade guidance
```

---

# 50. Helm Escape Hatch

Teams with legitimate requirements may extend or replace standard charts after architectural review where needed.

The platform must not become an obstacle to valid engineering.

---

# 51. GitOps Onboarding

New services should automatically enter GitOps management.

```text
Service Repository
      │
      ▼
Build Artifact
      │
      ▼
GitOps Repository
      │
      ▼
Argo CD
      │
      ▼
Kubernetes
```

---

# 52. Argo CD Registration

Platform automation should create appropriate:

```text
Application
Project
Repository relationship
Environment mapping
RBAC
Sync policy
```

rather than requiring repetitive manual setup.

---

# 53. Git as Desired State

Production Kubernetes changes should flow through governed desired state.

```text
Git
 │
 ▼
Review
 │
 ▼
Merge
 │
 ▼
Argo CD
 │
 ▼
Cluster
```

Direct production mutation should be exceptional and auditable.

---

# 54. Environment Model

Mediverse should define standard environment semantics.

Potential model:

```text
LOCAL
DEV
TEST
UAT
PROD
```

Not every service automatically requires every environment.

---

# 55. Environment Proliferation

Creating:

```text
DEV1
DEV2
DEV3
TEST1
TEST2
UAT1
UAT2
UAT3
PREPROD1
PREPROD2
```

without clear purpose creates cost and operational complexity.

Environment creation must be requirement-driven.

---

# 56. Namespace Provisioning

Developers should request a workload environment rather than manually constructing namespaces.

```text
Environment Request
       │
       ▼
Namespace
       │
       ├── Quotas
       ├── RBAC
       ├── Network policy
       ├── Secrets integration
       └── Observability
```

---

# 57. Resource Quotas

Namespaces should receive sensible defaults for:

```text
CPU
Memory
Pods
Storage
Object counts
```

with an escalation mechanism for legitimate exceptions.

---

# 58. Database Self-Service

A service requiring PostgreSQL should declare the capability.

```text
Service
   │
   ▼
"Need PostgreSQL"
   │
   ▼
Platform
   │
   ├── Provision
   ├── Credentials
   ├── Backup
   ├── Monitoring
   └── Catalogue
```

---

# 59. Database Ownership Integration

ADR-076 must be encoded automatically.

Provisioning should register:

```text
Owner
Domain
Classification
Backup class
Environment
Lifecycle
```

---

# 60. Kafka Self-Service

Teams should be able to request governed topics.

```text
Topic Request
     │
     ▼
Schema + Owner + Retention
     │
     ▼
Policy Validation
     │
     ▼
Kafka Topic
     │
     ▼
Catalogue
```

A raw `kafka-topics --create` command is not enterprise topic governance.

---

## ADR-078 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The emerging platform architecture is:

```text
                         DEVELOPER
                            │
                            ▼
                  DEVELOPER EXPERIENCE
                            │
             ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
             ▼              ▼              ▼
           PORTAL           CLI            API
             │              │              │
             └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                            ▼
                       GOLDEN PATH
                            │
       ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
       ▼                    ▼                    ▼
    SOFTWARE            DELIVERY          INFRASTRUCTURE
       │                    │                    │
       ├─ Spring Boot       ├─ CI                 ├─ Namespace
       ├─ React             ├─ Artifacts          ├─ PostgreSQL
       ├─ Python            ├─ Helm               ├─ Kafka
       └─ AI                └─ GitOps             └─ Redis
       │                    │                    │
       └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                            ▼
                      GOVERNANCE
                            │
           ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
           ▼                ▼                ▼
        SECURITY       OBSERVABILITY       DATA/AI
           │                │                │
           └────────────────┼────────────────┘
                            ▼
                      KUBERNETES
                            │
                            ▼
                     RUNNING SYSTEM
                            │
                            ▼
                   SERVICE CATALOGUE
                            │
                            ▼
                     OPERATE / EVOLVE
```

The key rule from Sections 1–60 is:

> **Mediverse developers should declare engineering intent while the platform automates repeatable implementation detail and embeds organizational guardrails. The platform must reduce cognitive load without hiding the underlying architecture so completely that developers lose the ability to understand, debug and operate their systems.**

**Part 2 should continue from Section 61 — Redis & Cache Self-Service**, then cover **object-storage provisioning → DNS → certificates → secrets → configuration → observability-by-default → OpenTelemetry → logs/metrics/traces → dashboards → alerts → SLO templates → runbooks → security controls → policy-as-code → Terraform modules → self-service infrastructure → Crossplane/operator decision → preview/ephemeral environments → sandbox environments → environment TTL → test-data integration → API catalogue → event catalogue → data-product catalogue → AI capability catalogue → TechDocs → ADR discovery → dependency graph → ownership → on-call integration → service scorecards → production-readiness scorecards → cost visibility → sustainability visibility → DORA metrics → developer-experience metrics → platform telemetry → platform SLOs → portal vs CLI vs API → Backstage decision framework → platform APIs → escape hatches → exception governance → platform versioning → template migrations → deprecation → breaking platform changes → platform security boundary → multi-cluster/multi-cloud abstraction → platform team topology → product management → adoption → measuring platform success → platform maturity → anti-patterns → final Mediverse Internal Developer Platform reference architecture and ADR-078 decision outcome.**

# ADR-078 — Enterprise Developer Platform, Internal Developer Platform, Platform Engineering & Golden Path Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 61–150

Continuing directly from **Section 60 — Kafka Self-Service**.

---

# 61. Redis & Cache Self-Service

Teams should request caching as a governed capability rather than manually creating unmanaged Redis infrastructure.

```text
Service
   │
   ▼
Cache Requirement
   │
   ▼
Platform
   │
   ├── Provision
   ├── Credentials
   ├── Network access
   ├── Monitoring
   ├── Backup where required
   └── Catalogue registration
```

ADR-076 remains authoritative: Redis is normally derived or ephemeral state, not the system of record.

---

# 62. Cache Profiles

The platform may expose profiles such as:

```text
cache-small
cache-standard
cache-high-throughput
cache-ha
```

rather than exposing every infrastructure parameter.

Advanced configuration remains available through controlled escape hatches.

---

# 63. Object Storage Self-Service

Applications requiring object storage should declare:

```text
Purpose
Classification
Expected size
Retention
Access pattern
Public/private requirement
Recovery requirement
```

The platform translates this into governed storage.

---

# 64. Object Storage Lifecycle

Provisioning should automatically attach appropriate:

```text
Encryption
Access policy
Versioning
Lifecycle
Retention
Monitoring
Cost attribution
Ownership metadata
```

Creating a bucket is the easy part. Governing it for years is the actual platform responsibility.

---

# 65. DNS Self-Service

Applications should request DNS through a controlled interface.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
DNS Request
    │
    ▼
Ownership Validation
    │
    ▼
DNS Automation
    │
    ▼
Record
```

Manual production DNS changes should be exceptional.

---

# 66. Certificate Automation

TLS certificate lifecycle should be automated.

```text
Domain
  │
  ▼
Certificate Request
  │
  ▼
Validation
  │
  ▼
Issue
  │
  ▼
Deploy
  │
  ▼
Renew Automatically
```

Certificate expiry should not depend on calendar reminders.

---

# 67. Secrets Self-Service

Developers should reference secrets rather than manually distribute them.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Secret Reference
    │
    ▼
Secrets Platform
    │
    ▼
Runtime Injection
```

Secrets must not be embedded in:

```text
Git
Docker images
Helm values committed in plaintext
Application logs
CI output
```

---

# 68. Secret Ownership

Every important secret should have:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Consumers
Rotation policy
Environment
Classification
```

Anonymous credentials inevitably become permanent credentials.

---

# 69. Secret Rotation

The platform should automate rotation where practical.

```text
Current Credential
       │
       ▼
Create New
       │
       ▼
Distribute
       │
       ▼
Validate
       │
       ▼
Revoke Old
```

Applications should tolerate credential rotation without unnecessary downtime.

---

# 70. Configuration Management

Configuration and secrets must remain conceptually separate.

```text
CONFIGURATION

LOG_LEVEL=INFO
FEATURE_X=true

SECRETS

DB_PASSWORD=...
API_TOKEN=...
```

Both require lifecycle management, but their security properties differ.

---

# 71. Configuration Versioning

Production configuration should be traceable.

For material incidents, teams should be able to answer:

```text
What configuration was active?
Who changed it?
When?
Through which deployment?
```

---

# 72. Observability by Default

Every golden-path workload should automatically receive baseline observability.

```text
Service
  │
  ├── Logs
  ├── Metrics
  ├── Traces
  ├── Health
  └── Runtime metadata
```

Observability should not be an optional task developers remember three days before production.

---

# 73. OpenTelemetry Golden Path

OpenTelemetry should provide standardized instrumentation where appropriate.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
OpenTelemetry
    │
    ├── Traces
    ├── Metrics
    └── Context propagation
```

Application teams should not independently invent telemetry conventions.

---

# 74. Trace Context Propagation

Distributed requests should preserve trace context.

```text
Frontend
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Service A
   │
   ▼
Kafka
   │
   ▼
Service B
```

Without correlation, distributed debugging becomes substantially harder.

---

# 75. Structured Logging

Golden paths should provide structured logging.

Conceptually:

```json
{
  "service": "assessment-service",
  "environment": "uat1",
  "traceId": "...",
  "level": "ERROR",
  "event": "assessment_submission_failed"
}
```

Sensitive information must not be logged merely because structured logging makes it convenient.

---

# 76. Standard Service Metrics

Services should automatically expose baseline signals such as:

```text
Request rate
Error rate
Latency
CPU
Memory
Restarts
Dependency failures
JVM/runtime health
```

Domain-specific metrics remain the responsibility of the product team.

---

# 77. Dashboard Provisioning

A new service should receive a baseline dashboard automatically.

```text
Service Created
      │
      ▼
Telemetry Registered
      │
      ▼
Dashboard Generated
```

Developers then extend it with business-specific observability.

---

# 78. Alerting Templates

Golden paths should provide sensible alerts for:

```text
Availability
Error rate
Latency
Crash loops
Resource saturation
Dependency failure
SLO burn
```

but avoid generating hundreds of low-value alerts automatically.

---

# 79. Alert Quality

A platform that automatically creates noisy alerts is not helping.

An alert should generally indicate:

```text
User impact
Imminent user impact
Actionable infrastructure risk
SLO threat
```

not merely that a metric crossed an arbitrary threshold.

---

# 80. SLO Templates

Services should declare service criticality.

```text
Service Tier
     │
     ▼
Suggested SLO Profile
     │
     ├── Availability
     ├── Latency
     └── Error budget
```

Teams refine targets according to business requirements.

---

# 81. Runbook Integration

Operational alerts should link to relevant:

```text
Runbook
Dashboard
Logs
Traces
Service owner
Dependency information
```

An alert without diagnostic context unnecessarily increases MTTR.

---

# 82. Security by Default

Golden paths must automatically embed baseline security controls.

```text
Repository
   │
   ├── Dependency scanning
   ├── Secret scanning
   ├── SAST
   └── Branch protection

Artifact
   │
   ├── Vulnerability scanning
   ├── SBOM
   └── Signing

Runtime
   │
   ├── Non-root
   ├── RBAC
   ├── Network controls
   └── Policy
```

---

# 83. Policy as Code

Architecture/security policies that are machine-verifiable should be automated.

Examples:

```text
Container MUST NOT run privileged
Production workload MUST declare owner
Production workload MUST define resources
Public service MUST use approved ingress
Image MUST come from approved registry
```

---

# 84. Policy Enforcement Layers

Policies may operate at:

```text
IDE / local
      │
      ▼
Pull Request
      │
      ▼
CI
      │
      ▼
GitOps
      │
      ▼
Admission Control
      │
      ▼
Runtime
```

Earlier feedback is preferable to late rejection.

---

# 85. Terraform Module Catalogue

Infrastructure teams should publish supported modules.

Examples:

```text
PostgreSQL
Redis
Object Storage
DNS
Network
Kubernetes
Observability
IAM
```

Modules should encode organizational defaults.

---

# 86. Terraform Module Versioning

Infrastructure modules require semantic lifecycle management.

```text
postgres-module
      │
      ├── v1
      ├── v2
      └── v3
```

Consumers must not be forced into uncontrolled breaking upgrades.

---

# 87. Self-Service Infrastructure

Platform workflows should invoke approved infrastructure modules.

```text
Developer Intent
      │
      ▼
Platform API
      │
      ▼
Policy
      │
      ▼
Terraform
      │
      ▼
Cloud Infrastructure
```

Developers consume a capability rather than becoming infrastructure specialists for routine needs.

---

# 88. Crossplane / Operator Decision

Kubernetes-native provisioning technologies such as Crossplane or custom operators should be adopted only where their reconciliation model creates clear value.

```text
Need continuous reconciliation?
          │
      ┌───┴───┐
      ▼       ▼
     YES      NO
      │        │
Operator/    Terraform may
Crossplane   remain simpler
```

Adding another control plane without a concrete need is rejected.

---

# 89. Platform Resource API

The IDP may expose higher-level resources such as:

```yaml
apiVersion: platform.mediverse.io/v1
kind: Database
metadata:
  name: assessment-db

spec:
  engine: postgres
  profile: standard
  criticality: high
```

The platform determines implementation details.

---

# 90. Ephemeral Environments

Short-lived environments can support:

```text
Pull requests
Integration testing
Demonstrations
Experiments
```

when their value justifies their infrastructure cost.

---

# 91. Preview Environment

```text
Pull Request
    │
    ▼
Build
    │
    ▼
Preview Environment
    │
    ▼
Test / Review
    │
    ▼
PR Closed
    │
    ▼
Destroy
```

Lifecycle automation is mandatory.

---

# 92. Environment TTL

Ephemeral environments should have expiration.

```text
Created
   │
   ▼
TTL
   │
   ▼
Still required?
 ┌─┴───┐
 ▼     ▼
YES    NO
 │      │
Extend Destroy
```

Otherwise "ephemeral" environments become permanent cost.

---

# 93. Developer Sandbox

A sandbox should provide freedom within controlled boundaries.

```text
Developer
    │
    ▼
Sandbox
    │
    ├── Quotas
    ├── Restricted data
    ├── Restricted network
    ├── TTL
    └── Cost limits
```

---

# 94. Test Data Integration

ADR-076 should be integrated into platform workflows.

Non-production environments should default toward:

```text
Synthetic data
Masked data
Generated fixtures
Approved test datasets
```

rather than unrestricted production copies.

---

# 95. API Catalogue

The developer portal should expose discoverable APIs.

For each API:

```text
Owner
Purpose
Version
OpenAPI definition
Authentication
Consumers
Lifecycle
Documentation
```

---

# 96. API Discovery

Instead of:

```text
Developer
   │
   ▼
Ask Slack:
"Does anyone know the enrollment API?"
```

prefer:

```text
Developer Portal
      │
      ▼
Search "Enrollment"
      │
      ▼
API + Docs + Owner
```

---

# 97. Event Catalogue

Kafka events should also be discoverable.

```text
Topic
Event schema
Producer
Consumers
Owner
Retention
Classification
Documentation
```

ADR-076 event governance becomes visible to developers.

---

# 98. Data Product Catalogue

Governed data products should appear alongside software components.

```text
Software
APIs
Events
Datasets
```

should be navigable through a coherent developer experience.

---

# 99. AI Capability Catalogue

ADR-077 capabilities should be registered.

The catalogue may expose:

```text
AI capability
Owner
Risk tier
Model
RAG source
Evaluation status
Deployment
Documentation
```

---

# 100. Unified Catalogue

The long-term goal is not five disconnected catalogues.

```text
                     DOMAIN
                        │
                        ▼
                      SYSTEM
                        │
       ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
       ▼                ▼                ▼
    SERVICES           DATA              AI
       │                │                │
       ├── APIs          ├── Products     ├── Models
       └── Events        └── Stores       └── Agents
```

---

# 101. TechDocs

Documentation should live close to engineering ownership and be rendered through the platform where useful.

```text
Repository
    │
    ▼
Docs as Code
    │
    ▼
Developer Portal
```

---

# 102. Documentation Ownership

Documentation without ownership becomes stale.

Important documentation should inherit component ownership wherever possible.

---

# 103. ADR Discovery

Architecture decisions should be discoverable from relevant components.

```text
assessment-service
      │
      ├── ADR-076 Data Governance
      ├── ADR-077 AI Governance
      └── ADR-078 Platform Standard
```

Developers should not need to search an unrelated document repository manually.

---

# 104. Dependency Graph

The catalogue should increasingly expose relationships.

```text
Frontend
   │
   ▼
Gateway
   │
   ▼
Assessment Service
   │
   ├── PostgreSQL
   ├── Kafka
   └── Redis
          │
          ▼
     Progress Service
```

---

# 105. Dependency Impact

Dependency visibility supports questions such as:

```text
"If Kafka cluster X fails,
which systems are affected?"

"If assessment-service changes,
who consumes it?"
```

This materially improves incident response and change planning.

---

# 106. On-Call Integration

Production components should link to operational ownership.

```text
Service
  │
  ▼
Owning Team
  │
  ▼
On-call / Escalation
```

The catalogue should not stop at repository ownership.

---

# 107. Service Scorecards

The platform should evaluate baseline engineering health.

Potential dimensions:

```text
Owner
Documentation
CI
Security
Observability
SLO
Runbook
Dependencies
Recovery
Cost allocation
```

---

# 108. Scorecards Are Not Vanity Rankings

Scorecards should identify actionable engineering debt.

They must not become simplistic team leaderboards that incentivize gaming metrics.

---

# 109. Production Readiness Scorecard

Before production:

| Control             |      Required |
| ------------------- | ------------: |
| Owner               |             ✓ |
| CI/CD               |             ✓ |
| Security scans      |             ✓ |
| Resource limits     |             ✓ |
| Health probes       |             ✓ |
| Logs                |             ✓ |
| Metrics             |             ✓ |
| Dashboard           |             ✓ |
| Alerts              |             ✓ |
| SLO                 |    Risk-based |
| Runbook             |             ✓ |
| Backup/recovery     |   If stateful |
| Data classification | If applicable |
| Cost ownership      |             ✓ |

---

# 110. Cost Visibility

ADR-073 should surface directly in developer workflows.

Developers should be able to see:

```text
Service cost
Environment cost
Database cost
Storage cost
AI cost
Cost trend
```

without becoming cloud-billing experts.

---

# 111. Cost Before Provisioning

Self-service should expose approximate economic consequences.

```text
Request:
High-availability PostgreSQL

Estimated profile:
$$$$

Alternative:
Standard PostgreSQL
$$
```

Developers should make informed choices before infrastructure exists.

---

# 112. Sustainability Visibility

ADR-074 should expose relevant resource-efficiency signals.

Potential examples:

```text
Idle environments
Low-utilization workloads
Oversized requests
Unused storage
Idle GPU capacity
```

The objective is actionable efficiency, not decorative carbon dashboards.

---

# 113. DORA Metrics

The platform should help measure:

```text
Deployment frequency
Lead time for changes
Change failure rate
Recovery time
```

but metrics must be interpreted in context.

---

# 114. DORA Metrics Are Not Individual KPIs

Using delivery metrics to rank individual developers creates bad incentives and corrupts the data.

They should primarily support system and team-level improvement.

---

# 115. Developer Experience Metrics

Platform success should also measure:

```text
Time to first commit
Time to first deployment
Environment provisioning time
CI duration
Deployment duration
Developer satisfaction
Documentation discoverability
Platform support demand
```

---

# 116. Platform Telemetry

The platform itself requires product analytics.

```text
Which golden paths are used?
Where do workflows fail?
Which steps are slow?
Which templates are avoided?
Which escape hatches are common?
```

Escape-hatch frequency is particularly valuable architectural feedback.

---

# 117. Platform SLOs

The IDP should define SLOs for critical capabilities.

Examples:

```text
Service creation availability
Deployment pipeline availability
Provisioning latency
Portal availability
GitOps reconciliation
Artifact availability
```

A platform that product teams depend on is itself a production system.

---

# 118. Portal, CLI and API

No single interface should become mandatory for every workflow.

```text
                 PLATFORM API
                     │
          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
          ▼          ▼          ▼
        PORTAL      CLI       AUTOMATION
```

The API/control plane should provide the durable foundation.

---

# 119. Developer Portal

The portal is optimized for:

```text
Discovery
Service creation
Documentation
Status
Ownership
Scorecards
Common self-service
```

---

# 120. Platform CLI

The CLI is useful for:

```text
Developer automation
Local workflows
Bootstrap
Diagnostics
Advanced operations
```

It should use the same platform capabilities rather than implementing a second platform.

---

# 121. Platform API

A stable platform API enables:

```text
Portal
CLI
GitOps
CI/CD
Automation
External integrations
```

This reduces UI-specific coupling.

---

# 122. Backstage Decision Framework

[Backstage](https://backstage.io/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) is a strong candidate when Mediverse requires an extensible developer portal with a software catalogue, templates, documentation and plugin ecosystem.

But adopting Backstage does **not** automatically create an IDP.

```text
Backstage
    =
Portal Framework

Backstage
    ≠
Complete Platform
```

The underlying automation, APIs, ownership model and platform product still have to exist.

---

# 123. Backstage Adoption Decision

Adopt it if:

```text
Catalogue requirements are substantial
Plugin ecosystem provides leverage
TechDocs is useful
Templates align with workflows
Team can operate/customize it
```

Do not adopt it merely because "platform engineering uses Backstage."

---

# 124. GitOps as Platform Interface

Some advanced users may interact through declarative Git.

```text
Platform Resource
      │
      ▼
Git
      │
      ▼
Review
      │
      ▼
Reconciliation
```

Portal and GitOps interfaces should converge on the same underlying control model.

---

# 125. Escape Hatches

Golden paths must support legitimate exceptions.

```text
Golden Path
    │
    ▼
Requirement unsupported?
   ┌─┴────┐
   ▼      ▼
  NO     YES
   │      │
Use      Escape Hatch
Path       │
           ▼
       Document Reason
```

---

# 126. Exception Governance

Exceptions should record:

```text
Reason
Owner
Risk
Scope
Approver where required
Expiry/review date
Migration possibility
```

Permanent undocumented exceptions become shadow architecture.

---

# 127. Escape-Hatch Feedback Loop

Repeated exceptions indicate a platform problem.

```text
Same Escape Hatch
used 20 times
      │
      ▼
Not exceptional anymore
      │
      ▼
Platform capability candidate
```

---

# 128. Platform Versioning

Platform interfaces require versioning.

This includes:

```text
Templates
APIs
Terraform modules
Helm charts
CI workflows
Policies
Custom resources
```

---

# 129. Compatibility

Platform teams must consider backward compatibility for existing consumers.

A centralized platform can create a very large blast radius if it makes uncontrolled breaking changes.

---

# 130. Template Migration

When a template improves:

```text
Template v3
    │
    ▼
Existing v1 Services
    │
    ▼
Automated Analysis
    │
    ▼
Migration PR
```

The objective is continuous convergence, not permanent generation-time divergence.

---

# 131. Platform Deprecation

Deprecated capabilities require:

```text
Announcement
Replacement
Migration guidance
Timeline
Telemetry
Support
Retirement
```

Silent removal is unacceptable.

---

# 132. Breaking Platform Changes

Breaking changes require stronger rollout discipline because hundreds of services may depend on the platform.

Prefer:

```text
Introduce new version
      │
      ▼
Canary consumers
      │
      ▼
Migration
      │
      ▼
Measure
      │
      ▼
Retire old version
```

---

# 133. Platform Security Boundary

The IDP may hold substantial privilege.

It may be capable of creating:

```text
Repositories
Infrastructure
Credentials
Deployments
DNS
Databases
Permissions
```

Therefore compromise of the platform can have enterprise-wide consequences.

---

# 134. Platform Least Privilege

The platform should not operate as one universal administrator identity.

Prefer scoped identities for:

```text
Provisioning
Deployment
DNS
Secrets
Repository automation
Catalogue
```

with explicit authorization boundaries.

---

# 135. Platform Auditability

Sensitive platform actions should answer:

```text
Who requested it?
Which workflow?
Which identity executed it?
What changed?
When?
Was approval required?
```

---

# 136. Multi-Cluster Abstraction

Product teams should generally consume:

```text
Environment / workload capability
```

rather than hard-coding unnecessary cluster-specific assumptions.

The platform may map workloads to clusters according to policy.

---

# 137. Multi-Cloud Abstraction

Do not promise perfect cloud portability.

```text
"One abstraction hides every cloud"
```

usually degenerates into the lowest common denominator.

Abstract stable organizational capabilities, not every provider-specific feature.

---

# 138. Platform Team Topology

A possible model:

```text
                    PLATFORM ORGANIZATION
                            │
          ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
          ▼                 ▼                 ▼
     Developer          Runtime           Infrastructure
     Experience         Platform            Platform
          │                 │                 │
          └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                            ▼
                       Product Teams
```

Exact topology should follow organizational scale.

---

# 139. Enabling Teams

Specialists may temporarily help teams adopt:

```text
Kubernetes
Observability
Security
Data
AI
Platform capabilities
```

The objective is capability transfer, not permanent dependency.

---

# 140. Platform Product Management

The platform backlog should be prioritized using:

```text
Developer pain
Business impact
Adoption
Risk reduction
Support volume
Delivery friction
Cost
Strategic architecture
```

Platform roadmaps should not be driven only by what platform engineers find technically interesting.

---

# 141. Platform Adoption

Mandating platform usage before it is useful is a bad strategy.

The preferred path should win because it provides:

```text
Faster delivery
Less boilerplate
Better reliability
Better security
Better visibility
Less operational work
```

---

# 142. Measuring Platform Success

A successful platform should improve outcomes such as:

```text
↓ onboarding time
↓ provisioning time
↓ deployment friction
↓ duplicated infrastructure code
↓ security misconfiguration
↓ support tickets
↓ cognitive load

↑ deployment frequency
↑ standard compliance
↑ service ownership visibility
↑ developer satisfaction
↑ operational consistency
```

---

# 143. Platform Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1 — MANUAL

Teams manually assemble
infrastructure and pipelines.


LEVEL 2 — STANDARDIZED

Templates, modules and
documentation exist.


LEVEL 3 — SELF-SERVICE

Common capabilities are
automated behind golden paths.


LEVEL 4 — PRODUCTIZED

Portal, API, catalogue, scorecards,
SLOs and platform product management
operate coherently.


LEVEL 5 — ADAPTIVE

Platform telemetry, policy,
automated migrations and developer
feedback continuously evolve
the paved roads.
```

Mediverse should target **Level 4**, selectively progressing toward Level 5.

---

# 144. Platform Engineering Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Platform engineering = renamed DevOps team
❌ IDP = Kubernetes dashboard
❌ IDP = Backstage installation
❌ Platform team as ticket queue
❌ Self-service requiring manual approval everywhere
❌ Developers writing identical Kubernetes YAML repeatedly
❌ 100 copied Jenkinsfiles
❌ 100 independently maintained Helm charts
❌ Infrastructure modules without owners
❌ Golden paths that cannot be escaped
❌ Escape hatches without governance
❌ Hiding infrastructure so completely developers cannot debug it
❌ Requiring every developer to become a Kubernetes expert
❌ Requiring no developer to understand Kubernetes at all
❌ Service creation without ownership metadata
❌ Repositories without CODEOWNERS
❌ Production components absent from the catalogue
❌ Manual observability onboarding
❌ Dashboards without useful signals
❌ Alert generation without alert quality
❌ Secrets in Git
❌ Permanent credentials by default
❌ Manual certificate renewal
❌ Uncontrolled production DNS
❌ Production data copied freely into preview environments
❌ Ephemeral environments without TTL
❌ Self-service infrastructure without cost visibility
❌ DORA metrics used to rank developers
❌ Scorecards used as vanity leaderboards
❌ Portal as the only platform interface
❌ Platform UI containing business logic unavailable through APIs
❌ Perfect multi-cloud abstraction promises
❌ Template scaffolding with no migration strategy
❌ Platform breaking changes without consumer migration
❌ Platform administrator identity with unlimited privileges
❌ Platform roadmap driven entirely by technical novelty
❌ Mandating a bad platform to improve "adoption"
```

---

# 148. Cross-ADR Platform Control Model

ADR-078 operationalizes previous architecture decisions.

```text
                         ADR-078
                    DEVELOPER PLATFORM
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ▼                   ▼                   ▼
    GOLDEN PATH        SELF-SERVICE         CATALOGUE
       │                   │                   │
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ▼
                      GUARDRAILS
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       ▼                   ▼                   ▼
    ADR-077             ADR-076             ADR-075
       AI                 DATA             RESILIENCE
       │                   │                   │
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ▼
                       ADR-073
                        FINOPS
                           │
                           ▼
                       ADR-074
                   SUSTAINABILITY
                           │
                           ▼
                       ADR-072
               EVOLUTIONARY GOVERNANCE
```

The important architectural shift is:

```text
BEFORE

Architecture Document
       │
       ▼
Developer reads it
       │
       ▼
Developer manually implements it


AFTER

Architecture Decision
       │
       ▼
Platform Capability
       │
       ▼
Golden Path
       │
       ▼
Automated Guardrail
       │
       ▼
Developer consumes it
```

That is the difference between documented architecture and **executable architecture**.

# ADR-078 — COMPLETE ✅

The governing invariant is:

> **Mediverse architecture must not exist only as documents developers are expected to remember. Repeated architectural decisions must progressively become reusable platform capabilities, golden paths, templates, APIs and automated guardrails. Product teams retain ownership of their software and domain decisions, while the platform removes undifferentiated engineering work and makes secure, observable, resilient and cost-aware delivery the easiest path.**

The complete developer lifecycle becomes:

```text
IDEA
 │
 ▼
DISCOVER
 │
 ▼
SELECT GOLDEN PATH
 │
 ▼
CREATE
 │
 ├── Repository
 ├── Ownership
 ├── Documentation
 └── Catalogue
 │
 ▼
DEVELOP
 │
 ▼
TEST
 │
 ▼
CI
 │
 ├── Quality
 ├── Security
 ├── SBOM
 └── Artifact
 │
 ▼
GITOPS
 │
 ▼

 │
 ▼
OBSERVE
 │
 ├── Logs
 ├── Metrics
 ├── Traces
 ├── SLO
 └── Cost
 │
 ▼
OPERATE
 │
 ▼
SCORE
 │
 ▼
IMPROVE
 │
 ▼
MIGRATE
 │
 ▼
RETIRE
```

## Next — ADR-079

### **ADR-079 — Enterprise Testing Architecture, Quality Engineering, Test Automation & Continuous Verification Standard**

The platform can now create and operate standardized services, but the next weak point is obvious: **standardized deployment without standardized verification simply lets Mediverse ship defects faster.**

ADR-079 should establish the complete enterprise quality architecture across **quality ownership → shift-left vs shift-right → testing pyramid vs testing trophy → unit tests → component tests → Spring Boot testing → React testing → API tests → contract tests → consumer-driven contracts → database tests → migration tests → Kafka/event tests → asynchronous workflow tests → integration tests → Testcontainers → end-to-end tests → browser automation → Playwright → mobile/responsive testing → accessibility testing → visual regression → performance testing → load → stress → spike → soak → scalability → capacity validation → resilience/chaos testing → security testing → SAST/DAST/SCA → penetration testing → infrastructure testing → Terraform tests → Helm tests → Kubernetes manifest tests → policy tests → GitOps verification → data-quality tests → ETL/streaming tests → AI evaluation integration from ADR-077 → RAG regression → agent testing → test-data management → synthetic data → environment strategy → ephemeral test environments → service virtualization → mocks/stubs/fakes → flaky-test governance → deterministic testing → test isolation → parallelization → test selection → test impact analysis → mutation testing → code coverage and its limitations → quality gates → release confidence → canary verification → production synthetic monitoring → continuous verification → observability-driven testing → defect escape analysis → quality metrics → DORA integration → developer feedback speed → test-cost economics → quality scorecards → policy-as-code → golden testing paths → platform integration → maturity model → anti-patterns → final Mediverse enterprise quality-engineering reference architecture and ADR-079 decision outcome.**

# ADR-079 — Enterprise Testing Architecture, Quality Engineering, Test Automation & Continuous Verification Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-079
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)
**Primary Stakeholders:** Quality Engineering, Application Engineering, Platform Engineering, SRE, Security, Data Engineering, AI Engineering, Product Engineering, DevOps

ADR-078 established standardized golden paths for building and operating Mediverse services.

ADR-079 establishes how Mediverse determines whether those services are actually **correct, secure, compatible, performant, resilient and safe to release**.

The central principle is:

> **Testing is not a phase performed after development. Quality is a continuous property of the engineering system, and release confidence must be built from multiple independent forms of evidence.**

```text
                        REQUIREMENT
                            │
                            ▼
                         DESIGN
                            │
                            ▼
                          CODE
                            │
          ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
          ▼                 ▼                 ▼
        STATIC            UNIT            COMPONENT
          │                 │                 │
          └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                            ▼
                       INTEGRATION
                            │
               ┌────────────┼────────────┐
               ▼            ▼            ▼
              API        CONTRACT       EVENT
               │            │            │
               └────────────┼────────────┘
                            ▼
                           E2E
                            │
                            ▼
                PERFORMANCE / SECURITY
                            │
                            ▼
                      RELEASE GATE
                            │
                            ▼
                         CANARY
                            │
                            ▼
                       PRODUCTION
                            │
                            ▼
                 CONTINUOUS VERIFICATION
```

# 1. Quality Ownership

Quality belongs to the delivery team.

It is not delegated to a downstream QA department.

```text
Developer ─┐
QE        ─┤
SRE       ─┤──► PRODUCT QUALITY
Security  ─┤
Product   ─┘
```

Dedicated quality engineers provide specialization, frameworks and strategy; they do not become the only people responsible for defects.

# 2. Quality Engineering

Mediverse adopts **Quality Engineering**, not merely test execution.

Quality engineering includes:

```text
Requirements
Architecture
Code
Automation
Testability
Observability
Security
Performance
Resilience
Production feedback
```

# 3. Prevention Before Detection

The preferred hierarchy is:

```text
Prevent defect
     │
     ▼
Detect during coding
     │
     ▼
Detect during CI
     │
     ▼
Detect before production
     │
     ▼
Detect immediately in production
```

Finding the same defect later generally costs more.

# 4. Shift Left

Move appropriate verification earlier:

```text
IDE
 │
 ├── Formatting
 ├── Linting
 ├── Static analysis
 ├── Unit tests
 └── Security feedback
```

But "shift left" does not mean everything can be tested before production.

# 5. Shift Right

Production provides evidence unavailable in isolated test environments.

```text
Production
    │
    ├── Synthetic monitoring
    ├── Canary analysis
    ├── Real SLOs
    ├── Observability
    ├── Runtime security
    └── Real workload behavior
```

Mediverse therefore adopts:

> **Shift left + shift right.**

# 6. Continuous Verification

Verification occurs throughout the lifecycle.

```text
CODE
 │
 ▼
BUILD
 │
 ▼
TEST
 │
 ▼
DEPLOY
 │
 ▼
VERIFY
 │
 ▼
OBSERVE
 │
 ▼
LEARN
 │
 └────────► CODE
```

# 7. Testing Strategy

No single test type establishes confidence.

Mediverse combines:

```text
Static verification
Unit testing
Component testing
Contract testing
Integration testing
End-to-end testing
Performance testing
Security testing
Resilience testing
Production verification
```

# 8. Testing Pyramid

The classical model remains useful:

```text
              /\
             /E2E\
            /─────\
           / INTEG \
          /─────────\
         /   UNIT    \
        /_____________\
```

Most tests should generally be fast, isolated and inexpensive.

# 9. Testing Trophy

Modern applications also benefit heavily from integration/component verification.

```text
            E2E
             ▲
        Integration
      ▲▲▲▲▲▲▲▲▲▲
          Unit
            ▲▲
          Static
```

Mediverse does not mandate ideological adherence to either diagram.

Test distribution should reflect architecture and failure risk.

# 10. Test Portfolio

A service should have the **cheapest test portfolio capable of detecting its important failure modes**.

More tests are not automatically better.

# 11. Unit Tests

Unit tests validate small units of behavior.

Properties:

```text
Fast
Deterministic
Isolated
Repeatable
Easy to diagnose
```

# 12. Unit Test Scope

Good unit tests target:

```text
Domain logic
Validation
Transformations
Calculations
State transitions
Business rules
```

They should not waste effort testing framework internals.

# 13. Test Behavior, Not Implementation

Fragile:

```text
Verify private method X called exactly twice.
```

Prefer:

```text
Given valid enrollment
When enrollment is processed
Then learner becomes enrolled.
```

Implementation-coupled tests make refactoring unnecessarily expensive.

# 14. Spring Boot Unit Testing

The Spring Boot golden path should support:

```text
JUnit 5
Mockito where appropriate
AssertJ or equivalent assertions
Parameterized tests
```

Spring context should not be loaded when a plain unit test is sufficient.

# 15. Spring Context Cost

This is wasteful:

```text
@SpringBootTest
```

for every trivial class.

Use the smallest useful test boundary.

# 16. Slice Tests

Spring test slices can validate targeted framework integration:

```text
@WebMvcTest
@DataJpaTest
@JsonTest
```

where appropriate.

# 17. Controller Testing

Controller tests should verify:

```text
HTTP status
Request validation
Serialization
Authentication behavior
Response structure
Error mapping
```

not duplicate every domain rule already tested elsewhere.

# 18. Repository Testing

Persistence tests should verify actual persistence assumptions:

```text
Mappings
Queries
Constraints
Transactions
Indexes where relevant
Database-specific behavior
```

# 19. Real Database Semantics

H2 is not PostgreSQL.

```text
H2 tests pass
      │
      X
PostgreSQL guaranteed correct
```

Database-specific behavior should be tested against PostgreSQL when it matters.

# 20. Testcontainers

Testcontainers is the preferred pattern where realistic disposable dependencies materially improve confidence.

```text
Test
 │
 ├── PostgreSQL Container
 ├── Redis Container
 └── Kafka Container
```

This reduces dependence on permanently shared integration environments.

# 21. Testcontainers Scope

Do not containerize everything merely because it is possible.

Use realistic dependencies where fake substitutes would hide meaningful behavior.

# 22. Component Tests

Component tests validate a service as a meaningful unit while controlling external dependencies.

```text
        SERVICE
      ┌───────────┐
HTTP ─►           │
      │ Business  │
      │ Database  │
      └───────────┘
            │
            ▼
       Stub External API
```

# 23. API Testing

API verification should cover:

```text
Happy paths
Validation
Authentication
Authorization
Errors
Pagination
Filtering
Idempotency
Compatibility
Rate limits where relevant
```

# 24. OpenAPI Verification

ADR-078's API catalogue should integrate API contracts with tests.

```text
Implementation
      │
      ▼
OpenAPI
      │
      ▼
Contract Verification
```

Documentation and implementation should not silently diverge.

# 25. Contract Testing

Distributed systems require explicit compatibility verification.

```text
Consumer
   │
   ▼
Contract
   │
   ▼
Provider
```

Contract testing detects integration incompatibility without requiring complete end-to-end environments.

# 26. Consumer-Driven Contracts

Where appropriate:

```text
Consumer expectation
        │
        ▼
Published contract
        │
        ▼
Provider verification
```

This is particularly useful when multiple independently deployed services interact.

# 27. Contract Ownership

Contracts require lifecycle governance:

```text
Producer
Consumer
Version
Compatibility
Deprecation
```

Tests cannot compensate for undefined ownership.

# 28. Backward Compatibility

Changes should explicitly test compatibility.

Examples:

```text
Adding optional field       → usually compatible
Removing field              → potentially breaking
Changing semantic meaning   → potentially breaking
Changing enum behavior      → potentially breaking
```

# 29. Database Migration Testing

Database migrations are production code.

Test:

```text
Empty DB → latest
Previous version → latest
Representative data → latest
Rollback/recovery where supported
```

# 30. Migration Correctness

A migration that works on an empty database may fail against years of production data.

Representative migration testing is required for material changes.

# 31. Schema Evolution

Applications and database schemas should tolerate controlled rollout.

```text
EXPAND
  │
  ▼
Deploy compatible application
  │
  ▼
Migrate
  │
  ▼
CONTRACT
```

This reduces deployment coupling.

# 32. Kafka Testing

Event-driven services require testing beyond "message was sent."

Verify:

```text
Schema
Key
Headers
Partition assumptions
Serialization
Consumer behavior
Retries
Duplicates
Ordering assumptions
Dead-letter handling
```

# 33. Event Contract Testing

```text
Producer
   │
   ▼
Event Schema
   │
   ▼
Compatibility Check
   │
   ▼
Consumers
```

Breaking event contracts can impact consumers that the producer team never directly deploys.

# 34. Duplicate Delivery Testing

Distributed messaging should assume duplicate delivery is possible where relevant.

```text
EVENT
 │
 ├── Delivery 1
 └── Delivery 2
        │
        ▼
Same business result?
```

Idempotency must be tested, not assumed.

# 35. Ordering Testing

If business correctness depends on message ordering, tests must explicitly verify those assumptions.

Better still, avoid unnecessary global ordering dependencies.

# 36. Retry Testing

Verify behavior under:

```text
Transient failure
Permanent failure
Timeout
Partial processing
Retry exhaustion
```

Retries can create duplicate side effects.

# 37. Dead-Letter Testing

DLQ workflows require tests for:

```text
Routing
Metadata
Observability
Replay
Authorization
Poison-message handling
```

# 38. Asynchronous Workflow Testing

Avoid fixed sleeps:

```text
sleep(10000)
```

Prefer condition-based waiting:

```text
Wait until expected state
or timeout.
```

Fixed sleeps create slow, flaky tests.

# 39. Integration Tests

Integration tests verify real collaboration among components.

```text
Service
   │
   ├── PostgreSQL
   ├── Kafka
   ├── Redis
   └── External dependency
```

The integration boundary must be intentionally chosen.

# 40. Integration Environment

Shared environments remain useful for selected system-level scenarios.

But they should not become the only place integration defects can be discovered.

# 41. Service Virtualization

Unavailable or expensive external dependencies may be virtualized.

```text
Application
    │
    ▼
Virtual Service
```

Virtualization must model relevant behavior, not merely return `200 OK`.

# 42. Mocks

Mocks are useful for interaction isolation.

But excessive mocking creates tests that verify an imaginary system.

```text
Everything mocked
      │
      ▼
Everything passes
      │
      ▼
Production fails
```

# 43. Stubs

Stubs provide controlled responses and are useful for deterministic dependency scenarios.

# 44. Fakes

Fakes provide simplified functional implementations.

Example:

```text
Real S3
   ↕
Local object-store fake
```

Choose test doubles based on what behavior actually matters.

# 45. End-to-End Tests

E2E tests validate important user journeys.

Examples:

```text
Register
Login
Enroll
Learn
Take assessment
View progress
```

# 46. E2E Scope

Do not encode every edge case in E2E automation.

E2E tests are slower and harder to diagnose.

Use them for high-value cross-system journeys.

# 47. Browser Automation

For web applications, browser tests should execute against realistic user behavior.

# 48. Playwright Golden Path

Playwright is a strong standard candidate for Mediverse browser automation.

The platform path should support:

```text
Cross-browser testing
Screenshots
Tracing
Parallel execution
Network inspection
Retry diagnostics
```

# 49. Page Object Discipline

Page objects can improve reuse, but giant abstraction frameworks can hide test intent.

Prefer understandable test code over elaborate automation architecture.

# 50. Responsive Testing

Mediverse should test representative viewport classes:

```text
Mobile
Tablet
Desktop
```

not every possible pixel dimension.

# 51. Cross-Browser Testing

Coverage should reflect actual supported browsers and usage.

Testing 20 browser/version combinations without business justification is waste.

# 52. Accessibility Testing

Automated checks should detect appropriate accessibility violations.

But automated tools cannot establish complete accessibility compliance.

# 53. Manual Accessibility Verification

Human testing remains necessary for areas such as:

```text
Keyboard usability
Screen-reader experience
Cognitive clarity
Focus behavior
Meaningful interaction
```

# 54. Visual Regression Testing

Visual snapshots can detect unexpected UI changes.

```text
Baseline
   │
   ▼
New Screenshot
   │
   ▼
Diff
```

# 55. Visual Test Governance

Visual tests can become noisy when every minor rendering difference fails CI.

Use them selectively for valuable interfaces and components.

# 56. Performance Engineering

Performance is an architectural property.

Do not wait until production launch to ask whether the system can handle expected traffic.

# 57. Performance Test Types

```text
LOAD
Expected traffic

STRESS
Beyond expected capacity

SPIKE
Sudden traffic increase

SOAK
Sustained workload

SCALABILITY
Behavior as resources/load change
```

# 58. Workload Models

Performance tests must model realistic behavior.

```text
Login
Browse
Search
Watch content
Submit assessment
AI tutoring
```

A million requests to `/health` proves almost nothing.

# 59. Performance Baselines

Record baselines for:

```text
Throughput
p50 latency
p95 latency
p99 latency
Error rate
CPU
Memory
Database utilization
Queue depth
```

# 60. Performance Regression

Performance should be compared across releases where material.

```text
Release N
   │
   ▼
Baseline

Release N+1
   │
   ▼
Compare
```

A functionally correct release can still be operationally unacceptable.

---

## ADR-079 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–60 completed.**

The emerging quality architecture is:

```text
                         REQUIREMENT
                              │
                              ▼
                         TESTABILITY
                              │
                              ▼
                           CODE
                              │
       ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
       ▼                      ▼                      ▼
     STATIC                  UNIT                 SECURITY
       │                      │                      │
       └──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┘
                              ▼
                         COMPONENT
                              │
            ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
            ▼                 ▼                 ▼
           API             DATABASE            EVENT
            │                 │                 │
            └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                              ▼
                         CONTRACTS
                              │
                              ▼
                        INTEGRATION
                              │
                              ▼
                             E2E
                              │
           ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
           ▼                  ▼                  ▼
     ACCESSIBILITY       PERFORMANCE        RESILIENCE

           └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘

                              │
```
