* Compliance and regulatory mapping
* Audit retention
* Identity governance
* Access reviews and certification
* Identity risk scoring
* Session anomaly detection
* Identity telemetry
* Identity scorecards
* Enterprise maturity model
* Anti-patterns
* Final Mediverse Zero Trust reference architecture
* ADR-081 decision outcome.


# ADR-081 — Enterprise Identity, Authentication, Authorization, IAM, Zero Trust & Access Control Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — Identity Propagation**.

---

# 61. Cross-Cluster Identity

Workload identity must remain consistent across Kubernetes clusters.

```text
                 Cluster A
                     │
                     ▼
             Workload Identity
                     │
─────────────────────┼─────────────────────
                     │
                     ▼
                 Cluster B
```

Identity should not change merely because workloads move between clusters.

---

# 62. Multi-Cloud Identity

Cloud provider identity should remain an implementation detail.

Prefer:

```text
Application Identity
        │
        ▼
Enterprise Identity
        │
        ▼
Cloud Mapping
```

Avoid embedding AWS-, Azure-, or GCP-specific assumptions throughout application code.

---

# 63. Federation Between Clusters

Clusters should establish mutual trust through enterprise identity mechanisms rather than manually exchanged static credentials.

---

# 64. Workload Federation

A workload should authenticate using its workload identity.

Never:

```text
Pod
 │
 ▼
Username/password stored in ConfigMap
```

---

# 65. AI Agent Identity

ADR-077 defines AI agents as first-class enterprise actors.

Every AI agent requires:

```text
Identity

Owner

Purpose

Allowed Tools

Allowed Models

Allowed Data
```

Anonymous AI agents are prohibited.

---

# 66. AI Tool Identity

Each tool callable by an AI agent requires its own authorization boundary.

```text
Agent
 │
 ▼
Tool Request
 │
 ▼
Authorization
 │
 ▼
Execution
```

---

# 67. AI-to-AI Identity

When AI systems invoke other AI systems:

```text
Tutor Agent
      │
      ▼
Assessment Agent
```

both identities should remain observable and independently auditable.

---

# 68. Platform Identity

ADR-078's Internal Developer Platform is itself a privileged enterprise identity.

Platform automation must never execute as an anonymous superuser.

---

# 69. CI/CD Identity

Jenkins, GitHub Actions and GitOps pipelines require dedicated machine identities.

Avoid:

```text
Shared Admin Account
```

for automated delivery.

---

# 70. GitOps Identity

Argo CD should authenticate using dedicated workload identities with narrowly scoped permissions.

---

# 71. Infrastructure Identity

Terraform, Crossplane and other infrastructure automation require separate identities from application deployments.

Infrastructure automation should not inherit developer credentials.

---

# 72. SCIM Provisioning

Identity lifecycle should integrate with enterprise provisioning.

```text
HR System
    │
    ▼
SCIM
    │
    ▼
Identity Provider
    │
    ▼
Applications
```

Manual user creation should become the exception.

---

# 73. Joiner-Mover-Leaver Process

Identity lifecycle automation should support:

```text
Join

Transfer

Leave
```

Access rights should evolve automatically as employment status changes.

---

# 74. Orphan Identity Detection

Platform governance should regularly identify:

```text
Inactive Accounts

Unknown Service Accounts

Unused API Keys

Unused Certificates
```

Unused identities represent unnecessary attack surface.

---

# 75. Identity Recertification

Critical permissions require periodic review.

```text
Permission
      │
      ▼
Manager Review
      │
 ┌────┴────┐
 ▼         ▼
Keep    Remove
```

---

# 76. Segregation of Duties (SoD)

No single identity should possess conflicting business privileges where separation is required.

Example:

```text
Approve Payment

AND

Execute Payment
```

held by one user may violate governance requirements.

---

# 77. Access Certification

Enterprise access should undergo scheduled certification.

Questions include:

```text
Does this user still require access?

Does this workload still exist?

Is this privilege justified?
```

---

# 78. Identity Risk Scoring

Identity telemetry may contribute to adaptive risk.

Signals include:

```text
Impossible travel

Credential stuffing

Multiple failures

Privilege escalation

New device
```

---

# 79. Session Risk

Session trust may change after authentication.

Example:

```text
Login

↓

Normal Behavior

↓

Sudden Admin Action

↓

Re-authenticate
```

Authentication is not necessarily a one-time event.

---

# 80. Continuous Authorization

Zero Trust extends beyond login.

```text
Authenticate

↓

Authorize

↓

Continue Monitoring

↓

Re-evaluate
```

---

# 81. Secrets Integration

ADR-080 secrets management provides identity credentials.

Identity services should consume approved secret-management capabilities rather than embedded credentials.

---

# 82. Certificate Lifecycle

Certificates supporting workload identity require:

```text
Issue

Rotate

Expire

Revoke

Audit
```

Manual certificate management does not scale.

---

# 83. Key Management

Cryptographic keys require governance.

Key lifecycle:

```text
Generate

Store

Rotate

Archive

Destroy
```

---

# 84. Authorization Testing

ADR-079 requires authorization verification.

Every protected operation should test:

```text
Allowed

Denied

Boundary Cases

Cross-Tenant

Expired Session
```

---

# 85. Policy Testing

Authorization policies themselves require automated testing.

```text
Policy

↓

Known Inputs

↓

Expected Decision
```

---

# 86. Negative Identity Tests

Test:

```text
Invalid JWT

Expired JWT

Forged JWT

Wrong Tenant

Missing Claims

Revoked Session
```

Security testing should emphasize failure scenarios.

---

# 87. Identity in Observability

Telemetry should correlate:

```text
Trace

Identity

Tenant

Authorization Decision

Policy Version
```

Never expose credentials or secrets.

---

# 88. Identity Events

Important identity events include:

```text
Login

Logout

Token Refresh

Role Change

Policy Update

Failed Authorization
```

These become security telemetry.

---

# 89. OPA Integration

Open Policy Agent (OPA) is an appropriate enterprise policy engine where centralized policy evaluation is beneficial.

Policies should remain version controlled.

---

# 90. Cedar Decision

Policy languages such as Cedar may be appropriate for fine-grained authorization where their expressiveness and ecosystem align with enterprise requirements.

The architecture remains policy-engine agnostic.

---

# 91. Policy Versioning

Authorization policy changes are production changes.

Every policy should support:

```text
Version

History

Rollback

Review
```

---

# 92. Policy Audit

Every authorization decision should be explainable.

Questions should include:

```text
Which policy?

Which rule?

Which identity?

Which attributes?

Why denied?
```

Opaque authorization systems become operational liabilities.

---

# 93. Compliance Mapping

Identity architecture should support enterprise compliance obligations.

Examples include:

```text
Least Privilege

MFA

Audit

Access Review

Segregation of Duties

Traceability
```

without coupling ADR-081 to a specific regulatory framework.

---

# 94. Audit Retention

Identity audit records require defined retention policies consistent with enterprise governance and legal obligations.

---

# 95. Identity Telemetry

Platform analytics should observe:

```text
Login Success

Failure Rate

Authorization Failures

Privilege Usage

Token Refresh

Expired Credentials
```

---

# 96. Identity Scorecard

Each production system may expose:

| Capability        | Status |
| ----------------- | ------ |
| OIDC              | ✓      |
| MFA               | ✓      |
| Workload Identity | ✓      |
| RBAC              | ✓      |
| ABAC              | ✓      |
| Audit             | ✓      |
| Token Rotation    | ✓      |
| Access Reviews    | ✓      |

---

# 97. Platform Integration

ADR-078 should automatically provision:

```text
Repository

↓

Identity

↓

Permissions

↓

Secrets

↓

GitOps

↓

Observability
```

Identity becomes part of the platform golden path.

---

# 98. Runtime Integration

ADR-080 runtime configuration must never bypass authorization.

Changing configuration must not silently grant new privileges.

---

# 99. AI Governance Integration

ADR-077 AI agents consume the same identity architecture as human and machine actors.

No separate "AI security model" should emerge.

---

# 100. Data Governance Integration

ADR-076 data classification influences authorization.

Highly classified datasets require stronger access controls than public learning content.

---

# 101. Incident Response

Identity systems should support rapid investigation.

Investigators should answer:

```text
Who accessed?

When?

From where?

Which resource?

Which policy allowed it?
```

---

# 102. Emergency Revocation

Compromised identities require rapid revocation.

```text
Compromise

↓

Revoke

↓

Invalidate Sessions

↓

Rotate Credentials

↓

Audit
```

---

# 103. Break-Glass Review

Every emergency access event requires post-incident review.

Break-glass should remain exceptional.

---

# 104. Identity Availability

Identity infrastructure becomes mission critical.

Identity outages can prevent:

```text
Login

API Access

Deployments

Platform Operations
```

Identity services require high availability.

---

# 105. Identity Recovery

Recovery planning should include:

```text
Identity Provider

Certificate Authority

Secrets Platform

Policy Store
```

Identity recovery is part of disaster recovery.

---

# 106. Zero Trust Maturity

```text
LEVEL 1

Basic Authentication

LEVEL 2

Centralized IAM

LEVEL 3

Zero Trust

LEVEL 4

Continuous Authorization

LEVEL 5

Adaptive Enterprise Identity
```

Mediverse targets **Level 4**.

---

# 107. Identity Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Shared admin accounts
❌ Long-lived static tokens
❌ Cluster-admin everywhere
❌ Secrets inside source code
❌ Human credentials used by applications
❌ Authorization inside UI only
❌ Trust based on network location
❌ Permanent break-glass access
❌ Anonymous AI agents
❌ API keys for everything
❌ Default service account everywhere
❌ Hardcoded permissions
❌ Authorization duplicated inconsistently
❌ Missing audit
❌ Manual identity lifecycle
❌ JWTs containing sensitive data
❌ Feature flags replacing authorization
❌ Runtime configuration bypassing security
❌ Policy engines without testing
❌ Identity telemetry without privacy controls
```

---

# 108. Enterprise Zero Trust Architecture

```text
                     HUMAN / MACHINE / AI
                              │
                              ▼
                    ENTERPRISE IDENTITY
                              │
          ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
          ▼                   ▼                   ▼
       HUMAN              WORKLOAD              AGENT
          │                   │                   │
          └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                              ▼
                     AUTHENTICATION
                              │
          ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
          ▼                   ▼                   ▼
          OIDC               mTLS              SPIFFE
                              │
                              ▼
                      AUTHORIZATION
                              │
        ┌─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐
        ▼                     ▼                     ▼
       RBAC                  ABAC                 ReBAC
                              │
                              ▼
                        POLICY ENGINE
                              │
                              ▼
                     PDP / PEP DECISION
                              │
                    ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                    ▼                   ▼
                 ALLOW                DENY
                    │
                    ▼
               APPLICATION
                    │
      ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
      ▼             ▼             ▼
    AUDIT       TELEMETRY      OBSERVE
```

---

# 109. ADR-081 Decision Outcome

| Area                   | Decision                              |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Zero Trust             | Mandatory                             |
| Central IdP            | Mandatory                             |
| OIDC                   | Preferred                             |
| OAuth 2.1              | Supported                             |
| SAML                   | Legacy interoperability               |
| JWT                    | Standard access token                 |
| MFA                    | Risk-based mandatory                  |
| Workload identity      | Mandatory                             |
| SPIFFE/SPIRE           | Preferred for workloads               |
| RBAC                   | Supported                             |
| ABAC                   | Supported                             |
| ReBAC                  | Supported                             |
| PBAC                   | Supported                             |
| Hybrid authorization   | Adopt                                 |
| PDP/PEP                | Adopt                                 |
| API Gateway            | Authentication + coarse authorization |
| Business authorization | Service responsibility                |
| Kubernetes RBAC        | Least privilege                       |
| JIT access             | Preferred                             |
| Break-glass            | Controlled                            |
| PAM                    | Required                              |
| SCIM                   | Preferred                             |
| Identity telemetry     | Mandatory                             |
| AI identities          | First-class                           |
| Platform identities    | First-class                           |
| Policy engine          | OPA/Cedar or equivalent               |
| Status                 | **Accepted**                          |

---

# 110. Governing Invariant

> **Every request in Mediverse—whether initiated by a human, service, Kubernetes workload, AI agent or automation platform—must continuously establish identity, authenticate through approved mechanisms, authorize against governed enterprise policy, remain fully auditable and operate under the principles of Zero Trust and least privilege. Identity is treated as a core architectural capability rather than an application feature.**

---

```text
       ▼

       │
       ▼

       ▼
AUDIT
       │
       ▼

       │
       ▼

       │
       ▼
ROTATE CREDENTIALS
       │
       ▼

       │
       ▼
DECOMMISSION
```

# ADR-082 — Enterprise API Architecture, API Governance, API Lifecycle & Integration Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-082
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-081 established Zero Trust identity and authorization.

ADR-082 defines how every service in Mediverse exposes capabilities through governed APIs while ensuring consistency, interoperability, backward compatibility, security, observability and long-term evolution.

The governing principle is:

> **An API is a long-lived business contract, not merely an HTTP endpoint. Every API must be designed, versioned, governed, observed and evolved as a product.**

```text id="0xtcmx"
                    CONSUMER
                        │
                        ▼
                  API CONTRACT
                        │
        ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
        ▼               ▼               ▼
   Authentication   Validation    Documentation
        │               │               │
        └───────────────┼───────────────┘
                        ▼
                   API Gateway
                        │
                        ▼
                  Business Service
                        │
        ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
        ▼               ▼               ▼
      Database        Events        External APIs
                        │
                        ▼
                 Observability
```

---

# 1. API Philosophy

An API is the public language of a bounded context.

It should expose business capabilities rather than implementation details.

Poor:

```text id="eprz8q"
POST /saveCourseData
```

Better:

```text id="5jlwmq"
POST /courses
```

---

# 2. API First

Mediverse adopts an **API-First** approach.

```text id="m7pph5"
Business Requirement
        │
        ▼
API Contract
        │
        ▼
Review
        │
        ▼
Implementation
```

Consumers should understand the contract before implementation exists.

---

# 3. API as Product

Every API requires:

```text id="swnhvg"
Owner
Documentation
Version
Consumers
Lifecycle
Support
SLO
```

APIs without ownership inevitably degrade.

---

# 4. API Taxonomy

APIs are classified into:

```text id="jlwm0m"
Public APIs

Partner APIs

Internal APIs

System APIs

Platform APIs

AI APIs
```

Different categories require different governance.

---

# 5. Internal vs External APIs

Internal APIs may evolve faster.

Public APIs require stronger compatibility guarantees.

The governance model should reflect consumer impact.

---

# 6. REST

REST is the preferred default for synchronous business APIs.

It aligns well with:

```text id="ezl0z4"
CRUD

Business Resources

HTTP Semantics

Caching

Tooling
```

---

# 7. gRPC

gRPC is appropriate where:

```text id="0n8d7w"
Low latency

High throughput

Internal communication

Streaming
```

It should not replace REST indiscriminately.

---

# 8. GraphQL

GraphQL is appropriate when consumers genuinely require flexible data retrieval.

Avoid adopting GraphQL solely because it is fashionable.

---

# 9. Async APIs

Event-driven communication complements synchronous APIs.

Use events where:

```text id="cy5hkn"
Immediate response unnecessary

Loose coupling valuable

Scalability important
```

---

# 10. API Selection Matrix

| Requirement               | Preferred Style |
| ------------------------- | --------------- |
| CRUD                      | REST            |
| Internal High Performance | gRPC            |
| Flexible Query            | GraphQL         |
| Event Notification        | Async           |
| Long-running workflow     | Async + REST    |

No single protocol is universally optimal.

---

# 11. Resource-Oriented Design

REST resources represent business entities.

Examples:

```text id="v6e7oj"
courses

students

assessments

progress
```

Avoid exposing database tables or implementation artifacts.

---

# 12. URI Conventions

Prefer nouns.

Good:

```text id="kxgihd"
/courses

/students

/assessments
```

Avoid verbs.

```text id="o71o7v"
/createCourse

/deleteCourse
```

HTTP methods already express actions.

---

# 13. HTTP Methods

Standard semantics:

```text id="w9m2jv"
GET

Read

POST

Create

PUT

Replace

PATCH

Partial Update

DELETE

Remove
```

Avoid redefining established HTTP meaning.

---

# 14. Resource Hierarchy

Represent relationships carefully.

Example:

```text id="4dr1p9"
/courses/{id}

/courses/{id}/assessments
```

Deep nesting generally increases complexity.

---

# 15. Naming Standards

Use:

```text id="4t5x5r"
Plural resources

Lowercase

Hyphenated words where needed
```

Maintain consistency across all APIs.

---

# 16. Identifiers

Identifiers should remain stable.

Never expose internal implementation assumptions that may change.

---

# 17. Representation

Represent business concepts.

Avoid exposing ORM entities directly.

Introduce DTOs where appropriate.

---

# 18. HTTP Status Codes

Use standard semantics.

Examples:

```text id="r6fkg7"
200

201

202

204

400

401

403

404

409

422

500
```

Avoid returning HTTP 200 for every situation.

---

# 19. Error Model

Errors should be structured.

```json id="j8nztv"
{
  "code": "COURSE_NOT_FOUND",
  "message": "...",
  "traceId": "...",
  "timestamp": "...",
  "details": {}
}
```

---

# 20. Error Stability

Error contracts are part of the API.

Consumers should not need to parse free-form strings.

---

# 21. OpenAPI

Every REST API should publish an OpenAPI specification.

Documentation should derive from the contract rather than handwritten documents.

---

# 22. Contract Governance

The OpenAPI document becomes an architectural artifact.

It requires:

```text id="24n4u3"
Review

Versioning

Validation

Publication
```

---

# 23. Documentation

Consumers should discover:

```text id="q0m4mh"
Authentication

Examples

Errors

Limits

Lifecycle

Owner
```

Documentation should evolve with the API.

---

# 24. Consumer Experience

API usability is an architectural concern.

Questions include:

```text id="f0tdob"
Can new consumers onboard quickly?

Are examples complete?

Are errors understandable?
```

---

# 25. Backward Compatibility

Backward compatibility is the default expectation.

Breaking consumers should require explicit justification.

---

# 26. Breaking Changes

Examples:

```text id="4dybvl"
Removing fields

Changing meaning

Changing enum behavior

Removing endpoints

Changing authentication
```

These require lifecycle governance.

---

# 27. Additive Evolution

Prefer:

```text id="cy5zj5"
New optional field

New endpoint

New capability
```

These generally preserve compatibility.

---

# 28. API Versioning

Versioning should be deliberate.

Versioning every release creates unnecessary fragmentation.

---

# 29. URI Versioning

Example:

```text id="l3vx5m"
/v1/courses
```

Acceptable where organizational standards require it.

---

# 30. Semantic Versioning of Contracts

API contracts should evolve predictably.

Major compatibility changes require stronger governance.

---

# ADR-082 — Enterprise API Architecture, API Governance, API Lifecycle & Integration Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Semantic Versioning of Contracts**.

---

# 31. API Lifecycle

Every API follows a governed lifecycle.

```text id="api31"
Idea
 │
 ▼
Design
 │
 ▼
Review
 │
 ▼
Implement
 │
 ▼
Publish
 │
 ▼
Operate
 │
 ▼
Deprecate
 │
 ▼
Retire
```

APIs should never appear or disappear without governance.

---

# 32. API Publication

Before consumers use an API, it should publish:

```text id="api32"
OpenAPI Specification

Examples

Authentication

Owner

Support Contact

Version

SLA/SLO

Changelog
```

---

# 33. Consumer Registration

Critical enterprise APIs should know:

```text id="api33"
Who consumes them

Business Owner

Criticality

Environment

Version Used
```

Consumer awareness enables safe evolution.

---

# 34. Consumer Onboarding

New consumers should complete onboarding through standardized documentation and automated provisioning.

```text id="api34"
Read Docs
     │
     ▼
Obtain Credentials
     │
     ▼
Sandbox
     │
     ▼
Production
```

---

# 35. API Discovery

ADR-078's Internal Developer Platform should provide an API catalog.

Developers should discover APIs without tribal knowledge.

---

# 36. API Deprecation

Deprecation must precede removal.

```text id="api36"
Supported
     │
     ▼
Deprecated
     │
     ▼
Removal Date
     │
     ▼
Retired
```

---

# 37. Deprecation Communication

Deprecation notices should include:

```text id="api37"
Reason

Replacement

Migration Guide

Timeline

Support Contact
```

---

# 38. API Retirement

An API should only retire after:

```text id="api38"
Consumers migrated

Business approval

Monitoring confirms no usage

Documentation updated
```

---

# 39. Pagination

Large collections require pagination.

```text id="api39"
/courses?page=2&size=20
```

Avoid returning unlimited datasets.

---

# 40. Cursor Pagination

For very large or frequently changing datasets, cursor-based pagination is generally preferred.

```text id="api40"
GET /students?cursor=abc123
```

---

# 41. Filtering

Filtering should remain declarative.

```text id="api41"
/courses?status=ACTIVE
```

Avoid creating separate endpoints for every filter combination.

---

# 42. Sorting

Sorting should be explicit.

```text id="api42"
/students?sort=name,asc
```

Default ordering should be documented.

---

# 43. Search APIs

Search differs from filtering.

```text id="api43"
/search?q=cardiology
```

Search semantics should be clearly defined.

---

# 44. Partial Responses

Consumers may request subsets of data where supported.

```text id="api44"
GET /students?fields=id,name
```

Use selectively to reduce payload size.

---

# 45. Idempotency

Repeated requests should not create unintended side effects.

```text id="api45"
POST
 │
 ▼
Idempotency-Key
 │
 ▼
Single Business Result
```

Critical create operations should support idempotency where duplicate requests are possible.

---

# 46. Long-Running Operations

Operations requiring significant processing should avoid blocking clients.

```text id="api46"
POST

↓

202 Accepted

↓

Operation Resource

↓

Polling/Webhook/Event
```

---

# 47. Asynchronous Workflows

Long-running workflows should expose explicit state.

```text id="api47"
Queued

↓

Running

↓

Completed

↓

Failed
```

---

# 48. Retry Safety

Consumers should understand whether retrying is safe.

Document:

```text id="api48"
Safe

Unsafe

Idempotent

Retryable
```

---

# 49. Rate Limiting

APIs should protect themselves from abuse.

```text id="api49"
Requests

↓

Rate Limiter

↓

Allow / Reject
```

---

# 50. Quotas

Some APIs require long-term usage limits.

Examples:

```text id="api50"
Daily AI Requests

Storage

API Calls

Assessment Attempts
```

---

# 51. API Caching

Caching should follow HTTP semantics where appropriate.

```text id="api51"
Client

↓

Gateway

↓

Origin
```

Avoid caching sensitive or user-specific data incorrectly.

---

# 52. Conditional Requests

Support conditional requests where beneficial.

```text id="api52"
ETag

If-None-Match
```

This reduces unnecessary bandwidth.

---

# 53. API Gateway Responsibilities

The gateway should provide cross-cutting capabilities.

Examples:

```text id="api53"
Authentication

TLS

Rate Limiting

Logging

Routing

Basic Validation
```

Business logic belongs in downstream services.

---

# 54. Backend for Frontend (BFF)

Different clients may require different APIs.

```text id="api54"
Web

↓

Web BFF

Mobile

↓

Mobile BFF
```

Avoid forcing every client through identical payloads.

---

# 55. API Composition

Composition aggregates multiple service responses.

```text id="api55"
Course Service

Student Service

Assessment Service

↓

Composite Response
```

Composition should avoid excessive coupling.

---

# 56. Aggregation vs Orchestration

Aggregation collects information.

Orchestration coordinates business workflows.

These responsibilities should remain distinct.

---

# 57. Service Mesh Interaction

Service meshes provide transport capabilities.

They do **not** replace API governance.

```text id="api57"
Service Mesh

≠

API Contract
```

---

# 58. Event Integration

Synchronous APIs and asynchronous events should complement each other.

Example:

```text id="api58"
POST Enrollment

↓

Enrollment Created Event
```

Events should never surprise API consumers.

---

# 59. Consumer-Driven Evolution

API evolution should consider actual consumer usage.

Breaking changes require understanding consumer impact rather than assuming consumers can immediately upgrade.

---

# 60. API Governance Integration

ADR-082 integrates with previous ADRs:

```text id="api60"
ADR-077

AI APIs

ADR-078

Platform & Observability

ADR-079

API Testing

ADR-080

Runtime Configuration

ADR-081

Authentication & Authorization
```

API architecture is therefore an enterprise capability rather than an isolated application concern.

---

# ADR-082 — Enterprise API Architecture, API Governance, API Lifecycle & Integration Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — API Governance Integration**.

---

# 61. API Observability

Every API should produce sufficient telemetry to answer:

```text id="api61"
Who called?

Which endpoint?

Latency?

Status?

Errors?

Consumer?

Version?
```

API health is measured by behavior, not merely uptime.

---

# 62. OpenTelemetry Integration

ADR-078 establishes OpenTelemetry as the enterprise telemetry standard.

Every API request should generate:

```text id="api62"
Trace

Span

Correlation ID

Request Metadata

Response Metadata
```

Avoid proprietary tracing mechanisms when standardized telemetry is sufficient.

---

# 63. Correlation IDs

Every request should carry a correlation identifier.

```text id="api63"
Gateway

↓

Service A

↓

Kafka

↓

Service B

↓

Database
```

The correlation identifier enables end-to-end diagnostics.

---

# 64. Structured Logging

API logs should be machine-readable.

Example fields:

```text id="api64"
Timestamp

Trace ID

Consumer

Endpoint

Status

Latency

Tenant

Error Code
```

Avoid free-form log messages for operational events.

---

# 65. API Metrics

Core metrics include:

```text id="api65"
Request Rate

Error Rate

Latency

Availability

Payload Size

Retry Rate

Throttle Rate
```

---

# 66. Consumer Analytics

Understand API usage.

Track:

```text id="api66"
Consumer

Version

Endpoint

Frequency

Success Rate

Geographic Region
```

Analytics inform safe evolution and capacity planning.

---

# 67. API SLIs

Representative Service Level Indicators:

```text id="api67"
Availability

Latency

Correctness

Freshness

Error Rate
```

SLIs should map to observable technical behavior.

---

# 68. API SLOs

Each production API should define measurable objectives.

Example:

```text id="api68"
Availability

99.9%

P95 Latency

<300 ms

Error Rate

<0.1%
```

Targets vary according to business criticality.

---

# 69. Error Budgets

SLOs define acceptable failure.

```text id="api69"
SLO

↓

Error Budget

↓

Operational Decisions
```

Teams should avoid exhausting error budgets through uncontrolled releases.

---

# 70. Contract Testing

ADR-079 requires API contracts to become executable tests.

```text id="api70"
Consumer

↓

Contract

↓

Provider

↓

Verification
```

Documentation alone cannot guarantee compatibility.

---

# 71. Consumer-Driven Contracts

Consumer expectations should drive compatibility verification where appropriate.

```text id="api71"
Consumer

↓

Expected Contract

↓

Provider Verification
```

---

# 72. Mock Servers

OpenAPI specifications should support automatically generated mock services.

```text id="api72"
OpenAPI

↓

Mock Server

↓

Consumer Development
```

This enables parallel development before implementation is complete.

---

# 73. Sandbox Environments

Public and partner APIs should provide sandbox environments where feasible.

Sandboxes reduce onboarding friction and protect production systems.

---

# 74. API Testing Strategy

Combine multiple forms of verification.

```text id="api74"
Unit

↓

Integration

↓

Contract

↓

Security

↓

Performance

↓

E2E
```

No single test category provides complete confidence.

---

# 75. Security Testing

ADR-081 defines authentication and authorization.

ADR-082 requires API verification for:

```text id="api75"
Authentication

Authorization

Rate Limits

Input Validation

Injection

Object-Level Authorization
```

---

# 76. GraphQL Governance

GraphQL services require additional governance.

Examples:

```text id="api76"
Depth Limits

Complexity Limits

Introspection Policy

Persisted Queries
```

Prevent expensive or abusive queries.

---

# 77. GraphQL Schema Evolution

Schema changes require compatibility review.

Prefer additive evolution over breaking field removals.

---

# 78. gRPC Governance

gRPC contracts require:

```text id="api78"
Proto Versioning

Field Compatibility

Reserved Fields

Backward Compatibility
```

Protocol Buffers become long-lived contracts.

---

# 79. AsyncAPI Governance

Event APIs should publish AsyncAPI specifications.

```text id="api79"
Topic

Schema

Producer

Consumer

Version

Lifecycle
```

Events deserve governance equal to REST APIs.

---

# 80. Webhook Standards

Webhook producers should define:

```text id="api80"
Authentication

Retries

Signing

Ordering

Timeout

Idempotency
```

Consumers should never assume guaranteed delivery.

---

# 81. SDK Generation

SDKs should be generated from API contracts where practical.

```text id="api81"
OpenAPI

↓

SDK

↓

Java

TypeScript

Python
```

Generated SDKs reduce manual inconsistencies.

---

# 82. Documentation Portal

The Internal Developer Platform should expose a unified portal containing:

```text id="api82"
API Catalog

OpenAPI

Examples

SDKs

Lifecycle

Owners
```

---

# 83. Changelog

Every API should publish an understandable changelog.

Include:

```text id="api83"
Added

Changed

Deprecated

Removed

Fixed
```

Consumers should not infer changes from behavior.

---

# 84. Migration Guides

Breaking or significant changes require migration documentation.

Good migration guides include:

```text id="api84"
Old Pattern

New Pattern

Examples

Timeline

Compatibility Notes
```

---

# 85. API Governance Board

Enterprise-wide APIs should undergo architectural review.

Review areas include:

```text id="api85"
Naming

Security

Compatibility

Performance

Documentation

Ownership
```

---

# 86. API Inventory

Maintain a complete inventory.

```text id="api86"
Owner

Version

Consumers

Lifecycle

Criticality

Dependencies
```

Unknown APIs create unmanaged risk.

---

# 87. API Dependency Graph

Understand service relationships.

```text id="api87"
Consumer

↓

Gateway

↓

API A

↓

API B

↓

Event

↓

API C
```

Dependency graphs support impact analysis.

---

# 88. API Scorecard

Each API may expose:

| Capability     | Status |
| -------------- | ------ |
| OpenAPI        | ✓      |
| Authentication | ✓      |
| Authorization  | ✓      |
| Contract Tests | ✓      |
| Rate Limits    | ✓      |
| SLOs           | ✓      |
| Observability  | ✓      |
| Documentation  | ✓      |

Scorecards highlight improvement opportunities rather than serving as pass/fail checklists.

---

# 89. API Governance Automation

Governance should become automated where possible.

Examples:

```text id="api89"
Lint OpenAPI

Validate Naming

Detect Breaking Changes

Check Security Rules

Verify Documentation
```

Automation improves consistency and reduces manual effort.

---

# 90. Consumer Notifications

Consumers should receive advance notice of:

```text id="api90"
Deprecations

Breaking Changes

Security Changes

Maintenance

Retirements
```

Communication is part of API reliability.

---

# 91. Platform Integration

ADR-078 should automatically provision:

```text id="api91"
Repository

↓

OpenAPI

↓

Gateway Registration

↓

Developer Portal

↓

Monitoring
```

Publishing an API becomes part of the platform golden path.

---

# 92. Runtime Integration

ADR-080 governs runtime API behavior.

Examples:

```text id="api92"
Rate Limits

Feature Flags

Timeouts

Routing

Kill Switches
```

Runtime controls must remain observable and auditable.

---

# 93. Security Integration

ADR-081 governs identity.

API contracts should clearly define:

```text id="api93"
Authentication

Authorization

Scopes

Permissions

Error Codes
```

Security requirements belong in API documentation.

---

# 94. AI API Integration

ADR-077 AI services should expose governed APIs.

Examples:

```text id="api94"
Model Invocation

Embedding API

RAG Retrieval

Agent Execution

Evaluation API
```

AI endpoints follow the same governance standards as traditional APIs.

---

# 95. Event Integration

REST and event contracts should remain synchronized.

Example:

```text id="api95"
POST Enrollment

↓

Enrollment Created Event

↓

Notification

↓

Analytics
```

API and event lifecycles should evolve together.

---

# 96. Performance Governance

Every critical API should have a performance baseline.

Track:

```text id="api96"
P50

P95

P99

Throughput

Resource Usage
```

Performance regressions are contract regressions.

---

# 97. Enterprise API Maturity Model

```text id="api97"
LEVEL 1

Ad Hoc APIs

LEVEL 2

Documented APIs

LEVEL 3

Governed APIs

LEVEL 4

Observable API Platform

LEVEL 5

Adaptive API Ecosystem
```

Mediverse targets **Level 4**.

---

# 98. API Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text id="api98"
❌ RPC-style REST endpoints
❌ Verbs in URIs
❌ Returning HTTP 200 for errors
❌ Breaking changes without notice
❌ Undocumented APIs
❌ Missing owners
❌ Versioning every release
❌ No pagination
❌ Unlimited responses
❌ Business logic in API Gateway
❌ Gateway-only authorization
❌ Free-form error messages
❌ Inconsistent naming
❌ APIs without observability
❌ Events without contracts
❌ GraphQL without query limits
❌ gRPC without compatibility rules
❌ API documentation drifting from implementation
❌ Hidden internal APIs used by external consumers
```

---

# 99. Enterprise API Reference Architecture

```text id="api99"
                 CONSUMER
                     │
                     ▼
            Developer Portal
                     │
                     ▼
              API Contract
                     │
         ┌───────────┼───────────┐
         ▼           ▼           ▼
   Documentation   SDKs      Examples
         │
         ▼
             API Gateway
         │
 ┌───────┼────────┬─────────┐
 ▼       ▼        ▼         ▼
REST    gRPC   GraphQL   AsyncAPI
 │       │        │         │
 └───────┼────────┼─────────┘
         ▼
 Business Services
         │
 ┌───────┼──────────────┐
 ▼       ▼              ▼
 DB    Events      External APIs
         │
         ▼
 Observability + Security + Testing
```

---

| Breaking Change Review | Mandatory                           |
| Status                 | **Accepted**                        |

> **Every API in Mediverse is a governed business contract with an owner, documented lifecycle, measurable reliability objectives, standardized security, executable compatibility tests, complete observability and predictable evolution. APIs are treated as products rather than implementation details.**

# ADR-083 — Enterprise Event-Driven Architecture, Messaging, Streaming & Distributed Workflow Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-083
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-082 established enterprise API architecture.

ADR-083 defines how Mediverse communicates asynchronously using events, messaging and streaming while preserving consistency, reliability, observability and business autonomy.

The governing principle is:

> **Events represent facts that have already occurred. They are immutable business records—not commands, API calls or implementation shortcuts.**

```text
                  BUSINESS EVENT
                        │
                        ▼
                  EVENT CONTRACT
                        │
         ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
         ▼              ▼              ▼
     PRODUCER       SCHEMA         SECURITY
         │              │              │
         └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                        ▼
                MESSAGE BROKER
                        │
      ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
      ▼                 ▼                 ▼
  CONSUMER A       CONSUMER B       STREAM PROCESSOR
      │                 │                 │
      └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                        ▼
                 OBSERVABILITY
```

---

# 1. Event-Driven Philosophy

Events describe something that **already happened**.

Examples:

```text
StudentRegistered

AssessmentSubmitted

CoursePublished

VideoProcessed
```

Events should never describe future intentions.

---

# 2. Event vs Command

Commands request work.

Events announce completed work.

```text
Command

CreateCourse

↓

CourseCreated
```

Confusing commands with events creates tight coupling.

---

# 3. Event Ownership

Every event has exactly one producer.

```text
Enrollment Service

↓

EnrollmentCreated
```

Many consumers may exist.

Only one authoritative producer may publish the business fact.

---

# 4. Event Categories

Mediverse classifies events as:

```text
Domain Events

Integration Events

Platform Events

Audit Events

AI Events
```

Each serves a distinct purpose.

---

# 5. Domain Events

Represent business facts.

Example:

```text
AssessmentCompleted
```

They should remain technology-independent.

---

# 6. Integration Events

Integration events communicate between bounded contexts.

They may transform internal domain models into externally consumable contracts.

---

# 7. Platform Events

Platform events describe infrastructure.

Examples:

```text
DeploymentCompleted

CertificateRotated

ClusterScaled
```

They are not business events.

---

# 8. Audit Events

Audit events support governance.

Examples:

```text
RoleAssigned

PermissionRevoked

PolicyChanged
```

Audit events require strong retention guarantees.

---

# 9. AI Events

ADR-077 introduces AI events.

Examples:

```text
PromptEvaluated

ModelInvoked

EmbeddingGenerated

TutorCompleted
```

AI pipelines become first-class event producers.

---

# 10. Event Storming

Business event discovery should begin with domain experts.

```text
Business Process

↓

Business Events

↓

Commands

↓

Policies

↓

Services
```

Technology follows business language.

---

# 11. Event Naming

Use past tense.

Good:

```text
StudentRegistered

CourseArchived
```

Avoid:

```text
RegisterStudent

UpdateCourse
```

---

# 12. Event Immutability

Published events are immutable.

Never modify historical events.

Corrections generate new events.

---

# 13. Event Contracts

Events are contracts.

Consumers depend on:

```text
Schema

Meaning

Semantics

Ownership
```

---

# 14. Schema Registry

Event schemas should be centrally governed.

```text
Producer

↓

Schema Registry

↓

Broker

↓

Consumers
```

---

# 15. Event Schema Evolution

Prefer additive evolution.

Examples:

```text
Add Optional Field

✓

Remove Required Field

✗
```

Compatibility remains the default expectation.

---

# 16. CloudEvents

CloudEvents is the preferred standard for portable event metadata where interoperability is valuable.

---

# 17. Required Metadata

Every event should include:

```text
Event ID

Timestamp

Producer

Version

Trace ID

Correlation ID

Tenant

Subject
```

---

# 18. Event Payload

Payloads should represent business information.

Avoid embedding implementation-specific objects.

---

# 19. Kafka

Kafka is the preferred enterprise streaming platform for durable event streams.

Suitable for:

```text
Streaming

Event Replay

Analytics

Large Scale
```

---

# 20. RabbitMQ

RabbitMQ remains appropriate for:

```text
Task Queues

RPC

Short-lived Messaging

Work Distribution
```

Messaging requirements determine technology selection.

---

# 21. Topic Naming

Topics should express business intent.

Example:

```text
student.events

assessment.events

course.events
```

Avoid infrastructure-oriented names.

---

# 22. Producer Responsibility

Producers guarantee:

```text
Correct Event

Correct Schema

Correct Timing

Correct Ownership
```

Consumers should not repair invalid events.

---

# 23. Consumer Responsibility

Consumers own:

```text
Processing

Validation

Retries

Local State

Side Effects
```

---

# 24. Loose Coupling

Producers should not know their consumers.

```text
Producer

↓

Broker

↓

Many Consumers
```

Direct dependencies reduce scalability.

---

# 25. Event Routing

Routing should depend on business semantics rather than infrastructure convenience.

---

# 26. Event Partitioning

Partition keys determine ordering.

Choose stable business identifiers.

Example:

```text
Student ID

Course ID

Assessment ID
```

---

# 27. Ordering Guarantees

Ordering generally exists only within a partition.

Avoid assuming global ordering.

---

# 28. Event Time

Different timestamps exist.

```text
Occurred

Published

Consumed

Processed
```

Distinguish them explicitly.

---

# 29. Event Identity

Every event requires a globally unique identifier.

This supports deduplication and traceability.

---

# 30. Event Lifecycle

```text
Occurred

↓

Published

↓

Stored

↓

Consumed

↓

Archived
```

Events should follow governed lifecycle management.

---

# ADR-083 — Enterprise Event-Driven Architecture, Messaging, Streaming & Distributed Workflow Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Event Lifecycle**.

---

# 31. Delivery Semantics

Every messaging system provides delivery guarantees.

Mediverse recognizes three primary models:

```text id="evt31"
At-Most-Once

↓

May Lose Messages

No Duplicates


At-Least-Once

↓

No Loss

Duplicates Possible


Exactly-Once

↓

Single Logical Processing

Additional Complexity
```

Exactly-once semantics should not be assumed merely because a messaging platform advertises them.

---

# 32. At-Most-Once

Suitable when occasional message loss is acceptable.

Examples:

```text id="evt32"
Analytics

Metrics

Telemetry
```

Not appropriate for critical business transactions.

---

# 33. At-Least-Once

Default enterprise delivery model.

```text id="evt33"
Producer

↓

Broker

↓

Consumer

↓

Retry Until Success
```

Consumers must tolerate duplicate delivery.

---

# 34. Exactly-Once

Exactly-once guarantees are limited.

They generally apply only within defined transactional boundaries.

Business correctness still requires idempotent processing.

---

# 35. Idempotency

Processing the same event multiple times should produce the same business outcome.

```text id="evt35"
Event

↓

Processed

↓

State Updated

↓

Duplicate Event

↓

No Additional Effect
```

---

# 36. Idempotency Keys

Consumers should use stable identifiers.

Examples:

```text id="evt36"
Event ID

Payment ID

Enrollment ID

Assessment Submission ID
```

Never use timestamps as idempotency identifiers.

---

# 37. Deduplication

Deduplication should occur close to business processing.

```text id="evt37"
Incoming Event

↓

Already Processed?

↓

YES → Ignore

NO → Process
```

---

# 38. Retry Philosophy

Retries should address transient failures only.

Examples:

```text id="evt38"
Temporary Network Failure

Broker Timeout

Database Connection Loss
```

Retries should not endlessly repeat permanent failures.

---

# 39. Retry Strategy

Preferred retry behavior:

```text id="evt39"
Attempt

↓

Exponential Backoff

↓

Retry

↓

Maximum Attempts

↓

DLQ
```

---

# 40. Exponential Backoff

Spacing retries reduces cascading failures.

```text id="evt40"
1 sec

2 sec

4 sec

8 sec

16 sec
```

Avoid immediate retry storms.

---

# 41. Retry Jitter

Randomized delay prevents synchronized retries.

```text id="evt41"
Base Delay

+

Random Offset
```

This reduces thundering herd effects.

---

# 42. Poison Messages

Some events can never be processed successfully.

Examples:

```text id="evt42"
Invalid Schema

Corrupted Payload

Missing Mandatory Data

Unsupported Version
```

Permanent failures require different handling from transient failures.

---

# 43. Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)

After retry exhaustion:

```text id="evt43"
Consumer

↓

Retry

↓

Retry

↓

Retry

↓

DLQ
```

DLQs preserve failed events for investigation.

---

# 44. DLQ Governance

Dead-letter queues require ownership.

Track:

```text id="evt44"
Owner

Reason

Timestamp

Retry Count

Resolution
```

A DLQ that nobody monitors is operational debt.

---

# 45. Consumer Groups

Consumer groups enable horizontal scaling.

```text id="evt45"
Topic

↓

Consumer Group

↓

Consumer A

Consumer B

Consumer C
```

Each partition is processed by one consumer within a group.

---

# 46. Rebalancing

Scaling consumers changes partition ownership.

```text id="evt46"
Consumer Added

↓

Partitions Reassigned

↓

Resume Processing
```

Applications should tolerate rebalancing events gracefully.

---

# 47. Consumer Offsets

Consumers control processing progress through offsets.

```text id="evt47"
Message

↓

Process

↓

Commit Offset
```

Offset commits should align with successful business processing.

---

# 48. Offset Management

Avoid committing offsets before processing completes.

Incorrect:

```text id="evt48"
Commit

↓

Process
```

Preferred:

```text id="evt48b"
Process

↓

Commit
```

---

# 49. Outbox Pattern

Avoid dual-write inconsistency.

```text id="evt49"
Database Transaction

↓

Business Update

+

Outbox Record

↓

Commit

↓

Publisher

↓

Broker
```

The Outbox Pattern ensures that state changes and event publication remain consistent.

---

# 50. Inbox Pattern

Consumers may maintain an Inbox table.

```text id="evt50"
Receive Event

↓

Inbox

↓

Already Seen?

↓

Process Once
```

This supports idempotent consumption.

---

# 51. Transactional Messaging

Distributed consistency should avoid two-phase commit where simpler patterns suffice.

Prefer:

```text id="evt51"
Local Transaction

+

Outbox

+

Reliable Publisher
```

---

# 52. Distributed Transactions

Distributed transactions increase complexity.

Where possible:

```text id="evt52"
Local Consistency

+

Events

+

Compensation
```

is preferred over global locking.

---

# 53. Saga Pattern

Long-running business workflows should use Sagas.

```text id="evt53"
Service A

↓

Event

↓

Service B

↓

Event

↓

Service C
```

Failures trigger compensating actions rather than global rollback.

---

# 54. Orchestration

An orchestrator explicitly coordinates workflow.

```text id="evt54"
Saga Orchestrator

↓

Service A

↓

Service B

↓

Service C
```

Suitable when workflow visibility is important.

---

# 55. Choreography

Services react independently to events.

```text id="evt55"
Event

↓

Service A

↓

Event

↓

Service B

↓

Event

↓

Service C
```

Choreography reduces central coordination but can become difficult to understand at scale.

---

# 56. Choosing Orchestration vs Choreography

| Requirement                  | Preferred     |
| ---------------------------- | ------------- |
| Simple independent reactions | Choreography  |
| Complex business workflow    | Orchestration |
| Auditability                 | Orchestration |
| Loose coupling               | Choreography  |

Neither approach is universally superior.

---

# 57. CQRS Integration

Command Query Responsibility Segregation separates writes from reads.

```text id="evt57"
Commands

↓

Write Model

↓

Events

↓

Read Model
```

CQRS should solve genuine complexity rather than become a default architecture.

---

# 58. Event Sourcing

Event sourcing stores business history as events.

```text id="evt58"
Event 1

↓

Event 2

↓

Event 3

↓

Current State
```

Event sourcing should be adopted only where its benefits justify its operational complexity.

---

# 59. Change Data Capture (CDC)

CDC converts database changes into events.

```text id="evt59"
Database

↓

CDC

↓

Kafka

↓

Consumers
```

CDC is valuable for integration but should not replace intentional domain events.

---

# 60. Stream Processing

Stream processors transform continuous event streams.

Examples:

```text id="evt60"
Analytics

AI Features

Recommendations

Real-Time Dashboards

Fraud Detection
```

Stream processing should preserve event ordering and correctness appropriate to the workload.

---

# ADR-083 — Enterprise Event-Driven Architecture, Messaging, Streaming & Distributed Workflow Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — Stream Processing**.

---

# 61. Event Replay

Durable event streams enable controlled replay.

```text id="evt61"
Stored Events
      │
      ▼
Replay
      │
      ▼
Consumer
      │
      ▼
Rebuild State
```

Replay should be intentional and governed.

---

# 62. Replay Safety

Before replaying events, verify:

```text id="evt62"
Idempotency

Target Environment

Business Impact

Ordering

Dependencies
```

Replaying production events without safeguards can duplicate business effects.

---

# 63. Event Retention

Every topic requires an explicit retention policy.

Examples:

```text id="evt63"
7 Days

30 Days

1 Year

Permanent
```

Retention should reflect business, operational and compliance requirements.

---

# 64. Log Compaction

Some streams represent current state rather than historical audit.

```text id="evt64"
Student

↓

Latest Record Retained
```

Use log compaction where consumers require the latest value instead of the full history.

---

# 65. Event Archival

Historical events may be archived.

```text id="evt65"
Broker

↓

Archive Storage

↓

Analytics

Audit

Recovery
```

Broker retention and archival are separate concerns.

---

# 66. Event Replay Governance

Replay requests should record:

```text id="evt66"
Who

Why

Scope

Time

Approval

Outcome
```

Replay is an operational event requiring auditability.

---

# 67. AsyncAPI Governance

All asynchronous APIs should publish AsyncAPI specifications.

Include:

```text id="evt67"
Topics

Schemas

Security

Examples

Versions

Owners
```

---

# 68. Schema Compatibility

Schema evolution requires automated compatibility verification.

```text id="evt68"
Previous Version

↓

Compatibility Check

↓

New Version
```

Breaking schemas should fail governance before deployment.

---

# 69. Schema Registry Governance

Schema Registry responsibilities include:

```text id="evt69"
Version Control

Compatibility Rules

Ownership

Audit

Lifecycle
```

The registry is a governance platform, not merely a storage system.

---

# 70. Event Validation

Consumers should validate incoming events.

Checks include:

```text id="evt70"
Schema

Required Fields

Version

Tenant

Integrity
```

Invalid events should not silently enter business workflows.

---

# 71. OpenTelemetry for Events

ADR-078 telemetry extends to messaging.

Each event should carry:

```text id="evt71"
Trace ID

Span ID

Correlation ID

Producer

Consumer
```

This enables distributed tracing across asynchronous boundaries.

---

# 72. Distributed Tracing

Tracing should connect:

```text id="evt72"
API

↓

Kafka

↓

Consumer

↓

Database

↓

External Service
```

Asynchronous messaging should not break observability.

---

# 73. Event Logging

Logs should include:

```text id="evt73"
Topic

Partition

Offset

Consumer Group

Trace ID

Event ID
```

Sensitive payloads should not be logged indiscriminately.

---

# 74. Event Metrics

Key operational metrics:

```text id="evt74"
Publish Rate

Consume Rate

Consumer Lag

Retry Count

DLQ Count

Processing Latency
```

---

# 75. Consumer Lag

Lag measures processing delay.

```text id="evt75"
Broker Offset

↓

Consumer Offset

↓

Lag
```

Growing lag may indicate scaling or processing problems.

---

# 76. Event SLIs

Representative indicators:

```text id="evt76"
Delivery Success

Processing Latency

Consumer Lag

Retry Rate

DLQ Rate
```

---

# 77. Event SLOs

Critical streams should define measurable objectives.

Example:

```text id="evt77"
99.9% Delivered

P95 Processing <5 sec

DLQ <0.01%
```

---

# 78. Event Error Budgets

Streaming platforms should consume defined error budgets.

Excessive failures require operational attention before additional change.

---

# 79. Event Security

ADR-081 identity extends to messaging.

Every producer and consumer authenticates using approved workload identity.

---

# 80. Authorization

Authorization should control:

```text id="evt80"
Publish

Consume

Create Topic

Delete Topic

Replay

Schema Changes
```

Messaging infrastructure should enforce least privilege.

---

# 81. Event Encryption

Protect:

```text id="evt81"
In Transit

At Rest
```

Encryption requirements depend on data classification defined in ADR-076.

---

# 82. Event Signing

Where integrity verification is required, events may include cryptographic signatures.

Consumers verify authenticity before processing.

---

# 83. Sensitive Data

Avoid publishing:

```text id="evt83"
Passwords

Secrets

Private Keys

Sensitive Personal Data
```

unless explicitly required and appropriately protected.

---

# 84. Multi-Tenant Messaging

Tenant isolation applies to events.

```text id="evt84"
Tenant A

×

Tenant B
```

Consumers should never accidentally process another tenant's events.

---

# 85. Event Authorization Context

Events should propagate sufficient context.

Example:

```text id="evt85"
Tenant

Subject

Correlation

Authorization Context
```

Avoid embedding unnecessary identity information.

---

# 86. Event Testing

ADR-079 requires verification of:

```text id="evt86"
Producer

Schema

Consumer

Compatibility

Retries

DLQ
```

---

# 87. Contract Testing

Event contracts require automated compatibility checks before deployment.

Documentation alone is insufficient.

---

# 88. Runtime Controls

ADR-080 runtime configuration should support:

```text id="evt88"
Pause Consumer

Adjust Concurrency

Modify Retry

Disable Pipeline

Replay Controls
```

Runtime changes require auditability.

---

# 89. Platform Integration

ADR-078 should automatically provision:

```text id="evt89"
Topic

Schema

ACL

Monitoring

Dashboards
```

Messaging becomes part of the platform golden path.

---

# 90. AI Event Pipelines

ADR-077 AI architecture integrates through events.

Examples:

```text id="evt90"
Document Indexed

Embedding Generated

Evaluation Completed

Agent Finished
```

AI processing should remain observable and replayable where appropriate.

---

# 91. Event Catalog

The developer platform should publish:

```text id="evt91"
Topic

Owner

Schema

Consumers

Version

Lifecycle
```

Developers should discover events without tribal knowledge.

---

# 92. Dependency Graph

Understand event relationships.

```text id="evt92"
Producer

↓

Topic

↓

Consumer

↓

Database

↓

API
```

Dependency graphs support change impact analysis.

---

# 93. Event Inventory

Maintain inventory of:

```text id="evt93"
Topics

Schemas

Consumers

Owners

Criticality

Retention
```

Unknown topics create unmanaged operational risk.

---

# 94. Event Documentation

Each event should document:

```text id="evt94"
Business Meaning

Trigger

Producer

Consumers

Schema

Examples
```

The event name alone is rarely sufficient.

---

# 95. Event Analytics

Platform analytics should measure:

```text id="evt95"
Volume

Growth

Consumer Count

Replay Frequency

DLQ Trends
```

These metrics guide capacity planning.

---

# 96. Event Scorecard

| Capability       | Status |
| ---------------- | ------ |
| AsyncAPI         | ✓      |
| Schema Registry  | ✓      |
| Contract Tests   | ✓      |
| Replay           | ✓      |
| DLQ              | ✓      |
| Observability    | ✓      |
| Security         | ✓      |
| Retention Policy | ✓      |

Scorecards expose maturity and improvement opportunities.

---

# 97. Event Maturity Model

```text id="evt97"
LEVEL 1

Ad Hoc Messaging

LEVEL 2

Managed Topics

LEVEL 3

Governed Event Contracts

LEVEL 4

Observable Event Platform

LEVEL 5

Adaptive Event Ecosystem
```

Mediverse targets **Level 4**.

---

# 98. Event Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text id="evt98"
❌ Commands disguised as events
❌ Multiple producers for the same business event
❌ Shared event ownership
❌ Events without schemas
❌ Breaking schema changes
❌ Global ordering assumptions
❌ Consumers depending on producer internals
❌ Infinite retries
❌ Ignored DLQs
❌ Replays without governance
❌ Sensitive data in events
❌ Anonymous producers
❌ Static credentials
❌ Topic names exposing implementation details
❌ Event sourcing used by default
❌ CDC replacing business events
❌ Missing correlation IDs
❌ Missing observability
❌ Event-driven architecture without documentation
```

---

# 99. Enterprise Event-Driven Reference Architecture

```text id="evt99"
                 BUSINESS EVENT
                       │
                       ▼
                EVENT CONTRACT
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
        ▼              ▼              ▼
     PRODUCER      SCHEMA REGISTRY   SECURITY
        │              │              │
        └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                       ▼
                MESSAGE BROKER
                       │
      ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
      ▼                ▼                ▼
  CONSUMER A      CONSUMER B      STREAM PROCESSOR
      │                │                │
      ├── Inbox         ├── Retry        ├── Analytics
      ├── Idempotency   ├── DLQ          ├── AI
      └── Business      └── State        └── Dashboards
                       │
                       ▼
        Observability + Security + Governance
```

---

| Domain Events          | Mandatory                                          |
| Integration Events     | Mandatory                                          |
| Kafka                  | Preferred streaming platform                       |

| AsyncAPI               | Mandatory                                          |
| Schema Registry        | Mandatory                                          |
| CloudEvents            | Preferred metadata standard                        |
| At-least-once Delivery | Default                                            |
| Idempotent Consumers   | Mandatory                                          |
| Outbox Pattern         | Preferred                                          |
| Inbox Pattern          | Supported                                          |

| Event Sourcing         | Exceptional, not default                           |

| OpenTelemetry          | Mandatory                                          |
| Event Catalog          | Mandatory                                          |
| Event Security         | Mandatory                                          |
| Status                 | **Accepted**                                       |

---

# 101. Governing Invariant

> **Every event in Mediverse is an immutable business fact with a single authoritative producer, a governed schema, observable lifecycle, secure transport, explicit ownership, and compatibility guarantees. Messaging exists to reduce coupling while preserving correctness, traceability and business autonomy.**

# ADR-084 — Enterprise Data Storage, Database Architecture, Persistence & State Management Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-084
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-083 established enterprise event-driven architecture.

ADR-084 establishes how Mediverse stores, owns, manages, secures, scales and governs persistent state across transactional systems, caches, search platforms, object stores, analytical systems and AI knowledge stores.

The governing principle is:

> **Data is a strategic enterprise asset. Every piece of data must have a single authoritative owner, an explicitly chosen persistence technology, a governed lifecycle, and well-defined consistency guarantees. Storage technologies exist to serve business requirements—not the other way around.**

```text id="db01"
                     BUSINESS DATA
                          │
                          ▼
                   DATA OWNERSHIP
                          │
      ┌───────────────────┼────────────────────┐
      ▼                   ▼                    ▼
 Transactional       Analytical         AI Knowledge
      │                   │                    │
      ▼                   ▼                    ▼
 PostgreSQL         Data Lake         Vector Database
      │                   │                    │
      └───────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                          ▼
                    GOVERNANCE
                          │
                          ▼
                BACKUP • SECURITY
                OBSERVABILITY
                LIFECYCLE
```

---

# 1. Data Philosophy

Data is not merely an implementation detail.

It represents:

```text id="db02"
Business Facts

Business State

Business History

Business Decisions
```

Architecture should preserve data integrity above implementation convenience.

---

# 2. Data Ownership

Every business dataset has exactly one authoritative owner.

```text id="db03"
Student Service

↓

Owns Student Data
```

Other services consume data through APIs or events rather than direct ownership.

---

# 3. Single Source of Truth

Only one service may own mutable business state.

```text id="db04"
Student Service

↓

Students Table

✓
```

Avoid:

```text id="db05"
Student Service

AND

Course Service

Both Update Students
```

Shared ownership creates inconsistency.

---

# 4. Database per Service

Mediverse adopts the **Database-per-Service** principle.

```text id="db06"
Course Service

↓

Course DB


Student Service

↓

Student DB
```

Service autonomy depends on storage autonomy.

---

# 5. Shared Database Anti-Pattern

Avoid:

```text id="db07"
Service A

↓

Shared Database

↑

Service B
```

Shared schemas tightly couple deployment, evolution and ownership.

---

# 6. Polyglot Persistence

Different workloads justify different storage engines.

```text id="db08"
Relational

Cache

Search

Object

Vector

Graph
```

One database should not solve every problem.

---

# 7. Storage Selection Principle

Choose storage according to access patterns.

```text id="db09"
Business Need

↓

Access Pattern

↓

Consistency

↓

Latency

↓

Scale

↓

Technology
```

Technology selection follows business requirements.

---

# 8. Relational Databases

PostgreSQL is the enterprise default for transactional business systems.

Suitable for:

```text id="db10"
Transactions

Relationships

Integrity

Consistency

Reporting
```

---

# 9. PostgreSQL Standard

The Spring Boot golden path standardizes PostgreSQL as the primary operational database unless documented architectural requirements justify an alternative.

---

# 10. NoSQL

NoSQL technologies should solve clearly identified problems.

Examples:

```text id="db11"
Large Documents

Flexible Schema

Massive Scale

Specialized Access Patterns
```

Not merely "modern architecture."

---

# 11. MongoDB Decision

MongoDB is appropriate when document-oriented modeling materially improves the domain.

Avoid using MongoDB solely to avoid relational design.

---

# 12. Redis

Redis is an in-memory data platform.

Primary uses include:

```text id="db12"
Caching

Sessions

Rate Limits

Distributed Locks

Queues

Temporary State
```

Redis should not become the primary system of record.

---

# 13. Elasticsearch/OpenSearch

Search platforms serve search workloads.

Suitable for:

```text id="db13"
Full-text Search

Autocomplete

Ranking

Aggregations

Analytics
```

Search indexes are derived data.

---

# 14. Object Storage

Binary content belongs in object storage.

Examples:

```text id="db14"
Videos

Images

PDFs

Assignments

Medical Images
```

Avoid storing large binaries directly inside transactional databases.

---

# 15. Vector Databases

ADR-077 introduces vector stores.

Suitable for:

```text id="db15"
Embeddings

Semantic Search

RAG

Similarity Search
```

Vector stores complement—not replace—transactional databases.

---

# 16. Data Classification

ADR-076 data classification governs storage decisions.

Classification influences:

```text id="db16"
Encryption

Retention

Access

Replication

Backup
```

---

# 17. Database Selection Matrix

| Requirement   | Preferred Storage        |
| ------------- | ------------------------ |
| Transactions  | PostgreSQL               |
| Cache         | Redis                    |
| Search        | Elasticsearch/OpenSearch |
| Binary Files  | Object Storage           |
| AI Embeddings | Vector Database          |
| Documents     | MongoDB (when justified) |

---

# 18. Persistence Models

Business state may exist as:

```text id="db17"
Current State

Historical Events

Materialized Views

Search Indexes

Caches
```

Each serves a distinct architectural purpose.

---

# 19. Transaction Boundaries

Transactions should remain local whenever possible.

```text id="db18"
Application

↓

Database Transaction

↓

Commit
```

Cross-service transactions should use ADR-083 patterns instead.

---

# 20. ACID

Transactional systems prioritize:

```text id="db19"
Atomicity

Consistency

Isolation

Durability
```

Critical business workflows generally require ACID guarantees.

---

# 21. BASE

Highly distributed systems may adopt:

```text id="db20"
Basically Available

Soft State

Eventual Consistency
```

BASE should be a deliberate tradeoff rather than an accidental consequence.

---

# 22. Consistency Models

Choose consistency intentionally.

```text id="db21"
Strong

Eventual

Session

Read-Your-Writes
```

Business correctness determines acceptable consistency.

---

# 23. Eventual Consistency

Eventual consistency is acceptable only where temporary divergence does not violate business requirements.

Not every domain tolerates stale information equally.

---

# 24. Data Normalization

Transactional schemas should generally favor normalization.

Normalization reduces duplication and update anomalies.

---

# 25. Controlled Denormalization

Denormalization is acceptable when justified by measurable performance or query requirements.

It requires governance because duplicated data must remain consistent.

---

# 26. Primary Keys

Every persistent entity requires stable identifiers.

Prefer immutable identifiers over mutable business attributes.

---

# 27. Foreign Keys

Relational integrity should be enforced where ownership exists within the same bounded context.

Cross-service foreign keys are prohibited.

---

# 28. Constraints

Use database constraints to protect integrity.

Examples:

```text id="db22"
Unique

Check

Foreign Key

Not Null
```

Application validation complements rather than replaces database integrity.

---

# 29. Database Schema

Schemas are enterprise assets.

Schema evolution requires version control and review.

---

# 30. Migration Standard

All schema changes must be versioned through approved migration tooling.

Manual production schema modifications are prohibited.

---

**Sections 1–30 completed.**

This establishes the foundational enterprise data architecture:

* Data ownership
* Database-per-service
* Polyglot persistence
* PostgreSQL as transactional standard
* Redis, Elasticsearch, MongoDB, object storage and vector database decision framework
* Single source of truth
* ACID vs BASE
* Consistency models
* Normalization
* Constraints
* Schema governance
* Migration standards

**Part 2 (Sections 31–60)** will continue with:

* Indexing strategies
* Query optimization

* Partitioning and sharding
* Connection pooling
* Database transactions
* Isolation levels
* Optimistic vs pessimistic locking
* Soft deletes
* Audit tables
* Temporal data
* Time-series storage
* Database versioning
* Backup and PITR
* High availability
* Replication
* Disaster recovery
* Database observability
* Performance tuning

# ADR-084 — Enterprise Data Storage, Database Architecture, Persistence & State Management Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Migration Standard**.

---

# 31. Indexing Philosophy

Indexes accelerate reads at the cost of storage and write performance.

```text id="db31"
Table

↓

Index

↓

Fast Lookup
```

Indexes should be created based on measured query patterns rather than speculation.

---

# 32. Primary Indexes

Every table should define a stable primary key index.

Prefer immutable identifiers to avoid unnecessary index maintenance.

---

# 33. Secondary Indexes

Secondary indexes support common access paths.

Examples:

```text id="db32"
Student ID

Course ID

Status

Created Date
```

Unused indexes should be removed.

---

# 34. Composite Indexes

Multiple columns may form a composite index.

Example:

```text id="db33"
Tenant ID

+

Student ID

+

Status
```

Column order should reflect actual query patterns.

---

# 35. Query Optimization

Optimize queries before adding infrastructure.

Process:

```text id="db34"
Slow Query

↓

Execution Plan

↓

Index

↓

Rewrite

↓

Verify
```

Never optimize blindly.

---

# 36. Explain Plans

Every critical SQL query should be validated using execution plans.

```text id="db35"
SQL

↓

EXPLAIN

↓

Execution Plan

↓

Optimization
```

---

# 37. N+1 Queries

Applications should avoid repeated database lookups inside loops.

Poor:

```text id="db36"
100 Students

↓

100 Queries
```

Preferred:

```text id="db37"
100 Students

↓

Single Optimized Query
```

---

# 38. Read Replicas

Separate read traffic when justified.

```text id="db38"
Primary

↓

Replication

↓

Read Replica
```

Read replicas improve scalability but introduce replication lag.

---

# 39. Replica Consistency

Applications should understand replication delays.

Critical read-after-write scenarios may require primary database reads.

---

# 40. Partitioning

Large datasets may be partitioned.

Common strategies:

```text id="db39"
Time

Tenant

Region

Identifier Range
```

Partitioning should align with access patterns.

---

# 41. Sharding

Sharding distributes data across multiple databases.

```text id="db40"
Shard 1

Shard 2

Shard 3
```

Sharding significantly increases operational complexity and should be adopted only when scaling demands it.

---

# 42. Connection Pooling

Applications should use managed connection pools.

```text id="db41"
Application

↓

Connection Pool

↓

Database
```

Opening a new database connection for every request is inefficient.

---

# 43. Transaction Scope

Transactions should remain as short as practical.

Avoid:

```text id="db42"
Transaction

↓

External API Call

↓

Commit
```

External network calls should not occur within database transactions.

---

# 44. Isolation Levels

Choose isolation levels intentionally.

Examples:

```text id="db43"
Read Committed

Repeatable Read

Serializable
```

Higher isolation generally reduces concurrency.

---

# 45. Optimistic Locking

Preferred for most business workloads.

```text id="db44"
Version

↓

Update

↓

Version Check
```

Conflicts are detected rather than prevented.

---

# 46. Pessimistic Locking

Use only where concurrent modification risks outweigh reduced concurrency.

```text id="db45"
Lock

↓

Modify

↓

Unlock
```

Long-held locks reduce throughput.

---

# 47. Deadlock Handling

Applications should expect occasional deadlocks.

Recommended approach:

```text id="db46"
Detect

↓

Rollback

↓

Retry
```

Deadlocks are operational realities, not exceptional failures.

---

# 48. Soft Deletes

Some domains require logical deletion.

```text id="db47"
Record

↓

Deleted Flag

↓

Hidden
```

Soft deletes support recovery and auditing.

---

# 49. Hard Deletes

Permanent deletion should follow governance.

Examples:

```text id="db48"
Retention Expired

Privacy Request

Business Approval
```

---

# 50. Audit Tables

Critical business changes should be auditable.

```text id="db49"
Insert

Update

Delete

↓

Audit Record
```

Audit history should remain tamper-resistant.

---

# 51. Temporal Data

Historical state may require valid-time tracking.

```text id="db50"
Valid From

↓

Valid To
```

Temporal models support regulatory and business history requirements.

---

# 52. Time-Series Data

Operational metrics differ from transactional data.

Suitable storage:

```text id="db51"
Monitoring

Telemetry

Sensor Data

Usage Metrics
```

Time-series workloads should use technologies optimized for sequential writes and time-based queries where appropriate.

---

# 53. Schema Versioning

Schemas evolve continuously.

```text id="db52"
Version 1

↓

Migration

↓

Version 2
```

Schema history should remain traceable.

---

# 54. Database Migration Strategy

Migration execution should be:

```text id="db53"
Versioned

Repeatable

Automated

Auditable
```

Manual production changes bypass governance.

---

# 55. Backup Strategy

Every persistent datastore requires backup.

Backup plans should define:

```text id="db54"
Frequency

Retention

Encryption

Verification

Recovery Owner
```

Backups are valuable only if restoration succeeds.

---

# 56. Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)

Transactional databases should support recovery to a specific point in time where business requirements justify it.

```text id="db55"
Backup

+

Transaction Logs

↓

Restore to Timestamp
```

---

# 57. High Availability

Critical databases should tolerate infrastructure failures.

```text id="db56"
Primary

↓

Automatic Failover

↓

Standby
```

Availability requirements should match business criticality.

---

# 58. Replication

Replication provides redundancy and scalability.

```text id="db57"
Primary

↓

Replica A

↓

Replica B
```

Replication is not a substitute for backups.

---

# 59. Disaster Recovery

ADR-075 disaster recovery extends to databases.

Recovery planning should define:

```text id="db58"
RPO

RTO

Recovery Steps

Validation

Ownership
```

Recovery procedures should be rehearsed.

---

# 60. Database Observability

ADR-078 observability applies to persistence.

Core telemetry includes:

```text id="db59"
Query Latency

Connection Usage

Slow Queries

Replication Lag

Cache Hit Rate

Storage Growth

Lock Waits
```

Database behavior should be observable before users experience failures.

---
