# ADR-084 — Enterprise Data Storage, Database Architecture, Persistence & State Management Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — Database Observability**.

---

# 61. Database Security

ADR-081 governs identity.

Every database access requires:

```text id="db60"
Authenticated Identity

↓

Authorized Role

↓

Audited Access
```

Anonymous database access is prohibited.

---

# 62. Encryption at Rest

Persistent storage should encrypt data at rest.

```text id="db61"
Disk

↓

Encryption

↓

Database Files
```

Encryption keys should be managed independently of the database.

---

# 63. Encryption in Transit

All database communication should use encrypted transport.

```text id="db62"
Application

↓

TLS

↓

Database
```

Plain-text database connections are prohibited in production.

---

# 64. Row-Level Security (RLS)

Where supported, Row-Level Security may enforce tenant or ownership isolation.

```text id="db63"
Student A

↓

Own Records

Student B

↓

Own Records
```

RLS complements application authorization rather than replacing it.

---

# 65. Column-Level Protection

Sensitive attributes may require additional protection.

Examples:

```text id="db64"
National ID

Medical Data

Financial Data

Personal Contact Information
```

Not every column requires identical security controls.

---

# 66. Multi-Tenant Storage Models

Supported approaches include:

```text id="db65"
Shared Database
Shared Schema

Shared Database
Separate Schema

Separate Database
```

Selection depends on isolation, scale, compliance and operational requirements.

---

# 67. Tenant Isolation

Tenant boundaries are security boundaries.

```text id="db66"
Tenant A

×

Tenant B
```

Cross-tenant data exposure is considered a critical architectural failure.

---

# 68. Redis Governance

Redis should contain:

```text id="db67"
Cache

Sessions

Temporary Data

Distributed Locks
```

Redis should not become the enterprise system of record.

---

# 69. Cache Strategy

Caching should be intentional.

```text id="db68"
Application

↓

Cache

↓

Database
```

Caches improve latency but increase consistency complexity.

---

# 70. Cache Invalidation

Cache invalidation follows state changes.

```text id="db69"
Update Database

↓

Invalidate Cache

↓

Next Read Refreshes Cache
```

Stale caches should have bounded lifetimes.

---

# 71. Cache TTL

Every cache entry should define an expiration policy.

```text id="db70"
Write

↓

TTL

↓

Automatic Expiration
```

Infinite cache lifetimes are discouraged.

---

# 72. Cache Stampede Protection

Prevent many requests rebuilding the same cache simultaneously.

Strategies include:

```text id="db71"
Locking

Refresh Ahead

Request Coalescing
```

---

# 73. Search Index Governance

Search indexes are derived data.

```text id="db72"
Database

↓

Indexer

↓

Search Platform
```

The database remains the authoritative source.

---

# 74. Index Synchronization

Search indexes should remain synchronized through governed mechanisms.

Preferred:

```text id="db73"
Domain Event

↓

Indexer

↓

Search Update
```

Avoid manual synchronization.

---

# 75. Object Storage Governance

Object storage should manage:

```text id="db74"
Documents

Images

Videos

Assignments

Medical Media
```

Metadata belongs in transactional databases.

Binary objects belong in object storage.

---

# 76. Object Versioning

Where business requirements justify it:

```text id="db75"
Document

↓

Version 1

↓

Version 2

↓

Version 3
```

Version history supports audit and recovery.

---

# 77. Object Lifecycle

Objects require lifecycle policies.

```text id="db76"
Upload

↓

Active

↓

Archive

↓

Delete
```

Lifecycle policies should align with ADR-076 data governance.

---

# 78. Vector Database Governance

ADR-077 establishes vector databases for semantic retrieval.

They store:

```text id="db77"
Embeddings

Metadata

Similarity Indexes
```

They do not replace business databases.

---

# 79. Embedding Lifecycle

Embedding lifecycle:

```text id="db78"
Document

↓

Embedding

↓

Vector Store

↓

Re-index

↓

Delete
```

Embedding freshness should follow source document updates.

---

# 80. AI Knowledge Synchronization

RAG systems require synchronization.

```text id="db79"
Business Content

↓

Embedding Pipeline

↓

Vector Database

↓

Retriever
```

Outdated embeddings reduce AI response quality.

---

# 81. Data Lifecycle

Every dataset follows:

```text id="db80"
Create

↓

Use

↓

Archive

↓

Delete
```

Lifecycle ownership must be explicit.

---

# 82. Retention Policies

Retention should define:

```text id="db81"
Minimum Duration

Maximum Duration

Archive Rules

Deletion Rules
```

Retention differs across data classifications.

---

# 83. Archival Strategy

Historical information may move to lower-cost storage.

```text id="db82"
Operational Database

↓

Archive Storage
```

Archived data should remain discoverable where required.

---

# 84. Data Purging

Deletion should follow governed processes.

```text id="db83"
Retention Expired

↓

Approval

↓

Delete

↓

Audit
```

---

# 85. Data Quality

Data quality dimensions include:

```text id="db84"
Accuracy

Completeness

Consistency

Validity

Timeliness

Uniqueness
```

Quality should be continuously measured.

---

# 86. Referential Integrity

Integrity exists at multiple levels.

```text id="db85"
Database Constraints

+

Application Validation

+

Business Rules
```

No single layer is sufficient alone.

---

# 87. Database Testing

ADR-079 extends to persistence.

Required verification includes:

```text id="db86"
Migrations

Indexes

Constraints

Queries

Recovery

Performance
```

---

# 88. Runtime Controls

ADR-080 runtime configuration may control:

```text id="db87"
Connection Pool Size

Cache TTL

Query Timeout

Replica Routing

Feature Flags
```

Runtime controls should never compromise data integrity.

---

# 89. Platform Integration

ADR-078 should automatically provision:

```text id="db88"
Database

↓

Secrets

↓

Monitoring

↓

Backups

↓

Dashboards
```

Provisioning becomes part of the platform golden path.

---

# 90. AI Data Integration

ADR-077 integrates:

```text id="db89"
Transactional Data

↓

Events

↓

Embedding Pipeline

↓

Vector Store

↓

RAG
```

Business databases remain the source of truth.

---

# 91. Database Inventory

Maintain an enterprise inventory.

```text id="db90"
Owner

Technology

Criticality

Backup

Retention

Classification
```

Unknown databases represent unmanaged risk.

---

# 92. Storage Scorecard

Each datastore may expose:

| Capability          | Status |
| ------------------- | ------ |
| Encryption          | ✓      |
| Backup              | ✓      |
| PITR                | ✓      |
| Observability       | ✓      |
| Automated Migration | ✓      |
| Monitoring          | ✓      |
| Replication         | ✓      |
| Disaster Recovery   | ✓      |

---

# 93. Performance Baselines

Track:

```text id="db91"
P50 Query

P95 Query

P99 Query

TPS

IOPS

Storage Growth
```

Performance regressions require investigation.

---

# 94. Capacity Planning

Capacity planning should monitor:

```text id="db92"
Disk

Memory

Connections

CPU

Growth Rate
```

Planning should anticipate future demand rather than react to outages.

---

# 95. Database Automation

Platform automation should manage:

```text id="db93"
Provisioning

Backup

Scaling

Monitoring

Rotation

Recovery Validation
```

Manual operational work should be minimized.

---

# 96. Data Maturity Model

```text id="db94"
LEVEL 1

Ad Hoc Storage

LEVEL 2

Managed Databases

LEVEL 3

Governed Data Platform

LEVEL 4

Observable Enterprise Data Platform

LEVEL 5

Adaptive Intelligent Data Platform
```

Mediverse targets **Level 4**.

---

# 97. Data Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text id="db95"
❌ Shared databases between services
❌ Shared ownership
❌ Missing backups
❌ Manual production schema changes
❌ No migrations
❌ Missing indexes
❌ Index everything
❌ Redis as system of record
❌ Search index as source of truth
❌ Storing binaries in relational tables
❌ Cross-service foreign keys
❌ Infinite cache lifetime
❌ Unencrypted storage
❌ Anonymous database users
❌ Missing observability
❌ Event sourcing by default
❌ Vector database replacing transactional storage
❌ No retention policy
❌ No disaster recovery validation
```

---

# 98. Enterprise Data Reference Architecture

```text id="db96"
                  BUSINESS DATA
                       │
                       ▼
                BOUNDED CONTEXT
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼───────────────┐
        ▼              ▼               ▼
 PostgreSQL         Redis Cache   Object Store
        │              │               │
        ▼              ▼               ▼
 Search Index    Vector Store    Analytics
        │              │               │
        └──────────────┼───────────────┘
                       ▼
          Backup • Security • Governance
             Observability • Lifecycle
```

---

# 99. ADR-084 Decision Outcome

| Area                     | Decision                       |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| Database-per-Service     | Mandatory                      |
| PostgreSQL               | Default transactional database |
| Redis                    | Cache/session platform         |
| Elasticsearch/OpenSearch | Search platform                |
| Object Storage           | Binary content                 |
| Vector Database          | AI retrieval                   |
| Automated Migrations     | Mandatory                      |
| Encryption               | Mandatory                      |
| Backup                   | Mandatory                      |
| PITR                     | Preferred for critical systems |
| Read Replicas            | Supported                      |
| Sharding                 | Selective                      |
| Observability            | Mandatory                      |
| Lifecycle Governance     | Mandatory                      |
| Status                   | **Accepted**                   |

---

# 100. Governing Invariant

> **Every dataset in Mediverse has one authoritative owner, one governed lifecycle, explicitly chosen persistence technology, measurable reliability objectives, automated recovery, comprehensive observability and security controls aligned with enterprise identity and data governance. Data architecture is driven by business semantics rather than storage technology.**

# ADR-085 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, Web Platform, Mobile Architecture & User Experience Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-085
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-084 established enterprise data architecture.

ADR-085 defines how Mediverse builds web, mobile and desktop user interfaces that are scalable, accessible, secure, observable and maintainable while providing a consistent user experience across all digital products.

The governing principle is:

> **The frontend is not a collection of pages. It is a governed application platform that translates business capabilities into intuitive, secure and accessible user experiences while remaining independent of backend implementation details.**

```text
                     USER
                      │
                      ▼
                USER EXPERIENCE
                      │
      ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
      ▼               ▼                ▼
  Design System   Business Logic   Accessibility
      │               │                │
      └───────────────┼────────────────┘
                      ▼
              Frontend Platform
                      │
      ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
      ▼               ▼                ▼
     React        API Layer       State Layer
                      │
                      ▼
              Backend Services
                      │
                      ▼
         Observability + Security
```

---

# 1. Frontend Philosophy

The frontend is an enterprise application.

It should provide:

```text
Consistency

Accessibility

Responsiveness

Performance

Security

Maintainability
```

---

# 2. Frontend Responsibilities

The frontend is responsible for:

```text
Presentation

Interaction

Navigation

Validation

State Management

Accessibility
```

It is **not** responsible for business authority or persistence.

---

# 3. Thin UI Principle

Business rules belong in backend services.

Frontend responsibilities include:

```text
Display

Interaction

Client Validation

UX
```

Avoid duplicating complex backend business logic.

---

# 4. Separation of Concerns

Separate:

```text
Presentation

Business State

API Communication

Design System

Infrastructure
```

Independent evolution reduces coupling.

---

# 5. React Standard

React is the enterprise web framework.

Reasons include:

```text
Large Ecosystem

Component Model

Strong Tooling

Community

Platform Support
```

---

# 6. TypeScript Standard

TypeScript is mandatory.

Benefits:

```text
Static Types

Refactoring

Safer APIs

Documentation

Developer Productivity
```

---

# 7. Vite Standard

Vite is the preferred build platform.

Advantages:

```text
Fast Startup

Fast HMR

Modern Tooling

Simple Configuration
```

---

# 8. Component-Driven Architecture

Applications should be built from reusable components.

```text
Application

↓

Pages

↓

Features

↓

Components

↓

Primitive UI
```

---

# 9. Component Categories

Components belong to layers.

```text
Primitive

Composite

Feature

Page
```

Responsibilities should remain clear.

---

# 10. Design System

A shared design system ensures consistency.

It includes:

```text
Typography

Spacing

Colors

Buttons

Inputs

Cards

Dialogs

Tables
```

---

# 11. Design Tokens

Visual properties should be tokenized.

Example:

```text
Primary Color

Spacing Scale

Font Size

Border Radius
```

Avoid hardcoded visual values throughout the application.

---

# 12. UI Library

Material UI (MUI) is the default enterprise component library unless project-specific requirements justify an alternative.

---

# 13. Styling Standard

Preferred hierarchy:

```text
Design Tokens

↓

Theme

↓

Component Styles
```

Avoid ad hoc styling patterns.

---

# 14. Responsive Design

Applications should support:

```text
Mobile

Tablet

Desktop

Large Displays
```

Responsive behavior should be designed rather than retrofitted.

---

# 15. Mobile-First

Layouts should prioritize smaller screens first.

Enhancements scale upward for larger displays.

---

# 16. Accessibility

Accessibility is a functional requirement.

Support includes:

```text
Keyboard Navigation

Screen Readers

Focus Management

Semantic HTML

Color Contrast
```

---

# 17. WCAG

Target WCAG 2.2 AA compliance unless regulatory requirements specify a higher level.

---

# 18. Semantic HTML

Prefer semantic elements.

Good:

```text
<header>

<nav>

<main>

<section>

<footer>
```

Avoid replacing semantics with generic containers unnecessarily.

---

# 19. Forms

Forms should provide:

```text
Validation

Error Messages

Accessibility

Progress Indicators
```

---

# 20. Validation

Client validation improves user experience.

Server validation remains authoritative.

---

# 21. Form Libraries

Enterprise forms should use standardized libraries rather than custom validation frameworks.

---

# 22. Routing

Routing represents application navigation.

Routes should align with business capabilities rather than implementation structure.

---

# 23. Protected Routes

Authentication and authorization should integrate with ADR-081.

Protected resources must not rely solely on client-side routing.

---

# 24. State Categories

Frontend state includes:

```text
UI State

Server State

Form State

Session State
```

Different state requires different management strategies.

---

# 25. Local State

Component-local state should remain inside components whenever practical.

Avoid unnecessary global state.

---

# 26. Global State

Global state should contain only information genuinely shared across the application.

Examples:

```text
Authenticated User

Theme

Notifications
```

---

# 27. Server State

Server state differs from application state.

Preferred solution:

```text
Backend

↓

Query Layer

↓

Cache

↓

UI
```

---

# 28. State Management

Enterprise standard:

```text
Redux Toolkit

or

Zustand

for Global State

+

TanStack Query

for Server State
```

Each tool addresses different responsibilities.

---

# 29. API Layer

All backend communication should pass through a centralized API abstraction.

Avoid scattered HTTP calls throughout components.

---

# 30. Error Handling

UI should distinguish:

```text
Validation Error

Network Error

Authorization Error

Server Error
```

Each requires different user experience.

---

## ADR-085 — Part 1 Complete

**Sections 1–30 completed.**

This establishes the foundational enterprise frontend architecture:

* Frontend philosophy
* React + TypeScript + Vite standards
* Component-driven architecture
* Design systems and design tokens
* Responsive and mobile-first design
* Accessibility and WCAG
* Forms and validation
* Routing
* Protected routes
* State management (Redux/Zustand/TanStack Query)
* Centralized API layer
* Error handling

**Part 2 (Sections 31–60)** will continue with:

* Micro-frontends
* Module Federation
* Lazy loading and code splitting
* Performance optimization
* SSR vs CSR vs SSG vs ISR
* Progressive Web Apps (PWA)
* Offline-first architecture
* Internationalization (i18n)
* Localization (l10n)
* Frontend security (CSP, XSS, CSRF)
* Authentication integration (ADR-081)
* Frontend observability (ADR-078)
* Frontend testing (ADR-079)
* Runtime configuration (ADR-080)
* AI-assisted UI (ADR-077)
* Platform integration
* CI/CD
* UX governance
* Performance budgets
* Frontend architecture integration.


# ADR-085 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, Web Platform, Mobile Architecture & User Experience Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Error Handling**.

---

# 31. Micro-Frontend Decision

Micro-frontends should solve organizational scaling problems—not merely technical curiosity.

Suitable when:

```text id="fe31"
Independent Teams

Independent Releases

Large Platform

Multiple Domains
```

Avoid adopting micro-frontends for small applications.

---

# 32. Module Federation

Where micro-frontends are adopted, Module Federation is the preferred mechanism for runtime composition.

```text id="fe32"
Host

↓

Remote A

Remote B

Remote C
```

Shared dependencies should be governed to avoid version conflicts.

---

# 33. Independent Deployment

Micro-frontends should support independent deployment while maintaining compatibility with shared platform contracts.

---

# 34. Shared Design System

Every frontend—whether monolith or micro-frontend—must consume the same enterprise design system.

Visual consistency should not depend on deployment topology.

---

# 35. Code Splitting

Applications should load only the code required for the current user journey.

```text id="fe35"
Application

↓

Route

↓

Lazy Bundle
```

---

# 36. Lazy Loading

Lazy loading reduces initial bundle size.

Suitable for:

```text id="fe36"
Admin Panels

Reports

Large Editors

Settings
```

Core application functionality should remain responsive.

---

# 37. Asset Optimization

Optimize:

```text id="fe37"
Images

Fonts

JavaScript

CSS

Icons
```

Delivery performance is part of user experience.

---

# 38. Performance Budgets

Define measurable frontend limits.

Example:

```text id="fe38"
JS Bundle

<250 KB

LCP

<2.5 s

CLS

<0.1
```

Budgets create objective engineering targets.

---

# 39. Web Vitals

Track Core Web Vitals:

```text id="fe39"
LCP

INP

CLS
```

Performance should be continuously monitored rather than measured only before release.

---

# 40. Rendering Strategy

Choose rendering based on business requirements.

```text id="fe40"
CSR

SSR

SSG

ISR
```

No rendering strategy is universally optimal.

---

# 41. Client-Side Rendering (CSR)

CSR is appropriate for:

```text id="fe41"
Internal Applications

Dashboards

Authenticated Portals
```

---

# 42. Server-Side Rendering (SSR)

SSR benefits:

```text id="fe42"
SEO

Faster Initial Render

Social Sharing
```

SSR introduces operational complexity and should be justified.

---

# 43. Static Site Generation (SSG)

Suitable for mostly static content.

Examples:

```text id="fe43"
Documentation

Marketing Pages

Learning Resources
```

---

# 44. Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)

ISR combines static delivery with controlled freshness.

Useful for content that changes periodically without requiring full rebuilds.

---

# 45. Progressive Web Apps (PWA)

PWAs may provide:

```text id="fe45"
Offline Support

Installability

Push Notifications

Background Sync
```

PWAs should be adopted where they improve user experience.

---

# 46. Offline-First

Offline capability should focus on meaningful user workflows.

Example:

```text id="fe46"
View Cached Course

Read Notes

Continue Draft

Sync Later
```

Not every feature requires offline support.

---

# 47. Synchronization

Offline changes require reconciliation.

```text id="fe47"
Offline Edit

↓

Local Storage

↓

Reconnect

↓

Synchronization
```

Conflict resolution must be defined.

---

# 48. Internationalization (i18n)

Applications should separate language from code.

```text id="fe48"
Code

↓

Translation Keys

↓

Localized Text
```

Avoid hardcoded strings.

---

# 49. Localization (l10n)

Localization extends beyond language.

Examples:

```text id="fe49"
Date

Time

Currency

Number Format

Timezone
```

---

# 50. Frontend Security

The frontend contributes to security through:

```text id="fe50"
Content Security Policy

Input Validation

Output Encoding

Secure Headers
```

Security remains a shared responsibility with backend services.

---

# 51. Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

Prevent XSS by:

```text id="fe51"
Escape Output

Sanitize HTML

Avoid Unsafe DOM APIs
```

Never trust user-generated content.

---

# 52. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)

Applications using cookie-based authentication should protect against CSRF.

Mitigations include:

```text id="fe52"
CSRF Tokens

SameSite Cookies

Origin Validation
```

---

# 53. Secure Storage

Avoid storing sensitive credentials in browser storage when more secure alternatives exist.

Examples:

```text id="fe53"
Access Token

Refresh Token

Session
```

Storage decisions should align with ADR-081.

---

# 54. Authentication Integration

Frontend authentication integrates with ADR-081.

```text id="fe54"
Login

↓

OIDC

↓

Token

↓

Protected APIs
```

The frontend should never become the authority for authentication decisions.

---

# 55. Authorization Awareness

The UI may hide unauthorized functionality for usability.

Backend services remain responsible for authorization enforcement.

---

# 56. Frontend Observability

ADR-078 extends to browsers.

Collect:

```text id="fe56"
Errors

Performance

Navigation

API Failures

User Journey
```

Personal data collection should comply with governance policies.

---

# 57. Frontend Testing

ADR-079 testing strategy includes:

```text id="fe57"
Unit

Component

Integration

E2E

Accessibility

Visual Regression
```

Testing should reflect user behavior.

---

# 58. Runtime Configuration

ADR-080 runtime configuration may control:

```text id="fe58"
API Endpoints

Feature Flags

Branding

Analytics

Environment Settings
```

Frontend builds should remain environment-independent where practical.

---

# 59. AI-Assisted User Experience

ADR-077 AI capabilities may include:

```text id="fe59"
Tutor

Recommendations

Summaries

Search

Learning Assistant
```

AI features should behave consistently with the overall design system.

---

# 60. Platform Integration

ADR-078 Internal Developer Platform should automate frontend provisioning.

```text id="fe60"
Repository

↓

CI/CD

↓

Preview Environment

↓

Observability

↓

Deployment
```

Frontend engineering should follow the same platform standards as backend services.

---

# ADR-085 — Enterprise Frontend Architecture, Web Platform, Mobile Architecture & User Experience Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — Platform Integration**.

---

# 61. UX Governance

User Experience is an architectural capability.

Every feature should optimize:

```text
Usability

Accessibility

Consistency

Discoverability

Efficiency

Feedback
```

UX decisions should be evidence-driven rather than preference-driven.

---

# 62. User Journey Design

Design around complete user journeys instead of isolated screens.

```text
Login

↓

Dashboard

↓

Course

↓

Assessment

↓

Result

↓

Feedback
```

Every journey should have a clear start, progression, and completion.

---

# 63. Information Architecture

Organize content according to business domains.

```text
Learning

Assessments

Progress

Administration

Profile
```

Avoid navigation based on technical implementation.

---

# 64. Navigation Standards

Navigation should be predictable.

Primary navigation should remain stable throughout the application.

Users should never wonder where they are.

---

# 65. Breadcrumbs

Provide breadcrumbs where navigation hierarchy is meaningful.

```text
Dashboard

>

Courses

>

Cardiology

>

Assessment
```

---

# 66. Search Experience

Enterprise search should provide:

```text
Autocomplete

Suggestions

Recent Searches

Filters

Ranking
```

Search should tolerate imperfect user input.

---

# 67. Empty States

Empty states should guide users.

Poor:

```text
No Data
```

Better:

```text
No assessments available.

Create a new assessment.
```

---

# 68. Error States

Every error should answer:

```text
What happened?

Why?

Can the user recover?

What should they do next?
```

Avoid technical stack traces in production UI.

---

# 69. Loading States

Users should always receive visual feedback.

Examples:

```text
Skeleton Screen

Spinner

Progress Bar
```

Loading indicators should reflect expected duration.

---

# 70. Notifications

Notifications should be categorized.

```text
Success

Information

Warning

Error
```

Avoid overusing modal dialogs.

---

# 71. Toast Messages

Toast notifications are appropriate for temporary, non-critical feedback.

```text
Profile Saved

✓
```

They should disappear automatically after a reasonable interval.

---

# 72. Confirmation Dialogs

Require confirmation only for destructive or irreversible actions.

Examples:

```text
Delete Course

Reset Assessment

Archive Student
```

Avoid confirmation fatigue.

---

# 73. Undo Pattern

Where feasible:

```text
Delete

↓

Undo

↓

Permanent Delete
```

Undo often provides a better experience than repeated confirmations.

---

# 74. Accessibility Testing

Accessibility should be continuously verified.

Include:

```text
Keyboard Navigation

Screen Readers

Focus Order

Contrast

ARIA Labels
```

---

# 75. Design System Governance

The design system is an enterprise platform.

Governance includes:

```text
Ownership

Versioning

Documentation

Contribution Process

Release Notes
```

---

# 76. Storybook Standard

All reusable UI components should be documented in Storybook (or an equivalent component catalog).

Each component should include:

```text
Examples

Variants

States

Accessibility Notes
```

---

# 77. Component Versioning

Shared components require semantic versioning.

Breaking visual or behavioral changes require governance.

---

# 78. Frontend CI/CD

Frontend delivery should follow ADR-078.

```text
Commit

↓

Build

↓

Lint

↓

Tests

↓

Accessibility

↓

Deploy Preview

↓

Production
```

---

# 79. Preview Environments

Every pull request should automatically create an isolated preview environment.

Benefits:

```text
Early Feedback

UX Review

QA

Stakeholder Validation
```

---

# 80. Visual Regression Testing

Critical UI components should undergo automated visual comparison.

```text
Previous Screenshot

↓

Current Screenshot

↓

Difference Detection
```

---

# 81. Frontend Performance Monitoring

Monitor real-user performance.

Examples:

```text
Page Load

Interaction Delay

Rendering

Navigation Timing
```

Synthetic tests alone are insufficient.

---

# 82. Client Error Monitoring

Capture:

```text
JavaScript Errors

Unhandled Exceptions

Promise Rejections

Rendering Failures
```

Errors should correlate with backend traces where possible.

---

# 83. Analytics

Product analytics should measure:

```text
Feature Usage

Task Completion

Search Success

Drop-off Points
```

Analytics should inform product improvement.

---

# 84. Privacy & Consent

Analytics and personalization should respect user consent.

Requirements include:

```text
Consent Banner

Preference Management

Data Minimization
```

Applicable regulations determine implementation details.

---

# 85. International UX

Support:

```text
RTL Languages

Localized Images

Localized Icons

Cultural Formatting
```

Internationalization extends beyond text translation.

---

# 86. Offline UX

Users should understand synchronization status.

Example:

```text
Offline

↓

Changes Saved Locally

↓

Waiting to Sync

↓

Synced
```

Transparency builds trust.

---

# 87. AI User Experience

ADR-077 AI interactions should clearly distinguish:

```text
Human Content

AI Suggestions

AI Confidence

AI Limitations
```

Users should understand when AI generated the content.

---

# 88. Explainable AI UI

Where AI influences decisions, the interface should provide understandable explanations when appropriate.

Example:

```text
Recommendation

↓

Reason

↓

Supporting Evidence
```

---

# 89. Runtime Feature Flags

ADR-080 runtime controls enable:

```text
Progressive Rollout

A/B Testing

Kill Switch

Regional Features
```

The UI should tolerate feature availability changing dynamically.

---

# 90. API Integration

ADR-082 governs backend communication.

Frontend should consume:

```text
Versioned APIs

Documented APIs

Observable APIs
```

Never depend on undocumented endpoints.

---

# 91. Event Integration

ADR-083 enables real-time interfaces.

Examples:

```text
Assessment Completed

↓

Notification

↓

Dashboard Updated
```

Real-time updates should enhance rather than overwhelm users.

---

# 92. Data Integration

ADR-084 governs persistence.

Frontend should never assume database implementation details.

Backend APIs remain the abstraction layer.

---

# 93. Enterprise Frontend Scorecard

| Capability         | Status |
| ------------------ | ------ |
| TypeScript         | ✓      |
| Design System      | ✓      |
| Accessibility      | ✓      |
| Performance Budget | ✓      |
| Observability      | ✓      |
| Security           | ✓      |
| Testing            | ✓      |
| CI/CD              | ✓      |

---

# 94. Frontend Quality Gates

Production deployment should require:

```text
Build Success

Lint Success

Tests Pass

Accessibility Checks

Performance Budget

Security Scan
```

---

# 95. Frontend Documentation

Every application should document:

```text
Architecture

Components

State Management

Routing

Deployment

Dependencies
```

Documentation should evolve alongside the code.

---

# 96. Frontend Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1

Static Pages

LEVEL 2

Component-Based UI

LEVEL 3

Governed Frontend Platform

LEVEL 4

Observable Enterprise Frontend

LEVEL 5

Adaptive AI-Assisted Experience
```

Mediverse targets **Level 4**.

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Business logic in UI
❌ Inline HTTP calls everywhere
❌ Hardcoded colors
❌ Duplicate components
❌ Accessibility ignored
❌ Global state for everything
❌ Massive React components
❌ CSS without design tokens
❌ No lazy loading
❌ No performance monitoring
❌ Missing error states
❌ Missing loading states
❌ Client-side authorization as security
❌ Undocumented components
❌ Runtime configuration baked into builds
❌ AI features without transparency
❌ Inconsistent navigation
❌ No design system governance
❌ No visual regression testing
```

# ADR-086 — Enterprise Security Architecture, DevSecOps & Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-086
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Security Architecture Board (ESAB)

ADR-085 established the enterprise frontend architecture.

ADR-086 establishes the complete security architecture for Mediverse, integrating identity (ADR-081), APIs (ADR-082), events (ADR-083), data (ADR-084), frontend (ADR-085), platform engineering (ADR-078), observability (ADR-078), testing (ADR-079), runtime governance (ADR-080), AI governance (ADR-077), and data governance (ADR-076).

The governing principle is:

> **Security is a continuously verified architectural property embedded into every phase of software delivery—not a gate performed immediately before production deployment.**

```text id="sec01"
                BUSINESS REQUIREMENT
                       │
                       ▼
              THREAT MODELING
                       │
                       ▼
           SECURE ARCHITECTURE
                       │
                       ▼
            SECURE DEVELOPMENT
                       │
                       ▼
          CONTINUOUS SECURITY
                       │
        ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
        ▼              ▼              ▼
     BUILD         DEPLOYMENT      RUNTIME
        │              │              │
        └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                       ▼
                 OBSERVABILITY
```

---

# 1. Security Philosophy

Security is an architectural quality attribute.

It is not:

```text id="sec02"
Pen Testing

Compliance

Firewall

Authentication
```

alone.

Security emerges from the interaction of architecture, implementation, operations and governance.

---

# 2. Shared Responsibility

Security responsibilities span the enterprise.

```text id="sec03"
Architecture

Development

Platform

Operations

Security

Business
```

Security ownership cannot be delegated to one department.

---

# 3. Secure by Design

Every architecture decision should evaluate:

```text id="sec04"
Confidentiality

Integrity

Availability

Privacy

Resilience
```

before implementation begins.

---

# 4. Defense in Depth

No individual control should become a single point of failure.

```text id="sec05"
Identity

↓

Network

↓

Application

↓

Database

↓

Monitoring
```

Multiple independent controls increase resilience.

---

# 5. Zero Trust

ADR-081 remains the foundational trust model.

Never trust:

```text id="sec06"
Network

Cluster

VPN

Namespace

Location
```

Trust must be established continuously.

---

# 6. Least Privilege

Every component should receive only required permissions.

```text id="sec07"
Identity

↓

Minimum Permissions

↓

Business Task
```

---

# 7. Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC)

Security activities occur throughout delivery.

```text id="sec08"
Requirements

↓

Design

↓

Implementation

↓

Verification

↓

Deployment

↓

Operations
```

Security is continuous.

---

# 8. Security Requirements

Functional requirements should include explicit security requirements.

Examples:

```text id="sec09"
Encryption

Audit

Authentication

Authorization

Retention
```

---

# 9. Threat Modeling

Threat modeling is mandatory for significant architectural changes.

Threat modeling precedes implementation.

---

# 10. STRIDE

STRIDE remains an approved threat-modeling methodology.

Categories include:

```text id="sec10"
Spoofing

Tampering

Repudiation

Information Disclosure

Denial of Service

Elevation of Privilege
```

---

# 11. PASTA

PASTA may be used where risk-driven analysis provides additional value.

The organization remains methodology-agnostic.

---

# 12. Threat Model Deliverables

Every threat model should identify:

```text id="sec11"
Assets

Actors

Entry Points

Trust Boundaries

Threats

Mitigations

Residual Risk
```

---

# 13. Trust Boundaries

Architectures should explicitly document trust boundaries.

```text id="sec12"
Browser

↓

Gateway

↓

Service

↓

Database
```

Each boundary requires authentication and validation.

---

# 14. Secure Coding

Developers should follow approved enterprise coding standards.

Secure coding complements automated tooling rather than replacing it.

---

# 15. OWASP ASVS

Application verification should align with OWASP ASVS where applicable.

ASVS provides structured security verification objectives.

---

# 16. OWASP Top 10

Development teams should understand common application risks.

Examples include:

```text id="sec13"
Broken Access Control

Cryptographic Failures

Injection

Security Misconfiguration

Vulnerable Components
```

Security education should reinforce these categories.

---

# 17. Input Validation

All external input should be considered untrusted.

```text id="sec14"
Validate

↓

Normalize

↓

Process
```

Validation should occur at trust boundaries.

---

# 18. Output Encoding

Encode output according to destination context.

Examples:

```text id="sec15"
HTML

JSON

JavaScript

SQL

XML
```

---

# 19. Parameterized Queries

Database interactions should use parameterized statements.

String concatenation for SQL is prohibited.

---

# 20. Secrets

ADR-080 governs secret management.

Applications must never embed:

```text id="sec16"
Passwords

Tokens

Keys

Certificates
```

inside source repositories.

---

# 21. Cryptography

Use approved enterprise cryptographic algorithms and libraries.

Avoid custom cryptographic implementations.

---

# 22. Key Management

Cryptographic keys require lifecycle management.

```text id="sec17"
Generate

Store

Rotate

Archive

Destroy
```

---

# 23. Secure Defaults

Systems should fail securely.

Examples:

```text id="sec18"
Access Denied

Feature Disabled

Logging Enabled

TLS Enabled
```

---

# 24. Security Headers

Frontend applications should implement:

```text id="sec19"
CSP

HSTS

X-Frame-Options

X-Content-Type-Options

Referrer-Policy
```

---

# 25. Session Security

Session management integrates with ADR-081.

Requirements include:

```text id="sec20"
Expiration

Rotation

Revocation

Re-authentication
```

---

# 26. Error Handling

Security-sensitive information should never appear in user-facing error messages.

Internal details belong in protected logs.

---

# 27. Logging

Security logs should capture:

```text id="sec21"
Authentication

Authorization

Configuration Changes

Security Events
```

Sensitive data should be excluded.

---

# 28. Audit Trails

Security-relevant actions require immutable audit records.

Audit integrity is a security requirement.

---

# 29. Privacy by Design

Privacy considerations should be incorporated during architecture rather than after implementation.

ADR-076 governs data classification and privacy handling.

---

# 30. Secure Architecture Reviews

Major architectural changes require formal security review before implementation.

Security review is preventive rather than reactive.

---

# ADR-086 — Enterprise Security Architecture, DevSecOps & Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Secure Architecture Reviews**.

---

# 31. DevSecOps Philosophy

Security must become part of the delivery pipeline.

```text id="sec31"
Developer

↓

Commit

↓

Security Checks

↓

Deployment
```

Security should move as close as possible to code creation.

---

# 32. Security Gates

Every software change should pass defined security quality gates.

```text id="sec32"
Code

↓

Build

↓

Security

↓

Deploy
```

High-risk findings should prevent promotion.

---

# 33. Static Application Security Testing (SAST)

SAST analyzes source code without execution.

Suitable for detecting:

```text id="sec33"
Injection

Hardcoded Secrets

Unsafe APIs

Weak Cryptography
```

Run SAST early in the development lifecycle.

---

# 34. Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)

DAST evaluates running applications.

It helps identify:

```text id="sec34"
Authentication Issues

HTTP Misconfigurations

Runtime Vulnerabilities

Input Validation Failures
```

---

# 35. Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)

IAST combines runtime execution with application instrumentation.

It provides higher precision than purely static or dynamic approaches for some vulnerability classes.

---

# 36. Software Composition Analysis (SCA)

Modern software depends heavily on third-party libraries.

SCA identifies:

```text id="sec35"
Known CVEs

License Issues

Deprecated Components

Dependency Risk
```

Dependencies require governance equal to proprietary code.

---

# 37. Secret Scanning

Repositories should automatically detect:

```text id="sec36"
API Keys

Passwords

Private Keys

Cloud Credentials

Access Tokens
```

Secrets should never reach source control.

---

# 38. Dependency Governance

Every dependency requires evaluation.

Consider:

```text id="sec37"
Maintenance

Popularity

Security History

License

Support
```

Avoid unnecessary dependencies.

---

# 39. Dependency Updates

Security patches should be applied according to defined risk priorities.

Outdated dependencies increase attack surface.

---

# 40. Container Security

Container images should remain minimal.

```text id="sec38"
Application

↓

Minimal Base Image

↓

Runtime
```

Smaller images reduce attack surface.

---

# 41. Container Image Scanning

Every container image should undergo automated vulnerability scanning before deployment.

```text id="sec39"
Image

↓

Scanner

↓

Report

↓

Decision
```

---

# 42. Kubernetes Security

Kubernetes security includes:

```text id="sec40"
RBAC

Network Policies

Pod Security

Admission Control

Secrets
```

Cluster security is multi-layered.

---

# 43. Pod Security

Containers should avoid unnecessary privileges.

Examples:

```text id="sec41"
Run as Non-Root

Read-Only Filesystem

Drop Linux Capabilities

Resource Limits
```

---

# 44. Admission Controllers

Admission policies validate workloads before scheduling.

Examples:

```text id="sec42"
Image Policy

Security Context

Resource Limits

Labels
```

---

# 45. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Security

Terraform, Helm and Kubernetes manifests should undergo security validation before deployment.

Configuration is code and requires equivalent review.

---

# 46. SBOM (Software Bill of Materials)

Every production artifact should generate an SBOM.

```text id="sec43"
Artifact

↓

SBOM

↓

Dependencies

Versions

Licenses
```

SBOMs improve vulnerability response.

---

# 47. Supply Chain Security

Software supply chains require protection.

```text id="sec44"
Source

↓

Build

↓

Artifact

↓

Deploy
```

Trust should be verifiable at every stage.

---

# 48. SLSA

Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) provides a framework for strengthening build integrity.

Higher assurance levels require stronger provenance guarantees.

---

# 49. Artifact Signing

Release artifacts should be cryptographically signed.

```text id="sec45"
Build

↓

Sign

↓

Repository

↓

Verify

↓

Deploy
```

Unsigned artifacts should not be promoted to production.

---

# 50. Provenance

Every deployable artifact should answer:

```text id="sec46"
Who Built It?

Which Commit?

Which Pipeline?

Which Dependencies?

When?
```

Artifact provenance supports traceability and incident response.

---

# 51. Runtime Protection

Applications require runtime defenses.

Examples:

```text id="sec47"
Anomaly Detection

Runtime Policies

Behavior Monitoring
```

Runtime protection complements preventive controls.

---

# 52. Web Application Firewall (WAF)

Internet-facing applications should evaluate WAF protection where appropriate.

WAFs reduce exposure to common attack patterns but do not replace secure coding.

---

# 53. API Security

ADR-082 governs API architecture.

Security includes:

```text id="sec48"
Authentication

Authorization

Rate Limiting

Input Validation

Audit
```

Every public API requires explicit security controls.

---

# 54. Network Segmentation

Critical systems should be isolated through network policy.

```text id="sec49"
Internet

↓

Gateway

↓

Application

↓

Database
```

Segmentation limits lateral movement.

---

# 55. Service Mesh Security

Where a service mesh is deployed, it should provide:

```text id="sec50"
mTLS

Identity

Authorization

Observability
```

Business authorization remains within applications.

---

# 56. Vulnerability Management

Vulnerabilities require lifecycle management.

```text id="sec51"
Discover

↓

Assess

↓

Prioritize

↓

Remediate

↓

Verify

↓

Close
```

---

# 57. Risk Prioritization

Prioritize remediation based on:

```text id="sec52"
Exploitability

Business Impact

Exposure

Compensating Controls
```

Severity alone should not determine priority.

---

# 58. Security Observability

ADR-078 extends to security telemetry.

Monitor:

```text id="sec53"
Authentication Failures

Authorization Failures

Policy Violations

Suspicious Activity

Configuration Drift
```

---

# 59. Security Testing Integration

ADR-079 requires automated verification of security controls.

Examples:

```text id="sec54"
Authentication Tests

Authorization Tests

Penetration Tests

Regression Tests
```

Security testing should be repeatable.

---

# 60. Platform Integration

ADR-078 Internal Developer Platform should automate security.

```text id="sec55"
Repository

↓

Security Scans

↓

SBOM

↓

Image Signing

↓

Deployment
```

Security should become part of the platform's default workflow rather than an optional activity.

---

# ADR-086 — Enterprise Security Architecture, DevSecOps & Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — Platform Integration**.

---

# 61. Incident Response

Security incidents require a defined lifecycle.

```text
Detect
   │
   ▼
Analyze
   │
   ▼
Contain
   │
   ▼
Eradicate
   │
   ▼
Recover
   │
   ▼
Lessons Learned
```

Every production system must have an incident response plan.

---

# 62. Incident Classification

Security incidents should be categorized by impact.

Example levels:

```text
Critical

High

Medium

Low
```

Classification determines escalation and response expectations.

---

# 63. Security Playbooks

Standard playbooks should exist for common scenarios.

Examples:

```text
Credential Compromise

Ransomware

API Abuse

Data Leak

Kubernetes Breach

Cloud Account Compromise
```

Playbooks reduce response time and improve consistency.

---

# 64. Security Operations Center (SOC)

Enterprise monitoring should support a Security Operations Center.

Responsibilities include:

```text
Monitoring

Alert Triage

Investigation

Escalation

Incident Coordination
```

---

# 65. Digital Forensics

Security investigations should preserve evidence.

```text
Evidence Collection

↓

Preservation

↓

Analysis

↓

Reporting
```

Forensic activities should avoid modifying original evidence.

---

# 66. Chain of Custody

Evidence handling should document:

```text
Who Collected

When

Where Stored

Who Accessed

Integrity Verification
```

This supports legal and regulatory requirements.

---

# 67. Root Cause Analysis

Every major security incident should conclude with root cause analysis.

Questions include:

```text
What happened?

Why?

How detected?

Why not prevented?

What changes are required?
```

---

# 68. Corrective Actions

Security improvements should follow incidents.

```text
Incident

↓

Root Cause

↓

Architecture Change

↓

Verification
```

Recurring incidents indicate ineffective remediation.

---

# 69. Threat Intelligence

Security operations should consume relevant threat intelligence.

Examples:

```text
Known CVEs

Malicious IPs

Attack Campaigns

Exploit Trends
```

Threat intelligence informs proactive defense.

---

# 70. Security Monitoring

Continuous monitoring should observe:

```text
Authentication

Authorization

API Abuse

Container Runtime

Infrastructure

Network Activity
```

Monitoring should prioritize actionable signals over excessive noise.

---

# 71. Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)

Security telemetry should be centralized.

```text
Applications

↓

Infrastructure

↓

Cloud

↓

Identity

↓

SIEM
```

Centralization supports correlation across systems.

---

# 72. Detection Engineering

Detection rules should be version controlled.

```text
Threat

↓

Detection Rule

↓

Alert

↓

Investigation
```

Detection quality should evolve continuously.

---

# 73. Compliance Mapping

Security controls should map to applicable compliance frameworks without coupling architecture to any single standard.

Potential mappings include:

```text
ISO 27001

SOC 2

HIPAA

GDPR

PCI DSS
```

---

# 74. Continuous Compliance

Compliance should be continuously verified.

```text
Configuration

↓

Validation

↓

Evidence

↓

Compliance Status
```

Avoid relying solely on periodic manual audits.

---

# 75. Audit Readiness

Systems should produce audit evidence automatically.

Examples:

```text
Access Logs

Configuration History

Deployment Records

Security Reports
```

Preparing for audits should not require reconstructing historical evidence.

---

# 76. Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM)

Cloud environments should undergo continuous posture assessment.

Examples:

```text
Public Buckets

Overprivileged IAM

Unencrypted Storage

Open Security Groups
```

---

# 77. Kubernetes Security Posture

Continuously evaluate:

```text
RBAC

Network Policies

Pod Security

Secrets

Admission Policies
```

Security posture should not drift over time.

---

# 78. AI Security

ADR-077 introduces AI-specific risks.

Security architecture should address:

```text
Prompt Injection

Jailbreak Attempts

Training Data Poisoning

Model Abuse

Sensitive Data Leakage
```

---

# 79. Prompt Injection Defense

AI systems should treat prompts as untrusted input.

Strategies include:

```text
Input Validation

Context Isolation

Tool Restrictions

Output Verification
```

---

# 80. AI Tool Security

AI agents should invoke only explicitly authorized tools.

```text
Agent

↓

Authorization

↓

Tool

↓

Audit
```

Tool execution should never bypass enterprise authorization.

---

# 81. AI Output Validation

AI-generated output may require validation before execution.

Examples:

```text
Generated SQL

Generated Code

Infrastructure Changes

Security Policies
```

Human or automated verification should match risk.

---

# 82. Model Security

Protect:

```text
Model Files

Weights

Configuration

API Keys

Inference Endpoints
```

Models are enterprise assets.

---

# 83. Data Leakage Prevention

Security controls should reduce unintended disclosure.

Examples:

```text
Sensitive Prompts

PII

Secrets

Medical Data

Financial Data
```

---

# 84. Insider Threat

Security architecture should consider trusted identities becoming malicious or compromised.

Monitoring should focus on unusual behavior rather than assumptions of trust.

---

# 85. Business Continuity

Security integrates with business continuity planning.

Critical systems require:

```text
Recovery Plans

Communication

Fallback

Testing
```

---

# 86. Security Metrics

Representative KPIs include:

```text
Mean Time to Detect

Mean Time to Respond

Patch Time

Critical Vulnerabilities

False Positives
```

Metrics support operational improvement.

---

# 87. Key Risk Indicators (KRIs)

Examples include:

```text
Unpatched Critical CVEs

Expired Certificates

Privilege Creep

Open Incidents

Security Drift
```

KRIs indicate increasing organizational risk.

---

# 88. Security Scorecard

| Capability         | Status |
| ------------------ | ------ |
| SSDLC              | ✓      |
| Threat Modeling    | ✓      |
| SAST               | ✓      |
| DAST               | ✓      |
| SCA                | ✓      |
| SBOM               | ✓      |
| Artifact Signing   | ✓      |
| Runtime Protection | ✓      |
| Incident Response  | ✓      |
| AI Security        | ✓      |

Scorecards provide governance visibility.

---

# 89. Security Documentation

Maintain documentation for:

```text
Architecture

Threat Models

Playbooks

Policies

Standards

Incident Reports
```

Documentation should remain current.

---

# 90. Security Training

Security awareness extends beyond annual compliance training.

Training should cover:

```text
Secure Coding

Threat Modeling

Phishing

Incident Reporting

AI Security
```

---

# 91. Platform Integration

ADR-078 should automatically provide:

```text
Security Scanning

↓

SBOM

↓

Artifact Signing

↓

Policy Validation

↓

Deployment Approval
```

Security becomes part of the platform's golden path.

---

# 92. Runtime Integration

ADR-080 runtime governance should support:

```text
Emergency Feature Disable

Policy Updates

Credential Rotation

Runtime Configuration Changes
```

Emergency actions should remain auditable.

---

# 93. Observability Integration

ADR-078 observability should correlate:

```text
Trace ID

Identity

Security Events

Infrastructure

Application Logs
```

Security investigations benefit from unified telemetry.

---

# 94. Identity Integration

ADR-081 identity architecture provides:

```text
Authentication

Authorization

Workload Identity

Zero Trust

MFA
```

Security architecture builds upon these capabilities rather than duplicating them.

---

# 95. API Integration

ADR-082 APIs should expose:

```text
Secure Endpoints

Rate Limits

Audit

Authentication

Authorization
```

---

```text
LEVEL 1

Reactive Security

LEVEL 2

Managed Security

LEVEL 3

Integrated DevSecOps

LEVEL 4

Observable Zero Trust Enterprise

LEVEL 5

Adaptive Autonomous Security
```

Mediverse targets **Level 4**.

# 97. Security Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Security review only before release
❌ Shared administrator accounts
❌ Hardcoded secrets
❌ Anonymous production access
❌ Trusting internal networks
❌ Missing SBOM
❌ Unsigned artifacts
❌ Ignored security findings
❌ Manual production changes
❌ No threat modeling
❌ Disabled TLS
❌ Running containers as root
❌ Long-lived credentials
❌ No incident playbooks
❌ Missing audit logs
❌ No runtime monitoring
❌ AI tools with unrestricted execution
❌ Prompt injection ignored
❌ Security treated as a separate team responsibility
```

# ADR-087 — Enterprise Cloud-Native Infrastructure, Kubernetes Platform, Service Mesh & Multi-Cloud Operations Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-087
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Platform Engineering Board (EPEB)

ADR-086 established the enterprise security architecture.

ADR-087 defines the enterprise cloud-native platform that hosts every Mediverse workload, providing a standardized Kubernetes platform, networking model, service mesh, infrastructure automation, scalability, resilience, and multi-cloud operations.

The governing principle is:

> **Infrastructure is a programmable enterprise platform that provides secure, observable, resilient and self-service capabilities. Applications consume the platform rather than building infrastructure independently.**

```text
                  DEVELOPERS
                       │
                       ▼
             Internal Developer Platform
                       │
                       ▼
                 GitOps Platform
                       │
                       ▼
              Kubernetes Platform
                       │
     ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
     ▼                 ▼                 ▼
 Networking       Compute         Storage
     │                 │                 │
     └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                       ▼
      Security • Observability • Runtime
```

---

# 1. Cloud-Native Philosophy

Cloud-native architecture emphasizes:

```text
Automation

Elasticity

Resilience

Observability

Self-Service
```

Infrastructure should enable rapid delivery without compromising governance.

---

# 2. Kubernetes Standard

Kubernetes is the standard orchestration platform for Mediverse.

It provides:

```text
Scheduling

Self-Healing

Scaling

Networking

Resource Isolation
```

All production workloads should target Kubernetes unless a documented exception is approved.

---

# 3. Platform Engineering

Infrastructure should be delivered as an Internal Developer Platform (IDP), not as ticket-driven operations.

```text
Developer

↓

Platform API

↓

Automated Provisioning

↓

Running Workload
```

---

# 4. Immutable Infrastructure

Infrastructure changes occur through declarative configuration rather than manual modification.

```text
Git

↓

Pipeline

↓

Cluster
```

---

# 5. Declarative Configuration

Infrastructure should be defined declaratively.

Examples:

```text
Kubernetes YAML

Helm

Kustomize

Terraform
```

Declarative state enables repeatable deployments.

---

# 6. Infrastructure as Code

All infrastructure must be managed as code.

IaC repositories become enterprise assets subject to version control, testing and review.

---

# 7. GitOps

Git is the authoritative source of desired infrastructure state.

```text
Git

↓

ArgoCD / Flux

↓

Cluster
```

Direct production changes are prohibited.

---

# 8. GitOps Workflow

```text
Commit

↓

Review

↓

Merge

↓

GitOps Sync

↓

Cluster
```

Synchronization should be automated and observable.

---

# 9. Cluster Philosophy

Clusters are shared enterprise platforms—not application-specific assets.

Application teams consume namespaces rather than owning clusters.

---

# 10. Cluster Topology

Environment separation:

```text
Development

↓

Testing

↓

Staging

↓

Production
```

Production workloads should not share clusters with development workloads.

---

# 11. Multi-Cluster Strategy

Multiple clusters improve:

```text
Isolation

Availability

Regional Deployment

Compliance

Disaster Recovery
```

Cluster count should reflect operational needs rather than organizational preferences.

---

# 12. Namespace Governance

Namespaces provide logical isolation.

```text
Platform

Monitoring

Ingress

Application

AI

Data
```

Namespaces should represent ownership boundaries.

---

# 13. Resource Quotas

Namespaces should define:

```text
CPU

Memory

Storage

Pods
```

Resource governance prevents noisy-neighbor problems.

---

# 14. Limit Ranges

Every namespace should define reasonable default resource requests and limits.

Applications should not rely on unlimited resource consumption.

---

# 15. Workload Types

Standard workload types include:

```text
Deployment

StatefulSet

DaemonSet

Job

CronJob
```

Workload selection should align with application behavior.

---

# 16. Stateless Workloads

Stateless applications should use Deployments.

Horizontal scaling becomes straightforward.

---

# 17. Stateful Workloads

Stateful applications require:

```text
Persistent Storage

Stable Identity

Ordered Deployment
```

StatefulSets provide these guarantees.

---

# 18. Batch Processing

Short-lived processing should use Jobs.

Recurring processing should use CronJobs.

---

# 19. Pod Design

Pods should contain tightly coupled containers only.

Avoid using Pods as miniature virtual machines.

---

# 20. Sidecar Pattern

Sidecars remain appropriate for:

```text
Proxy

Logging

Security

Telemetry
```

Business logic should remain in the primary container.

---

# 21. Labels and Selectors

Every workload should use standardized labels.

Examples:

```text
Application

Environment

Version

Owner

Component
```

Labels enable automation and observability.

---

# 22. Node Pools

Separate node pools may support:

```text
General

AI

GPU

Batch

System
```

Scheduling should reflect workload requirements.

---

# 23. Taints and Tolerations

Specialized workloads should use taints and tolerations to prevent inappropriate scheduling.

---

# 24. Affinity Rules

Affinity and anti-affinity improve availability.

```text
Replica A

Node 1

Replica B

Node 2
```

Avoid concentrating replicas on a single node.

---

# 25. Autoscaling

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) is preferred for stateless workloads.

Scaling policies should reflect measured demand.

---

# 26. Vertical Scaling

Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) may assist workload tuning.

Avoid uncontrolled automatic resizing without operational understanding.

---

# 27. Cluster Autoscaler

Infrastructure should scale worker nodes automatically where supported.

Capacity should follow workload demand.

---

# 28. Resource Requests

Every workload should define:

```text
CPU Request

Memory Request
```

Scheduling depends on accurate requests.

---

# 29. Resource Limits

Production workloads should define:

```text
CPU Limit

Memory Limit
```

Limits protect cluster stability.

---

# 30. Health Probes

Applications should implement:

```text
Startup Probe

Liveness Probe

Readiness Probe
```

Health checks enable Kubernetes self-healing.

---

**Sections 1–30 completed.**

This establishes the foundational enterprise Kubernetes platform:

* Cloud-native principles
* Kubernetes standard

**Part 2 (Sections 31–60)** will continue with:

* Secrets and ConfigMaps
* Certificate management
* Backup
* High availability
* Disaster recovery
* Multi-region deployment
* Multi-cloud architecture
* Runtime integration (ADR-080)
* Platform integration (ADR-078).

# ADR-086 — Enterprise Security Architecture, DevSecOps & Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — Platform Integration**.

---

# 61. Incident Response

Security incidents require a defined lifecycle.

```text
Detect
   │
   ▼
Analyze
   │
   ▼
Contain
   │
   ▼
Eradicate
   │
   ▼
Recover
   │
   ▼
Lessons Learned
```

Every production system must have an incident response plan.

---

# 62. Incident Classification

Security incidents should be categorized by impact.

Example levels:

```text
Critical

High

Medium

Low
```

Classification determines escalation and response expectations.

---

# 63. Security Playbooks

Standard playbooks should exist for common scenarios.

Examples:

```text
Credential Compromise

Ransomware

API Abuse

Data Leak

Kubernetes Breach

Cloud Account Compromise
```

Playbooks reduce response time and improve consistency.

---

# 64. Security Operations Center (SOC)

Enterprise monitoring should support a Security Operations Center.

Responsibilities include:

```text
Monitoring

Alert Triage

Investigation

Escalation

Incident Coordination
```

---

# 65. Digital Forensics

Security investigations should preserve evidence.

```text
Evidence Collection

↓

Preservation

↓

Analysis

↓

Reporting
```

Forensic activities should avoid modifying original evidence.

---

# 66. Chain of Custody

Evidence handling should document:

```text
Who Collected

When

Where Stored

Who Accessed

Integrity Verification
```

This supports legal and regulatory requirements.

---

# 67. Root Cause Analysis

Every major security incident should conclude with root cause analysis.

Questions include:

```text
What happened?

Why?

How detected?

Why not prevented?

What changes are required?
```

---

# 68. Corrective Actions

Security improvements should follow incidents.

```text
Incident

↓

Root Cause

↓

Architecture Change

↓

Verification
```

Recurring incidents indicate ineffective remediation.

---

# 69. Threat Intelligence

Security operations should consume relevant threat intelligence.

Examples:

```text
Known CVEs

Malicious IPs

Attack Campaigns

Exploit Trends
```

Threat intelligence informs proactive defense.

---

# 70. Security Monitoring

Continuous monitoring should observe:

```text
Authentication

Authorization

API Abuse

Container Runtime

Infrastructure

Network Activity
```

Monitoring should prioritize actionable signals over excessive noise.

---

# 71. Security Information and Event Management (SIEM)

Security telemetry should be centralized.

```text
Applications

↓

Infrastructure

↓

Cloud

↓

Identity

↓

SIEM
```

Centralization supports correlation across systems.

---

# 72. Detection Engineering

Detection rules should be version controlled.

```text
Threat

↓

Detection Rule

↓

Alert

↓

Investigation
```

Detection quality should evolve continuously.

---

# 73. Compliance Mapping

Security controls should map to applicable compliance frameworks without coupling architecture to any single standard.

Potential mappings include:

```text
ISO 27001

SOC 2

HIPAA

GDPR

PCI DSS
```

---

# 74. Continuous Compliance

Compliance should be continuously verified.

```text
Configuration

↓

Validation

↓

Evidence

↓

Compliance Status
```

Avoid relying solely on periodic manual audits.

---

# 75. Audit Readiness

Systems should produce audit evidence automatically.

Examples:

```text
Access Logs

Configuration History

Deployment Records

Security Reports
```

Preparing for audits should not require reconstructing historical evidence.

---

# 76. Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM)

Cloud environments should undergo continuous posture assessment.

Examples:

```text
Public Buckets

Overprivileged IAM

Unencrypted Storage

Open Security Groups
```

---

# 77. Kubernetes Security Posture

Continuously evaluate:

```text
RBAC

Network Policies

Pod Security

Secrets

Admission Policies
```

Security posture should not drift over time.

---

# 78. AI Security

ADR-077 introduces AI-specific risks.

Security architecture should address:

```text
Prompt Injection

Jailbreak Attempts

Training Data Poisoning

Model Abuse

Sensitive Data Leakage
```

---

# 79. Prompt Injection Defense

AI systems should treat prompts as untrusted input.

Strategies include:

```text
Input Validation

Context Isolation

Tool Restrictions

Output Verification
```

---

# 80. AI Tool Security

AI agents should invoke only explicitly authorized tools.

```text
Agent

↓

Authorization

↓

Tool

↓

Audit
```

Tool execution should never bypass enterprise authorization.

---

# 81. AI Output Validation

AI-generated output may require validation before execution.

Examples:

```text
Generated SQL

Generated Code

Infrastructure Changes

Security Policies
```

Human or automated verification should match risk.

---

# 82. Model Security

Protect:

```text
Model Files

Weights

Configuration

API Keys

Inference Endpoints
```

Models are enterprise assets.

---

# 83. Data Leakage Prevention

Security controls should reduce unintended disclosure.

Examples:

```text
Sensitive Prompts

PII

Secrets

Medical Data

Financial Data
```

---

# 84. Insider Threat

Security architecture should consider trusted identities becoming malicious or compromised.

Monitoring should focus on unusual behavior rather than assumptions of trust.

---

# 85. Business Continuity

Security integrates with business continuity planning.

Critical systems require:

```text
Recovery Plans

Communication

Fallback

Testing
```

---

# 86. Security Metrics

Representative KPIs include:

```text
Mean Time to Detect

Mean Time to Respond

Patch Time

Critical Vulnerabilities

False Positives
```

Metrics support operational improvement.

---

# 87. Key Risk Indicators (KRIs)

Examples include:

```text
Unpatched Critical CVEs

Expired Certificates

Privilege Creep

Open Incidents

Security Drift
```

KRIs indicate increasing organizational risk.

---

```text
Playbooks

Policies

Standards

Incident Reports
```

Documentation should remain current.

---

# 90. Security Training

Security awareness extends beyond annual compliance training.

Training should cover:

```text
Secure Coding

Threat Modeling

Phishing

Incident Reporting

AI Security
```

---

# 91. Platform Integration

```text
↓

Policy Validation
```

Security becomes part of the platform's golden path.

# 93. Observability Integration

ADR-078 observability should correlate:

```text
Identity

Security Events

Infrastructure

Application Logs
```

---

# 94. Identity Integration

ADR-081 identity architecture provides:

```text
Authentication

Authorization

Workload Identity

MFA
```

Security architecture builds upon these capabilities rather than duplicating them.

---

# 95. API Integration

ADR-082 APIs should expose:

```text
Rate Limits

Audit

Authorization
```

---

# 96. Enterprise Security Maturity Model

```text
Reactive Security

LEVEL 2

Managed Security

LEVEL 3

Integrated DevSecOps
```

```text
❌ Security review only before release
```

# ADR-087 — Enterprise Cloud-Native Infrastructure, Kubernetes Platform, Service Mesh & Multi-Cloud Operations Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Health Probes**.

---

# 31. Kubernetes Networking

Networking should provide secure, observable and reliable communication.

```text id="k831"
Pod

↓

Service

↓

Ingress / Gateway

↓

Client
```

Applications should not depend on Pod IP addresses.

---

# 32. Container Network Interface (CNI)

A standard CNI implementation should provide:

```text id="k832"
Pod Networking

Network Policies

IP Management

Performance
```

The CNI becomes part of the platform architecture rather than an application concern.

---

# 33. Kubernetes Services

Services provide stable discovery.

Supported types:

```text id="k833"
ClusterIP

NodePort

LoadBalancer

ExternalName
```

ClusterIP should be the default for internal communication.

---

# 34. Service Discovery

Applications should discover services through Kubernetes DNS.

```text id="k834"
Application

↓

DNS

↓

Service

↓

Pods
```

Avoid hardcoded IP addresses.

---

# 35. Ingress

Ingress exposes HTTP/HTTPS applications.

```text id="k835"
Internet

↓

Ingress

↓

Service

↓

Pods
```

Ingress focuses on north-south traffic.

---

# 36. Gateway API

Gateway API is the preferred long-term Kubernetes networking standard.

Advantages include:

```text id="k836"
Improved Extensibility

Role Separation

Advanced Routing

Standardization
```

---

# 37. North-South Traffic

Traffic entering the cluster should pass through governed gateways.

```text id="k837"
Client

↓

Gateway

↓

Application
```

Direct access to workloads should be avoided.

---

# 38. East-West Traffic

Internal service communication should remain secure and observable.

```text id="k838"
Service A

↓

Service B

↓

Service C
```

---

# 39. Service Mesh

A service mesh provides infrastructure capabilities for service-to-service communication.

Examples:

```text id="k839"
mTLS

Traffic Policies

Retries

Telemetry
```

Business logic remains inside applications.

---

# 40. Istio Standard

Istio is the preferred enterprise service mesh where advanced traffic management is required.

Linkerd may be appropriate for environments prioritizing operational simplicity.

---

# 41. Mutual TLS (mTLS)

Internal service communication should use mutual TLS.

```text id="k840"
Service A

⇄

Encrypted & Authenticated

⇄

Service B
```

---

# 42. Traffic Policies

The service mesh may manage:

```text id="k841"
Retries

Timeouts

Circuit Breakers

Load Balancing
```

Application logic should not duplicate mesh behavior unnecessarily.

---

# 43. Circuit Breakers

Prevent cascading failures.

```text id="k842"
Failures

↓

Circuit Opens

↓

Temporary Isolation

↓

Recovery
```

---

# 44. Retry Policies

Retries should address transient failures.

Mesh retries should remain coordinated with application retry strategies to avoid amplification.

---

# 45. Timeout Policies

Every network request should define explicit timeouts.

Unlimited waiting reduces overall system resilience.

---

# 46. Canary Deployments

Progressively expose new versions.

```text id="k843"
Version 1

95%

Version 2

5%
```

Traffic percentages should increase based on observed health.

---

# 47. Blue-Green Deployments

Maintain two production environments.

```text id="k844"
Blue

↓

Switch

↓

Green
```

Rollback becomes rapid and predictable.

---

# 48. Progressive Delivery

Release decisions should depend on observed metrics rather than deployment completion.

```text id="k845"
Deploy

↓

Observe

↓

Promote

↓

Complete
```

---

# 49. Persistent Storage

Persistent workloads require Kubernetes storage abstraction.

```text id="k846"
Application

↓

Persistent Volume Claim

↓

Persistent Volume

↓

Storage
```

---

# 50. Container Storage Interface (CSI)

CSI standardizes storage integration.

Benefits include:

```text id="k847"
Provisioning

Snapshots

Expansion

Portability
```

---

# 51. Storage Classes

Different workloads may require different storage profiles.

Examples:

```text id="k848"
Standard

SSD

High IOPS

Archive
```

---

# 52. Volume Snapshots

Critical persistent data should support snapshots.

```text id="k849"
Volume

↓

Snapshot

↓

Recovery
```

Snapshots complement backups rather than replacing them.

---

# 53. ConfigMaps

Configuration should be externalized.

```text id="k850"
Application

↓

ConfigMap

↓

Runtime Configuration
```

Configuration changes should not require image rebuilds.

---

# 54. Secrets

Sensitive configuration belongs in Kubernetes Secrets integrated with enterprise secret management.

Secrets should never be stored in Git repositories.

---

# 55. Certificate Management

Certificates require automated lifecycle management.

```text id="k851"
Issue

↓

Deploy

↓

Rotate

↓

Expire
```

Manual certificate renewal does not scale.

---

# 56. Backup Strategy

Cluster backup should include:

```text id="k852"
Persistent Volumes

Kubernetes Resources

GitOps Configuration

Secrets Metadata
```

Recovery procedures should be regularly validated.

---

# 57. High Availability

Production clusters should tolerate infrastructure failures.

```text id="k853"
Multiple Control Plane Nodes

+

Multiple Worker Nodes

+

Redundant Networking
```

Single points of failure should be eliminated where practical.

---

# 58. Disaster Recovery

Disaster recovery planning should define:

```text id="k854"
Recovery Point Objective

Recovery Time Objective

Recovery Procedures

Validation
```

Recovery should be rehearsed rather than assumed.

---

# 59. Multi-Region Deployment

Critical services may span multiple geographic regions.

Benefits include:

```text id="k855"
Lower Latency

Higher Availability

Regional Resilience
```

Multi-region architecture introduces additional consistency and operational considerations.

---

# 60. Multi-Cloud Strategy

Multi-cloud should solve specific business requirements such as resilience, regulatory constraints or vendor risk.

It should not be adopted solely to avoid perceived vendor lock-in.

---
