# ADR-087 — Enterprise Cloud-Native Infrastructure, Kubernetes Platform, Service Mesh & Multi-Cloud Operations Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — Multi-Cloud Strategy**.

---

# 61. Platform Observability

ADR-078 defines enterprise observability.

Every Kubernetes cluster should expose:

```text
Infrastructure Metrics

Platform Logs

Distributed Traces

Events

Health Signals
```

Platform behavior must be measurable before users experience failures.

---

# 62. Cluster Monitoring

Every cluster should continuously monitor:

```text
API Server

etcd

Scheduler

Controller Manager

Kubelet

CoreDNS
```

The control plane is production infrastructure and requires the same operational visibility as business applications.

---

# 63. Node Monitoring

Worker nodes should expose:

```text
CPU

Memory

Disk

Filesystem

Network

Pressure Conditions
```

Capacity issues should be detected before workloads are affected.

---

# 64. Pod Monitoring

Monitor every workload for:

```text
Restarts

OOMKilled

CrashLoopBackOff

Pending

Evictions
```

Frequent restarts often indicate application or resource configuration problems.

---

# 65. Prometheus Standard

Prometheus is the enterprise metrics platform.

Responsibilities:

```text
Metrics Collection

Alert Evaluation

Service Discovery

Recording Rules
```

Metrics should follow standardized naming conventions.

---

# 66. Grafana Standard

Grafana is the enterprise visualization platform.

Dashboards should exist for:

```text
Platform

Applications

Infrastructure

Security

Business KPIs
```

---

# 67. OpenTelemetry Integration

All workloads should emit:

```text
Metrics

Logs

Traces
```

using OpenTelemetry instrumentation where practical.

---

# 68. Logging Architecture

Centralized logging should aggregate:

```text
Application Logs

Platform Logs

Audit Logs

Security Logs
```

Logs should be searchable and retained according to governance policies.

---

# 69. Kubernetes Events

Cluster events provide operational insight.

Examples:

```text
Scheduling

Scaling

Eviction

Deployment

Node Failure
```

Events should complement metrics rather than replace them.

---

# 70. Alerting Strategy

Alerts should prioritize actionable conditions.

Examples:

```text
API Server Down

Node Not Ready

High Error Rate

High Latency

Certificate Expiry
```

Avoid excessive alert noise.

---

# 71. SLO Monitoring

Platform SLOs should define measurable objectives.

Example:

```text
API Availability

99.95%

Control Plane Latency

<100 ms

Pod Scheduling

<30 sec
```

---

# 72. Capacity Planning

Platform growth should be forecast using:

```text
CPU

Memory

Storage

Pods

Network

Growth Trends
```

Planning should anticipate demand rather than react to shortages.

---

# 73. Cluster Scaling

Scaling decisions should combine:

```text
Historical Trends

Current Demand

Forecasted Growth
```

Reactive scaling alone may be insufficient during predictable demand spikes.

---

# 74. FinOps

Infrastructure cost should become observable.

Track:

```text
Namespace Cost

Application Cost

Storage Cost

Idle Resources

GPU Usage
```

Engineering teams should understand the financial impact of architectural decisions.

---

# 75. Resource Optimization

Regularly identify:

```text
Overprovisioned Pods

Underutilized Nodes

Unused Volumes

Idle Load Balancers
```

Optimization should preserve reliability while reducing waste.

---

# 76. Identity Integration

ADR-081 governs workload identity.

Every workload should authenticate using enterprise workload identity mechanisms.

Long-lived static credentials are prohibited.

---

# 77. Runtime Policy Enforcement

ADR-080 runtime controls should support:

```text
Feature Flags

Policy Updates

Traffic Controls

Emergency Disable

Configuration Changes
```

Changes should remain observable and auditable.

---

# 78. Kubernetes Security Integration

ADR-086 security controls apply to the platform.

Examples:

```text
RBAC

Network Policies

Pod Security

Image Verification

Admission Policies
```

Platform security should be continuously validated.

---

# 79. GitOps Operations

GitOps controllers continuously reconcile:

```text
Git

↓

Desired State

↓

Cluster

↓

Actual State
```

Configuration drift should trigger investigation.

---

# 80. Drift Detection

Detect unauthorized differences between:

```text
Git

↓

Cluster
```

Manual production modifications should be treated as exceptions.

---

# 81. Progressive Delivery Integration

GitOps should integrate with:

```text
Canary

Blue-Green

Traffic Shifting

Automatic Rollback
```

Deployment success depends on runtime health rather than rollout completion.

---

# 82. Platform Automation

The Internal Developer Platform should automate:

```text
Namespace Creation

Secrets

Certificates

Monitoring

Ingress

Policies
```

Self-service reduces operational bottlenecks.

---

# 83. Self-Service Platform

Developers should request platform capabilities through standardized APIs or templates.

```text
Developer

↓

Platform API

↓

Provisioned Environment
```

---

# 84. Golden Paths

Platform engineering should publish approved implementation paths.

Examples:

```text
Spring Boot

React

Kafka

PostgreSQL

AI Services
```

Golden paths improve consistency without eliminating flexibility.

---

# 85. Platform Documentation

Document:

```text
Architecture

Cluster Standards

Networking

Security

Operations

Runbooks
```

Documentation should remain version-controlled.

---

# 86. Platform Runbooks

Standard operational procedures should exist for:

```text
Node Failure

Certificate Rotation

Cluster Upgrade

Backup

Recovery

Scaling
```

Runbooks reduce operational uncertainty.

---

# 87. Platform Testing

ADR-079 extends to infrastructure.

Testing includes:

```text
Disaster Recovery

Scaling

Failover

Network Policies

Backup Restoration
```

Operational assumptions should be validated.

---

# 88. Upgrade Strategy

Cluster upgrades should follow:

```text
Development

↓

Testing

↓

Staging

↓

Production
```

Upgrade plans should include rollback procedures.

---

# 89. Platform Inventory

Maintain an inventory of:

```text
Clusters

Namespaces

Node Pools

Storage

Ingress

Gateways

Service Meshes
```

Unknown infrastructure introduces operational risk.

---

# 90. Platform Governance

Governance should review:

```text
Architecture

Security

Cost

Performance

Compliance

Reliability
```

Platform evolution should remain intentional.

---

# 91. Infrastructure Scorecard

| Capability        | Status |
| ----------------- | ------ |
| GitOps            | ✓      |
| Kubernetes        | ✓      |
| Service Mesh      | ✓      |
| Observability     | ✓      |
| Security          | ✓      |
| Autoscaling       | ✓      |
| Backup            | ✓      |
| Disaster Recovery | ✓      |

---

# 92. Platform KPIs

Representative KPIs include:

```text
Deployment Frequency

Lead Time

Change Failure Rate

Recovery Time

Platform Availability
```

These metrics align platform performance with engineering outcomes.

---

# 93. Enterprise Platform Maturity Model

```text
LEVEL 1

Manual Infrastructure

LEVEL 2

Infrastructure as Code

LEVEL 3

GitOps Platform

LEVEL 4

Self-Service Platform Engineering

LEVEL 5

Autonomous Cloud Platform
```

Mediverse targets **Level 4**.

---

# 94. Infrastructure Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text
❌ Manual kubectl changes in production
❌ Snowflake clusters
❌ Shared admin accounts
❌ Unlimited namespaces
❌ Missing resource limits
❌ Applications using Pod IPs

❌ No GitOps
❌ No monitoring
❌ No backups
❌ No disaster recovery testing
❌ Uncontrolled autoscaling
❌ No health probes
❌ No workload identity
❌ Ignored configuration drift
❌ Infrastructure without documentation
```

# ADR-088 — Enterprise Reliability Engineering (SRE), High Availability, Disaster Recovery & Operational Excellence Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-088
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Reliability Engineering Board (EREB)

ADR-087 established the enterprise cloud-native platform.

ADR-088 defines how Mediverse achieves measurable reliability, operational excellence, resilience, disaster recovery, and sustainable operations through Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) principles.

The governing principle is:

> **Reliability is engineered through continuous measurement, automation, fault tolerance and operational discipline—not by reacting to failures after they occur.**

```text id="sre01"
              BUSINESS SERVICE
                     │
                     ▼
          Reliability Objectives
                     │
                     ▼
        Engineering + Operations
                     │
      ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
      ▼              ▼              ▼
 Monitoring     Automation     Recovery
      │              │              │
      └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                     ▼
          Continuous Improvement
```

---

# 1. Reliability Philosophy

Reliability is a product feature.

It includes:

```text id="sre02"
Availability

Performance

Correctness

Recoverability

Resilience
```

Reliability should be designed rather than assumed.

---

# 2. Site Reliability Engineering (SRE)

SRE applies software engineering principles to operations.

Objectives include:

```text id="sre03"
Automation

Measurement

Scalability

Reliability

Operational Excellence
```

---

# 3. Reliability as an Architectural Concern

Every architectural decision should consider:

```text id="sre04"
Failure

Recovery

Observability

Scalability
```

Operational behavior is part of architecture.

---

# 4. Shared Ownership

Reliability is jointly owned by:

```text id="sre05"
Engineering

Platform

Security

Operations

Business
```

No single team can ensure reliability independently.

---

# 5. Service Level Indicators (SLIs)

SLIs measure observable behavior.

Examples:

```text id="sre06"
Availability

Latency

Error Rate

Throughput

Freshness
```

SLIs should represent user experience.

---

# 6. Service Level Objectives (SLOs)

Every critical service should define measurable objectives.

Example:

```text id="sre07"
Availability

99.9%

P95 Latency

<300 ms

Error Rate

<0.1%
```

---

# 7. Service Level Agreements (SLAs)

SLAs define contractual commitments.

Unlike SLOs, they include business consequences.

Not every internal service requires an SLA.

---

# 8. Error Budgets

Error budgets balance innovation with stability.

```text id="sre08"
SLO

↓

Allowed Failure

↓

Engineering Decisions
```

Teams exhausting error budgets should prioritize reliability over feature delivery.

---

# 9. Reliability Metrics

Track:

```text id="sre09"
Availability

Latency

Success Rate

MTTR

MTBF
```

Measurements should be automated.

---

# 10. Mean Time to Detect (MTTD)

Measure:

```text id="sre10"
Failure

↓

Detection
```

Reducing detection time improves recovery outcomes.

---

# 11. Mean Time to Respond (MTTRsp)

Measure:

```text id="sre11"
Alert

↓

Response Begins
```

Rapid acknowledgement reduces operational impact.

---

# 12. Mean Time to Recover (MTTR)

Measure:

```text id="sre12"
Failure

↓

Recovery
```

Recovery speed is often more important than preventing every failure.

---

# 13. Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF)

Measure operational stability.

```text id="sre13"
Failure

↓

Normal Operation

↓

Failure
```

Higher MTBF generally indicates greater reliability.

---

# 14. Reliability Budgeting

Engineering capacity should explicitly allocate time for:

```text id="sre14"
Reliability

Technical Debt

Automation

Performance
```

Reliability work should not rely solely on spare capacity.

---

# 15. Automation First

Operational tasks should be automated whenever practical.

Examples:

```text id="sre15"
Deployment

Scaling

Recovery

Monitoring
```

Automation reduces operational variability.

---

# 16. Operational Simplicity

Architectures should minimize unnecessary operational complexity.

Complex systems fail in more ways.

---

# 17. Observability Integration

ADR-078 provides telemetry.

Reliability depends on:

```text id="sre16"
Metrics

Logs

Traces

Events
```

Without observability, reliability cannot be measured.

---

# 18. Alert Philosophy

Alerts should require action.

Avoid alerts that:

```text id="sre17"
Inform Only

Duplicate

Self-Recover
```

Actionable alerts improve operational focus.

---

# 19. Alert Severity

Alerts should distinguish:

```text id="sre18"
Critical

High

Medium

Low
```

Severity determines escalation.

---

# 20. Alert Routing

Alerts should reach the correct responders automatically.

Manual forwarding increases response time.

---

# 21. Operational Dashboards

Dashboards should present:

```text id="sre19"
Availability

Latency

Errors

Capacity

Deployments
```

Operators should understand system health quickly.

---

# 22. Health Model

Service health should include:

```text id="sre20"
Healthy

Degraded

Unavailable
```

Binary up/down status is insufficient.

---

# 23. Readiness vs Availability

A running service is not necessarily ready to serve traffic.

Readiness should reflect actual operational capability.

---

# 24. Operational Readiness Reviews

Before production release verify:

```text id="sre21"
Monitoring

Runbooks

Alerts

Recovery

Ownership
```

---

# 25. Dependency Awareness

Reliability depends on downstream systems.

```text id="sre22"
Application

↓

API

↓

Database

↓

Messaging
```

Dependencies influence SLOs.

---

# 26. Failure Domains

Architectures should isolate failures.

Examples:

```text id="sre23"
Node

Zone

Region

Cluster
```

Smaller failure domains improve resilience.

---

# 27. Redundancy

Critical services should avoid single points of failure.

```text id="sre24"
Replica A

Replica B

Replica C
```

---

# 28. Graceful Degradation

During failures:

```text id="sre25"
Core Features

Remain Available

↓

Noncritical Features

Temporarily Disabled
```

Maintain essential business capability whenever possible.

---

# 29. Fail Fast

Detect failures quickly.

```text id="sre26"
Failure

↓

Immediate Detection

↓

Recovery
```

Waiting rarely improves outcomes.

---

# 30. Retry Strategy

Retries should remain coordinated across the platform.

Uncontrolled retries increase system instability.

---

# ADR-088 — Enterprise Reliability Engineering (SRE), High Availability, Disaster Recovery & Operational Excellence Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Retry Strategy**.

---

# 31. Circuit Breakers

Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures.

```text id="sre31"
Healthy

↓

Failures Increase

↓

Circuit Opens

↓

Requests Rejected

↓

Recovery Check

↓

Closed
```

Applications should fail predictably rather than indefinitely waiting on failing dependencies.

---

# 32. Bulkhead Pattern

Isolate resources so one failure does not consume the entire system.

```text id="sre32"
Service

├── Pool A

├── Pool B

└── Pool C
```

Resource isolation improves overall resilience.

---

# 33. Load Shedding

When demand exceeds capacity:

```text id="sre33"
Incoming Requests

↓

Prioritize

↓

Reject Low Priority

↓

Protect Core Services
```

Serving fewer requests successfully is preferable to failing all requests.

---

# 34. Backpressure

Consumers should communicate when they cannot process additional work.

```text id="sre34"
Producer

↓

Consumer Busy

↓

Slow Down
```

Backpressure prevents uncontrolled queue growth.

---

# 35. Rate Limiting for Reliability

Rate limiting protects infrastructure.

Examples:

```text id="sre35"
Requests/User

Requests/API

Requests/Tenant
```

Rate limits should align with service capacity.

---

# 36. Queue Management

Queues should remain observable.

Track:

```text id="sre36"
Depth

Age

Processing Rate

Retry Rate
```

Growing queues often indicate downstream bottlenecks.

---

# 37. High Availability (HA)

Critical services should tolerate component failures.

```text id="sre37"
Load Balancer

↓

Replica A

Replica B

Replica C
```

No single replica should become a dependency.

---

# 38. Multi-Zone Deployment

Production workloads should span availability zones where supported.

```text id="sre38"
Zone A

Zone B

Zone C
```

Zone failure should not interrupt critical services.

---

# 39. Multi-Region Resilience

Only business-critical systems requiring regional resilience should operate across multiple regions.

Multi-region architecture increases operational complexity.

---

# 40. Disaster Recovery Philosophy

Disaster recovery should be planned before disasters occur.

Recovery procedures require validation through regular exercises.

---

# 41. Recovery Point Objective (RPO)

RPO defines acceptable data loss.

```text id="sre39"
Failure

↓

Maximum Recoverable Data Loss
```

Different systems require different RPOs.

---

# 42. Recovery Time Objective (RTO)

RTO defines acceptable recovery duration.

```text id="sre40"
Failure

↓

Service Restored
```

Recovery targets should align with business criticality.

---

# 43. Backup Validation

Backups should be restored regularly.

```text id="sre41"
Backup

↓

Restore Test

↓

Verification
```

Untested backups cannot be assumed to be usable.

---

# 44. Disaster Recovery Exercises

Conduct regular recovery simulations.

Examples:

```text id="sre42"
Cluster Failure

Database Failure

Region Failure

Network Isolation
```

Exercises improve organizational readiness.

---

# 45. Chaos Engineering

Controlled experiments improve confidence in system resilience.

```text id="sre43"
Inject Failure

↓

Observe

↓

Improve
```

Chaos testing should occur in controlled environments.

---

# 46. Fault Injection

Introduce realistic failures.

Examples:

```text id="sre44"
Latency

Packet Loss

Pod Failure

Disk Failure

Node Failure
```

Experiments should have defined objectives.

---

# 47. Capacity Engineering

Capacity should support expected growth.

Monitor:

```text id="sre45"
CPU

Memory

Storage

Network

Concurrency
```

Capacity planning should be proactive.

---

# 48. Auto-Healing

Infrastructure should recover automatically when appropriate.

```text id="sre46"
Failure

↓

Detection

↓

Restart

↓

Healthy
```

Automation reduces recovery time.

---

Every critical service should have documented operational procedures.

Examples:

```text id="sre47"
Restart

Scaling

Recovery

Certificate Rotation

Rollback
```

---

# 50. On-Call Engineering

Production systems require clearly defined on-call ownership.

Responsibilities include:

```text id="sre48"

Escalation

Recovery

Communication
```

---

```text id="sre49"
↓

Triage

↓

Mitigation

↓

Recovery

↓

Review
```

---

Responsibilities:

```text id="sre50"

Track Status

Manage Communication

Prioritize Actions
```

# 53. Communication

During incidents communicate:

```text id="sre51"
Impact

Current Status

Actions

Estimated Recovery
```

Clear communication reduces uncertainty.

---

```text id="sre52"
Root Cause

Contributing Factors

Corrective Actions

Lessons Learned
```

The objective is systemic improvement rather than assigning blame.

```text id="sre53"
↓

↓

Implementation

↓

Verification
```

```text id="sre54"
Scaling

Certificate Renewal

Backup

Health Validation
```

Automation improves consistency and reduces operational toil.

---

# 57. Operational Toil

```text id="sre55"

Repeated Deployments

Manual Scaling

Log Collection
```

Reducing toil allows engineers to focus on system improvement.

---

# 58. Reliability Reviews

Periodically review:

```text id="sre56"
SLOs

Incidents

Capacity

Risk

Architecture
```

Reliability should evolve continuously.

---

ADR-078 platform engineering should automatically provision:

```text id="sre57"
Alerting

Dashboards

Runbooks

SLO Templates
```

Reliability becomes part of the platform's default capabilities.

# ADR-088 — Enterprise Reliability Engineering (SRE), High Availability, Disaster Recovery & Operational Excellence Standard

# 61. Error Budget Policy

Every production service should define an explicit policy for consuming error budgets.

```text id="sre61"
SLO

↓

Error Budget

↓

Engineering Decision
```

When the error budget is exhausted, engineering effort should prioritize reliability improvements over feature delivery until the service returns within target.

---

# 62. Reliability Governance

Reliability should be reviewed regularly by the Enterprise Reliability Board.

Governance includes:

```text id="sre62"
SLO Compliance

Incident Trends

Capacity

Operational Risk

Technical Debt
```

Reliability becomes a managed business capability.

---

# 63. Reliability Reviews

Review areas include:

```text id="sre63"
Architecture

Operational Readiness

Monitoring

Recovery

Security Dependencies
```

---

# 64. Operational Audits

Operational audits verify that documented practices are followed.

Examples:

```text id="sre64"
Runbooks

On-call Coverage

Backup Validation

Disaster Recovery

Alert Quality
```

---

# 65. Continuous Verification

Production systems should continuously verify critical assumptions.

```text id="sre65"
Health Checks

Synthetic Transactions

Configuration Validation

Dependency Verification
```

Monitoring alone is insufficient.

---

# 66. Synthetic Monitoring

```text id="sre66"
Login

↓

Open Course

↓

Start Assessment

↓

Submit Answers
```

Synthetic tests detect failures before users report them.

---

```text id="sre67"
Latency

Errors

Navigation

Failures
```

```text id="sre68"
Error Rate

Traffic

Deployments

Incidents
```

Dashboards should support both engineering and operations.

---

# 69. Golden Signals

```text id="sre69"
Latency

Traffic

Errors

Saturation
```

These provide a concise operational health overview.

---

# 70. USE Method

Infrastructure monitoring should include:

```text id="sre70"
Utilization

Saturation

Errors
```

The USE method complements application-level metrics.

---

# 71. RED Method

```text id="sre71"
Errors

Duration
```

# 72. Reliability KPIs

```text id="sre73"
Likelihood

Impact

Owner

Mitigation

Review Date
```

```text id="sre74"
↓

Forecast

↓

Provision

↓

Validate
```

Forecasts should account for seasonal demand and business growth.

---

# 75. Reliability Testing

ADR-079 testing extends to operational behavior.

Examples:

```text id="sre75"
Load Testing

Stress Testing

Spike Testing

Endurance Testing

Recovery Testing
```

Reliability should be validated under realistic conditions.

# 76. Resilience Validation

```text id="sre76"

Retries

Failover

Auto-Healing

Load Balancing
```

Controls should be proven rather than assumed.

# 77. Continuous Improvement

```text id="sre77"

↓

Analyze

↓

Improve

↓

Verify

↓

Repeat
```

```text id="sre83"
Cost
```

# 94. Reliability Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text id="sre94"

❌ Untested backups
❌ No disaster recovery exercises
❌ Unlimited retries
❌ Single points of failure
❌ Manual production recovery
❌ Missing runbooks
❌ Blame-focused postmortems
❌ Ignored error budgets
❌ No capacity planning
❌ Hidden operational dependencies
❌ Chaos engineering in production without safeguards
❌ No operational documentation
❌ Reactive scaling only
❌ Reliability treated as an operations-only responsibility
```

# ADR-089 — Enterprise Governance, Architecture Review Board (ARB), Technical Standards, Decision Management & Architecture Compliance Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-089
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Review Board (ARB)

ADR-088 established enterprise reliability engineering.

ADR-089 establishes how architecture is governed, how decisions are made, how standards evolve, and how technical consistency is maintained across Mediverse.

The governing principle is:

> **Architecture is a continuously governed decision-making capability. Governance exists to enable consistent, scalable engineering—not to create bureaucracy.**

```text id="gov01"
             BUSINESS STRATEGY
                    │
                    ▼
          Enterprise Architecture
                    │
                    ▼
         Architecture Governance
                    │
      ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
      ▼             ▼             ▼
 Standards      Reviews      Decisions
      │             │             │
      └─────────────┼─────────────┘
                    ▼
            Continuous Improvement
```

---

# 1. Governance Philosophy

Governance enables engineering.

It provides:

```text id="gov02"
Consistency

Quality

Risk Reduction

Reuse

Long-Term Sustainability
```

Governance should accelerate delivery through clear standards rather than slowing it through unnecessary approvals.

---

# 2. Architecture Review Board (ARB)

The Architecture Review Board governs enterprise architecture.

Responsibilities include:

```text id="gov03"
Architecture Approval

Standards

Technology Direction

Risk Management

Strategic Decisions
```

---

# 3. ARB Membership

The ARB should include representatives from:

```text id="gov04"
Enterprise Architecture

Platform Engineering

Security

Data

Frontend

Backend

SRE

Business
```

Decisions should balance technical and business concerns.

---

# 4. Architecture Principles

Every architectural decision should align with:

```text id="gov05"
Business Value

Security

Scalability

Maintainability

Observability

Automation
```

---

# 5. Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)

All significant architectural decisions require ADRs.

Every ADR should document:

```text id="gov06"
Context

Decision

Alternatives

Consequences

Status
```

---

# 6. ADR Lifecycle

```text id="gov07"
Proposed

↓

Under Review

↓

Accepted

↓

Superseded

↓

Archived
```

Architecture decisions should remain traceable over time.

---

# 7. Decision Ownership

Every ADR should identify:

```text id="gov08"
Decision Owner

Approvers

Review Date

Status
```

Ownership prevents ambiguity.

---

# 8. Decision Traceability

Every major implementation should trace back to one or more ADRs.

```text id="gov09"
Requirement

↓

ADR

↓

Implementation

↓

Verification
```

---

# 9. Architecture Reviews

Major initiatives require formal architecture review before implementation.

Reviews should focus on risk, alignment and long-term sustainability.

---

# 10. Review Triggers

Architecture review is required for:

```text id="gov10"
New Platform

New Technology

Major Refactoring

External Integration

AI Systems

Production Services
```

---

# 11. Review Outcomes

Possible outcomes:

```text id="gov11"
Approved

Approved with Conditions

Deferred

Rejected
```

Every decision should include rationale.

---

# 12. Technical Standards

Enterprise standards define approved engineering practices.

Examples:

```text id="gov12"
Coding

Testing

Deployment

Security

Documentation
```

---

# 13. Standard Lifecycle

```text id="gov13"
Draft

↓

Review

↓

Approved

↓

Published

↓

Retired
```

Standards evolve alongside technology.

---

# 14. Technology Catalog

Maintain an approved catalog of:

```text id="gov14"
Languages

Frameworks

Databases

Messaging

Cloud Services

Developer Tools
```

---

# 15. Technology Classification

Technologies should be categorized.

```text id="gov15"
Strategic

Approved

Trial

Deprecated

Prohibited
```

Classification guides adoption decisions.

---

# 16. Technology Radar

Maintain a technology radar tracking:

```text id="gov16"
Adopt

Trial

Assess

Hold
```

The radar supports informed technology evolution.

---

# 17. Reference Architectures

Provide reusable reference architectures for common solution types.

Examples:

```text id="gov17"
Microservices

AI Platform

Data Platform

Frontend

Analytics
```

---

# 18. Golden Paths

Publish approved implementation patterns.

```text id="gov18"
Spring Boot

React

Kafka

PostgreSQL

Kubernetes
```

Golden paths reduce unnecessary variation.

---

# 19. Reusable Components

Promote reuse through:

```text id="gov19"
Shared Libraries

Templates

Platform APIs

Design System
```

---

# 20. Documentation Governance

Architecture documentation should remain:

```text id="gov20"
Version Controlled

Reviewed

Searchable

Current
```

Documentation is an engineering asset.

---

# 21. Documentation Hierarchy

Maintain a structured hierarchy.

```text id="gov21"
Vision

↓

Architecture

↓

Design

↓

Implementation

↓

Operations
```

---

# 22. Architecture Repository

All ADRs, standards and reference architectures should reside in a centralized repository.

The repository becomes the authoritative architectural knowledge base.

---

# 23. Architecture Compliance

Projects should demonstrate alignment with approved standards.

Compliance should emphasize guidance before enforcement.

---

# 24. Compliance Reviews

Periodic reviews should evaluate:

```text id="gov22"
Architecture

Security

Performance

Reliability

Documentation
```

---

# 25. Exception Management

Exceptions should be formally documented.

Every exception requires:

```text id="gov23"
Business Justification

Risk Assessment

Owner

Expiration Date
```

---

# 26. Waiver Process

Temporary deviations may be approved through waivers.

Waivers should:

```text id="gov24"
Be Time-Bound

Track Risk

Define Exit Plan
```

---

# 27. Risk Governance

Architecture decisions should identify:

```text id="gov25"
Technical Risk

Operational Risk

Business Risk

Security Risk
```

---

# 28. Technical Debt

Technical debt should be visible.

Track:

```text id="gov26"
Description

Impact

Priority

Owner

Target Resolution
```

---

# 29. Architecture Metrics

Measure:

```text id="gov27"
ADR Coverage

Standard Compliance

Technical Debt

Review Time

Exception Count
```

Metrics drive continuous improvement.

---

# 30. Continuous Architecture

Architecture should evolve continuously alongside product development.

Architecture is an ongoing practice rather than a one-time design activity.

With ADR-089 complete, the foundational enterprise architecture series now covers:

* **ADR-076:** Enterprise Data Governance & Information Architecture

* **ADR-080:** Runtime Configuration & Feature Management

These ADRs collectively define a comprehensive enterprise architecture baseline spanning governance, software architecture, platform engineering, security, operations, AI, data, frontend, backend, infrastructure, and organizational decision-making.

Given the enterprise ADR foundation we've built (ADR-076 through ADR-089), I recommend **continuing with ADR-090** as the next major enterprise standard.

Unlike the original uploaded list, this ADR is broader than just "DevOps" or "Git strategy." It governs **how engineering teams build software from idea to production**.

# ADR-090 — Enterprise Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC), Engineering Workflow & Delivery Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-090
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Engineering Excellence Board (EEEB)

ADR-089 established enterprise governance.

ADR-090 establishes the enterprise engineering operating model, defining how software moves from business ideas through planning, implementation, testing, deployment, operation, and continuous improvement.

The governing principle is:

> **Software delivery is a governed, repeatable, measurable engineering process that maximizes business value while ensuring quality, security, reliability, and maintainability.**

```text
Business Idea
      │
      ▼
Product Discovery
      │
      ▼
Architecture
      │
      ▼
Implementation
      │
      ▼
Verification
      │
      ▼
Deployment
      │
      ▼
Operations
      │
      ▼
Continuous Improvement
```

---

# 1. SDLC Philosophy

Software delivery is a continuous lifecycle.

It includes:

```text
Planning

Design

Development

Testing

Deployment

Operations

Feedback
```

Engineering is not complete when software is deployed.

---

# 2. Engineering Principles

Every engineering activity should optimize:

```text
Quality

Automation

Security

Reliability

Developer Experience

Business Value
```

---

# 3. Agile First

Mediverse adopts Agile as the default delivery model.

Supported approaches:

```text
Scrum

Kanban

Scrumban
```

Methodology should serve product delivery rather than become a goal itself.

---

# 4. Product-Driven Development

Engineering work begins with business outcomes.

```text
Business Goal

↓

Capability

↓

Feature

↓

Implementation
```

Technology decisions should support measurable product value.

---

# 5. Product Backlog

All engineering work originates from a managed backlog.

Examples:

```text
Epic

Feature

Story

Bug

Technical Debt

Spike
```

---

# 6. Epic Management

Epics represent large business capabilities.

```text
Epic

↓

Features

↓

Stories
```

Epics should deliver measurable business outcomes.

---

# 7. Feature Definition

Features describe end-user capabilities.

Each feature should define:

```text
Business Value

Acceptance Criteria

Dependencies

Priority
```

---

# 8. User Stories

Stories should follow INVEST principles where practical.

Each story should remain independently deliverable.

---

# 9. Technical Stories

Engineering work includes technical improvements.

Examples:

```text
Refactoring

Performance

Security

Automation

Infrastructure
```

Technical work should remain visible.

---

# 10. Spikes

Spikes reduce uncertainty.

Examples:

```text
Prototype

Research

Technology Evaluation

Performance Experiment
```

---

# 11. Definition of Ready (DoR)

A story is ready when:

```text
Requirements Clear

Acceptance Criteria Defined

Dependencies Known

Estimate Available
```

---

# 12. Definition of Done (DoD)

Work is complete only when:

```text
Code Complete

Tests Pass

Security Checks Pass

Documentation Updated

Reviewed

Deployable
```

---

# 13. Sprint Planning

Planning should define:

```text
Sprint Goal

Committed Work

Risks

Dependencies
```

---

# 14. Daily Collaboration

Teams should synchronize frequently.

Focus:

```text
Progress

Risks

Blockers

Coordination
```

---

# 15. Sprint Review

Completed work should be demonstrated to stakeholders.

Feedback informs future planning.

---

# 16. Sprint Retrospective

Teams continuously improve.

Review:

```text
What Worked

Problems

Actions

Experiments
```

---

# 17. Engineering Estimation

Estimate effort—not guarantees.

Supported methods:

```text
Story Points

T-Shirt Sizes

Relative Estimation
```

---

# 18. Backlog Prioritization

Prioritize using:

```text
Business Value

Risk

Dependencies

Urgency

Technical Impact
```

---

# 19. Release Planning

Releases should align with business milestones.

Deployment frequency and release frequency may differ.

---

# 20. Continuous Delivery

Software should remain deployable at all times.

Deployment should become a routine engineering activity.

---

# 21. Git Workflow

Enterprise Git workflow defines:

```text
Repository

↓

Branch

↓

Commit

↓

Pull Request

↓

Review

↓

Merge
```

---

# 22. Branch Strategy

Preferred long-lived branches:

```text
main

develop (optional)

release (when needed)
```

Feature branches should remain short-lived.

---

# 23. Commit Standards

Commits should be:

```text
Atomic

Traceable

Descriptive
```

Conventional commit messages are recommended.

---

# 24. Pull Requests

Every production change should be introduced through a Pull Request.

Direct commits to protected branches are prohibited.

---

# 25. Code Reviews

Code review evaluates:

```text
Correctness

Maintainability

Security

Performance

Architecture
```

Reviews are collaborative, not approval rituals.

---

# 26. Pair Programming

Pair programming is encouraged for:

```text
Critical Features

Knowledge Transfer

Complex Changes

Onboarding
```

---

# 27. Mob Programming

Mob programming may be used for:

```text
Architecture

Major Refactoring

Incident Resolution
```

---

# 28. Engineering Documentation

Every significant implementation should produce:

```text
ADR

Design Document

API Documentation

Operational Notes
```

---

# 29. Technical Design Documents (TDD)

Complex changes require Technical Design Documents before implementation.

Design review reduces downstream rework.

---

# 30. RFC Process

Major engineering proposals should follow a Request for Comments (RFC) process.

RFCs encourage early collaboration and structured feedback.

---

# ADR-090 — Enterprise Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC), Engineering Workflow & Delivery Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — RFC Process**.

---

# 31. Continuous Integration (CI)

Every code change should automatically trigger validation.

```text
Developer Commit
        │
        ▼
Build
        │
        ▼
Static Analysis
        │
        ▼
Tests
        │
        ▼
Artifact
```

CI should provide rapid feedback to developers.

---

# 32. Continuous Delivery (CD)

Every successful build should produce a deployable artifact.

Deployment approval remains a business decision.

```text
Validated Build
        │
        ▼
Deployable Artifact
        │
        ▼
Environment Promotion
```

---

# 33. Trunk-Based Development

Trunk-Based Development is the preferred engineering model.

Characteristics:

```text
Short-lived Branches

Frequent Merges

Small Changes

Continuous Integration
```

Long-running feature branches should be avoided.

---

# 34. GitFlow

GitFlow may be adopted for products requiring scheduled releases.

```text
main

↓

release

↓

hotfix

↓

feature
```

GitFlow introduces additional coordination and should be used only when justified.

---

# 35. Merge Policies

Protected branches require:

```text
Passing CI

Code Review

Security Checks

No Merge Conflicts
```

Direct force pushes to protected branches are prohibited.

---

# 36. Merge Strategy

Preferred merge strategy:

```text
Feature Branch

↓

Squash Merge

↓

Main
```

This maintains a clean and understandable commit history.

---

# 37. Semantic Versioning

Enterprise releases follow Semantic Versioning.

```text
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH

2.4.7
```

* **MAJOR** — Breaking changes
* **MINOR** — Backward-compatible features
* **PATCH** — Bug fixes

---

# 38. Release Trains

Where multiple teams contribute to the same product, scheduled release trains are preferred.

```text
Sprint

↓

Integration

↓

Release Train

↓

Production
```

Release cadence should be predictable.

---

# 39. Hotfix Process

Critical production issues require an expedited workflow.

```text
Incident

↓

Hotfix Branch

↓

Validation

↓

Production

↓

Merge Back
```

Hotfixes must be merged back into the main development line.

---

# 40. Feature Flags

ADR-080 governs runtime feature management.

Feature flags enable:

```text
Progressive Rollout

A/B Testing

Emergency Disable

Beta Features
```

Features should not remain permanently hidden behind stale flags.

---

# 41. Release Notes

Every release should include:

```text
Features

Bug Fixes

Breaking Changes

Known Issues

Migration Steps
```

Release notes improve transparency for stakeholders.

---

# 42. Environment Strategy

Standard environments include:

```text
Local

↓

Development

↓

Integration

↓

Testing

↓

Staging

↓

Production
```

Each environment has a defined purpose.

---

# 43. Developer Workstations

Developer environments should be reproducible.

Requirements:

```text
Containerized Development

Standard Toolchain

Automated Setup

Version Consistency
```

---

# 44. Development Containers

# ADR-091 — Enterprise DevOps, CI/CD, Release Engineering & Software Supply Chain Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-091
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise DevOps & Platform Engineering Board (EDPEB)

ADR-090 established the Enterprise Software Development Lifecycle.

ADR-091 defines the enterprise DevOps architecture, Continuous Integration (CI), Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD), Release Engineering, Artifact Management, and Software Supply Chain standards that transform source code into trusted production software.

The governing principle is:

> **Every production artifact must be reproducible, traceable, verifiable, secure, and automatically delivered through standardized pipelines. Software delivery is treated as an engineering product rather than a collection of manual activities.**

```text id="devops01"
Developer
    │
    ▼
Source Code
    │
    ▼
Continuous Integration
    │
    ▼
Quality & Security
    │
    ▼
Artifact Repository
    │
    ▼
Continuous Delivery
    │
    ▼
GitOps
    │
    ▼
Production
```

---

# 1. DevOps Philosophy

DevOps integrates development, platform engineering, security, quality engineering, and operations into a continuous delivery model.

Goals:

```text id="devops02"
Automation

Quality

Speed

Reliability

Security

Feedback
```

DevOps optimizes the entire software value stream.

---

# 2. Continuous Everything

Every engineering activity should be automated where practical.

```text id="devops03"
Continuous Integration

Continuous Testing

Continuous Security

Continuous Delivery

Continuous Monitoring

Continuous Improvement
```

Automation reduces variability and accelerates feedback.

---

# 3. Pipeline as Product

CI/CD pipelines are enterprise platform products.

They should be:

```text id="devops04"
Reusable

Versioned

Observable

Secure

Self-Service
```

---

# 4. Pipeline Architecture

Standard delivery flow:

```text id="devops05"
Source

↓

Build

↓

Test

↓

Security

↓

Package

↓

Publish

↓

Deploy

↓

Verify
```

Every stage should be deterministic.

---

# 5. Source Control Integration

Every pipeline begins from version-controlled source.

Supported repositories:

```text id="devops06"
GitHub

GitLab

Azure DevOps
```

The Git repository is the single source of truth for application code.

---

# 6. Build Triggers

Pipeline execution may be triggered by:

```text id="devops07"
Commit

Pull Request

Merge

Tag

Release

Manual Approval
```

Trigger selection should align with the delivery workflow.

---

# 7. Build Reproducibility

Builds should produce identical outputs from identical inputs.

Requirements:

```text id="devops08"
Pinned Dependencies

Versioned Tools

Immutable Build Environment
```

---

# 8. Build Isolation

Each pipeline execution should run in an isolated environment.

```text id="devops09"
Pipeline

↓

Ephemeral Runner

↓

Dispose
```

Shared mutable build environments should be avoided.

---

# 9. Build Systems

Approved build systems include:

```text id="devops10"
Maven

Gradle

npm

pnpm
```

Tool selection should follow enterprise technology standards.

---

# 10. Dependency Resolution

Dependencies should originate from approved repositories.

```text id="devops11"
Source

↓

Repository Manager

↓

Build
```

Direct internet downloads during production builds should be minimized.

---

# 11. Artifact Philosophy

Artifacts are immutable.

Examples:

```text id="devops12"
JAR

WAR

Docker Image

Helm Chart
```

Artifacts should never be modified after publication.

---

# 12. Artifact Repositories

Approved repositories include:

```text id="devops13"
Nexus

JFrog Artifactory

GitHub Packages
```

Artifacts require centralized lifecycle management.

---

# 13. Artifact Versioning

Every artifact should include:

```text id="devops14"
Version

Commit SHA

Build Number

Timestamp
```

Traceability is mandatory.

---

# 14. Build Metadata

Each build should record:

```text id="devops15"
Source Revision

Pipeline Version

Builder Identity

Dependencies

Environment
```

Metadata supports auditing and troubleshooting.

---

# 15. Docker Image Standards

Container images should:

```text id="devops16"
Be Minimal

Be Immutable

Be Versioned

Be Scanned

Be Signed
```

Image construction should follow enterprise security standards.

---

# 16. Base Images

Only approved base images may be used.

Criteria:

```text id="devops17"
Supported

Minimal

Secure

Frequently Updated
```

---

# 17. Multi-Stage Builds

Multi-stage Docker builds are preferred.

Benefits:

```text id="devops18"
Smaller Images

Reduced Attack Surface

Cleaner Artifacts
```

---

# 18. Helm Packaging

Kubernetes applications should be packaged using Helm.

Helm charts should be version-controlled and released alongside applications.

---

# 19. Build Caching

Caching may improve build performance.

Examples:

```text id="devops19"
Maven Cache

Gradle Cache

npm Cache

Docker Layers
```

Caches should not compromise build reproducibility.

---

# 20. Pipeline Observability

Pipelines should expose:

```text id="devops20"
Duration

Success Rate

Failure Rate

Queue Time

Stage Metrics
```

Pipeline health is an engineering metric.

---

# 21. Quality Gates

Every pipeline should evaluate:

```text id="devops21"
Compilation

Tests

Code Quality

Security

Coverage
```

Quality gates prevent defective software from progressing.

---

# 22. Static Analysis

Static analysis should execute automatically.

Examples:

```text id="devops22"
SonarQube

Linting

Formatting

Complexity Analysis
```

---

# 23. Test Automation

Testing integrates with ADR-079.

Pipeline stages should include:

```text id="devops23"
Unit Tests

Integration Tests

Contract Tests

Smoke Tests
```

---

# 24. Security Integration

ADR-086 security controls execute automatically.

Pipeline should include:

```text id="devops24"
SAST

SCA

Secret Scan

SBOM

Artifact Signing
```

---

# 25. Pipeline Failure Policy

Pipeline failures should stop promotion.

```text id="devops25"
Failure

↓

Notify

↓

Investigate

↓

Fix

↓

Rebuild
```

Failed quality gates should not be bypassed except through governed emergency procedures.

---

# 26. Notifications

Pipeline events should notify appropriate stakeholders.

Examples:

```text id="devops26"
Build Failure

Deployment Complete

Security Findings

Release Created
```

---

# 27. Parallel Execution

Independent stages should execute in parallel where appropriate.

```text id="devops27"
Build
   ├── Tests
   ├── Security
   └── Quality
```

Parallelism reduces delivery time.

---

# 28. Pipeline Templates

Reusable pipeline templates should be published by Platform Engineering.

Templates improve consistency and reduce duplicated configuration.

---

# 29. Self-Service Pipelines

Developers should provision pipelines without manual platform intervention.

Self-service accelerates onboarding and delivery.

---

# 30. Enterprise Integration

ADR-091 integrates with:

```text id="devops28"
ADR-078 Platform Engineering

ADR-079 Testing

ADR-086 Security

ADR-087 Infrastructure

ADR-090 SDLC
```

The DevOps platform operationalizes the enterprise software delivery lifecycle.

---

# ADR-091 — Enterprise DevOps, CI/CD, Release Engineering & Software Supply Chain Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Enterprise Integration**.

---

# 31. Release Engineering Philosophy

Release engineering transforms validated artifacts into reliable production releases.

Objectives:

```text id="devops31"
Repeatability

Reliability

Traceability

Automation

Recoverability
```

Releases should be engineered, not manually assembled.

---

# 32. Release Lifecycle

Every release follows a standard lifecycle.

```text id="devops32"
Build

↓

Validate

↓

Package

↓

Promote

↓

Deploy

↓

Verify

↓

Operate
```

Each stage should generate auditable evidence.

---

# 33. Environment Promotion

Artifacts move through controlled environments.

```text id="devops33"
Development

↓

Integration

↓

Testing

↓

Staging

↓

Production
```

Artifacts are promoted, never rebuilt.

---

# 34. Artifact Promotion

The exact same artifact should progress across environments.

```text id="devops34"
Artifact

↓

QA

↓

Staging

↓

Production
```

Rebuilding between environments is prohibited.

---

# 35. Release Candidates

Candidate releases should undergo production-like validation.

Requirements:

```text id="devops35"
Functional Validation

Security

Performance

Compatibility
```

---

# 36. GitOps Deployment

ADR-087 governs deployment.

Deployment flow:

```text id="devops36"
Git

↓

ArgoCD / Flux

↓

Cluster

↓

Running Application
```

Git remains the desired-state authority.

---

# 37. Deployment Strategies

Supported deployment models:

```text id="devops37"
Rolling

Blue-Green

Canary

Recreate
```

Strategy selection depends on workload characteristics.

---

# 38. Progressive Delivery

Traffic should shift gradually.

```text id="devops38"
Deploy

↓

Observe

↓

Increase Traffic

↓

Complete
```

Promotion depends on observed health.

---

# 39. Blue-Green Releases

Maintain two production environments.

```text id="devops39"
Blue

↓

Validation

↓

Switch

↓

Green
```

Rollback should be immediate.

---

# 40. Canary Releases

Expose new versions incrementally.

```text id="devops40"
1%

↓

5%

↓

20%

↓

50%

↓

100%
```

Traffic increases should depend on health metrics.

---

# 41. Deployment Verification

Every deployment should validate:

```text id="devops41"
Availability

Latency

Error Rate

Health Checks
```

Verification determines deployment success.

---

# 42. Automated Rollback

Rollback should occur automatically for predefined failure conditions.

```text id="devops42"
Deploy

↓

Health Check

↓

Failure

↓

Rollback
```

---

# 43. Manual Rollback

Manual rollback procedures should exist for complex operational scenarios.

Runbooks should define the required steps.

---

# 44. Deployment Windows

Organizations may define deployment windows based on business requirements.

Emergency releases should follow an expedited but governed workflow.

---

# 45. Release Approvals

Production deployment approvals should be risk-based.

Examples:

```text id="devops43"
Low Risk

Automated

Medium Risk

Engineering Approval

High Risk

Business Approval
```

---

# 46. Change Records

Every production release should record:

```text id="devops44"
Version

Approver

Deployment Time

Rollback Plan

Associated ADRs
```

---

# 47. Deployment Audit Trail

Deployment history should include:

```text id="devops45"
Who

What

When

Where

Result
```

Audit information supports compliance and incident analysis.

---

# 48. Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)

ADR-086 requires SBOM generation.

Pipeline flow:

```text id="devops46"
Source

↓

Build

↓

SBOM

↓

Artifact
```

SBOMs should accompany released artifacts.

---

# 49. Artifact Provenance

Every artifact should record:

```text id="devops47"
Commit

Builder

Pipeline

Dependencies

Timestamp
```

Provenance strengthens supply chain integrity.

---

# 50. Artifact Signing

Production artifacts should be digitally signed.

```text id="devops48"
Artifact

↓

Sign

↓

Repository

↓

Verification
```

Unsigned artifacts should not be deployed.

---

# 51. Image Verification

Deployment should verify:

```text id="devops49"
Signature

Integrity

Trusted Source
```

Verification occurs before runtime.

---

# 52. Supply Chain Security

Software supply chain controls include:

```text id="devops50"
Trusted Source

Verified Build

SBOM

Signing

Policy Validation
```

Supply chain integrity extends beyond source code.

---

# 53. Release Governance

Governance evaluates:

```text id="devops51"
Quality

Security

Compliance

Risk

Approval
```

Release readiness should be evidence-based.

---

# 54. Multi-Environment Management

Environment configuration should remain externalized.

```text id="devops52"
Application

↓

Configuration

↓

Environment
```

Configuration changes should not require rebuilding artifacts.

---

# 55. Deployment Metrics

Representative deployment metrics:

```text id="devops53"
Deployment Time

Rollback Rate

Failure Rate

Recovery Time
```

Metrics support continuous improvement.

---

# 56. Release Dashboards

Dashboards should display:

```text id="devops54"
Pipeline Status

Release History

Deployment Health

Failures

Approvals
```

Visibility improves operational awareness.

---

# 57. DevOps KPIs

Track:

```text id="devops55"
Deployment Frequency

Pipeline Success Rate

Lead Time

Rollback Frequency

Release Duration
```

These complement the DORA metrics defined in ADR-090.

---

# 58. Platform Automation

The platform should automate:

```text id="devops56"
Pipeline Creation

Artifact Publishing

Release Notes

Approvals

Notifications
```

Automation improves consistency and reduces manual effort.

---

# 59. Release Operating Model

```text id="devops57"
Source Code

↓

CI Pipeline

↓

Quality Gates

↓

Artifact Repository

↓

GitOps

↓

Production

↓

Monitoring
```

The release operating model standardizes software promotion from source code to production.

---

# 60. Enterprise Integration

ADR-091 integrates with:

```text id="devops58"
ADR-078 Platform Engineering

ADR-079 Testing

ADR-080 Runtime
```

Release engineering connects software development with secure, observable and reliable production operations.

# 61. Enterprise DevOps Organization

DevOps is an organizational capability rather than a standalone team.

Engineering responsibilities include:

```text id="devops61"
Application Teams

↓

Platform Engineering

↓

SRE

↓

Security

↓

Operations
```

Shared ownership improves delivery and operational outcomes.

---

# 62. Platform Engineering Ownership

ADR-078 establishes Platform Engineering as the owner of reusable delivery capabilities.

Responsibilities include:

```text id="devops62"
CI/CD Platform

Pipeline Templates

Developer Portal

Golden Paths

Self-Service
```

Application teams consume platform capabilities instead of building them independently.

---

# 63. Pipeline Governance

Enterprise pipelines should follow approved standards.

Governance covers:

```text id="devops63"
Security

Quality

Compliance

Traceability

Versioning
```

Pipelines themselves are governed software assets.

---

# 64. Pipeline Versioning

Pipeline definitions should be version-controlled.

```text id="devops64"
Pipeline

↓

Version

↓

Release

↓

Migration
```

Pipeline changes should be reviewed like application code.

---

# 65. Reusable Pipeline Components

Common pipeline stages should be reusable.

Examples:

```text id="devops65"
Build

Test

Security Scan

SBOM

Deployment
```

Reuse improves consistency and reduces maintenance effort.

---

# 66. Self-Service Delivery

Developers should provision delivery pipelines through standardized templates.

```text id="devops66"
Repository

↓

Template

↓

Pipeline

↓

Deployment
```

Manual ticket-based provisioning should be minimized.

---

# 67. Policy as Code

Deployment policies should be executable.

Examples:

```text id="devops67"
Branch Protection

Quality Gates

Security Policies

Approval Rules
```

Policy enforcement should be automated.

---

# 68. Multi-Repository Coordination

Complex products may require coordinated releases across repositories.

Governance should define:

```text id="devops68"
Dependencies

Release Order

Compatibility

Version Alignment
```

---

# 69. Monorepo vs Polyrepo

Both repository strategies are supported.

Selection depends on:

```text id="devops69"
Team Size

Architecture

Release Independence

Tooling
```

Repository structure should align with organizational needs.

---

# 70. Multi-Cluster GitOps

GitOps controllers should manage multiple Kubernetes clusters.

```text id="devops70"
Git

↓

GitOps

↓

Cluster B

Cluster C
```

Desired state remains centralized while execution is distributed.

---

# 71. Multi-Region Releases

Global deployments should support coordinated regional rollout.

```text id="devops71"

↓

Region 2

↓

Region 3
```

Regional deployment order should reduce business risk.

---

# 72. Deployment Policy Engine

The deployment platform should evaluate:

```text id="devops72"
Environment

Risk

Approval

Compliance

Health
```

Deployment decisions should be policy-driven.

---

# 73. Release Scheduling

Release cadence should balance:

```text id="devops73"
Business Value

Operational Risk

Customer Impact
```

Continuous deployment does not require continuous feature exposure.

---

# 74. Configuration Promotion

Configuration should follow controlled promotion.

```text id="devops74"
Development

↓

Testing

↓

Staging

↓

Production
```

Configuration drift should be minimized.

---

# 75. Infrastructure Promotion

Infrastructure changes should follow the same promotion principles as application releases.

Infrastructure should not bypass engineering governance.

---

# 76. Release Communication

Production releases should communicate:

```text id="devops75"
Scope

Risk

Timeline

Rollback Plan

Support Contacts
```

Communication improves operational coordination.

# 77. Deployment Freeze

Examples:

```text id="devops76"
Major Business Events

Regulatory Windows
```

```text id="devops77"

Rapid Validation

↓

Approval

↓

Deployment

↓

Post Review
```

Expedited delivery should remain auditable.

---

# 79. Value Stream Management

DevOps should optimize the complete engineering value stream.

Measure:

```text id="devops78"
Lead Time

Queue Time

Cycle Time

Deployment Time
```

Optimization should target the entire workflow rather than individual stages.

---

# 80. Flow Efficiency

Reduce waiting between engineering stages.

```text id="devops79"
Work

↓

Minimal Waiting

↓

Continuous Flow
```

Flow efficiency often has greater impact than isolated stage optimization.

---

# 81. AI-Assisted DevOps

ADR-077 enables AI support for delivery operations.

Examples:

```text id="devops80"
Pipeline Analysis

Failure Diagnosis

Release Notes

Dependency Updates

Risk Summaries
```

AI recommendations should remain reviewable by engineers.

# 82. Deployment Intelligence

Use operational telemetry to guide deployment decisions.

```text id="devops81"
Metrics

↓

Analysis

↓

Promotion Decision
```

Health data should influence release progression.

---

# 83. DevOps Documentation

Maintain documentation for:

```text id="devops82"
Pipelines

Templates

Runbooks

Release Procedures

Recovery
```

Documentation should evolve alongside the platform.

---

# 84. Release Runbooks

Every production release should have documented operational procedures.

Include:

```text id="devops83"
Deployment

Verification

Rollback

Escalation
```

Representative KPIs:

KPIs should support continuous improvement.

Mediverse rejects:

```text id="devops86"

❌ Direct kubectl changes in production
❌ Pipeline secrets stored in source code
❌ Unsigned production artifacts
❌ Missing rollback procedures
❌ Unversioned pipelines
❌ Environment-specific application binaries
❌ Manual release notes
❌ Bypassing quality gates
❌ Deploying without verification
❌ Pipeline ownership ambiguity
❌ Untracked release changes
```

# ADR-092 — Enterprise Quality Engineering, Test Automation & Verification Architecture Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-092
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Quality Engineering Board (EQEB)

ADR-091 established the Enterprise DevOps & Release Engineering architecture.

ADR-092 establishes the enterprise Quality Engineering (QE) strategy, defining how Mediverse verifies software quality continuously across the Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC), CI/CD pipelines, production environments, and operational feedback loops.

The governing principle is:

> **Quality is continuously engineered into software through automated verification, measurable quality objectives, risk-based testing, and continuous feedback. Testing is one activity within a broader Quality Engineering discipline.**

```text id="qe01"
Business Requirement
        │
        ▼
Architecture
        │
        ▼
Development
        │
        ▼
Quality Engineering
        │
        ▼
CI/CD Verification
        │
        ▼
Deployment
        │
        ▼
Production Validation
        │
        ▼
Continuous Improvement
```

---

# 1. Quality Engineering Philosophy

Quality Engineering extends beyond software testing.

It encompasses:

```text id="qe02"
Prevention

Verification

Validation

Measurement

Continuous Improvement
```

Quality should be designed into systems rather than inspected in after implementation.

---

# 2. Quality as a Shared Responsibility

Quality is owned collectively by:

```text id="qe03"
Product

Engineering

QA

Platform

Security

SRE
```

No single team should act as the sole gatekeeper for quality.

---

# 3. Shift-Left Testing

Quality activities should begin as early as possible.

```text id="qe04"
Requirements

↓

Architecture

↓

Development

↓

Testing
```

Early defect detection reduces cost and delivery risk.

---

# 4. Shift-Right Testing

Quality verification continues after deployment.

Examples:

```text id="qe05"
Synthetic Monitoring

Canary Analysis

Feature Flags

Production Observability
```

Production is an additional source of validation, not the first.

---

# 5. Continuous Quality

Quality verification should occur throughout the SDLC.

```text id="qe06"
Code

↓

Build

↓

Test

↓

Deploy

↓

Observe
```

Continuous verification replaces isolated testing phases.

---

# 6. Risk-Based Testing

Testing effort should align with business and technical risk.

Consider:

```text id="qe07"
Business Impact

Probability

Complexity

Security Exposure
```

Critical capabilities require proportionally greater verification.

---

# 7. Test Strategy

Every major product should define a documented test strategy.

It should identify:

```text id="qe08"
Scope

Objectives

Approach

Automation

Risks
```

---

# 8. Test Planning

Test planning should occur before implementation.

Planning includes:

```text id="qe09"
Objectives

Coverage

Environment

Data

Responsibilities
```

---

# 9. Verification vs Validation

Verification asks:

```text id="qe10"
Did we build the system correctly?
```

Validation asks:

```text id="qe11"
Did we build the correct system?
```

Both are required.

---

# 10. Quality Gates

Every delivery pipeline should evaluate:

```text id="qe12"
Compilation

Tests

Coverage

Security

Quality Rules
```

Failed quality gates prevent promotion.

---

# 11. Test Pyramid

The enterprise testing strategy follows the Test Pyramid.

```text id="qe13"
        UI Tests
           ▲
Integration Tests
           ▲
     Unit Tests
```

Automation should emphasize lower, faster, and more isolated test layers.

---

# 12. Test Trophy

Some products may adopt the Test Trophy approach.

```text id="qe14"
Static Analysis

↓

Unit Tests

↓

Integration Tests

↓

End-to-End Tests
```

Selection depends on system characteristics.

---

# 13. Unit Testing

Unit tests verify isolated business logic.

Characteristics:

```text id="qe15"
Fast

Deterministic

Independent

Automated
```

---

# 14. Integration Testing

Integration tests verify collaboration between components.

Examples:

```text id="qe16"
API + Database

API + Queue

Service + Cache
```

---

# 15. Contract Testing

Contract testing validates service interactions.

```text id="qe17"
Consumer

⇄

Contract

⇄

Provider
```

Contracts reduce integration failures between independently deployed services.

---

# 16. End-to-End Testing

End-to-end tests validate complete business workflows.

Examples:

```text id="qe18"
Login

↓

Course Enrollment

↓

Assessment

↓

Certification
```

They should focus on critical user journeys rather than exhaustive coverage.

---

# 17. Smoke Testing

Smoke tests confirm basic application health after deployment.

Typical checks:

```text id="qe19"
Application Starts

Health Endpoint

Database Connection

Core API
```

---

# 18. Sanity Testing

Sanity tests verify that recent changes behave as expected without executing the entire regression suite.

---

# 19. Regression Testing

Regression testing ensures previously working functionality remains correct.

Regression suites should evolve with the product.

---

# 20. Test Automation

Automation should be the default approach.

```text id="qe20"
Manual

↓

Automated

↓

Continuous
```

Manual testing should focus on exploratory and exceptional scenarios.

---

# 21. Automation Principles

Test automation should be:

```text id="qe21"
Reliable

Maintainable

Repeatable

Independent
```

Automation that produces inconsistent results reduces confidence.

---

# 22. Test Isolation

Tests should execute independently.

Avoid:

```text id="qe22"
Shared State

Execution Order Dependencies

External Side Effects
```

Independent tests improve repeatability.

---

# 23. Deterministic Testing

Tests should produce consistent results under the same conditions.

Flaky tests require investigation and remediation.

---

# 24. Test Naming

Test names should clearly describe expected behavior.

Example format:

```text id="qe23"
Given

When

Then
```

Readable test names improve maintainability.

---

# 25. Test Data Management

Test data should be managed intentionally.

Sources include:

```text id="qe24"
Synthetic Data

Anonymized Production Data

Generated Data
```

Sensitive production data should not be exposed in test environments.

---

# 26. Test Environment Strategy

Standard environments include:

```text id="qe25"
Local

↓

Development

↓

Integration

↓

Staging

↓

Production
```

Each environment supports a defined verification objective.

---

# 27. Environment Parity

Higher environments should resemble production as closely as practical.

Configuration drift increases testing risk.

---

# 28. Mocking Strategy

Use mocks appropriately for isolated testing.

Examples:

```text id="qe26"
External APIs

Payment Gateways

Messaging Systems
```

Overuse of mocks may reduce confidence in integration behavior.

---

# 29. Test Doubles

Supported test doubles include:

```text id="qe27"
Mocks

Stubs

Spies

Fakes
```

Select the appropriate test double based on the testing objective.

---

# 30. Enterprise Integration

ADR-092 integrates with:

```text id="qe28"
ADR-078 Platform Engineering

ADR-079 Testing Standards

ADR-086 Security

ADR-090 SDLC

ADR-091 DevOps
```

Quality Engineering becomes a continuous capability spanning development, delivery, deployment, and operations.

---

# ADR-092 — Enterprise Quality Engineering, Test Automation & Verification Architecture Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Enterprise Integration**.

---

# 31. Performance Engineering

Performance should be engineered continuously rather than evaluated only before release.

Quality attributes include:

```text id="qe31"
Latency

Throughput

Scalability

Resource Efficiency

Stability
```

Performance requirements should be defined during system design.

---

# 32. Load Testing

Load testing verifies expected production workload.

```text id="qe32"
Normal Users

↓

Expected Load

↓

Performance Validation
```

Load tests confirm that the system meets defined Service Level Objectives (SLOs).

---

# 33. Stress Testing

Stress testing evaluates behavior beyond expected capacity.

```text id="qe33"
Expected Load

↓

Peak Load

↓

Breaking Point

↓

Recovery
```

The objective is to understand system limits and recovery characteristics.

---

# 34. Spike Testing

Spike testing evaluates sudden traffic increases.

Examples:

```text id="qe34"
Flash Sale

Exam Start

Registration Opening

Breaking News
```

Systems should degrade predictably under sudden demand.

---

# 35. Endurance Testing

Endurance testing validates long-running system stability.

```text id="qe35"
Continuous Load

↓

Hours / Days

↓

Performance Stability
```

Memory leaks and resource exhaustion often emerge during extended execution.

---

# 36. Scalability Testing

Scalability testing evaluates growth behavior.

```text id="qe36"
Users ↑

↓

Resources ↑

↓

Performance
```

Scaling characteristics should align with architectural expectations.

---

# 37. Capacity Testing

Capacity testing determines maximum sustainable workload.

Measure:

```text id="qe37"
Concurrent Users

Transactions

Requests

Storage Growth
```

Capacity planning should use measured evidence.

---

# 38. API Testing

Every public API should undergo automated verification.

Validate:

```text id="qe38"
Correctness

Status Codes

Contracts

Error Handling

Latency
```

API testing integrates with ADR-082.

---

# 39. Database Testing

Database validation includes:

```text id="qe39"
Schema

Constraints

Transactions

Indexes

Performance
```

Persistence correctness is part of application quality.

---

# 40. Security Testing

ADR-086 governs security verification.

Quality Engineering integrates:

```text id="qe40"
Authentication

Authorization

Input Validation

Session Handling

Security Regression
```

Security testing should be automated where practical.

---

# 41. Accessibility Testing

Applications should verify accessibility requirements.

Representative areas:

```text id="qe41"
Keyboard Navigation

Screen Readers

Color Contrast

Focus Management
```

Accessibility should be considered throughout development rather than after implementation.

---

# 42. Cross-Browser Testing

Frontend applications should verify compatibility across supported browsers.

Examples:

```text id="qe42"
Chrome

Firefox

Edge

Safari
```

Browser support should follow documented product requirements.

---

# 43. Responsive Testing

Applications should validate supported screen sizes.

```text id="qe43"
Desktop

Tablet

Mobile
```

Responsive behavior should be verified automatically where possible.

---

# 44. Mobile Testing

Mobile experiences should validate:

```text id="qe44"

Navigation

Touch Interaction

Offline Behavior
```

Testing should reflect supported devices and operating systems.

---

# 45. Mutation Testing

Mutation testing measures test effectiveness.

```text id="qe45"
Code Mutation

↓

Execute Tests

↓

Mutation Score
```

A surviving mutation indicates potential gaps in the test suite.

---

# 46. Code Coverage

Coverage is a supporting metric—not a quality objective.

Measure:

```text id="qe46"

Branch Coverage

Function Coverage
```

High coverage does not guarantee meaningful verification.

---

# 47. Quality Coverage

Quality coverage should evaluate:

```text id="qe47"

Security

Performance

Integration

Recovery
```

Coverage should extend beyond source code metrics.

---

# 48. Continuous Verification

Verification continues after deployment.

```text id="qe48"
Deployment

↓

Health Checks

↓

Synthetic Monitoring

↓

Observability
```

Continuous verification complements pre-release testing.

---

# 49. Production Testing

Limited production validation may include:

```text id="qe49"
Smoke Tests

Canary Verification

Feature Flags

Health Validation
```

Production testing should minimize customer impact.

---

# 50. Synthetic Monitoring

Synthetic transactions verify critical business flows.

Examples:

```text id="qe50"
Login

Course Search

Assessment

Certificate Download
```

Synthetic monitoring supports early detection of production issues.

---

# 51. Test Reporting

Test execution should produce standardized reports.

Include:

```text id="qe51"
Executed Tests

Failures

Coverage

Duration

Environment
```

Reports should be retained for trend analysis.

---

# 52. Quality Dashboards

Dashboards should present:

```text id="qe52"
Pass Rate

Coverage

Pipeline Health

Defects

Quality Trends
```

Dashboards improve engineering visibility.

---

# 53. Defect Lifecycle

Every defect should follow a managed lifecycle.

```text id="qe53"
Reported

↓

Triaged

↓

Assigned

↓

Fixed

↓

Verified

↓

Closed
```

Defect management should support traceability.

---

# 54. Defect Severity

Representative severity levels:

```text id="qe54"
Critical

High

Medium

Low
```

Severity reflects technical impact.

---

# 55. Defect Priority

Priority determines implementation order.

Examples:

```text id="qe55"
Immediate

High

Normal

Deferred
```

Priority should consider business impact alongside technical severity.

---

# 56. Test Governance

Quality governance should review:

```text id="qe56"
Coverage

Automation

Defect Trends

Risk

Quality Objectives
```

Governance supports continuous improvement rather than policing teams.

---

# 57. AI-Assisted Testing

ADR-077 enables AI support for quality engineering.

Examples:

```text id="qe57"
Test Generation

Test Data

Regression Analysis

Failure Summaries

Coverage Suggestions
```

AI-generated artifacts should be reviewed before adoption.

---

# 58. Quality KPIs

Representative KPIs:

```text id="qe58"
Defect Escape Rate

Automation Coverage

Regression Pass Rate

Test Duration

Production Defects
```

KPIs should encourage sustainable quality improvements.

---

# 59. Enterprise Verification Model

```text id="qe59"
Requirements

↓

Design

↓

Implementation

↓

Verification

↓

Deployment

↓

Continuous Validation
```

Verification becomes a continuous engineering capability.

---

# 60. Enterprise Integration

ADR-092 integrates with:

```text id="qe60"
ADR-078 Platform Engineering
```

# 61. Enterprise Quality Organization

```text id="qe61"
↓

↓

Security
```

Dedicated Quality Engineers enable engineering teams rather than acting as independent gatekeepers.

Core principles:

```text id="qe62"
Ownership

Prevention

Automation
```
