# ADR-093 — Enterprise Domain-Driven Design (DDD), Strategic Design, Tactical Design & Product Architecture Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-093
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Architecture Board (EAB)

ADR-092 established the Enterprise Quality Engineering architecture.

ADR-093 establishes the enterprise Domain-Driven Design (DDD) standard, defining how Mediverse models business domains, organizes software architecture, and aligns engineering with business capabilities.

The governing principle is:

> **Software architecture should reflect the business domain. Domain models—not databases, frameworks, or infrastructure—should drive system design.**

```text id="ddd01"
Business Vision
       │
       ▼
Business Domains
       │
       ▼
Bounded Contexts
       │
       ▼
Domain Models
       │
       ▼
Applications
       │
       ▼
Infrastructure
```

---

# 1. Domain-Driven Design Philosophy

Domain-Driven Design prioritizes business understanding over technical implementation.

Core focus:

```text id="ddd02"
Business Knowledge

Domain Model

Collaboration

Continuous Refinement
```

The domain model becomes the primary representation of business behavior.

---

# 2. Business-First Architecture

Architecture should emerge from business capabilities.

```text id="ddd03"
Business Capability

↓

Domain

↓

Software Architecture
```

Technology choices should support the business model.

---

# 3. Strategic Design

Strategic design identifies:

```text id="ddd04"
Domains

Subdomains

Bounded Contexts

Relationships
```

Strategic design establishes the high-level architecture.

---

# 4. Domain Discovery

Discover domains through collaboration.

Participants include:

```text id="ddd05"
Business Experts

Product Owners

Architects

Engineers
```

Business knowledge is essential for accurate domain modeling.

---

# 5. Core Domain

The Core Domain provides competitive differentiation.

Examples for Mediverse:

```text id="ddd06"
Learning

Assessment

Adaptive Education

AI Tutoring
```

The Core Domain receives the highest engineering investment.

---

# 6. Supporting Domains

Supporting domains enable the Core Domain.

Examples:

```text id="ddd07"
Notifications

Reporting

Scheduling

Search
```

Supporting domains should remain modular and reusable.

---

# 7. Generic Domains

Generic domains provide common enterprise capabilities.

Examples:

```text id="ddd08"
Authentication

Email

Payments

Logging
```

These are often implemented using established platforms or services.

---

# 8. Bounded Contexts

Every domain should define clear boundaries.

```text id="ddd09"
Domain

↓

Bounded Context

↓

Model

↓

Implementation
```

Each bounded context owns its model and business rules.

---

# 9. Ubiquitous Language

Business and engineering should share a common vocabulary.

Examples:

```text id="ddd10"
Student

Course

Assessment

Instructor

Enrollment
```

Terms should have a single agreed meaning within a bounded context.

---

# 10. Context Mapping

Relationships between bounded contexts should be explicitly documented.

```text id="ddd11"
Learning

⇄

Assessment

⇄

Certification
```

Context maps clarify ownership and integration.

---

# 11. Context Relationships

Supported relationships include:

```text id="ddd12"
Customer/Supplier

Partnership

Conformist

Shared Kernel

Open Host Service
```

Relationship selection depends on organizational and technical constraints.

---

# 12. Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)

External models should not directly influence internal domain models.

```text id="ddd13"
External System

↓

ACL

↓

Domain Model
```

ACLs preserve model integrity.

---

# 13. Shared Kernel

Only stable, jointly owned concepts should reside in a Shared Kernel.

Minimize shared code to reduce coupling.

---

# 14. Open Host Service

Expose stable integration interfaces for external consumers.

Interfaces should evolve through versioning rather than breaking changes.

---

# 15. Published Language

Shared communication between bounded contexts should use well-defined contracts.

Examples:

```text id="ddd14"
REST APIs

Events

Schemas
```

Published language should be versioned.

---

# 16. Domain Model

The domain model represents:

```text id="ddd15"
Business Rules

Behavior

State

Relationships
```

The model should remain independent of infrastructure concerns.

---

# 17. Rich Domain Model

Business logic belongs inside the domain model.

Avoid placing business rules exclusively in service layers.

---

# 18. Anemic Domain Model

Anemic domain models separate data from behavior.

This pattern is discouraged for complex business domains.

---

# 19. Domain Boundaries

Each domain owns:

```text id="ddd16"
Rules

Data

Events

APIs
```

Ownership should be explicit.

---

# 20. Domain Ownership

Every domain requires:

```text id="ddd17"
Business Owner

Technical Owner

Product Owner
```

Clear ownership improves accountability.

---

# 21. Domain Independence

Domains should minimize unnecessary dependencies.

```text id="ddd18"
Loose Coupling

High Cohesion
```

---

# 22. Domain Events

Domains publish meaningful business events.

Examples:

```text id="ddd19"
StudentRegistered

CourseCompleted

AssessmentSubmitted
```

Events describe completed business facts.

---

# 23. Event Naming

Events should use past-tense business language.

Examples:

```text id="ddd20"
PaymentProcessed

CertificateIssued

LessonCompleted
```

Names should describe what happened, not what should happen.

---

# 24. Event Ownership

Only the owning bounded context publishes its domain events.

Consumers should not redefine producer-owned events.

---

# 25. Business Invariants

Critical business rules must always remain true.

Examples:

```text id="ddd21"
Enrollment Required

Unique Certificate

Valid Assessment Attempt
```

Invariants protect domain integrity.

---

# 26. Domain Consistency

Consistency boundaries align with aggregates.

Distributed consistency should use asynchronous coordination where appropriate.

---

# 27. Domain Collaboration

Domains collaborate through:

```text id="ddd22"
Events

APIs

Queries
```

Collaboration should preserve autonomy.

---

# 28. Product Architecture

Product architecture is the composition of bounded contexts.

```text id="ddd23"
Product

↓

Domains

↓

Bounded Contexts

↓

Services
```

---

# 29. Strategic Modeling Workshops

Conduct regular collaborative modeling sessions.

Examples:

```text id="ddd24"
Event Storming

Domain Mapping

Capability Mapping
```

These workshops refine shared understanding.

---

# 30. Enterprise Integration

ADR-093 integrates with:

```text id="ddd25"
ADR-082 APIs

ADR-083 Events

ADR-084 Data

ADR-089 Governance

ADR-090 SDLC

ADR-091 DevOps

ADR-092 Quality
```

Domain-Driven Design provides the business-centric architectural foundation for the enterprise platform.

---

# ADR-093 — Enterprise Domain-Driven Design (DDD), Strategic Design, Tactical Design & Product Architecture Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Enterprise Integration**.

---

# 31. Tactical Domain-Driven Design

Tactical DDD defines the building blocks used to implement business domains.

Core building blocks:

```text id="ddd31"
Entities

Value Objects

Aggregates

Repositories

Factories

Domain Services
```

Tactical patterns realize the strategic design.

---

# 32. Entities

Entities represent objects with a continuous identity.

Characteristics:

```text id="ddd32"
Identity

Lifecycle

Behavior

State
```

Examples:

```text
Student
Instructor
Course
Assessment
```

Identity distinguishes entities even when their attributes change.

---

# 33. Entity Identity

Entity identity should be stable.

```text id="ddd33"
ID

↓

Persistence

↓

Lifecycle
```

Business identity is preferred over infrastructure-generated identifiers where practical.

---

# 34. Value Objects

Value Objects represent immutable concepts.

Examples:

```text id="ddd34"
Address

Money

Duration

Email

Percentage
```

Value Objects are compared by value rather than identity.

---

# 35. Immutability

Value Objects should be immutable.

Benefits:

```text id="ddd35"
Thread Safety

Predictability

Simpler Reasoning
```

Changes produce new instances rather than modifying existing ones.

---

# 36. Aggregates

Aggregates enforce business consistency.

```text id="ddd36"
Aggregate

↓

Entities

↓

Value Objects
```

Aggregates define transactional boundaries.

---

# 37. Aggregate Root

Every aggregate has one Aggregate Root.

```text id="ddd37"
Aggregate Root

↓

Child Entities

↓

Value Objects
```

External access occurs only through the Aggregate Root.

---

# 38. Aggregate Invariants

Aggregate Roots enforce:

```text id="ddd38"
Business Rules

Consistency

Validation
```

No external component should bypass aggregate invariants.

---

# 39. Aggregate Size

Aggregates should remain small.

Large aggregates reduce scalability and concurrency.

Prefer consistency boundaries over object graphs.

---

# 40. Transaction Boundary

Transactions should align with aggregate boundaries.

```text id="ddd39"
Aggregate

↓

Transaction

↓

Commit
```

Cross-aggregate consistency should use eventual consistency where appropriate.

---

# 41. Repositories

Repositories provide collection-like access to aggregates.

Responsibilities:

```text id="ddd40"
Load

Save

Query

Delete
```

Repositories abstract persistence concerns from domain logic.

---

# 42. Repository Rules

Repositories should operate on Aggregate Roots only.

Avoid exposing persistence implementation details to domain code.

---

# 43. Factories

Factories encapsulate complex object creation.

Examples:

```text id="ddd41"
StudentFactory

AssessmentFactory

CertificateFactory
```

Creation logic belongs in factories when constructors become complex.

---

# 44. Domain Services

Domain Services implement business behavior that does not naturally belong to a single entity.

Examples:

```text id="ddd42"
EnrollmentService

SchedulingService

RecommendationService
```

---

# 45. Application Services

Application Services coordinate use cases.

Responsibilities:

```text id="ddd43"
Orchestration

Transactions

Authorization

Integration
```

Business rules should remain inside the domain model.

---

# 46. Infrastructure Services

Infrastructure provides technical capabilities.

Examples:

```text id="ddd44"
Email

Storage

Messaging

Cache
```

Infrastructure should not contain domain rules.

---

# 47. Specifications

Specifications encapsulate business rules.

Examples:

```text id="ddd45"
EligibleForExam

PassedCourse

CertificateAvailable
```

Specifications improve reuse and readability.

---

# 48. Domain Policies

Policies define reusable business decisions.

```text id="ddd46"
Discount Policy

Enrollment Policy

Exam Policy
```

Policies should remain independent of infrastructure.

---

# 49. CQRS

Separate read and write responsibilities when justified.

```text id="ddd47"
Commands

↓

Domain

↓

Events

↓

Read Model
```

CQRS should be introduced only where complexity provides measurable value.

---

# 50. Event Sourcing

Event Sourcing stores business events as the source of truth.

```text id="ddd48"
Event

↓

Event Store

↓

Aggregate State
```

Use Event Sourcing selectively for domains requiring complete auditability or temporal reconstruction.

---

# 51. Command Model

Commands express business intent.

Examples:

```text id="ddd49"
EnrollStudent

SubmitAssessment

IssueCertificate
```

Commands request changes; they do not represent completed facts.

---

# 52. Query Model

Queries retrieve information without changing business state.

```text id="ddd50"
Student Transcript

Course Catalog

Assessment Results
```

Queries should remain side-effect free.

---

# 53. Hexagonal Architecture

Separate business logic from external technologies.

```text id="ddd51"
Domain

↓

Ports

↓

Adapters

↓

Infrastructure
```

The domain remains independent of frameworks.

---

# 54. Clean Architecture

Dependencies point inward.

```text id="ddd52"
Frameworks

↓

Adapters

↓

Use Cases

↓

Entities
```

Business rules should not depend on external libraries.

---

# 55. Onion Architecture

Organize software into concentric layers.

```text id="ddd53"
Infrastructure

↓

Application

↓

Domain

↓

Core
```

Inner layers remain independent of outer layers.

---

# 56. Modular Monolith

A modular monolith may be preferred during early product evolution.

Characteristics:

```text id="ddd54"
Single Deployment

Strong Module Boundaries

Independent Domains
```

Internal modularity reduces future migration effort.

---

# 57. Microservices Alignment

Microservices should align with bounded contexts rather than technical layers.

```text id="ddd55"
Bounded Context

↓

Microservice
```

Service decomposition should follow business boundaries.

---

# 58. Persistence Model

Persistence models should support domain models without leaking database concerns into business logic.

Domain behavior should not be dictated by relational schemas.

---

# 59. Tactical Architecture Model

```text id="ddd56"
Application Service

↓

Aggregate

↓

Repository

↓

Database

↓

Events
```

Each layer has clearly defined responsibilities.

---

# 60. Enterprise Integration

ADR-093 integrates with:

```text id="ddd57"
ADR-082 APIs

ADR-083 Events

ADR-084 Data

ADR-085 Frontend

ADR-089 Governance

ADR-090 SDLC

ADR-091 DevOps

ADR-092 Quality
```

Tactical Domain-Driven Design provides the implementation patterns that realize the strategic business architecture.

---

# ADR-093 — Enterprise Domain-Driven Design (DDD), Strategic Design, Tactical Design & Product Architecture Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — Enterprise Integration**.

---

# 61. Event Storming

Event Storming should be the preferred collaborative domain discovery technique.

Participants:

```text id="ddd61"
Business Experts

↓

Product Owners

↓

Architects

↓

Engineers
```

Outputs include:

* Domain Events
* Commands
* Aggregates
* Policies
* External Systems
* Hotspots

---

# 62. Domain Storytelling

Business workflows should be modeled using domain stories.

```text id="ddd62"
Actor

↓

Action

↓

Business Rule

↓

Outcome
```

Stories expose business language and hidden domain concepts.

---

# 63. Capability Mapping

Business capabilities should drive software architecture.

```text id="ddd63"
Enterprise

↓

Capability

↓

Domain

↓

Bounded Context

↓

Service
```

Capabilities change less frequently than organizational structures.

---

# 64. Service Decomposition

Microservices should be decomposed according to domain boundaries.

Avoid decomposition based on:

```text id="ddd64"
Database Tables

Technical Layers

Teams
```

Business capabilities remain the primary decomposition driver.

---

# 65. Domain Ownership

Every bounded context should define:

```text id="ddd65"
Business Owner

Technical Owner

Product Team

Architecture Owner
```

Ownership includes both functional evolution and operational responsibility.

---

# 66. Domain Governance

Domain governance should define:

```text id="ddd66"
Boundaries

Ownership

Contracts

Events

APIs
```

Governance protects domain autonomy.

---

# 67. Domain Lifecycle

Each domain progresses through a lifecycle.

```text id="ddd67"
Discovery

↓

Design

↓

Implementation

↓

Evolution

↓

Retirement
```

Architecture should evolve alongside business needs.

---

# 68. Domain Evolution

Domains change through controlled evolution.

Examples:

```text id="ddd68"
Split Context

Merge Context

Rename Concepts

Refine Language
```

Evolution should preserve business continuity.

---

# 69. Legacy Modernization

Legacy systems should migrate incrementally.

Preferred approach:

```text id="ddd69"
Legacy

↓

Anti-Corruption Layer

↓

New Domain

↓

Gradual Migration
```

Avoid large-scale "big bang" migrations where feasible.

---

# 70. Strangler Pattern

Incrementally replace legacy functionality.

```text id="ddd70"
Legacy System

↓

New Capability

↓

Traffic Shift

↓

Legacy Retirement
```

This reduces migration risk.

---

# 71. Domain Versioning

Domain contracts should evolve using versioning.

```text id="ddd71"
v1

↓

v2

↓

Deprecation

↓

Removal
```

Backward compatibility should be maintained when practical.

---

# 72. Domain APIs

Each bounded context exposes well-defined interfaces.

Supported interfaces include:

```text id="ddd72"
REST

gRPC

Events

GraphQL
```

Interfaces should reflect domain language.

---

# 73. Domain Events Governance

Domain events should define:

```text id="ddd73"
Owner

Schema

Version

Lifecycle

Consumers
```

Events become long-lived enterprise contracts.

---

# 74. Service Contracts

Every service contract should specify:

```text id="ddd74"
Inputs

Outputs

Errors

Version

Compatibility
```

Contracts should be treated as stable public interfaces.

---

# 75. Domain Security

Security should align with domain boundaries.

Examples:

```text id="ddd75"
Authorization

Data Ownership

Privacy

Audit
```

Security rules belong to the business domain where appropriate.

---

# 76. Domain Observability

Every bounded context should expose:

```text id="ddd76"
Metrics

Logs

Traces

Business Events
```

Observability should include both technical and business telemetry.

---

# 77. Domain Quality

Quality Engineering integrates with DDD.

Each domain should verify:

```text id="ddd77"
Business Rules

API Contracts

Events

Performance
```

Testing should follow bounded context boundaries.

---

# 78. Domain Metrics

Representative metrics include:

```text id="ddd78"
Business KPIs

Error Rate

Latency

Throughput

Domain Events
```

Metrics should measure domain outcomes rather than only infrastructure.

---

# 79. Domain Documentation

Every domain should maintain:

```text id="ddd79"
Context Map

Domain Model

Events

APIs

ADRs
```

Documentation should evolve with the domain.

---

# 80. Domain Knowledge Base

Maintain a centralized repository containing:

```text id="ddd80"
Glossary

Context Maps

Patterns

Business Rules

Architecture Decisions
```

Knowledge should be searchable and version-controlled.

---

# 81. Enterprise Product Architecture

Product architecture is composed of multiple collaborating domains.

```text id="ddd81"
Product

↓

Capabilities

↓

Domains

↓

Contexts

↓

Services
```

Products evolve through domain evolution rather than technology-first changes.

---

# 82. Product Modularity

Products should support:

```text id="ddd82"
Independent Domains

Independent Releases

Loose Coupling

High Cohesion
```

Modularity improves scalability and maintainability.

---

# 83. Domain Collaboration Model

Domains collaborate through:

```text id="ddd83"
Events

APIs

Queries

Shared Language
```

Communication mechanisms should preserve autonomy.

---

# 84. Enterprise Context Map

Maintain an enterprise-wide context map.

```text id="ddd84"
Learning

⇄

Assessment

⇄

Certification

⇄

Billing

⇄

Identity
```

The context map is a strategic architectural artifact.

---

# 85. Enterprise Domain Catalog

Maintain a catalog of:

```text id="ddd85"
Core Domains

Supporting Domains

Generic Domains

Owners

Dependencies
```

The catalog supports governance and portfolio planning.

---

# 86. Enterprise DDD Scorecard

| Capability             | Status |
| ---------------------- | ------ |
| Strategic Design       | ✓      |
| Tactical Design        | ✓      |
| Bounded Contexts       | ✓      |
| Context Maps           | ✓      |

---

# 87. Enterprise DDD Maturity Model

```text id="ddd86"
LEVEL 1

Layered CRUD Applications

LEVEL 2

Modular Applications

LEVEL 3

Domain-Oriented Architecture

LEVEL 4

Enterprise Domain Platform

LEVEL 5

Adaptive Autonomous Business Architecture
```

Mediverse targets **Level 4**.

---

# 88. DDD Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text id="ddd87"
❌ Database-Driven Design
❌ Anemic Domain Model
❌ Shared Database Between Domains
❌ Shared Business Logic
❌ Technical Service Decomposition
❌ God Services
❌ Generic Service Layer
❌ Leaking Infrastructure into Domain
❌ Missing Ubiquitous Language
❌ Missing Context Boundaries
❌ Large Aggregates
❌ Distributed Transactions Across Domains
❌ Domain Ownership Ambiguity
❌ Framework-Driven Architecture
❌ Business Logic Inside Controllers
```

---

# 89. Enterprise DDD Reference Architecture

```text id="ddd88"
Business Vision
      │
      ▼
Business Capabilities
      │
      ▼
Domains
      │
      ▼

      ▼
Aggregates

      ▼

      ▼

```

---

# 90. Product Operating Model

```text id="ddd89"
Business Strategy
      │
      ▼
Product
      │
      ▼
Domains
      │
      ▼
Engineering Teams
      │
      ▼
Platform
      │
      ▼
Operations
```

Cross-functional teams own domains throughout their lifecycle.

---

# 91. Enterprise Integration

ADR-093 operationalizes:

```text id="ddd90"
ADR-082 APIs

ADR-083 Events

ADR-084 Data

ADR-085 Frontend

ADR-089 Governance

ADR-090 SDLC

ADR-091 DevOps

ADR-092 Quality
```

DDD becomes the business-centric architectural model underpinning the enterprise.

---

# 92. Domain Governance Board

The Domain Governance Board should oversee:

```text id="ddd91"
Context Boundaries

Naming

Ownership

Evolution

Standards
```

Its role is to preserve domain consistency across the enterprise.

---

# 93. Enterprise Modeling Standards

Approved modeling artifacts include:

```text id="ddd92"
Context Maps

Domain Models

Event Storming Outputs

Capability Maps

Sequence Diagrams
```

Standardized artifacts improve communication and governance.

---

# 94. Architecture Fitness

Periodically assess:

```text id="ddd93"
Domain Coupling

Model Complexity

Context Boundaries

Business Alignment
```

These assessments help identify architectural erosion.

---

# 95. Engineering Investment

Investment priorities include:

```text id="ddd94"
Core Domains

Architecture Evolution

Domain Refactoring

Business Knowledge Capture
```

Engineering effort should favor the areas that differentiate the business.

# 97. Governing Invariant

> **Every Mediverse system must model business capabilities through explicit domains, bounded contexts, ubiquitous language, and well-defined ownership. Business concepts drive architectural structure, while technology remains an implementation concern supporting the domain model.**

# ADR-094 — Enterprise Integration Architecture, External Systems, B2B Connectivity & Interoperability Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-094
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Integration Architecture Board (EIAB)

ADR-093 established the Enterprise Domain-Driven Design architecture.

ADR-094 establishes the enterprise integration architecture, defining how Mediverse communicates with internal services, external platforms, healthcare systems, partner organizations, cloud services, and third-party applications while maintaining scalability, security, reliability, and interoperability.

The governing principle is:

> **Every enterprise integration must be secure, loosely coupled, observable, versioned, resilient, and governed. Integration should preserve domain autonomy while enabling seamless business collaboration.**

```text id="int01"
Business Domains
        │
        ▼
Integration Layer
        │
 ┌──────┼──────────────┐
 ▼      ▼              ▼
APIs   Events    File Exchange
 │      │              │
 └──────┼──────────────┘
        ▼
External Systems
```

---

# 1. Enterprise Integration Philosophy

Integration enables business capabilities across systems.

Objectives:

```text id="int02"
Interoperability

Loose Coupling

Scalability

Reliability

Security

Observability
```

Integration should connect systems without tightly coupling them.

---

# 2. Integration Principles

Every integration should satisfy:

```text id="int03"
Standardized

Versioned

Observable

Secure

Resilient
```

---

# 3. Integration Styles

Supported enterprise integration styles include:

```text id="int04"
Synchronous

Asynchronous

Streaming

Batch

File-Based
```

The style should match business and technical requirements.

---

# 4. Synchronous Integration

Used when immediate responses are required.

Examples:

```text id="int05"
REST APIs

gRPC

GraphQL
```

Latency requirements should justify synchronous communication.

---

# 5. Asynchronous Integration

Preferred when immediate responses are unnecessary.

Examples:

```text id="int06"
Kafka

RabbitMQ

Cloud Messaging
```

Asynchronous messaging improves resilience and scalability.

---

# 6. Streaming Integration

Continuous event streams support real-time processing.

Examples:

```text id="int07"
Telemetry

Audit Events

Learning Analytics

Notifications
```

---

# 7. Batch Integration

Batch processing is appropriate for scheduled workloads.

Examples:

```text id="int08"
Reporting

Billing

Analytics

Data Synchronization
```

---

# 8. File-Based Integration

File exchange remains appropriate for legacy systems.

Supported formats:

```text id="int09"
CSV

JSON

XML

Parquet
```

File transfers should be encrypted and validated.

---

# 9. API-Led Connectivity

Enterprise integrations should prioritize APIs.

```text id="int10"
System APIs

↓

Process APIs

↓

Experience APIs
```

API layers improve reuse and separation of concerns.

---

# 10. Integration Layer

Applications should not integrate directly with every external system.

```text id="int11"
Application

↓

Integration Layer

↓

External Platform
```

The integration layer centralizes policies and transformations.

---

# 11. Enterprise Service Bus (ESB)

Existing ESBs may be supported during migration.

New architectures should prefer lightweight integration patterns over centralized orchestration where appropriate.

---

# 12. API Gateway Integration

ADR-082 governs API exposure.

Integration gateways should provide:

```text id="int12"
Routing

Authentication

Rate Limiting

Observability
```

---

# 13. Message Brokers

Approved messaging platforms include:

```text id="int13"
Kafka

RabbitMQ

Cloud Pub/Sub
```

Broker selection depends on workload characteristics.

---

# 14. Integration Contracts

Every integration should define:

```text id="int14"
Inputs

Outputs

Schemas

Errors

Version
```

Contracts should evolve through governed versioning.

---

# 15. Schema Management

Schemas should be centrally managed.

Examples:

```text id="int15"
JSON Schema

Avro

Protocol Buffers

FHIR Profiles
```

Schema evolution should preserve compatibility where practical.

---

# 16. Data Transformation

Transformation belongs within the integration layer.

```text id="int16"
Source Model

↓

Transformation

↓

Target Model
```

Domain models should remain insulated from external formats.

---

# 17. Canonical Data Model

A canonical model may be used selectively for cross-enterprise integration.

Avoid forcing all systems into a single universal schema.

---

# 18. Data Mapping

Mappings should be:

```text id="int17"
Documented

Versioned

Tested

Traceable
```

Mapping logic should be independently maintainable.

---

# 19. Integration Security

ADR-086 governs integration security.

Controls include:

```text id="int18"
TLS

OAuth2

mTLS

JWT

API Keys
```

---

# 20. Enterprise Integration Governance

Integration governance defines:

```text id="int19"
Ownership

Standards

Versioning

Lifecycle

Monitoring
```

Integration assets require the same governance as application code.

---

# 21. Integration Observability

Every integration should expose:

```text id="int20"
Metrics

Logs

Traces

Business Events
```

Integration failures should be diagnosable end-to-end.

---

# 22. Correlation IDs

Requests should propagate a unique correlation identifier.

```text id="int21"
Client

↓

Gateway

↓

Service A

↓

Service B

↓

Database
```

Correlation IDs support distributed tracing and troubleshooting.

---

# 23. Idempotency

Operations that may be retried should be idempotent.

Examples:

```text id="int22"
Payment Requests

Enrollment Requests

Webhook Processing
```

Idempotency prevents duplicate processing.

---

# 24. Retry Strategy

Retries should use controlled policies.

```text id="int23"
Retry

↓

Exponential Backoff

↓

Circuit Breaker

↓

Dead Letter Queue
```

Retries should not amplify failures.

---

# 25. Dead Letter Queues (DLQ)

Failed asynchronous messages should be isolated.

```text id="int24"
Message

↓

Failure

↓

DLQ

↓

Investigation
```

DLQs preserve failed events for analysis and recovery.

---

# 26. Timeout Management

Integration calls should define explicit timeouts.

Waiting indefinitely is prohibited.

---

# 27. Circuit Breakers

Integration endpoints should implement circuit breakers for unstable dependencies.

This complements ADR-088 reliability standards.

---

# 28. Bulkheads

Resource isolation should prevent one failing integration from exhausting shared resources.

---

# 29. Integration Testing

Every integration should include:

```text id="int25"
Contract Tests

API Tests

End-to-End Tests

Failure Scenarios
```

Testing should verify interoperability, not just individual systems.

---

# 30. Enterprise Integration

ADR-094 integrates with:

```text id="int26"
ADR-082 APIs

ADR-083 Events

ADR-086 Security

ADR-088 Reliability

ADR-091 DevOps

ADR-093 DDD
```

Enterprise integration provides the connective layer between autonomous domains, internal platforms, and external ecosystems.

---

# ADR-094 — Enterprise Integration Architecture, External Systems, B2B Connectivity & Interoperability Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Enterprise Integration**.

---

# 31. Webhook Integration

Webhooks enable event-driven communication between systems.

```text id="int31"
Event

↓

Webhook

↓

Consumer

↓

Acknowledgement
```

Webhook deliveries should support retries, authentication, and signature verification.

---

# 32. Callback APIs

Long-running operations should use callback APIs where appropriate.

```text id="int32"
Request

↓

Processing

↓

Callback

↓

Result
```

Callbacks reduce unnecessary client polling.

---

# 33. Polling Strategy

Polling should be used only when push-based integration is unavailable.

Requirements:

```text id="int33"
Configurable Interval

Timeout

Backoff

Caching
```

Polling frequency should minimize unnecessary system load.

---

# 34. Event Choreography

Independent services collaborate using domain events.

```text id="int34"
Service A

↓

Event

↓

Service B

↓

Event

↓

Service C
```

Choreography promotes autonomy but requires strong event governance.

---

# 35. Event Orchestration

A central orchestrator coordinates complex workflows.

```text id="int35"
Orchestrator

├── Service A

├── Service B

└── Service C
```

Orchestration is appropriate for processes requiring centralized control.

---

# 36. Saga Pattern

Distributed business transactions should use Saga patterns.

```text id="int36"
Step 1

↓

Step 2

↓

Step 3

↓

Compensation (if required)
```

Avoid distributed ACID transactions across services.

---

# 37. Compensation

Every Saga should define compensation actions.

Examples:

```text id="int37"
Cancel Payment

Reverse Enrollment

Release Reservation
```

Compensation restores business consistency after partial failure.

---

# 38. Change Data Capture (CDC)

CDC enables asynchronous synchronization.

```text id="int38"
Database

↓

CDC

↓

Event Stream

↓

Consumers
```

CDC should avoid direct database polling.

---

# 39. Data Synchronization

Synchronization strategies include:

```text id="int39"
Real-Time

Scheduled

Batch

Event-Driven
```

Selection depends on business latency requirements.

---

# 40. ETL & ELT

Data movement strategies include:

```text id="int40"
Extract

↓

Transform

↓

Load
```

or

```text
Extract

↓

Load

↓

Transform
```

Approach selection depends on analytical architecture.

---

# 41. Healthcare Interoperability

Healthcare integrations should support recognized standards.

Examples:

```text id="int41"
FHIR

HL7

DICOM
```

Profiles and implementation guides should be version-controlled.

---

# 42. HL7 Integration

HL7 interfaces should include:

```text id="int42"
Validation

Transformation

Acknowledgement

Error Handling
```

Legacy healthcare messaging should remain isolated behind integration adapters.

---

# 43. FHIR APIs

FHIR resources should be exposed through governed APIs.

Examples:

```text id="int43"
Patient

Practitioner

Observation

Medication

Encounter
```

FHIR implementations should preserve interoperability.

---

# 44. DICOM Integration

Medical imaging systems should integrate through DICOM services where required.

Image metadata should remain synchronized with enterprise systems.

---

# 45. ERP Integration

Enterprise systems may integrate with:

```text id="int44"
SAP

Oracle ERP

Microsoft Dynamics
```

ERP integration should occur through well-defined interfaces rather than direct database access.

---

# 46. CRM Integration

Supported CRM integrations include:

```text id="int45"
Salesforce

Microsoft Dynamics

HubSpot
```

Customer data synchronization should follow enterprise data governance.

---

# 47. Payment Gateway Integration

Payment providers should integrate through adapters.

Examples:

```text id="int46"
Stripe

Razorpay

PayPal

Adyen
```

Payment-specific logic should remain isolated from business domains.

---

# 48. Identity Federation

Identity integration should support:

```text id="int47"
OIDC

OAuth2

SAML

LDAP
```

Identity federation aligns with ADR-081.

---

# 49. Partner Onboarding

New partners should complete a standardized onboarding process.

```text id="int48"
Security Review

↓

API Access

↓

Contract Validation

↓

Testing

↓

Production
```

---

# 50. B2B Integration

Business-to-business integrations should define:

```text id="int49"
Contracts

Authentication

SLAs

Monitoring

Ownership
```

Long-term interoperability depends on stable agreements.

---

# 51. API Monetization

External APIs may support:

```text id="int50"
Free Tier

Subscription

Usage-Based Billing
```

Commercial APIs require governance and lifecycle management.

---

# 52. Third-Party Dependency Management

Maintain an inventory of external integrations.

Track:

```text id="int51"
Owner

Version

SLA

Security

Business Criticality
```

Dependency visibility supports operational resilience.

---

# 53. Integration Quality

Integration quality should evaluate:

```text id="int52"
Availability

Latency

Compatibility

Error Rate

Throughput
```

---

# 54. Integration Metrics

Representative metrics:

```text id="int53"
Request Rate

Success Rate

Retry Rate

DLQ Count

Response Time
```

Metrics should support operational decision-making.

---

# 55. Integration Dashboards

Dashboards should display:

```text id="int54"
API Health

Broker Health

Partner Status

Failures

Latency
```

Operational visibility reduces troubleshooting time.

---

# 56. Integration Governance

Governance should review:

```text id="int55"
Contracts

Versions

Security

Ownership

Lifecycle
```

Integration assets should evolve through controlled processes.

---

# 57. AI-Assisted Integration

ADR-077 enables AI support for integration engineering.

Examples:

```text id="int56"
Schema Mapping

Transformation Suggestions

Contract Validation

Error Analysis
```

AI recommendations should be reviewed before production adoption.

---

# 58. Enterprise Interoperability Model

```text id="int57"
Internal Domains

↓

Integration Layer

↓

External Platforms

↓

Partners

↓

Customers
```

Interoperability extends across the enterprise ecosystem.

---

# 59. Integration Operating Model

```text id="int58"
Request

↓

Validation

↓

Transformation

↓

Routing

↓

Execution

↓

Observation
```

The operating model standardizes enterprise integration flows.

---

# 60. Enterprise Integration

ADR-094 integrates with:

```text id="int59"
ADR-081 Identity

ADR-082 APIs

ADR-083 Events

ADR-084 Data

ADR-086 Security

ADR-088 Reliability

ADR-093 DDD
```

Integration architecture enables secure, resilient, and interoperable communication across business domains and external ecosystems.

# ADR-094 — Enterprise Integration Architecture, External Systems, B2B Connectivity & Interoperability Standard

## Part 3 — Sections 61–120

Continuing from **Section 60 — Enterprise Integration**.

---

# 61. Enterprise Integration Platform (iPaaS)

The enterprise should provide a standardized Integration Platform as a Service (iPaaS).

Capabilities:

```text id="int61"
API Integration

Event Routing

Transformation

Monitoring

Security
```

The platform reduces duplicated integration logic.

---

# 62. Integration Center of Excellence (ICoE)

The Integration CoE establishes enterprise standards.

Responsibilities:

```text id="int62"
Architecture

Standards

Governance

Training

Platform Evolution
```

The ICoE enables teams rather than becoming an implementation bottleneck.

---

# 63. API Mediation

API mediation handles protocol and message adaptation.

```text id="int63"
Consumer

↓

Gateway

↓

Transformation

↓

Provider
```

Mediation should not contain business logic.

---

# 64. Protocol Translation

Integration platforms may translate between protocols.

Examples:

```text id="int64"
REST ↔ gRPC

REST ↔ SOAP

AMQP ↔ Kafka
```

Translation should preserve contract semantics.

---

# 65. Service Mesh Integration

Service mesh capabilities complement the integration platform.

Examples:

```text id="int65"
mTLS

Traffic Routing

Retries

Observability
```

Business integration remains outside the service mesh.

---

# 66. Multi-Cloud Integration

Integration architecture should support multiple cloud providers.

```text id="int66"
AWS

↓

Azure

↓

Google Cloud
```

Cloud selection should not fundamentally alter integration contracts.

---

# 67. Hybrid Cloud Integration

Enterprise systems may span cloud and on-premises environments.

```text id="int67"
Cloud

↓

Secure Connectivity

↓

On-Premises
```

Connectivity should follow enterprise security standards.

---

# 68. Edge Integration

Edge systems should synchronize with central platforms using secure integration channels.

Offline operation should be supported where business requirements demand it.

---

# 69. Cross-Region Integration

Regional deployments should exchange data using governed integration channels.

Cross-region traffic should respect latency and regulatory constraints.

---

# 70. Data Residency

Integration architecture should respect regional data residency policies.

```text id="int68"
Region

↓

Policy

↓

Routing

↓

Storage
```

Data movement must comply with applicable regulations.

---

# 71. Cross-Border Data Transfer

International integrations should define:

```text id="int69"
Legal Basis

Encryption

Audit

Retention
```

Cross-border transfers require governance.

---

# 72. Integration Security Operations

Operational monitoring should include:

```text id="int70"
Authentication Failures

API Abuse

Certificate Status

Traffic Anomalies
```

Security events should integrate with enterprise monitoring.

---

# 73. Certificate Lifecycle

Integration certificates should follow managed lifecycle processes.

```text id="int71"
Issue

↓

Deploy

↓

Rotate

↓

Revoke
```

Expired certificates should not interrupt critical integrations.

---

# 74. Secret Management

Integration credentials should be stored securely.

Examples:

```text id="int72"
API Keys

OAuth Secrets

Client Certificates

Signing Keys
```

Secrets should never be embedded in source code.

---

# 75. Integration Lifecycle

Every integration should progress through:

```text id="int73"
Design

↓

Build

↓

Validate

↓

Deploy

↓

Operate

↓

Retire
```

Lifecycle management ensures maintainability.

---

# 76. Integration Versioning

Integration interfaces should evolve predictably.

```text id="int74"
Current

↓

Compatible

↓

Deprecated

↓

Retired
```

Consumers require sufficient migration time.

---

# 77. Deprecation Policy

Deprecated integrations should define:

```text id="int75"
Notice Period

Migration Guide

Retirement Date
```

Unexpected removal of interfaces is prohibited.

---

# 78. Consumer Management

Every published integration should identify:

```text id="int76"
Consumers

Usage

Version

Owner
```

Consumer visibility supports impact analysis.

---

# 79. Provider Responsibilities

Integration providers are responsible for:

```text id="int77"
Availability

Documentation

Versioning

Monitoring

Support
```

Provider obligations should be clearly documented.

---

# 80. Consumer Responsibilities

Consumers are responsible for:

```text id="int78"
Correct Usage

Version Upgrades

Error Handling

Retry Policies
```

Integration reliability is a shared responsibility.

---

# 81. Integration Documentation

Every integration should include:

```text id="int79"
Architecture

Contracts

Examples

Error Codes

Operational Runbooks
```

Documentation should be version-controlled.

---

# 82. Enterprise Integration Catalog

Maintain a centralized catalog containing:

```text id="int80"
APIs

Events

Schemas

Partners

Owners
```

The catalog becomes the enterprise integration inventory.

---

# 83. Integration Scorecard

| Capability          | Status |
| ------------------- | ------ |
| API Governance      | ✓      |
| Event Integration   | ✓      |
| Contract Testing    | ✓      |
| Security            | ✓      |
| Observability       | ✓      |
| Versioning          | ✓      |
| Partner Integration | ✓      |
| CDC                 | ✓      |

---

# 84. Enterprise Integration KPIs

Representative KPIs:

```text id="int81"
API Availability

Partner Success Rate

Message Throughput

Retry Rate

Integration Latency
```

KPIs should measure interoperability effectiveness.

---

# 85. Continuous Integration Improvement

Integration capabilities should improve through:

```text id="int82"
Measure

↓

Analyze

↓

Improve

↓

Validate

↓

Repeat
```

Operational insights should drive architectural evolution.

---

# 86. Enterprise Integration Maturity Model

```text id="int83"
LEVEL 1

Point-to-Point

LEVEL 2

Managed APIs

LEVEL 3

Event-Driven Enterprise

LEVEL 4

Unified Integration Platform

LEVEL 5

Autonomous Intelligent Integration
```

Mediverse targets **Level 4**.

---

# 87. Integration Anti-Patterns

Mediverse rejects:

```text id="int84"
❌ Point-to-point spaghetti integrations
❌ Shared databases between systems
❌ Hardcoded endpoints
❌ No contract versioning
❌ Direct ERP database access
❌ Missing retries
❌ Infinite retry loops
❌ Missing idempotency
❌ Manual schema changes
❌ Business logic in integration middleware
❌ Unmonitored partner integrations
❌ Credentials stored in source code
❌ Missing API documentation
❌ Synchronous calls for long-running workflows
❌ Hidden integration dependencies
```

---

```text id="int85"
API Layer

       ▼

 ▼     ▼               ▼
Events APIs      File Exchange
 │     │               │
 └─────┼───────────────┘
       ▼
External Systems
```

# 89. Enterprise Interoperability Operating Model

```text id="int86"
Business Need
      │
      ▼
Integration Design

      ▼
Contract

      ▼

      ▼

      ▼

      ▼
Operations
```

Interoperability should follow the same engineering discipline as application development.

```text id="int87"
ADR-081 Identity
```

# ADR-095 — Enterprise Analytics, Business Intelligence (BI), Data Warehouse, Lakehouse & Decision Intelligence Architecture Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-095
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Data & Analytics Architecture Board (EDAAB)

ADR-094 established the Enterprise Integration Architecture.

ADR-095 establishes the enterprise analytics architecture, defining how Mediverse transforms operational data into trusted business insights, predictive intelligence, executive dashboards, and AI-ready analytical assets.

The governing principle is:

> **Operational systems execute the business. Analytical systems explain, optimize, and predict the business. Analytics must be trustworthy, governed, scalable, and accessible while preserving a single version of business truth.**

```text
Operational Systems
        │
        ▼
Data Integration
        │
        ▼
Lakehouse
        │
        ▼
Semantic Layer
        │
        ▼
Analytics
        │
        ▼
Business Decisions
```

---

# 1. Enterprise Analytics Philosophy

Analytics exists to support decision-making rather than data collection.

Objectives:

```text
Trusted Data

Business Insight

Prediction

Optimization

Continuous Learning
```

Analytics should create measurable business value.

---

# 2. Decision Intelligence

Analytics should evolve from reporting toward decision intelligence.

```text
Data

↓

Information

↓

Insight

↓

Decision

↓

Action
```

The objective is better business decisions, not more dashboards.

---

# 3. Analytical Architecture

Enterprise analytical architecture consists of:

```text
Data Sources

↓

Integration

↓

Storage

↓

Semantic Layer

↓

Analytics
```

---

# 4. Operational vs Analytical Systems

Separate operational processing from analytical processing.

```text
OLTP

↓

Integration

↓

OLAP
```

Operational workloads should not be degraded by analytical queries.

---

# 5. OLTP

Operational databases support:

```text
Transactions

Updates

Consistency

Business Operations
```

---

# 6. OLAP

Analytical systems support:

```text
Reporting

Aggregation

Forecasting

Trend Analysis
```

---

# 7. Enterprise Data Warehouse

The Data Warehouse stores integrated historical business data.

Characteristics:

```text
Integrated

Historical

Subject-Oriented

Non-Volatile
```

---

# 8. Enterprise Data Lake

The Data Lake stores raw structured and unstructured data.

Examples:

```text
Logs

Images

Audio

Video

Documents
```

---

# 9. Lakehouse Architecture

Preferred enterprise analytical architecture:

```text
Data Lake

↓

Governance

↓

Warehouse Capabilities
```

Lakehouse combines flexibility with governance.

---

# 10. Data Zones

Organize data into governed zones.

```text
Raw

↓

Validated

↓

Curated

↓

Published
```

---

# 11. Data Ingestion

Supported ingestion methods:

```text
Batch

Streaming

CDC

API
```

Selection depends on latency requirements.

---

# 12. Batch Analytics

Batch processing supports:

```text
Daily Reports

Financial Reports

Historical Trends
```

---

# 13. Streaming Analytics

Streaming supports:

```text
Real-Time Dashboards

Alerts

Fraud Detection

Learning Analytics
```

---

# 14. Data Transformation

Transformation should produce business-ready datasets.

```text
Extract

↓

Clean

↓

Transform

↓

Publish
```

---

# 15. Data Modeling

Enterprise analytical models should prioritize business understanding.

Supported approaches:

```text
Dimensional

Data Vault

Normalized
```

---

# 16. Star Schema

Preferred for reporting.

```text
Fact

↓

Dimension

Dimension

Dimension
```

Optimized for analytical queries.

---

# 17. Snowflake Schema

Normalization may be appropriate for large shared dimensions.

Trade-offs should be evaluated against reporting performance.

---

# 18. Fact Tables

Facts measure business activity.

Examples:

```text
Enrollment

Revenue

Assessment

Usage
```

---

# 19. Dimension Tables

Dimensions describe business context.

Examples:

```text
Student

Course

Instructor

Date
```

---

# 20. Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD)

Dimension history should follow documented SCD strategies.

Examples:

```text
Type 1

Type 2

Type 3
```

Historical accuracy should guide implementation.

---

# 21. Semantic Layer

The semantic layer exposes business-friendly definitions.

Examples:

```text
Revenue

Completion Rate

Active Students

Retention
```

Business users should not require SQL knowledge.

---

# 22. Business Metrics

Enterprise metrics require standardized definitions.

Examples:

```text
Monthly Active Users

Revenue

Course Completion

Customer Lifetime Value
```

---

# 23. Enterprise KPIs

KPIs should align with business strategy.

```text
Growth

Quality

Efficiency

Customer Success
```

---

# 24. Business Intelligence Platform

BI platforms should provide:

```text
Dashboards

Reports

Ad Hoc Analysis

Self-Service
```

---

# 25. Self-Service Analytics

Business users should independently explore approved datasets.

Governance remains mandatory.

---

# 26. Dashboard Standards

Dashboards should emphasize:

```text
Clarity

Consistency

Actionability

Accuracy
```

---

# 27. Executive Dashboards

Executive dashboards summarize enterprise health.

Typical metrics:

```text
Revenue

Growth

Customer Satisfaction

Platform Health
```

---

# 28. Operational Dashboards

Operational dashboards support day-to-day execution.

Examples:

```text
System Health

Admissions

Assessments

Support
```

---

# 29. Embedded Analytics

Analytics should be available within business applications where appropriate.

Users should not always need separate BI tools.

---

# 30. Enterprise Integration

ADR-095 integrates with:

```text
ADR-076 Data Governance

ADR-084 Data Platform

ADR-090 SDLC

ADR-091 DevOps

ADR-094 Integration
```

Analytics transforms governed enterprise data into actionable business intelligence.

---

# ADR-095 — Enterprise Analytics, Business Intelligence (BI), Data Warehouse, Lakehouse & Decision Intelligence Architecture Standard

## Part 2 — Sections 31–60

Continuing from **Section 30 — Enterprise Integration**.

---

# 31. Data Lineage

Every analytical dataset should maintain end-to-end lineage.

```text id="an31"
Source

↓

Ingestion

↓

Transformation

↓

Warehouse

↓

Dashboard
```

Lineage enables impact analysis, troubleshooting, and regulatory compliance.

---

# 32. Metadata Management

Enterprise metadata should include:

```text id="an32"
Business Metadata

Technical Metadata

Operational Metadata

Governance Metadata
```

Metadata improves discoverability and trust.

---

# 33. Enterprise Data Catalog

A centralized catalog should document:

```text id="an33"
Datasets

Reports

Dashboards

Owners

Definitions
```

The catalog becomes the primary discovery mechanism for analytical assets.

---

# 34. Data Quality for Analytics

Analytical datasets should satisfy quality dimensions.

```text id="an34"
Accuracy

Completeness

Consistency

Timeliness

Validity
```

Poor data quality leads to unreliable business decisions.

---

# 35. Data Profiling

Profiling should evaluate:

```text id="an35"
Null Values

Distribution

Patterns

Duplicates

Outliers
```

Profiling should occur before publishing datasets.

---

# 36. Data Validation

Validation rules should verify:

```text id="an36"
Business Rules

Formats

Ranges

Relationships
```

Validation should be automated where practical.

---

# ADR-096 — Enterprise AI Platform, Agentic AI, LLMOps, RAG & Autonomous Systems Architecture Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-096
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise AI Architecture Board (EAIAB)

ADR-095 established the Enterprise Analytics & Decision Intelligence architecture.

ADR-096 establishes the enterprise architecture for Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), Agentic AI, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), AI Platforms, Knowledge Graphs, LLMOps, Model Governance, and Autonomous Systems.

The governing principle is:

> **Artificial Intelligence is an enterprise capability that must be trustworthy, explainable, secure, observable, governable, and aligned with business objectives. AI systems should augment human decision-making while remaining accountable, measurable, and continuously improvable.**

```text
Business Problems
        │
        ▼
AI Platform
        │
 ┌──────┼──────────────┐
 ▼      ▼              ▼
LLMs   ML Models     Agents
 │      │              │
 └──────┼──────────────┘
        ▼
Business Applications
```

---

# 1. Enterprise AI Philosophy

AI should augment—not replace—human expertise.

Objectives:

```text
Trust

Automation

Intelligence

Productivity

Innovation
```

AI adoption should produce measurable business outcomes.

---

# 2. AI Platform

The enterprise AI platform provides reusable capabilities.

```text
Models

↓

Knowledge

↓

Agents

↓

Applications
```

The platform standardizes AI development across the organization.

---

# 3. AI Architecture Layers

Enterprise AI consists of:

```text
Applications

↓

AI Services

↓

Knowledge Layer

↓

Models

↓

Infrastructure
```

Each layer has independent responsibilities.

---

# 4. AI Workload Types

Supported AI workloads include:

```text
Prediction

Classification

Generation

Recommendation

Optimization

Reasoning
```

Different workloads may require different model architectures.

---

# 5. Foundation Models

Foundation models provide general-purpose reasoning capabilities.

Examples:

```text
Large Language Models

Vision Models

Speech Models

Multimodal Models
```

Selection depends on business requirements.

---

# 6. Enterprise LLM Strategy

LLMs should be treated as enterprise infrastructure.

```text
LLM

↓

Guardrails

↓

Knowledge

↓

Applications
```

Applications should not directly depend on raw model behavior.

---

# 7. Model Selection

Model selection should evaluate:

```text
Accuracy

Latency

Cost

Privacy

Security
```

No single model is optimal for every workload.

---

# 8. Multi-Model Architecture

Support multiple AI models.

```text
Application

↓

Model Router

↓

LLM A

LLM B

LLM C
```

Routing enables workload-specific optimization.

---

# 9. Model Routing

Routing decisions may consider:

```text
Task

Cost

Latency

Quality

Availability
```

Routing policies should be configurable.

---

# 10. AI Gateway

Applications access models through an AI Gateway.

```text
Application

↓

AI Gateway

↓

Models
```

The gateway centralizes authentication, quotas, logging, safety, and routing.

---

# 11. Prompt Engineering

Prompts are managed assets.

Every production prompt should define:

```text
Purpose

Inputs

Constraints

Output Format
```

Prompt changes should follow version control.

---

# 12. Prompt Templates

Prompt templates should be reusable.

```text
Template

↓

Variables

↓

Execution
```

Avoid hardcoded prompts in application code.

---

# 13. Prompt Versioning

Prompt evolution should support:

```text
Draft

↓

Approved

↓

Released

↓

Deprecated
```

Applications should reference versioned prompts.

---

# 14. Prompt Library

Maintain a centralized prompt repository.

Examples:

```text
Customer Support

Assessment

Tutoring

Summarization

Translation
```

---

# 15. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

Enterprise AI should prefer RAG over embedding business knowledge directly into prompts.

```text
Question

↓

Retriever

↓

Knowledge

↓

LLM

↓

Answer
```

RAG improves factual grounding and reduces hallucinations.

---

# 16. Enterprise Knowledge Base

Knowledge sources may include:

```text
Documents

Policies

ADRs

Medical Content

APIs
```

Knowledge should be governed and version-controlled.

---

# 17. Vector Database

Embeddings should be stored in vector databases.

Examples:

```text
Embeddings

↓

Vector Store

↓

Similarity Search
```

Vector search complements structured querying.

---

# 18. Embeddings

Embeddings represent semantic meaning.

Applications include:

```text
Search

Recommendation

Clustering

RAG
```

Embedding models should be versioned.

---

# 19. Chunking Strategy

Documents should be chunked intentionally.

Consider:

```text
Size

Overlap

Metadata

Context
```

Chunk quality strongly influences retrieval quality.

---

# 20. Metadata Filtering

Retrieval should support:

```text
Department

Language

Version

Access Level

Source
```

Metadata improves retrieval precision.

---

# 21. Knowledge Freshness

Knowledge repositories should define:

```text
Update Frequency

Validation

Expiration

Ownership
```

Stale knowledge reduces AI reliability.

---

# 22. Knowledge Graphs

Knowledge graphs model enterprise relationships.

```text
Entities

↓

Relationships

↓

Reasoning
```

Graphs complement vector search for structured reasoning.

---

# 23. Graph + RAG

Hybrid retrieval combines:

```text
Knowledge Graph

+

Vector Search

↓

LLM
```

Hybrid retrieval improves accuracy for complex enterprise queries.

---

# 24. AI Context Management

Context should include:

```text
Conversation

Knowledge

User Role

Business Rules
```

Context should remain relevant and bounded.

---

# 25. Context Windows

Applications should optimize:

```text
Relevant Context

↓

LLM

↓

Efficient Response
```

Excessive context increases cost and latency.

---

# 26. AI Memory

Memory types include:

```text
Session

Short-Term

Long-Term
```

Memory should respect privacy and governance policies.

---

# 27. AI Tool Calling

LLMs should invoke enterprise tools through governed interfaces.

Examples:

```text
Search

CRM

ERP

Database

Calendar
```

Models should not bypass enterprise authorization.

---

# 28. Function Calling

Function schemas should define:

```text
Inputs

Outputs

Permissions

Validation
```

Structured tool invocation improves reliability.

---

# 29. Enterprise Integration

ADR-096 integrates with:

```text
ADR-077 AI Governance

ADR-082 APIs

ADR-084 Data

ADR-090 SDLC

ADR-095 Analytics
```

---

# 30. AI Platform Foundation

The enterprise AI platform provides:

```text
Models

Knowledge

Agents

Tools

Governance
```

These components establish a reusable foundation for AI-powered applications.

```text
↓

↓

Reasoning

↓

Tool Execution

↓

Observation

↓

Completion
```

```text
↓

↓

↓

↓

↓
```

```text
Workflow Agents

Decision Support Agents

Automation Agents
```

```text
↓

↓

↓
```

```text
↓

↓

↓

Monitoring
```

# 38. Agent Memory

```text
Working Memory

↓

Conversation Memory

↓

Long-Term Memory
```

---

# 39. Agent Reflection

Agents may evaluate their own outputs before responding.

```text
Generate

↓

Review

↓

Improve

↓

Return
```

Reflection can improve quality but increases latency and cost.

---

# 40. Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)

Critical workflows require human approval.

```text
AI Recommendation

↓

Human Review

↓

Approval

↓

Execution
```

Examples include medical recommendations, financial decisions, and legal actions.

---

# 41. AI Guardrails

Every AI system should implement guardrails.

Examples:

```text
Input Validation

Output Validation

Safety Policies

Content Filtering

Rate Limits
```

Guardrails operate independently of model behavior.

---

# 42. AI Safety

Safety mechanisms should mitigate:

```text
Hallucinations

Prompt Injection

Data Leakage

Unsafe Recommendations

Bias
```

Safety is a continuous engineering capability.

---

# 43. Hallucination Mitigation

Reduce hallucinations through:

```text
RAG

Grounded Prompts

Citation

Verification

Human Review
```

Generated content should be traceable to trusted sources where possible.

---

# 44. Prompt Injection Protection

AI systems should detect and mitigate prompt injection attacks.

Controls include:

```text
Input Sanitization

Policy Enforcement

Context Isolation

Tool Restrictions
```

User prompts should not override system governance.

---

# 45. Output Validation

AI responses should be validated before execution.

Validation may include:

```text
Schema Validation

Business Rules

Security Checks

Confidence Thresholds
```

---

# 46. AI Evaluation

```text

Relevance

Latency

Cost

Safety
```

Evaluation should be continuous.

---

```text

Coding

Summarization

Reasoning

Translation
```

Benchmarks enable objective comparison across models.

---

Core areas:

```text
Prompt Management

Model Deployment

Evaluation

Monitoring

Governance
```

LLMOps extends MLOps for generative AI.

---

# 49. Model Lifecycle

Every model progresses through:

```text
Selection

↓

Evaluation

↓

Deployment

↓

Monitoring

↓

Retirement
```

Lifecycle governance ensures continuous quality.

# ADR-097 — Enterprise FinOps, Cloud Financial Management, Resource Optimization & Sustainable Cloud Architecture Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-097
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise FinOps & Cloud Governance Board (EFCGB)

ADR-096 established the Enterprise AI Platform architecture.

ADR-097 establishes the enterprise FinOps architecture, defining how Mediverse governs cloud spending, optimizes infrastructure costs, aligns engineering decisions with business value, and enables financially accountable cloud operations.

The governing principle is:

> **Every cloud resource must have a measurable business purpose, an accountable owner, and continuously optimized cost throughout its lifecycle. Financial accountability is a shared engineering responsibility—not solely a finance activity.**

```text
Business Strategy
        │
        ▼
Cloud Governance
        │
        ▼
Resource Provisioning
        │
        ▼
Cost Monitoring
        │
        ▼
Optimization
        │
        ▼
Business Value
```

---

# 1. Enterprise FinOps Philosophy

FinOps enables continuous financial optimization.

Objectives:

```text
Visibility

Accountability

Optimization

Forecasting

Business Alignment
```

Cloud spending should directly support business outcomes.

---

# 2. FinOps Operating Model

FinOps is a collaboration between:

```text
Finance

↓

Engineering

↓

Platform

↓

Product

↓

Leadership
```

Financial ownership is shared across the organization.

---

# 3. Cloud Financial Governance

Governance defines:

```text
Budgets

Policies

Approvals

Reporting

Optimization
```

Financial controls should be automated where possible.

---

# 4. Cloud Cost Lifecycle

```text
Plan

↓

Provision

↓

Monitor

↓

Optimize

↓

Retire
```

Cost management spans the full resource lifecycle.

---

# 5. Cost Visibility

Every cloud resource should expose:

```text
Owner

Environment

Project

Department

Business Unit
```

Resources without ownership should not remain in production.

---

# 6. Resource Tagging Standard

Mandatory tags include:

```text
Application

Owner

Environment

Cost Center

Business Domain

Lifecycle
```

Tags enable allocation, governance, and automation.

---

# 7. Cost Allocation

Cloud costs should be allocated by:

```text
Business Unit

Product

Team

Project

Environment
```

Shared infrastructure should use documented allocation rules.

---

# 8. Chargeback Model

Business units are billed for actual cloud consumption.

```text
Cloud Cost

↓

Business Unit

↓

Financial Accountability
```

Chargeback promotes responsible consumption.

---

# 9. Showback Model

Where chargeback is not adopted:

```text
Cloud Usage

↓

Business Reports

↓

Cost Awareness
```

Showback increases transparency without direct billing.

---

# 10. Budget Management

Budgets should exist for:

```text
Teams

Projects

Products

Departments
```

Budgets should include warning thresholds.

---

# 11. Forecasting

Forecasts should consider:

```text
Historical Usage

Growth Trends

Seasonality

Business Plans
```

Forecast accuracy should improve over time.

---

# 12. Cost Anomaly Detection

Automatically detect:

```text
Unexpected Spend

Resource Spikes

Idle Resources

Misconfigurations
```

Anomalies should generate actionable alerts.

---

# 13. Cost Optimization

Optimization targets:

```text
Compute

Storage

Networking

Databases

AI Workloads
```

Optimization should preserve required service levels.

---

# 14. Compute Optimization

Evaluate:

```text
CPU Utilization

Memory Utilization

Instance Size

Scaling Efficiency
```

Rightsizing should use actual utilization data.

---

# 15. Storage Optimization

Optimize:

```text
Storage Tier

Retention

Compression

Lifecycle Policies
```

Inactive data should migrate to lower-cost storage.

---

# 16. Network Optimization

Evaluate:

```text
Data Transfer

Cross-Region Traffic

Ingress

Egress
```

Architecture should minimize unnecessary network costs.

---

# 17. Kubernetes Cost Optimization

Kubernetes workloads should optimize:

```text
Requests

Limits

Autoscaling

Node Utilization

Namespaces
```

Resource requests should reflect observed usage rather than peak estimates.

---

# 18. Container Efficiency

Monitor:

```text
Idle Pods

Over-Provisioning

Restart Frequency

Resource Waste
```

Container efficiency directly affects cloud costs.

---

# 19. Autoscaling Economics

Autoscaling policies should balance:

```text
Performance

Availability

Cost
```

Scaling decisions should consider financial impact.

---

# 20. Enterprise Integration

ADR-097 integrates with:

```text
ADR-078 Platform Engineering

ADR-087 Kubernetes

ADR-088 Reliability

ADR-091 DevOps

ADR-096 AI Platform
```

FinOps becomes an operational capability spanning engineering, finance, and cloud governance.

---

# 21. Reserved Capacity Strategy

Use committed capacity where workloads are predictable.

Examples:

```text
Reserved Instances

Savings Plans

Committed Use Discounts
```

Commitments should be based on historical utilization.

---

# 22. Spot Capacity Strategy

Spot or preemptible instances should be used for fault-tolerant workloads.

Suitable workloads include:

```text
Batch Processing

CI/CD Jobs

ML Training

Rendering
```

Critical workloads should not rely solely on spot capacity.

---

# 23. Rightsizing Policy

Rightsizing should occur continuously.

Evaluate:

```text
CPU

Memory

Disk

Network
```

Changes should be validated against workload behavior.

---

# 24. Idle Resource Management

Identify and remove:

```text
Unused Volumes

Idle Load Balancers

Stopped Instances

Unused IPs

Abandoned Snapshots
```

Idle resources create avoidable costs.

---

# 25. Cost Optimization KPIs

Representative KPIs:

```text
Cloud Cost per User

Cloud Cost per Transaction

Resource Utilization

Idle Resource %

Optimization Savings
```

Engineering teams should review these metrics regularly.

---

# 26. Sustainable Cloud Architecture (GreenOps)

Cloud optimization should also consider environmental impact.

Focus areas:

```text
Efficient Compute

Storage Lifecycle

Energy-Aware Scheduling

Carbon Reduction
```

Efficiency and sustainability often reinforce each other.

---

# 27. Engineering Accountability

Engineering teams are responsible for:

```text
Resource Efficiency

Tag Compliance

Cost Awareness

Optimization Reviews
```

Cost optimization is part of software engineering.

---

# 28. FinOps Dashboards

Dashboards should display:

```text
Spend by Team

Forecast vs Actual

Cost Trends

Savings

Anomalies
```

Dashboards support proactive cost management.

---

# 29. Enterprise FinOps Metrics

Track:

```text
Monthly Cloud Spend

Budget Variance

Optimization Rate

Forecast Accuracy

Resource Efficiency
```

Metrics should guide investment decisions.

---

# 30. Enterprise Integration

ADR-097 integrates with:

```text
ADR-076 Data Governance

ADR-078 Platform Engineering

ADR-087 Infrastructure

ADR-088 SRE

ADR-091 DevOps

ADR-096 AI
```

Financial governance becomes an integral part of enterprise cloud architecture.

---

# 39. Kubernetes Platform Economics

# ADR-098 — Enterprise Compliance, Privacy, Risk Management, Legal Architecture & Regulatory Governance Standard

**Document Version:** 1.0
**ADR ID:** ADR-098
**Status:** Accepted
**Priority:** Critical
**Owner:** Enterprise Governance, Risk & Compliance Board (GRCB)

ADR-097 established the Enterprise FinOps & Cloud Financial Governance architecture.

ADR-098 establishes the enterprise Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC) architecture, defining how Mediverse complies with regulatory obligations, protects privacy, manages enterprise risk, and demonstrates continuous compliance.

The governing principle is:

> **Compliance is an architectural capability embedded throughout the software lifecycle rather than a post-development audit activity. Every business capability must be designed to satisfy applicable legal, regulatory, contractual, and organizational obligations.**

```text
Business Strategy
        │
        ▼
Governance
        │
        ▼
Risk Management
        │
        ▼
Compliance Controls
        │
        ▼
Continuous Monitoring
        │
        ▼
Audit & Improvement
```

---

# 1. Enterprise Compliance Philosophy

Compliance exists to protect:

```text
Customers

Patients

Employees

Partners

Organization
```

Compliance should enable trusted business operations rather than merely satisfy auditors.

---

# 2. Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC)

Enterprise GRC integrates:

```text
Governance

↓

Risk

↓

Compliance

↓

Continuous Assurance
```

These disciplines should operate as a unified capability.

---

# 3. Enterprise Governance

Governance defines:

```text
Policies

Standards

Decision Rights

Ownership

Accountability
```

Governance establishes how architectural and operational decisions are made.

---

# 4. Enterprise Risk Management

Risk management should identify:

```text
Business Risk

Technology Risk

Security Risk

Operational Risk

Compliance Risk
```

Risk treatment should be proportionate to business impact.

---

# 5. Risk Lifecycle

```text
Identify

↓

Assess

↓

Treat

↓

Monitor

↓

Review
```

Risk management is continuous.

---

# 6. Compliance-by-Design

Compliance requirements should be addressed during:

```text
Requirements

↓

Architecture

↓

Development

↓

Deployment

↓

Operations
```

Late compliance remediation is costly and disruptive.

---

# 7. Privacy-by-Design

Privacy should be embedded into every system.

Core principles:

```text
Data Minimization

Purpose Limitation

Transparency

Security

Accountability
```

---

# 8. Security-by-Design

Security and compliance are complementary.

Security controls should satisfy both technical and regulatory objectives.

---

# 9. Regulatory Landscape

Enterprise systems may need to comply with:

```text
GDPR

HIPAA

SOC 2

ISO 27001

PCI DSS

Local Regulations
```

Applicable regulations depend on business context and jurisdiction.

---

# 10. Compliance Classification

Requirements should be categorized.

```text
Mandatory

Required

Recommended

Internal Policy
```

Classification helps prioritize implementation.

---

# 11. Personal Data

Personally identifiable information (PII) should be identified and classified.

Examples:

```text
Name

Email

Phone

National ID

Medical Identifier
```

---

# 12. Sensitive Data

Sensitive information includes:

```text
Medical Records

Financial Data

Authentication Data

Biometrics
```

Sensitive data requires stronger controls.

---

# 13. Data Classification

Enterprise data should be classified.

```text
Public

Internal

Confidential

Restricted
```

Classification determines required protections.

---

# 14. Data Ownership

Every regulated dataset requires:

```text
Business Owner

Technical Owner

Data Steward
```

Ownership supports accountability.

---

# 15. Consent Management

Systems processing personal information should support:

```text
Consent Capture

Consent Withdrawal

Consent Audit

Consent History
```

Consent should be traceable.

---

# 16. Purpose Limitation

Collected information should only be used for approved business purposes.

Secondary use requires governance approval where applicable.

---

# 17. Data Minimization

Only necessary information should be collected.

Avoid excessive data collection.

---

# 18. Data Retention

Retention policies should define:

```text
Retention Period

Legal Basis

Deletion

Archiving
```

Retention should align with legal and business requirements.

---

# 19. Secure Disposal

Expired information should be securely destroyed.

Examples:

```text
Cryptographic Erasure

Secure Deletion

Physical Destruction
```

---

# 20. Enterprise Integration

ADR-098 integrates with:

```text
ADR-076 Data Governance

ADR-081 Identity

ADR-084 Data Platform

ADR-086 Security

ADR-091 DevOps

ADR-097 FinOps
```

Compliance requirements span the complete enterprise architecture.

---

# 21. Audit Logging

Systems should maintain immutable records for:

```text
Authentication

Authorization

Administrative Changes

Sensitive Data Access
```

Logs should be protected against tampering.

---

# 22. Records Management

Business records should define:

```text
Creation

Retention

Archive

Disposal
```

Records differ from ordinary operational data.

---

# 23. Legal Hold

When required, records should be preserved beyond normal retention schedules.

Deletion processes should respect legal hold requirements.

---

# 24. Evidence Management

Maintain evidence for:

```text
Compliance

Audits

Controls

Policies
```

Evidence should be versioned and traceable.

---

# 25. Policy Management

Enterprise policies should define:

```text
Owner

Version

Review Date

Approval

Scope
```

Policies should be periodically reviewed.

---

# 26. Control Framework

Controls should be mapped to:

```text
Risks

Policies

Regulations
```

Control traceability simplifies audits.

---

# 27. Third-Party Risk

Assess third parties for:

```text
Security

Privacy

Compliance

Business Continuity
```

Third-party risk should be reviewed before onboarding.

---

# 28. Vendor Compliance

Vendors should provide evidence of applicable certifications and contractual commitments where required.

---

# 29. Regulatory Reporting

Required reports should define:

```text
Owner

Frequency

Recipients

Approval
```

Reporting processes should be repeatable and auditable.

---

# 30. Enterprise Integration

ADR-098 integrates with:

```text
ADR-076 Data Governance

ADR-081 Identity

ADR-084 Data

ADR-086 Security

ADR-089 Governance

ADR-091 DevOps

ADR-097 FinOps
```

Compliance becomes an enterprise capability embedded into architecture, operations, and governance.

---
